records.text: Fundamental of Database Systems

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Study notes
records.text: Fundamental of Database Systems Design a correct schema from explicit business rules, then use constraints, dependency tests and queries to justify it. This chapter covers all three official design outcomes alongside related database concepts. Work in order: requirements → ER/EER → relational mapping → keys/FDs → normalization → SQL and physical choices. Practice drawing and constructing the registration/dormitory schema without looking; explain why every key and reference exists. For each MCQ, check literal syntax, assumptions and overlapping choices; justify the answer using database rules. Recalculate closure, product counts, join preservation and group filters; compare similar terms through concrete examples.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Practice questions
records.text: Fundamental of Database Systems

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Revision outline
records.text: Fundamental of Database Systems

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Database approach, benefits and costs
records.text: A database is a coherent collection of related facts with meaning for an application. A DBMS is software that defines, stores, retrieves, updates, protects and shares that data. The database is the content; the DBMS manages it. A database system also includes applications, people and infrastructure. Traditional file applications define their own formats and access procedures. Separate files can repeat facts, disagree after updates, isolate useful data and make shared integrity or concurrent updates difficult. A DBMS centralizes metadata and supports multiple views, authorization, transactions, backup and recovery. It controls redundancy rather than guaranteeing zero duplication. Complexity, administration, storage and licensing can outweigh benefits for a tiny fixed application; lightweight embedded DBMSs also exist. Concurrent access itself is useful; uncontrolled concurrent access causes anomalies. The DBA manages access authorization, backup/recovery, availability, monitoring, tuning and routine maintenance, coordinating database use; designers define the schema and application developers build user-facing programs. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Data models and product names
records.text: A data model supplies concepts for structure, relationships, constraints and operations. Conceptual ER models describe entities and relationships. Relational models use tables; hierarchical models organize records in a parent–child tree; classic network models connect records through pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents. Object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior. A physical model specifies record layouts and access paths. These are different representation choices, not stages of one query. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and IBM Db2 are relational DBMS products. MongoDB is a document DBMS. Java is a programming language. IBM alone names a vendor, not a database product. Distinguish a vendor such as IBM from a specific database product. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Relations, schemas, instances and metadata
records.text: A relation is a set of tuples, represented as a table. A tuple/row/record contains related attribute values; an attribute/column/field describes a property. Degree counts columns; cardinality counts rows. Classical relations have distinct tuples, atomic cells and domains for attributes; row order has no meaning. Column order has no logical meaning when attributes are identified by name. SQL tables can contain duplicate rows unless constrained. A schema describes names, structures and constraints; an instance, state or snapshot is the data at a particular time. Inserting a student changes the state, while adding a column changes the schema. Metadata is data describing data. The catalog or data dictionary records table definitions, types, constraints and often access privileges and optimizer statistics. A schema diagram draws tables and key references; labels such as database diagram can overlap. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Three-schema architecture and data independence
records.text: The external level gives each user group a selected view. The conceptual level describes the whole logical database: entity types, relationships, data types and constraints. The internal/physical level describes files, record placement and access paths. These are abstraction levels, distinct from client/server deployment tiers. Physical data independence permits changing internal storage without changing the conceptual schema, for example adding an index. Logical data independence permits conceptual changes while preserving affected external views and application interfaces, for example splitting a table while maintaining a compatible view. It is harder because applications depend on logical meaning. Data abstraction hides irrelevant details; program–data insulation separates data definitions from application code. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Requirements through implementation
records.text: First collect business facts, required transactions, reports, volumes, privacy rules and quality targets. Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model. Logical design maps the conceptual model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Physical design chooses file organization, indexes and storage. Implementation creates and loads the actual objects; testing checks requirements. Logical relational design is tied to a data model but can remain independent of a particular DBMS. Vendor-specific implementation details may be introduced during later refinement. Whether logical design is DBMS-dependent depends on the stated design methodology. Conceptual design usually proceeds from a whole enterprise view downward; normalization can refine structures from dependencies upward. These are useful approaches rather than mandatory directions for every modeling activity. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Entities, attributes and ER notation
records.text: An entity is a distinguishable real or conceptual thing, such as one student or one course. An entity type describes common properties; its current collection of entities is an entity set. A relationship associates entities. In Chen notation rectangles represent entity types, diamonds relationships and ellipses attributes; double ellipses denote multivalued attributes and dashed ellipses derived attributes. Always inspect the diagram legend. Simple versus composite asks whether a value has meaningful components: Address may split into City and Street. Single-valued versus multivalued asks how many values one entity may have: a student may have several phone numbers. These dimensions differ: one address may be composite and single-valued. Age derived from birth date is derived, even if also single-valued. Attribute names alone do not establish multiplicity. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Superkeys, candidate keys and primary keys
records.text: A superkey uniquely identifies a tuple. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any component loses uniqueness. Minimal means no unnecessary attribute, not necessarily the fewest columns among all keys. A primary key is one selected candidate key; remaining candidates are alternate keys. A composite key contains multiple attributes and need not be the chosen primary key. If ID is unique, both {ID} and {ID,City} are superkeys, but only {ID} is minimal. A table can have several candidates and foreign keys but at most one declared primary-key constraint, possibly containing several columns. String columns can be keys. Prefer stable, compact identifiers when practical, but Email, SSN or EmployeeID is a candidate only if business rules guarantee uniqueness. A composite-key example must include multiple columns; a single-column key is not composite. Example Worked example Given candidate keys CustID, Email and ContactNo, all are eligible primary keys. CustID is preferable only with an explicit stability/size policy; uniqueness alone does not choose it. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Weak entities and identifying relationships
records.text: A weak entity lacks a complete independent key. Its owner is normally a strong entity, so owner entity set and strong entity set may both describe the associated set. Its partial key, also called discriminator, distinguishes weak entities of the same owner. Identification combines the owner key and partial key. For Dependent(EmployeeID,DependentName,BirthDate), suppose names are unique only within one employee's dependents. Then (EmployeeID,DependentName) is the key, and EmployeeID is a foreign key. The weak entity participates totally in its identifying relationship. Chen notation uses a double rectangle, double identifying diamond and dashed underline for a partial key. A weak entity is not merely any table with a foreign key. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Cardinality, participation and direction
records.text: Cardinality specifies maximum associated occurrences: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. Minimum cardinality specifies optional/partial participation (zero permitted) or mandatory/total participation (at least one). A maximum of one does not mean participation is compulsory. Relationship degree counts participating entity roles: unary recursive, binary or ternary. Read business rules in both directions. If each employee belongs to one department and each department has many employees, Employee→Department is N:1; Department→Employee is 1:N. Building→Location could also be N:1, so names alone cannot select a unique example. Under the common arrow convention, arrows from advisor to both Instructor and Student impose maximum-one at both ends, giving 1:1. Without a notation convention, arrows are unsafe evidence. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Map entities, composite and multivalued attributes
records.text: Create one relation per strong entity type, preserve its simple attributes and select a candidate key. Expand composite attributes into their useful simple components; do not copy a composite ER structure unchanged into a flat atomic design. Derived values can usually be calculated, avoiding stale stored copies. Map each multivalued attribute to a separate relation containing the owner key and one value. StudentPhone(StudentID,Phone) has primary key (StudentID,Phone) and a foreign key to Student. Store separate rows for two phone numbers, not a comma-separated list or repeated Phone1/Phone2 columns. Include the relational mapping step when translating an ER/EER design into tables. Table names may follow entity names; naming does not invalidate a mapping. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module University of Texas: ER-to-relational mapping

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Map 1:1 and 1:N relationships
records.text: For 1:N, place the one-side key as a foreign key in the many-side table; store relationship attributes there. Department(DeptID) and Employee(EmpID,DeptID,HireDate) implement many employees per department. If participation is total, make the reference NOT NULL. If partial, a nullable reference can represent no assignment. For 1:1, one side may hold the other key with a UNIQUE constraint. Prefer the totally participating side to reduce NULLs; NOT NULL enforces that side's mandatory reference. Merging entities is reasonable only when their lifecycle and participation rules permit it. For A→B many-to-one, A can absorb the relationship reference under either total or partial participation; requiring total participation as the only possible case overstates the rule. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Map M:N, recursive and n-ary relationships
records.text: A binary M:N relationship needs an association table in addition to the two entity tables. Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) references Student and Course; (StudentID,CourseID) is a key if one enrollment per pair is allowed. Repeated attempts require Term or AttemptNo in the key. This ordinarily produces three tables. A recursive M:N friendship uses UserLink(UserID,OtherUserID), two foreign keys to User; decide whether links are directed and whether self-links are allowed. A recursive 1:N supervision uses a nullable SupervisorID reference in Employee. For a ternary Supply(SupplierID,PartID,ProjectID,Quantity), preserve all participating references; binary replacements can lose which triple occurred. Choose the association key from actual cardinalities rather than automatically assuming every reference is necessary. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module University of Texas: ER-to-relational mapping

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — EER inheritance and category constraints
records.text: EER extends ER with superclass/subclass structure. A subclass inherits the superclass attributes and relationships. Specialization divides Student into Undergraduate and Graduate; generalization combines common properties into Student. Disjoint subclasses cannot overlap; overlapping subclasses can. Total specialization requires every superclass member in some subclass; partial specialization does not. Map Person(PersonID,Name) and Student(PersonID,Program) with Student.PersonID both primary key and foreign key to Person. This preserves inherited identity. A category/union subclass draws members from a union of different superclasses, such as Owner drawn from Person or Company; it differs from an intersection subclass requiring membership in both. Object models also support inheritance; distinguish basic ER notation from EER when comparing models. Structural EER inheritance alone does not define executable object methods. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Fan traps and chasm traps
records.text: A fan trap occurs when two 1:N relationships fan from a common entity and a path suggests an association it cannot determine. Department→Employee and Department→Project do not reveal which employee works on which project; joining through Department pairs every employee with every project in that department. Record WorksOn explicitly when that is the fact needed. A chasm trap occurs when an apparently useful path fails for some occurrences because an optional relationship breaks it. For example, a branch's property may be lost from a path that requires an assigned staff member when some properties have none. Add the required direct relationship or revise the model. Multiple 1:N relationships are legitimate; eliminating all fans is not a universal repair. A missing path describes a chasm, not the defining ambiguity of a fan. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Dr G. Russell, Napier University: Database Systems notes

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Integrity and constraint taxonomy
records.text: Domain integrity restricts type and allowed values. Key integrity enforces uniqueness. Entity integrity requires every primary-key component to be non-NULL. Referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign-key value to match an eligible referenced unique/candidate key; self-references are allowed. A parent need not have a child. Inherent constraints come from the data model; schema-based constraints are declared through the DDL; semantic/application rules may need triggers or application logic when DDL cannot express them. Integrity improves data validity; authorization controls who may access it. Uniqueness and domain validation are both integrity mechanisms. If a Department primary key is NULL and Manager=107 lacks a referenced employee, entity integrity certainly fails and referential integrity also fails if that foreign key is declared. One INSERT can violate multiple constraints. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Write and enforce SQL constraints
records.text: Example: CREATE TABLE Enrollment (StudentID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(StudentID), CourseID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Course(CourseID), Grade INTEGER CHECK (Grade BETWEEN 0 AND 100), PRIMARY KEY (StudentID,CourseID)); Each column declaration gives its name then type, with commas between declarations. CHECK is a constraint clause, not a standalone GRANT-like statement. POSITIVE is not a general SQL constraint keyword; CHECK (Amount > 0) expresses positivity. PRIMARY KEY implies uniqueness and non-NULL. UNIQUE does not generally imply NOT NULL; NULL treatment differs by DBMS. A CHECK can pass when its result is unknown, so add NOT NULL if missing values must be forbidden. Parent updates/deletes may use NO ACTION/RESTRICT, CASCADE or SET NULL. A referenced key is not inherently unchangeable: legality depends on matching children and the declared action. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module PostgreSQL: Constraints

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Functional dependencies and attribute closure
records.text: X→Y means every legal pair of tuples agreeing on X also agrees on Y. It is a business constraint, not a correlation observed in one sample. Full dependency requires all determinant attributes; partial dependency holds through a proper subset. A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key; a nonprime attribute belongs to none. To compute X+, start with X and repeatedly add the right-hand side of any dependency whose left side is already present. Stop when nothing changes. X is a superkey exactly when X+ contains the whole relation. Remove attributes and recompute to test minimality. Reflexivity gives X→Y when Y⊆X; augmentation permits XZ→YZ from X→Y; transitivity derives X→Z from X→Y and Y→Z. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Find all keys before deciding normal form
records.text: For R(A,B,C,D), let C→D, C→B and B→C. A never appears on a right-hand side, so every key needs A. (AB)+ gives ABCD through B→C→D; (AC)+ also gives ABCD. AB and AC are minimal keys. BC cannot derive A and is not a key. A, B and C are prime; D is nonprime. D depends on C alone and also on B through transitivity, proper subsets of those keys. Thus 2NF fails; assuming atomic values, the highest form is 1NF. Use the stated functional dependencies to justify each key and normal-form conclusion. Confirm the actual dependency set before calculating closures; do not infer dependencies from unclear symbols. Example Worked example For F={A→B,B→C} on R(A,B,C), A+=ABC makes A the key. The chain through nonkey B causes a 3NF violation. If instead B were a candidate key, a dependency chain would not by itself prove such a violation. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Insertion, deletion and update anomalies
records.text: Suppose Enrollment repeats StudentName for every course. An update anomaly requires changing every copy of the student's name; missed copies disagree. An insertion anomaly prevents recording a new student until some enrollment exists. A deletion anomaly loses the only record of a student's details when their last enrollment is deleted. Revoke anomaly is not a normalization anomaly. Normalization separates facts according to their determinants, reducing avoidable repetition and associated anomalies. It does not require seeing bad current data: declared dependencies suffice. Adding a generated row ID may make insertion technically possible, but does not remove repeated facts or fix the dependency design. Reduced redundancy can improve integrity and storage use, but extra keys and joins mean neither storage savings nor faster retrieval is guaranteed. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — First and second normal forms
records.text: 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen relational domains and no repeating groups in cells. It does not mean merely declaring a primary key. A mapped ER design that correctly splits composite and multivalued structures gives ordinary 1NF tables; ER drawing alone guarantees no higher form. 2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key. For Enrollment(SID,CID,SName,CTitle,Grade), assume key (SID,CID), SID→SName and CID→CTitle. Split into Student(SID,SName), Course(CID,CTitle) and Enrollment(SID,CID,Grade). Grade still depends on the whole pair. A relation whose every candidate key is single-attribute has no nonprime partial-key dependency. Higher forms inherit 2NF, so no partial dependencies establishes the minimum guaranteed stage only when 1NF is also assumed. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Third normal form, BCNF and higher forms
records.text: For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF requires X to be a superkey. The mnemonic whole key and nothing but the key describes the common single-key case; it cannot replace the full tests when keys overlap. Remove dependencies of nonprime facts on nonkey determinants. In Sale(Date,Customer,Product,Vendor,VendorCity,SalesRep), assume key (Date,Customer,Product), Product→Vendor and Vendor→VendorCity. Product is a proper subset of the key, so Vendor and VendorCity violate 2NF. With atomic values the highest form is 1NF, even though a transitive dependency also exists. 4NF addresses nontrivial multivalued dependencies with nonsuperkey determinants; 5NF addresses join dependencies. Do not confuse a multivalued dependency with a list stored inside a cell. Example Worked example Employee(EID,DeptID,DeptName), EID→DeptID and DeptID→DeptName, splits into Employee(EID,DeptID) and Department(DeptID,DeptName). Each department name is stored once. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Decomposition: lossless and dependency preserving
records.text: A lossless decomposition reconstructs exactly the original legal tuples by joining its parts; a lossy one creates spurious combinations. For a binary decomposition into R1 and R2 under FDs, it is lossless when their common attributes determine all of R1 or all of R2. Sharing a column without this condition is insufficient. Dependency preservation means the original constraints can be enforced on the individual relations without joining them. Losslessness and dependency preservation are separate properties. A practical 3NF synthesis uses a minimal FD cover, creates a relation for each determinant and its dependent attributes, removes contained relations, and adds a relation containing a candidate key if none already does. BCNF decomposition removes an offending X→Y by separating XY and the remaining attributes with X; it can sacrifice dependency preservation. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Jan Chomicki, University at Buffalo: Relational database design

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Choose data types and storage levels
records.text: CHAR(n) is fixed length; VARCHAR(n) has variable length up to a limit. DATE represents a date and BLOB binary content such as images. INTEGER represents whole numbers; DECIMAL(p,s) represents exact decimal values, making it suitable for money when scale is specified. FLOAT/REAL/DOUBLE are approximate; names, widths and precision depend on the DBMS. Numeric type widths depend on the DBMS and type; do not assume one universal width. Primary storage includes RAM and processor cache and is usually volatile. Secondary storage includes persistent SSDs/HDDs used online; database pages are copied into buffers before CPU processing. Tertiary storage includes tape or removable archive media. Choose types from meaning, range and accuracy requirements, not a blanket rule that integers are always faster than strings. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Records, pages and primary file organization
records.text: A page/block is a unit of database I/O and holds several records. For fixed unspanned records of size r in usable page space B, the blocking factor is floor(B/r), and n records occupy ceil(n/blocking factor) pages. Page headers and slots reduce usable space. A heap has no search-key order and supports simple inserts, but searches may scan all pages. A sorted file supports efficient range scans and binary search on the ordering field, with more costly insertions or overflow handling. A hashed file chooses a bucket by hash(key), supports equality lookup well and requires collision/overflow handling; hash order does not support ordinary ranges. Choose organization from actual reads, writes and predicates. Partitioning splits a large dataset; replication copies it; migration moves it; archiving removes older data from active service. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Ordered, dense, sparse and multilevel indexes
records.text: An index stores search keys with pointers or row identifiers. It often speeds selective retrieval but consumes space and must be maintained on writes. A full scan can win for a tiny table or a query returning most rows. Indexes do not themselves establish referential integrity. In ordered-file indexing terminology, a primary ordered index is on the file’s ordering key and can have one entry per page, hence sparse. A clustering index is on a nonunique ordering field, often with an entry per distinct value. Secondary indexes provide other access paths and must represent all searchable values with record pointers or pointer lists. A dense index represents each search value; sparse indexes rely on ordered data between entries. Multilevel indexes index lower index levels. B/B+ trees support ordered and range search; hashing targets equality; bitmap indexes suit some analytic workloads. No one type is universally best. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — SQL command categories and exact scope
records.text: DDL changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, commonly RENAME and TRUNCATE in textbook classifications. DML retrieves or changes data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. Some texts separate SELECT as DQL. DCL manages privileges through GRANT and REVOKE. TCL includes COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. Classify a statement by its effect, not its length. DELETE removes rows and keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table object; ALTER changes its definition. TRUNCATE empties a table using implementation-specific mechanisms. PostgreSQL allows transactional rollback of TRUNCATE, so no rollback information is retained is not a universal SQL property. SQL Server permits DROP DATABASE Sales, suppliers; that comma-list syntax is vendor-specific. SQLite's .databases lists attached names/files in its command-line shell; .database is not the documented command. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module PostgreSQL: TRUNCATE Microsoft: DROP DATABASE (Transact-SQL) SQLite: Command-line shell

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — SELECT and its result columns
records.text: SELECT Name,Address FROM Customer; produces only those mailing-label fields. SELECT * selects all columns; DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; AS supplies an alias; ALL permits duplicates and does not mean all columns. SQL normally preserves duplicates without DISTINCT. A query reading table columns needs an appropriate FROM source. A literal-only query such as SELECT 1 may legally omit FROM. Typical written clause order is SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY …. Conceptually form FROM/JOIN rows, filter WHERE, group, filter HAVING, select expressions and then order the result. SELECT alone normally reads without changing the database state. WHERE alone is a clause rather than a complete read-only statement, so it cannot be compared as an equivalent executable command. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Predicates, strings and NULL
records.text: Use single quotes for SQL string literals: WHERE ID = 'B001'. Standard double quotes delimit identifiers, although some vendor modes accept them for strings. Qualify ambiguous columns with aliases such as E.Department. Conditions use =, <>, <, >, AND, OR and NOT; use parentheses to make precedence clear. LIKE 'Ab%' matches a prefix, and BETWEEN includes its endpoints. NULL represents a missing/unknown value. Comparisons such as Salary = NULL are unknown, not true; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. WHERE retains only true conditions. An index-friendly year predicate for timestamps is BirthDate >= DATE '2000-01-01' AND BirthDate < DATE '2001-01-01', avoiding omitted times on December 31. Expression indexes can support functions, so functions do not universally prevent indexing. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
records.text: INSERT INTO Hotel(HotelID,HotelName,SubCity) VALUES (1,'Hilton','Yeka'); pairs each named column with a compatible value. Counts and types must match; keys and other constraints still apply. Without a column list, values must follow the table's declared column order. UPDATE Book SET Price = 600 WHERE ID = 'B001'; changes matching rows. UPDATE without WHERE targets every row. DELETE FROM Publisher WHERE Name = 'XWZ'; deletes matching publisher rows, subject to reference policies. DELETE FROM r; removes every row but leaves r defined. Both clear relation entries and delete rows describe that effect. Several UPDATE statements can all be valid while performing different tasks; most appropriate requires a requested change and a specified quoting dialect. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — CREATE and ALTER tables
records.text: CREATE TABLE Employee (EmpID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80)); declares two columns. The name and its type stay together; the comma separates whole column declarations. To add a primary key later: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (EmpID); existing data must be unique and non-NULL. A table cannot gain a second primary key without replacing the existing constraint. ALTER TABLE Employee ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(120); adds a column in PostgreSQL-style syntax. ALTER TABLE Employee DROP COLUMN Email; removes it. ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (Email); adds a named constraint. Use ALTER rather than DALTER, and do not separate column_name and column_type with a comma; validate the resulting SQL before execution. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Join behavior and preservation
records.text: An inner join returns matching pairs satisfying ON. An equijoin uses equality; a theta join permits another comparison. A natural join is ordinarily an inner equality join on every same-named column and merges those duplicate columns. JOIN … USING (DeptID) specifies shared join columns explicitly. CROSS JOIN forms every pair without a matching condition. LEFT OUTER JOIN also preserves unmatched left rows, padding right columns with NULL; RIGHT preserves right rows and FULL preserves both. Therefore inner and natural inner joins both discard unmatched rows. A self-join uses aliases for two occurrences of one base table. Each ordinary join operator combines two inputs, but its inputs can be earlier joins, so one query can join many tables. Distinguish base-table count, table occurrences and binary operator arity. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module PostgreSQL: Table expressions

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING
records.text: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(x) counts non-NULL x values; SUM and AVG summarize non-NULL numeric values. SQL's usual average function is AVG, not AVERAGE. GROUP BY creates one group per distinct grouping value; HAVING tests aggregate groups after WHERE has filtered individual rows. SELECT Department, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department <> 'Sales' GROUP BY Department HAVING AVG(Salary) > 35000; lists qualifying department averages. An ordinary AVG(Salary) predicate cannot be placed directly in WHERE. Selecting EmpID, FirstName and LastName while grouping only by Department is also invalid unless the DBMS can establish the required functional dependence. The grouping column need not itself appear in SELECT; check the functional dependence of other selected columns. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module PostgreSQL: GROUP BY and HAVING

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Subqueries and views
records.text: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement. It may appear in WHERE, HAVING or FROM, not only the first two. IN tests membership; EXISTS tests whether at least one qualifying row exists. Correlated subqueries refer to the outer row. A scalar subquery must produce an appropriate single value. Beware NOT IN when its subquery can return NULL; NOT EXISTS often expresses the intended absence more safely. CREATE VIEW CSStudent AS SELECT StudentID,Name FROM Student WHERE Major = 'CS'; stores a query definition and presents a virtual table. Views can simplify repeated queries, expose derived values and restrict access when configured correctly. An ordinary view does not necessarily store its result; a materialized view does. Rewriting a subquery as a join can change duplicates, and does not guarantee faster execution. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Set operations and type conversion in SQL
records.text: SELECT ID FROM A UNION SELECT ID FROM B; combines compatible result columns and removes duplicate rows by default. UNION ALL retains duplicates. Explicit UNION DISTINCT is accepted in some dialects, including PostgreSQL; it is not a separate algebra rule. INTERSECT returns common rows; EXCEPT returns first-result rows absent from the second. Inputs need the same column count and compatible corresponding types. CAST('42' AS INTEGER) converts an expression to a requested type if the value permits it. CONVERT is vendor-specific and can also perform type conversion; specify the SQL dialect when comparing it with CAST. In SELECT xyz FROM table1 UNION xyz FROM table2, the second SELECT is missing. In the corrected query, xyz is a selected column/expression, not a table name. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module PostgreSQL: Combining queries PostgreSQL: Value expressions

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Relational algebra: calculate results
records.text: Selection σ filters tuples; projection π retains attributes and removes duplicate tuples under set semantics. Rename ρ changes relation or attribute names. Union, difference and intersection require union-compatible schemas. Difference R−S is not commutative; union and intersection are. Inner joins are commutative up to attribute order when predicates are adjusted; left outer joins are not generally commutative. Identify the join variant before predicting its behavior. A Cartesian product has |R|×|S| tuples and degree degree(R)+degree(S), renaming conflicting attributes if necessary. Thus 200×100=20,000 and 5×7=35. Join equals selection over a product; intersection can be derived from difference. A common minimal basis contains selection, projection, union, difference, product and rename. Assignment is a useful notation, not an indispensable primitive; lists of basic operations vary across textbooks. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Relational calculus: state the desired facts
records.text: Relational algebra specifies a sequence of operations and is procedural at the logical level. Relational calculus specifies a predicate describing desired results and is declarative/nonprocedural. A tuple variable ranges over tuples; a domain variable ranges over individual attribute values. Safe/range-restricted expressions produce results bounded by the database's active domain. Tuple form {s | Student(s) AND s.Major='CS'} selects student tuples with that major. A domain form can request names n satisfying ∃i,m (Student(i,n,m) AND m='CS'). Existential quantification means some matching tuple exists; universal quantification means every required case meets a condition. SQL is declarative even though an optimizer later chooses a procedural execution plan. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Transactions and the ACID properties
records.text: A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity applies all its effects or none. Consistency means a correct transaction preserves declared invariants. Isolation controls interference between concurrent transactions; serializable isolation provides behavior equivalent to some serial execution. Durability preserves committed effects after a crash, typically through durable logging rather than forcing every data page immediately. For a transfer, subtracting 100 from one balance and adding 100 to another must commit together; losing either half violates atomicity and may violate the total-balance invariant. BEGIN starts work, COMMIT completes it, ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted work and SAVEPOINT marks an intermediate rollback point. A failed transaction may roll back while other users' committed transactions remain. SQL transaction syntax and error-handling constructs differ by DBMS; @@ERROR/IF is SQL Server-specific. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Choose a design technique from the requirement
records.text: Normalization reduces dependency-driven anomalies. Indexing supplies search paths. Denormalization deliberately repeats or precomputes facts to reduce selected read costs, increasing maintenance work. Partitioning divides rows or columns; replication creates copies to improve locality or availability while complicating updates. These techniques can coexist. An e-commerce or gaming label alone does not select one. Privacy requires a threat model. Authentication verifies identity; role-based authorization limits allowed records/actions; encryption protects data at rest or in transit; auditing records activity. Both encryption and access control can protect patient data. Scalability, availability, fast retrieval, redundancy control and security are all reasonable design considerations. Functional requirements describe behavior; nonfunctional requirements quantify qualities such as 99.9% uptime or response time. Authentication and encryption mechanisms alone do not uniquely establish that distinction. In a CMS, tags/categories describe meaning, while foreign keys preserve valid references between content and tags. A ContentTag(ContentID,TagID) association models multiple tags per item; these functions complement each other. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Integrated design: student registration and dormitory allocation
records.text: State the rules first: each student belongs to one department, may enroll in many courses, and has at most one current dorm assignment. Each course accepts many students; each dorm holds at most six students. Identify Department, Student, Course and Dorm entities; Enrollment is the M:N relationship with Grade. Use Department(DeptID,Name), Student(SID,Name,DeptID,DormID), Course(CID,Title), Enrollment(SID,CID,Grade) and Dorm(DormID,FloorNumber). Declare all entity IDs primary keys; Student.DeptID and Student.DormID reference their parents; Enrollment has composite key (SID,CID) and both references. Make DormID nullable until assignment. Separate StudentPhone(SID,Phone) for multiple contacts. Normalize repeated department/course facts into their owning tables. A simple foreign key does not enforce the six-student capacity; use a concurrency-safe trigger, allocation transaction or explicit slot design with six unique slots per dorm. Example Worked example Complete the reference as FOREIGN KEY (DormID) REFERENCES Dorm(DormID). STUDENT is the referencing child; DORM is referenced. Consistent names and an added Student.DormID column are required before execution. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Check SQL syntax and question assumptions
records.text: Justify each answer using the schema, SQL rules and stated assumptions. Owner and strong entity can both describe the entity supporting a weak entity; row and record are synonyms in a relational table; difference and set-difference are the same operator. DELETE, UPDATE and the invalid command REMOVE are not DROP; a question asking which is not DROP can therefore admit several choices. Compare all choices with the relevant rule before selecting an answer. For invalid SQL, identify the syntax error and validate the corrected statement before analyzing its result. For unsupported cardinalities, request business rules and direction. For best/efficient/important questions, specify workload, quality goal or comparison baseline. A diagram-dependent conclusion needs the missing diagram or an explicit description of its relevant symbols. Identify the smallest clarification needed when a question does not support a unique answer. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Algebra operator lists and derivable operations
records.text: A list of basic relational-algebra operators is a teaching convention, distinct from a claim that every listed operation is logically indispensable. The course module uses selection, projection, Cartesian product, set difference, union and intersection as its basic-operation list. Natural join and assignment are not members of that particular list. Under set semantics, union includes tuples from either compatible input, intersection retains tuples common to both, and difference keeps first-input tuples absent from the second. Intersection can be expressed using difference, while a matching join can be expressed as selection over a Cartesian product. A smaller primitive basis may therefore omit intersection even when it is introduced as a basic operation. Fundamental of Database Systems module · page 24

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Relational systems with richer types
records.text: An object-relational DBMS retains relational data management while supporting richer extensions such as user-defined data types, functions and operators. PostgreSQL is an example. Richer relational types do not by themselves require all data to form a parent–child tree; that representation is the defining concern of hierarchical modeling. PostgreSQL documentation — What Is PostgreSQL?

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 2 · Q00038
records.text: Q00038 Question 2 FDB05 In DBMS-independent logical relational design, before vendor-specific refinement, which statement is NOT correct? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A It consider a particular DBMS B Normalization is undertaken in logical phase C It is based on specific data model D It is independent from physical considerations A. It consider a particular DBMS Logical design maps the conceptual model into relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. It therefore uses a particular data model while separating storage decisions from logical structure. Under the stated DBMS-independent methodology, considering a particular vendor's DBMS is the false claim. Normalization, a chosen model and independence from physical storage are all consistent with this phase. A correct False in the stated phase: particular-DBMS implementation choices are deferred. B incorrect True: normalization checks the mapped relations. C incorrect True: relational logical design uses a specific data model. D incorrect True: file layouts and indexes belong to physical design.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 5 · Q00043
records.text: Q00043 Question 5 FDB15 Which database constraints are specified in the data definition language? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Implicit or inherent model based constraints B Semantic constraints C Application based constraints D Schema based constraints Schema-based constraints. The question asks how constraints are specified, rather than which business meaning they express. FDB15 distinguishes constraints inherent in a data model from constraints explicitly declared in schema DDL. That second category is schema-based. Semantic or application rules may require triggers or application code when ordinary DDL cannot express them. A incorrect Inherent model constraints follow from the data model rather than explicit schema declarations. B incorrect Semantic rules express application meaning and may exceed what ordinary schema DDL can enforce. C incorrect Application-based constraints may require program logic rather than declarations in the database definition. D correct Schema-based constraints are explicitly specified in data definition language declarations.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 6 · Q00080
records.text: Q00080 Question 6 FDB26 Which SQL command removes an existing relation's table object, including its definition? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Delete B Drop C Remove D UPDATE B. Drop Removing a relation object means removing its definition as well as its contents. DROP TABLE performs that operation. DELETE affects rows while retaining the table, and UPDATE changes values within rows. REMOVE is not the SQL table-removal command. The distinction is between schema removal and operations on data in an existing schema. A incorrect DELETE removes rows and retains the table definition. B correct DROP TABLE removes the table object and its definition. C incorrect REMOVE is not the SQL command for dropping a table. D incorrect UPDATE changes existing row values.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 7 · Q00106
records.text: Q00106 Question 7 FDB02 FDB03 Which of the following statement best describe relational data model? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A It is a database model that allows multiple records to be linked to the same owner file. B It structures data in a tree like structure using parent to child relationship. C It is a database model to manage data as tuples grouped into relations D It is a model that use concepts such as entities, attributes, and relationships E Describe how data is stored in the computer, representing information such as record structures, record ordering, and access paths. It is a database model to manage data as tuples grouped into relations A relational database consists of relations with tuple rows and attribute columns. A incorrect Owner-file links do not define tuple relations (PDF 13, 7.) B incorrect A tree is not the stated relational representation (PDF 13, 7.) C correct Tuple rows in relations match the definition (PDF 13, 7.) D incorrect Entities and relationships describe conceptual ER modeling (PDF 13, 7.) E incorrect Storage details define the physical model (PDF 13, 7.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 8 · Q00107
records.text: Q00107 Question 8 FDB15 Department(Dept_Name, Manager) has primary key Dept_Name and foreign key Manager referencing Employee(Emp_ID). Employee contains IDs 101–105 only. Consider INSERT INTO Department (Dept_Name, Manager) VALUES (NULL, 107); Which named integrity rules are violated? Select all that apply. Treat key integrity as uniqueness and domain integrity as type/allowed-value checks. Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Domain constraint B Key constraint C Entity Integrity constraint D Referential Integrity constraint C. Entity Integrity constraint; D. Referential Integrity constraint The inserted row has two independent defects. Dept_Name is the primary key, so NULL violates entity integrity. Manager is a non-NULL foreign key, yet employee 107 is absent, violating referential integrity. These are separate requirements and the same insertion fails both. Under the question's taxonomy, neither a duplicate-key violation nor an incompatible-domain value is being asserted. A incorrect The stated domain checks are satisfied; primary-key NULL is classified separately. B incorrect No duplicate key value is inserted; this category tests uniqueness. C correct NULL in the primary key violates entity integrity. D correct Manager 107 has no referenced employee and violates referential integrity.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 9 · Q00108
records.text: Q00108 Question 9 FDB18 FDB20 FDB21 Assume atomic attribute values. Consider R(A,B,C,D) with functional dependencies F = {C→D, C→B, B→C}. Which statement about R is true? Derive every candidate key before testing dependency-based normal forms. A The relation R is in second normal form B The relation R is in third normal form C The candidate key for R is BC D The relation R is in Boyce–Codd normal form E None of the other statements is true None of the other statements is true Every candidate key must contain A because no dependency derives it. Both AB and AC determine all attributes and are minimal; BC determines only B, C and D. The nonprime attribute D depends on B or C alone, a proper subset of either composite key, so 2NF fails. The dependency C→D also violates 3NF and BCNF because C is not a superkey and D is nonprime. None of the other statements is true. A incorrect False: D depends on a proper subset of a candidate key, violating 2NF. B incorrect False: C→D has a nonsuperkey determinant and a nonprime dependent attribute, violating 3NF. C incorrect False: (BC)+ = {B,C,D}, so BC cannot determine A and is not a key. D incorrect False: C determines D but is not a superkey, violating BCNF. E correct Correct: each of the other four claims is false.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 11 · Q00110
records.text: Q00110 Question 11 FDB01 Which of the following is the disadvantage of a database approach? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A Data consistency B Sharing of data C Improved data integrity D Increased concurrency E Enforcement of standards F Complexity G None Complexity is a database-approach disadvantage. FDB01 identifies complexity and administration costs as possible disadvantages of a DBMS. Consistency, sharing, integrity and centrally supported standards are benefits. Increased concurrency means useful concurrent access here; only uncontrolled concurrent access causes anomalies. Thus complexity is the sole listed disadvantage, even though database management can improve the other listed properties. A incorrect Data consistency is improved by shared definitions and controlled updates, making it a benefit. B incorrect Sharing data is a purpose and benefit of the database approach. C incorrect Improved integrity means better enforcement of valid data and is a benefit. D incorrect Concurrent access is useful; uncontrolled interference, rather than increased concurrency itself, causes problems. E incorrect Central management supports consistent definitions and standards, which is a benefit. F correct A DBMS introduces administrative and technical complexity that can outweigh benefits for small applications. G incorrect A listed disadvantage exists: the complexity of database management.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 12 · Q00111
records.text: Q00111 Question 12 FDB03 FDB20 Which of the following is a correct statement about relation? (Choose all that applies) Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Values of each columns is a repeating group/array B Values in a column can be from different domain C A relation is in the INF D Two rows in a relational table can be identical E The sequence of columns and rows is insignificant F None A relation is in the INF; The sequence of columns and rows is insignificant Read INF as 1NF. Relations have atomic cells rather than repeating groups; the relational representation is independent of tuple sequence. The column sequence likewise does not alter named attributes. Distinct tuples and typed attribute domains rule out A,B,D. A incorrect Repeating arrays violate atomicity (PDF 14, 17.) B incorrect An attribute has a constrained domain (PDF 14, 17.) C correct Atomic relation values satisfy 1NF (PDF 14, 17.) D incorrect Duplicate tuples conflict with relation uniqueness (PDF 14, 17.) E correct Presentation order does not change named tuple values (PDF 14, 17.) F incorrect C and E already supply valid statements (PDF 14, 17.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 13 · Q00112
records.text: Q00112 Question 13 FDB32 Which of the following statement is correct about executing the following SQL query on the employee database given in question 2? (Choose all that applies) SELECT Emp_ID, First_Name, Last_Name FROM Employee E, Department D WHERE Department <> Sales' and AVG (salary) > 35000 and E.Department=D.Dept_Name GROUP BY Department; Apply grouping before filtering groups and computing aggregate output. A the query will execute successfully and will obtain all departments with an average salary higher than 35,000 B the query will not execute because Department attribute in Group by statement was not included in the select statement list C the query will not execute because we can't include aggregate function in the where statement D the query will execute successfully and will obtain employees of all departments with an average salary higher than 35,000 AVG(salary) cannot be used directly in WHERE. The query places AVG(salary) > 35000 in WHERE. FDB32 requires ordinary aggregate predicates in HAVING. Omitting Department from SELECT is not itself an error. Selecting ungrouped employee details is another defect unless functional dependence is established. The query therefore does not successfully produce either claimed result. A incorrect The aggregate predicate in WHERE prevents this query from successfully producing department averages. B incorrect A grouping column need not appear in SELECT; that omission is not the stated error. C correct WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so the ordinary AVG predicate belongs in HAVING. D incorrect The invalid aggregate predicate prevents execution; employee columns also require valid grouping or functional dependence.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 24 · Q00307
records.text: Q00307 Question 24 FDB09 Read each pair left→right. Buildings and locations are 1:1; each employee belongs to one department and a department may have many employees; a hospital serves many patients, each registered at one hospital; authors and books are M:N. Which pair is many-to-one? Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints. A [ Building — Location] B [ Employee — Department] C [ Hospital — Patient] D [ Author — Book] B. [ Employee — Department] Many-to-one means several left-side entities may share a right-side entity while each left entity has at most one right partner. Employees share departments under the stated assignment rule. Building→Location is one-to-one, Hospital→Patient is one-to-many and Author→Book is many-to-many. Reading the direction and both maximum counts determines the answer rather than the entity names. A incorrect Building→Location is explicitly 1:1. B correct Many employees can share one department; each employee has one department. C incorrect Hospital→Patient is 1:N under the registration rule. D incorrect Author→Book is explicitly M:N.

records.text: Q00374 Question 25 FDB03 FDB06 __________ is a single elementary unit of information representing an attribute of an entity. Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Entity Set B Record C File D Field Field. A field corresponds to one attribute rather than the collection of attributes describing a whole record. FDB03 equates attribute, column and field, while tuple, row and record refer to related attribute values together. An entity set groups entities, and a file groups stored records, so both are larger collections. A incorrect An entity set collects entities of one type rather than representing a single attribute. B incorrect A record contains related values for multiple attributes, rather than one elementary field. C incorrect A file groups records and is not an elementary attribute unit. D correct A field represents one attribute or property within a record.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 26 · Q00548
records.text: Q00548 Question 26 FDB11 An ER model has entity types A and B connected by an attribute-free relationship R. Cardinalities are read A→B. Which conditions allow R to be represented by a single B-key foreign-key column in A, permitting NULL for partial participation? Select all that apply. Locate the relationship's cardinality and participation before placing a foreign key. A Relationship R is one -to —many and the participation of A in R is Total. B Relationship R is one -to —many and the participation of A in R is Partial. C Relationship R is many —to —one and the participation of A in R is Total. D Relationship R is many —-to —one and the participation of A in R is Partial. C. Relationship R is many —to —one and the participation of A in R is Total.; D. Relationship R is many —-to —one and the participation of A in R is Partial. A single foreign-key column in A can represent R whenever each A is related to at most one B. This is exactly the many-to-one direction. Total participation makes the reference mandatory; partial participation permits NULL. One-to-many in the opposite direction needs the reference on B or another representation, because one A may have multiple related B values. A incorrect For A→B one-to-many, B normally holds A's key; total participation does not reverse that mapping. B incorrect Partial participation does not make a one-to-many collection fit a single ordinary foreign key in A. C correct Many-to-one with total A participation stores a non-NULL B reference in A. D correct Many-to-one with partial A participation stores a nullable B reference in A.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 27 · Q00567
records.text: Q00567 Question 27 FDB35 Under set relational algebra, which listed operation is not commutative? Interpret Join as an inner join, adjust its predicate when swapping inputs, and ignore attribute order. Apply each algebra operator to the input relations step by step. A Union B Join C Intersection D None D. None Union and intersection give the same tuple sets when their inputs are exchanged. An inner join also gives corresponding matches after the predicate is adjusted for the swapped inputs; the question explicitly ignores attribute order. Thus none of the three named operations lacks commutativity here. This conclusion depends on the stated inner-join interpretation; preservation of one designated outer side would use a different rule. A incorrect Union is commutative on union-compatible relations. B incorrect Inner join is commutative under the stated predicate and schema convention. C incorrect Intersection is commutative on union-compatible relations. D correct All three named operators are commutative under these assumptions.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 28 · Q00595
records.text: Q00595 Question 28 FDB19 Which of the following is a benefit of normalization rather than a potential cost or disadvantage? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A May require joins to reconstruct decomposed records B May reduce system performance C Time consuming D Reduce duplicate data Reduce duplicate data Normalization organizes facts according to their dependencies to reduce avoidable duplication and update anomalies. That reduction is a benefit. Decomposing a table may require joins when an application needs the original combined information, which can increase retrieval cost for some workloads. Dependency analysis and schema design also take time. These are possible costs, not claims that normalization always slows a system. Declared dependencies suffice for normalization even when the current sample data shows no errors. A incorrect A possible cost: reconstructing information from decomposed tables may require joins. B incorrect A possible cost: additional joins can reduce performance for some workloads, although this is not inevitable. C incorrect A possible cost: analyzing dependencies and designing a decomposition takes time. D correct Correct: reducing duplicate facts is a principal benefit, rather than a disadvantage.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 29 · Q00617
records.text: Q00617 Question 29 FDB35 Let you have two relations A and B, each table has 200 and 100 rows of records respectively. So after applying cross product on those tables, how many rows of records you will have? Apply each algebra operator to the input relations step by step. A 300 B 20000 C 2000 D 100 20000 The Cartesian-product example explicitly creates 1000*50 tuples from inputs of sizes 1000 and 50 (PDF p.28, lines 6–8). Applying the same all-pairs construction to 200 and 100 rows yields 200*100 = 20000. Each of the 200 rows is paired with each of the 100 rows; no filtering or duplicate-eliminating projection is specified. A incorrect 300 adds input sizes instead of counting pairs (PDF p.28). B correct 20000 is 200*100, the illustrated Cartesian pair-count rule (PDF p.28). C incorrect 2000 is ten times too small for the all-pairs count (PDF p.28). D incorrect 100 counts only one input and omits its 200 pairings per row (PDF p.28).

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 31 · Q00676
records.text: Q00676 Question 31 FDB05 Which database-design stage primarily builds an ER model from the users' requirements? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Applications and security B Physical refinement C Conceptual database D Schema refinement Conceptual database Conceptual design represents the required entities, attributes and relationships in an ER model. Logical design later maps that conceptual model into relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Physical refinement chooses storage organizations and access paths, while application and security work concerns behavior and protection rather than the modeling stage requested. The stem asks for the primary stage building the ER model, not every later activity that might consult it. A incorrect Incorrect: application and security work addresses behavior and protection, rather than building the conceptual ER model. B incorrect Incorrect: physical refinement chooses storage organization and access paths. C correct Correct: conceptual design turns requirements into the ER model. D incorrect Incorrect: schema refinement checks or improves a logical schema, rather than naming the initial ER-model stage.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 32 · Q00678
records.text: Q00678 Question 32 FDB30 Employee(empid, ...) already exists, has no primary key, and empid values are unique and non-NULL. Which SQL statement adds a primary key on empid? Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A ADD TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (empid) B ATTACH TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (empid) C ADD TABLE Employee ATTACH PRIMARY KEY (empid) D ALTER TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (empid); D. ALTER TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (empid); Adding a constraint to an existing table uses ALTER TABLE, followed by ADD PRIMARY KEY and the parenthesized key column. The existing unique, non-NULL empid values satisfy the prerequisite for the constraint. Option D has this structure. ADD TABLE and ATTACH TABLE do not perform this alteration, and ATTACH PRIMARY KEY is not the required constraint clause. A incorrect ADD TABLE does not modify an existing table's constraints. B incorrect ATTACH TABLE is not the required table-alteration syntax. C incorrect Neither ADD TABLE nor ATTACH PRIMARY KEY forms this SQL alteration. D correct The corrected ALTER TABLE statement adds the primary-key constraint.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 34 · Q00680
records.text: Q00680 Question 34 FDB27 You need to produce a report for mailing labels for customers. The mailing label must have only the customer name and address. The CUSTOMERS table has these columns, ID ,NAME,ADDRESS,PHONE ,the SELECT statement to accomplishes this task? * Trace how SELECT forms its result columns and rows. B and C include unwanted ID and PHONE fields, while D uses column names not supplied by the question. A correct It selects exactly the two existing columns required for the mailing label. records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 36 · Q00682
records.text: Q00682 Question 36 FDB29 FDB26 Which SQL statement sets PRICE to 600 in BOOK for rows whose ID is 'B001'? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A CHANGE BOOK SET PRICE =600 Where ID ='B001'; B UPDATE TO CHANGE BOOK SET PRICE =600 Where ID ='B001'; C UPDATE BOOK SET PRICE =600 Where ID ='B001'; D GRANT BOOK SET PRICE =600 Where ID ='B001'; UPDATE BOOK SET PRICE =600 Where ID ='B001'; UPDATE changes existing row values. The table name follows UPDATE, SET supplies the assignment and WHERE restricts the rows. C therefore assigns 600 only where ID equals the quoted string B001. CHANGE is not the row-update command, the extra TO CHANGE words break the required UPDATE structure, and GRANT controls privileges rather than performing a row assignment. These malformed alternatives are definite incorrect selections. A incorrect Incorrect: the required row-change statement begins UPDATE, not CHANGE BOOK SET. B incorrect Incorrect: UPDATE must be followed by its target table, not TO CHANGE. C correct Correct: the statement assigns 600 to PRICE for precisely the matching ID rows. D incorrect Incorrect: GRANT manages privileges; it cannot perform this SET assignment.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 40 · Q00686
records.text: Q00686 Question 40 FDB35 If relation R has 5 tuples and relation S has also 7 tuples, then Cartesian product of R and S will have Apply each algebra operator to the input relations step by step. A 5+7 tuples B 7-5 tuples C 5X7 tuples D 5/7 tuples 5X7 tuples The module explicitly multiplies input tuple counts for a Cartesian product (PDF p.28, lines 6–8). Hence 5 rows paired with 7 rows give 5*7 = 35 distinct concatenated tuples, before any filtering/projection. A incorrect 5+7 is the sum, not all pair combinations (PDF p.28). B incorrect 7-5 is the size difference, not the pair count (PDF p.28). C correct 5*7 gives the 35 combinations required by the product construction (PDF p.28). D incorrect 5/7 is not even an integer tuple count and is not pair enumeration (PDF p.28).

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 42 · Q00730
records.text: Q00730 Question 42 FDB29 FDB28 Using standard SQL string literals, which update changes only the name of the student whose ID is '123' to 'abel'? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A UPDATE student ID='123'; B UPDATE student SET ID='123'; C UPDATE student SET name='abel' WHERE ID='123'; D UPDATE student SET name='abel'; C. UPDATE student SET name='abel' WHERE ID='123'; UPDATE needs SET to state the assignment and WHERE to restrict the target rows. C assigns the desired name only to the student with ID '123'. B changes IDs in every row, while D changes every student's name because it has no filter. A omits SET and is malformed. Correct syntax and the requested scope both matter. A incorrect SET is missing before the assignment. B incorrect This sets every student's ID and does not change the name. C correct SET changes name and WHERE restricts the operation to ID '123'. D incorrect Without WHERE, every name is changed.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 43 · Q00899
records.text: Q00899 Question 43 FDB08 A weak entity is identified by its partial key together with the key of an independently keyed associated entity. Which listed terms describe that associated entity set? Select all that apply. Check how a dependent entity obtains its complete identity. A Identifying set B Strong entity set C Neighbor set D Owner set B. Strong entity set; D. Owner set A weak entity cannot identify itself using its own attributes alone. Its owner contributes the missing key component, and in the specified case that owner has an independent key, so it is a strong entity set. Both owner set and strong entity set describe it. The identifying relationship connects the sets; neighbor does not identify the required ownership role. A incorrect Identifying normally names the owner relationship rather than the defined owner entity-set role. B correct The owner supplying the independent key is normally a strong entity set. C incorrect Neighbor does not express the ownership and identification needed for a weak entity. D correct Owner set names the entity set whose key contributes to weak-entity identification.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 45 · Q00907
records.text: Q00907 Question 45 FDB03 FDB01 In relational-table terminology, which listed terms name a unit of related field values treated together by an application? Select all that apply. Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Rows B Field C Record D Database A. Rows; C. Record A relational tuple groups related attribute values into one unit. Row and record are names for that same unit, so both options qualify even though one is plural. A field refers to one property rather than the whole grouping. A database is the larger coherent collection containing tables and their data, rather than one individual tuple. A correct A relational row groups related field values and is synonymous with a record. B incorrect A field represents one attribute, not the collection of related fields in the definition. C correct A record is the unit containing related fields described by the stem. D incorrect A database contains a larger coherent collection, rather than this single field grouping.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 46 · Q00927
records.text: Q00927 Question 46 FDB30 Which template correctly creates a table with one column? Treat table_name, column_name and column_type as placeholders for valid identifiers and a data type. Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A CREATE table_name (column_name, column type); B CREATE table_name (column_type, column name); C CREATE TABLE table_name (column_name column_type); D CREATE TABLE table_name (column_type, column_name); C. CREATE TABLE table_name (column_name column_type); A column declaration places its name immediately before its data type. Commas separate complete declarations when more than one column is present. The corrected C uses CREATE TABLE and a properly paired name and type. A and B omit TABLE, while D separates and reverses the name/type parts rather than declaring the intended column. A incorrect TABLE is missing and the name/type pair is split by a comma. B incorrect TABLE is missing and the type/name order is wrong. C correct CREATE TABLE is followed by one correctly ordered name/type declaration. D incorrect A comma separates type from name and no valid intended declaration is formed.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 48 · Q00943
records.text: Q00943 Question 48 FDB09 Consider a directed line(->) from the relationship set advisor to both entity sets instructor and student. This indicates cardinality Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints. A Many to one B Many to many C ¢. One to one D One to many One-to-one, under the common relationship-arrow convention. FDB09 explicitly states the convention used for this example: arrows from advisor toward both Instructor and Student impose maximum-one at both ends. Each instructor can therefore be associated with at most one student and each student with at most one instructor. That is 1:1, without implying mandatory participation. A different notation would need an explicit legend. A incorrect Many-to-one constrains only one end to maximum one, whereas both ends have arrows here. B incorrect Many-to-many permits multiple associations at both ends, contrary to both maximum-one arrows. D incorrect One-to-many allows multiple associations at one end, which the second arrow rules out.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 50 · Q00964
records.text: Q00964 Question 50 FDB07 For a relation with attributes ID, CITY and NAME, ID is guaranteed unique and non-NULL; CITY and NAME are not unique. Which listed attribute sets are superkeys? Select all that apply. Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A NAME B ID C CITY D CITY, ID B. ID; D. CITY, ID A superkey is any attribute set guaranteed to identify a tuple; it need not be minimal. ID has the stated uniqueness guarantee, and adding CITY cannot destroy it. Thus ID and (CITY, ID) are superkeys. CITY and NAME individually lack uniqueness guarantees. Only ID is a minimal candidate key among the two qualifying choices, but minimality is not required here. A incorrect Repeated names are permitted, so NAME is not a guaranteed identifier. B correct ID is guaranteed unique and identifies each tuple. C incorrect Repeated cities are permitted, so CITY alone is not a superkey. D correct The set includes unique ID and therefore retains uniqueness.

records.text: Q01153 Question 54 FDB03 Which listed terms denote database contents at one particular moment, rather than the database definition? Select all that apply. Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Database instance B Database state / snapshot C Database schema D None of the above A. Database instance; B. Database state / snapshot An instance, state or snapshot describes the actual data at a selected time. Those contents can change after an insertion or update without changing the database definition. A schema describes names, structures and constraints instead. Therefore both the instance option and the state/snapshot option fit, while none of the above cannot be selected because these matching terms are present. A correct A database instance denotes its data at a particular time. B correct State and snapshot are synonyms for the same time-specific database contents. C incorrect A schema describes structure and constraints rather than current data values. D incorrect Both instance and state/snapshot are provided and correctly fit the definition.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 55 · Q01154
records.text: Q01154 Question 55 FDB04 What is the capacity to change the conceptual schema while preserving affected external schemas and application interfaces? Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A Logical data independence B Physical data independence C Conceptual database D All of the above Logical data independence Logical data independence allows changes to the conceptual schema while preserving the external views and application interfaces that depend on it. A conceptual database or schema describes the logical structure itself; naming that structure does not express the ability to preserve external interfaces during a change. Consequently A names the requested property and the all-of-the-above choice is false. A correct Correct: logical data independence preserves external interfaces across conceptual-schema changes. B incorrect Incorrect: physical data independence concerns internal-storage changes while preserving the conceptual schema. C incorrect Incorrect: conceptual database names the logical structure, not the property preserving external interfaces when that structure changes. D incorrect Incorrect: physical independence and the conceptual database are not the requested change-preservation property.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 57 · Q01157
records.text: Q01157 Question 57 FDB32 Common functions applied to collections of numeric values: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT. records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 61 · Q01163
records.text: Q01163 Question 61 FDB20 FDB21 In the usual normalization sequence, which is the first normal form that excludes partial dependencies of nonprime attributes on any candidate key? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First Normal Form (1NF) B Third Normal Form (3NF) C Second Normal Form (2NF) D Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF) Second Normal Form (2NF) Second normal form is the first stage requiring atomic relations to have no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key. First normal form addresses atomic values, so it does not impose that dependency rule. Third normal form and BCNF are stronger stages that inherit the absence of partial dependencies, but they are not the first stage introducing it. BCNF specifically requires every nontrivial functional-dependency determinant to be a superkey. A incorrect Incorrect: 1NF requires atomic values but does not exclude partial dependencies. B incorrect Incorrect: 3NF inherits 2NF and imposes its additional determinant/prime-attribute condition; it is not the first stage. C correct Correct: 2NF is the first stage excluding nonprime partial dependencies on candidate keys.
