D incorrect Incorrect: BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey; it is stronger than the first stage imposing the partial-dependency rule.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 62 · Q01164
records.text: Q01164 Question 62 FDB20 FDB21 In the usual normalization sequence, which is the first normal form that excludes transitive dependence of nonprime attributes on a key through a nonkey determinant? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A Third Normal Form (3NF) B Fourth Normal Form (4NF) C First Normal Form (1NF) D All of the above Third Normal Form (3NF) In the stated single-key teaching case, 2NF excludes partial dependencies but can still allow a nonprime fact to depend on the key through a nonkey determinant. The next defining stage is 3NF, summarized by the whole-key-and-nothing-but-the-key mnemonic. BCNF strengthens the determinant rule, and 4NF addresses multivalued dependencies. Stronger forms inherit earlier conditions, so the explicit first-stage scope makes 3NF the unique selection rather than treating inherited properties as rival answers. A correct Correct: 3NF is the first stage imposing the specified nonprime transitive-dependency restriction in this teaching case. B incorrect Incorrect: 4NF addresses multivalued dependencies and is a later stage; it is not the first stage imposing the 3NF condition. C incorrect Incorrect: 1NF concerns atomic values and does not eliminate the specified transitive dependencies. D incorrect Incorrect: Not all options identify the requested first stage: 1NF does not eliminate the specified transitive dependency and 4NF is later.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 63 · Q01217
records.text: Q01217 Question 63 FDB04 A conceptual level refers to: Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A Describes the represents global view of the entire database B Describes the part of the database that a particular user group views of the data environment C Describes how data is actually stored on disk D Describes the physical storage structure of the database Describes the represents global view of the entire database The conceptual schema describes the whole database while hiding storage details. External views show a particular group's part, and internal schema describes storage. A correct Whole-database structure is conceptual. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) B incorrect A user-group subset is external. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) C incorrect Actual storage is internal. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) D incorrect Physical storage structure is internal. (PDF pp. 7, 8.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 64 · Q01226
records.text: Q01226 Question 64 FDB05 FDB19 Suppose you want to design a database for a certain company after you know the need of all users of the database. What is the next step you are expected to do? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Logical design B Normalization C Query Processing D Conceptual design Conceptual design After collecting users' information requirements, conceptual design develops the ER/EER model that represents those needs. Logical design then maps that model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization. Normalization refines dependency structure rather than replacing the initial conceptual modeling step. Query processing evaluates database requests instead of defining the initial enterprise model. D is therefore the next step under the stated sequence, rather than a claim that design can never iterate. A incorrect Incorrect: logical design maps an already developed conceptual model into relations and constraints. B incorrect Incorrect: normalization refines relation dependencies during logical design; the initial conceptual model must first be developed. C incorrect Incorrect: query processing evaluates requests rather than creating the initial model from requirements. D correct Correct: conceptual design follows the collection of requirements in the stated sequence.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 65 · Q01278
records.text: Q01278 Question 65 FDB01 FDB03 FDB04 All are true about the Database except: Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A Program data independence. B Self-describing nature C Sharing of data and multi-user transaction processing D Support of single views of the data Support of single views of the data The listed characteristics include insulation between data and programs, self-description, sharing, and multiple views. The exception is single views, interpreted as support restricted to one view; a DBMS can of course also display a single view. A incorrect Program/data insulation is expressly a characteristic. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) B incorrect Self-description is expressly listed. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) C incorrect Sharing and multiuser transactions are expressly listed. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) D correct The stated characteristic is multiple views, rather than restriction to a single view. (PDF pp. 5, 6.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 66 · Q01326
records.text: Q01326 Question 66 FDB26 Which one of the following provides the ability to query information from the database and to insert tuples into, delete tuples from, and modify tuples in the database? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML(Data Manipulation Langauge) B DDL(Data Definition Langauge) C Query D Relational Schema DML(Data Manipulation Langauge) DML includes SELECT, INSERT, DELETE, UPDATE and therefore covers both retrieval and tuple changes. The second list is misprinted as Basic DDL commands but sits under the DML heading; the heading and separation resolve that typo. A correct DML is the category covering all named operations. (PDF pp. 26.) B incorrect DDL describes structural commands. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect A query is a request, not the complete language category for all modifications. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect A relational schema describes structure rather than performing operations. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 67 · Q01327
records.text: Q01327 Question 67 FDB30 FDB26 Which command is used to modifies an existing database object, such as a table? Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A Create B Alter C Drop D Modify ALTER. ALTER changes the definition of an existing database object. FDB30 demonstrates adding or removing columns and adding constraints with ALTER TABLE. CREATE establishes an object and DROP removes it. MODIFY can occur within some vendor-specific alteration syntax, but it is not the general top-level command requested here. A incorrect CREATE defines a new object rather than altering the definition of an existing one. B correct ALTER is the command used to change an existing database object definition. C incorrect DROP removes the object instead of modifying its existing definition. D incorrect MODIFY is not the general standalone command; some dialects use it inside ALTER syntax.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 68 · Q01328
records.text: Q01328 Question 68 FDB29 Which command is used to modifies records? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A Insert B Update C Delete D Modify Update The module puts UPDATE in DML (PDF p.26). Its UPDATE(Salary) privilege example explicitly permits the Finance user to change Salary values (PDF pp.54–55), grounding UPDATE as the command for modifying existing record values. A incorrect INSERT is a separate DML operation, illustrated as adding VALUES rows on PDF p.77. B correct UPDATE is explicitly tied to changing Salary values on PDF p.55. C incorrect DELETE is a separate operation illustrated with a row predicate on PDF p.77. D incorrect MODIFY is not the command used for the demonstrated change-value privilege on PDF pp.54–55.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 69 · Q01329
records.text: Q01329 Question 69 FDB26 In the SQLite command-line shell, which command lists the names and files of attached databases? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A db B use C .databases D database C. .databases The command belongs to the SQLite shell rather than ordinary SQL statement syntax. Its documented spelling is .databases, including the leading dot and final s, and it lists attached database names and files. The corrected C has that spelling. The alternatives db, use and database do not form this SQLite attached-database listing command. A incorrect db is not the SQLite shell listing command. B incorrect use does not list SQLite attached names and files. C correct The .databases command performs the requested listing. D incorrect database lacks the required shell-command spelling.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 70 · Q01330
records.text: Q01330 Question 70 FDB02 FDB03 FDB15 What is an RDBMS? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Database that stores data elements that are not linked B Database that accesses data elements that are not linked C Database that stores and allows access to data elements that are linked D None of the mentioned Database that stores and allows access to data elements that are linked A relational DBMS manages a database represented by relations/tables, with references maintaining relationships between tuples. Among these broad descriptions C is closest, although linked data alone is not a complete definition distinguishing relational from other models. A incorrect A description excluding links omits the relationships modeled by references. (PDF pp. 5, 13, 14.) B incorrect Accessing only unlinked elements also omits those relationships. (PDF pp. 5, 13, 14.) C correct Storage and access to related elements agrees with tables and relational constraints. (PDF pp. 5, 13, 14.) D incorrect C supplies the compatible broad description, though it is not a formal definition. (PDF pp. 5, 13, 14.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 71 · Q01331
records.text: Q01331 Question 71 FDB03 FDB07 What is a relation in RDBMS? Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Key B Table C Row D Data Types Table The relational model represents relations in table format. A tuple is one row; a key identifies tuples rather than being the relation itself. A incorrect A key is an identifying attribute set. (PDF pp. 13.) B correct A relation is represented as a table. (PDF pp. 13.) C incorrect A row is a tuple within the relation. (PDF pp. 13.) D incorrect Data types constrain values rather than constituting a relation. (PDF pp. 13.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 72 · Q01332
records.text: Q01332 Question 72 FDB36 FDB35 Relational Algebra is a __________ query language that takes two relations as input and produces another relation as an output of the query. Distinguish a declarative condition from a prescribed evaluation procedure. A Relational B Structural C Procedural D Fundamental Procedural Relational algebra is procedural because it specifies a sequence of operations. The stem overgeneralizes arity: operations can take one or more input relations, not always two. A incorrect Relational describes the model but misses the procedural/calculus distinction. (PDF pp. 24, 24.) B incorrect Structural is not the stated classification. (PDF pp. 24, 24.) C correct Procedural is expressly justified by the required sequence. (PDF pp. 24, 24.) D incorrect Fundamental is not the procedural classification used in the definition. (PDF pp. 24, 24.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 73 · Q01333
records.text: Q01333 Question 73 FDB-S01 FDB35 Which of the following is a fundamental operation in relational algebra? Use the operator convention stated in the question and distinguish membership from derivability. A Set intersection B Natural join C Assignment D None of the mentioned Set intersection Under the stated Basic operations list, intersection is basic. A smaller primitive basis may instead treat intersection as derived; the answer uses the stated list. A correct Intersection is explicitly under Basic operations. (PDF pp. 24.) B incorrect Natural join is absent from this basic list. (PDF pp. 24.) C incorrect Assignment is absent from this basic list. (PDF pp. 24.) D incorrect False because intersection is listed as basic. (PDF pp. 24.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 74 · Q01334
records.text: Q01334 Question 74 FDB35 Which of the following is used to denote the selection operation in relational algebra? Apply each algebra operator to the input relations step by step. A Pi (Greek) B Sigma (Greek) C Lambda (Greek) D Omega (Greek) Sigma (Greek) Selection filters tuples and is conventionally denoted by sigma, σ. Projection keeps attributes and is denoted by pi, π. Lambda and omega are different Greek symbols and therefore cannot identify the requested sigma operation under this notation. This is a question about the operator's conventional symbol, rather than whether another symbol could be assigned a new meaning in a custom notation. B is the unique selection symbol among the choices. A incorrect Incorrect: pi, π, denotes projection, which retains attributes. B correct Correct: sigma, σ, denotes selection, which filters tuples. C incorrect Incorrect: lambda, λ, is a different symbol from the conventional selection symbol σ. D incorrect Incorrect: omega, ω, is a different symbol from the conventional selection symbol σ.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 75 · Q01335
records.text: Q01335 Question 75 FDB-S01 FDB35 For union-compatible relations, which listed names denote the minus operation R−S, returning tuples in R but not S? Select all that apply. Use the operator convention stated in the question and distinguish membership from derivability. A Union B Set-difference C Difference D Intersection B. Set-difference; C. Difference R−S tests membership asymmetrically: a tuple must occur in R and must not occur in S. Difference and set-difference are names for this same operator, so both should be selected. Union combines membership from either input, whereas intersection requires membership in both. Swapping the inputs to difference can change the result because the exclusion direction matters. A incorrect Union combines compatible input tuples rather than retaining only first-input tuples absent from the second. B correct Set-difference returns tuples in the first relation that do not occur in the second. C correct Difference is the same minus operator as set-difference. D incorrect Intersection keeps tuples common to both relations, the opposite membership condition.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 76 · Q01336
records.text: Q01336 Question 76 FDB26 Which one of the following is used to define the structure of the relation, deleting relations and relating schemas? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML(Data Manipulation Langauge) B DDL(Data Definition Langauge) C Query D Relational Schema DDL(Data Definition Langauge) Defining and deleting relation structures are schema operations in DDL. DML operates on their data. Relating schemas here is interpreted as defining schema structure rather than retrieving joins. A incorrect DML is for data operations. (PDF pp. 26.) B correct DDL is the schema-definition category. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect A query request is not the schema language category. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect A schema is a description, not a language for changing it. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 77 · Q01337
records.text: Q01337 Question 77 FDB26 FDB30 CREATE TABLE employee (name VARCHAR(80), id INTEGER); What kind of SQL statement is this? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML B DDL C View D Integrity constraint DDL CREATE TABLE defines a new table and its columns, so it is a data-definition-language statement. DML instead retrieves or changes stored rows. A view is a query-based logical object, while this statement creates a base table. Integrity constraints can be included inside a table definition, but this whole statement is not merely a constraint expression. VARCHAR has the stated length in this table definition. A incorrect Incorrect: DML acts on stored data, whereas this statement defines a table. B correct Correct: creating a table and declaring its columns is DDL. C incorrect Incorrect: CREATE TABLE defines a table rather than a view. D incorrect Incorrect: the statement defines an entire table, not just an integrity-constraint expression.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 78 · Q01338
records.text: Q01338 Question 78 FDB26 FDB27 FDB33 SELECT * FROM employee What type of statement is this? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML B DDL C View D Integrity constraint DML SELECT is in the list under the DML heading. The line's repeated DDL word is a typographical error in that DML subsection, as shown by the preceding separate DDL list. A correct SELECT is classified under DML. (PDF pp. 26.) B incorrect SELECT is not in the preceding DDL list. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect No view is defined by this standalone retrieval. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect The retrieval is not an integrity constraint. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 79 · Q01339
records.text: Q01339 Question 79 FDB23 The basic data type char(n) is a _____ length character string and varchar(n) is _____ length character. Relate the value domain and access requirements to storage and type choices. A Fixed, equal B Equal, variable C Fixed, variable D Variable, equal Fixed, variable The attribute-type section directly defines CHAR as fixed-length and VARCHAR as variable-length. Neither blank means equal length. A incorrect Fixed is right for CHAR but equal is wrong for VARCHAR. (PDF pp. 19.) B incorrect Variable is right for VARCHAR but equal is not the stated CHAR class. (PDF pp. 19.) C correct Fixed followed by variable matches both definitions. (PDF pp. 19.) D incorrect Both descriptions miss the given definitions. (PDF pp. 19.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 80 · Q01340
records.text: Q01340 Question 80 FDB26 To remove a relation from an SQL database, we use the ______ comman d. Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Delete B Purge C Remove D Drop table DROP TABLE. Removing a relation means removing the table object, rather than just its tuples. FDB26 distinguishes DROP TABLE from DELETE: DELETE preserves the table definition while removing rows. DROP TABLE removes the object itself. PURGE and REMOVE are not the general SQL command specified here for this task. A incorrect DELETE removes tuples while preserving the relation definition, so it does not remove the relation. B incorrect PURGE is not the general table-removal command established here. C incorrect REMOVE is not the SQL command used here to remove a relation object. D correct DROP TABLE removes the table object, including its relation definition.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 81 · Q01341
records.text: Q01341 Question 81 FDB29 Assume constraints permit the deletion. Which descriptions apply to executing DELETE FROM r; on an existing table r? Select all that apply. Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A Remove relation B Clear relation entries C Delete fields D Delete rows B. Clear relation entries; D. Delete rows Without WHERE, DELETE targets every row in r. If the operation succeeds, the table's entries are cleared but its column definitions and table object remain. Clear relation entries and delete rows describe this same effect. Removing the relation itself requires a schema operation such as DROP TABLE, while deleting fields would change columns rather than row contents. A incorrect The table definition remains; DELETE does not remove the relation object. B correct Without WHERE, every relation entry is removed while the table remains available. C incorrect Fields are columns; DELETE removes rows rather than column definitions. D correct Every row is targeted because the statement contains no filtering WHERE clause.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 82 · Q01342
records.text: Q01342 Question 82 FDB26 FDB29 INSERT INTO instructor VALUES (10211, 'Smith', 'Biology', 66000); What type of statement is this? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Query B DML C Relational D DDL DML INSERT belongs to the DML list. Classification follows from the operation name; it does not require assuming an instructor schema or proving that these particular values satisfy its constraints. A incorrect Query is a generic request rather than the displayed language category. (PDF pp. 26.) B correct INSERT is expressly a DML command. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect Relational names a model, not this statement class. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect INSERT is not in the DDL list. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 83 · Q01343
records.text: Q01343 Question 83 FDB31 Which joins discard unmatched tuples from both inputs? Interpret Natural join as an ordinary natural inner join. Select all that apply. Compute matching pairs, then account for any preserved unmatched rows. A Left outer join B Right outer join C Inner join D Natural join C. Inner join; D. Natural join An inner join returns only pairs that satisfy its matching condition, so unmatched tuples from either input disappear. An ordinary natural join is an inner equality join using all common column names and has the same preservation behavior. Left and right outer joins instead preserve unmatched tuples from their designated side by adding NULLs for the other side. A incorrect A left outer join preserves unmatched left rows, filling right-side columns with NULL. B incorrect A right outer join preserves unmatched right rows, filling left-side columns with NULL. C correct An inner join returns matching pairs only, so unmatched tuples do not survive. D correct An ordinary natural join is an inner equality join and discards unmatched tuples.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 84 · Q01344
records.text: Q01344 Question 84 FDB31 What type of join is needed when you wish to include rows that do not have matching values? Compute matching pairs, then account for any preserved unmatched rows. A Equi-join B Natural join C Outer join D All of the mentioned Outer join. An outer join retains unmatched rows from one or both inputs and fills the missing side with NULL. FDB31 contrasts that behavior with ordinary matching-only joins. Equijoin describes an equality condition, and an ordinary natural join is an inner equality join; neither alone guarantees unmatched-row preservation. Therefore all of the mentioned is false. A incorrect An equality condition alone does not retain rows that fail to match. B incorrect An ordinary natural join uses matching shared-column values and discards unmatched rows. C correct Outer joins preserve unmatched rows from the left, right or both inputs. D incorrect The other named joins do not all guarantee preservation of unmatched rows.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 85 · Q01345
records.text: Q01345 Question 85 FDB31 How many input relations does one ordinary binary join operator combine? Count operator inputs, not distinct base tables used by a complete query. Compute matching pairs, then account for any preserved unmatched rows. A One B Two C Three D All of the mentioned B. Two One binary join operator combines two input relations. Either input may itself be the output of an earlier join, so the complete query can involve more base tables. A self-join can refer twice to one base table, but still supplies two relation occurrences to the operator. The question fixes the count at the operator level, making two the unique choice. A incorrect One distinct base table can support a self-join, but the operator still has two inputs. B correct A binary join operator has exactly two inputs. C incorrect Three base tables require a chain of binary joins, not one operator. D incorrect The input count of the specified binary operator is fixed, so all counts do not apply.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 86 · Q01346
records.text: Q01346 Question 86 FDB31 Which option gives the complete set of valid SQL join forms among the listed alternatives? Choose the most complete single answer. Compute matching pairs, then account for any preserved unmatched rows. A Cross join B Natural join C Join with USING clause D All of the mentioned All of the mentioned CROSS JOIN forms every pair of input rows without a matching predicate. NATURAL JOIN matches all same-named columns and merges the duplicate join columns. JOIN USING explicitly names shared equality columns. All three are valid join forms, although they do not all express a join condition in the same way. The revised stem requests the complete single answer, so the aggregate D is selected; each individually true alternative is incomplete on its own. A incorrect Incorrect as the complete selection: CROSS JOIN is a valid join form without a matching condition, but B and C also qualify. B incorrect Incorrect as the complete selection: NATURAL JOIN is valid and matches same-named columns, but A and C also qualify. C incorrect Incorrect as the complete selection: JOIN USING is valid and names shared equality columns, but A and B also qualify. D correct Correct: all three named constructs are valid SQL join forms, so the aggregate is the complete answer.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 87 · Q01347
records.text: Q01347 Question 87 FDB-S01 FDB35 The operation which is not considered a basic operation of relational algebra is Use the operator convention stated in the question and distinguish membership from derivability. A Join B Selection C Union D Cross product Join The stated basic-operation list contains selection, union, cross-product, projection, difference, and intersection. Join is not included, even though it appears in later execution-plan examples. A correct Join is absent from the basic list and is the requested exception. (PDF pp. 24.) B incorrect Selection is explicitly basic. (PDF pp. 24.) C incorrect Union is explicitly basic. (PDF pp. 24.) D incorrect Cross-product is explicitly basic. (PDF pp. 24.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 88 · Q01348
records.text: Q01348 Question 88 FDB12 A many to many relationship between two entities usually results in how many tables? Identify relationship degree and cardinality before choosing a relational mapping. A One B Two C Three D Four Three tables: two entity tables and one association table. Each of the two entity types normally has its own relation. Their many-to-many relationship requires an additional association relation holding references to both entities and any relationship attributes. FDB12 illustrates Student, Course and Enrollment. Thus the usual total is three, rather than only the one new association table. A incorrect One counts only the association table and omits the two participating entity tables. B incorrect Two entity tables alone do not record arbitrary many-to-many pairs. C correct The two entity tables plus their association table produce the usual total of three. D incorrect No fourth table is required by the ordinary binary many-to-many mapping.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 89 · Q01349
records.text: Q01349 Question 89 FDB06 FDB03 An ________ is a set of entities of the same type that share the same properties, or attributes. Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Entity set B Attribute set C Relation set D Entity model Entity set. FDB06 distinguishes an individual entity from the type describing its properties and the set containing the current entities of that type. The stem asks for that collection of similarly described entities, which is an entity set. Attributes describe properties; a model describes representation rather than the current collection itself. A correct An entity set is the collection of entities belonging to one common entity type. B incorrect An attribute set groups properties, rather than the entities possessing those properties. C incorrect Relation set is not the ER term for the stated collection of entities. D incorrect An entity model describes structures, rather than naming the current set of entity instances.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 90 · Q01350
records.text: Q01350 Question 90 FDB06 Entity is a _________ Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Object of relation B Present working model C Thing in real world D Model of relation Thing in real world An entity is an object with physical or conceptual existence. It need not be a physical thing; the real-world thing option includes conceptual objects such as a course. A incorrect Object of relation is not the module's definition. (PDF pp. 10.) B incorrect A present working model is not an entity definition. (PDF pp. 10.) C correct Thing in the real world matches physical or conceptual objects. (PDF pp. 10.) D incorrect A model describes entities rather than being the object described. (PDF pp. 10.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 91 · Q01351
records.text: Q01351 Question 91 FDB05 E-R modeling technique is a : Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Top-down approach B Bottom-up approach C Left-right approach D None of the above Top-down is the usual conceptual ER approach. FDB05 describes conceptual design as usually starting with an enterprise view and working downward into entity and relationship details. This is the usual top-down classification of ER modeling. Bottom-up refinement is associated here with normalization from dependencies. This is a useful conventional approach, rather than a claim that every ER modeling activity must follow one direction. A correct Conceptual ER modeling usually moves from an overall enterprise view toward detailed entities and relationships. B incorrect Bottom-up dependency refinement describes normalization here, rather than the usual ER conceptual approach. C incorrect Left-right is not a database design methodology identified here. D incorrect Top-down is an available and appropriate description of the usual conceptual ER approach.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 92 · Q01352
records.text: Q01352 Question 92 FDB09 The number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set is expressed as : Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints. A Entity B Cardinality C Schema D Attributes Cardinality Cardinality measures how often an entity participates and distinguishes one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many. That is the number of possible associations asked about. A incorrect Entity is a participating object. (PDF pp. 11, 12.) B correct Cardinality is the association-count constraint. (PDF pp. 11, 12.) C incorrect Schema describes structure rather than the count. (PDF pp. 11, 12.) D incorrect Attributes are properties, not the association-count classification. (PDF pp. 11, 12.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 93 · Q01353
records.text: Q01353 Question 93 FDB20 FDB21 Relations produced from an E-R model will always be in : Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First normal form B Second normal form C Third normal form D Fourth normal form First normal form, assuming correct ER-to-relational mapping. FDB20 states that properly splitting composite and multivalued ER structures produces ordinary 1NF relations. Nothing in an ER drawing alone proves absence of partial, transitive or multivalued dependencies needed for higher forms. Thus A is the guaranteed level under correct relational mapping; the word always must not be read as excusing an incorrect mapping. A correct Correctly mapped atomic relations are in 1NF; this is the guaranteed level described here. B incorrect An ER model alone does not rule out partial dependencies on a composite candidate key. C incorrect An ER model alone does not establish the full dependency conditions required for 3NF. D incorrect An ER model alone does not rule out the nontrivial multivalued dependencies addressed by 4NF.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 94 · Q01354
records.text: Q01354 Question 94 FDB04 FDB13 In ER model the details of the entities are hidden from the user. This process is called : Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A generalization B specialization C abstraction D none of these above abstraction Abstraction hides unwanted or irrelevant details. Generalization groups subclasses; specialization divides a superclass. Thus hiding entity details describes abstraction. A incorrect Generalization combines common characteristics, rather than the general detail-hiding process. (PDF pp. 6, 13.) B incorrect Specialization separates narrower classes. (PDF pp. 6, 13.) C correct Abstraction is explicitly the process of hiding details. (PDF pp. 6, 13.) D incorrect The required term is present. (PDF pp. 6, 13.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 95 · Q01355
records.text: Q01355 Question 95 FDB06 The attributes made up of more than one single attributes are called Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Composite attribute B Derived attribute C Single value attribute D Multi value attribute Composite attribute Composite attributes have smaller meaningful subparts. This differs from multiple values of one attribute and from calculating a value from another. A correct Composite is the stated divisible structure. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) B incorrect Derived concerns computation from stored attributes. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) C incorrect Single-valued concerns count of values, not internal composition. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) D incorrect Multivalued concerns a set of values rather than components of one value. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 96 · Q01356
records.text: Q01356 Question 96 FDB06 The attribute AGE is calculated from DATE_OF_BIRTH. The attribute AGE is Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Single valued B Multi valued C Composite D Derived Derived The exact Age/Birth_date example identifies Age as derived. Age can also be single-valued, but the stem asks the classification indicated by calculating it from another attribute; D describes that dependency, while A describes a different axis. A incorrect Age can be single-valued, but that does not express the calculation relationship asked for. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) B incorrect No set of ages per person is described. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) C incorrect No meaningful component attributes of Age are specified. (PDF pp. 10, 10.) D correct Derived directly matches the module's example and the calculation clause. (PDF pp. 10, 10.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 97 · Q01357
records.text: Q01357 Question 97 FDB06 A student has one official Name and one Date_of_birth, but may have several Phone_number values. Which listed attribute is multivalued for a student? Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Phone_number B Name C Date_of_birth D All of the mentioned A. Phone_number Multiplicity asks how many values of one attribute may belong to the same entity. The student may have several phone numbers, making Phone_number multivalued. The stated rules allow one official name and one birth date, so those attributes are single-valued. These classifications follow the supplied requirements rather than the names or internal structure of the values. A correct Several phone values are permitted for one student. B incorrect The model permits one official name per student. C incorrect One birth date is permitted per student. D incorrect Name and birth date are single-valued under the stated rules.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 98 · Q01358
records.text: Q01358 Question 98 FDB06 For each student, Register_number has one value; Address records all residences and permits several values; SUBJECT_TAKEN permits several subjects; Reference permits several referees. Which listed attribute is single-valued? Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Register_number B Address C SUBJECT_TAKEN D Reference A. Register_number Single-valued means one value per entity, independently of whether that value can be broken into components. Register_number is single-valued under the stated student rule. Address, SUBJECT_TAKEN and Reference each explicitly permit multiple values for one student. An address can be composite without necessarily being multivalued, but this particular model permits multiple residences. A correct One register number is assigned per student. B incorrect Several residence addresses are permitted. C incorrect Several subjects can be taken by one student. D incorrect Several referee references are permitted.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 99 · Q01359
records.text: Q01359 Question 99 FDB06 FDB03 An association of several entities in an Entity-Relation model is called : Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Tuple B Record C Relationship D Field Relationship A relationship represents an association between entity types. Tuples and records instead represent individual table rows. A incorrect Tuple is a row. (PDF pp. 11, 13.) B incorrect Record is row data, not the ER association category. (PDF pp. 11, 13.) C correct Relationship is the explicit association term. (PDF pp. 11, 13.) D incorrect Field is an attribute component, not the association. (PDF pp. 11, 13.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 100 · Q01360
records.text: Q01360 Question 100 FDB30 FDB26 To include integrity constraint in an existing relation use: Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A Modify table B Drop table C Alter table D Create table Alter table Adding an integrity constraint to an existing table changes its definition, so ALTER TABLE is the appropriate command family. It can add a named constraint or a primary key, provided existing data satisfies the rule. DROP TABLE removes the object, and CREATE TABLE defines a new one. MODIFY TABLE does not follow the ALTER TABLE command form required for this structural change. The remaining constraint clause depends on the integrity rule to be enforced. A incorrect Incorrect: the required command family for this definition change is ALTER TABLE, not MODIFY TABLE. B incorrect Incorrect: DROP TABLE removes the existing object instead of adding a constraint. C correct Correct: ALTER TABLE can add a constraint to an existing table definition. D incorrect Incorrect: CREATE TABLE defines a new table rather than changing this existing one.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 101 · Q01361
records.text: Q01361 Question 101 FDB16 Which option is not a general SQL integrity-constraint keyword or clause? Distinguish a constraint clause from a business condition that could be expressed inside one. Read each SQL constraint's scope and enforcement rule. A Not null B Positive C Unique D Check predicate Positive NOT NULL forbids missing values, UNIQUE enforces uniqueness under the DBMS's NULL rules, and CHECK evaluates a declared predicate. POSITIVE by itself is not a general SQL constraint keyword. A positivity requirement is still a valid business rule and can be written as a CHECK predicate such as CHECK (Amount > 0). The question therefore distinguishes clause syntax from the meaning of a possible rule, making B the unique incorrect keyword rather than rejecting positivity as an integrity requirement. A incorrect Incorrect selection: NOT NULL is a constraint that forbids NULL values. B correct Correct selection: POSITIVE is not the standalone constraint keyword; a CHECK predicate can enforce positivity. C incorrect Incorrect selection: UNIQUE is a constraint enforcing uniqueness. D incorrect Incorrect selection: CHECK is the clause for enforcing a declared predicate.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 102 · Q01362
records.text: Q01362 Question 102 FDB15 Foreign key is the one in which the ________ of one relation is referenced in another relation. Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Foreign key B Primary key C References D Check constraint Primary key A foreign key references a matching candidate, usually primary, key in the parent. B is the offered conventional primary-key case; the definition also permits a candidate key, so primary is not an exclusive universal requirement. A incorrect An arbitrary foreign key is not the required parent unique target. (PDF pp. 48.) B correct Primary key is the listed usual referenced key. (PDF pp. 48.) C incorrect References names a mechanism rather than the key category. (PDF pp. 48.) D incorrect A CHECK predicate is not the referenced key. (PDF pp. 48.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 103 · Q01363
records.text: Q01363 Question 103 FDB15 Which are uses of data integrity constraints, rather than access authorization? Select all that apply. Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Control who is allowed access to the data B Ensure that duplicate records are not entered into the table C Improve the quality of data entered for a specific property (i.e., table column) D Prevent users from changing the values stored in the table B. Ensure that duplicate records are not entered into the table; C. Improve the quality of data entered for a specific property (i.e., table column) Integrity constraints test whether data is valid according to the schema's rules. Uniqueness constraints can reject duplicate keyed records, while domain constraints reject inappropriate values for a column. These support the two selected purposes. Authorization controls who may access the data. Integrity rejects invalid changes rather than prohibiting all changes, so it does not imply that every stored value is immutable. A incorrect Controlling who may access data is authorization rather than data integrity itself. B correct Key or uniqueness constraints prevent duplicate keyed records. C correct Domain constraints validate types and allowed values for a specific column. D incorrect Integrity permits valid updates; it does not prohibit every change to stored values.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 104 · Q01364
records.text: Q01364 Question 104 FDB15 FDB07 FDB16 The relationship between the two tables are created using __________ Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Candidate Key B Primary Key C Foreign Key D Check Constraint Foreign Key A foreign key links child occurrences to the matching parent candidate key. Primary/candidate keys identify the target, but foreign-key referencing creates the intertable link. A incorrect Candidate keys identify potential reference targets rather than expressing the link alone. (PDF pp. 48.) B incorrect A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key expresses the reference. (PDF pp. 48.) C correct The foreign key is explicitly the linking mechanism. (PDF pp. 48.) D incorrect CHECK restricts values rather than defining this intertable reference. (PDF pp. 48.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 105 · Q01365
records.text: Q01365 Question 105 FDB07 Customer has candidate keys CustId, Email and ContactNo. CustId is an immutable compact generated identifier; Email and ContactNo may change. A policy prefers stable compact candidate keys. Which is the best primary key under that policy? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A CustId B Email C ContactNo D CustId and ContactNo A. CustId Every candidate key is eligible for primary-key selection, but the policy gives a reason to prefer one. CustId is explicitly stable and compact, while the contact attributes may change. Choosing CustId follows that policy without denying the uniqueness of the other candidates. Combining CustId and ContactNo is nonminimal because CustId alone already identifies each customer. A correct Its stated stability and compactness satisfy the preference policy. B incorrect Email is eligible but may change, so it loses under this policy. C incorrect ContactNo is eligible but may change, so it loses under this policy. D incorrect Adding ContactNo to an already unique CustId is unnecessary and nonminimal.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 106 · Q01366
records.text: Q01366 Question 106 FDB07 FDB16 Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about primary key? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A There can be more than one primary key for a table B Columns with string data types cannot be made Primary Key because they are large C Both A and B D None of the above Both A and B The designer selects one candidate key as the primary key; a composite primary key is still one key. No numeric-only restriction appears: a key is defined by uniqueness, not by a prohibition on string type. Thus both A and B are false claims. A incorrect False: several candidate keys do not mean several primary keys. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) B incorrect False: the definition imposes uniqueness, not a ban on strings. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) C correct Both preceding claims conflict with the key definition. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) D incorrect There are false claims, so none is not correct. (PDF pp. 11, 14.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 107 · Q01367
records.text: Q01367 Question 107 FDB26 Which is the subset of SQL commands used to manipulate Oracle Database structures, including tables? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Data Definition Language(DDL) B Data Manipulation Language(DML) C DML and DDL D None of the Mentioned Data Definition Language(DDL) Schema-structure manipulation falls under definition language, despite the everyday word manipulate. DML is the separate category for data manipulation. A correct DDL contains the structural commands. (PDF pp. 26.) B incorrect DML concerns data operations. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect The asked subset for structures is DDL, not a combined category. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect DDL is offered. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 108 · Q01368
records.text: Q01368 Question 108 FDB26 Using the course's textbook SQL command categories, with RENAME treated as DDL, which listed commands are outside DDL? Select all that apply. Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A RENAME B REVOKE C GRANT D UPDATE B. REVOKE; C. GRANT; D. UPDATE DDL concerns structural definitions and includes RENAME in this course classification. GRANT and REVOKE manage privileges, placing them in DCL, while UPDATE changes existing data and belongs to DML. All three are consequently outside DDL. Classifying by each statement's effect distinguishes schema operations, access permissions and data changes even though all are expressed using SQL. A incorrect RENAME is commonly classified as DDL in the note's textbook taxonomy. B correct REVOKE removes privileges and is DCL rather than DDL. C correct GRANT assigns privileges and is DCL rather than DDL. D correct UPDATE changes data and is DML rather than DDL.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 109 · Q01369
records.text: Q01369 Question 109 FDB26 Which command empties an existing table while retaining its definition, using DBMS-specific table-emptying mechanisms rather than asserting that rollback is impossible? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A TRUNCATE command B Create command C Drop table command D Alter table command A. TRUNCATE command TRUNCATE empties a table while retaining the table object. Its implementation, logging and transaction behavior depend on the DBMS, so the answer does not rely on a claim that rollback is impossible. CREATE defines an object, DROP TABLE removes it, and ALTER changes its definition. Only TRUNCATE has the requested table-emptying role among these choices. A correct TRUNCATE empties the table and keeps its definition. B incorrect CREATE defines objects rather than emptying an existing table. C incorrect DROP TABLE removes the definition as well as the table. D incorrect ALTER changes the table definition rather than serving as the table-emptying command.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 110 · Q01370
records.text: Q01370 Question 110 FDB26 Which SQL command form removes a database object together with its contained database objects? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DROP DATABASE B DELETE DATABASE C REMOVE DATABASE D None of the mentioned DROP DATABASE DROP removes a database object, whereas DELETE removes rows from an existing table. DROP DATABASE is consequently the correct command form for removing a database and its contained objects. DELETE DATABASE does not express that structural operation, and REMOVE DATABASE does not follow the taught DROP syntax. Since the correct DROP DATABASE form is one of the options, the none-of-the-mentioned alternative is also incorrect. A correct Correct: DROP DATABASE removes the database object and its contained objects. B incorrect Incorrect: DELETE is row removal; deleting rows does not remove the database object. C incorrect Incorrect: the database-removal command form uses DROP, not REMOVE. D incorrect Incorrect: DROP DATABASE is present and performs the requested structural operation.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 111 · Q01371
records.text: Q01371 Question 111 FDB26 In SQL Server, which statement drops the two databases named Sales and suppliers? Assume permissions and database state allow the operation. Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DROP DATABASE Sales, NewSales B DROP DATABASE Sales, suppliers C DROP DATABASE Sales and suppliers D DROP DATABASE Sales-suppliers B. DROP DATABASE Sales, suppliers SQL Server permits a comma-separated list of database names after DROP DATABASE. B names exactly Sales and suppliers using that syntax. A names a different second database, while AND and a hyphen do not form the required two-name list. The answer is specific to SQL Server and does not assert that the same multi-database syntax works in every SQL dialect. A incorrect The second target is NewSales rather than suppliers. B correct The supported comma list names both required databases. C incorrect AND is not the separator in this DROP DATABASE syntax. D incorrect A hyphen does not separate these two database names.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 112 · Q01372
records.text: Q01372 Question 112 FDB30 Command that is used to add attributes to an existing relation, is said to be Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A Alter B Modify C Tailor D Eliminate ALTER. Adding attributes changes a relation schema. FDB30 demonstrates ALTER TABLE Employee ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(120), keeping the column name next to its type. ALTER is therefore the required command family. The remaining alternatives do not name the general SQL schema-change command shown by the complete note. A correct ALTER changes an existing relation definition and supports adding a column. B incorrect MODIFY alone is not the general command for adding attributes to an existing relation. C incorrect TAILOR is not an SQL schema-change command established here. D incorrect ELIMINATE is not the SQL command for adding a relation attribute.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 113 · Q01373
records.text: Q01373 Question 113 FDB30 FDB26 FDB29 Which keyword pair changes a table definition to remove a specified column, rather than changing or deleting row values? Treat the comma in an option as separating keyword names. Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A UPDATE TABLE B TRUNCATE COLUMN C ALTER, DROP D DELETE COLUMN ALTER, DROP Removing a column changes the table's definition. The appropriate form is ALTER TABLE followed by DROP COLUMN, so the keyword pair represented by C is correct. Its comma separates the two keyword names rather than belonging in executable SQL. UPDATE changes stored row values, DELETE removes rows, and TRUNCATE empties a table while retaining its definition; none of those operations removes the specified column definition. A incorrect Incorrect: UPDATE changes row values rather than removing a column definition. B incorrect Incorrect: TRUNCATE empties a table; TRUNCATE COLUMN is not the column-removal form. C correct Correct: ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN removes a column definition. D incorrect Incorrect: DELETE removes rows, not a column from the schema.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 114 · Q01374
records.text: Q01374 Question 114 FDB27 Which one of these is used with SELECT clause to fetch all columns from a table? Trace how SELECT forms its result columns and rows. A ALL B * C DISTINCT D AS The asterisk (*). FDB27 explicitly says SELECT * selects all columns. ALL and DISTINCT instead govern duplicate result rows, so neither means every column. AS introduces an alias. A query still needs the appropriate FROM source for table columns; the question asks only which SELECT-list symbol requests them all. A incorrect ALL permits duplicate result rows and does not expand the result to every column. B correct The wildcard * requests every column from the selected table source. C incorrect DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows rather than selecting all available columns. D incorrect AS supplies an alias for a result expression or source, not a wildcard column list.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 115 · Q01375
records.text: Q01375 Question 115 FDB16 A parent table has a DATE column, a nullable data column and a primary-key column referenced by existing child rows with ON UPDATE RESTRICT. Which column's change to a different otherwise valid value is blocked specifically because the old key is still referenced? No other constraints or triggers block changes. Read each SQL constraint's scope and enforcement rule. A DATE type columns in the table B Columns which allows NULL values in the table C A primary key column which also serves as foreign key reference in another table D All of the above C. A primary key column which also serves as foreign key reference in another table The stated restrictive action prevents changing the parent key while existing children still refer to its old value. This is a consequence of the particular reference state and action, rather than inherent immutability of every primary key. DATE and nullable columns can accept otherwise valid changes. Therefore only the referenced primary-key column has the specified update block. A incorrect DATE values can be changed to other permitted dates. B incorrect Allowing NULL does not itself block valid updates. C correct Existing child references plus ON UPDATE RESTRICT block this key change. D incorrect The date and nullable columns are not blocked under the given conditions.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 116 · Q01376
records.text: Q01376 Question 116 FDB26 Using the course classification that includes SELECT in DML, which listed language terms can describe application requests to retrieve database data? Select all that apply. Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML B DDL C Query language D All of the Mentioned A. DML; C. Query language A query language expresses requests for data. The course also includes SELECT retrieval within DML, alongside insertion, update and deletion. Both terms can therefore describe the application's retrieval request at different levels of terminology. DDL changes structural definitions instead of expressing the requested retrieval. Since DDL does not fit, the aggregate all-of-the-mentioned choice is also false. A correct DML includes retrieval with SELECT in the note's classification. B incorrect DDL changes schema structure rather than expressing ordinary data retrieval requests. C correct A query language expresses requests for data, directly matching the stem. D incorrect DDL does not fit the retrieval role, so the inclusive choice is false.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 117 · Q01377
records.text: Q01377 Question 117 FDB26 Which of the following is not included in DML (Data Manipulation Language)? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Insert B Update C Delete D Alter Alter INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are all in the DML subsection. ALTER is instead in the preceding DDL list. A incorrect INSERT is listed as DML. (PDF pp. 26.) B incorrect UPDATE is listed as DML. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect DELETE is listed as DML. (PDF pp. 26.) D correct ALTER is the DDL exception. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 118 · Q01378
records.text: Q01378 Question 118 FDB26 In the course's SQL command taxonomy, how is TRUNCATE classified? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DDL B DML C DCL D TCL DDL The course groups TRUNCATE with DDL commands. It empties a table through mechanisms that depend on the implementation, but that fact does not turn it into a privilege-management or transaction-boundary command. DML covers commands such as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; DCL covers GRANT and REVOKE; TCL covers COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. The requested classification is the course convention, not a claim that TRUNCATE has identical recovery behavior in every DBMS. A correct Correct: the course's textbook classification includes TRUNCATE under DDL. B incorrect Incorrect: DML includes row operations such as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; TRUNCATE is assigned to DDL in this taxonomy. C incorrect Incorrect: DCL manages privileges through commands such as GRANT and REVOKE. D incorrect Incorrect: TCL controls transaction boundaries or rollback points, unlike TRUNCATE.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 119 · Q01379
records.text: Q01379 Question 119 FDB33 A type of query that is placed within a WHERE or HAVING clause of another query is called Distinguish a stored query definition from stored data and trace subquery scope. A Master query B Sub query C Super query D Multi-query Sub query The optimization section identifies nested queries as separate query blocks, and the view example places a SELECT inside an outer WHERE. Subquery is the offered name matching this inner/nested query; WHERE or HAVING placement does not define every possible subquery location. A incorrect Master describes neither the inner query nor the module's nesting distinction. (PDF pp. 34, 58.) B correct Subquery corresponds to the nested inner SELECT demonstrated. (PDF pp. 34, 58.) C incorrect Super query does not name the inner block. (PDF pp. 34, 58.) D incorrect Multi-query does not identify the nesting relationship. (PDF pp. 34, 58.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 120 · Q01380
records.text: Q01380 Question 120 FDB31 FDB35 A data manipulation command the combines the records from one or more tables is called Compute matching pairs, then account for any preserved unmatched rows. A SELECT B PROJECT C JOIN D PRODUCT JOIN The DML list contains JOIN, and the query-plan example describes joining Staff and Branch into a joined relation. This directly matches combining records rather than selecting columns alone. A incorrect SELECT can retrieve data, but JOIN names the combining operation illustrated. (PDF pp. 26, 28.) B incorrect PROJECT selects columns rather than linking records by the illustrated condition. (PDF pp. 26, 28.) C correct JOIN is explicitly used to combine the example relations. (PDF pp. 26, 28.) D incorrect PRODUCT combines all pairs; it is the broader Cartesian operation rather than the illustrated join command. (PDF pp. 26, 28.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 121 · Q01382
records.text: Q01382 Question 121 FDB26 Data manipulation language (DML) includes statements that modify the _____ of a database. Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Structure B Data C User D Size Data Data-definition commands are distinct from data-manipulation commands such as INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE. Their category concerns the stored data, while SELECT is also included as a retrieval command that need not modify state. A incorrect Structure belongs to definition language. (PDF pp. 26.) B correct Data is the manipulated content. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect User administration is not the target category here. (PDF pp. 26.) D incorrect Size can change as a consequence, not the category manipulated. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 122 · Q01383
records.text: Q01383 Question 122 FDB34 Which listed term names the standard SQL expression form for converting a value to a requested data type, rather than vendor-specific conversion syntax? Check set membership, duplicates and compatible result types. A Cast B Drop type C Alter type D Convert A. Cast CAST is the standard expression form that requests conversion of a value to a target type. CONVERT can also perform conversions in supporting vendor dialects, but the question specifically excludes vendor-specific syntax. DROP TYPE and ALTER TYPE act on type definitions rather than converting one expression value. The target value must still be representable in the requested type. A correct CAST supplies the requested standard expression conversion. B incorrect DROP TYPE removes a type definition. C incorrect ALTER TYPE changes a type definition. D incorrect CONVERT is vendor-specific in the supplied course distinction.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 123 · Q01384
records.text: Q01384 Question 123 FDB34 FDB31 Which SQL keyword combines the rows returned by two compatible SELECT statements into one result set, removing duplicates by default? Check set membership, duplicates and compatible result types. A COMBINE B CONCAT C JOIN D UNION UNION UNION combines the rows of compatible query results and removes duplicates by default. It is written between the SELECT statements. JOIN instead combines input rows through matching or product behavior within a query, rather than taking the set union of completed results. CONCAT concerns concatenation of values, and COMBINE does not form the required SQL set-operation syntax. D is therefore the unique correct selection for this result-set operation. A incorrect Incorrect: COMBINE is not the UNION set-operation keyword required between these SELECT statements. B incorrect Incorrect: concatenating values does not perform the requested union of query-result rows. C incorrect Incorrect: JOIN forms combinations of input rows rather than this union of compatible SELECT results. D correct Correct: UNION combines compatible query results and removes duplicates by default.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 124 · Q01385
records.text: Q01385 Question 124 FDB34 What is xyz in the following SQL statement? SELECT xyz FROM table1 UNION xyz FROM table2; Check set membership, duplicates and compatible result types. A row name B column name C table name D database name xyz denotes a selected column/expression; the second SELECT is missing. The printed statement is malformed because the second branch says UNION xyz rather than UNION SELECT xyz. Nevertheless, the role of xyz in the first SELECT list is clear: it is a column or expression, not a row, table or database name. FDB34 explicitly identifies that role and the required repair, so the terminology question remains answerable. A incorrect SQL does not select a row by placing its row name in this SELECT-list position. B correct xyz occupies the selected-column position; the second branch needs its missing SELECT keyword. C incorrect The table sources are table1 and table2, which follow FROM rather than SELECT. D incorrect No database identifier occupies xyz's SELECT-list position in this statement.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 125 · Q01386
records.text: Q01386 Question 125 FDB34 In a dialect that accepts explicit UNION DISTINCT, which listed modifier requests duplicate elimination when used with UNION? Check set membership, duplicates and compatible result types. A ALL B NARROW C STRICT D DISTINCT DISTINCT UNION eliminates duplicate result rows by default. In the stated dialect, DISTINCT explicitly requests that same behavior, while ALL retains duplicates. NARROW and STRICT are not modifiers in the UNION [ALL | DISTINCT] form being tested. This classification does not imply that every DBMS accepts the explicit DISTINCT spelling: the question states that support, and bare UNION remains sufficient to request duplicate elimination. A incorrect Incorrect: ALL retains duplicates, the opposite of the requested behavior. B incorrect Incorrect: NARROW is not an ALL or DISTINCT modifier in the stated UNION form. C incorrect Incorrect: STRICT is not an ALL or DISTINCT modifier in the stated UNION form. D correct Correct: DISTINCT explicitly requests duplicate elimination in the stated dialect.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 126 · Q01387
records.text: Q01387 Question 126 FDB19 The database design prevents some data from being stored due to _______. Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A Deletion anomalies B Insertion anomalies C Update anomalies D Selection anomalies Insertion anomalies Insertion anomaly is explicitly the inability to insert a new record properly when the whole primary key is unknown. The other anomalies concern losing information on deletion or inconsistent/multiple updates. A incorrect Deletion anomaly loses existing related information. (PDF pp. 16.) B correct Insertion anomaly prevents a proper new insertion. (PDF pp. 16.) C incorrect Update anomaly concerns changing existing values. (PDF pp. 16.) D incorrect Selection anomaly is not among the module's stated three types. (PDF pp. 16.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 127 · Q01388
records.text: Q01388 Question 127 FDB03 FDB06 In the course terminology, which labels can name a drawing of relational tables and their primary-key/foreign-key references? Select all that apply. ER Diagram means a conceptual entity/relationship drawing; Relational Schema means a textual table definition here. Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A ER Diagram B Database Diagram C Schema Diagram D Relational Schema B. Database Diagram; C. Schema Diagram A schema diagram draws relational tables and their key references. Database diagram is also used for that depiction in the course terminology, so both labels qualify. The question explicitly distinguishes a conceptual ER drawing and a textual relational schema from the requested table-reference drawing. This makes the two accepted names compatible without treating every representation of a database as the same artifact. A incorrect A conceptual ER diagram represents entities and relationships rather than specifically depicting mapped table key references. B correct Database diagram can denote the table-and-key depiction also called a schema diagram. C correct A schema diagram explicitly draws tables and their primary/foreign-key references. D incorrect A relational schema defines structures and constraints but need not itself be a diagram.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 128 · Q01389
records.text: Q01389 Question 128 FDB20 FDB21 FDB17 R(A,B,C) has atomic attributes and exactly the dependencies implied by A→B and B→C. A is the sole candidate key; B is not a superkey and C is nonprime. Moving upward through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF, which listed normal form is the first that R fails? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A BCNF B 1NF C 2NF D 3NF D. 3NF The atomic relation satisfies 1NF. Its only candidate key is the single attribute A, so no nonprime dependency can involve a proper part of that key, and 2NF holds. However, B→C has a determinant that is not a superkey and a dependent that is nonprime. This violates the stated 3NF test, so 3NF is the listed form it fails. A incorrect BCNF also fails, but 3NF is the earlier failed level in the stated hierarchy. B incorrect Atomic values satisfy 1NF. C incorrect A single-attribute candidate key has no nonprime partial-key dependency. D correct B→C violates 3NF because B is not a superkey and C is nonprime.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 129 · Q01390
records.text: Q01390 Question 129 FDB21 Consider the relation Sale(Date, Customer, Product, Vendor, VendorCity, SalesRep){Date, Customer, Product} is the composite candidate key and the following functional dependencies are also given:Vendor => VendorCity, Product => VendorWhat is the highest normal form of the sale relation? Test determinants and prime attributes against the stated normal-form rules. A 0NF B 1NF C 2NF D 3NF 1NF Assuming atomic values as customary for a relation, Product is a proper subset of the stated composite key and determines non-prime Vendor. Vendor→VendorCity adds another non-key dependency. Product→Vendor alone violates 2NF, so the highest supported form is 1NF. No stated dependency makes these non-prime attributes alternative keys. A incorrect 0NF is not warranted when attributes are atomic. (PDF pp. 15, 17.) B correct 1NF is the highest form under the explicit atomicity assumption. (PDF pp. 15, 17.) C incorrect 2NF fails because Vendor depends on Product alone. (PDF pp. 15, 17.) D incorrect 3NF requires 2NF, which already fails. (PDF pp. 15, 17.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 130 · Q01391
records.text: Q01391 Question 130 FDB21 Third normal form is based on the concept of _________ Test determinants and prime attributes against the stated normal-form rules. A Closure Dependency B Transitive Dependency C Normal Dependency D Functional Dependency Transitive Dependency The defining extra condition of 3NF over 2NF is non-transitive dependence of non-prime attributes on keys. Functional dependency is the broader framework, but transitive dependency is the particular concept distinguishing this stage. A incorrect Closure dependency is not the stated criterion. (PDF pp. 18.) B correct Transitive dependency is the specific concept addressed. (PDF pp. 18.) C incorrect Normal dependency is not a defined dependency category. (PDF pp. 18.) D incorrect Functional dependency is broader and does not identify the distinctive 3NF condition. (PDF pp. 18.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 131 · Q01392
records.text: Q01392 Question 131 FDB27 Which of the following statements does not change the state of the database? Trace how SELECT forms its result columns and rows. A Where B Select C Insert D Drop Select The read-only transaction example uses SELECT to retrieve rows from two tables. SELECT is the complete retrieval statement among these choices; WHERE is only a clause and not a standalone SQL statement. The question is read as asking about valid statements. A incorrect WHERE alone is not a complete statement, so it cannot be the requested statement. (PDF pp. 52, 26.) B correct SELECT is demonstrated in a read-only transaction. (PDF pp. 52, 26.) C incorrect INSERT is a manipulation command, not the demonstrated read-only request. (PDF pp. 52, 26.) D incorrect DROP is a structural DDL command, not the demonstrated retrieval. (PDF pp. 52, 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 132 · Q01500
records.text: Q01500 Question 132 FDB20 FDB21 A relation is in 1NF and has no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key. What is the strongest normal form guaranteed by these facts alone? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First B BCNF C Third D Second D. Second The two stated conditions are exactly the requirements for 2NF: 1NF plus the absence of nonprime partial dependencies on candidate keys. First normal form is also true but is a weaker guarantee. Third normal form and BCNF need additional conditions on other functional dependencies. The relation might satisfy those higher forms, but the given facts alone establish only 2NF. A incorrect 1NF is given, but 2NF is the stronger guaranteed form. B incorrect BCNF additionally requires all nontrivial determinants to be superkeys. C incorrect 3NF needs further checks on determinants and prime dependents. D correct The conditions directly establish 2NF as the strongest guaranteed form.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 133 · Q01502
records.text: Q01502 Question 133 FDB07 The minimal set of super key is called Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A Foreign key B None of the choices is correct C Candidate key D Primary key Candidate key A candidate key is a minimal superkey. Minimal means no removable attribute while retaining uniqueness, not necessarily the fewest attributes among all keys. A incorrect Foreign key links relations, not the minimal-superkey definition. (PDF pp. 11.) B incorrect A matching definition is offered. (PDF pp. 11.) C correct Candidate key is the exact definition. (PDF pp. 11.) D incorrect Primary key is the selected candidate key rather than the category of every minimal superkey. (PDF pp. 11.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 134 · Q01581
records.text: Q01581 Question 134 FDB15 Assume every foreign-key column is NOT NULL and references a declared primary key. Which statement expresses referential integrity under these assumptions? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A Every primary-key value must match a primary-key value in an associated table B Every primary-key value must match a foreign-key value in an associated table C Every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value in an associated table D Every foreign-key value must match a foreign-key value in an associated table C. Every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value in an associated table A foreign key is a reference from a child row to an eligible key in the parent. Because the question makes every reference non-NULL and targets primary keys, each foreign-key value must match a primary-key value. A parent row need not have children, and primary keys do not themselves have to reference another table. Merely matching a foreign-key column is not sufficient. A incorrect A primary key can exist without referencing another table. B incorrect A parent can have no child references. C correct Every non-NULL child reference must match its targeted parent primary key. D incorrect The target must be an eligible referenced key, not an arbitrary foreign-key column.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 135 · Q01582
records.text: Q01582 Question 135 FDB26 Which of the following is generally used for performing tasks like creating the structure of the relations, deleting relation? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A DML(Data Manipulation Language) B Query C Relational Schema D DDL(Data Definition Language) DDL(Data Definition Language) Creating/deleting relation structure falls under DDL's structural command category. It is distinguished from data manipulation and from the schema description itself. A incorrect DML is the data-operation category. (PDF pp. 26.) B incorrect Query is not the schema-definition category. (PDF pp. 26.) C incorrect A relational schema is a description, not a command language. (PDF pp. 26.) D correct DDL is the named structural-language category. (PDF pp. 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 136 · Q01583
records.text: Q01583 Question 136 FDB26 Which of the following is used in the application programs to request data from the database management system? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Data Manipulation language B Data Definition Language C Data Control Language D All choices are correct Data Manipulation language DML is the offered language category that includes retrieval requests such as SELECT. DDL handles definition, while authorization is separate from retrieval commands. A correct DML includes retrieval. (PDF pp. 26, 24.) B incorrect DDL is definition rather than ordinary data requests. (PDF pp. 26, 24.) C incorrect Access-control language is not the category that retrieves the requested data. (PDF pp. 26, 24.) D incorrect DDL and control are not all retrieval categories. (PDF pp. 26, 24.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 137 · Q01331B
records.text: Q01331B Question 137 FDB02 Which single choice completely identifies the relational DBMS products in the list? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Oracle Database B Microsoft SQLServer C IBM Db2 D All of the mentioned D. All of the mentioned Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and IBM Db2 are all relational DBMS products named in the note. Replacing the vendor-only IBM label with IBM Db2 makes every product entry well-defined. The question asks for the complete set, so All of the mentioned is the best answer. Each individual product is genuinely relational but identifies only part of the full set. A incorrect Oracle Database is relational, but this alone is an incomplete set. B incorrect SQL Server is relational, but this alone is an incomplete set. C incorrect IBM Db2 is relational, but this alone is an incomplete set. D correct The aggregate choice includes all three relational products.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 138 · Q01388B
records.text: Q01388B Question 138 FDB06 In ER diagram Diamond/Ellipses represent Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Relationship sets/Attributes B Entity sets/Attributes C Attributes/Relationships sets D Relationship sets/Entity sets Diamonds represent relationship sets; ellipses represent attributes. FDB06 maps rectangles to entity types, diamonds to relationships and ellipses to attributes in Chen notation. The question asks for the diamond/ellipse pair in that order. A preserves that order and meaning; the other choices either substitute entity sets or reverse the symbol meanings. A diagram-specific legend would override the generic convention. A correct The two shapes map to relationships and attributes respectively in Chen notation. B incorrect Entity types use rectangles, so a diamond does not represent the first item listed. C incorrect This reverses the requested meanings: diamonds indicate relationships, while ellipses indicate attributes. D incorrect The first meaning fits, but ellipses represent attributes rather than entity sets.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 139 · Q01388C
