records.text: Q01388C Question 139 FDB20 A relation is in 2NF if: Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A All the values of non-key attributes are dependent fully on the candidate key. B Any non-key attribute that are dependent on only part of the candidate key should be moved to another relation where the partial key is the actual full key. C It must be already in the 1NF. D All of the above. All of the above. Second normal form requires 1NF and full dependence of each non-prime attribute on candidate keys; partial dependencies must be moved to another relation. A states the criterion, B the repair, and C the prerequisite; D collects all three. A alone is not a complete definition without C. A incorrect Full dependency is a required 2NF property. (PDF pp. 17.) B incorrect Moving a partially dependent attribute to the relation where its determinant is the whole key is the stated repair. (PDF pp. 17.) C incorrect 1NF is expressly required. (PDF pp. 17.) D correct All three agree with the module's definition and repair rule. (PDF pp. 17.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 140 · SM0017
records.text: SM0017 Question 140 FDB25 Which one of the following is NOT a single level ordered index? Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs. A Secondary index B Primary index C Clustering index D Multilevel index Multilevel index In this single-level ordered-index classification, the listed types are primary, clustering and secondary indexes. A multilevel index is the exception to that listed single-level classification. A incorrect Secondary is listed as single level. (PDF pp. 21.) B incorrect Primary is listed as single level. (PDF pp. 21.) C incorrect Clustering is listed as single level. (PDF pp. 21.) D correct Multilevel is outside the specified single-level group. (PDF pp. 21.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 141 · SM0023
records.text: SM0023 Question 141 FDB01 Among the following, which one best describes a Database Management System (DBMS)? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A It is responsible for creating and maintaining a database B It can help users to manage computer's activity C It can assist process images D It can assist you to process document It is responsible for creating and maintaining a database A DBMS is software facilitating definition, construction, manipulation and sharing of databases. This directly matches creating and maintaining a database. A correct Matches the module's DBMS definition. (PDF pp. 5.) B incorrect Managing general computer activity describes a broader different role. (PDF pp. 5.) C incorrect Image processing is not the database-management role. (PDF pp. 5.) D incorrect Document processing is not the database-management definition. (PDF pp. 5.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 142 · SM0034
records.text: SM0034 Question 142 FDB29 FDB16 FDB15 Given the schemas: BOOK (Book_id, Title, Publisher_name), BOOK_AUTHOR (Book_id, Author_name), PUBLISHER (Name, Address, Phone). Which one of the following SQL is correct to delete the publisher named 'XWZ' from the PUBLISHER table? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A DELETE FROM BOOK_AUTHOR WHERE Address = 'XWZ' B DELETE FROM PUBLISHER WHERE Name = 'XWZ' C DELETE FROM PUBLISHER WHERE Address = 'XWZ' D DELETE FROM BOOK WHERE Name = 'XWZ' DELETE FROM PUBLISHER WHERE Name = 'XWZ' The module illustrates DELETE FROM HumanResources.JobCandidate WHERE JobCandidateID = 13 (PDF p.77). Substitute the requested relation PUBLISHER and its identifying Name predicate: DELETE FROM PUBLISHER WHERE Name = 'XWZ'. The stem's schemas distinguish Name from Address and omit both from BOOK_AUTHOR. This identifies the requested statement; successful execution may additionally depend on existing referencing rows and the deletion policy (PDF pp.48–49). A incorrect BOOK_AUTHOR is the wrong target and has no Address column in the supplied schema (compare the target/predicate form on PDF p.77). B correct PUBLISHER is the target and Name is the requested name filter, matching the module's DELETE FROM ... WHERE example (PDF p.77). C incorrect Filtering Address does not select by publisher name, despite a valid target table (PDF p.77's predicate pattern). D incorrect BOOK is the wrong target and has no Name column in the supplied schema (PDF p.77's target/predicate pattern).

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 143 · SM0048
records.text: SM0048 Question 143 FDB04 What does program data independence in the database approach entail? Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A The application may be affected when data changes B Data and applications are defined separately C Programs can create redundant data independently D Both program and data are defined together Data and applications are defined separately Program/data insulation separates application definitions from data definitions, allowing schema changes without corresponding higher-level changes under the relevant independence conditions. A incorrect Says changes necessarily affect applications, contrary to insulation. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) B correct Separate definitions express program/data insulation. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) C incorrect Creating redundant data independently is not the defined independence. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) D incorrect Defining both together contradicts insulation. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 144 · SM0071
records.text: SM0071 Question 144 FDB14 Which statements are NOT correct descriptions of a fan trap or its general remedy in an ER diagram? Select all that apply. Treat B as a warning pattern, not a sufficient condition. Trace the actual relationship paths and check whether the requested association follows. A It occurs when there is no pathway between related entities B Highly likely when more than two one-to-many relationships fan out from an entity C When there is ambiguous pathway between some entity occurrences in related entity types D It can be resolved by readjusting the model so that no one-to-many relationships fan out from an entity A. It occurs when there is no pathway between related entities; D. It can be resolved by readjusting the model so that no one-to-many relationships fan out from an entity A fan trap concerns an ambiguous association inferred through branches from a common entity. A missing or broken path is instead a chasm-type issue. Also, legitimate one-to-many branches need not all be eliminated: the model should record the actual missing association. Multiple branches can warn of a fan trap, and ambiguity is its defining issue, so B and C are not false. A correct This is false about fan traps: a missing or broken path describes a chasm-type problem. B incorrect Several 1:N branches from a common entity can create the ambiguous association characteristic of fan traps. C incorrect Ambiguity about associations between entity occurrences is the defining fan-trap problem. D correct This is false as a general remedy: valid 1:N fans may remain after explicitly modeling the required association.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 145 · SM0086
records.text: SM0086 Question 145 FDB01 In which situation does using a DBMS become costly and not recommended? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A In embedded systems having too small storage space B In situation where more than one user should access the database C To deny access to unauthorized users D To control redundancy Severely storage-constrained embedded systems can make a DBMS too costly. FDB01 says storage, administration and complexity may outweigh DBMS benefits in a tiny fixed application, while also recognizing lightweight embedded DBMSs. A is therefore the listed situation where resource constraints can make a DBMS inappropriate. The other scenarios are central reasons for using a DBMS: sharing, authorization and redundancy control. Embedded use alone does not forbid a DBMS. A correct Severely limited storage can make DBMS overhead unjustified, though lightweight embedded DBMSs may still fit. B incorrect Controlled multiuser access is a benefit supplied by database management rather than a reason to avoid it. C incorrect Authorization helps deny unauthorized access and is a reason to use DBMS protection. D incorrect Controlling redundancy is a benefit of shared database management rather than a contraindication.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 146 · SM0208
records.text: SM0208 Question 146 FDB25 Indexes in database tables speed up the _______ operations. Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs. A Read operations B Delete operations C Update operations D Write operations Read operations Indexes are auxiliary access structures explicitly used to speed record retrieval for search conditions. This is a read-performance purpose; it does not claim that maintaining indexes makes every change operation faster. A correct Read retrieval is the stated purpose. (PDF pp. 21.) B incorrect Deletion may require maintenance; it is not the stated general benefit. (PDF pp. 21.) C incorrect Updating data is not the stated general purpose. (PDF pp. 21.) D incorrect Writing is not the stated retrieval purpose. (PDF pp. 21.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 147 · SM0226
records.text: SM0226 Question 147 FDB38 FDB25 An e-commerce database already has a suitable normalized schema. Customer-order queries repeatedly select a small fraction of rows by a search key. Which technique directly adds a maintained search path for those lookups? Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A Normalization B Denormalization C Partitioning D Indexing D. Indexing Indexing stores search keys and pointers that support selective retrieval without scanning every row. That directly meets the requested search-path improvement. Normalization addresses dependency anomalies, denormalization stores redundant or precomputed facts, and partitioning divides a dataset. Those techniques can be useful elsewhere, but the specified task is to add an access path to the existing normalized schema. A incorrect Normalization organizes dependencies; it does not add the requested search path. B incorrect Denormalization repeats or precomputes facts rather than directly adding an index path. C incorrect Partitioning divides the dataset rather than adding the requested maintained search-key structure. D correct Indexing directly supplies the selective lookup search path.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 148 · SM0251
records.text: SM0251 Question 148 FDB29 FDB26 Which SQL command is used to modify existing data in a table? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A ALTER B UPDATE C MODIFY D CHANGE UPDATE UPDATE changes existing row values using a target table, SET assignments and an optional WHERE predicate. ALTER instead changes an object's definition. The bare words MODIFY and CHANGE do not form the UPDATE statement required for changing stored row values in the stated SQL forms. They should not be treated as synonyms for the command merely because they describe the task in everyday language. B names the actual row-update command. A incorrect Incorrect: ALTER changes schema definitions rather than stored row values. B correct Correct: UPDATE changes existing rows using SET and, when needed, WHERE. C incorrect Incorrect: MODIFY is not the UPDATE command required for the stated row-value operation. D incorrect Incorrect: CHANGE is not the UPDATE command required for the stated row-value operation.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 149 · SM0252
records.text: SM0252 Question 149 FDB20 FDB21 Which is the first normal form in the usual normalization sequence that requires atomic values and no repeating groups? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A Second Normal Form (2NF) B Third Normal Form (3NF) C Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF) D First Normal Form (1NF) First Normal Form (1NF) First normal form is the first stage requiring atomic values and no repeating groups in cells. It does not by itself remove partial or transitive functional dependencies. Second normal form adds the full-dependency condition, third normal form adds the determinant/prime-attribute rule, and BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. These stronger forms inherit atomicity, but the question asks for the first stage defining it. A incorrect Incorrect: 2NF inherits atomicity and additionally excludes nonprime partial dependencies; it is a later stage. B incorrect Incorrect: 3NF inherits the earlier atomicity condition and adds a stronger dependency test. C incorrect Incorrect: BCNF adds the superkey-determinant rule and is not the first stage requiring atomicity. D correct Correct: 1NF is the first stage defining atomic values and no repeating groups.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 150 · SM0254
records.text: SM0254 Question 150 FDB19 FDB38 What is the purpose of normalization in database design? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A To increase data redundancy B To decrease data integrity C To eliminate data duplication D To simplify data retrieval To eliminate data duplication Normalization systematically decomposes relations to eliminate or reduce duplication and insertion/update/deletion anomalies. Eliminate is understood as the design goal, not a claim that every possible repeated value or necessary key reference disappears. A incorrect Increasing redundancy reverses the goal. (PDF pp. 16.) B incorrect Decreasing integrity reverses the anomaly-prevention goal. (PDF pp. 16.) C correct Eliminating duplicated data is directly stated. (PDF pp. 16.) D incorrect Simplifying retrieval is not the stated normalization purpose and does not follow automatically from decomposition. (PDF pp. 16.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 151 · SM0262
records.text: SM0262 Question 151 FDB02 Which of the following IS NOT a type of database management system (DBMS)? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A PostgreSQL B MongoDB C Java D MySQL Java is a programming language, not a DBMS. The question uses type loosely to list named systems. FDB02 identifies PostgreSQL and MySQL as relational DBMS products and MongoDB as a document DBMS. Java is explicitly a programming language. Its ability to connect to databases does not make it a database management system, so C alone fits the negative question. A incorrect PostgreSQL is a relational DBMS product, so it does not satisfy the negative question. B incorrect MongoDB is a document DBMS, even though it is not a relational system. C correct Java is a programming language rather than a database management system. D incorrect MySQL is a relational DBMS product and therefore is not the requested exception.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 152 · SM0273
records.text: SM0273 Question 152 FDB06 The E-R data model is based on a perception of the real world that consists of a set of basic objects called ______. Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Objects B Classes C Entities D Attributes Entities The ER model uses entities, attributes and relationships; the actual physical/conceptual objects are entities. Objects is a generic word, while entities is the model-specific category requested. A incorrect Objects is the generic description, not the requested ER term. (PDF pp. 9, 10.) B incorrect Classes are not the basic-object term in this ER definition. (PDF pp. 9, 10.) C correct Entities is the named category for those real-world objects. (PDF pp. 9, 10.) D incorrect Attributes are properties of entities rather than the objects themselves. (PDF pp. 9, 10.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 153 · SM0275
records.text: SM0275 Question 153 FDB07 What is the primary key in a relational database? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A A unique identifier for each row in a table B A foreign key from another table C A key used for encryption D An index on a non-unique column A unique identifier for each row in a table A primary key is the selected candidate key used to identify tuples uniquely; its values must be unique and non-null. The key may consist of more than one attribute. A correct Uniquely identifies each row, consistent with the key definition. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) B incorrect A foreign key serves a reference role and need not be this table's primary key. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) C incorrect Encryption keys have a different security role. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) D incorrect A non-unique index does not meet key uniqueness. (PDF pp. 11, 14.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 154 · SM0280
records.text: SM0280 Question 154 FDB01 What is the role of a database administrator (DBA)? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A Designing user interfaces for database applications B Developing front-end applications C Writing complex SQL queries D Managing and maintaining databases Managing and maintaining databases The DBA administers the database and DBMS, authorizes access, coordinates/monitors use and acquires resources. Those responsibilities fit management and maintenance. A incorrect User-interface design is not the defining DBA responsibility described. (PDF pp. 6.) B incorrect Front-end development is not the defining responsibility. (PDF pp. 6.) C incorrect Writing a difficult query may occur, but is not the administration role defined. (PDF pp. 6.) D correct Management and maintenance match the listed administration duties. (PDF pp. 6.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 155 · SM0304
records.text: SM0304 Question 155 FDB02 Which of the following IS NOT a type of database model? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Linear B Object-Oriented C Hierarchical D Relational Linear The model taxonomy names object-oriented, hierarchical/network, and relational concepts. Linear is not among the stated database-model categories; this is a taxonomy question within that stated list, not a universal claim about every possible model name. A correct Linear is outside the supplied taxonomy. (PDF pp. 7, 13.) B incorrect Object-Oriented is explicitly a conceptual-model example. (PDF pp. 7, 13.) C incorrect Hierarchical is named in the model discussion. (PDF pp. 7, 13.) D incorrect Relational is explicitly defined as a database model. (PDF pp. 7, 13.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 156 · SS133
records.text: SS133 Question 156 FDB20 FDB21 A relation has atomic values with no repeating groups, and no nonprime attribute partially depends on any candidate key. What is the strongest normal form guaranteed by these facts alone? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A 4NF B 2NF C 1NF D 3NF B. 2NF Atomic values without repeating groups establish 1NF. Adding the absence of nonprime partial dependencies establishes 2NF. Higher normal forms have additional requirements involving nonkey determinants or multivalued dependencies, and none of those requirements follows from the stated facts. Thus 2NF is the strongest guaranteed level, even though the relation could also happen to satisfy higher forms. A incorrect No restriction on nontrivial multivalued dependencies has been established. B correct 1NF plus the absence of nonprime partial dependencies guarantees 2NF. C incorrect 1NF holds, but 2NF is the stronger guarantee. D incorrect 3NF requires additional determinant/prime-attribute conditions.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 157 · SS142
records.text: SS142 Question 157 FDB01 FDB03 FDB04 Which one of the following is not among the characterizing features of database approach? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A Sharing of data B @-tTM Application-data dependency C j Oc. Self-describing D Data abstraction @-tTM Application-data dependency Database systems support sharing, self-description and abstraction/insulation. Application-data dependency is the opposite of insulation and independence. A incorrect Sharing is expressly a characteristic. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) B correct Application-data dependency contradicts the stated insulation characteristic. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) C incorrect Self-description is expressly a characteristic. (PDF pp. 5, 6.) D incorrect Abstraction is expressly a characteristic. (PDF pp. 5, 6.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 158 · SS146
records.text: SS146 Question 158 FDB01 FDB06 FDB07 "Database is a logically coherent collection of data with some inherent meaning" describes that Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A the entity should be physical object B number of attributes should be limited C there should be one primary key attribute D all attributes of the entity should be related all attributes of the entity should be related A database is a collection of related data with implicit meaning. D is the closest reading of coherence in the question: attributes should describe related subject matter, not arbitrary unrelated data. It does not mean every attribute functionally determines every other. A incorrect Entities may have conceptual existence too. (PDF pp. 5, 10, 11.) B incorrect No bound on the number of attributes is implied. (PDF pp. 5, 10, 11.) C incorrect A primary key may have multiple attributes; coherence does not require a single attribute. (PDF pp. 5, 10, 11.) D correct Related attributes are the offered interpretation consistent with meaningful related data. (PDF pp. 5, 10, 11.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 159 · SS157
records.text: SS157 Question 159 FDB29 FDB07 FDB15 For HOTEL(Hotel_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Hotel_Name STRING, Sub_city STRING), which statement correctly inserts one row? Assume Hotel_id = 1 is unused and no other constraints prevent the insert. Track which rows each data-changing command affects. A INSERT INTO HOTEL(Hotel_id,Hotel_Name,Sub_city) Values('Hilton', Yeka') B INSERT INTO HOTEL(Hotel_id,Hotel_Name,Sub_city) Values (1,'Hilton','Yeka') C INSERT INTO HOTEL(1,'Hilton','Yeka') D INSERT Values INTO HOTEL(Hotel_id,Hotel_Name,Sub_city) Values(1,'Hilton','Yeka') INSERT INTO HOTEL(Hotel_id,Hotel_Name,Sub_city) Values (1,'Hilton','Yeka') An INSERT must match each named column with a compatible value and follow INSERT INTO ... VALUES syntax. B supplies the integer identifier and the two text values in the named order; the stated unused-key assumption removes a possible primary-key conflict. A supplies too few values and has damaged string quoting. C puts values where column names belong and omits VALUES, while D places an extra Values token before INTO. These are incorrect statements, not unresolved alternatives. A incorrect Incorrect: three named columns require three compatible values; this text supplies only two and also has malformed quoting. B correct Correct: it supplies an unused integer key and two strings in the named column order with the required INSERT syntax. C incorrect Incorrect: literal values occupy the column-list position and the VALUES clause is absent. D incorrect Incorrect: INSERT Values INTO has an extra token before INTO and breaks the required INSERT structure.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 160 · SS172
records.text: SS172 Question 160 FDB39 DORM(DormID, FloorNumber) has primary key DormID. STUDENT(IdNo, Name, Department, DormID) has primary key IdNo. Which table-constraint fragment correctly declares STUDENT.DormID as a reference to DORM? Capacity six is enforced separately; the surrounding CREATE TABLE syntax is supplied. Trace keys and cardinalities through the integrated schema. A FOREIGN KEY (DormID) REFERENCED BY DORM(DormID) B DORM table is a referencing relation C FOREIGN KEY (DormID) REFERENCES DORM(DormID) D STUDENT table is a referenced relation C. FOREIGN KEY (DormID) REFERENCES DORM(DormID) The student row stores the dorm identifier, making STUDENT the referencing child and DORM the referenced parent. The required clause names the child column and uses REFERENCES to identify Dorm's key. C has this syntax after the naming repair. The foreign key validates a dorm reference; it does not by itself enforce the six-student capacity rule, which the question handles separately. A incorrect REFERENCED BY is not the required child-to-parent clause. B incorrect DORM is the referenced parent, not the referencing child. C correct REFERENCES DORM(DormID) correctly targets the parent key. D incorrect STUDENT is the referencing child.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 161 · SS189
records.text: SS189 Question 161 FDB05 Which one of the following is an appropriate sequence of database design processes? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Logical database design, Enterprise data modeling, Physical database design, Database implementation B Enterprise data modeling, Logical database design, Database implementation, Physical database design C Logical database design, Enterprise data modeling, Physical database design, Database implementation D Enterprise data modeling, Logical database design, Physical database design, Database implementation Enterprise modeling → logical design → physical design → implementation. FDB05 starts with business requirements and conceptual ER modeling, then maps to relations and constraints in logical design, chooses storage and indexes in physical design, and creates/loads actual objects in implementation. D preserves that order. The other choices either begin logical design before enterprise modeling or place implementation before the storage decisions it must implement. A incorrect Logical design should use the conceptual enterprise model rather than precede its creation. B incorrect Physical storage decisions precede implementation, not follow it in the stated design sequence. C incorrect This duplicates A and again places logical design before enterprise modeling. D correct It follows conceptual enterprise modeling, relational mapping, storage design and actual implementation.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 162 · AM0132
records.text: AM0132 Question 162 FDB07 FDB16 Which of the following is a primary key in a relational database? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A A unique identifier for a row in a table B A foreign key from another table C A non-unique attribute in a table D A combination of attributes in a table A unique identifier for a row in a table A primary key is selected from candidate keys to uniquely identify a row and must be unique/non-null. Multiple attributes alone do not make a set a primary key unless those requirements and selection hold. A correct Gives the essential identifying property. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) B incorrect A foreign key is a reference and is not necessarily the selected primary identifier. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) C incorrect Non-unique attributes cannot uniquely identify rows. (PDF pp. 11, 14.) D incorrect A combination can be a composite primary key, but an arbitrary combination is not sufficient. (PDF pp. 11, 14.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 163 · AM0133
records.text: AM0133 Question 163 FDB15 FDB07 FDB38 What is the purpose of foreign keys in a relational database? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A To establish relationships between tables B To store encrypted data C To enforce data types in columns D To improve query performance To establish relationships between tables Foreign keys link child records to matching parent keys and preserve consistency between related tables. A correct Establishes the described reference relationship. (PDF pp. 48, 14.) B incorrect Encryption is a security mechanism, not the FK purpose. (PDF pp. 48, 14.) C incorrect Data types are controlled by domain constraints. (PDF pp. 48, 14.) D incorrect Performance improvement is not the stated FK purpose. (PDF pp. 48, 14.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 164 · AM0134
records.text: AM0134 Question 164 FDB20 FDB21 In the usual normalization sequence, which is the first normal form requiring every nonprime attribute to depend fully on every candidate key, rather than on a proper subset? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First normal form (1NF) B Second normal form (2NF) C Third normal form (3NF) D Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) Second normal form (2NF) Second normal form is the first stage requiring atomic relations to have no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key. First normal form addresses atomic values, so it does not impose that dependency rule. Third normal form and BCNF are stronger stages that inherit the absence of partial dependencies, but they are not the first stage introducing it. BCNF specifically requires every nontrivial functional-dependency determinant to be a superkey. A incorrect Incorrect: 1NF requires atomic values but does not exclude partial dependencies. B correct Correct: 2NF is the first stage excluding nonprime partial dependencies on candidate keys. C incorrect Incorrect: 3NF inherits 2NF and imposes its additional determinant/prime-attribute condition; it is not the first stage. D incorrect Incorrect: BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey; it is stronger than the first stage imposing the partial-dependency rule.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 165 · AM0135
records.text: AM0135 Question 165 FDB07 What defines a composite key in database design? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A A key made up of two or more attributes B A foreign key that references multiple tables C A unique identifier for a column in a table D A key used for data encryption A. A key made up of two or more attributes Composite describes the number of attributes in a key: it contains two or more attributes. It does not mean the key has necessarily been selected as the primary key, nor does it refer to the number of tables reached by a reference. A column name alone is not a multicolumn identification key. Encryption uses a different meaning of key. A correct Two or more key attributes are the defining feature. B incorrect The number of referenced tables does not define composition. C incorrect A column identifier does not describe a multicolumn key. D incorrect An encryption key is a different concept.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 166 · AM0136
records.text: AM0136 Question 166 FDB25 FDB23 FDB15 FDB38 What is the purpose of an index in a database? Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs. A To store large binary objects B To enforce referential integrity C To improve data retrieval performance D To encrypt sensitive data To improve data retrieval performance Indexes are auxiliary structures used to speed retrieval for search conditions, rather than stored binary values or security mechanisms. A incorrect BLOB is the named large-binary-object type. (PDF pp. 21, 19.) B incorrect Foreign keys handle referential links; indexes are defined for retrieval. (PDF pp. 21, 19.) C correct Exactly the stated retrieval-performance purpose. (PDF pp. 21, 19.) D incorrect Encryption is a separate security mechanism. (PDF pp. 21, 19.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 167 · AM0137
records.text: AM0137 Question 167 FDB03 What is a data dictionary in database design? Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A A database table that stores user information B A collection of tables in a database C A file system used to store database files D A repository of metadata about the database structure A repository of database metadata. A data dictionary describes the database rather than serving as ordinary application data storage. FDB03 says it records definitions, types, constraints and often privileges and optimizer statistics. User information may appear in an application table, but that is not the dictionary definition. Nor is a dictionary simply all tables or the physical file system. A incorrect Ordinary user records are application data, not the defining purpose of a metadata repository. B incorrect A collection of tables is not specifically the repository describing those tables and constraints. C incorrect The physical file system stores files; a dictionary records descriptive database metadata. D correct The dictionary is the repository describing database structure, data types and constraints.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 168 · AM0138
records.text: AM0138 Question 168 FDB16 FDB26 Which of the following is an example of a database constraint? Read each SQL constraint's scope and enforcement rule. A UNIQUE B SELECT C INSERT D DELETE UNIQUE Uniqueness constrains distinct tuple identifiers, whereas SELECT, INSERT and DELETE are language operations in the DML list. UNIQUE is the offered constraint name matching that property. A correct Uniqueness is explicitly an integrity condition. (PDF pp. 14, 26.) B incorrect SELECT is a retrieval command. (PDF pp. 14, 26.) C incorrect INSERT is a manipulation command. (PDF pp. 14, 26.) D incorrect DELETE is a manipulation command. (PDF pp. 14, 26.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 169 · AM0139
records.text: AM0139 Question 169 FDB15 FDB38 FDB25 What is the purpose of referential integrity in a database? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A To prevent unauthorized access to data B To ensure data consistency and integrity across related tables C To improve query performance D To encrypt sensitive data To ensure data consistency and integrity across related tables Referential integrity maintains consistency between related tuples by requiring non-null child references to resolve to existing parent keys. It controls valid relationships rather than authorization, performance, or encoding. A incorrect Unauthorized access is a security issue. (PDF pp. 14, 48.) B correct Matches the module's consistency-between-relations definition. (PDF pp. 14, 48.) C incorrect Query performance is not the referential validity rule. (PDF pp. 14, 48.) D incorrect Encryption is a separate security mechanism. (PDF pp. 14, 48.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 170 · AM0140
records.text: AM0140 Question 170 FDB38 What is denormalization in database design? Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A The process of breaking down a complex table into smaller tables B The process of adding redundancy to improve data retrieval performance C The process of eliminating duplicate values from a table D The process of converting data into a different format for storage Deliberately adding redundancy to improve selected retrieval workloads. FDB38 defines denormalization as deliberately repeating or precomputing facts to reduce selected read costs, with extra maintenance work. It is a workload-driven trade-off rather than elimination of all duplication. Breaking tables apart typically describes normalization; changing storage format is a different concern. Thus B captures both the mechanism and its intended retrieval benefit. A incorrect Splitting tables according to dependencies is normalization, rather than the redundancy introduced by denormalization. B correct Denormalization deliberately repeats or precomputes information to improve selected retrieval workloads. C incorrect Eliminating duplication describes a different direction from deliberately introducing useful redundant facts. D incorrect Changing storage format does not define the dependency and redundancy trade-off of denormalization.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 171 · AM0141
records.text: AM0141 Question 171 FDB33 What is the purpose of a view in a database? Distinguish a stored query definition from stored data and trace subquery scope. A To define the structure of a table B To store complex queries for reuse C To encrypt sensitive data D To enforce data types in columns Store a query definition for reuse as a virtual table. FDB33 says CREATE VIEW stores a query definition and presents a virtual table. B describes reusing that query, although a view need not be complex. Ordinary views do not inherently store result rows. Table definitions and column types belong to schema DDL, and views do not encrypt sensitive content merely by hiding columns or rows. A incorrect A view defines a virtual query result rather than the base table's storage structure. B correct A view saves a query definition that can be reused as a virtual table. C incorrect Restricting exposed data through a view does not encrypt that data. D incorrect Column data types are enforced by schema definitions and constraints rather than the view's primary purpose.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 172 · AM0142
records.text: AM0142 Question 172 FDB02 Which database model represents data as a collection of objects? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Hierarchical model B Relational model C Object-oriented model D Network model Object-oriented model. FDB02 says object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior. That matches a collection of objects directly. Hierarchical models use a parent-child tree, relational models use tables, and classic network models link records through owner/member pointers. Those representations should not be conflated merely because programming languages can wrap their data in objects. A incorrect The hierarchical model organizes records in a parent-child tree rather than primarily as objects. B incorrect The relational model represents data in tables with tuples and attributes. C correct The object model represents objects with identity, state and behavior. D incorrect The network model represents linked records through owner/member connections rather than object behavior.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 173 · AM0143
records.text: AM0143 Question 173 FDB19 What is the purpose of data normalization in database design? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A To improve data storage efficiency B To simplify the database structure C To eliminate data redundancy D To optimize query performance To eliminate data redundancy Normalization organizes/decomposes tables to avoid redundancy and anomalies. Storage may benefit, but the explicit defining purpose among these choices is reducing/eliminating repeated data. A incorrect Storage efficiency can be a consequence, but the cited definition does not guarantee a storage result. (PDF pp. 16.) B incorrect Decomposition does not necessarily simplify the whole schema. (PDF pp. 16.) C correct Eliminating redundancy is explicitly stated. (PDF pp. 16.) D incorrect Query speed is not the stated normalization goal. (PDF pp. 16.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 174 · AM0143_2
records.text: AM0143_2 Question 174 FDB20 FDB21 In the customary single-key teaching case, which is the first normalization stage summarized as dependence on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First normal form (1NF) B Second normal form (2NF) C Third normal form (3NF) D Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) Third normal form (3NF) In the stated single-key teaching case, 2NF excludes partial dependencies but can still allow a nonprime fact to depend on the key through a nonkey determinant. The next defining stage is 3NF, summarized by the whole-key-and-nothing-but-the-key mnemonic. BCNF strengthens the determinant rule, and 4NF addresses multivalued dependencies. Stronger forms inherit earlier conditions, so the explicit first-stage scope makes 3NF the unique selection rather than treating inherited properties as rival answers. A incorrect Incorrect: 1NF concerns atomic values and does not eliminate the specified transitive dependencies. B incorrect Incorrect: 2NF excludes partial dependencies but can retain a nonprime transitive dependency through a nonkey determinant. C correct Correct: 3NF is the first stage imposing the specified nonprime transitive-dependency restriction in this teaching case. D incorrect Incorrect: BCNF strengthens 3NF by requiring every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey; it is not the first stage described.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 175 · AM0144
records.text: AM0144 Question 175 FDB02 Which database model represents data as a collection of records linked through pointers? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Hierarchical model B Relational model C Object-oriented model D Network model Network model. FDB02 specifically describes the classic network model as records connected by pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents. That is the representation in the stem. Hierarchical data is restricted to a parent-child tree; relational data uses tables; object-oriented data emphasizes identity, state and behavior. Pointer-linked records therefore identify the network model in this comparison. A incorrect A hierarchical model restricts record organization to a parent-child tree rather than general network links. B incorrect A relational model uses tables and logical keys rather than the classic pointer-based network representation. C incorrect Object modeling is defined by identity, state and behavior, not this classic linked-record formulation. D correct Classic network databases connect records through pointer-based owner/member links.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 176 · AM0145
records.text: AM0145 Question 176 FDB25 FDB38 FDB15 What is the purpose of database indexing? Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs. A To encrypt sensitive data B To enforce data integrity constraints C To improve data retrieval performance D To ensure data consistency To improve data retrieval performance Indexes provide additional access paths and explicitly speed retrieval in response to search conditions; the purpose is performance of reads. A incorrect Encoding data is not the defined indexing purpose. (PDF pp. 21.) B incorrect The cited purpose is access speed, not integrity enforcement. (PDF pp. 21.) C correct Directly matches the retrieval definition. (PDF pp. 21.) D incorrect Consistency is a constraint/transaction concern rather than the indexing purpose defined. (PDF pp. 21.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 177 · AM0146
records.text: AM0146 Question 177 FDB02 FDB03 Which database model represents data as a collection of tables with rows and columns? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Hierarchical model B Relational model C Object-oriented model D Network model Relational model The relational model represents data using relations, conventionally shown as tables of tuples and attributes. The other choices have different defining structures: a hierarchical model uses a parent–child tree, a classic network model uses pointer-based owner/member links, and an object model uses objects with identity, state and behavior. Products may combine features, but the question asks for the model defined by rows and columns, which is relational. A incorrect Incorrect: the hierarchical model organizes records in a parent–child tree. B correct Correct: the relational model uses relations represented as tables of rows and columns. C incorrect Incorrect: the object model represents objects with identity, state and behavior. D incorrect Incorrect: the classic network model uses pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 178 · AM0147
records.text: AM0147 Question 178 FDB03 What is the purpose of a database schema? Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A To enforce data types in columns B To store database files C To define the structure and organization of a database D To ensure data integrity To define the structure and organization of a database A schema is the database description specified during design. It expresses structure, types, relationships and constraints; enforcing a particular constraint is narrower than the description's overall purpose. A incorrect Types are included, but enforcement alone is narrower than the schema description. (PDF pp. 7, 7.) B incorrect Files hold data physically; the schema describes the database. (PDF pp. 7, 7.) C correct Structure and organization match the schema definition. (PDF pp. 7, 7.) D incorrect Integrity conditions can be specified in a schema, but integrity alone is not its overall descriptive purpose. (PDF pp. 7, 7.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 179 · AM0148
records.text: AM0148 Question 179 FDB01 What is the role of a database administrator (DBA) in database management? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A To design and implement the database schema B To write complex SQL queries C To manage and maintain the database system D To develop database applications To manage and maintain the database system The DBA administers database and DBMS resources, authorizes access and coordinates/monitors use. Management and maintenance summarize those system responsibilities. A incorrect Schema design may be a duty in practice but is not the defining administrator role stated. (PDF pp. 6.) B incorrect Complex query writing is not the defining administrative responsibility. (PDF pp. 6.) C correct Matches resource administration and monitoring. (PDF pp. 6.) D incorrect Developing applications is a different role from the stated administration duties. (PDF pp. 6.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 180 · AM0149
records.text: AM0149 Question 180 FDB02 Which database model represents data as a hierarchical structure with parent-child relationships? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Hierarchical model B Relational model C Object-oriented model D Network model Hierarchical model. The defining phrase is a hierarchical parent-child structure. FDB02 assigns that tree organization to the hierarchical model. The relational model uses tables; the object model represents identity, state and behavior; the network model permits more general links including multiple parents. A parent-child tree therefore selects A directly. A correct The hierarchical model organizes records into a parent-child tree. B incorrect The relational model represents data as tables rather than a prescribed parent-child tree. C incorrect The object model represents object identity, state and behavior rather than requiring a tree. D incorrect The network model permits more general connections and multiple parents rather than the restricted tree structure.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 181 · AM0150
records.text: AM0150 Question 181 FDB05 What is the first step in the database design process? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Defining relationships between tables B Determining the database schema C Analyzing the information requirements D Creating database queries Analyzing the information requirements The initial design step is to understand the organization's information needs, required transactions, reports and constraints. Those requirements guide conceptual modeling, which is then mapped into a logical schema. Defining table relationships and determining the schema therefore depend on the earlier analysis. Queries express required operations against a model rather than replacing the initial work of identifying what information and behavior are needed. C is the first step in that sequence. A incorrect Incorrect: table relationships are designed to satisfy requirements already identified. B incorrect Incorrect: schema choices follow the analysis of required information and operations. C correct Correct: analyze information requirements before choosing the model and schema. D incorrect Incorrect: query construction depends on understanding the required information and intended database structure.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 182 · AM0151
records.text: AM0151 Question 182 FDB09 Read pairs left→right. Student↔Course and Product↔Supplier permit many occurrences in both directions. Each employee belongs to one department with many employees. Each order belongs to one customer, who may place many orders. Which pair is one-to-many? Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints. A Student and Course B Employee and Department C Customer and Order D Product and Supplier C. Customer and Order Customer→Order is one-to-many because one customer can place several orders and each order belongs to one customer. Employee→Department runs in the opposite direction: many employees share one department, making it many-to-one. The student/course and product/supplier pairs explicitly permit many partners in both directions and are many-to-many. Cardinality follows these rules and the direction of the pair. A incorrect Student→Course is M:N under the stated enrollment rule. B incorrect Employee→Department is N:1. C correct Customer→Order is 1:N under the ownership rule. D incorrect Product→Supplier is M:N under the stated supply rule.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 183 · AM0153
records.text: AM0153 Question 183 FDB25 Which of the following is a benefit of using database indexes? Compare index organization with its access benefits and maintenance costs. A Increased data redundancy B Decreased data integrity C Improved data retrieval performance D Simplified data modeling Improved data retrieval performance The auxiliary index provides alternative access paths to speed retrieval under search conditions. This is the directly supported benefit. A incorrect Redundancy is not the benefit identified by the index definition. (PDF pp. 21.) B incorrect Reduced integrity is not a stated benefit. (PDF pp. 21.) C correct Retrieval improvement is explicitly stated. (PDF pp. 21.) D incorrect Simplification of the logical model is not the index's stated function. (PDF pp. 21.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 184 · AM0155
records.text: AM0155 Question 184 FDB07 Employee has required, unique SSN and Employee ID values. Names and salaries may repeat. Which listed individual attributes are candidate keys? Select all that apply. Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A Social Security Number (SSN) B Employee Name C Employee ID D Employee Salary A. Social Security Number (SSN); C. Employee ID A candidate key is a minimal attribute set guaranteed to identify a tuple. Each required unique single-attribute identifier is already minimal, so SSN and Employee ID both qualify. Names and salaries may repeat and therefore cannot guarantee identification. The question asks for candidate keys rather than the one candidate later selected as the primary key, allowing both identifiers. A correct Required unique SSN identifies each employee and is minimal. B incorrect Repeated names are permitted, so Name is not a candidate key. C correct Required unique Employee ID independently identifies each employee. D incorrect Repeated salaries are permitted, so Salary is not a candidate key.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 185 · AM0156
records.text: AM0156 Question 185 FDB15 FDB07 What is the purpose of a foreign key in database design? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A To enforce data types in columns B To define primary key constraints C To establish relationships between tables D To optimize query performance To establish relationships between tables A foreign key links a child occurrence to the matching parent candidate/primary key. Its defining purpose is the intertable relationship. A incorrect Domain constraints specify legal types. (PDF pp. 48.) B incorrect The parent key is an identifying constraint, while the child FK expresses the reference. (PDF pp. 48.) C correct Matches the stated linking purpose. (PDF pp. 48.) D incorrect Performance is not the defining reference function. (PDF pp. 48.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 186 · AM0157
records.text: AM0157 Question 186 FDB04 FDB05 FDB19 FDB25 Which of the following database design principles promotes data independence? Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling B Normalization C Database indexing D Data abstraction Data abstraction Abstraction hides irrelevant details and helps achieve data independence. Three-schema separation then permits changes at one level without forcing higher-level schema changes. A incorrect ER modeling describes conceptual structure but is not the explicit independence principle here. (PDF pp. 6, 8.) B incorrect Normalization addresses redundancy/anomalies. (PDF pp. 6, 8.) C incorrect Indexes address retrieval paths and performance. (PDF pp. 6, 8.) D correct Abstraction is explicitly connected to independence. (PDF pp. 6, 8.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 187 · AM0158
records.text: AM0158 Question 187 FDB12 FDB11 Which type of database relationship is represented by a join table? Identify relationship degree and cardinality before choosing a relational mapping. A One-to-one relationship B One-to-many relationship C Many-to-many relationship D Hierarchical relationship Many-to-many relationship. A join table stores pairs of references to the two participating entity tables, optionally with relationship attributes. FDB12 uses Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) for the many-to-many Student–Course relationship. One-to-one and one-to-many relationships normally use a foreign key in an entity table instead. A hierarchy is a structural pattern, not the relationship cardinality represented by this usual association mapping. A incorrect A 1:1 relationship normally uses a UNIQUE foreign key rather than requiring a join table. B incorrect A 1:N relationship normally stores the one-side key in the many-side entity table. C correct A join or association table stores the pairs making up a many-to-many relationship. D incorrect Hierarchical organization is not the standard cardinality category represented by this association-table mapping.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 188 · AM0159
records.text: AM0159 Question 188 FDB17 Employee ID uniquely identifies an employee and their name, salary and department. Names may repeat; the same salary may occur in different departments, and a department may contain different salaries. Which listed functional dependency is guaranteed? Compute closures using the declared dependencies and test minimality. A Employee ID -> Employee Name B Employee Name -> Employee ID C Employee Salary -> Employee Department D Employee Department -> Employee Salary A. Employee ID -> Employee Name A functional dependency is guaranteed by business rules for every legal state. Unique Employee ID determines all employee attributes, including Name, so A follows. Repeated names can correspond to different IDs, equal salaries can occur in different departments, and one department may contain different salaries. Those permissions prevent the other proposed directions from being guaranteed dependencies. A correct The unique employee identifier determines the employee's name. B incorrect Repeated names can belong to different IDs. C incorrect The same salary may occur in different departments. D incorrect One department may contain employees with different salaries.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 189 · AM0160
records.text: AM0160 Question 189 FDB03 What is the purpose of a data dictionary in database design? Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A To store user credentials B To manage database backups C To define the structure and attributes of data elements D To enforce referential integrity constraints To describe the structure and attributes of data elements. The dictionary contains metadata explaining table definitions, attribute types and constraints. FDB03 therefore supports C as its purpose. It may record privileges, but storing user credentials is not its defining function. Backup management is an administrative operation, and enforcing a reference requires DBMS constraint machinery rather than merely the repository that describes the constraint. A incorrect Credential storage is not the defining purpose of the database structure metadata repository. B incorrect Backup management is an administrative activity rather than the dictionary's structural-description purpose. C correct The dictionary records definitions, attributes, data types and constraints describing database elements. D incorrect It describes constraints; the DBMS enforcement machinery actually checks referential integrity during operations.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 190 · AM0161
records.text: AM0161 Question 190 FDB38 FDB01 FDB25 Compared with scanning all pages of a large heap file, which advantage can an RDBMS with a suitable index provide for a query selecting a small fraction of rows? Assume index lookup costs less than the scan. Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A Easy integration with external systems B Lower storage requirements C No need for data normalization D Faster data retrieval D. Faster data retrieval The suitable index provides a search path for the selective query, reducing the work compared with scanning the large heap under the stated cost assumption. This supports faster retrieval for this workload. It does not remove normalization concerns, guarantee smaller storage or establish external-system compatibility. Index space and maintenance costs remain separate trade-offs from the query's retrieval advantage. A incorrect External integration is outside the stated lookup comparison. B incorrect Indexes consume additional storage rather than guaranteeing a reduction. C incorrect An index does not remove the need for dependency-aware design. D correct The stated cheaper indexed lookup supports faster retrieval for this query.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 191 · AM0163
records.text: AM0163 Question 191 FDB07 OrderLine has one row per line number within an order. OrderID and LineNo together uniquely identify a row; neither alone does. Which listed attribute set is a composite key? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A Employee ID B Product SKU C Customer Name D (OrderID, LineNo) D. (OrderID, LineNo) A composite key contains more than one attribute. OrderID identifies an order and LineNo identifies a line within it; the stated rules make their pair unique while neither component alone is sufficient. That establishes a minimal composite key. The other options each name only one attribute and therefore do not illustrate a composite key, regardless of any separate uniqueness policy. A incorrect Employee ID is a single attribute. B incorrect Product SKU is a single attribute. C incorrect Customer Name is a single listed attribute. D correct The pair is unique and requires both stated attributes.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 192 · AM0164
records.text: AM0164 Question 192 FDB15 FDB19 FDB25 What is the purpose of data validation in database design? Match the validity requirement to the appropriate constraint definition. A To enforce referential integrity constraints B To improve query performance C To eliminate data redundancy D To ensure data integrity and quality To ensure data integrity and quality Validation checks that input values meet legal domains/criteria, protecting integrity and consistency. D is the broad purpose; referential validation is one narrower kind rather than the whole definition. A incorrect Referential checks are one specific constraint, not the overall purpose of validation. (PDF pp. 47, 48, 49.) B incorrect Performance is not the legal-input goal. (PDF pp. 47, 48, 49.) C incorrect Redundancy reduction belongs to normalization. (PDF pp. 47, 48, 49.) D correct Integrity and input quality match domain validation and CHECK criteria. (PDF pp. 47, 48, 49.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 193 · AM0165
records.text: AM0165 Question 193 FDB21 FDB20 Which normal forms have defining restrictions on functional dependencies? Select all that apply. Treat 1NF as the atomic-value/no-repeating-groups requirement. Test determinants and prime attributes against the stated normal-form rules. A First Normal Form (1NF) B Second Normal Form (2NF) C Third Normal Form (3NF) D Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) B. Second Normal Form (2NF); C. Third Normal Form (3NF); D. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) Second normal form excludes nonprime partial functional dependencies on candidate keys. Third normal form checks each nontrivial dependency using the determinant's superkey status or the dependent's prime status. BCNF strengthens that test by requiring a superkey determinant. These three therefore use functional-dependency restrictions. First normal form instead establishes the atomic-value foundation and absence of repeating groups. A incorrect 1NF addresses atomic values and repeating groups rather than the stated dependency-based tests. B correct 2NF is defined through absence of nonprime partial functional dependencies on candidate keys. C correct 3NF tests nontrivial FDs using determinant superkeys and prime dependent attributes. D correct BCNF requires every nontrivial FD determinant to be a superkey.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 194 · AM0166
records.text: AM0166 Question 194 FDB05 FDB02 Which are direct representational purposes of conceptual/logical data modeling, rather than DBMS enforcement or physical query tuning? Select all that apply. Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A To enforce data constraints B To optimize query performance C To define the structure and organization of a database D To represent real-world entities and their relationships C. To define the structure and organization of a database; D. To represent real-world entities and their relationships Conceptual modeling represents domain entities and their relationships, while logical modeling defines database structures, keys and constraints. Both are direct representational purposes, so C and D qualify. Modeling can describe constraints, but the DBMS and application implementation enforce them during operations. Query performance can inform physical design, yet it is not the direct representational task specified in this question. A incorrect A model describes constraints, while implementation and DBMS machinery enforce them on actual operations. B incorrect Query performance can inform physical design, but it is not the general representational purpose asked here. C correct Modeling specifies the database's structure and organization. D correct Conceptual modeling represents real-world entities and their relationships.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 195 · AM0167
records.text: AM0167 Question 195 FDB38 FDB05 FDB19 Which option states a measurable nonfunctional quality requirement for a database system? Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A The database service must achieve at least 99.9% uptime. B User authentication C Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram D Data normalization A. The database service must achieve at least 99.9% uptime. A nonfunctional requirement states a quality target such as availability or response time. The uptime threshold specifies a measurable availability requirement and fits that category. User authentication names system behavior, while an ER diagram is a modeling artifact and normalization is a design technique. These may support requirements, but they do not themselves state the quantified quality requested here. A correct The 99.9% uptime threshold is a measurable availability target. B incorrect Authentication names behavior rather than a quantified quality target. C incorrect An ER diagram is a design artifact. D incorrect Normalization is a design technique.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 196 · AM0168
records.text: AM0168 Question 196 FDB26 What is the purpose of data manipulation in database management? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A To define the database schema B To create database backups C To insert, update, and delete data D To manage concurrent access to data To insert, update, and delete data The DML subsection includes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. SQL examples show insertion/deletion and an UPDATE privilege permits changing values, grounding the data-manipulation purpose. DML also includes retrieval, so C describes its modification part rather than all of DML. A incorrect Schema definition is DDL. (PDF pp. 26, 55, 77.) B incorrect Backup is not the DML purpose identified. (PDF pp. 26, 55, 77.) C correct Insertion, updating and deletion are explicitly DML operations. (PDF pp. 26, 55, 77.) D incorrect Concurrency control is a separate transaction-management responsibility. (PDF pp. 26, 55, 77.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 197 · AM0170
records.text: AM0170 Question 197 FDB05 FDB38 During conceptual database design, which listed goal directly concerns representing the business domain before choosing storage layouts and access paths? Identify the design phase from its inputs and intended deliverable. A Efficient storage of data B Secure data transmission C Optimal query performance D Effective representation of real-world entities D. Effective representation of real-world entities Conceptual design turns business facts into an ER/EER representation of entities and relationships. Effective representation of the domain is therefore the direct goal in this phase. Storage efficiency and query access paths are later physical design concerns. Secure transmission can be an important requirement, but it is not the conceptual representational task singled out by the revised question. A incorrect Storage layout efficiency belongs to physical decisions. B incorrect Transmission security is a requirement or mechanism, not the specified conceptual representation goal. C incorrect Query performance is addressed through later physical design and tuning. D correct Representing real-world entities directly matches conceptual design.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 198 · AM0171
records.text: AM0171 Question 198 FDB38 Which are legitimate considerations when designing a database for a large e-commerce site? Select all that apply. Minimal redundancy means controlling avoidable duplication while permitting deliberate replicas. Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A High availability and scalability B Minimal data redundancy C Fast data retrieval D Secure user authentication A. High availability and scalability; B. Minimal data redundancy; C. Fast data retrieval; D. Secure user authentication Large e-commerce databases need several complementary qualities. Availability and scalability support continued service and growth; retrieval speed supports interactive use; security protects accounts and records. Controlling avoidable redundancy reduces consistency and maintenance problems even where intentional replicas are useful. All listed considerations therefore belong in the design discussion, with their relative priority determined by the site's actual requirements. A correct High availability and scalability support growth and continued service for a large site. B correct Controlling unnecessary redundancy improves consistency and maintenance even when deliberate copies are retained. C correct Fast retrieval is a legitimate quality target for browsing, orders and customer-facing operations. D correct Secure authentication is a legitimate security consideration for customer and administrative access.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 199 · AM0172
records.text: AM0172 Question 199 FDB38 FDB19 FDB25 Which listed mechanisms directly protect patient confidentiality, covering both protected stored/transmitted content and restrictions on authorized user actions? Select all that apply. Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A Database normalization B Data encryption C Role-based access control D Database indexing B. Data encryption; C. Role-based access control Encryption protects patient content at rest or in transit against the disclosure threats it covers. Role-based access control restricts which users can read or change patient records. These are complementary privacy protections and both qualify. Normalization reduces dependency anomalies, while indexing supplies retrieval paths; neither mechanism by itself decides who may see patient information or protects encoded content. A incorrect Normalization reduces dependency anomalies but does not itself restrict unauthorized disclosure. B correct Encryption protects patient content at rest or in transit against appropriate disclosure threats. C correct Role-based access control limits which users may access patient records or perform actions. D incorrect Indexes provide search paths and do not by themselves enforce patient confidentiality.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 200 · AM0173
records.text: AM0173 Question 200 FDB38 FDB25 FDB24 Which techniques can improve query performance for some suitable workloads, without implying that they always help? Select all that apply. Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A Indexing B Data replication C Denormalization D Partitioning A. Indexing; B. Data replication; C. Denormalization; D. Partitioning Indexes add search paths for selective queries. Replicas can improve read locality, denormalization can reduce selected joins or computations, and partitioning can reduce relevant data access when aligned with queries. Each technique can therefore help some workloads. Their benefits are conditional and can involve extra storage or update costs, so selecting all four does not mean every database should use all of them. A correct Indexes can reduce reads for selective predicates when maintenance and lookup costs are justified. B correct Replication can place read copies near users or spread suitable read workloads. C correct Denormalization can avoid selected joins or repeated computation by storing redundant/precomputed facts. D correct Partitioning can limit relevant data or improve locality when partitioning matches query predicates.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 201 · AM0174
records.text: AM0174 Question 201 FDB12 FDB09 FDB07 FDB15 Users may follow many other users, and each user may be followed by many users. Which option describes the cardinality of this recursive user relationship, rather than a key constraint or procedural enforcement mechanism? Identify relationship degree and cardinality before choosing a relational mapping. A Primary key constraints B Foreign key constraints C Many-to-many relationships D Triggers and stored procedures C. Many-to-many relationships The follow rules permit multiple related users in both directions, which is many-to-many cardinality. A recursive association table can store two user references to represent those links. Primary and foreign keys support identification and referential integrity, but they are constraint mechanisms rather than the requested multiplicity classification. Triggers and stored procedures are also not a cardinality category. A incorrect Primary keys identify rows rather than name relationship multiplicity. B incorrect Foreign keys validate references rather than describe the many-to-many cardinality. C correct Both endpoints permit many partners, establishing M:N. D incorrect Procedures are implementation mechanisms rather than a cardinality type.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 202 · AM0175
records.text: AM0175 Question 202 FDB20 FDB21 In the usual normalization sequence, which is the first normal form excluding transitive dependence of nonprime attributes on a key through a nonkey determinant? Check atomicity, candidate keys and partial dependencies in that order. A First Normal Form (1NF) B Second Normal Form (2NF) C Third Normal Form (3NF) D Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) Third Normal Form (3NF) In the stated single-key teaching case, 2NF excludes partial dependencies but can still allow a nonprime fact to depend on the key through a nonkey determinant. The next defining stage is 3NF, summarized by the whole-key-and-nothing-but-the-key mnemonic. BCNF strengthens the determinant rule, and 4NF addresses multivalued dependencies. Stronger forms inherit earlier conditions, so the explicit first-stage scope makes 3NF the unique selection rather than treating inherited properties as rival answers. A incorrect Incorrect: 1NF concerns atomic values and does not eliminate the specified transitive dependencies. B incorrect Incorrect: 2NF excludes partial dependencies but can retain a nonprime transitive dependency through a nonkey determinant. C correct Correct: 3NF is the first stage imposing the specified nonprime transitive-dependency restriction in this teaching case. D incorrect Incorrect: BCNF strengthens 3NF by requiring every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey; it is not the first stage described.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 203 · AM0176
records.text: AM0176 Question 203 FDB38 FDB15 What is the purpose of denormalization in database design for real-world scenarios? Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A To eliminate data redundancy B To optimize query performance C To enforce referential integrity D To simplify the database schema To improve selected query performance. Denormalization repeats or precomputes facts so that selected queries can perform less work, such as fewer joins. FDB38 also states the cost: more maintenance when underlying facts change. It does not aim to eliminate redundancy or enforce foreign-key references. A simpler query path may result, but a simpler schema is not the essential purpose. A incorrect Denormalization introduces controlled redundancy instead of eliminating it. B correct Its goal is to reduce costs of selected read queries using repeated or precomputed information. C incorrect Foreign-key constraints enforce references; denormalization itself does not establish referential integrity. D incorrect It may simplify selected reads, but schema simplicity is not the defining or guaranteed goal.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 204 · AM0178
records.text: AM0178 Question 204 FDB13 Which listed modeling technique directly includes superclass/subclass inheritance? Interpret ER modeling in A as basic ER without the EER extension, relational modeling as ordinary tables/keys, and XML modeling as document structure. Review inheritance, specialization and category constraints. A Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling B Object-oriented data modeling C Relational data modeling D XML data modeling B. Object-oriented data modeling Object-oriented data modeling directly represents superclass/subclass inheritance. Enhanced ER also supports inheritance, but A is explicitly limited to basic ER in this question. Ordinary relational tables can encode subtype data through references without making inheritance a direct modeling construct, and document structure is not the object inheritance mechanism being tested. The scope distinction makes the selected technique definite. A incorrect Basic ER excludes the EER inheritance extension under the stated scope. B correct Object models directly support superclass/subclass inheritance. C incorrect Ordinary relational tables encode facts and references rather than directly declaring this inheritance construct. D incorrect Document structure is not the direct object inheritance model asked for.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 205 · AM0179
records.text: AM0179 Question 205 FDB38 FDB15 Which CMS features directly support either semantic grouping of content or valid stored references between content and tags? Select all that apply. Compare design techniques by the specific problem each solves. A Referential integrity constraints B Full-text search capabilities C Content categorization and tagging D Distributed database architecture A. Referential integrity constraints; C. Content categorization and tagging Categories and tags describe semantic associations among content items. Referential integrity constraints keep the stored links between content and tags valid. These two features address meaning and reference validity respectively, so both fit. Full-text search supports finding text, while a distributed architecture concerns data placement and coordination. Neither is the requested direct representation or validation of content-to-tag relationships. A correct Referential constraints preserve valid links between content and related rows, such as tags. B incorrect Full-text search finds textual content rather than primarily defining or validating item relationships. C correct Categories and tags describe semantic groupings and associations among content items. D incorrect Distribution determines placement and coordination rather than directly representing the stated content relationships.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 206 · AM0180
records.text: AM0180 Question 206 FDB02 FDB-S02 Which database design technique is used to represent a hierarchical structure of data elements? Compare the data models by how they organize records and relationships. A Relational data modeling B Network data modeling C Hierarchical data modeling D Object-relational data modeling Hierarchical data modeling. A hierarchical structure organizes elements into parent-child levels. FDB02 assigns this representation to the hierarchical model, so C directly matches the requested design concept. Relational modeling instead uses tables, network modeling permits more general record links, and richer object-relational types do not by themselves require a hierarchical organization. A incorrect Relational modeling represents facts in tables rather than requiring a hierarchical tree. B incorrect Network modeling permits linked records with multiple parents rather than a restricted hierarchy. C correct Hierarchical modeling explicitly represents the parent-child structure asked for in the stem.
