D incorrect An object-relational approach adds richer types to relational storage rather than defining this tree organization.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 207 · AM0181
records.text: AM0181 Question 207 FDB19 Which benefit directly follows from reducing dependency-driven insertion, deletion and update anomalies through normalization, without assuming reduced storage or simpler queries? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A Simplified data retrieval B Increased data redundancy C Enhanced data integrity D Reduced storage requirements C. Enhanced data integrity Normalization separates facts according to their determinants, reducing repeated facts and the insertion, deletion and update anomalies they cause. That directly supports enhanced data integrity. Storage savings and simpler retrieval are not guaranteed because decomposition can introduce additional keys and joins. Increased redundancy is opposite to the intended reduction of avoidable repetition, so it is not the benefit identified by this question. A incorrect Normalized retrieval may require more joins, so simplification does not follow. B incorrect Normalization aims to reduce avoidable repetition. C correct Reducing inconsistent updates and related anomalies improves integrity. D incorrect Storage savings can be offset by extra keys and relation overhead.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 208 · AM0182
records.text: AM0182 Question 208 FDB24 Which database design concept allows the division of a large database into smaller, manageable units? Distinguish logical records, disk pages and physical file organization. A Data partitioning B Database replication C Data migration D Data archiving Data partitioning. FDB24 explicitly contrasts partitioning, replication, migration and archiving. Partitioning divides the dataset into smaller portions, matching the question. Replication makes additional copies, migration moves data, and archiving takes older data out of active service. Those operations can accompany partitioning, but none of them defines division into manageable units. A correct Partitioning divides a large dataset into smaller portions or manageable units. B incorrect Replication creates copies rather than dividing the original dataset into distinct units. C incorrect Migration moves data to another location or system rather than defining a split. D incorrect Archiving removes older data from active service rather than generally dividing the database.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 209 · AM0183
records.text: AM0183 Question 209 FDB06 FDB02 Which database design technique is used to capture the relationships between entities in a graphical representation? Review entity, attribute and relationship notation before interpreting the model. A Relational data modeling B Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling C Object-oriented data modeling D Document data modeling Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling ERD is explicitly a graphical database-schema technique showing modeled entities and their important relationships. This directly establishes ER modeling for the graphical representation asked about. A incorrect Relational modeling describes tables; ERD is the named graphical technique. (PDF pp. 9.) B correct ER modeling is the explicit graphical entities/relationships technique. (PDF pp. 9.) C incorrect Object-oriented is named but not the described ERD technique. (PDF pp. 9.) D incorrect Document modeling is not the technique defined in the module. (PDF pp. 9.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 210 · CS0049
records.text: CS0049 Question 210 FDB04 In contrary to the traditional file-based approach, in the database approach: Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A Programs define and access their own data B Store data items in multiple copies C Don't care about the definition of programs and data D Data and programs are defined independently Data and programs are defined independently The database approach insulates programs from data definitions and supports data independence. This is the relevant distinction from programs managing their own files. A incorrect Own program-specific definitions do not express the database approach's insulation. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) B incorrect Multiple uncontrolled copies are not the defining benefit and can cause inconsistency. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) C incorrect The approach explicitly maintains metadata and definitions, not indifference to them. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.) D correct Independent definitions match program/data insulation and independence. (PDF pp. 5, 6, 8.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 211 · CS0050
records.text: CS0050 Question 211 FDB04 Assume you are a database designer and you are given a task to specify entities, relationships, constraints on relations and data types for the data to be stored. At which level of the three-schema architecture would this be addressed? Trace which schema levels a proposed change affects. A View level B Internal level C External level D Conceptual level Conceptual level The conceptual level describes the whole database and explicitly concentrates on entities, data types, relationships, operations and constraints while hiding physical storage. The stem repeats those conceptual responsibilities. A incorrect View level shows a user-group subset. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) B incorrect Internal level describes physical storage and access paths. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) C incorrect External is another name for user view, not the global description. (PDF pp. 7, 8.) D correct Conceptual is the level explicitly listing the requested structural components. (PDF pp. 7, 8.)

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 212 · NS0217
records.text: NS0217 Question 212 FDB19 What is the purpose of normalization in database design? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A To reduce redundancy and improve data integrity B To speed up query performance C To create complex relationships between tables D To encrypt sensitive data Reduce avoidable redundancy and associated integrity anomalies. FDB19 defines normalization as separating facts according to their determinants, reducing avoidable repetition and insertion, deletion and update anomalies. That supports both parts of A. It does not promise universally faster queries, deliberately create complexity for its own sake or encrypt content. Performance and security need their own workload and threat-model choices. A correct Normalization reduces repeated facts and the anomalies that threaten data consistency. B incorrect More joins may be needed, so faster query execution is not a universal normalization purpose. C incorrect Relationships follow fact dependencies; creating complexity is not the goal. D incorrect Normalization restructures facts and does not encrypt sensitive values.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 213 · NS0295
records.text: NS0295 Question 213 FDB08 A weak entity uses its partial key together with the key of an independently keyed owner. Which terms describe that associated entity set? Select all that apply. Check how a dependent entity obtains its complete identity. A Identifying set B Strong entity set C Neighbor set D Owner set B. Strong entity set; D. Owner set The weak entity lacks a complete independent identifier. Its owner's key combines with the partial key to identify it. Because the owner is independently keyed in this question, strong entity set and owner set both describe the associated set. Identifying describes the relationship connecting the sets, while neighbor does not state the necessary ownership and identification dependency. A incorrect Identifying is normally the relationship role rather than the defined name of the owner entity set. B correct The owner that supplies an independent identifying key is normally a strong entity set. C incorrect Neighbor does not express the necessary ownership and identification dependency. D correct Owner set is the associated entity set whose key identifies the weak entity together with its partial key.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 214 · NS0297
records.text: NS0297 Question 214 FDB26 A language that allows the DBA or user to describe and name the entities, attributes, and relationships required for the application is__________ Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. A Transaction control language (TCL) B Data control language (DCL) C Data Manipulation Language (DML) D Data Definition Language (DDL) Data Definition Language. Describing and naming application entities, attributes and relationships defines schema structure. FDB26 assigns structural changes to DDL through CREATE, ALTER and DROP. TCL manages transaction boundaries, DCL controls privileges and DML retrieves or changes data. These categories have different effects, so DDL uniquely matches the schema-description role in the stem. A incorrect TCL manages commit, rollback and savepoints rather than defining schema elements. B incorrect DCL manages privileges through GRANT and REVOKE rather than describing entities and attributes. C incorrect DML retrieves or changes instance data rather than defining the application schema. D correct DDL defines and changes schema structure, including tables, attributes and constraints.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 215 · NS0302
records.text: NS0302 Question 215 FDB03 In relational-table terminology, which terms describe a unit of related field values treated together by an application? Select all that apply. Distinguish a relation's structure from its current contents and its descriptive metadata. A Rows B Field C Record D Database A. Rows; C. Record A tuple holds a set of related attribute values as one table unit. Row and record are synonymous names for that unit, so both alternatives qualify. A field is only an individual property, and a database is the larger coherent collection of related data. Grammatical number in Rows does not create a different relational concept from Record. A correct Rows contain related field values and are the relational counterpart of records. B incorrect A field is an individual property rather than a collection of related fields. C correct Record is the stated unit that groups related fields for application use. D incorrect A database contains a larger coherent collection of data rather than just one record.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 216 · NS0315
records.text: NS0315 Question 216 FDB30 Which template creates a table with one column? Treat table_name, column_name and column_type as placeholders for valid identifiers and a data type. Distinguish table definition changes from changes to stored rows. A CREATE table_name (column_name, column type); B CREATE table_name (column_type, column name); C CREATE TABLE table_name (column_name column_type); D CREATE TABLE table_name (column_type, column name); C. CREATE TABLE table_name (column_name column_type); CREATE TABLE introduces a new table definition. Within its parentheses, each column declaration places the column name before its data type, without a comma between those two parts. Commas separate whole declarations. Option C matches this pattern. A and B omit TABLE, while D reverses and separates the intended name/type pair and therefore fails the requested template. A incorrect TABLE is absent and the column declaration is split incorrectly. B incorrect TABLE is absent and the name/type order is reversed. C correct The name/type pair forms one complete column declaration. D incorrect The type/name order and comma do not form the intended declaration.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 217 · NS0320
records.text: NS0320 Question 217 FDB01 FDB36 FDB25 From the following alternatives which one is FALSE about database system? Review the database approach and match each claimed benefit or cost to its mechanism. A It is very difficult to protect a file under the system B In database system the user is not required to write the procedures C In database system, DBMS provides a good protection mechanism. D It contains a wide variety of sophisticated techniques to store and retrieve the data. The claim that protection is very difficult under a database system is false. FDB01 contrasts unmanaged file difficulties with DBMS authorization, shared integrity, transactions and recovery. A therefore reverses a stated database benefit. B is understood in the data-access sense: declarative requests need not prescribe retrieval procedures, as FDB36 explains; it does not mean applications never contain code. Protection and sophisticated storage/access facilities in C and D are consistent with the note. A correct This reverses the note's benefit: a DBMS provides coordinated protection rather than inherently making protection very difficult. B incorrect Declarative data requests need not prescribe retrieval procedures; this does not exclude ordinary application code. C incorrect Authorization and controlled data access are explicit DBMS protection mechanisms. D incorrect DBMS storage and access facilities include indexes, buffers, query processing and other sophisticated mechanisms.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 218 · NS0329
records.text: NS0329 Question 218 FDB09 Consider a directed line(->) from the relationship set advisor to both entity sets instructor and student. This indicates _________ cardinality Read the relationship in both directions and check participation constraints. A Many to one B Many to many C One to one D One to many One-to-one under the common ER arrow convention. FDB09 explicitly discusses arrows from advisor to both Instructor and Student. Under its common convention, each arrow imposes a maximum of one on the corresponding end. Both ends are therefore maximum-one, producing 1:1. This does not imply total participation, and another diagram notation would require a legend, but the complete note supplies the convention for this example. A incorrect Many-to-one permits many at one end, contrary to maximum-one arrows at both ends. B incorrect Many-to-many imposes neither of the maximum-one constraints stated by the arrows. C correct Maximum one at both ends produces a one-to-one relationship. D incorrect One-to-many permits multiple associations at one end rather than maximum one at both.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 219 · NS0339
records.text: NS0339 Question 219 FDB19 FDB21 What is the basic goal of Normalization? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. A To decrease data integrity B To reduce redundancy C To maximize transitive dependency D To increase dependency Reduce avoidable redundancy. Normalization separates facts by their determinants to reduce repeated storage and the anomalies that repetition can cause. FDB19 therefore supports reducing redundancy as the basic listed goal. Decreasing integrity is the opposite intended effect, and maximizing transitive or unspecified dependencies is not a normalization objective. Proper dependencies are analyzed rather than increased indiscriminately. A incorrect Normalization aims to improve integrity by reducing anomalies, not decrease it. B correct Reducing avoidable repeated facts is a basic normalization goal. C incorrect Problematic nonkey transitive dependencies are removed or separated rather than maximized. D incorrect Dependencies are analyzed to place facts correctly; increasing them indiscriminately is not the objective.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 220 · NS0344
records.text: NS0344 Question 220 FDB07 For a relation with ID, CITY and NAME, ID is guaranteed unique and non-NULL while CITY and NAME may repeat. Which listed sets are superkeys? Select all that apply. Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A NAME B ID C CITY D CITY, ID B. ID; D. CITY, ID A superkey is any set of attributes guaranteed to identify a tuple. ID has that guarantee, and the larger set containing CITY and ID keeps it. Both sets therefore qualify, even though the larger one is not minimal. CITY and NAME may repeat and cannot independently identify all tuples. Minimality would distinguish candidate keys, but it is not required for superkeys. A incorrect Repeated names are permitted, so NAME is not guaranteed unique. B correct ID uniquely identifies every tuple. C incorrect Repeated cities are permitted, so CITY is not guaranteed unique. D correct Including unique ID preserves identification even with the extra CITY attribute.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 221 · NS0357
records.text: NS0357 Question 221 FDB07 ______________is one of the candidate keys chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify the entity set. Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A Super key B Candidate key C Social security key D Primary key Primary key. FDB07 defines a primary key as the selected candidate key, with the remaining candidates called alternate keys. The stem asks specifically for the designer's selection rather than every unique attribute set. Superkey is broader and candidate key denotes eligibility before selection. A social-security identifier could be chosen, but is not the generic name of that role. A incorrect A superkey is any unique identifier set and may include unnecessary attributes. B incorrect Candidate keys are eligible minimal identifiers, not specifically the one selected for the primary role. C incorrect A social-security identifier is a possible attribute choice, not the generic selected-key category. D correct The selected candidate key is the primary key.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 222 · NS0627
records.text: NS0627 Question 222 FDB07 FDB15 FDB16 What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key? Test uniqueness and minimality separately when classifying keys. A primary key is the selected unique non-NULL identifier; a foreign key references an eligible key. FDB07 defines the primary key as a selected candidate key. FDB15 requires non-NULL foreign-key values to match an eligible referenced unique/candidate key; foreign keys need not be unique and may permit NULL.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 223 · NS0628
records.text: NS0628 Question 223 FDB19 Why is database normalization important? What problems does it solve? Distinguish dependency-based design problems from the contents of one sample table. Normalization reduces repeated facts and insertion, deletion and update anomalies. Repeating a student name across enrollments risks inconsistent updates, prevents storing some facts without unrelated rows and can lose a fact when its last repeated row is deleted. Normalization separates facts by their determinants to reduce these anomalies.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 224 · NS0629
records.text: NS0629 Question 224 FDB29 FDB16 What happens if you UPDATE a row but forget to include a WHERE clause? Track which rows each data-changing command affects. UPDATE without WHERE targets every row, subject to constraints and transaction outcome. FDB29 states that an UPDATE without WHERE targets every row. The SET expressions are therefore applied to all rows rather than one intended row; constraints or errors can still prevent completion.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 225 · NS0630
records.text: NS0630 Question 225 FDB37 Why would you use a ROLLBACK command in a transaction? Match each transaction guarantee to its precise failure or interference scenario. ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted transaction work, for example after a failure or unwanted change. FDB37 contrasts COMMIT, which completes transaction work, with ROLLBACK, which undoes uncommitted work. Rollback restores the prior transactional state after errors or a decision not to keep the changes; it does not erase other users' committed transactions.

records.title: Fundamental of Database Systems — Question 226 · NS0631
records.text: NS0631 Question 226 FDB26 FDB29 What is the difference between DELETE and DROP? Classify each SQL command by the kind of change it performs. DELETE removes rows and retains the table; DROP TABLE removes the table object. FDB26 distinguishes data deletion from structural removal. DELETE may target selected rows with WHERE, or all rows without it, while leaving the table defined. DROP TABLE removes that relation object.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Course module
records.text: Advanced Database Systems

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Study notes
records.text: Advanced Database Systems Use object semantics, recovery algorithms, distributed design and explicit query costs to reason about system behavior. Worked traces and explicit assumptions support the study of object models, recovery and distributed databases. For each schedule, mark conflicting items and build the precedence graph; test commit dependencies separately. For recovery, write the durable commit set, buffer policy and checkpoint/ARIES assumptions before choosing undo or redo. Compare equivalent plans with stated page counts, memory and network bytes; show the arithmetic rather than memorizing a preferred join. Construct one homogeneous and one heterogeneous distributed design, including ownership, reconstruction, replication and failure behavior. Review OID versus values, encapsulation versus abstraction, 2PL versus 2PC and rollback versus redo through short examples.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Practice questions
records.text: Advanced Database Systems

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Revision outline
records.text: Advanced Database Systems

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Objects, identity, classes and persistence
records.text: An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity. Persistence lets an object survive beyond the program execution that created it. An OODBMS adds durable storage, transactions, querying and controlled sharing to object concepts. It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables. An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables. These three approaches differ. Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design. University of Pittsburgh: Object-oriented databases

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Encapsulation, abstraction and object associations
records.text: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details. Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage. Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented. These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation. An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects. It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types. Methods can invoke operations on other objects, supporting collaboration. A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation. Do not treat each of these as an interchangeable name for the whole object. University of Pittsburgh: Object-oriented databases

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Inheritance, polymorphism and safe substitutability
records.text: Inheritance derives a subtype from a superclass, reusing applicable attributes and behavior. GraduateStudent is a Student; association instead says Student belongs to Department. EER teaches inherited attributes and relationships, while a programming object model also specifies behavior. Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses. The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object. This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation. Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface. Distinguish inheritance as a structural relationship from polymorphism as a use of that relationship at runtime. Oracle Java Tutorials: Polymorphism

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Object type constructors
records.text: In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state). An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string. A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B'). It is not a collection of records. A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions. Constructors can be nested to represent complex objects, such as a tuple with a set of phone numbers. An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable. A type constructor defines the shape of a value; it is not the same as an executable constructor operation that creates a new object. University of Pittsburgh: Object type constructors

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — ODL, OQL and inverse relationships
records.text: Object Definition Language (ODL) is the ODMG schema-definition language for object databases; it describes interfaces/classes, attributes, operations and relationships. Object Query Language (OQL) expresses queries. Host-language bindings connect these definitions and operations to languages such as Java or C++. Defining a logical schema is different from implementing its storage. An inverse declaration pairs opposite directions of the same relationship. Conceptually, Department.employees is inverse to Employee.department: when an employee belongs to department D, the corresponding employee appears in D's collection. The declaration expresses relationship consistency; it is not an inheritance keyword or an ordinary scalar attribute. An MCQ calling ODL both a DDL and a language for developing logical schemas offers overlapping true descriptions, so its exact wording matters. Juniata College: Object Databases

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Transactions, ACID and state transitions
records.text: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent. Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions. Example Worked example A=5,000 and B=8,000 become 4,250 and 8,750 after transferring 750 from A to B. Both balances total 13,000. Unchanged or reverse-transfer balances can also preserve that sum; only the requested debit/credit implements the specified successful transfer. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Read/write operations, buffers and log records
records.text: read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable. write_item(X) copies the new program value into the buffered page, marking it dirty. Writing that page to disk can occur later according to the buffer policy; write_item is not inherently an immediate disk flush. Insert and delete also modify data; sorting is a query-processing operation rather than a primitive item update. A conceptual log can contain START, UPDATE(T,X,old,new), COMMIT, ABORT and END records. Before-images support undo; after-images support redo. Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read. COMMIT records successful completion; an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace
records.text: Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read. Nonrepeatable read means a repeated read of one row sees a committed change. A phantom means repeating a predicate query finds a changed qualifying set after another transaction inserts, deletes or changes matching rows. Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200. A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs
records.text: A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict. For conflict serializability, make one graph vertex per transaction. For every earlier conflicting operation of Ti and later operation of Tj, add Ti→Tj. Acyclic means conflict-serializable; a topological ordering gives a valid serial order. Cyclic means not conflict-serializable. This test is stronger than view serializability, which also compares read-from relationships and final writers and may permit some schedules with blind writes. Example Worked example r1(X), w2(X), r2(Y), w1(Y) gives T1→T2 on X and T2→T1 on Y, a cycle. r1(X), w1(X), r2(X), w2(X) gives only T1→T2 and is conflict-serializable. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules
records.text: Recoverable means if Tj reads Ti's value, Tj cannot commit before Ti commits. Otherwise Ti might abort after Tj already committed dependent work. Cascadeless means a transaction reads only values written by committed transactions, avoiding cascading aborts. Strict means no other transaction reads or overwrites an item written by an uncommitted transaction. Strict ⇒ cascadeless ⇒ recoverable. For w1(X), r2(X), c2, a1, T2 committed a dirty dependency, so the schedule is unrecoverable. Moving c2 after c1 makes that dependency recoverable, but the earlier dirty read still makes it not cascadeless. Serializability and recoverability are separate tests: one concerns equivalent transaction order and the other safe commit/rollback dependencies. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers
records.text: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior. A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers. Held / requested S X S Compatible Conflict X Conflict Conflict Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Two-phase locking and its variants
records.text: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts. Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort. Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point. Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock. It requires knowing the lock set and can reduce concurrency. Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation
records.text: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work. Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder
records.text: A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names. Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive. Starvation avoidance additionally assumes holders eventually finish and scheduling is fair. In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one; a younger transaction requesting a resource held by an older one aborts. Deadlock-prevention priority rules are also different from basic timestamp ordering's read/write validity tests. Requester relative to holder Wait–die Wound–wait Older Wait Abort younger holder Younger Abort requester Wait Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module San Jose State University: Deadlocks and distributed databases

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests
records.text: Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order. For TS(T)=10 and write_TS(X)=20, T cannot read X: it would observe a logically later write. Thus the transaction aborted can be older, contrary to the guides' blanket younger-always-aborts claim. The Thomas write rule can ignore an obsolete write instead of aborting in one case, but that is a different protocol and must be stated. Basic timestamp ordering avoids lock-wait deadlocks but may cause repeated restarts. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Virginia Tech: Timestamp protocols

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity
records.text: Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts. Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot. Snapshot isolation is not automatically serializable: concurrent writes to different rows can violate a shared invariant. Fine-grained row locks permit more independent operations but require tracking many locks. Coarse table/database locks simplify management but block unrelated rows and reduce concurrency. Intention locks advertise planned descendant locks in a hierarchy; escalation replaces many small locks with a coarser one. Small granularity does not inherently cause more logical conflicts. Choose granularity from contention and management overhead, not a universal rule. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Query processing: representation before execution
records.text: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries. A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates. A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms. Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization. DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Heuristic and semantic query rewrites
records.text: Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile. Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input. Semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, such as a key proving a join cannot multiply matching rows. Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone. Outer joins, NULLs, duplicates and aggregation restrict equivalences: moving a right-table filter from ON to WHERE after a left join may delete its preserved unmatched rows. Fewer intermediate rows is a useful heuristic, not proof of minimum runtime. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity
records.text: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches. For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module CMU 15-445/645 Spring 2024 Query Optimization slides Leis et al., How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Join algorithms and access-path tradeoffs
records.text: Tuple nested loops scan the inner relation for each outer tuple. Page nested loops approximately cost B(R)+B(R)×B(S) page reads. With M buffers, block nested loops can cost B(R)+ceil(B(R)/(M−2))×B(S), reserving an inner and output buffer. Try both outer choices. An indexed nested-loop join probes an inner index for each qualifying outer tuple; it suits a small outer result and a useful index. Sort-merge joins sorted join keys and must include any sorting cost. Hash join partitions/builds a hash structure and probes it; equality joins suit it, ranges generally do not. A one-pass in-memory hash join can read each input once when the build side fits. Include output/materialization cost if the exercise requires it. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Compare actual query strategies
records.text: Compare only plans returning the same result under the same assumptions. Add scans, probes, sorting, intermediate writes and communication as applicable; do not count an omitted cost in only one plan. Record memory limits and whether inputs are already ordered. Choose the lowest estimated cost for the specified objective, then test estimates against actual execution. Example: R has 100 pages, S has 1,000 pages and M=12 buffers. Block nested loops with R outer cost 100+ceil(100/10)×1,000=10,100 reads; S outer costs 1,000+ceil(1,000/10)×100=11,000. If a selective R index costs 3 reads and returns 20 outer tuples, with each S index probe costing 4 reads including matches, indexed nested loops cost 3+20×4=83 reads. That wins under these stated assumptions; it is not a universal join ranking. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Pipelining, parallelism and caching
records.text: Materialization stores an intermediate result before the next operator consumes it. Pipelining passes tuples as they become available, overlapping producer and consumer work and reducing temporary I/O. A sort is normally blocking; a hash join must build its hash table before probing can output, though later probe/output can stream. Pipelining does not require separate CPUs. Parallel execution uses multiple workers, for example partitioned scans/joins, independent subplans or operator pipelines. Interleaving on one CPU is concurrency; simultaneous cores provide parallelism. Result caching reuses answers and needs invalidation when underlying data changes. Plan caching reuses an execution strategy, not the rows returned. Buffer caching keeps data pages; materialization retains intermediate rows. Specify the kind of query caching being discussed. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Indexes, statistics and re-optimization
records.text: B/B+ tree indexes support ordered and range predicates; hash indexes target equality; bitmap indexes can help some analytic selections. Clustered storage keeps related rows close. An index may reduce reads but adds space and update work; scanning can be faster when most rows qualify. Commonly useful is not a unique property of one index type. Re-optimization chooses a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest the old plan is unsuitable. Updating statistics does not itself execute the query. Use EXPLAIN and measured execution to compare estimates, spills, scans and join choices. Avoid universal rules that joins always beat subqueries, functions can never use indexes or more indexes always improve performance. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Security, integrity and inference control
records.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction. Inference control concerns learning protected individual facts indirectly from allowed aggregate answers. Releasing SUM for a group and SUM for the same group excluding one known person may disclose that person's value by subtraction. Suppressing individual rows alone is insufficient; protections may restrict queries, aggregate sizes or add appropriately designed noise. Access-restricted views can expose aggregates while hiding details; inference control additionally concerns preventing indirect disclosure. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Jagannathan and Wright: Private Inference Control for Aggregate Database Queries

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — GRANT, REVOKE and privilege scope
records.text: GRANT SELECT ON Catalogue TO Mohammed; permits reads. REVOKE DELETE, UPDATE (Price,Year) ON Catalogue FROM Mohammed; removes the specified table deletion and column update grants in SQL dialects supporting that form. DELETE applies to rows/table access rather than particular columns; UPDATE can be column-scoped. REVOKE removes permission, whereas GRANT gives it. Roles group privileges. WITH GRANT OPTION permits a recipient to grant a privilege onward; removing an upstream grant can cascade or be restricted according to the chosen command and DBMS. Removing one direct grant may leave effective access through another role or grant path. A view is a stored query definition, not encryption. Least privilege assigns only the access needed for the task. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Classify failures and choose the starting resource
records.text: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation. Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects. Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy. These are cooperating mechanisms, not four mutually exclusive complete alternatives. Buffer management is not durable backup. Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification. A full backup copies the database to separate storage; scheduled backups plus archived logs support restoration to a chosen recoverable point. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — WAL, undo and redo
records.text: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment. Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Steal and force determine recovery work
records.text: Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo. No-steal prevents those uncommitted effects reaching the persistent database. Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo. For the conventional page/log model: steal/no-force needs undo and redo; steal/force needs undo but no redo; no-steal/no-force needs redo but no undo; no-steal/force needs neither data-page undo nor redo after a system crash. Logging/atomic commit machinery may still be necessary. These policies are independent of whether an update overwrites an old page or uses a separate location. Immediate update alone does not uniquely specify every recovery requirement. Buffer policy Force No-force Steal UNDO UNDO + REDO No-steal Neither data-page UNDO nor REDO REDO Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates
records.text: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately. In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Checkpoints and recovery boundaries
records.text: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing. A fuzzy checkpoint permits ongoing transactions and records active-transaction and dirty-page information without forcing all pages simultaneously. Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position. A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions. Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery
records.text: ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table. Analysis reconstructs active/loser transactions and dirty-page information. Redo repeats history, starting from the relevant earliest dirty-page update; pageLSNs help skip already-installed actions. Undo reverses loser transactions. Compensation log records (CLRs) describe undo actions and their continuation information. They can be redone but are not themselves undone. This makes recovery restartable: after a second crash, durable undo progress need not be undone again as if no progress occurred. Absence of checkpoints alone does not imply identical undo/redo lists. State the recovery algorithm, durable logs/page state and progress before predicting repeated-crash behavior. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: Recovery System slides

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Execute a small recovery problem
records.text: Assume steal/no-force, durable WAL and a simple undo/redo method. Initially X=100,Y=50. The durable log contains START T1; UPDATE T1 X 100→120; COMMIT T1; START T2; UPDATE T2 Y 50→70; crash. T1 is a winner and T2 a loser. Redo X=120 if needed; undo Y=50 if T2's change reached disk. Under no-steal, Y never reached the persistent database, so no undo of it is needed. To solve larger cases, list transactions and durable commit status, identify the checkpoint type and buffer policy, select the algorithm, apply redo/undo in its required order and recompute final values. Transactions active at failure are not automatically restarted and committed. Business-level retries require a new controlled attempt; idempotency prevents duplicate effects when the client is unsure whether a commit succeeded. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems
records.text: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization. Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics. ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction. Locality, expansion and replicated availability are potential benefits. Distribution adds communication, coordination and security costs; a site outage can still make needed data unavailable if no usable replica exists. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Architectures and local autonomy
records.text: In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types. A tightly integrated distributed system can present one global schema and shared control. A federation integrates autonomous databases through mappings; a loosely coupled multidatabase system may preserve more independence without one complete global schema. State how much schema, transaction and administrative autonomy local sites retain. Calling a system heterogeneous does not require all sites to surrender autonomy or to copy every row everywhere. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Transparency: what exactly is hidden?
records.text: Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three. If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent. Distinguish whether fragment names, storage sites or both are hidden from the user. Column subsets define vertical fragmentation, not a type of transparency. Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction
records.text: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches. Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order. Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces. A full outer join is not universally required. Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy. Losing the only site containing a fragment makes that fragment unavailable, even while other sites continue. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Replication policies and their costs
records.text: Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups. Eager/synchronous replication coordinates propagation before the specified commit/acknowledgment point, increasing update latency. Lazy/asynchronous replication propagates later and may expose stale reads or need conflict resolution. Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes. These dimensions can coexist, so commonly used does not identify one unique policy. Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Distributed query plans and semijoin arithmetic
records.text: Distributed processing decomposes a logical query, localizes referenced relations to fragments/replicas, chooses global placement/order and optimizes local subplans. Include bytes moved, message latency, bandwidth and local work. Apply filters and projections before shipping when equivalent. A semijoin retains only rows of one input that have a match in the other, returning that input's attributes. Suppose R at A occupies 100 MB and S at B 20 MB; compute the result at A. Shipping all S costs 20 MB. A semijoin can send 0.2 MB of distinct R join keys to B, then return 1 MB of matching S rows: 1.2 MB before other costs. It wins on transferred bytes, but extra messages may dominate on high-latency links. If nearly all S matches, key shipping may not help. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Distributed atomic commit and Oracle commit points
records.text: Two-phase commit (2PC) first asks participants to prepare and durably promise they can commit. If all vote yes, the coordinator records commit durably and tells participants; otherwise it decides abort. A prepared participant must retain enough state to obey the final decision. Coordinator/communication failure can leave it in doubt and block progress until the decision is learned. Timeout after preparation is not permission to invent a commit or abort. 2PC coordinates atomic outcome; locking/other concurrency protocols provide isolation. Oracle's COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH helps choose the commit point site in its distributed transaction mechanism, with higher eligible strength preferred. This is an Oracle-specific 2PC role rule, not a lock phase or checkpoint setting. The transaction coordinator coordinates decisions rather than physically storing every site's rows. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module Oracle: COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Construct homogeneous and heterogeneous designs
records.text: For a bank using one compatible DBMS at three branches, horizontally fragment branch accounts by BranchID; keep each account at its home branch and replicate selected read-mostly reference data. For cross-branch transfers, use global identifiers, coordinated commit and a stated isolation policy. Choose replica placement so the required service remains available after the specified failure. Verify reconstruction, capacity, latency and recovery procedures. For a merger retaining different branch DBMSs, add mappings for AccountID, currency, time zones and numeric precision, plus middleware/gateways for supported operations. Decide whether all engines support atomic distributed commits; if not, define an explicit compensating workflow and its intermediate-state limits. Compare retaining autonomy against coordination and availability requirements. A good design answers who owns each fact, where copies live, what a failed link permits and how conflicting writes are resolved. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Warehouses, OLTP, OLAP and columnar storage
records.text: OLTP handles frequent operational transactions, such as account updates; OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets for analysis. A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading. These are workload tendencies: OLTP can retain history and warehouses can be updated. A star schema places measurements at a declared grain in a fact table linked to descriptive dimensions, such as time, product and store. A snowflake normalizes dimension structure further. Columnar storage groups values by column, reducing unnecessary column reads and aiding compression in scans; row-oriented storage groups each record's fields. Neither physical layout alone determines whether the logical model is relational. Indexes and denormalization choices depend on workload. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — NoSQL families, wide columns and CAP
records.text: Key-value stores retrieve values by key; document stores hold structured documents; wide-column/column-family systems organize sparse rows and related column families; graph systems model nodes and edges for relationship traversal. Wide-column systems such as Cassandra are not simply interchangeable with analytic columnar relational engines. Flexible schema does not mean no schema rules, and NoSQL does not imply no transactions. CAP states that under a network partition, a distributed service cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request at nonfailed nodes. It is not a universal menu saying casually pick any two forever. Systems choose failure behavior and may vary it by operation. CAP consistency is a single-copy visibility/order property, distinct from ACID consistency's preservation of application invariants. Gilbert and Lynch: Perspectives on the CAP Theorem

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Data sources and association rules
records.text: Structured data follows explicit fields, such as a registrar's relational tables. Unstructured data includes free text, images and audio; web/search collections can include these alongside structured content. A DBMS can also store text or BLOBs, so a storage product does not prove all its contents are structured. An association rule X⇒Y describes co-occurrence. Support=count(X and Y)/N; confidence=count(X and Y)/count(X)=P(Y|X). If 75 of 100 shoe purchases include socks, confidence(shoes⇒socks)=0.75. This does not prove causation or specify support without total transaction count. Clustering groups similar cases without target labels; classification predicts categories and regression predicts numeric outcomes. Purchasing co-occurrence is association mining even when its result informs store layout. University of Tennessee: Association rules

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Data-mining workflow and evaluation
records.text: CRISP-DM starts with business understanding: define the decision and success criteria. Then understand data, prepare it, model, evaluate and deploy; the process is iterative. Cleaning, integration and feature selection occur during preparation, not before the business problem exists. Within modeling, split data appropriately, train on training data, tune using validation and evaluate once on a held-out test set before deployment. Testing and evaluation are sometimes overlapping labels rather than universally distinct sequential phases. If an MCQ asks training→testing→evaluation→deployment, state that convention; another valid workflow can evaluate during model selection before final testing. Deployment includes monitoring and may trigger another preparation/modeling cycle. Do not leak future or test outcomes into training. IBM SPSS Modeler: CRISP-DM View

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Compare database mechanisms under explicit assumptions
records.text: Database mechanisms can overlap: ARIES and deferred update can both be log-based; restart recovery can use checkpoints, rollback and redo; NO-UNDO/REDO equals redo-only. Questions using best, important, common or faster need a workload and comparison criterion. Read the literal scope rather than treating one familiar term as automatically unique. State the minimum missing information: exact DBMS/version for vendor behavior; OID/type convention for object constructors; requester/holder ages for waiting; durable log, page state and policy for recovery; fragment definitions and network cost for distribution. Evaluate each description separately when several database mechanisms apply. Use the stated assumptions to explain which database mechanisms apply to each question. Fundamental of Database Systems module Advanced Database Systems module

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Query representations and relational operators
records.text: A relation is represented by a table of tuples. Selection filters its rows by a predicate; projection retains chosen columns. A Cartesian product constructs every pair of input tuples. A matching join combines tuples satisfying its predicate, and can be represented as a selection over a product. Sorting orders results, while grouping collects rows sharing grouping values; these are different operations. A query tree corresponds to a relational-algebra expression: base relations appear at leaves and operators at internal nodes. A query graph represents the predicate relationships of a relational-calculus expression without itself prescribing an operator execution order. An optimizer can transform the representation and choose access paths; the representation is not the query result. Advanced Database Systems module · page 24 Advanced Database Systems module · page 34 PostgreSQL documentation — Table Expressions PostgreSQL documentation — Sorting Rows

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Transaction boundaries and savepoints
records.text: In SQL transaction-block notation, BEGIN starts a block, COMMIT completes it successfully, and ROLLBACK cancels its uncommitted changes. Committing requests a durable transaction outcome; it is distinct from merely finishing the last read or write operation. SAVEPOINT marks an intermediate position inside the current transaction. ROLLBACK TO discards changes made after that position while retaining earlier work in the transaction. A savepoint is not an independent durable commit, and rolling back to it does not itself commit the retained changes. PostgreSQL documentation — Transactions

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Availability and evidence against false denial
records.text: Availability concerns keeping services and resources accessible to their authorized users. Non-repudiation concerns evidence that an event or action occurred and who originated it, so a participant cannot falsely deny it. Neither property specifies which particular user has permission to change a database row; that is the separate authorization decision. Computer Security module · page 4

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Elementary binary locks and shared-lock compatibility
records.text: An elementary binary lock has two states: free and held. A request on a free item sets the lock to held; a request on an already-held item waits until release. That simple model does not distinguish shared readers from a writer. Shared/exclusive locking adds modes so multiple shared readers can coexist while incompatible exclusive access is excluded. Advanced Database Systems module · page 83

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Classify a failure by its stated cause
records.text: A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault. A hardware failure originates in malfunctioning physical equipment; loss of disk contents is media failure. An accidental user deletion is human error even if the software executes the requested command correctly. Physical catastrophes such as fire can also cause failure. The observed symptom of a crash does not alone identify which cause occurred. Advanced Database Systems module · page 98

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 2 · Q00022
records.text: Q00022 Question 2 ADB29 Which update-timing policy permits a transaction's changes to reach the persistent database before the transaction commits? Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary. A In-Place Update B Immediate update C Shadow update D Deferred update Immediate update Immediate update permits a transaction's changes to be written to the persistent database before commit. If that transaction later aborts, recovery may need to undo those changes. Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. In-place update describes overwriting an existing location, while shadow update describes writing a separate version. Those location strategies do not, by their names alone, specify the timing policy requested here. Immediate update need not flush every cache write immediately. A incorrect Describes overwriting the existing location, not the commit-timing policy. B correct Correct: immediate update permits persistent database changes before commit and may require undo. C incorrect Describes writing a separate version while preserving the committed one, not the requested timing policy. D incorrect Deferred update excludes uncommitted changes from the persistent database.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 3 · Q00026
records.text: Q00026 Question 3 ADB18 ADB19 Which query-optimization approach applies relational-algebra properties and equivalences to rewrite a query and reduce intermediate work? Consider which equivalent transformation changes intermediate work and what assumptions preserve meaning. A Database storage without query rewriting B Heuristic approach C Deterministic execution without query rewriting D Physical-plan cost estimation Heuristic approach Heuristic optimization uses algebraic rules to reduce intermediate work, for example applying selective filters earlier, replacing a product plus join predicate with a join and projecting away unneeded columns. Storage and execution without rewriting do not perform those transformations. Cost estimation predicts resources for candidate plans rather than naming the algebraic rewrite approach itself. A practical optimizer can combine rewriting and costing, but the question isolates the rule-based transformation role. A incorrect Incorrect: storage without rewriting does not transform the algebraic query representation. B correct Correct: heuristic rewriting uses operator properties and equivalences to reduce intermediate work. C incorrect Incorrect: repeatable execution without rewriting does not apply the requested query transformations. D incorrect Incorrect: cost estimation predicts candidate-plan resource use rather than identifying the algebraic rewrite approach.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 4 · Q00046
records.text: Q00046 Question 4 ADB12 In which phase of the two phase locking protocol can a transaction obtain locks? Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary. A Release phase B Roll back phase C Shrinking phase D Growing phase Growing phase Two-phase locking acquires locks in the growing phase, then releases them in the shrinking phase without acquiring new ones. A incorrect Release is the unlocking portion, not acquisition. (PDF pp. 86.) B incorrect Rollback is not one of the two acquisition/release phases. (PDF pp. 86.) C incorrect Shrinking forbids new locks. (PDF pp. 86.) D correct Growing allows acquisition and forbids release. (PDF pp. 86.)

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 5 · Q00053
records.text: Q00053 Question 5 ADB08 ADB06 Which one of the following is not problem if concurrency is not controlled properly? Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A Lost update problem B Consistent database C Incorrect summary D Dirty read Consistent database Lost update, temporary update/dirty read, and incorrect summary are concurrency problems. A consistent database is the desired outcome of concurrency control. A incorrect Lost update is explicitly a concurrency anomaly. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.) B correct Consistency is a desired state, so this is the exception. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.) C incorrect Incorrect summary mixes values from different update stages. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.) D incorrect Dirty read exposes an update before its transaction has safely committed. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 6 · Q00078
records.text: Q00078 Question 6 ADB09 Which one of the following is not a condition for two operations in a schedule to be said to conflict? Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence. A If they access the same item X B If they belong to the same transactions C If Write_item (X) is at least one of the operations D If they belong to different transactions If they belong to the same transactions Conflict requires different transactions, the same item, and at least one write. Membership in the same transaction is therefore the exception. A incorrect Accessing the same item is required. (PDF pp. 70, 71.) B correct Same-transaction operations fail the different-transaction requirement. (PDF pp. 70, 71.) C incorrect At least one write is required. (PDF pp. 70, 71.) D incorrect Different transactions is required, so D is not the exception. (PDF pp. 70, 71.)

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 7 · Q00079
records.text: Q00079 Question 7 ADB26 ADB27 ADB06 ADB25 During restart recovery after a crash, which operation removes the database effects of a transaction that had not committed? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A View B Commit C Rollback D Redo Rollback Atomicity requires removing the effects of an incomplete transaction after a crash. Rollback performs that undo work, restoring before-images as needed. Commit instead accepts successful transaction effects, and a view is a query representation rather than a recovery action. Redo installs logged after-images to recover missing work; it does not name the removal of uncommitted effects requested here. These actions occur during restart recovery after the system is operating again. A incorrect Incorrect: a view is not an operation that reverses transaction effects. B incorrect Incorrect: commit accepts transaction effects rather than undoing the incomplete work. C correct Correct: rollback undoes the effects of the uncommitted transaction. D incorrect Incorrect: redo installs logged after-images; the requested removal requires undo/rollback.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 8 · Q00081
records.text: Q00081 Question 8 ADB13 A system is in a ______ state if there exists a set of transactions such that every transaction in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set. Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A Idle B Waiting C Deadlock D Ready Deadlock Mutual waiting among transactions for locks held by one another is a deadlock condition. A incorrect Idle does not express mutual lock waiting. (PDF pp. 87.) B incorrect Waiting alone need not involve a cycle. (PDF pp. 87.) C correct Deadlock is mutual waiting that prevents progress. (PDF pp. 87.) D incorrect Ready does not describe transactions blocked on one another. (PDF pp. 87.)

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 9 · Q00113
records.text: Q00113 Question 9 ADB24 Users may request permitted aggregates but must not infer protected individual values by subtracting overlapping aggregate answers. Which security measure specifically addresses this indirect-disclosure threat? Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values. A Inference control B Access control C Integrity control D Encryption E None of the above A. Inference control Inference control targets learning protected individual facts from aggregate answers.
