records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 76 · AM0187
records.text: AM0187 Question 76 ADB03 In the object-oriented model, inheritance allows: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface. A Objects to have multiple parents B Objects to inherit attributes and behaviors from a superclass C Objects to be created dynamically at runtime D Objects to establish relationships with other objects Inherit applicable attributes and behavior from a superclass. ADB03 defines inheritance as deriving a subtype from a superclass and reusing its applicable attributes and behavior. B captures that idea. It does not inherently require multiple parents, dynamically create objects, or merely link unrelated objects. Those alternatives concern particular inheritance forms, instantiation or association rather than the general meaning of inheritance. A incorrect Multiple parents are not a general requirement or guarantee of inheritance. B correct A subtype inherits applicable superclass attributes and behavior. C incorrect Dynamic object creation is instantiation, not the capability defined by inheritance. D incorrect Relationships between separate objects are associations rather than the is-a subtype relationship.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 77 · AM0188
records.text: AM0188 Question 77 ADB03 Which concept in the object-oriented model allows different classes to share the same method name but with different implementations? Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface. A Polymorphism B Abstraction C Encapsulation D Inheritance Polymorphism. ADB03 illustrates Shape.area dispatching to Circle.area or Rectangle.area according to the actual object. The common operation name has different compatible implementations, which is polymorphism. Inheritance can provide the subtype structure used by that mechanism, but is not itself the runtime dispatch behavior. Abstraction and encapsulation concern contracts and implementation access instead. A correct Polymorphism lets the same interface operation invoke different implementations for compatible object types. B incorrect Abstraction exposes a relevant contract rather than selecting among differing method implementations. C incorrect Encapsulation controls internal access rather than providing type-dependent method dispatch. D incorrect Inheritance supplies a structural subtype relation; polymorphism describes the differing implementations through a common interface.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 78 · AM0189
records.text: AM0189 Question 78 ADB02 The process of combining data and methods into a single entity is known as: Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects. A Inheritance B Polymorphism C Abstraction D Encapsulation Encapsulation. The question specifically asks about placing data and methods inside one entity. ADB02 identifies that grouping as encapsulation, along with controlled access to implementation details. Abstraction concerns what the contract exposes; inheritance derives compatible subtypes; polymorphism invokes different implementations through a common interface. None of those replaces the state-and-method grouping named in the stem. A incorrect Inheritance derives a subtype and reuses superclass features rather than naming state/method grouping. B incorrect Polymorphism varies implementations behind a compatible common interface rather than grouping data and methods. C incorrect Abstraction presents a relevant contract; the specific grouping asked for is encapsulation. D correct Encapsulation packages state and operations together within the object boundary.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 79 · AM0190
records.text: AM0190 Question 79 ADB02 The object-oriented model supports the concept of association, which represents: Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects. A Inheritance relationships between classes B Shared attributes among objects C The interactions between objects D Data duplication in the database Links and interactions between objects. ADB02 defines association as links between objects, commonly implemented with references, and describes methods invoking operations on other objects. C is the closest description of that collaboration. An association is not an is-a inheritance hierarchy, shared attribute definitions or duplication. For example, Student belonging to Department links objects without making either a subtype of the other. A incorrect Inheritance is an is-a relationship between types, distinct from association links between objects. B incorrect Having similar attributes does not itself define an association between particular objects. C correct Associations link objects and support their interactions or collaboration through references. D incorrect Association represents relationships rather than duplicated copies of the same database facts.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 80 · AM0191
records.text: AM0191 Question 80 ADB03 ADB02 Circle and Rectangle already inherit from Shape. A Shape reference can hold either object and dispatch area() to its actual implementation at runtime. Which concept names this common-interface use, rather than the structural subtype relationship? Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface. A Polymorphism B Inheritance C Abstraction D Encapsulation A. Polymorphism Subtype polymorphism allows a common superclass or interface reference to denote different compatible subclass objects. Dispatching area() according to whether the actual object is a Circle or Rectangle is that runtime use. Inheritance establishes the subtype relationship already given in the stem. Abstraction exposes a contract and encapsulation controls representation, but neither names this particular substitutable runtime dispatch. A correct Using one superclass interface with subclass-specific dispatch is subtype polymorphism. B incorrect Inheritance is the established structural prerequisite, not the runtime use requested. C incorrect Abstraction describes a contract rather than the dispatch behavior. D incorrect Encapsulation controls internal representation and access.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 81 · AM0192
records.text: AM0192 Question 81 ADB02 ADB03 What is the purpose of abstraction in the object-oriented model? Separate the object boundary, the exposed contract and links between objects. A To combine multiple classes into a single entity B To hide the internal details of an object C To establish relationships between objects D To define the attributes and behaviors of a class Hide implementation details while exposing a relevant contract. ADB02 explains abstraction through an operation's relevant contract: what withdrawal does is exposed without showing how storage implements it. B captures hiding those irrelevant internal details. This overlaps encapsulation, but abstraction emphasizes the view or contract. Combining classes, creating associations or listing class members is not its defining purpose. A incorrect Abstraction does not mean merging several classes into one entity. B correct Abstraction exposes relevant behavior while hiding implementation details from the client view. C incorrect Establishing links between objects is association rather than abstraction's defining purpose. D incorrect A class specifies attributes and behavior; abstraction chooses the relevant contract exposed to users.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 82 · AM0193
records.text: AM0193 Question 82 ADB03 The concept of polymorphism allows objects to: Distinguish the subtype relationship from use through a common interface. A Inherit attributes from multiple classes B Change their class dynamically at runtime C Access private methods of other objects D Be treated as objects of different classes Use an object through a compatible superclass or interface type. ADB03 allows a superclass or interface reference to denote compatible subclass objects. D is correct in that sense: the same object can be treated through its actual type and a compatible supertype. This does not permit arbitrary conversion to unrelated classes. Multiple inheritance, runtime class mutation and access to another object's private methods are different concepts and are not granted by polymorphism. A incorrect Inheriting from multiple classes is multiple inheritance, not the operation described by polymorphism. B incorrect Polymorphism does not change the actual class of an object dynamically. C incorrect Polymorphism does not bypass private-access restrictions on other objects. D correct An object can be used through compatible superclass/interface types; this does not mean arbitrary unrelated classes.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 83 · AM0194
records.text: AM0194 Question 83 ADB01 Which concept in the object-oriented model defines the structure and behavior of objects? Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity. A Class B Object C Attribute D Method Class. A class is the specification that defines attributes and operations for its instances, as ADB01 states. An object is an instance conforming to that specification. An attribute accounts for part of state and a method for one operation, but neither individually defines the whole structure and behavior of the object type. A correct A class specifies the structure and available operations for its object instances. B incorrect An object is one instance of the specification rather than the specification itself. C incorrect An attribute represents part of an object's state rather than its whole structure and behavior. D incorrect A method implements an operation but does not alone define the complete object type.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 84 · AM0195
records.text: AM0195 Question 84 ADB27 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method aims to restore the database to a previous consistent state by undoing the effects of incomplete or failed transactions? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Rollback recovery B Redo recovery C Checkpoint recovery D Restart recovery Rollback recovery Undo restores before images and removes after images; failed transactions that updated the database must roll back (p.107). This directly answers the specific action, although undo may be one phase of broader crash recovery. A correct Rollback is the direct undo operation. B incorrect Redo restores after images instead. C incorrect Checkpoints synchronize database and log; they do not name the undo action. D incorrect A restart can include undo, but is broader than the requested failed-transaction reversal.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 85 · AM0196
records.text: AM0196 Question 85 ADB27 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method involves reapplying the changes made by committed transactions from a log file to restore the database? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Redo recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery Redo recovery If a transaction committed but its buffers did not reach disk, recovery redoes its updates for durability (p.103). Redo restores after images (p.107), whose log records are required before commit (p.104). A correct Redo is exactly reapplying logged committed updates. B incorrect A checkpoint reduces the amount of recovery work; it is not the replay operation. C incorrect Restart recovery can invoke redo but names a larger process. D incorrect A backup restores a stored database copy, not this specific logged replay.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 86 · AM0197
records.text: AM0197 Question 86 ADB30 ADB27 Which recovery method involves creating checkpoints at regular intervals to save the current state of the database and transaction logs? Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it. A Checkpoint recovery B Redo recovery C Rollback recovery D Restart recovery Checkpoint recovery Checkpointing synchronizes database and log (p.105); its listed steps force modified buffers to disk, write a checkpoint record, and save the log (p.107). This is not necessarily a full database backup. A correct The named synchronization procedure matches. B incorrect Redo reapplies after images, not periodic synchronization. C incorrect Rollback restores before images. D incorrect Restart follows failure, whereas checkpoints are established during operation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 87 · AM0198
records.text: AM0198 Question 87 ADB26 ADB27 ADB30 Which recovery method involves restarting the system and recovering the database by applying the necessary redo and undo operations? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Restart recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Redo recovery D Rollback recovery Restart recovery Recovery from a non-catastrophic crash may combine undo and redo (pp.103,107). A is the best descriptive name for restarting and performing that combined recovery, although the module does not define four mutually exclusive method classes under these exact option names. A correct Restart recovery describes the complete post-crash recovery process stated in the stem. B incorrect Checkpointing supplies a saved starting boundary rather than the whole restart process. C incorrect Redo supplies only the forward part of the stated combination. D incorrect Rollback supplies only the undo part.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 88 · AM0199
records.text: AM0199 Question 88 ADB26 ADB27 Which recovery method involves restoring the database from a backup copy taken prior to the failure? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Backup recovery B Rollback recovery C Redo recovery D Restart recovery Backup recovery For catastrophic damage the module restores a past database copy from backup storage and reconstructs committed operations from the backup log (p.103). A names restoration of that backup copy; a backup alone may need subsequent log replay. A correct Restoration from a stored copy is the stated backup operation. B incorrect Rollback reverses updates using before images, not a backup copy. C incorrect Redo replays logged changes, which may supplement backup restoration. D incorrect Restart names an overall recovery process rather than its backup-copy source.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 89 · AM0200
records.text: AM0200 Question 89 ADB26 ADB27 ADB30 Which recovery method is used to recover the database after a media failure, such as a disk crash? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Backup recovery B Redo recovery C Checkpoint recovery D Rollback recovery Backup recovery Disk-head crash is media failure (p.97). Where that destroys database contents, the catastrophic-recovery strategy restores a past backup and then reconstructs committed operations from the backup log (p.103). A correct A backup supplies contents lost in the media failure. B incorrect Redo can advance a restored copy but alone assumes data pages available to update. C incorrect A checkpoint is not a replacement copy of a destroyed database. D incorrect Undo cannot recreate arbitrary destroyed pages by reversing incomplete transactions alone.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 90 · AM0201
records.text: AM0201 Question 90 ADB30 ADB26 ADB27 A crash-recovery system has a long log history and wants to reduce the log-search work compared with scanning all history. Which method adds durable recovery-state records for that purpose? Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it. A Redo recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Backup recovery D Rollback recovery B. Checkpoint recovery Checkpoints record durable recovery state so recovery need not inspect all old history. That is the requested mechanism for reducing log-search work. Redo reinstalls missing changes, rollback removes incomplete effects and backup recovery starts from a separate copy. They may cooperate with checkpoints, but their defining actions do not name the added recovery-state boundary specified in this question. A incorrect Redo applies logged after-images rather than defining the recovery-state boundary. B correct Checkpoint information reduces how much old history must be searched. C incorrect A backup is a separate stored copy rather than the stated history-bounding record. D incorrect Rollback reverses incomplete effects rather than adding this recovery-state boundary.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 91 · AM0202
records.text: AM0202 Question 91 ADB27 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method is focused on ensuring that all committed changes are durable and can survive system failures? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Redo recovery B Restart recovery C Rollback recovery D Checkpoint recovery Redo recovery Durability requires committed effects to survive crashes (p.97). The module specifically redoes committed updates lost between commit and buffer flushing (p.103), making redo the direct mechanism asked for. A correct Redo reapplies the missing committed updates. B incorrect Restart is a broader process that can invoke redo and undo. C incorrect Rollback preserves atomicity by removing uncommitted effects. D incorrect Checkpoints reduce replay work but are not the committed-update replay operation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 92 · AM0203
records.text: AM0203 Question 92 ADB27 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method uses the transaction log to identify the changes made by transactions and undo the effects of incomplete or failed transactions? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Rollback recovery B Redo recovery C Checkpoint recovery D Restart recovery Rollback recovery Before images logged under WAL permit undo of failed transaction effects (p.104); rollback restores them (p.107). The stem specifies this particular operation rather than all crash-recovery phases. A correct Rollback is the direct log-based undo operation. B incorrect Redo restores new values instead of removing failed updates. C incorrect Checkpointing records a synchronization boundary. D incorrect Restart can include rollback, but is broader than the named reversal.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 93 · AM0204
records.text: AM0204 Question 93 ADB26 ADB27 ADB30 Which recovery method is used to recover the database after a system crash or power failure? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Restart recovery B Backup recovery C Redo recovery D Checkpoint recovery Restart recovery For a recoverable system crash, recovery uses undo/redo to restore consistency (pp.103,107). A is the broad descriptive answer for restarting the failed system. If power failure also destroys media, backup restoration may additionally be required; the question supplies no such destruction. A correct Restart recovery denotes the overall post-crash process. B incorrect Backup is required for damaged/lost storage, which is not specified here. C incorrect Redo alone may be insufficient when incomplete transactions reached disk. D incorrect A checkpoint assists recovery but does not itself execute the full crash recovery.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 94 · AM0205
records.text: AM0205 Question 94 ADB26 What is the primary goal of database recovery after a failure? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Restoring the database to a previous state B Preventing future failures from occurring C Optimizing database performance D Enforcing data integrity constraints Restoring the database to a previous state The explicit purpose is bringing the database into its last consistent state before failure (p.97). A is correct only with this consistency qualification; restoring an arbitrary earlier corrupt state is not the goal. A correct Read previous state as the last consistent state, as stated. B incorrect Recovery handles failures rather than preventing all future ones. C incorrect Performance is not the stated recovery purpose. D incorrect Integrity is relevant, but constraint enforcement is not the direct restoration objective stated here.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 95 · AM0206
records.text: AM0206 Question 95 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method involves periodically making a copy of the entire database onto a separate storage medium? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery Backup recovery A full backup copies the database to separate storage so it can later be restored, often followed by replay of archived logs. Rollback reverses failed transaction work; restart recovery restores a valid state after a crash. A checkpoint records recovery state to reduce log-search and recovery work and is not a full independent database copy. The question's periodic separate copy is therefore the backup mechanism, represented by backup recovery. A incorrect Incorrect: rollback reverses transaction effects rather than making an independent database copy. B incorrect Incorrect: checkpointing records recovery state and limits recovery work; it is not a full backup. C incorrect Incorrect: restart recovery is the crash-recovery process, not the periodic creation of a separate copy. D correct Correct: backup recovery relies on a stored independent database copy.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 96 · AM0207
records.text: AM0207 Question 96 ADB27 ADB26 ADB30 Which recovery method involves undoing the effects of incomplete or failed transactions? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery Rollback recovery The module calls undoing a failed transaction rollback and specifies restoring before images (p.107). A therefore directly names removal of incomplete effects. A correct Rollback is the named undo operation. B incorrect Checkpoint is synchronization, not transaction reversal. C incorrect Restart can include undo but is the wider process. D incorrect Backup restores a past copy instead of directly reversing this transaction.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 97 · AM0208
records.text: AM0208 Question 97 ADB30 ADB07 What is the purpose of a checkpoint in the recovery process? Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it. A To save the current state of the database B To recover from a system crash C To log all transaction operations D To enforce data integrity constraints To save the current state of the database A checkpoint synchronizes database and log by forcing modified buffers and recording the checkpoint (pp.105,107), saving a durable recovery boundary and reducing later work. It is not necessarily a full snapshot copy. A correct Saving synchronized current state best matches the listed procedure. B incorrect Crash recovery uses checkpoints, but this is a later use rather than checkpoint creation itself. C incorrect Logging every operation is the transaction log’s role, not checkpoint’s distinguishing purpose. D incorrect Constraint enforcement is not the checkpoint procedure.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 98 · AM0209
records.text: AM0209 Question 98 ADB30 ADB26 ADB27 In a log-based crash restart that uses durable checkpoint state plus relevant transaction logs, which listed labels describe the checkpoint-assisted technique and its overall restoration process? Select all that apply. Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery B. Checkpoint recovery; C. Restart recovery Checkpoint-assisted recovery uses recorded recovery state to limit the necessary log history. Restart recovery is the overall process that restores a valid state after the crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects. Both labels describe the specified procedure at different levels. Rollback names only undo work, and backup recovery would require starting from a separate stored copy. A incorrect Rollback specifically undoes incomplete effects rather than naming the checkpoint-plus-log restart procedure. B correct Checkpoint-assisted recovery uses durable checkpoint information with the relevant log history. C correct Restart recovery can use checkpoints and transaction logs to reconstruct valid state. D incorrect Backup recovery starts from a separate database copy, which the description does not mention.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 99 · AM0210
records.text: AM0210 Question 99 ADB26 ADB32 Which overall crash-recovery process preserves durable committed work and removes incomplete effects after a system failure, leaving any business-level retry of formerly active transactions to a new controlled attempt? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery C. Restart recovery Restart recovery restores a valid database state after a crash. It preserves durable committed effects and removes incomplete effects using the required recovery mechanisms. Transactions active at failure are not automatically rerun and committed; a business retry is a separate controlled attempt. Rollback and checkpoint processing can be components, while backup recovery starts from another stored copy when that is needed. A incorrect Rollback names undo of incomplete work rather than the entire restart process. B incorrect Checkpoint information guides recovery rather than naming its whole process. C correct Restart recovery is the overall crash-restoration process described. D incorrect Backup restoration starts from a separate copy, which this scenario does not require.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 100 · AM0212
records.text: AM0212 Question 100 ADB26 ADB27 ADB30 After a power failure loses volatile memory but leaves persistent storage intact, which term names the overall process that restores a valid database while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects? Choose the umbrella process rather than one component. Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery C. Restart recovery Restart recovery is the overall restoration process following a system crash or power loss when persistent storage survives. It preserves durable commits and removes incomplete effects using the appropriate logged recovery work. Rollback may supply undo and checkpoints can shorten log searches, but these are cooperating mechanisms within the process. Backup restoration addresses a separate stored copy and is not required by this stated failure. A incorrect Rollback is an undo component rather than the overall process. B incorrect Checkpoint-assisted work guides restart rather than naming its umbrella process. C correct Restart recovery names the complete restoration after this system crash. D incorrect The stated intact persistent storage does not call for restoring a separate backup.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 101 · AM0213
records.text: AM0213 Question 101 ADB27 ADB30 ADB26 In a conventional transaction-log system, which listed mechanisms use logged updates or checkpoint/log state for undo or restart? Select all that apply. Backup recovery in D means restoring only a standalone full backup, without replaying archived logs. Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery A. Rollback recovery; B. Checkpoint recovery; C. Restart recovery Logged rollback uses before-images to remove incomplete effects. Checkpoint-assisted recovery combines durable recovery state with relevant log history, and log-based restart uses that history to preserve commits and remove incomplete work. All three fit the specified model. A standalone backup restore instead copies a separately stored database image; the question excludes archived-log replay from D so that this alternative does not overlap. A correct The logged rollback uses before-images for undo. B correct Checkpoint-assisted recovery uses recovery-state records and relevant log history. C correct The specified log-based restart uses durable transaction history. D incorrect A standalone image restore without log replay does not use the specified logged recovery mechanism.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 102 · AM0214
records.text: AM0214 Question 102 ADB26 Which recovery method is used to recover from media failures, such as disk crashes? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Rollback recovery B Checkpoint recovery C Restart recovery D Backup recovery Backup recovery For disk media destruction, restore a backup copy and reconstruct committed operations from the backup log (p.103). D supplies the missing database contents. A incorrect Undo alone does not recreate a destroyed database copy. B incorrect Checkpoint synchronization alone is not an independent media backup. C incorrect A restart without restoring lost storage is insufficient. D correct Backup recovery is the required catastrophic/media restoration approach.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 103 · AM0215
records.text: AM0215 Question 103 ADB33 What is a distributed database system? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A A database system that is spread across multiple locations B A database system that uses multiple database management systems C A database system that supports multiple database schemas D A database system that is used for storing distributed data A database system that is spread across multiple locations A DDB is multiple logically related databases distributed over a computer network, managed transparently (p.114). A captures the physical distribution; logical relatedness and coordinated management are implicit qualifications. A correct Multiple locations captures the defining distribution. B incorrect Different DBMS products are not required; homogeneous DDBs exist. C incorrect Multiple schemas are not the physical distribution definition. D incorrect Storing distributed data is circular and omits the network/location criterion.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 104 · AM0216
records.text: AM0216 Question 104 ADB33 ADB37 What is the key advantage of a distributed database system? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A Improved data security B Reduced data redundancy C Enhanced data availability D Simplified data querying Enhanced data availability Multiple nodes allow others to do the job if one fails (p.116), improving availability. The module lists integrity/security difficulty and complexity among disadvantages (p.117). A incorrect Improved security is not guaranteed; distributed access complicates control. B incorrect Replication stores multiple copies rather than necessarily reducing redundancy. C correct Availability is explicitly improved through multiple nodes. D incorrect Querying across sites adds network and optimization complexity rather than inherently simplifying it.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 105 · AM0217
records.text: AM0217 Question 105 ADB33 ADB34 What is a homogenous distributed database system? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A A system that uses the same database management system across all sites B A system that stores the same type of data across all sites C A system that uses a single database schema across all sites D A system that shares the same network infrastructure across all sites A system that uses the same database management system across all sites A homogeneous distributed database uses the same or compatible DBMS technology at its sites. Sharing data types, a schema or network infrastructure does not by itself establish that DBMS property. In particular, identical DBMS technology does not force all local schemas to be identical, and compatible structures alone do not prove identical DBMSs. The definition concerns the database-management technology, so A identifies the relevant criterion without adding unnecessary sameness requirements. A correct Correct: the same DBMS technology across sites meets the homogeneous-system criterion. B incorrect Incorrect: matching data types alone does not establish that the sites use the same DBMS technology. C incorrect Incorrect: schema agreement alone does not establish DBMS homogeneity, and same DBMS technology need not imply identical local schemas. D incorrect Incorrect: shared networking does not establish the database-management technology used at the sites.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 106 · AM0218
records.text: AM0218 Question 106 ADB33 What is a heterogeneous distributed database system? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A A system that uses different database management systems across all sites B A system that stores different types of data across all sites C A system that uses different database schemas across all sites D A system that uses different network infrastructures across all sites A system that uses different database management systems across all sites Heterogeneous means at least one database is from a different vendor (p.119), supporting different DBMS software. It does not require every pair of sites to differ; A’s all sites must be read as across the participating sites, not pairwise uniqueness. A correct Different database-system vendors/software captures the defining distinction with the stated qualification. B incorrect Different content/types alone do not establish vendor heterogeneity. C incorrect Federated systems may have one conceptual schema despite heterogeneity. D incorrect Network differences are not the database-vendor definition.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 107 · AM0219
records.text: AM0219 Question 107 ADB36 ADB37 ADB24 What is data fragmentation in a distributed database system? Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation. A Storing data in multiple copies at different sites B Dividing data into smaller subsets and storing them at different sites C Merging data from different sites into a single copy D Replicating data across all sites in the system Dividing data into smaller subsets and storing them at different sites Fragmentation splits a relation into logically related correct parts (p.117); horizontal fragments select rows and vertical fragments select columns (p.118). B describes storing these subsets across sites. A incorrect Multiple identical copies describe replication. B correct Smaller subsets describe fragmentation. C incorrect Merging is reconstruction/integration, the opposite direction from splitting. D incorrect Copying data to all sites is replication rather than fragmentation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 108 · AM0220
records.text: AM0220 Question 108 ADB37 ADB36 ADB24 What is data replication in a distributed database system? Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost. A Storing data in multiple copies at different sites B Dividing data into smaller subsets and storing them at different sites C Merging data from different sites into a single copy D Deleting data that is no longer needed from the database Storing data in multiple copies at different sites Replication maintains several identical copies of a relation at different sites (p.117). This differs from dividing it into fragments. A correct Multiple copies at different sites exactly matches. B incorrect Subsets describe fragmentation. C incorrect Merging into one copy is not maintaining multiple copies. D incorrect Deletion removes data rather than replicating it.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 109 · AM0221
records.text: AM0221 Question 109 ADB35 Which transparency hides the physical site storing a named database object, so users can refer to that object without specifying its site? Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user. A Local-only data access B Fragmentation transparency C Location transparency D Replication transparency Location transparency Location transparency hides the physical site holding a named logical object. Fragmentation transparency instead hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments, while replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. Those properties can coexist in a distributed database, so a vague single-logical-database experience would not identify only one. The revised stem isolates hidden site placement. Local-only access restricts what can be accessed rather than making remote placement transparent. A incorrect Incorrect: restricting access to local data does not hide the placement of a named distributed object. B incorrect Incorrect: fragmentation transparency hides splitting and reconstruction, not specifically the object's physical site. C correct Correct: location transparency hides which physical site stores the named object. D incorrect Incorrect: replication transparency hides copy selection and maintenance, not specifically site placement.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 110 · AM0222
records.text: AM0222 Question 110 ADB35 A user explicitly names a fragment and can query it without specifying or knowing the physical site that stores it. Which transparency is being provided? The existence of the fragment is visible. Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user. A Local-only data access B Fragmentation transparency C Location transparency D Replication transparency Location transparency Location transparency hides the physical site storing a named object. The user in this scenario still names the fragment, so fragmentation remains visible; fragmentation transparency would hide the split and reconstruction. Replication transparency hides which copy is selected or maintained. Restricting users to local data is an access limitation rather than concealment of a remote fragment's placement. C therefore identifies the particular hidden detail without treating all transparency properties as interchangeable. A incorrect Incorrect: local-only access restricts accessible data rather than hiding a named remote fragment's physical site. B incorrect Incorrect: the user explicitly names the fragment, so its existence is not hidden. C correct Correct: the fragment's physical site is hidden while its logical name remains usable. D incorrect Incorrect: replica selection and maintenance are different hidden details from the specified site placement.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 111 · AM0223
records.text: AM0223 Question 111 ADB35 Which data transparency level ensures that users are not aware of the presence of multiple copies of data in different sites? Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user. A Local data transparency B Fragmentation transparency C Location transparency D Replication transparency Replication transparency The module combines transparent distribution (p.114) with replication as storing copies at multiple sites (pp.116–117). Hiding this copying is replication transparency. A incorrect Local transparency does not identify multiple copies. B incorrect Fragmentation concerns subsets rather than duplicates. C incorrect Location hides placement but does not specifically name the copying aspect. D correct Replication transparency is the copy-specific aspect.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 112 · AM0224
records.text: AM0224 Question 112 ADB38 ADB39 ADB24 ADB34 What is the role of a distributed query processor in a distributed database system? Compare local processing with the bytes and messages moved between sites. A It ensures the consistency of data across all sites. B It manages the distribution and retrieval of data across multiple sites. C It controls the access permissions of users in the system. D It handles the physical storage of data at each site. It manages the distribution and retrieval of data across multiple sites. Distributed query processing compares moving source relations and results among sites, selecting the lower-transfer strategy (pp.120–121). B best captures distributed retrieval, understood as planning transfers for a query rather than deciding the physical database design. A incorrect Global consistency is assigned to concurrency control/recovery rather than query transfer planning. B correct Managing query data transfer and retrieval matches the worked example. C incorrect Access permissions are authorization, not the worked query role. D incorrect Physical local storage management is not choosing distributed query strategies.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 113 · AM0230
records.text: AM0230 Question 113 ADB33 ADB37 Which condition specifically makes a distributed database environment homogeneous, rather than merely being useful for distributed operation? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A Consistency of database schemas across all sites B Compatibility of network infrastructures across all sites C Standardization of database management systems across all sites D Replication of data at each site for fault tolerance Standardization of database management systems across all sites Homogeneity is defined by using the same or compatible DBMS technology across sites. Schema compatibility, functioning network connections and replication can be useful design concerns, but none alone establishes that common DBMS technology. A homogeneous system may have different local schemas, and replication is not required merely because data is distributed. Narrowing the question to the defining condition preserves C while acknowledging that the other design concerns can matter in practice. A incorrect Incorrect: schema compatibility can be useful but does not establish common DBMS technology. B incorrect Incorrect: compatible networking supports communication but does not establish DBMS homogeneity. C correct Correct: DBMS standardization supplies the defining common technology across sites. D incorrect Incorrect: replication can improve availability but is optional and does not define homogeneity.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 114 · AM0231
records.text: AM0231 Question 114 ADB33 ADB40 ADB37 A heterogeneous distributed database retains different local DBMSs and schemas and must integrate them without requiring full replication. Which integration requirements apply? Select all that apply. D means coherent schema semantics through mappings, not identical schemas. Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A Replication of data at each site for fault tolerance B Standardization of database management systems across all sites C Compatibility of network infrastructures across all sites D Consistency of database schemas across all sites C. Compatibility of network infrastructures across all sites; D. Consistency of database schemas across all sites Integration requires interoperable communication so requests and results can move between sites. It also requires coherent mappings for names, types, identifiers and other schema meanings. These support C and D. Replacing every DBMS with one product would remove the retained heterogeneity, and full replication is an optional placement decision rather than a requirement for integrating different local systems. A incorrect Copying all data everywhere is not required for the stated integration. B incorrect The scenario retains differing DBMSs rather than replacing all with one standard. C correct Interoperable communication is needed to exchange requests and results. D correct Mappings must reconcile schema meanings without requiring identical local schemas.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 115 · AM0232
records.text: AM0232 Question 115 ADB38 ADB22 Which approach is commonly used for query processing in a distributed database system? Compare local processing with the bytes and messages moved between sites. A Centralized query processing B Distributed query processing C Parallel query processing D Sequential query processing Distributed query processing The module’s distributed-query section compares execution and data-transfer locations among multiple sites (pp.120–121). B names the overall approach. A chosen plan may execute a particular join at one site; that does not make the whole system centralized. A incorrect A local execution site can be part of a distributed plan, but centralized processing does not name the chapter’s overall approach. B correct Distributed query processing matches the section and cross-site strategies. C incorrect Parallelism may be used, but simultaneous execution is not required by these examples. D incorrect A plan may contain sequential operations; this does not identify cross-site processing.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 116 · AM0233
records.text: AM0233 Question 116 ADB39 ADB06 ADB38 ADB24 What is the role of a distributed transaction coordinator in a distributed database system? Distinguish coordinated transaction outcome from concurrent access and local storage. A It ensures the consistency of data across all sites. B It manages the distribution and retrieval of data across multiple sites. C It controls the access permissions of users in the system. D It handles the physical storage of data at each site. It ensures the consistency of data across all sites. Global consistency is required of concurrency/recovery (p.122). Under the primary-site technique a coordinator manages transaction concurrency and commit (p.123). A is supported in that transaction-coordination sense, rather than as an unconditional guarantee against every error. A correct Coordination of concurrency and commit maintains transaction consistency across sites. B incorrect Query transfer/retrieval is a separate distributed-query task. C incorrect User permissions are authorization, not commit coordination. D incorrect Local physical storage is not the primary coordinator’s stated function.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 117 · AM0234
records.text: AM0234 Question 117 ADB37 Which listed approaches are replication policies or transfer methods in distributed databases, allowing dimensions to coexist? Select all that apply. Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost. A Eager replication B Lazy replication C Snapshot replication D Incremental replication A. Eager replication; B. Lazy replication; C. Snapshot replication; D. Incremental replication Eager and lazy replication differ in when propagation occurs relative to the acknowledgment or commit point. Snapshot and incremental replication differ in whether a copy or changes are transferred. These are legitimate replication dimensions and can coexist, so all four qualify. The question asks for recognized approaches rather than claiming that one policy is most prevalent or universally preferable. A correct Eager replication coordinates propagation before the specified acknowledgment or commit point. B correct Lazy replication propagates changes later and can expose stale reads or require conflict handling. C correct Snapshot replication distributes a copy at intervals rather than necessarily sending each individual update. D correct Incremental replication transfers changes and can coexist with a propagation-timing policy.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 118 · AM0235
records.text: AM0235 Question 118 ADB19 ADB38 When comparing distributed query strategies, which factors can affect estimated execution cost or replica placement decisions? Select all that apply. Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies. A Cost of query execution B Size of the database C Network bandwidth D Data replication A. Cost of query execution; B. Size of the database; C. Network bandwidth; D. Data replication Execution cost summarizes the resources consumed by a candidate plan. Relation sizes affect scans and intermediate work, network bandwidth affects data-transfer time, and replica placement changes which copies are available near the computation. All these inputs can alter a distributed strategy's cost. They are complementary considerations rather than competing names for one exclusively important factor. A correct Estimated execution cost is the explicit basis for comparing candidate strategies. B correct Database and relation sizes affect scan work, intermediate sizes and algorithm feasibility. C correct Bandwidth affects transfer time when data or results move between sites. D correct Replica locations affect which copy can serve a query and its communication cost.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 119 · AM0236
records.text: AM0236 Question 119 ADB17 ADB19 ADB06 ADB24 What is the purpose of query optimization in a database system? Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A To ensure data consistency B To minimize query execution time C To maximize data replication D To manage database security To minimize query execution time Query optimization chooses an efficient execution strategy and minimizes resource usage including response time (p.27). Page 30 explicitly seeks faster queries and the most efficient sequence of steps. A incorrect Consistency is a transaction correctness concern, not the stated optimization objective. B correct Minimizing execution/response time captures the efficiency objective. C incorrect Maximizing replication is not the execution-plan goal. D incorrect Authorization/security is not query optimization’s stated purpose.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 120 · AM0237
records.text: AM0237 Question 120 ADB17 ADB-S01 ADB23 What is a query plan in a database system? Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A A set of database schemas B A representation of the query result C A sequence of operations to execute a query D A collection of database indices A sequence of operations to execute a query An execution plan includes a relational-algebra query tree, access methods and operator implementations (p.44). Its operations run from leaves toward the root (p.29), so C captures the execution procedure, which can have a tree structure rather than a single linear list. A incorrect Schemas describe data structure rather than the executable operations. B incorrect The result is the output, whereas the plan specifies how to obtain it. C correct An operation sequence/tree with access methods is the stated plan concept. D incorrect Indices may be access methods within a plan but do not alone constitute it.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 121 · AM0238
records.text: AM0238 Question 121 ADB19 What is a cost model in query optimization? Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies. A A statistical model of query execution times B A model for estimating the cost of query plans C A model for analyzing database schemas D A statistical model for data distribution A model for estimating the cost of query plans The cost function combines I/O, CPU, communication and storage (p.41); optimization estimates and compares alternative strategy costs (p.42). A cost model therefore estimates costs of query plans. A incorrect Execution time can contribute, but this is narrower than the listed resource-cost model. B correct Estimating plan costs is the defining function. C incorrect Schema analysis is not evaluation of competing execution strategies. D incorrect Data distribution statistics are possible inputs, not the whole cost model.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 122 · AM0239
records.text: AM0239 Question 122 ADB-S01 ADB18 What is a join operation in query processing? Separate the query's representation from the operations used to calculate its result. A Combining tuples from multiple tables based on a common attribute B Sorting the query result in ascending order C Grouping the query result based on a specific attribute D Filtering the query result based on a condition Combining tuples from multiple tables based on a common attribute The query joins Staff and Branch by matching branchNo (p.27). The heuristic combines a Cartesian product and selection on the join condition into a join (p.41); the distributed example similarly matches Employee.Dno and Department.Dnumber (p.120). A expresses this equijoin case; joins in general need not always use equality or identical attribute names. A correct Combining tuples that satisfy the matching attribute condition describes these joins. B incorrect Sorting changes order rather than combining source tuples. C incorrect Grouping builds groups/aggregates, not cross-relation matching. D incorrect Filtering alone selects rows rather than combining related tuples from tables.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 123 · AM0240
records.text: AM0240 Question 123 ADB23 Which listed index or clustered-storage approaches can speed a suitable query workload, without a claim that any always wins? Select all that apply. Match the predicate and workload to the access structure or reasons to choose a plan again. A B-tree index B Hash index C Bitmap index D Clustered index A. B-tree index; B. Hash index; C. Bitmap index; D. Clustered index B-tree indexes support ordered and range access, hash indexes target equality, and bitmap indexes can support analytic selections. Clustered storage places related rows close together and can reduce access work for suitable queries. Each approach can therefore help an appropriate workload. Space, maintenance and selectivity still matter, so accepting all four does not claim that every query benefits or that one design is universally best. A correct B-tree indexes support selective ordered and range access for suitable queries. B correct Hash indexes can accelerate equality lookups on the indexed key. C correct Bitmap indexes can accelerate suitable analytic selection workloads. D correct Clustered storage keeps related rows close and can reduce reads for appropriate access patterns.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 124 · AM0241
records.text: AM0241 Question 124 ADB23 What is query re-optimization in a database system? Match the predicate and workload to the access structure or reasons to choose a plan again. A Re-executing the query with different parameters B Re-evaluating the query cost based on updated statistics C Re-writing the query in a different query language D Re-organizing the database schema to improve performance Reconsider the plan using updated cost information or statistics. ADB23 defines re-optimization as choosing a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest that the existing plan is unsuitable. B is the listed description of this cost reconsideration. Merely executing again with other values does not necessarily re-optimize, and changing the query language or redesigning the schema is not the definition. A incorrect Re-execution with new parameters can reuse the same plan and is not inherently re-optimization. B correct Updated statistics can change cost estimates and lead to choosing a new execution plan. C incorrect Changing query language is not required to reconsider an execution strategy. D incorrect Schema reorganization is a design change rather than the definition of query re-optimization.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 125 · AM0242
records.text: AM0242 Question 125 ADB22 What is query pipelining in query processing? Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects. A Dividing a query into subqueries and executing them in parallel B Dividing a query into stages and executing them sequentially C Dividing a query into multiple queries and executing them in parallel D Dividing a query into multiple stages and executing them concurrently Dividing a query into multiple stages and executing them concurrently Pipelined evaluation evaluates several operations simultaneously and passes results directly from one to the next (p.44). D means overlapping producer/consumer stages, not necessarily executing independent whole queries. A incorrect Parallel independent subqueries are not the defining inter-operator tuple stream. B incorrect Pure sequential completion of each whole stage loses the stated simultaneous overlap. C incorrect Multiple independent queries are not the defining pipeline within an expression tree. D correct Concurrent overlapping stages passing tuples match the explicit definition.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 126 · AM0243
records.text: AM0243 Question 126 ADB22 ADB19 What is query result caching, specifically caching returned answers rather than execution plans or intermediate rows? Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects. A Storing query results for future reuse B Storing intermediate results during query execution C Storing database metadata for query optimization D Storing query plans for efficient execution A. Storing query results for future reuse Result caching stores a query's returned rows or answer for future reuse. It needs suitable invalidation when underlying data changes. Plan caching instead stores the execution strategy without its returned rows. Intermediate rows retained during one execution are materialization, while database metadata supports optimization. Naming the cached object makes result caching distinct from these other useful storage mechanisms. A correct This stores final query answers for future reuse. B incorrect Intermediate-row storage is materialization rather than final-answer caching. C incorrect Metadata supports optimization but is not the query's returned answer. D incorrect Plan caching stores strategy rather than returned rows.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 127 · AM0244
records.text: AM0244 Question 127 ADB22 ADB17 What is query parallelization in query processing? Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects. A Dividing a query into subqueries and executing them in parallel B Dividing a query into stages and executing them sequentially C Dividing a query into multiple queries and executing them in parallel D Dividing a query into multiple stages and executing them concurrently Dividing a query into subqueries and executing them in parallel The fragmentation discussion says a transaction can be divided into several subqueries operating on fragments, increasing concurrency (p.117). A matches this parallel decomposition; it is distinct from pipelining a dependent stream of stages. A correct Independent fragment subqueries can run in parallel as described. B incorrect Sequential stages do not supply parallelism. C incorrect Replacing one query with multiple separate whole queries is not the stated subquery decomposition. D incorrect Concurrent stages describe pipelining when results flow between dependent operators, not the specific fragment-subquery approach.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 128 · CS0066
records.text: CS0066 Question 128 ADB27 ADB06 If power went off while processing a transaction, what should the DBMS do to reverse any changes made to the database? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Read_transaction B Fail transaction C Commit transaction D Rollback Rollback To reverse changes of an incomplete failed transaction, recovery undoes its effects (p.103) by restoring before images (p.107). This is rollback. A committed transaction instead requires durability, so the answer assumes the interrupted transaction had not committed, as implied by reverse any changes. A incorrect Reading a transaction is not an undo operation. B incorrect Marking failure does not itself restore old values. C incorrect Committing would preserve rather than reverse the changes. D correct Rollback/undo is the direct reversal mechanism.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 129 · NS0051
records.text: NS0051 Question 129 ADB33 What is the main difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous distributed databases? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. Homogeneous systems use compatible DBMS technology; heterogeneous systems integrate differing DBMSs, models, schemas or interfaces. ADB33 defines the distinction through compatibility of database technology and representation. Operating-system differences can occur but do not define heterogeneity. Homogeneous sites need not have identical schemas or automatic replication. Heterogeneous integration requires explicit mappings for names, types and semantics, rather than assuming that common connectivity alone reconciles their meanings.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 130 · NS0052
records.text: NS0052 Question 130 ADB36 Why is data fragmentation useful in distributed databases? Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation. Fragmentation improves locality, manageable placement and parallelism by splitting data across useful site boundaries. ADB36 splits rows with predicates and columns with projections while preserving reconstruction through unions or key joins. This can place frequently used data near its consumers and allow independent work on pieces. Correct fragments must preserve completeness and required disjointness. Fragmentation alone creates no spare copy, so losing the only site containing a fragment still makes it unavailable.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 131 · NS0053
records.text: NS0053 Question 131 ADB12 What is the purpose of two-phase locking (2PL) in concurrency control? Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability by separating lock acquisition from release. During the growing phase a transaction acquires or upgrades locks; after it releases any lock, the shrinking phase forbids acquiring new ones. For well-formed transactions this guarantees conflict serializability. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and permit cascading aborts, so strict or conservative variants add different protections. It is distinct from distributed two-phase commit.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 132 · NS0054
records.text: NS0054 Question 132 ADB27 Why is write-ahead logging important for database recovery? Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. WAL makes recovery information durable before its changed data pages, enabling safe undo/redo after crashes. ADB27 requires needed update logs to reach stable storage before corresponding changed pages. A durable commit also forces required log records, including commit. Recovery can then use before-images for undo and after-images for redo if buffered data was lost. WAL orders durable writes; modifying an in-memory buffer before the log flush does not itself violate it.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 133 · NS0055
records.text: NS0055 Question 133 ADB41 How does a data warehouse differ from an operational database? Distinguish operational transactions, analytical workloads and physical storage layout. A warehouse integrates historical data for analysis; an operational database serves frequent business transactions. OLTP handles account updates and other frequent operational transactions, while OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets. A warehouse commonly integrates sources through extraction, transformation and loading for historical analysis. These are workload tendencies rather than absolute restrictions: operational databases may retain history, and warehouses may receive updates. Schema and storage choices should follow the actual workload.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 134 · NS0056
records.text: NS0056 Question 134 ADB06 What does ACID stand for in the context of database transactions? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability B Accuracy, Consistency, Integrity, Durability C Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Data D Availability, Consistency, Isolation, Durability Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. ADB06 names all four ACID properties and assigns distinct roles: all-or-none effects, preserved invariants, controlled interference and durable commits. Only A lists those names in the correct order. Accuracy, integrity, concurrency, data and availability are related database concepts but do not replace the letters of this established transaction acronym. A correct It lists the four ACID properties in the proper acronym order. B incorrect Accuracy and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, changing the defined acronym. C incorrect Concurrency and Data incorrectly replace Consistency and Durability. D incorrect Availability is not the A in the ACID transaction acronym.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 135 · NS0057
records.text: NS0057 Question 135 ADB06 Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is treated as an indivisible unit — either all steps succeed or none are applied? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Consistency B Isolation C Atomicity D Durability Atomicity. The question specifies indivisibility of the transaction effects: partial success must not remain if the transaction fails. ADB06 assigns that guarantee to atomicity. Consistency concerns valid invariants, isolation controls interference, and durability protects already committed work. Those properties support correctness too, but none directly means all-or-none effects. A incorrect Consistency concerns preserving integrity rules rather than specifically making effects indivisible. B incorrect Isolation controls interactions between concurrent transactions rather than partial transaction application. C correct Atomicity applies every transaction effect together or discards the incomplete work. D incorrect Durability protects committed effects after failure rather than defining all-or-none completion.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 136 · NS0058
records.text: NS0058 Question 136 ADB06 Account A = 5,000 Birr, Account B = 8,000 Birr. After transferring 750 Birr from A to B, which values maintain CONSISTENCY? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A A = 4,000, B = 9,000 B A = 4,250, B = 8,750 C A = 5,750, B = 7,250 D A = 4,250, B = 8,000 A = 4,250 Birr and B = 8,750 Birr. The requested transfer subtracts 750 from 5000 and adds 750 to 8000, giving 4250 and 8750. The invariant total remains 13000. A and C also sum to 13000, but implement a different amount or the reverse direction. Preserving the total alone does not implement the specified successful transfer; D loses the credit. A incorrect The sum remains 13000, but the changes transfer 1000 rather than the requested 750. B correct It debits 750 from A, credits 750 to B and preserves the 13000 total. C incorrect It preserves the total but transfers 750 in the reverse direction. D incorrect It debits A without crediting B, reducing the total to 12250.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 137 · NS0059
records.text: NS0059 Question 137 ADB06 Which ACID property guarantees that committed transaction changes persist even after a system crash? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Atomicity B Consistency C Isolation D Durability Durability. ADB06 defines durability as preserving committed effects despite failure. A system may leave data pages buffered at commit provided durable recovery information can restore the changes after a crash. Atomicity controls partial outcomes, consistency protects declared invariants and isolation controls concurrent interference; they do not name this persistence guarantee. A incorrect Atomicity means all-or-none effects, not specifically persistence after a successful commit. B incorrect Consistency concerns valid integrity rules before and after correct work. C incorrect Isolation controls concurrent interference rather than persistence across a crash. D correct Durability ensures committed changes survive failures through the supported recovery mechanisms.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 138 · NS0060
records.text: NS0060 Question 138 ADB07 In the Read_item(X) operation, what is the THIRD and final step? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A Store the updated block back to disk B Find the disk block address containing X C Copy the disk block into main memory buffer D Copy item X from the buffer to the program variable named x Copy X from the buffer into the program variable x. ADB07 first locates the page containing X, brings it into a buffer if absent and then copies X into a program variable. Thus D is the final conceptual read step. Locating and loading precede it, and storing an updated block to disk belongs to writing/flushing rather than completing read_item. A buffer hit can avoid physical I/O. A incorrect A read does not update and write the block back to disk. B incorrect Locating the containing page is the first conceptual step, not the final one. C incorrect Loading the page into a buffer precedes copying the item into the program variable. D correct The final read step copies the requested item from its buffer into x.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 139 · NS0061
records.text: NS0061 Question 139 ADB06 A transaction that has started and is currently executing its operations is in which state? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Committed B Partially Committed C Active D Failed Active. ADB06 defines Active as the state while transaction operations are executing. Partially committed follows completion of the last operation but precedes assured durable commitment. Committed means commitment succeeded, while Failed means execution encountered a failure. Merely starting and continuing its operations therefore places this transaction in Active. A incorrect Committed requires successful commitment, which has not occurred while operations are still executing. B incorrect Partially committed follows the last operation rather than ordinary ongoing execution. C correct Active is the state during execution of the transaction operations. D incorrect Failed requires an execution failure, which the stem does not report.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 140 · NS0062
records.text: NS0062 Question 140 ADB06 Which transaction state means all operations executed successfully but the commit has NOT been finalized yet? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Active B Partially Committed C Committed D Aborted Partially committed. Finishing all operations does not yet establish durable commitment. ADB06 names this intermediate state Partially committed. The transaction becomes Committed only after commitment succeeds, or can fail before that boundary. Active describes operations still running, while Aborted means rollback completed, so neither matches successful operations awaiting finalized commit. A incorrect Active means operations are still executing, whereas the last operation has finished here. B correct Partially committed means execution finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. C incorrect Committed requires the commit itself to have succeeded, which the stem excludes. D incorrect Aborted follows rollback rather than successful execution awaiting a commit decision.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 141 · NS0063
records.text: NS0063 Question 141 ADB07 What does the log record [abort, T] indicate? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A Transaction T has just started execution B Transaction T committed successfully C Transaction T was aborted and ALL its changes must be discarded D Transaction T read a data item T is aborting/aborted and its transaction effects must be discarded. ADB07 includes ABORT among conceptual log records and warns that it can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is already complete. C is correct because it says the changes must be discarded, not that all undo has finished. START, COMMIT and ordinary read activity have different meanings. A incorrect A START record, rather than ABORT, marks beginning transaction execution. B incorrect COMMIT records successful completion; ABORT means the opposite outcome. C correct Abort requires discarding transaction effects, though this record need not prove all undo is already complete. D incorrect The record denotes abort handling rather than a read_item operation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 142 · NS0064
records.text: NS0064 Question 142 ADB07 Which of the following is NOT one of the four basic transaction operations on a database? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A Read B Write C Sort D Delete Sort. ADB07 distinguishes read_item and write_item and notes that inserts and deletes also modify data. Sorting is instead an operation used in query processing, not a primitive item update in this classification. The exact count four is a teaching convention, but the note directly supplies the relevant distinction that singles out Sort. A incorrect Reading is an explicitly defined primitive database item operation. B incorrect Writing is an explicitly defined primitive database item modification operation. C correct Sorting is a query-processing operation rather than the primitive item access/update category. D incorrect Delete modifies stored data and belongs with the listed primitive data operations.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 143 · NS0065
records.text: NS0065 Question 143 ADB06 ADB09 The Isolation property of ACID ensures that concurrent transactions: Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Always read the same data at the same time B Do not interfere with each other; each executes independently C Commit in the same order they started D Always complete successfully without any errors Concurrent work is isolated from improper interference. ADB06 defines isolation as controlling interference between concurrent transactions. B captures logical independence under the specified isolation guarantee; it does not mean transactions literally use separate hardware or never wait. Isolation does not require identical reads, start-order commits or universal successful completion. Strong serializable isolation makes behavior equivalent to some serial order. A incorrect Isolation does not require all transactions to read identical values at the same time. B correct Isolation controls interference so concurrent transactions retain the promised logical execution semantics. C incorrect Isolation does not require commit order to match transaction start order. D incorrect Conflicts and failures can still cause aborts; isolation is not a success guarantee.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 144 · NS0066
records.text: NS0066 Question 144 ADB07 ADB27 In a simplified teaching sequence, write_item(X) updates a buffered page and then the buffer manager immediately flushes that page, after required WAL records are durable. What is the final physical step of this specified sequence? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A Copy item X to program variable B Find the disk block address C Store the updated buffer block back to disk D Read the old value of X first C. Store the updated buffer block back to disk After X's program value has been copied into the buffered page, the specified sequence completes by writing the changed page back to disk. That is C. In ordinary buffering this flush may be deferred, but the question explicitly includes it. Locating a page or reading its old value occurs before or separately from the final physical output, and copying into a program variable describes reading. A incorrect Copying into a program variable is a read operation. B incorrect The page address is located before the final output. C correct The explicitly included flush stores the updated buffered page on disk. D incorrect Reading the old value is not the final physical output step.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 145 · NS0067
records.text: NS0067 Question 145 ADB06 A transaction that encountered an error during execution and could not complete is in which state? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Aborted B Failed C Terminated D Partially Committed Failed. ADB06 places a transaction in Failed when an error prevents successful execution. After rollback removes its effects it reaches Aborted. The stem reports the execution error but does not say rollback has completed, so Failed is the precise state. Partially committed follows successful final operation execution, not an error that prevents completion. A incorrect Aborted requires completed rollback, which is not stated after the execution error. B correct Failed is the immediate state when an error prevents completing the transaction. C incorrect Termination is later lifecycle handling rather than the immediate error state. D incorrect Partially committed follows completion of the last operation rather than failed execution.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 146 · NS0068
records.text: NS0068 Question 146 ADB07 ADB24 Transaction log records serve primarily for which purpose? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.
