A Speeding up query execution B Encrypting sensitive data C Enabling database recovery after failures by recording all changes D Enforcing access control permissions Enable recovery by recording the information needed to undo or redo changes. ADB07 records starts, updates, commits and aborts, with before-images for undo and after-images for redo. That makes recovery the primary purpose among the choices. Actual log formats may be physical or logical and need not record every read, so all changes should be understood as the change information required by the recovery design, not every operation indiscriminately. A incorrect The primary log purpose here is recovery rather than speeding query execution. B incorrect Transaction logging does not inherently encrypt the stored sensitive data. C correct Logged update and transaction-state information supports recovery of valid committed state after failures. D incorrect Access privileges control authorization; transaction log records are not themselves that enforcement mechanism.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 147 · NS0069
records.text: NS0069 Question 147 ADB22 Which processing type uses multiple CPUs to execute different transactions simultaneously, achieving higher throughput? Distinguish overlapping dependent operators, independent workers and reused cached objects. A Sequential processing B Interleaved processing C Parallel processing D Batch processing Parallel processing. ADB22 distinguishes concurrency by interleaving on one CPU from actual simultaneous work on multiple cores. The stem explicitly uses multiple CPUs to execute different transactions at the same time, making Parallel the correct classification. Batch describes grouping work, and sequential processing performs work in order; neither guarantees the stated simultaneous execution. A incorrect Sequential processing does not execute different transactions simultaneously on multiple CPUs. B incorrect Interleaving alternates execution and need not provide simultaneous CPU work. C correct Multiple CPUs working simultaneously provide parallel execution. D incorrect Batch describes grouped submission or handling, not necessarily simultaneous multi-CPU execution.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 148 · NS0070
records.text: NS0070 Question 148 ADB06 Why are transactions important in database systems? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A They make queries run faster B They ensure the database remains consistent and reliable through ACID properties C They allow the database to store more data D They simplify the SQL syntax for users Transactions support consistent, reliable work through ACID guarantees. ADB06 groups operations into a logical unit with all-or-none effects, invariant preservation, isolation and durable commits. These guarantees support consistent and reliable database behavior when application logic is correct. They do not inherently speed queries, expand storage capacity or simplify syntax. In particular a DBMS cannot make an incorrect business operation consistent merely by wrapping it in a transaction. A incorrect Transactions can add coordination costs and do not inherently make queries faster. B correct ACID guarantees support valid and recoverable logical work, provided business logic is correct. C incorrect Transaction semantics do not increase the database's physical storage capacity. D incorrect Grouping work atomically does not inherently simplify the SQL language for users.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 149 · NS0071
records.text: NS0071 Question 149 ADB08 ADB13 T1 reads balance=$500 and adds $100, planning to write $600. T2 reads the same $500, adds $200, and writes $700. T1 then writes $600. What problem occurred? Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A Dirty Read B Lost Update (Write-Write Problem) C Incorrect Summary Problem D Deadlock Lost update: T1 overwrites T2’s increment with its stale calculation. Both transactions read 500. T2 writes 700 after adding 200, but T1 then writes its previously computed 600, erasing T2’s increment. A serial execution would produce 800. This matches the lost-update trace in ADB08; no waiting cycle or aggregate calculation is described, and reading an uncommitted value is not the stated cause. A incorrect Neither transaction is described as reading the other's uncommitted write. B correct T1's stale write of 600 overwrites T2's added 200; the correct combined result is 800. C incorrect No aggregate over mutually inconsistent versions is being calculated. D incorrect No circular waiting or blocked resource requests are present.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 150 · NS0072
records.text: NS0072 Question 150 ADB08 A dirty read occurs when transaction T1 reads data that: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A T1 itself wrote earlier in the same transaction B T2 modified but has NOT yet committed, and T2 may later abort C Was permanently deleted from the database D Was last read more than one hour ago Read another transaction’s uncommitted modification. ADB08 defines dirty read as consuming a value written by an uncommitted other transaction. If that writer aborts, the dependent read used a value that should not survive. Reading one’s own changes is allowed and is not this anomaly; the age of a value or a completed permanent deletion does not define dirty reading. A incorrect Reading changes made earlier by the same transaction is not a dirty read. B correct The read depends on T2's uncommitted update, which may later need undo. C incorrect Permanent deletion is not the defining uncommitted-value dependency. D incorrect Elapsed time since a read does not determine whether the writer committed.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 151 · NS0073
records.text: NS0073 Question 151 ADB11 ADB-S04 Which lock type allows MULTIPLE transactions to simultaneously READ a data item? Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Exclusive Lock B Write Lock C Shared Lock D Binary Lock Shared lock. ADB11 states that a shared lock permits reading and multiple shared holders can coexist on the same item. Exclusive/write locks conflict with another transaction’s shared or exclusive lock on that item. Thus shared locking provides the requested concurrent-reader behavior. A generic binary locked/unlocked label does not establish shared-reader compatibility in the supplied model. A incorrect An exclusive lock conflicts with other transactions' read locks on the same item. B incorrect A write/exclusive lock does not grant multiple independent readers the requested shared ownership. C correct Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, permitting multiple readers. D incorrect The binary label does not provide the explicit S/S compatibility defined in the note.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 152 · NS0074
records.text: NS0074 Question 152 ADB12 ADB16 In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), a transaction can acquire new locks ONLY during which phase? Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary. A Shrinking Phase B Termination Phase C Growing Phase D Validation Phase Growing phase. Basic 2PL separates acquiring/upgrading locks from releasing/downgrading them. ADB12 permits acquisition only in the growing phase; after any release, no new lock may be acquired. Termination is a transaction boundary and validation belongs to a different control approach. The growing/shrinking rule is what distinguishes 2PL from unrestricted use of locks. A incorrect The shrinking phase releases or downgrades locks and forbids new acquisitions. B incorrect Termination is not the 2PL phase in which new locks are acquired. C correct Growing permits acquiring and upgrading locks before any release begins. D incorrect Validation is an optimistic-control stage, not the lock-acquisition phase of 2PL.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 153 · NS0075
records.text: NS0075 Question 153 ADB12 What does Two-Phase Locking (2PL) guarantee that locking alone does NOT guarantee? Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary. A That no deadlocks will occur B Serializability — results equivalent to some serial execution C That all transactions complete without aborting D That every transaction reads the most current data Conflict serializability for well-formed transactions. ADB12 explicitly guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed 2PL transactions. Locking without its phase discipline need not provide that ordering guarantee. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and may permit cascading aborts, so it does not guarantee successful completion. Nor does serializability require every read to observe the latest wall-clock update. A incorrect Basic 2PL can deadlock, so deadlock freedom is not its general guarantee. B correct The phase discipline guarantees conflict-serializable schedules for well-formed transactions. C incorrect Deadlock resolution or failures can still abort transactions. D incorrect Serializability does not require every read to see the newest wall-clock version.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 154 · NS0076
records.text: NS0076 Question 154 ADB13 ADB26 What is a deadlock in database systems? Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A A transaction that executes too slowly B A circular wait where each transaction holds a resource another needs, and none can proceed C A type of hardware failure causing data loss D When a transaction violates the ACID consistency property A circular wait among transactions holding resources needed by others. ADB13 defines deadlock through a waiting cycle: each participant holds a resource another needs, so none can advance without an intervention. Slow work alone can still make progress and is not deadlock. Hardware loss and consistency violations are distinct problems that do not require a resource-wait cycle. A incorrect A slow transaction may still make progress and need not participate in a wait cycle. B correct Circular hold-and-wait prevents the involved transactions from progressing without intervention. C incorrect Hardware failure is a different failure category and does not define a lock wait cycle. D incorrect A consistency violation concerns invalid data states rather than necessarily circular waiting.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 155 · NS0077
records.text: NS0077 Question 155 ADB14 In the Wait-Die deadlock prevention strategy, when a YOUNGER transaction needs a resource held by an OLDER transaction, the younger transaction: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action. A Wounds (aborts) the older transaction B Waits for the older transaction to release the resource C Is immediately aborted and restarted D Receives the resource immediately due to higher priority Abort the younger requester; retry with its original timestamp. The requester is younger and the resource holder older. ADB14 says wait–die permits an older requester to wait but aborts a younger requester needing an older holder. C therefore gives the correct action. Restart should retain the original timestamp to improve relative priority; immediately aborted does not require an immediate successful retry or resource grant. A incorrect Wait–die does not let the younger requester abort the older holder. B incorrect In wait–die, the younger requester dies rather than waiting for the older holder. C correct The younger requester is aborted and may restart using its original timestamp. D incorrect The older holder retains priority; the younger requester does not receive the resource immediately.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 156 · NS0078
records.text: NS0078 Question 156 ADB14 ADB13 In the Wound-Wait strategy, when an OLDER transaction needs a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action. A The older transaction waits for the younger B The older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger transaction C Both transactions are simultaneously aborted D A deadlock detection algorithm runs The older requester aborts the younger holder. ADB14 distinguishes wound–wait from wait–die: an older requester wounds the younger holder, while a younger requester waits for an older holder. Here the requester is explicitly older, so B applies. The rule prevents waiting cycles through age-based action; it does not require detecting an existing deadlock first or aborting both participants. A incorrect An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under wound–wait. B correct The older requester causes the younger resource holder to abort and release its lock. C incorrect The protocol aborts the younger holder, not both transactions. D incorrect This is a prevention action based on ages, not a requirement to run cycle detection first.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 157 · NS0079
records.text: NS0079 Question 157 ADB16 Optimistic concurrency control is BEST suited for environments where: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead. A Transactions frequently write to the same data items B Write operations always conflict with read operations C Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads) D All transactions must complete in strict timestamp order Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads) Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions read and compute privately, then validates overlapping read/write activity before publishing changes. When conflicts are rare, most work can commit without being discarded. Frequent competing writes or persistent read/write conflicts instead lead to costly retries. Strict timestamp completion describes a separate ordering constraint; it does not supply the low-conflict condition that makes optimistic execution suitable. Read-heavy activity is useful here only insofar as actual conflicts remain uncommon. A incorrect Incorrect: frequent competing writes cause validation failures and discarded work. B incorrect Incorrect: persistent read/write conflicts increase retry costs rather than favoring optimistic execution. C correct Correct: rare conflicts allow most private work to validate and commit. D incorrect Incorrect: a required completion order does not imply low contention; optimistic suitability depends on conflicts and retry cost.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 158 · NS0080
records.text: NS0080 Question 158 ADB11 Lock upgrade refers to changing a lock from: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Exclusive → Shared B Shared → Exclusive C No lock → Shared D Exclusive → No lock Shared → Exclusive. ADB11 explicitly names S→X an upgrade and X→S a downgrade. The stronger exclusive lock permits writing and can be granted only after conflicting other holders leave. Acquiring a new shared lock is initial acquisition rather than conversion, while releasing an exclusive lock is unlocking. Thus B alone names a lock upgrade. A incorrect Exclusive-to-shared weakens permissions and is a downgrade. B correct Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the held lock to permit writing, subject to compatibility. C incorrect No-lock-to-shared is initial acquisition, not conversion of an already held lock. D incorrect Exclusive-to-no-lock is release rather than upgrade.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 159 · NS0081
records.text: NS0081 Question 159 ADB08 Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly? The intended anomaly is a mixed-version aggregate, distinct from a nonrepeatable read. Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A Two transactions both delete the same record simultaneously B Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200. C A transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction D A transaction fails to acquire all necessary locks B. Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200. The transfer preserves the total balance at 200, but T1 combines the pre-transfer debit balance with the post-transfer credit balance. Its computed 100+110=210 is not a valid summary of a consistent state. This is an incorrect-summary anomaly. Dirty reading is defined by an uncommitted dependency, and lock failure or simultaneous deletion alone does not establish this mixed aggregate. A incorrect Concurrent deletion alone does not specify an inconsistent aggregate. B correct The mixed old/new balances yield 210 instead of the invariant 200. C incorrect Reading another transaction's uncommitted value defines a dirty read. D incorrect Failure to acquire locks concerns scheduling rather than this aggregate result.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 160 · NS0082
records.text: NS0082 Question 160 ADB13 Starvation in a database system occurs when: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A A transaction consumes excessive memory resources B A transaction is repeatedly bypassed by higher-priority transactions and never executes C A deadlock persists longer than the timeout period D The transaction log becomes completely full Indefinite postponement while other transactions keep progressing. ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without requiring any waiting cycle. Repeatedly favoring higher-priority work can prevent a transaction from executing, matching B. Memory consumption, a full log or a long deadlock are different resource/failure conditions; none alone defines the fairness failure of starvation. A incorrect Excessive memory use is a resource problem rather than the definition of indefinite postponement. B correct Repeated bypass by other transactions can indefinitely postpone this transaction while work continues. C incorrect Deadlock requires a waiting cycle; starvation can occur without one. D incorrect A full log can block work but does not itself define unfair indefinite postponement.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 161 · NS0083
records.text: NS0083 Question 161 ADB15 ADB12 ADB29 ADB16 Which concurrency control technique assigns a unique start-time value to each transaction and uses this to order execution and resolve conflicts? Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps. A Two-Phase Locking B Shadow Paging C Timestamp-Based Concurrency Control D Optimistic Concurrency Control Timestamp-based concurrency control. ADB15 assigns TS(T) to each transaction and compares it with item read_TS and write_TS values. Those tests reject operations that would violate timestamp order, so C matches the start-time ordering technique. 2PL orders locking, optimistic control validates private work, and shadow paging is a recovery/storage technique rather than this conflict-ordering protocol. A incorrect 2PL orders lock acquisition and release rather than defining the timestamp validity tests. B incorrect Shadow paging preserves page versions for recovery rather than ordering concurrent transaction operations by timestamp. C correct Timestamp ordering compares transaction timestamps with item read/write timestamps to resolve conflicts. D incorrect Optimistic control validates private read/write work rather than being defined by these timestamp-order tests.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 162 · NS0084
records.text: NS0084 Question 162 ADB11 ADB13 A well-formed transaction must follow which rule regarding locking? Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Lock all items at the end of the transaction B Lock a data item BEFORE reading or writing it C Lock items only when modifying them, not when reading D Acquire all locks in alphabetical order by item name Acquire the appropriate lock before accessing the item. ADB11 requires ownership of an appropriate lock before access and permits releasing only one’s own locks. Reads therefore need shared or suitable stronger locks in this basic model; writes need exclusive ownership. Alphabetical acquisition may be a separate prevention convention, but it is not the general well-formedness rule and locks cannot be postponed until after access. A incorrect Locking only at the end leaves the earlier accesses unprotected. B correct A well-formed transaction holds an appropriate lock before reading or writing an item. C incorrect Basic lock-based access also requires an appropriate read lock, not only locks for writes. D incorrect A fixed resource order can help prevention, but alphabetical order is not the general well-formedness definition.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 163 · NS0085
records.text: NS0085 Question 163 ADB13 ADB12 Lock timeout as a deadlock solution works by: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A Detecting cycles in the wait-for graph B Building a priority queue of all waiting transactions C Automatically aborting a transaction that has waited too long for a lock D Locking all required data items before execution begins Abort a transaction after its lock wait exceeds the timeout. ADB13 describes timeout as aborting long waits, while warning it may mistake slow progress for deadlock. C directly states that mechanism. Detecting cycles is a different method; acquiring all needed locks first is conservative locking; a priority queue alone neither defines a timeout nor guarantees elimination of waiting cycles. A incorrect Cycle detection is graph-based deadlock detection rather than a wait-duration timeout. B incorrect A priority queue alone does not enforce the stated wait-duration abort policy. C correct The policy aborts work whose lock wait exceeds the chosen threshold. D incorrect Obtaining all locks before execution is conservative locking, not timeout handling.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 164 · NS0086
records.text: NS0086 Question 164 ADB17 What are the three phases of query processing in the correct order? Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A Optimization, Parsing, Evaluation B Parsing & Translation, Optimization, Evaluation C Evaluation, Translation, Optimization D Parsing, Evaluation, Optimization Parsing/translation → optimization → evaluation. ADB17 checks grammar and semantics, constructs a logical representation, chooses an equivalent efficient execution plan and evaluates it. B groups parsing and translation into the first phase and preserves that dependency order. Plans cannot sensibly be evaluated before construction and selection, and optimization does not precede understanding the query’s syntax and meaning. A incorrect Optimization cannot precede parsing and understanding the query in the stated pipeline. B correct It preserves analysis/translation, plan optimization and then execution/evaluation. C incorrect Evaluation cannot be the first phase before the query is represented and planned. D incorrect It executes before selecting the optimized plan, reversing optimization and evaluation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 165 · NS0087
records.text: NS0087 Question 165 ADB17 During query translation, SQL is typically converted into which internal representation for processing? Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A Machine code instructions B Binary decision trees C Relational algebra expressions D Compressed byte code Relational algebra expressions or a logical query tree. ADB17 states that translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. This allows equivalent rewrites and plan choice before physical execution. Machine code or bytecode may appear in particular execution implementations, but they are not the general logical translation target asked for here; a binary decision tree is also not the defined representation. A incorrect Machine code is not the logical relational representation described for query translation. B incorrect A binary decision tree is not the note's general query-algebra representation. C correct Relational algebra expresses the logical operators that can be rewritten and optimized. D incorrect Compressed bytecode is not the stated general logical query representation.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 166 · NS0088
records.text: NS0088 Question 166 ADB19 ADB18 ADB23 The query optimizer's primary goal is to: Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies. A Ensure queries return results in sorted order B Find an execution plan that minimizes the overall cost of retrieving data C Maximize the number of indexes used in the query D Ensure all tables are accessed in the order written in SQL Choose a low-cost equivalent execution plan. ADB19 estimates resource costs such as I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and communication for candidate plans. Optimization compares equivalent ways to return the same result and chooses a suitable low-cost strategy. It does not seek index count, force textual table order or impose sorting that the query never requested. The estimate need not prove a global real-world minimum. A incorrect Sorting is required only when query semantics need it, not as the universal optimizer goal. B correct The optimizer seeks an efficient equivalent plan under the selected resource-cost model. C incorrect More indexes used does not necessarily mean lower cost or better execution. D incorrect Equivalent join reordering can reduce cost; SQL textual order need not dictate access order.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 167 · NS0089
records.text: NS0089 Question 167 ADB19 In the textbook local rotating-disk cost model, data is not memory-resident and query execution is disk-bound; client/network and CPU costs are negligible by comparison. Which component dominates the estimated query cost? Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies. A CPU processing time B Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time) C Memory allocation overhead D Network latency to the client B. Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time) The specified disk-bound model estimates the cost of seeks and transferred blocks. Because CPU, memory-management and network costs are negligible by assumption, disk I/O dominates this query's estimated cost. This is a contextual model rather than a universal fact about all databases: memory-resident or distributed workloads can have different dominant resources. The answer follows the scenario's stated objective. A incorrect CPU cost is negligible in the specified model. B correct Seek and transfer time dominate the stated disk-bound workload. C incorrect Memory-management overhead is negligible here. D incorrect Client/network cost is negligible in this local scenario.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 168 · NS0090
records.text: NS0090 Question 168 ADB19 In the disk I/O cost formula Cost = (S x tS) + (B x tT), what does 'B' represent? Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies. A Block size in bytes B Number of disk blocks transferred C Buffer pool size D Binary search operations The number of transferred disk blocks. ADB19 computes disk cost as seeks times seek duration plus transferred blocks times per-block transfer time. Therefore B in the formula is a block count, making B×tT the total transfer time. Block size, buffer capacity and search-operation count are different quantities and would not have the units required by this expression. A incorrect Block size is bytes per block rather than the number multiplied by per-block transfer time. B correct B counts transferred blocks, so B×tT gives their total transfer time. C incorrect Buffer-pool capacity is not the transferred-block count in this formula. D incorrect Binary-search operation count is not the disk-block transfer term.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 169 · NS0091
records.text: NS0091 Question 169 ADB27 ADB30 ADB07 The UNDO operation in database recovery is used to: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk B Create new checkpoint entries in the log C Reverse changes made by incomplete or aborted transactions D Transfer data from cache to permanent disk storage Reverse incomplete or aborted transaction effects. ADB27 uses undo to restore before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing a transaction’s updates backward. This removes changes that must not survive. Reapplying committed changes is redo, checkpoint records bound recovery searches, and transferring dirty buffers to storage is page flushing. Only C describes undo rather than another recovery or storage operation. A incorrect Reapplying missing committed updates is redo rather than undo. B incorrect Checkpoint creation records recovery state and is not reversal of incomplete effects. C correct Undo restores old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction changes. D incorrect Writing a buffer to disk is flushing rather than restoring before-images.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 170 · NS0092
records.text: NS0092 Question 170 ADB27 ADB29 The REDO operation in database recovery is used to: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Abort all active transactions found in the log B Reverse changes made by failed transactions C Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk D Create shadow copies of database pages Reapply required logged after-images, including committed changes missing from pages. ADB27 describes redo as installing logged after-images when necessary. In the simple teaching model it preserves committed work not yet on disk, matching C. ARIES may repeat history more broadly before loser undo, so C describes the ordinary purpose rather than every algorithm’s full phase. Aborting transactions and reversing failed changes are different actions. A incorrect Aborting active transactions is not the operation of applying logged after-images. B incorrect Reversing incomplete effects is undo rather than redo. C correct Redo can restore committed changes whose data pages were not durable at the crash. D incorrect Shadow-page creation is a separate copy-on-write technique rather than logged redo.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 171 · NS0093
records.text: NS0093 Question 171 ADB27 What is the fundamental durable-write ordering rule of write-ahead logging? In B, 'actual data changes' means writing the corresponding changed data page to persistent storage, not modifying a volatile buffer. Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Write data to disk before creating the log record B Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes C All transactions must commit before any log entries are written D Log records are written only after a system crash occurs B. Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes WAL requires the recovery log for an update to reach stable storage before its corresponding changed page is written to disk. A volatile buffer may already contain the change, so this rule does not order every CPU assignment after a log flush. A reverses the required durable order; C and D postpone logs until too late to support recovery of earlier persistent changes. A incorrect Data-before-log reverses WAL's required durable ordering. B correct With the defined durable-write scope, the log reaches stable storage first. C incorrect Update logs may need to be durable before commit and before data flushing. D incorrect Recovery requires logs that were durable before the crash.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 172 · NS0094
records.text: NS0094 Question 172 ADB30 In a simple quiescent checkpoint exercise, all transactions have completed and the required log/data pages are flushed at the checkpoint. How does that checkpoint reduce later recovery search work? Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it. A Preventing all types of hardware failures B Encrypting log records for faster access C Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning D Automatically committing all active transactions periodically C. Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning The quiescent checkpoint supplies a durable boundary for the simplified exercise. With no active transaction spanning it and the required pages flushed, recovery need not scan all earlier history to redo those completed changes. C captures that bounded search. Checkpointing does not prevent hardware failure, gain its benefit from encryption or automatically commit active transactions. Fuzzy checkpoints require different starting-point qualifications. A incorrect Recording recovery state does not prevent hardware failures. B incorrect Encryption is not the mechanism reducing log-search work. C correct The specified durable checkpoint bounds the history needed in this exercise. D incorrect Transactions have completed here; a checkpoint does not automatically commit active work.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 173 · NS0095
records.text: NS0095 Question 173 ADB29 In deferred update (No-Undo) recovery, actual database modifications are written to disk: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary. A Immediately as each SQL statement executes B Only AFTER the transaction successfully commits C When a checkpoint operation is triggered D At regular 5-minute intervals regardless of transaction state After successful commit, in the deferred-update model. ADB29 keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. Only committed effects may therefore be installed in its actual database pages, which is the property B expresses. This does not require every committed page to be flushed immediately. Checkpoints and periodic timers cannot independently authorize writing uncommitted changes while retaining the claimed No-Undo model. A incorrect Immediate per-statement persistent writes can expose uncommitted effects and do not define deferred update. B correct The model does not install uncommitted effects in the persistent database; committed changes can be written later. C incorrect A checkpoint alone does not make an uncommitted transaction eligible for persistent installation. D incorrect A fixed timer cannot ignore transaction commit status while preserving deferred-update semantics.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 174 · NS0096
records.text: NS0096 Question 174 ADB29 ADB26 ADB24 Shadow paging recovery technique preserves the original database pages by: Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary. A Creating a backup on a separate server B Writing all modifications to NEW shadow pages, keeping originals intact until commit C Encrypting pages before any modification D Storing pages in sorted order for faster access Write changed data to new pages while preserving the committed page map. ADB29 preserves the committed version and writes changed data at new locations. Shadow paging keeps the old page map plus a modified map; commit atomically installs the new durable root after needed pages are durable. B captures the copy-on-write preservation, although the unchanged old map is the shadow rather than the name of each newly modified page. A incorrect A separate-server backup is not the page-map copy-on-write mechanism of shadow paging. B correct Changes use new pages, preserving the originals until the new committed map is safely installed. C incorrect Encryption does not preserve the old page mapping or provide the stated rollback mechanism. D incorrect Sorting pages is an access-layout choice rather than preserving committed copies.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 175 · NS0097
records.text: NS0097 Question 175 ADB26 ADB-S05 Which type of database failure is caused by accidental deletion of important data by a user? Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required. A Hardware failure B Natural disaster C Software error D Human error Human error. The described cause is an accidental user action, not faulty hardware, a natural event or a software defect. ADB26 treats human mistakes separately and notes they may need point-in-time restoration before a bad committed operation. Ordinary crash redo would otherwise preserve a committed deletion rather than recognize the user’s intention. A incorrect No hardware malfunction is stated; the cause is the user's mistaken deletion. B incorrect A natural disaster is not the cause described in the prompt. C incorrect The software may have executed the requested deletion correctly; the stated mistake belongs to the user. D correct Accidental deletion by a user is a human error.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 176 · NS0098
records.text: NS0098 Question 176 ADB27 ADB19 ADB24 The transaction log records 'before and after values' for data modifications primarily to support: Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects. A Query optimization B User access control C UNDO (restore old value) and REDO (apply new value) operations during recovery D Database compression and storage efficiency Undo with old values and redo with logged new values. ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete work and installs after-images when redoing logged effects. Recording both values therefore supports reversal and reapplication after failure. Query costing uses catalog statistics, access control uses privileges, and compression is a different storage concern; none explains the specific recovery value pair as directly. A incorrect Query optimization estimates plan cost rather than restoring old/new transaction values. B incorrect Access control checks privileges rather than using before/after images to authorize users. C correct Old values support reversal and new values support necessary reapplication during recovery. D incorrect Recording two values can add storage overhead and is not primarily a compression mechanism.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 177 · NS0099
records.text: NS0099 Question 177 ADB33 ADB34 ADB37 Which type of distributed database uses the SAME DBMS software at every site? Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration. A Heterogeneous distributed database B Homogeneous distributed database C Middleware-based database D Partially replicated database Homogeneous distributed database. ADB33 identifies homogeneous systems by compatible DBMS technology across sites. Using the same DBMS software fits that classification. Heterogeneous systems integrate differing engines, models or interfaces. Middleware describes integration architecture and partial replication describes placement of copies, so neither substitutes for the homogeneity classification asked for here. A incorrect Heterogeneous systems integrate differing database technologies rather than the same DBMS throughout. B correct Using the same DBMS at each site fits homogeneous distributed database technology. C incorrect Middleware describes communication/integration responsibilities, not whether DBMS technology is the same. D incorrect Partial replication describes where selected copies reside rather than which DBMS software sites use.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 178 · NS0100
records.text: NS0100 Question 178 ADB36 ADB37 Horizontal fragmentation divides a table based on: Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation. A Splitting columns into separate subsets B Splitting rows into subsets based on a condition C Combining two tables into one larger table D Replicating the table to multiple sites Split rows by predicates. ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation as selecting row subsets using predicates and reconstructing the relation by union. Column subsets belong to vertical fragmentation. Combining tables is not fragmentation, and copying a whole table is replication. Thus B identifies both the item being split and the rule used to decide fragment membership. A incorrect Column splitting is vertical fragmentation rather than horizontal fragmentation. B correct Horizontal fragments contain rows selected by stated predicates. C incorrect Combining tables increases the combined relation rather than splitting one table into row subsets. D incorrect Replicating copies preserves the whole table at more sites rather than partitioning its rows.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 179 · NS0101
records.text: NS0101 Question 179 ADB36 In vertical fragmentation, why must the PRIMARY KEY be included in every fragment? Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation. A To speed up INSERT operations B To prevent duplicate rows C To enable reconstruction of the original table by joining fragments on the primary key D To ensure proper replication across sites A repeated key or row identifier lets vertical pieces join back losslessly. ADB36 repeats a key or row identifier across vertical fragments so attributes from the same original row can be matched during reconstruction. C states that purpose. The general requirement is a suitable identifier, not necessarily the particular declared primary key if another row identifier is used. It is unrelated to mandatory replication or inherently faster inserts. A incorrect Faster insertion is not why vertical fragments share a row identifier. B incorrect Avoiding duplicate values is not sufficient to align column pieces from the same original row. C correct The shared key identifies matching original rows when the column fragments are joined. D incorrect Replication copies data and is distinct from reconstructing vertical column fragments.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 180 · NS0102
records.text: NS0102 Question 180 ADB37 Which data replication scheme stores each data fragment at ONLY ONE site with NO copies? Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost. A Full replication B Partial replication C No replication (non-redundant allocation) D Hybrid replication No replication, or nonredundant allocation. ADB37 explicitly calls storing each fragment once nonredundant allocation. Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site, while partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites. A hybrid can mix strategies, but the stem specifies exactly one location and no copies for every fragment, so C is the precise classification. A incorrect Full replication stores copies throughout the relevant sites rather than one copy per fragment. B incorrect Partial replication still copies selected fragments and therefore does not mean no copies. C correct Nonredundant allocation stores each fragment at one site without replicas. D incorrect A hybrid can combine policies, but the stated universal no-copy arrangement is specifically nonreplicated.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 181 · NS0103
records.text: NS0103 Question 181 ADB35 ADB24 ADB33 Transparency in distributed databases means that: Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user. A All data is encrypted and transparent to hackers B The distribution complexity is hidden from users who interact as if using a single database C Users can see all technical details of how data is distributed D All sites must use the same operating system Hide distribution details behind a single logical database experience. ADB35 defines transparency through which distribution details are hidden: sites, fragment reconstruction or replica selection/maintenance. Together these can let clients work with a single logical database abstraction. B captures that broad meaning. Transparency is not encryption, disclosure of every technical detail or a requirement that operating systems be identical. A incorrect Encryption protects content; transparency here concerns hiding distribution complexity from legitimate users. B correct Distribution details can be hidden so users work with one logical database abstraction. C incorrect Transparency hides selected implementation details rather than exposing all of them. D incorrect Operating-system uniformity does not define distribution transparency.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 182 · NS0104
records.text: NS0104 Question 182 ADB36 ADB37 ADB34 ADB33 Hybrid fragmentation combines which two fragmentation types? Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation. A Replication and Partitioning B Horizontal and Vertical fragmentation C Client-Server and Middleware architectures D Homogeneous and Heterogeneous distribution Horizontal and vertical fragmentation. ADB36 defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in a suitable order. Reconstructing reverses those operations using unions for horizontal pieces and key joins for corresponding vertical pieces. Replication, deployment architectures and DBMS homogeneity are different design dimensions rather than the two fragmentation types combined by hybrid fragmentation. A incorrect Replication copies data and is not the second fragmentation dimension in the hybrid definition. B correct Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row splits with vertical column splits. C incorrect Client-server and middleware classify architectures rather than fragmentation operations. D incorrect Homogeneous/heterogeneous classifies system technology compatibility rather than row/column splitting.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 183 · NS0105
records.text: NS0105 Question 183 ADB37 With full replication and synchronous propagation before acknowledgment, which listed disadvantage specifically concerns maintaining copies during an update-heavy workload? Assume usable replicas can serve reads. Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost. A Data becomes unavailable when any site fails B Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment. C It requires all sites to use the same DBMS software D Queries can only be answered from the primary site B. Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment. Full replication stores the entire database at each relevant site, so updates create propagation and coordination work. The stated synchronous policy places that work before acknowledgment, adding update latency in the update-heavy scenario. This is the disadvantage described by B. Usable copies can serve reads and improve availability; full replication neither implies identical DBMS software nor restricts queries to one primary site. A incorrect Usable replicas can keep data available after one site fails. B correct The stated synchronous policy adds propagation and coordination work before acknowledgment. C incorrect Full replication is a copy-placement policy, not a requirement to standardize every DBMS. D incorrect Usable replicas can serve reads in the stated scenario.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 184 · NS0106
records.text: NS0106 Question 184 ADB06 What does ACID stand for in database transactions? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Durability B Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability C Availability, Consistency, Integrity, Durability D Atomicity, Correctness, Isolation, Distribution Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. ADB06 gives all-or-none effects, preservation of declared rules, controlled interference and persistence after failure as the four ACID properties. B names them correctly. The other options substitute concurrency, availability, integrity, correctness or distribution for the defined terms, changing the acronym rather than describing an equivalent expansion. A incorrect Concurrency incorrectly replaces Consistency in the acronym. B correct The expansion exactly matches the four ACID property names. C incorrect Availability and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, which are the defined terms. D incorrect Correctness and Distribution do not replace Consistency and Durability in ACID.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 185 · NS0107
records.text: NS0107 Question 185 ADB06 Which ACID property ensures that either ALL operations of a transaction complete or NONE do? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Consistency B Isolation C Atomicity D Durability Atomicity. The requested property concerns whether partial transaction effects can survive. ADB06 assigns all-or-none application to atomicity. A correct transaction also preserves consistency, concurrency needs isolation and completed commits need durability, but those are different guarantees. C is therefore the property matching the explicit ALL or NONE condition. A incorrect Consistency concerns preservation of integrity rules rather than the indivisible effect boundary itself. B incorrect Isolation governs concurrent interference rather than all-or-none transaction effects. C correct Atomicity makes the transaction effects succeed together or be removed together. D incorrect Durability protects committed effects rather than defining partial-success handling.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 186 · NS0108
records.text: NS0108 Question 186 ADB06 If A=5000 and B=8000, and 750 is transferred from A to B, what values satisfy the Consistency property? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A A=4250, B=8750, sum=13000 B A=4250, B=8000, sum=12250 C A=5000, B=8750, sum=13750 D A=5000, B=8000, sum=13000 A=4250, B=8750, total=13000. Subtracting 750 from A gives 4250 and adding it to B gives 8750; their total remains 13000. A implements both the specified operation and its total-balance invariant. B and C apply only one side. D preserves the initial total but does not perform the requested transfer, so invariant preservation alone does not make it the successful-transfer result. A correct It performs the 750 debit and credit and preserves the total of 13000. B incorrect The debit occurs without its credit, reducing the total to 12250. C incorrect The credit occurs without its debit, increasing the total to 13750. D incorrect It preserves the starting total but leaves both accounts unchanged rather than performing the transfer.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 187 · NS0109
records.text: NS0109 Question 187 ADB06 Which ACID property ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Atomicity B Durability C Consistency D Isolation Isolation. ADB06 assigns concurrent-interference control to isolation. That is the distinguishing phrase in the stem. Atomicity handles partial effects, durability handles committed persistence, and consistency means correct work preserves declared rules. Different isolation levels provide different detailed guarantees, so this classification does not imply that all implementations offer serializability by default. A incorrect Atomicity governs partial effects within a transaction rather than concurrent interference. B incorrect Durability concerns persistence of committed changes after failures. C incorrect Consistency concerns declared integrity rules under correct business logic. D correct Isolation controls interference among concurrently executing transactions.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 188 · NS0110
records.text: NS0110 Question 188 ADB06 Which ACID property guarantees committed changes survive system crashes? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Atomicity B Consistency C Isolation D Durability Durability. ADB06 defines durability by persistence of committed effects despite failure. Recovery information can provide this even when changed data pages were buffered at the instant of commit. All-or-none application, invariant preservation and concurrent isolation serve different transaction guarantees, so only durability matches survival of successful commits after a crash. A incorrect Atomicity concerns all-or-none application rather than the persistence of completed commits. B incorrect Consistency concerns validity of declared invariants rather than crash survival of commits. C incorrect Isolation controls concurrent interactions rather than persistence after a crash. D correct Durability preserves committed effects across system failures.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 189 · NS0111
records.text: NS0111 Question 189 ADB06 A transaction that has executed all operations but NOT YET committed is in which state? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Active B Partially Committed C Committed D Failed Partially committed. ADB06 places a transaction in Partially committed after its last operation finishes but before durable commitment is assured. The stem states exactly that boundary. Active means operations are still executing; Committed needs successful commit; Failed needs an error. Finishing the operation list alone does not establish the committed state. A incorrect Active describes ongoing operation execution, not the interval after the last operation finishes. B correct The last operation finished, but commitment is not yet assured. C incorrect The stem explicitly says the transaction has not yet committed. D incorrect No execution or commit failure is reported.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 190 · NS0112
records.text: NS0112 Question 190 ADB06 ADB27 In the Aborted state, what happens to all changes made by the transaction? Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario. A Changes are permanently saved B All changes are rolled back restoring the database to its pre-transaction state C The transaction waits for resources D The transaction restarts automatically Its effects have been rolled back; other committed transactions remain. ADB06 reaches Aborted after rollback. Thus the aborted transaction’s own changes are removed rather than permanently saved. Restoring pre-transaction state must be understood relative to its effects, not erasing unrelated concurrent commits. A restart can be a new attempt, but is not automatic merely because the aborted state was reached. A incorrect Permanent saving is a committed outcome, not an aborted outcome. B correct Rollback removes this transaction's effects while retaining other transactions' legitimate committed work. C incorrect Waiting for a lock describes a blocked executing transaction rather than completed rollback. D incorrect An aborted transaction may be retried, but automatic restart is not guaranteed.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 191 · NS0113
records.text: NS0113 Question 191 ADB07 Which log record signals successful completion of transaction T? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A [start_transaction, T] B [abort, T] C [write_item, T, X, old, new] D [commit, T] [commit, T]. ADB07 identifies COMMIT as the record of successful transaction completion. START begins work, UPDATE records a data change and ABORT marks failed termination/rollback handling. A data write by itself does not prove the enclosing transaction committed, and an abort record can begin rollback rather than confirm it has completed. A incorrect The start record indicates beginning work rather than successful completion. B incorrect Abort records failure/rollback handling instead of successful commitment. C incorrect An update record describes one changed item, not successful transaction completion. D correct The commit record signals successful completion of transaction T.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 192 · NS0114
records.text: NS0114 Question 192 ADB07 The Read_item(X) command transfers data in which order? Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event. A Disk -> Program variable -> Buffer B Buffer -> Disk -> Program variable C Disk -> Buffer -> Program variable D Program variable -> Buffer -> Disk Disk page → buffer → program variable. ADB07 locates X’s page, loads it into a buffer if absent and copies the item from that buffer into the program variable. C gives that conceptual data movement order. A cached page may avoid the physical disk read, but the program still reads through the buffer. The reverse direction describes a write path rather than read_item. A incorrect The page is buffered before the item is copied to the program variable. B incorrect A read does not first send the buffer to disk before obtaining the variable value. C correct The page enters the buffer if needed, then its item is copied into the program variable. D incorrect Program-variable-to-buffer-to-disk describes writing, not reading into a variable.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 193 · NS0115
records.text: NS0115 Question 193 ADB11 ADB15 ADB09 ADB26 ADB24 In a multi-user system, which mechanisms does the DBMS use to manage concurrent access? Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Only backup systems B Locks, timestamps, and scheduling algorithms C Physical user separation D Only file system permissions Locks, timestamp rules and transaction scheduling. ADB11 defines compatible shared/exclusive locks and ADB15 orders conflicting operations with timestamp tests. These are actual concurrency-control mechanisms that constrain transaction schedules. Backups provide copies for recovery, and file permissions determine access rather than safe interleavings. Physical separation of people also does not coordinate their concurrent database operations. A incorrect Backups support restoration rather than scheduling safe concurrent reads and writes. B correct Locks and timestamp rules control conflicting accesses and permissible schedules. C incorrect Separating users physically does not coordinate their concurrent operations on shared database items. D incorrect File permissions alone do not enforce isolation among authorized concurrent transactions.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 194 · NS0116
records.text: NS0116 Question 194 ADB08 The Lost Update problem is also called: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A Read-Read Problem B Write-Write Problem C Read-Write Problem D Phantom Read Problem Write-write problem, as shorthand for a lost-update overwrite. ADB08 illustrates both transactions reading 500, one writing 700 and the other later overwriting it with stale 600. The conflict is between their writes, which explains the offered write-write shorthand. This is not a claim that every pair of writes loses an update: the stale calculation and overwrite are essential. Read/read and phantom behavior describe different situations. A incorrect Two reads alone do not overwrite and lose an update. B correct The stale write overwrites another write, motivating this write-write shorthand. C incorrect The defining loss is the later stale overwrite, not merely an arbitrary read/write pair. D incorrect A phantom changes a predicate query's qualifying row set rather than overwriting one balance.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 195 · NS0117
records.text: NS0117 Question 195 ADB08 A Dirty Read occurs when: Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A A transaction reads only committed data B A transaction reads data modified by another uncommitted transaction C Two transactions read the same record simultaneously D A transaction writes invalid format data Reading another transaction’s uncommitted data. ADB08 defines dirty read through another transaction’s uncommitted write. The value can disappear if its writer aborts, leaving dependent work based on invalid data. Reading committed data or two readers accessing one item is not inherently dirty. Invalid-format writes concern data validity rather than whether the read-from transaction has committed. A incorrect Reading only committed values avoids the defining uncommitted-writer dependency. B correct The read consumes another transaction's modification before that writer commits. C incorrect Multiple readers alone do not create an uncommitted data dependency. D incorrect Invalid format concerns validation or integrity rather than the definition of a dirty read.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 196 · NS0118
records.text: NS0118 Question 196 ADB08 Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly, meaning an aggregate that mixes mutually inconsistent versions? Treat nonrepeatable read as a separate anomaly. Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs. A A transaction reads data after another commits B Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200. C Two transactions delete the same record D A transaction reads its own uncommitted data B. Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200. The transfer subtracts and adds the same amount, preserving a total of 200. T1 instead adds an old A balance to a new B balance and obtains 210, combining versions that do not form a consistent summary. That is the incorrect-summary anomaly. Reading committed data, deleting a record or reading one's own uncommitted changes alone does not establish this aggregate defect. A incorrect A read after another commit is not by itself an inconsistent aggregate. B correct 100+110=210 mixes versions and violates the preserved total 200. C incorrect Concurrent deletions alone do not show this summary anomaly. D incorrect Reading one's own changes is not the stated mixed-version aggregate.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 197 · NS0119
records.text: NS0119 Question 197 ADB11 A Shared Lock allows: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Only one transaction to read an item B Multiple transactions to read simultaneously but not write C One transaction to read and write exclusively D Multiple transactions to write simultaneously Compatible readers, with no writing under a shared lock. ADB11 permits multiple shared locks on one item, each for reading. Writing requires a suitable exclusive lock, which conflicts with other shared holders. Thus B describes shared-lock behavior in the basic lock-based model. Exclusive read/write ownership and multiple simultaneous writers are not shared locking; multiversion snapshot rules are a separate model. A incorrect More than one transaction may hold compatible shared read locks on the same item. B correct Shared locks permit multiple readers but do not authorize writes under that lock mode. C incorrect Sole read/write ownership describes an exclusive lock. D incorrect Shared locks do not allow multiple transactions to write simultaneously.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 198 · NS0120
records.text: NS0120 Question 198 ADB11 An Exclusive Lock allows: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Multiple transactions to read concurrently B Multiple transactions to write simultaneously C Only one transaction to both read and write, blocking all other access D Multiple readers and one writer simultaneously The exclusive holder may read and write; conflicting access to that item is blocked. ADB11 permits an exclusive lock holder to read and write and makes that item’s X lock conflict with another S or X. C is correct in this basic model. Blocking all other access means conflicting access to the same item, not the entire database; locks on other items remain independent and multiversion systems can have additional snapshot-reader behavior. A incorrect Other transactions' shared reads conflict with an exclusive lock on the same item in this model. B incorrect Two exclusive writers cannot hold compatible locks on the same item. C correct One holder can read/write the locked item while incompatible same-item accesses wait or abort. D incorrect Concurrent same-item shared readers conflict with this exclusive writer under the basic rules.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 199 · NS0121
records.text: NS0121 Question 199 ADB12 In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), during the Growing Phase a transaction: Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary. A Releases locks only B Acquires locks without releasing any C Acquires and releases locks freely D Makes no lock requests Acquire or upgrade locks without releasing them. ADB12 defines growing as the acquisition/upgrade phase and shrinking as the release/downgrade phase. Once any lock is released, no further acquisition is allowed. B therefore matches growing. Freely mixing acquisition and release would abandon the two-phase discipline that guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions. A incorrect Releasing locks belongs to shrinking rather than growing. B correct Growing acquires or upgrades locks before any release occurs. C incorrect Freely acquiring after release violates the defining 2PL phase restriction. D incorrect Growing is precisely the phase in which lock requests may be made.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 200 · NS0122
records.text: NS0122 Question 200 ADB15 ADB11 ADB16 ADB29 Which concurrency control technique uses start-times to order transaction execution? Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps. A Locking B Optimistic Concurrency Control C Timestamp-based Concurrency Control D Shadow Paging Timestamp-based concurrency control. ADB15 assigns each transaction a timestamp and checks reads and writes against item read/write timestamps. These checks preserve timestamp order and can abort stale operations. Locking instead uses ownership compatibility, optimistic control validates private work and shadow paging concerns recovery page maps. Only C names the start-time ordering technique described. A incorrect Locking uses lock compatibility and protocols rather than being defined by transaction start-time ordering. B incorrect Optimistic control validates private read/write sets rather than applying these timestamp-order tests. C correct Timestamp-based control orders valid conflicting operations using transaction timestamps. D incorrect Shadow paging preserves committed page maps for recovery rather than ordering concurrent operations.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 201 · NS0123
records.text: NS0123 Question 201 ADB16 Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is best suited for: Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead. A High-conflict write-heavy workloads B Read-heavy workloads where conflicts are rare C Single-user database systems D Distributed transactions only Read-heavy, low-conflict workloads. ADB16 computes privately, validates and publishes, retrying failed validation. Low-conflict workloads let most work succeed; high write contention wastes computation on aborts. B states that criterion explicitly. Single-user systems do not need intertransaction conflict control, and OCC is not restricted to distributed transactions. Actual conflict frequency matters more than the read-heavy label alone. A incorrect High conflicts cause validation failures and repeated wasted work. B correct Rare conflicts allow optimistic private work to validate successfully with few retries. C incorrect A single-user setting lacks the concurrent conflict problem motivating this choice. D incorrect Optimistic control is not limited to distributed transaction environments.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 202 · NS0124
records.text: NS0124 Question 202 ADB13 ADB11 Deadlock occurs when: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A One transaction waits for a resource held by no one B Two or more transactions each wait for resources held by the other in a circular chain C A transaction commits too slowly D Multiple transactions read identical data A circular resource-wait chain. ADB13 requires a waiting cycle: participants hold resources needed by others and cannot make progress without a victim release or another intervention. Waiting for an unheld resource does not state such a cycle. Slow commit and simultaneous reads can occur without deadlock; compatible shared readers in particular need not block one another. A incorrect A resource held by no one does not create the stated circular hold-and-wait dependency. B correct Each participant waits for another holder in a cycle, preventing independent progress. C incorrect A slow commit may still progress and need not form a waiting cycle. D incorrect Compatible shared reads of the same data do not inherently deadlock.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 203 · NS0125
records.text: NS0125 Question 203 ADB14 In the Wait-Die protocol, when a YOUNGER transaction requests a resource held by an OLDER transaction: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action. A The younger transaction dies (aborts) B The older transaction dies C The younger transaction waits D Both transactions abort The younger requester aborts. The requester is younger and the holder older. ADB14 makes that requester die in wait–die; only an older requester may wait for a younger holder. On retry the aborted transaction retains its original timestamp. Wounding a holder belongs to a different protocol, and both participants need not be aborted. A correct Wait–die aborts the younger requester when the needed resource is held by an older transaction. B incorrect The older holder keeps its resource; this protocol does not kill it for a younger requester. C incorrect Waiting is allowed for an older requester facing a younger holder, not this case. D incorrect The policy aborts the younger requester, not both participants.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 204 · NS0126
records.text: NS0126 Question 204 ADB14 In the Wound-Wait protocol, when an OLDER transaction requests a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction: Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action. A The older transaction waits B The younger is wounded (aborted), allowing the older to proceed C Both transactions are aborted D A new transaction takes over Abort the younger holder so the older requester can proceed. ADB14 says an older requester wounds a younger holder, while a younger requester waits. B is therefore the rule for the given ages. The protocol uses priority to prevent cycles rather than arbitrarily aborting both or handing the work to a new transaction. Any retry should preserve the original timestamp to reduce starvation. A incorrect An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under this policy. B correct The younger holder is aborted, releasing the resource for the older requester. C incorrect Aborting both is unnecessary and is not the wound–wait rule. D incorrect No replacement transaction takes over; the older requester continues after the conflicting holder releases.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 205 · NS0127
records.text: NS0127 Question 205 ADB13 ADB12 ADB14 Lock Timeout as a deadlock solution works by: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A Building and analyzing wait-for graphs B Aborting any transaction that waits longer than a specified time limit C Locking all items before a transaction starts D Assigning age-based priorities Abort a transaction whose wait exceeds the configured limit. ADB13 defines timeout by excessive wait duration and warns it can mistake slow progress for deadlock. B matches that mechanism. Wait-for graphs detect cycles, conservative locking obtains all locks before execution and age priorities define wait–die/wound–wait decisions. Those are distinct policies rather than implementations of a time limit. A incorrect Graph analysis detects cycles rather than deciding from elapsed lock-wait time. B correct Timeout aborts a waiting transaction after its configured wait limit is exceeded. C incorrect Preacquiring all locks is conservative locking rather than timeout handling. D incorrect Age-based priorities define other prevention policies, not an elapsed-wait threshold.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 206 · NS0128
records.text: NS0128 Question 206 ADB09 A schedule is serializable if: Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence. A All transactions execute one after another with no overlap B Its concurrent execution produces the same result as some serial execution of those transactions C All transactions commit at the same time D No two transactions access the same table Equivalent behavior to some serial execution, even if interleaved. ADB09 defines a serializable schedule as equivalent to a serial order while permitting interleaving. B matches when same result means the required full transaction equivalence, not an accidental equality of one final value. A describes a serial schedule, which is a special case but not the general definition. Commit simultaneity and disjoint tables are not required. A incorrect This defines serial execution, a stricter special case that omits permitted serializable interleavings. B correct Serializable behavior is equivalent to some serial ordering; coincidental equality of one value alone is insufficient. C incorrect Simultaneous commits do not establish the required transaction-execution equivalence. D incorrect Serializable transactions may access the same tables if their operations are correctly ordered.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 207 · NS0129
records.text: NS0129 Question 207 ADB11 Lock Upgrade refers to: Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request. A Releasing an exclusive lock to a shared lock B Converting a shared (read) lock to an exclusive (write) lock C Removing all locks at commit D Granting a lock to multiple transactions Convert Shared to Exclusive. ADB11 identifies S→X as an upgrade, possible only after incompatible other holders leave. It strengthens an existing read lock to permit writing. X→S is a downgrade, releasing all locks is transaction cleanup and granting compatible readers is shared acquisition. Only B names the requested conversion of a held lock. A incorrect Exclusive-to-shared is a downgrade rather than an upgrade. B correct Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the lock to permit writing when compatibility allows. C incorrect Removing locks is release rather than conversion to a stronger mode. D incorrect Granting compatible shared readers is not the upgrade of one existing lock.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 208 · NS0130
records.text: NS0130 Question 208 ADB13 Starvation in concurrency control means: Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement. A A transaction holding too many locks B A transaction is perpetually delayed and never executes due to other transactions always taking priority C The database runs out of storage space D A transaction commits before completing all operations Indefinite postponement caused by repeated priority to other work. ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other transactions progress, without requiring a deadlock cycle. B states that repeated bypass precisely. Holding many locks can create contention but does not itself prove starvation. Storage exhaustion and premature commit are different failures, so neither supplies the scheduling-fairness definition. A incorrect Holding many locks describes resource use rather than being perpetually denied execution. B correct Repeated priority to others can indefinitely postpone the transaction while other work continues. C incorrect Running out of storage is a capacity failure rather than the defined scheduling starvation. D incorrect Premature commit concerns transaction correctness rather than indefinite postponement.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 209 · NS0131
records.text: NS0131 Question 209 ADB17 The first step in SQL query processing is: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A Optimization B Evaluation C Parsing and Translation D Result Delivery Parsing and translation. ADB17 first checks syntax and semantics and constructs a logical query representation, before optimization and evaluation. C groups those initial activities. Result delivery follows execution, while optimization needs an understood query to compare valid plans. The phase grouping is conventional, but the ordering dependency is explicit in the complete note. A incorrect Optimization follows understanding and representing the query rather than preceding it. B incorrect Evaluation executes a selected plan and is not the first processing activity. C correct Parsing/translation establishes query meaning and logical representation before optimization. D incorrect Results can be delivered only after the required evaluation produces them.

records.title: Advanced Database Systems — Question 210 · NS0132
records.text: NS0132 Question 210 ADB17 SQL queries are internally translated into: Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution. A Machine code B Relational algebra C Python scripts D XML documents Relational algebra. ADB17 translates a query into relational algebra or a logical query tree for equivalent rewrites and plan selection. B names that logical representation. A particular engine may later compile execution code, but machine code, Python scripts and XML documents are not the general logical translation target taught here. Logical meaning precedes implementation-specific execution choices. A incorrect Machine code may be an implementation detail but is not the stated logical translation target.
