records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 158 · Q01255
records.text: Q01255 Question 158 OOP25 OOP-S03 For this valid Java instance method inside a class, which input/output statement is correct? public void test(boolean a, boolean b) { if (a) { System.out.println("A"); } else if (a && b) { System.out.println("A && B"); } else { if (!b) { System.out.println("!B"); } else { System.out.println("None"); } } } Trace condition tests, control transfers and printing as separate steps. A If a and b are both true, the output is "A && B". B If a is true and b is false, the output is "!B". C If a is false and b is true, the output is "None". D If a and b are both false, the output is "None". a=false and b=true prints None. If a is true, the first branch prints A regardless of b. If a is false, the else-if condition a && b is necessarily false, so execution enters the final else. There !b selects !B when b is false and None when b is true. Only C pairs its input values with the resulting output. A incorrect When a is true the first branch prints A, not the unreachable A && B branch. B incorrect a=true selects A immediately regardless of b, so !B does not print. C correct a=false bypasses both earlier tests and b=true makes !b false, selecting None. D incorrect With both false, the final !b test is true and prints !B rather than None.

records.text: Q01505 Question 162 OOP09 OOP10 Which statements about Java 17 constructors are false? Select all that apply. records.text: Q01585 Question 163 OOP21 What is the output of the following program? The cast is type-checkable because Ferrari is a subclass, but it fails at runtime as OOP21 states. Execution stops at the cast with ClassCastException, before a.drive() or d.brake() can print any of their messages. A incorrect The failing cast occurs before either drive or brake, so neither listed message prints. B incorrect No Ferrari object exists here; the cast throws before any dynamic drive or brake call. C incorrect The program never reaches any of the three proposed messages because the cast fails first. D incorrect The related-class cast can pass compile-time checking; the actual object type causes a runtime failure. E correct Casting a plain Car object to Ferrari throws ClassCastException at runtime before any method output.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 174 · SM0243
records.text: SM0243 Question 174 OOP19 OOP02 OOP20 Which purposes apply to a Java interface viewed as a capability contract? “Blueprint” means an operation contract for implementing classes, and “multiple inheritance” means multiple type inheritance rather than multiple superclass state inheritance. Select all that apply. Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. A To define a blueprint for a class B To allow multiple inheritance C To create objects directly D To hide internal implementation details To define a blueprint for a class; To allow multiple inheritance; To hide internal implementation details An interface specifies an operation contract that implementing classes satisfy, so the qualified blueprint description is valid. A class can implement multiple interfaces, gaining multiple type inheritance. Clients can use the contract without depending on a particular implementation’s internals, supporting abstraction. Interfaces are not directly instantiated, so creating objects directly is not their purpose. The multi-select form therefore accepts A, B and D. A correct An operation blueprint is the contract that implementations must satisfy. B correct Implementing multiple interfaces supports multiple type inheritance. C incorrect An interface cannot be instantiated directly. D correct The public contract lets callers use capabilities without depending on internal implementation details.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 182 · SS109
records.text: SS109 Question 182 OOP19 OOP18 OOP11 Assume you have an interface called Payable as follows: public interface Payable { double getPaymentAmount(); } If you have another class Invoice that implements this interface and getQuantity() and getPricePerItem() methods that return quantity and price per item, which options correctly implement the Payable contract? Treat each option as an independent class skeleton with accessible getQuantity() and getPricePerItem() methods supplied and compatible with multiplication returning double. An abstract class may supply a concrete implementation. Select all that apply. Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. A public abstract class Invoice implements Payable { public double getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } } B public class Invoice implements Payable { public double getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } } C public class Invoice implements Payable { public getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } } D public class Invoice extends Payable { public double getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } } public abstract class Invoice implements Payable { public double getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } }; public class Invoice implements Payable { public double getPaymentAmount() { return getQuantity() * getPricePerItem(); } } Both A and B provide public double getPaymentAmount() with the required quantity-times-unit-price result. Declaring A abstract does not prevent it from implementing the interface method concretely; it only prevents direct construction of Invoice itself. The assumed helper methods make both skeletons complete for this comparison. C omits the return type, while D incorrectly uses extends for the interface relationship. Thus A and B satisfy the contract. A correct An abstract class may still provide this concrete public double implementation. B correct The concrete class provides the required public double implementation. C incorrect The method lacks a return type and is not a valid implementation declaration. D incorrect A class implements Payable; it cannot extend that interface as a superclass.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 183 · SS117
records.text: SS117 Question 183 OOP30 OOP31 Which statement is wrong about a Java try-catch construct? Assume any exception considered has a matching catch, and no earlier control transfer prevents reaching it. Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. A The execution control is moved to catch block after exception occur in try block B When exception occurs, the execution of try block is interrupted C The catch block is executed once regardless of exceptions in try block D The catch block is used to handle exceptions that occur in try block The catch block is executed once regardless of exceptions in try block If the try block completes normally, its catch does not execute. If an exception occurs, normal execution of the try is interrupted and the matching handler runs. Thus the claim that catch runs once regardless of exceptions is false. Catch is conditional handling, whereas finally normally provides cleanup after the try and any selected handler. The matching-handler assumption makes the other transfer statements precise. records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 231 · NS0292
records.text: NS0292 Question 231 OOP17 Consider this C++17 class and statements inside a valid main function: struct Meter { int reading = 0; void set(int reading) { this->reading = reading; } static int twice(int x) { return 2 * x; } }; Meter first, second; first.set(4); second.set(9); int doubled = Meter::twice(3); Which statement correctly describes the implicit object context during second.set(9) and the call to twice? records.text: NS0335 Question 234 OOP14 OOP12 OOP02 Consider the following code snippet class Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Animal sound"); } } class Dog extends Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Bark!"); } } Which OOP concept is illustrated when Dog provides its own version of sound? records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 246 · NS0641
records.text: NS0641 Question 246 OOP22 What is the difference between a.equals(b) and a == b when comparing objects? Separate identity, content equality, immutable values and references that may be reassigned. == compares reference identity; equals uses the class’s equality policy. For object references, == asks whether they denote the same object. equals invokes a method whose policy may compare content or value; Object.equals remains identity-based unless overridden. String.equals compares character content. Therefore equals does not automatically mean value equality for every class, and two distinct objects may be equal under an appropriate override.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 247 · NS0642
records.text: NS0642 Question 247 OOP13 In Java, a class extends two classes simultaneously: public class Dog extends Animal, Mammal {}. What is the result? A class can instead implement multiple interfaces for multiple type contracts, and composition can combine separately held collaborators where multiple state/implementation sources are needed.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 248 · NS0643
records.text: NS0643 Question 248 OOP14 A private method in a superclass is 'overridden' in a subclass with the same name and signature. What actually happens? The parent’s private method is not an eligible inherited method for runtime overriding. Thus equal spelling and parameters alone do not establish polymorphic replacement, and this is not ordinary static-method hiding either. records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 249 · NS0644
records.text: NS0644 Question 249 OOP15 Animal a = new Dog(); — What is the declared type and actual type? records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 250 · NS0645
records.text: NS0645 Question 250 OOP15 OOP21 You have Animal a = new Dog(); and Dog has a method fetch() not in Animal. What happens when you call a.fetch()? Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class. Compilation fails because fetch() is absent from the declared Animal type. Because fetch() exists only in Dog, a.fetch() is rejected. A checked/safe narrowing to a suitable Dog reference could expose Dog-specific members, but the original expression does not perform that narrowing.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 251 · NS0646
records.text: NS0646 Question 251 OOP15 OOP16 What is dynamic binding (late binding) in Java? Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class. Eligible overridden instance methods are selected at runtime from the actual object class. The compiler first verifies accessible members and selects the method signature from declared types. Runtime dispatch then selects the most specific eligible override in the object’s actual class. For Animal a=new Dog(), a.sound() can therefore invoke Dog.sound(). This rule does not make Dog-only methods compile through Animal, and static methods/fields follow different selection rules.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 252 · NS0647
records.text: NS0647 Question 252 OOP18 An abstract class has 3 abstract methods. A subclass implements only 2. What is the result? Check whether a class is concrete and whether every inherited abstract contract has an implementation. The subclass must remain abstract unless it provides or inherits the third implementation; a concrete incomplete subclass fails compilation. Implementing only two of three required methods leaves an abstract obligation. OOP18 requires a concrete subclass to provide or inherit implementations for every required method. If the third is still unimplemented, declaring the subclass abstract is permitted; declaring it concrete is not. Merely implementing a majority of the methods does not satisfy the parent contract.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 253 · NS0648
records.text: NS0648 Question 253 OOP18 OOP10 Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can it be instantiated? Check whether a class is concrete and whether every inherited abstract contract has an implementation. Yes, it can have constructors; no, it cannot be directly instantiated. OOP18 allows an abstract class to define constructors alongside fields and concrete/abstract methods. Its constructor participates in initializing the inherited part of a concrete subclass object. That initialization role does not permit new of the abstract class itself. Direct instantiation remains prohibited even if the abstract class happens to contain no abstract methods.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 254 · NS0649
records.text: NS0649 Question 254 OOP13 OOP19 What is the difference between implementing an interface and extending a class? Identify the subtype or ownership relationship and distinguish class inheritance from interface contracts. extends forms a single superclass relationship; implements fulfills one or more interface contracts. A class can extend one superclass, gaining a subtype relationship and appropriate inherited implementation/state. It can also implement multiple interfaces, satisfying their required public operations through provided or inherited methods. Interfaces supply capability contracts rather than per-instance fields or constructors. Modern default/static interface methods mean the distinction cannot simply be summarized as interfaces never contain bodies.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 255 · NS0650
records.text: NS0650 Question 255 OOP19 For an ordinary bodyless Java interface method declaration with no private, default or static modifier, which two method modifiers are implicit? Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. public and abstract. The specified bodyless interface method is implicitly public and abstract. An implementing concrete class must satisfy the public contract without reducing its visibility. This scoped rule does not describe every modern interface method: default and static methods may have bodies, and Java 9 and later allow private helper methods. Those forms are explicitly outside the declaration being classified.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 256 · NS0651
records.text: NS0651 Question 256 OOP19 Can an interface have instance fields (instance variables)? Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. No. Interface fields are implicitly public static final, not per-instance variables. OOP19 explicitly excludes interface instance fields. Any field declared in an interface is a public static final class-level constant under the note’s rule, even when some modifiers are not written. Implementing classes may define their own instance fields, but those belong to the implementing objects rather than being instance state supplied by the interface.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 257 · NS0652

Animal a = new Cat(); a.makeNoise(); — Cat overrides makeNoise() to print 'Meow' Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class. records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 258 · NS0653
records.text: NS0653 Question 258 OOP21 When is downcasting (Dog dog = (Dog) animal;) safe to use? Separate compile-time cast compatibility from the object’s actual runtime type.
