records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 259 · NS0654
records.text: NS0654 Question 259 OOP07 OOP22 What does the final keyword prevent when applied to a class like: final class String {}? Decide whether a member belongs to a class or an object, then check initialization and final restrictions. It prevents subclasses from extending that class. OOP07 says final on a class prohibits extension. Developers therefore cannot declare a subclass of String. This differs from final on a variable, which prevents reassignment, and final on a method, which prevents overriding. A final class is not automatically immutable merely because subclassing is prohibited; String’s immutability is an additional property discussed in OOP22.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 260 · NS0655
records.text: NS0655 Question 260 OOP16 Can a static method be overridden in Java? Distinguish the current instance, parent context, hidden fields and static dispatch. No. A same-signature subclass static method hides the parent static method. OOP16 states that static methods hide rather than override. Selecting a static method through a reference uses the compile-time type, unlike eligible instance-method dispatch based on the object’s runtime class. Thus Animal a=new Dog(); a.staticMethod() selects Animal’s static declaration. ClassName.method() is the clearer recommended spelling and makes that selection explicit.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 261 · NS0656
records.text: NS0656 Question 261 OOP13 What is the 'is-a' relationship and how does it relate to inheritance? Identify the subtype or ownership relationship and distinguish class inheritance from interface contracts. A subtype is a valid instance of its parent contract: Dog is an Animal. OOP13 recommends inheritance when a subtype can satisfy its parent’s contract, as Dog satisfies Animal. That is the is-a relationship rather than mere code reuse. Car containing Engine is instead has-a composition. Reusing fields or methods alone does not justify declaring a subclass if its behavior cannot honor the parent’s promised operations.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 262 · NS0657
records.text: NS0657 Question 262 OOP10 OOP09 You call super() in a subclass constructor but the superclass has no no-arg constructor. What happens? Trace constructor delegation and initialization in the specified Java version. Compilation fails unless an accessible matching no-argument superclass constructor exists. An explicit super() requests the immediate superclass’s no-argument constructor. OOP10 requires a matching accessible parent constructor, so a superclass with only parameterized constructors cannot satisfy that invocation. The subclass must instead call an appropriate super(arguments) or the superclass must provide an accessible no-argument constructor. Java does not synthesize one after another constructor has been declared.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 263 · NS0658
records.text: NS0658 Question 263 OOP08 What is the purpose of the protected access modifier specifically for inheritance? Locate the accessing code, declaring type, package and receiver before applying visibility rules. It permits inherited access in subclasses across packages, and also same-package access. protected supports subclass use of a parent member without making it universally public. OOP08 also grants access to unrelated code in the same package, so it is not subclasses-only. Across packages an instance member must be accessed in the inherited context or through an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, rather than any arbitrary superclass object.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 264 · NS0659
records.text: NS0659 Question 264 OOP19 OOP20 OOP18 An interface Drawable extends both Shape and Colorable interfaces. A class Circle implements Drawable. What must Circle implement? Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. A concrete Circle must satisfy all inherited abstract operations from Drawable, Shape and Colorable. Drawable can extend both interfaces, combining their contracts. Circle implements Drawable and must therefore provide or inherit suitable public implementations of every remaining abstract operation from the full hierarchy. One compatible implementation can satisfy a shared signature; inherited defaults may supply implementations where applicable. If obligations remain unresolved, Circle must be abstract rather than an incomplete concrete class.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 265 · NS0660
records.text: NS0660 Question 265 OOP20 What happens if you declare the same method in both an abstract class and the interface it implements? Check the kind of inherited method and whether competing contracts require an explicit resolution. Compatible declarations can coexist; implementation obligations depend on abstract, concrete and default status. OOP20 says a concrete inherited class method takes precedence over an interface default. An abstract class declaration can instead leave an implementation obligation for a concrete subclass. A compatible public implementation may satisfy the interface contract, but incompatible signatures/return types may be impossible. Without declaration details, these conditional rules are the answer rather than one unconditional outcome.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 266 · NS0661
records.text: NS0661 Question 266 OOP19 Can you instantiate an interface? If not, how do you use it? Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. Not directly. Use an interface reference holding an implementing object, anonymous implementation or suitable lambda. OOP19 prohibits direct interface instantiation while allowing a reference of interface type to hold an implementing object. Calls then use the interface contract with the object’s implementation. Anonymous class syntax still creates an implementing class instance, and a compatible functional-interface lambda supplies an implementation; neither means constructing a bare interface with no implementation.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 267 · NS0662
records.text: NS0662 Question 267 OOP30 What is the difference between throw and throws in Java? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. throw actively raises an exception value; throws declares a method’s possible checked-exception obligation. OOP30 contrasts throw new IOException("message") with throws IOException in a method signature. The first performs an action in control flow, skipping the remaining try body; the second declares an obligation that callers must handle or propagate. A throws clause does not itself throw anything, and throwing a checked exception still requires handling or declaration.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 268 · NS0663
records.text: NS0663 Question 268 OOP30 OOP31 What happens if an exception occurs in a try block and there is no matching catch block? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. It propagates outward to a matching enclosing handler; if uncaught, its thread terminates. Without a matching local catch, the exception is not ignored and execution does not resume with the next ordinary statement in the try. OOP30 sends it outward through enclosing calls/handlers. Relevant finally blocks normally execute during that exit under OOP31’s limits. If no handler catches it, the uncaught exception terminates its thread, not necessarily every JVM thread.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 269 · NS0664
records.text: NS0664 Question 269 OOP29 OOP30 Is it mandatory to handle an ArithmeticException? Separate source errors from runtime exceptions and determine the hierarchy and checked obligation. No catch-or-declare obligation applies: ArithmeticException is unchecked. OOP29 lists ArithmeticException among unchecked exceptions, so Java does not require a surrounding catch or throws declaration merely because it may occur. A program can still catch it when that provides useful recovery. Unchecked means no mandatory compile-time handling obligation, not harmless behavior: an uncaught occurrence propagates and may terminate its thread.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 270 · NS0665
records.text: NS0665 Question 270 OOP30 OOP31 What is the order of execution in: try { ... } catch(E e) { ... } finally { ... }? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. Run try, then a matching catch if thrown, then normally finally. If try completes normally, no catch executes and finally follows. If an exception is thrown, the remaining try body is skipped, a matching catch runs if available, and finally normally executes before continuation or outward propagation. finally also normally runs on return. Process/JVM exit, a crash or control never leaving try prevents an unconditional always claim.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 271 · NS0666
records.text: NS0666 Question 271 OOP30 You catch a general Exception before a specific IOException. What is the result? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. Compilation fails because the IOException catch after Exception is unreachable. Exception already catches IOException values because IOException is a subtype. The later subtype handler can never be selected, and OOP30 says this ordering prevents compilation rather than merely causing the general handler to win at runtime. Place the specific IOException catch before Exception if both handlers are needed.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 272 · NS0667
records.text: NS0667 Question 272 OOP31 What does e.printStackTrace() actually print? Track pending returns or exceptions and distinguish normal cleanup from process termination. Exception information plus recorded call-stack frames for diagnosis. OOP31 distinguishes getMessage, toString and printStackTrace. The stack trace reports exception information together with recorded call frames, helping locate the call path associated with the failure. It is more diagnostic context than the message alone and does not repair or handle the error by itself. Exact text depends on the exception and recorded frames.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 273 · NS0668
records.text: NS0668 Question 273 OOP31 Can a finally block change the return value of a try block? Track pending returns or exceptions and distinguish normal cleanup from process termination. Yes. A return from finally overrides the pending try/catch return; avoid it. A try return expression is evaluated before finally runs. A return statement inside finally can replace that pending return and can even suppress an exception, which OOP31 warns against. Merely changing a local after a primitive return expression was evaluated does not automatically recompute that earlier result. The explicit finally return is the clear override mechanism.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 274 · NS0669
records.text: NS0669 Question 274 OOP29 What is the difference between Error and Exception in Java? Separate source errors from runtime exceptions and determine the hierarchy and checked obligation. They are Throwable branches: Error usually denotes serious conditions; Exception contains checked and unchecked application exceptions. OOP29 places Error and Exception below Throwable. Error normally signals serious conditions for which routine recovery is inappropriate and its subclasses are unchecked. Exception includes unchecked RuntimeException subclasses and other checked exceptions requiring catch-or-declare handling. It is technically possible to catch Error, so the distinction must not be stated as errors can never be caught.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 275 · NS0670
records.text: NS0670 Question 275 OOP30 FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException. Which catch block executes: catch(IOException e) or catch(FileNotFoundException e)? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. For FileNotFoundException, the first applicable catch wins; put it before IOException. Both handler types can match a FileNotFoundException, so catch order matters. If FileNotFoundException is first, that specific block executes. If IOException is placed first with FileNotFoundException afterward, the latter is unreachable and compilation fails. If only IOException is present, it can handle the subclass. The prompt omits order, so these cases must be distinguished.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 276 · NS0671
records.text: NS0671 Question 276 OOP21 What does ClassCastException indicate? Separate compile-time cast compatibility from the object’s actual runtime type. An attempted reference cast is incompatible with the actual object type. A cast can be syntactically and type-checkably permitted between related reference types while still fail at runtime. OOP21’s plain Car cannot become a Ferrari merely by casting, so ClassCastException occurs before subsequent method calls. The exception reports an incompatible dynamic type, not object transformation, allocation or a numeric conversion failure.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 277 · NS0672
records.text: NS0672 Question 277 OOP30 Can you use multiple catch blocks for one try block? Can one catch block catch multiple exceptions? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. Yes to both: use ordered catches or a multi-catch such as catch(IOException | SQLException e). One try can have several catch blocks; source order and specific-before-general reachability still apply. A single multi-catch can also handle alternative exception types. OOP30 prohibits alternatives related by subclassing, so IOException and FileNotFoundException cannot be paired in one union catch. Their hierarchy instead calls for an appropriate common catch or ordered handlers.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 278 · NS0673
records.text: NS0673 Question 278 OOP24 OOP06 What is the output? int x = 5; int y = ++x * x--; System.out.println(x + ' ' + y); Track the old and updated values separately and distinguish a character operand from a string. 73. The expression leaves x=5 and y=36, then adds the space character’s value 32. Java evaluates ++x first, changing 5 to 6 and supplying 6. x-- then supplies 6 and restores x to 5, so y=36. In x + ' ' + y the space is char, not String, and numeric promotion gives 5+32+36=73. Replacing it with a double-quoted space would instead concatenate separated values.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 279 · NS0674
records.text: NS0674 Question 279 OOP11 OOP08 OOP16 Circle and Sphere are separately declared top-level Java classes. Circle declares private double radius; and Sphere extends Circle. What happens if an instance method of Sphere attempts this.radius = 5.0;? Separate parameters from arguments and operations that read state from operations that change it. Compilation fails for an ordinary separately declared Sphere: the inherited radius field is private. The direct field access fails compilation. Circle’s private field is not accessible from a separately declared top-level subclass, and this only identifies the current object; it does not relax visibility. Sphere must use an accessible operation supplied by Circle if it needs to request a radius change. Declaring the classes separately removes the shared-nest exception from the scenario.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 280 · NS0675
records.text: NS0675 Question 280 OOP18 What is the difference between a concrete class and an abstract class? Check whether a class is concrete and whether every inherited abstract contract has an implementation. A concrete class can be instantiated and must satisfy abstract obligations; an abstract class cannot be directly instantiated. An abstract class can hold state, constructors, concrete methods and abstract methods, and need not contain an abstract method. A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of every required abstract operation before it can serve as an instantiable class. Abstract is therefore a class-level instantiation/contract restriction, not a prohibition on implemented behavior.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 281 · NS0676
records.text: NS0676 Question 281 OOP07 OOP22 String is declared as a final class. What does this mean for developers? Decide whether a member belongs to a class or an object, then check initialization and final restrictions. Developers cannot subclass String; final prohibits extension. Applying final to String prevents any class from extending String. It does not prevent constructing or referencing String instances, nor does the class modifier alone explain immutability of arbitrary objects. OOP22 treats String’s immutable content as a distinct property. Developers should use existing String operations rather than attempting a String subclass.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 282 · NS0677
records.text: NS0677 Question 282 OOP16 OOP15 What is method hiding in Java and how does it differ from overriding? Distinguish the current instance, parent context, hidden fields and static dispatch. A subclass static method hides a same-signature parent static method; overriding is runtime instance dispatch. For static hiding, the selected declaration follows the compile-time type used to qualify the call. For eligible overridden instance methods, the object’s runtime class determines the implementation. OOP16’s Animal a=new Dog() static call therefore resolves to Animal, unlike a virtual instance sound call that could invoke Dog. Class qualification makes static selection clearer.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 283 · NS0678
records.text: NS0678 Question 283 OOP19 OOP18 OOP14 Given: interface A { void m1(); } interface B { void m2(); } class C implements A, B {} — What must C define? Identify the interface contract, effective modifiers and permitted implementation forms. C must provide public void m1() and public void m2(), or inherit suitable implementations. Both unmodified interface declarations are implicitly public abstract. A concrete C implementing A and B must satisfy both signatures, not merely one. In the shown class with no suitable superclass implementation, define public void m1() and public void m2(). Package-private implementations would narrow the public contract; otherwise C must be declared abstract instead of concrete.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 284 · NS0679
records.text: NS0679 Question 284 OOP29 What is the significance of the java.lang.Throwable class? Separate source errors from runtime exceptions and determine the hierarchy and checked obligation. Throwable is the common root of Java’s throwable Error and Exception hierarchy. OOP29 places both Error and Exception under Throwable, establishing the common type for Java throwable values. The distinction between checked and unchecked branches controls catch-or-declare obligations, not whether an exception happens during compilation. Throwable therefore unifies the hierarchy without implying that every subclass is an ordinary recoverable application exception.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 285 · NS0680
records.text: NS0680 Question 285 OOP30 OOP29 A method throws a checked exception but neither catches it nor declares throws. What happens? Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output. Compilation fails because the checked exception is neither handled nor declared. OOP30 requires callers and methods to handle or propagate checked obligations. A method that may throw a checked exception but neither catches it nor declares it in throws violates that compile-time requirement. The failure is not that checked exceptions occur during compilation: the compiler is checking a possible future runtime throw.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 286 · NS0681
records.text: NS0681 Question 286 OOP15 What does 'extensibility' mean in the context of polymorphism? Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class. New subtypes can supply behavior while existing common-type client code remains reusable. OOP15 describes a common Animal array loop invoking speak on Dog and Cat objects. Adding another conforming Animal subtype can supply its own override without rewriting that generic loop. That ability is extensibility through polymorphism: clients depend on the shared contract, while runtime dispatch supplies subtype behavior. The new subtype must still satisfy that contract.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 287 · NS0682
records.text: NS0682 Question 287 OOP21 OOP-S04 You have: Object obj = 'Hello'; String s = (String) obj; Is this valid? What about Integer i = (Integer) obj;? Separate compile-time cast compatibility from the object’s actual runtime type. Literal single-quoted Hello is invalid. With "Hello", the String cast succeeds and the Integer cast throws ClassCastException. A Java character literal cannot contain the multi-character text 'Hello', so the printed declaration fails before either cast executes. OOP21 explicitly separates that defect from the intended double-quoted version. After changing it to a String literal, obj refers to a String: narrowing back to String succeeds, but narrowing it to Integer fails at runtime.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 288 · NS0683
records.text: NS0683 Question 288 OOP10 If a subclass constructor doesn't explicitly call super(), what does Java do? Trace constructor delegation and initialization in the specified Java version. If no explicit this(...) or super(...) delegation exists, Java inserts super(); this(...) instead delegates within the class. Omitting explicit super() alone is insufficient to determine what happens. A constructor may explicitly call this(...), delegating to another same-class constructor that eventually reaches superclass construction. Only when there is no explicit constructor delegation does OOP10 insert super(), requiring an accessible matching parent no-argument constructor. Otherwise the program fails to compile.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 289 · NS0734
records.text: NS0734 Question 289 OOP01 What is the difference between a class and an object? Use a concrete example. Distinguish an object’s stored state, operations, identity and class definition. A class defines common structure/behavior; an object is one instance, such as a particular Rectangle with width and height. Rectangle can define width, height, getArea and getPerimeter for every rectangle. A particular rectangle object stores its own width and height values and responds to those operations. OOP01 distinguishes that instance from the type description: two objects can have equal field values and still have distinct identities. The class is shared structure, not one particular rectangle.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 290 · NS0735
records.text: NS0735 Question 290 OOP02 OOP11 Why is encapsulation important? How is it achieved? Identify whether the emphasis is grouping state, hiding implementation, exposing essentials or varying behavior. Encapsulation protects invariants and stable interfaces by grouping state with validated operations and controlling access. OOP02 groups state and operations with controlled access, keeping representation decisions behind stable interfaces. A private account balance exposed through deposit(amount) can reject invalid negative changes rather than permitting unrestricted assignment. This localizes responsibility and lets clients use meaningful operations without depending on internal representation. OOP11 cautions that automatically exposing setters for every field is not required.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 291 · NS0736
records.text: NS0736 Question 291 OOP12 OOP14 OOP15 What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding? Provide examples. Compare names and parameter signatures before considering return types or access modifiers. Overloading changes parameter signatures; overriding replaces eligible inherited instance behavior with the same signature. For overloading, f(int), f(double) and f(int,int) share a name but have distinct signatures selected using declared arguments at compile time. For overriding, Dog extends Animal and supplies void sound() matching Animal’s eligible void sound(); a superclass reference can then dispatch to Dog at runtime. Changing only the return type cannot create an overload, and override return compatibility still matters.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 292 · NS0737
records.text: NS0737 Question 292 OOP13 OOP20 Why can't Java classes inherit from multiple parent classes? How is this limitation overcome? Identify the subtype or ownership relationship and distinguish class inheritance from interface contracts. Java permits one direct superclass. Use multiple interfaces for type contracts and composition for cooperating implementation/state. The immediate reason the declaration is rejected is Java’s one-direct-superclass rule in OOP13. Multiple interfaces supply multiple type contracts, while contained collaborators model has-a reuse without multiple class inheritance. This does not eliminate every diamond problem: OOP20 requires explicit resolution of conflicting unrelated interface defaults. The note supplies these mechanisms, rather than a historical language-design rationale.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 293 · NS0738
records.text: NS0738 Question 293 OOP15 What is polymorphism? Explain with a code example. Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class. Polymorphism lets a common-type reference invoke behavior appropriate to the actual subtype. Example: class Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Animal"); } } class Dog extends Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Bark"); } } Then Animal a=new Dog(); a.sound(); prints Bark. The declared Animal type makes sound available; the actual Dog object supplies its eligible override at runtime. A new Animal subtype can participate through the same common operation.

records.title: Object Oriented Programming — Question 294 · NS0739
records.text: NS0739 Question 294 OOP20 OOP19 OOP18 When would you use an abstract class versus an interface? Check the kind of inherited method and whether competing contracts require an explicit resolution. Use an abstract class for shared state/construction/implementation; use an interface for capabilities across unrelated classes and multiple type contracts. An abstract class can centralize common fields, constructor initialization and concrete operations while leaving selected operations abstract. An interface specifies a capability that otherwise unrelated classes can implement, and a class may implement several interfaces. Modern interface defaults do not supply per-instance fields or constructors, so shared object state/construction remains a reason to choose an abstract class.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Course module
records.text: Computer Organization and Architecture

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Study notes
records.text: Computer Organization and Architecture Understand how representation, registers, memory, control and I/O cooperate to execute a program. Use the stated machine model: architectural labels alone do not fix timing, power, word size or core count. For each problem identify the representation, operand width, addressing mode and timing assumptions before calculating. Practice Boolean simplification, signed subtraction, effective addresses, cache traces, register transfers and pipeline timing; comparisons should explain the mechanism. Give the four blueprint outcomes equal attention: hardware/software structure, CPU operations, I/O communication and performance enhancement. Use historical architecture facts as a small supplement to the core principles.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Practice questions
records.text: Computer Organization and Architecture

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Revision outline
records.text: Computer Organization and Architecture

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Architecture, organization and system structure
records.text: Architecture describes programmer-visible behavior: instructions, registers, data types, address spaces and I/O conventions. Organization is the implementation: control signals, internal buses, pipelines and memory technology. Different organizations can implement the same architecture; neither definition imposes a maximum lifetime. Microarchitecture names the internal processor design. CPU, main memory, I/O and their interconnection are the major structural parts. The CPU contains an ALU, control unit and registers; a microcontroller is a complete integrated control system, not another mandatory CPU subunit. A motherboard physically connects components. Gates are fundamental logic building blocks; distinguish that level from CPU, memory, disk and motherboard components. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Stored programs and software roles
records.text: In the textbook Von Neumann model, instructions and data share an addressed memory system; the CPU normally advances sequentially unless control flow changes. Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths. Modern systems may combine a unified address-space view with separate instruction/data caches, so “architecture used nowadays” is not an exclusive choice. Separate program/data regions within one memory do not make a Harvard machine. An operating system manages resources and provides services. Applications solve user tasks. A compiler translates source into target code; assembly is a symbolic form of machine instructions. JIT compilation happens during program execution, often translating intermediate code. Translation before execution alone does not distinguish JIT from an ahead-of-time compiler. Machine-language programming depends on the register set, supported types and memory/addressing structure. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Gates, truth tables and symbols
records.text: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1. NOT complements a bit. NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR. For two inputs XOR is 1 when inputs differ, and XNOR when they agree. An enabled buffer copies its input. A bubble at a gate output indicates inversion: an AND-shaped symbol with a bubble is NAND. With n binary inputs, enumerate 2^n truth-table rows. Evaluate complements, products and then sums. A plus sign means Boolean OR, not integer addition. Example Worked microexample F=x+y'z at x=0,y=1,z=1: y'=0, so F=0 OR (0 AND 1)=0. Four independent inputs give 16 rows. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Boolean reduction and universal gates
records.text: Useful identities are A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, AA=A, A+A'=1, AA'=0, A+AB=A and A(A+B)=A. De Morgan gives (AB)'=A'+B' and (A+B)'=A'B'. Check a proposed simplification with a truth table if uncertain. NAND and NOR are each universal: feeding the same input to both inputs constructs NOT; combine complemented gates to construct AND or OR. For Karnaugh maps, use Gray-code order, group adjacent 1s in rectangles of powers of two, allow wraparound and overlap, cover every required 1, and remove variables changing within a group. Do not group diagonally or include a required 0. Example Worked microexample AB+AB'=A(B+B')=A. A NAND A=A'; NAND followed by inversion gives AND. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Combinational versus sequential circuits
records.text: A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay. Adders, multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders and decoders have no stored logical state. A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples. This is the defensible criterion when comparing a shift register against decoder, encoder and multiplexer. A flip-flop stores one bit while powered. State retention during operation does not mean nonvolatile storage. Ordinary flip-flops and SRAM lose state when power is removed. Clocked sequential circuits update at designated clock events; combinational logic does not inherently require a clock. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Flip-flop and counter state traces
records.text: For an active-high SR latch, S=1,R=0 sets, S=0,R=1 resets, and S=R=0 holds; S=R=1 is forbidden for the NOR-latch model. Active-low NAND-latch conventions differ. A D flip-flop copies D at its active edge. JK holds for 00, resets for 01, sets for 10 and toggles for 11. T toggles when T=1 and holds when T=0. Trace a sequential circuit one clock at a time from the given initial state. A k-bit binary counter has 2^k states and wraps modulo 2^k unless extra control changes the sequence. Ripple counters propagate changes asynchronously; synchronous counters share a clock. Example Worked microexample A 3-bit counter at 110 advances to 111, then 000. A T flip-flop starting at 0 with T inputs 1,0,1 gives states 1,1,0. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Adders, selectors and code converters
records.text: A half-adder has sum A XOR B and carry AB. A full-adder includes carry-in: sum=A XOR B XOR Cin and carry=AB+Cin(A XOR B). Cascading full-adders propagates carry across a word. A 2^k-to-1 multiplexer uses k select bits to choose one data input. A demultiplexer routes one input to a selected output. A k-to-2^k decoder asserts the selected output, subject to enable and active-level conventions. An ordinary encoder assumes one active input; a priority encoder defines which wins if several are active. Registers are storage, not combinational code converters. Example Worked microexample For a full-adder with A=B=Cin=1, binary total is 11: sum=1 and carry=1. An 8-to-1 mux needs 3 select bits. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Base conversion and binary codes
records.text: In base b, a digit at position i has value digit×b^i. Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15. Convert a positive integer to binary by repeated division by 2 and read remainders upward. For fractions, repeatedly multiply by 2 and read integer parts downward. Group binary bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal, outward from the radix point. BCD encodes each decimal digit separately in four bits; BCD 12 is 0001 0010, while ordinary binary 12 is 1100. ASCII is a character code, not a physical I/O interface. Example Worked microexample 1011₂=8+2+1=11. 2F₁₆=47. 101.101₂=5.625. Decimal 13 gives remainders 1,0,1,1 and hence 1101₂. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Signed arithmetic, subtraction and overflow
records.text: For n-bit unsigned values the range is 0 through 2^n−1. Two’s complement ranges from −2^(n−1) through 2^(n−1)−1. Negate by inverting all n bits and adding one. Compute A−B as A+(two’s complement of B), retaining n result bits. Signed magnitude and one’s complement have two zero encodings; two’s complement has one. Unsigned carry and signed overflow are different. Signed addition overflows when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result. Keep the width fixed throughout the calculation. Example Worked microexample In 4 bits, 7−3 = 0111+1101 = 1 0100; discard carry to get 4. But 0111+0001=1000 is signed overflow, since +8 is outside −8…+7. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Floating point and arithmetic pipelines
records.text: A normalized binary floating-point value is sign×significand×2^exponent. For ordinary IEEE binary32 normal values, value=(−1)^s(1.f)2^(e−127); binary64 uses 11 exponent bits and bias 1023. Special exponent patterns represent zero/subnormal values or infinities/NaNs, so the implicit leading 1 is not universal. For floating addition, compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add or subtract, normalize and round. Alignment may lose low-order bits. Overflow concerns exponent range; rounding error concerns finite precision. An arithmetic pipeline overlaps these steps for different operand pairs; it need not perform all steps in one cycle. Example Worked microexample 1.10₂×2³ + 1.00₂×2¹ becomes (1.10₂+0.01₂)×2³=1.11₂×2³=14. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Register transfers, buses and memory cycles
records.text: R2←R1 copies R1 into R2; it does not erase R1. A control condition P:R2←R1 performs the transfer only when P is true at the relevant clock event. Simultaneous transfers read old register values; sequential statements can use a newly written value. A common bus selects one source at a time, while destination load signals select receivers. A read places an address in MAR/AR, asserts read, waits for memory and captures data in MDR/MBR/DR. A write supplies both address and data and asserts write. The ALU computes; the control unit sequences and enables the transfers. A microoperation is one elementary operation on register contents. Example Worked microexample With R1=3,R2=7, simultaneous R1←R2,R2←R1 swaps to 7,3. Executed sequentially, both end at 7. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Address, data and control buses
records.text: Address signals select a location; data signals carry values; control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements. In the simple CPU-master model, addresses flow from CPU to memory, while data travels in either direction. A DMA controller can also become bus master. Aggregate control signals include both CPU outputs and device inputs; both data and control buses can therefore be bidirectional under that scope. With a address bits there are 2^a addressable locations. Multiply by bytes per location before calling this a byte capacity. Word width, data-bus width, instruction width and address width need not match. Example Worked microexample 32 address bits and byte addressing give 2^32 bytes=4 GiB (often called 4 GB in introductory questions). A 16-bit data bus does not itself imply a 16-bit address space. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Logic masks and shifts
records.text: To set selected bits use A OR mask; to clear them use A AND NOT(mask); to toggle use A XOR mask; to retain only selected bits use A AND mask. A XOR A clears the entire register. Clearing with XOR is valid only with the appropriate operand, not any arbitrary mask. Logical shifts insert zero. Arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit. Left shift inserts zero and may overflow; it does not preserve the sign in every case. Rotate returns a shifted-out bit at the opposite end. SISO shift registers delay serial streams; SIPO collects a word and PISO serializes a parallel word. Example Worked microexample A=1010, mask=1100: set→1110, selective clear→0010, toggle→0110. Arithmetic-right 1100 gives 1110 (−4 to −2 in two’s complement); logical-right gives 0110. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — CPU registers and control-word construction
records.text: PC identifies the next instruction to fetch. IR holds the fetched instruction; MAR holds an address used for the current memory access; MDR holds transferred data. The accumulator holds operands/results, SP tracks the stack, and status flags report conditions. “Address of the instruction” without a phase can describe PC or MAR. Registers and cache both store temporary information, but registers are explicit execution operands and cache holds copies of memory blocks. A control word chooses ALU sources, destination and operation. Use the machine’s encoding table rather than guessing opcodes. In this 14-bit control-word example, SELA, SELB and SELD each have 3 bits, followed by a 5-bit operation field. Example Worked microexample For R1←R2−R3 in this encoding, select 010,011,001 and subtraction 00101: 010 011 001 00101. Source and destination order matters. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Fetch, decode, execute and next-PC choice
records.text: A conceptual instruction cycle fetches an instruction, decodes opcode/addressing fields, obtains operands, executes, writes results where required and checks permitted interrupts. A five-stage implementation may name stages IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB; these stages are not mandatory for every architecture. A sample fetch is MAR←PC; MDR←M[MAR]; IR←MDR; PC←PC+instruction_length. A branch can replace the sequential PC later. Thus “which phase determines the next instruction?” needs to distinguish reading the current PC from calculating a branch target. The control unit coordinates fetching and data flow; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic. A write-back/result-storage phase is not another fetch. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Opcode fields and address-count formats
records.text: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation. A 4-bit opcode permits at most 16 encodings, not necessarily 16 implemented instructions. A 6-bit operand-reference field has 64 encodings; what they designate depends on the machine. Three-address ADD X,Y,Z means X←Y+Z under destination-first notation. Two-address ADD X,Y overwrites X with X+Y. One-address accumulator ADD X means AC←AC+M[X]. Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands. Count explicit operand fields; an instruction such as INC X does not become an accumulator instruction merely because it has one written operand. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Stacks and evaluation order
records.text: A stack is last-in, first-out. PUSH adds an item and POP removes the logical top. A register stack uses registers; a memory stack uses RAM and a stack pointer. Check whether SP points to the top or the next free location, whether addresses increase or decrease, and whether the update occurs before or after access. Overflow means pushing a full stack; underflow means popping an empty one. Zero-address arithmetic typically pops the second operand first, then the first operand; subtraction therefore needs careful order. PUSH and POP may still contain an explicit address even on a stack machine. Example Worked microexample For (A+B)×(C+D): PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL. For a downward-growing full stack, PUSH commonly decrements SP before storing and POP reads before incrementing. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Effective addresses and addressing modes
records.text: Let A be an instruction field, R a register value and M[x] the contents at x. Immediate uses value A; direct uses EA=A and operand M[A]; indirect uses EA=M[A] then operand M[EA]. Register uses operand R; register-indirect uses EA=R. Indexed/base displacement uses EA=R+A; PC-relative uses the architecture-defined PC plus a signed displacement. Auto-increment/decrement also updates the register by operand size. A transfer between a register and memory does not uniquely specify addressing mode; either direct, indexed or indirect addressing may produce it. Example Worked microexample A=100,R=20,M[100]=300,M[300]=9: direct operand is 300; indirect operand is 9; indexed EA is 120. An immediate field 100 is the value 100, not M[100]. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Instruction classes and control flow
records.text: Data-transfer instructions copy values. Arithmetic/logic instructions compute values. TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining the arithmetic result. Branch instructions choose a target, conditionally or unconditionally. CALL saves a return point; RETURN restores it. SKIP, where supported, bypasses the next instruction when its condition holds. “Jump to the next instruction” does not clearly mean skip. External interrupts arise from devices or timers; synchronous internal exceptions arise from the executing instruction, such as divide errors, illegal opcodes or access violations. A software interrupt is deliberately requested by an instruction. Arithmetic overflow trapping depends on architecture and instruction; ordinary overflow flags need not trigger an interrupt. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — RISC, CISC and control implementation
records.text: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control. CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths. Hardwired control directly generates control signals; microprogrammed control sequences stored control words. These are tendencies, not universal guarantees. One instruction completing per pipeline cycle is throughput, not proof that every instruction has one-cycle latency. Modern RISC instructions can take multiple cycles and modern CISC processors can translate instructions into simpler internal operations. Neither label guarantees lower power, cost or execution time. The semantic gap is the distance between high-level constructs and machine operations; reducing it is associated with richer instructions, not a universal shared objective of both design approaches. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — x86 register names and classification
records.text: In Intel x86 notation, AX/BX/CX/DX, BP/SP and SI/DI are 16-bit general-purpose registers, with conventional special roles. AL is AX’s low byte and AH its high byte; analogous byte names apply to BX/CX/DX. EAX is 32-bit and RAX 64-bit. FLAGS/EFLAGS/RFLAGS report status; IP/EIP/RIP identifies instruction position. CS and SS are code/stack segment registers. DX is programmer-visible; IR/MDR are conceptual internal registers. SP’s stack role does not remove it from Intel’s general-purpose register classification. EAX/EIP existed with the 80386, before Pentium; R8–R15 belong to the 64-bit extension, not original Pentium. State the textbook convention when using a narrower “multipurpose” register category. Intel Software Developer Manual, Volume 1

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — x86 instruction legality and implicit operands
records.text: Assume Intel destination-first syntax and ordinary legacy x86 forms. MOV AL,BP is invalid because operand widths differ (8 versus 16 bits). INC CX and DEC CX are valid word operations. Segment-register MOV has register/memory forms, not a direct immediate-to-segment form: load an immediate into AX, then MOV DS,AX. Unsigned MUL with a byte operand multiplies AL by that byte and writes AX. With a word operand it multiplies AX and writes DX:AX. Thus AL=8 and BH=10 gives AX=80 after MUL BH; CL is irrelevant. MOVS and LODS are string transfer operations, XCHG exchanges operands, and INC is arithmetic. “Different” requires the transfer-versus-arithmetic criterion. Intel Software Developer Manual, Volume 2B

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Memory hierarchy and timing measures
records.text: A usual speed/cost-per-bit order is registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM, SSD, HDD and archival tape. Faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit. Access time measures latency of a read/write; cycle time is the minimum interval before another operation and may include recovery. Transfer rate measures data per time, not individual-request delay. Temporal locality reuses recent data; spatial locality uses nearby locations. Cache copies memory blocks near the CPU. Hit ratio=hits/accesses; miss ratio=1−hit ratio. Distinguish capacity, latency, bandwidth and hit ratio before comparing alternatives. Example Worked microexample For 90 hits in 100 accesses, hit ratio=0.9. If hit time is 2 ns and an additional miss penalty is 50 ns, AMAT=2+0.1×50=7 ns. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — RAM, firmware and memory-chip capacity
records.text: SRAM uses powered bistable storage: fast and costly per bit, without periodic refresh. DRAM stores charge and requires refresh: denser and commonly used for main memory. Both are ordinarily volatile. ROM and flash retain contents without power; erasable/programmed variants mean “ROM can never be modified” is too broad. Firmware is low-level system code, commonly in nonvolatile storage. For a chip described as 2^a×w, a is the number of address inputs and w the data width. Combine chips in parallel to increase word width and in banks to increase the number of words. Distinguish address decoding from data selection. Example Worked microexample Eight 1K×1 chips in parallel make 1K×8 storage: 10 shared address lines and 8 data bits. Four such banks make 4K×8 and require 12 address bits overall. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Cache placement, index bits and conflicts
records.text: Let B be block size in bytes and L the number of cache lines. Block number=floor(address/B); offset=address mod B. Direct mapping uses line=block mod L. Fully associative placement permits any line. A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block. For power-of-two sizes, offset bits=log2 B, index bits=log2 S and remaining address bits form the tag. Compare tags and valid bits to identify a hit. Two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together. Associations reduce placement conflicts but require more tag comparisons. Example Worked microexample 16-byte blocks and four direct-mapped lines: addresses 0 and 64 have block numbers 0 and 4, both index 0, so alternating them causes conflict misses. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Cache replacement and write-policy traces
records.text: FIFO evicts the earliest inserted line; LRU evicts the least recently accessed line. On each access, record hit/miss, the set involved and policy state. Hits update LRU order but do not reset FIFO insertion order. Direct mapping has no replacement choice within a line. Write-through updates the lower level on each write; write-back modifies cache and marks a dirty bit, writing to the lower level on eviction. Write-allocate fetches a missed block before writing; no-write-allocate writes below without installing it. L1/L2 describe hierarchy levels; split cache means separate instruction/data caches and unified means combined. Internal/external location is another classification, not synonymous with split/unified. Example Worked microexample Two fully associative lines, references A,B,A,C: all except the second A are misses. LRU evicts B for C; FIFO evicts A. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Virtual addresses, MMU and page faults
records.text: Virtual memory gives processes translated address spaces and protection; backing storage can hold nonresident pages. The MMU translates virtual/logical addresses to physical addresses, using page tables and often a TLB of recent translations. Virtual memory is not just extra disk disguised as RAM. With page size P, page=floor(virtual_address/P), offset=virtual_address mod P and physical_address=frame×P+offset. A valid nonresident page access faults and may require loading data; invalid or forbidden accesses can also fault. A cache miss, TLB miss and page fault are different events; not every page fault reads a disk, since zero-fill and already-resident shared pages exist. Example Worked microexample With 1024-byte pages, address 2053 is page 2, offset 5. If page 2 maps to frame 7, physical address=7173. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Persistent storage and access methods
records.text: An HDD stores magnetic patterns on tracks divided into sectors; reads/writes access addressed blocks while platters rotate. A head normally stays over a track while reading but moves radially for seeks. It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits. SSDs use nonvolatile semiconductor storage without mechanical seek. Optical media use lasers; tape is suited to sequential streaming and archives. An Ethernet cable is a communication medium, not a disk or RAM. In textbook access taxonomy, tape is sequential, disk is direct access with positioning delay, RAM is random access with broadly address-independent timing, and associative access matches content. “Random-access disk” is also common informal usage; specify the taxonomy when comparing direct and random access. Optical access ranges such as 100–300 ms are historical examples, not universal device specifications. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — I/O interfaces, registers and commands
records.text: A peripheral performs input, output or storage outside the CPU’s execution core; CPU itself is not a peripheral. Input units encode external information and output units present processed results. A device controller handles device protocol/timing; its interface commonly exposes data, status and control registers. Buffers absorb speed differences and error/status bits report conditions. Control commands start actions, test/status commands inspect readiness or errors, read commands bring device data toward the system, and write/output commands send system data to the device. “Issue” describes sending a command, not a standard fourth command category. A controller is hardware; a driver is software that operates it. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Polling, interrupts and DMA
records.text: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device. DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup. Completion or errors can interrupt the CPU. DMA does not eliminate CPU involvement in configuration, ownership, address mapping or completion. Burst mode can hold the bus for a block; cycle stealing takes individual transfer opportunities, and transparent DMA uses idle opportunities. DMA reduces per-word CPU work but competes for memory bandwidth. Choose it for substantial blocks; mapping devices to addresses is a separate design dimension. Example Worked microexample For 1000 words, polling or interrupt transfer may require CPU work per word. DMA replaces much of that work with setup and completion, although the actual memory transfers still take time. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — I/O address spaces, priorities and handshaking
records.text: Memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable load/store operations. Isolated/port-mapped I/O has a separate port space and special instructions such as IN/OUT. MMIO must respect device access widths, ordering and side effects; a status read is not necessarily a harmless RAM read. Asynchronous handshaking uses request/ready and acknowledgement signals to tolerate unequal speeds: sender presents data and requests, receiver accepts and acknowledges, then each withdraws its signal. A single strobe lacks this feedback. Interrupt priority selects among simultaneous requests, using schemes such as polling, daisy chains or priority hardware. Serial sends bits over time; parallel transfers multiple bits on multiple lines, without guaranteeing higher real-world speed. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Named interfaces: choose by connection role
records.text: USB is a serial peripheral interconnect used by keyboards and external storage; RS-232 specifies a traditional point-to-point serial electrical/interface standard. Both RS-232 and USB use serial communication; distinguish their interface roles and specifications. HDMI carries digital video and audio. Ethernet connects network devices; it is not memory. SATA is a storage interface; legacy IDE/PATA and SCSI represent other storage connections, while iSCSI carries SCSI commands over IP. PCI is a peripheral expansion interconnect, not a disk protocol; connecting unlike bus segments requires suitable bridge/controller logic. “Extends processor-bus connectivity” without topology does not uniquely identify PCI or Multibus. POSIX is a software interface standard with operations such as open/read/write/close; ASCII is a character encoding. An unqualified “standard PC disk interface” needs an era or device requirement. USB Implementers Forum, mass storage transport specification Texas Instruments AN-216 HDMI Licensing Administrator specifications overview Linux libATA Developer Guide

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Analog interfaces and component identification
records.text: An ADC measures an analog input and produces a digital code; a DAC produces an analog output from a digital code. ADC080x parts are 8-bit successive-approximation analog-to-digital converters; DAC0830 is a digital-to-analog converter, while 82C55 denotes a programmable parallel I/O interface, not an ADC. Component names are not interchangeable with the direction of conversion. For an ideal n-bit converter spanning a voltage range V, one code step is approximately V/2^n; actual endpoint conventions and specifications must be stated. Quantization rounds an analog range into discrete codes; sample rate and resolution measure different properties. Example Worked microexample An ideal 8-bit ADC over a 5.12 V span has 256 codes and a 0.02 V step. Greater bit depth reduces the quantization step for the same span. Texas Instruments ADC0804-N

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Execution-time calculations and bottlenecks
records.text: CPU time=instruction_count×CPI×clock_period=instruction_count×CPI/clock_rate. CPI may be a weighted average across instruction classes; IPC is its reciprocal only under a consistent whole-program definition. Raising clock frequency does not guarantee a faster program when instruction count or stalls increase. Throughput counts completed work per unit time; latency measures one job’s delay. When a fraction f of execution is sped up by factor s, overall speedup=1/((1−f)+f/s). The unaffected fraction limits gains. Compare the same workload and include memory and branch penalties instead of equating clock speed with performance. Example Worked microexample 10^6 instructions, CPI=2 and 1 GHz take 2 ms. If half the time becomes twice as fast, overall speedup=1/(0.5+0.25)=4/3, not 2. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Pipelines: overlap and timing
records.text: A pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions; it primarily improves throughput. In an ideal k-stage single-issue pipeline, n instructions take k+n−1 cycles when stages are balanced and there are no stalls. Without overlap, comparable work takes nk stage cycles. The ideal steady-state completion rate is one instruction per cycle, while an individual instruction still spans multiple stages. Choose the pipeline clock using the slowest stage plus register overhead. Fill/drain overhead matters for short streams. “Fetch/decode one instruction while executing another” describes pipelining, whereas issuing several instructions in one cycle requires multiple-issue resources. Example Worked microexample A five-stage pipeline processing 10 instructions takes 14 ideal cycles versus 50 without overlap: speedup=50/14≈3.57. It does not reach the limiting factor of five for this short stream. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Pipeline hazards and instruction-level parallelism
records.text: Structural hazards compete for one resource. Data hazards arise when an instruction needs a result not yet available; forwarding can supply results early, but some dependencies still stall. Control hazards arise when the next PC depends on an unresolved branch. Branch prediction guesses direction/target and continues speculatively; wrong guesses discard work. Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to multiple functional units in a cycle when dependencies permit. Out-of-order execution schedules ready operations before stalled older ones while preserving architectural results and exception behavior. Dynamic resource allocation assigns available internal entries/units at runtime. These mechanisms exploit instruction-level parallelism; wider fetch improves instruction supply, not necessarily individual memory latency. Computer Organization and Architecture module INFLIBNET Computer Architecture, Multiple Issue Processors I

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Multiprocessing, vectors and Flynn classification
records.text: Flynn classifies instruction and data streams: SISD has one of each; SIMD applies one instruction stream to multiple data elements; MIMD uses multiple instruction and data streams; MISD has multiple instruction streams for a common data stream and is uncommon. A vector instruction describes an operation over a sequence of elements; physical lanes may process them in batches, not all in one instant. SMP processors share memory/I/O and have peer roles under an OS. Distributed-memory systems communicate between separate address spaces. More cores increase available parallel work, but serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup. “Core i7” is a product family rather than one core count; a model number is essential. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Historical conventions and processor-width caveats
records.text: The familiar generation convention associates first with vacuum tubes, second with transistors, third with integrated circuits and fourth with microprocessor/VLSI-era personal computers. Stored-program machines arose in the first era. High-level languages became prominent around the transition into the second; introduction dates do not fit every generation boundary. Magnetic-core memory spanned more than one era, so “witnessed use” cannot identify exactly one. Several generations improved performance. Integration generally reduced individual component dimensions while capacity, density and processor performance grew; these are trends rather than guarantees for every model. Intel’s 80386 introduced 32-bit x86 execution in 1985, before 80486/Pentium; the 80286 was a 16-bit predecessor. An n-bit processor label does not force its PC, IR or address register to be n bits. Columbia University Computing History, Computer Generations Intel 1987 Annual Report Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Identify architecture assumptions before answering
records.text: Main memory, registers and cache can all provide temporary storage; identify the scope and role. Memory can also include nonvolatile ROM/flash, so distinguish RAM when comparing power-off data retention with disk storage. Architecture lifetime, power efficiency and generational improvements require assumptions; definitions alone do not make these exclusive. For a TEST-instruction question, identify the instruction and the complete statements being compared before drawing a conclusion. Identify a logic gate from its actual graphical symbol. An opcode can be identified from an explicit description of its operation-field role even without a figure. Check that the question includes the phrase, choices or diagram needed to apply the relevant architecture rule. Computer Organization and Architecture module

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Model-specific core and thread counts
records.text: Intel’s desktop comparison chart lists the Core i7-920 with four physical cores and eight hardware threads. Core count and thread count are distinct specification fields: use the exact processor model and the field requested rather than inferring a count from the Core i7 family name. Intel Core i7 Desktop Processor Comparison Chart

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Buses as shared communication paths
records.text: A bus is a set of common signal lines used to transfer binary information among connected units. In a parallel register bus, one line carries each bit position; control signals select a source and enable the intended destination. Storage registers and memory retain information, while the bus provides a transfer path. Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 40 Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 6

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — The basic single-accumulator memory instruction
records.text: In the textbook single-accumulator organization, a memory-reference instruction has an operation part and an address part. The address locates a memory operand; the operation combines that operand with the accumulator as required. The address field is not the operand value itself, and this simple format does not describe every addressing mode or instruction set. Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 47

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Textbook instruction-set and control tendencies
records.text: RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer; CISC means Complex Instruction Set Computer. The textbook RISC design pairs a relatively large register set, load/store access and easily decoded instructions with hardwired rather than microprogrammed control and an efficient pipeline. These are design tendencies, not guarantees of one-cycle latency or lower power for every implementation. Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 77 Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 78

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Instruction and stack pointers in 64-bit x86
records.text: In Intel 64-bit mode, RIP holds the offset of the next instruction to execute. RSP is the 64-bit stack pointer, extending the ESP/SP stack role. These pointers are distinct from CS and SS, which are code and stack segment registers. Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer’s Manual, Volume 1 · §§3.4–3.5 and 6.1

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Exclusive-OR notation
records.text: The circled plus symbol ⊕ denotes exclusive OR. For two Boolean inputs, A⊕B is 1 exactly when the inputs differ; an overbar or output inversion would complement this result. Texas Instruments SNx4HC86 Quadruple 2-Input XOR Gates · description

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Bistable one-bit state
records.text: A flip-flop is bistable: it has two stable states representing 0 and 1. While powered, it can retain one bit until an input or designated clock event changes its state. Multiple flip-flops are required to represent a multi-bit counter state. Computer Organization and Architecture module · page 16

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 1 · Q00029
records.text: Q00029 Question 1 COA30 Which one of the following is responsible for controlling the flow of bits between memory and controllers with no need for a constant intervention from the CPU? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Disk fragmenting B Memo, manager C Device controller D Direct memory access Direct memory access DMA transfers a block directly between device and memory; the CPU supplies setup information and receives completion notification, rather than moving every word (PDF pp.107–108). This precisely meets the absence of constant intervention. A generic device controller alone does not establish DMA capability. A incorrect Disk fragmenting is not the block-transfer mechanism described on pp.107–108. B incorrect The corrupted name “Memo, manager” does not identify the DMA mechanism on p.107. C incorrect An I/O controller can notify the CPU under interrupt I/O; that still leaves CPU data movement (p.106). D correct Direct transfers and only beginning/end CPU involvement are explicit on p.108.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 2 · Q00044
records.text: Q00044 Question 2 COA-S02 COA01 Which one of the following is a communication pathway connecting transmitting signals in binary digits between two or more devices? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Memory B Register C CPU D Bus Bus The common bus is a set of shared lines used to transfer binary information among registers (PDF p.40). The structural definitions distinguish storage and processing components from their communication mechanism (p.6). A incorrect Main memory stores data; it is an endpoint (p.6). B incorrect Registers store bits, rather than naming the pathway (p.35). C incorrect CPU processes and controls; it is a communicating component (p.6). D correct A bus supplies common bit lines and selection controls (p.40).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 3 · Q00056
records.text: Q00056 Question 3 COA24 COA28 Which memory is characterized by the need for periodic change in order to maintain data storage? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Static RAM B Dynamic RAM C Disk D Tape Dynamic RAM Interpret “periodic change” as periodic charge refreshing: capacitor charge leaks, so DRAM needs refresh (PDF p.80). This is different from SRAM power retention and nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91). A incorrect SRAM uses flip-flops and holds data while powered (p.80), without the stated charge refresh. B correct DRAM capacitor discharge explicitly requires periodic refreshing (p.80). C incorrect Disk is nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91), not capacitor-refresh RAM. D incorrect Tape is also nonvolatile secondary storage (p.91), not refresh RAM.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 4 · Q00060
records.text: Q00060 Question 4 COA28 In the ordinary HDD model, which statement is incorrect? Read/write refers to accessing sectors on the current track; seeking to another track is a separate operation. Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Data is arranged in sectors within tracks B The head stays over the selected track while its sectors rotate beneath it C Its data is organized in tracks D It needs continuous power to keep bit contents It needs continuous power to keep bit contents An HDD records magnetic patterns in sectors arranged on tracks. During access to a selected track, rotation brings sectors under the head; seeking moves the head radially to another track. The medium retains its magnetic contents without continuous power, so the claimed power requirement is false. Power is needed to operate the drive, but that differs from power needed merely to retain the stored bits. A incorrect Sectors are subdivisions of tracks in the stated HDD organization. B incorrect This describes track-local access; a separate seek changes which track is under the head. C incorrect Magnetic disk data is organized on tracks, so this statement is true. D correct An HDD is nonvolatile: retaining stored patterns does not require continuous power.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 5 · Q00093
records.text: Q00093 Question 5 COA05 COA03 Which listed circuit category requires stored state so that output can depend on past input behavior as well as present inputs? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A Combinational circuit B Sequential circuits C A two-input AND gate with no feedback D A combinational multiplexer with no storage Sequential circuits A sequential circuit contains state that preserves information about prior behavior. A combinational circuit computes its outputs from current inputs after propagation delay. The specified AND gate and multiplexer are combinational examples without storage or feedback. They therefore do not require remembered state, while the sequential-circuit category does. This distinction concerns logical state, not whether physical propagation takes time. A incorrect Combinational output depends on current inputs rather than stored history. B correct Sequential circuits retain state and can make output depend on past behavior. C incorrect The specified AND gate computes a truth function of its present inputs without storage. D incorrect The specified multiplexer selects a present data input; it has no stored logical state.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 6 · Q00134
records.text: Q00134 Question 6 COA09 In computers, subtraction is carried out generally by __________. Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order. A 1's complement method B 2's complement method C Signed magnitude method D BCD subtraction method 2's complement method Subtraction is described as complementation plus addition: add one to the inverted subtrahend, then add that two’s complement to the minuend (PDF p.42). Hence R1 + (~R2+1) represents R1−R2 within the register width. A incorrect One’s complement alone omits the added 1 in p.42’s subtraction procedure. B correct The inversion-plus-one subtrahend is exactly two’s complement (p.42). C incorrect The cited procedure does not use separate sign and magnitude arithmetic. D incorrect The cited general register subtraction is not BCD digit subtraction.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 7 · Q00135
records.text: Q00135 Question 7 COA05 Pick the different _ Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A Decoder B Encoder C Multiplexer D Shift Register Shift register: the sequential circuit. COA05 distinguishes combinational circuits from sequential storage. Decoder, encoder and multiplexer are explicitly combinational; the shift register retains state and therefore belongs to the sequential class. The image confirms the four option texts. Using the state criterion provides the technically supported odd-one-out distinction without relying on the source emphasis. A incorrect A decoder is combinational and has no stored logical state in this circuit classification. B incorrect An encoder is also combinational, grouping it with the decoder and multiplexer. C incorrect A multiplexer selects among present inputs and is explicitly a combinational circuit. D correct A shift register retains and shifts stored state, distinguishing it from the three combinational devices.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 8 · Q00136
records.text: Q00136 Question 8 COA11 COA16 An operation performed on the contents of a register is known as Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Instruction code B Micro-operation C Accumulator D Register Micro-operation An elementary operation on information stored in one or more registers is explicitly defined as a micro operation (PDF p.38). An instruction code tells the computer what operation to execute, while registers are the storage objects (pp.35,47). A incorrect An instruction code specifies work; it is not the elementary register operation itself (p.47). B correct Matches the exact definition and examples shift, count, clear, load (p.38). C incorrect Accumulator denotes a processing register, not the operation. D incorrect A register stores the information being operated on (p.35).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 9 · Q00137
records.text: Q00137 Question 9 COA-S04 COA20 Which one is true about RISC computers? Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor. A RISC are with few numbers of registers when compared to CISC B RISC use complex and efficient machine instructions when compared to CISC C RISC is with hardwired control unit with pipelining processing D RISC uses extensive addressing capabilities for memory operations E None RISC is with hardwired control unit with pipelining processing RISC characteristics explicitly include hardwired control, many registers, few addressing modes and an efficient pipeline (PDF p.77). These jointly support C and contradict the reversed CISC-like descriptions. A incorrect A reverses the relatively large register count on p.77. B incorrect Complex instructions are the CISC characteristic (p.78), whereas RISC has few, easily decoded instructions (p.77). C correct Both hardwired control and efficient pipeline are explicitly listed (p.77). D incorrect RISC has relatively few addressing modes and memory access limited to loads/stores (p.77). E incorrect C is supported, so “None” fails.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 10 · Q00138
records.text: Q00138 Question 10 COA01 Which of the following is not a basic element within the microprocessor? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Microcontroller B Arithmetic logic unit (ALU) C Register array D Control unit Microcontroller The module divides the CPU into the register set, ALU and control unit (PDF p.57). Treating microprocessor as the CPU implementation, A is the only choice outside that list; the module does not separately define microcontrollers. A correct Microcontroller is not one of the three CPU components listed on p.57. B incorrect ALU performs the micro-operations (p.57). C incorrect The register set stores intermediate data (p.57). D incorrect Control unit supervises transfers and ALU operations (p.57).
