records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 11 · Q00139
records.text: Q00139 Question 11 COA30 COA19 After CPU setup, which transfer method moves a block between an I/O device and memory without the CPU copying each data word? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Software interrupts B Interrupt-driven I/O C Polled I/O D Direct memory access (DMA) Direct memory access (DMA) DMA assigns the block movement to a controller after the CPU configures the transfer. Polling and ordinary interrupt-driven I/O still make the CPU execute item transfers. A software interrupt is an instruction-requested control transfer to a handler, not a block-copy engine. CPU setup and completion handling remain part of DMA; bypass refers specifically to avoiding CPU copying for every word. A incorrect A software interrupt requests handler execution; it does not itself move a block directly between device and memory. B incorrect The interrupt handler still uses CPU execution to service the device and move items. C incorrect The CPU checks status and moves items itself in polled I/O. D correct The DMA controller performs the block transfer after setup, avoiding per-word CPU copies.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 12 · Q00140
records.text: Q00140 Question 12 COA12 In the simple CPU-master bus model, which bus carries instruction or operand values in both directions during memory reads and writes? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Address bus B Control bus C Data bus D None of the above Data bus Data signals carry the values transferred between processor and memory. A read brings those values toward the CPU, while a write sends them toward memory, so the data bus serves both directions. Address signals select a location. Control signals coordinate operations and can include signals in both directions, but the question specifically asks about instruction or operand values rather than aggregate control direction. A incorrect The address bus selects locations rather than carrying payload values. B incorrect Control signals coordinate transfers rather than carrying the instruction or operand payload. C correct The data bus carries values toward the CPU on reads and toward memory on writes. D incorrect The data bus supplies the requested role.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 13 · Q00365
records.text: Q00365 Question 13 COA35 COA36 Which specific instruction-processing technique overlaps fetch or decode of a later instruction with execution of an earlier instruction? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Superscalar processing B None of the above C Parallel Computation D Pipe-lining Pipe-lining Fetching or decoding one instruction while another is being executed overlaps different instruction stages, which is pipelining. Superscalar processing instead permits issuing multiple instructions to execution resources during a cycle. These techniques can coexist, but the specific fetch/decode-versus-execute overlap identifies the pipeline mechanism rather than the processor’s issue width. A incorrect Superscalar processing names multiple-issue execution resources; the stated overlap of different stages specifically describes pipelining. B incorrect Pipelining is an available matching choice. C incorrect Parallel computation is broader simultaneous processing (p.114); it does not identify the staged instruction mechanism as precisely as D. D correct The instruction pipeline reads consecutive instructions while previous ones execute (p.117).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 14 · Q00366
records.text: Q00366 Question 14 COA19 Which instruction class, where supported, bypasses the immediately following instruction when its condition is met? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Branch instruction B Return instruction C Skip instruction D Jump instruction Skip instruction A SKIP instruction conditionally bypasses the next instruction. That differs from an ordinary branch, which chooses a target, and from RETURN, which restores a saved return point. The original phrase jump to the next instruction did not express bypassing it; the revised wording states that intended control-flow effect precisely. The classification is based on behavior rather than an unstated machine-specific opcode. A incorrect A branch chooses a target rather than naming the specific next-instruction-bypass class. B incorrect RETURN restores a saved return point. C correct SKIP is the conditional next-instruction-bypass operation described. D incorrect A general jump chooses a target rather than naming this specific conditional operation.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 15 · Q00367
records.text: Q00367 Question 15 COA19 An interrupt that is caused by register overflow, attempt to divide by zero, an invalid operation code, stack overflow can be? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A None of the above B Software interrupt C External interrupt D Internal interrupt Internal interrupt (synchronous exception). COA19 classifies divide errors and illegal opcodes as synchronous internal exceptions because they arise from the executing instruction. Register or stack overflow belongs to that category when the machine traps it. Overflow does not invariably interrupt: ordinary flags may merely record it. Deliberate software requests and asynchronous external device events describe different causes. A incorrect The internal-exception category directly covers these instruction-related faults when trapping is enabled. B incorrect A software interrupt is deliberately requested by an instruction, rather than caused by an execution fault. C incorrect External interrupts originate from devices or timers, rather than the faulting instruction. D correct These execution-generated faults are internal exceptions; overflow trapping still depends on the architecture.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 16 · Q00368
records.text: Q00368 Question 16 COA12 Computer address bus is Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Unidirectional B None of the above C Multidirectional D Bidirectional Unidirectional For the CPU-initiated memory operations described, CPU-held address registers supply the memory address (PDF pp.82–83 and 70). Thus the address path runs CPU→memory; this is a direction within that model, not a rule excluding DMA bus masters. A correct CPU loads MAR to select memory; the addressed memory does not return an address (pp.82–83). B incorrect The described CPU-address path supplies a matching option A. C incorrect The module’s CPU-memory operation does not require simultaneous multidirectional address flow. D incorrect Read/write data can go both ways, but the initiating CPU supplies the address.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 17 · Q00369
records.text: Q00369 Question 17 COA-S03 The simplest way to organize a computer is to have one processor register and an instruction code format with two parts. The first part specifies the operation to be performed and the second specifies . Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A address B output C Input D operand address The module reproduces this two-part instruction description: operation first, address second; that address locates the operand (PDF p.47). The operand itself and its address must not be conflated. A correct The second field specifies an address (p.47). B incorrect Output is not the second field in this format. C incorrect Input is not the second field in this format. D incorrect The operand is fetched using the address; it is not generally embedded in this field (p.47).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 18 · Q00370
records.text: Q00370 Question 18 COA23 Which of the following computer memory is fastest? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A RAM B Register C None of the above D Hard disk Register The hierarchy figure on PDF p.79 places registers before cache, RAM and disk. Register organization also avoids time-consuming memory accesses (p.58). Although p.84 calls cache the fastest memory-hierarchy component, it qualifies cache as approaching CPU component speed; registers are the CPU storage meant here. A incorrect RAM requires memory access, avoided by retaining intermediate values in registers (p.58). B correct Registers are the fastest offered CPU storage tier in Figure 6.1 (p.79). C incorrect A listed choice fits. D incorrect Disk lies at the slow, large secondary-storage end of the hierarchy (p.79).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 19 · Q00539
records.text: Q00539 Question 19 COA31 COA30 It is a method used to synchronize the I/O device with the microprocessor Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Interrupt B Handshaking C Interface D None Handshaking. COA31 describes asynchronous handshaking as an exchange of request/ready and acknowledgement signals. The sender presents data, the receiver accepts it, and the feedback coordinates transfer despite unequal device and processor speeds. An interrupt requests service but does not itself name this two-sided transfer protocol. An interface is the broader connection exposing the signals and registers. A incorrect Interrupts request processor attention; they do not specifically identify the request-and-acknowledgement transfer protocol. B correct Request and acknowledgement signals synchronize the sender and receiver despite unequal operating speeds. C incorrect An interface provides the connection; handshaking names the synchronization method implemented through it. D incorrect Handshaking is an explicitly supported synchronization method, so an affirmative option fits.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 20 · Q00542
records.text: Q00542 Question 20 COA22 Which one of the following instructions is incorrect? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A MOV AL, BP B INC CX C DEC CX D All MOV AL, BP is invalid. Under the ordinary Intel forms specified in COA22, AL is an 8-bit destination while BP is a 16-bit source. MOV does not implicitly resize these operands, so MOV AL, BP is invalid. INC CX and DEC CX are legal 16-bit operations. Consequently the all-invalid alternative fails because two listed instructions are valid. A correct The 8-bit AL and 16-bit BP widths do not match for this MOV instruction. B incorrect INC CX legally increments a 16-bit register under the stated legacy x86 assumptions. C incorrect DEC CX legally decrements a 16-bit register under the stated legacy x86 assumptions. D incorrect INC CX and DEC CX are valid, so the instructions are not all incorrect.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 21 · Q00544
records.text: Q00544 Question 21 COA21 A register used to indicate the condition of the microprocessor is Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A SI B FLAG C DI D EIP FLAG register. COA21 states that FLAGS/EFLAGS/RFLAGS report processor status. This is the register family indicated by the option FLAG. SI and DI are general-purpose registers with conventional index roles, and EIP identifies the instruction position. Neither the index registers nor the instruction pointer is the processor condition/status register requested. A incorrect SI has an index/general-purpose role rather than collecting the processor condition flags. B correct FLAG denotes the status-register family reporting processor conditions such as arithmetic status. C incorrect DI has an index/general-purpose role rather than serving as the processor status register. D incorrect EIP identifies instruction position; it does not contain the collection of processor condition flags.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 22 · Q00545
records.text: Q00545 Question 22 COA22 Which one of the following instructions is correct Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A MOV DS, 20 B MOV ES, 40 C MOV SS, 60 D None None of these immediate-to-segment MOV forms is valid. COA22 excludes a direct immediate-to-segment-register MOV in the assumed legacy x86 syntax. DS, ES and SS are segment registers, and each listed source is an immediate number. A permitted sequence first loads the value into a suitable general register and then moves that register to the segment register. Therefore all three displayed forms fail. A incorrect MOV DS, 20 attempts the unsupported direct transfer of an immediate into a segment register. B incorrect MOV ES, 40 also attempts an unsupported immediate-to-segment-register transfer in the stated syntax. C incorrect MOV SS, 60 has the same unsupported direct immediate source for a segment destination. D correct All three proposed segment-register instructions require an intermediate register or supported memory source.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 23 · Q00546
records.text: Q00546 Question 23 COA-S05 A register used to address the next instruction in a section of memory is Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A RSP B CS C RIP D SS RIP, the instruction pointer. COA21 identifies IP/EIP/RIP as the instruction-position register family; COA14 identifies the PC role as locating the next instruction to fetch. RIP is the corresponding 64-bit x86 instruction pointer. CS selects the code segment and SS the stack segment, while RSP is the stack pointer. A segment selector alone does not identify the next instruction offset. A incorrect RSP tracks the stack, not the next instruction position within the instruction stream. B incorrect CS identifies the code segment; the instruction pointer supplies the instruction position within it. C correct RIP is the x86 instruction pointer used to identify the next instruction position. D incorrect SS identifies the stack segment rather than the location of the next instruction.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 24 · Q00562
records.text: Q00562 Question 24 COA38 The Intel's first true 32-bit microprocessor is Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A Pentium B 80486 C 80286 D 80386 80386, within the offered x86 lineage. COA38 explicitly dates 32-bit x86 execution to the 80386 in 1985. It precedes the 80486 and Pentium, while the 80286 is a 16-bit predecessor. The offered choices therefore select 80386. This conclusion concerns the x86 sequence represented by the options; it should not be expanded into a claim about every historical Intel processor family. A incorrect Pentium follows the 80386; it was not the first 32-bit member among these x86 choices. B incorrect The 80486 follows the 80386, which had already introduced 32-bit x86 execution. C incorrect The note identifies the 80286 as a 16-bit predecessor, rather than the 32-bit introduction. D correct The 80386 introduced 32-bit x86 execution before the other offered 32-bit processors.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 25 · Q00569
records.text: Q00569 Question 25 COA22 The content of BH is 10, AL is 8, CL is 4 how much is the content of AX after MUL BH Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A 40 B 80 C 32 D 320 AX = 80. The operand BH is a byte register. COA22 states that unsigned byte MUL multiplies AL by the explicit byte operand and stores the product in AX. Substituting the given values yields 8 × 10 = 80. CL is not an operand of MUL BH; multiplying by its value would change the instruction being evaluated. A incorrect 40 multiplies BH by CL, but byte MUL uses AL as its implicit multiplicand. B correct AL × BH equals 8 × 10 = 80, written into AX. C incorrect 32 multiplies AL by CL, whereas the explicit operand is BH, not CL. D incorrect 320 incorrectly includes CL as a third factor; MUL BH multiplies only AL and BH.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 26 · Q00573
records.text: Q00573 Question 26 COA22 Which legacy x86 instruction is arithmetic rather than a data-transfer or operand-exchange operation? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A MOVS B LODS C XCHG D INC INC MOVS and LODS are string-transfer operations, and XCHG exchanges operand values. INC instead increments an operand, making it arithmetic. The revised stem states the classification criterion, so different no longer depends on whether the reader groups string operations, operand counts or another property. This retains the original instruction set and intended comparison while giving every choice a definite classification. A incorrect MOVS transfers string data. B incorrect LODS loads string data. C incorrect XCHG exchanges operands rather than performing arithmetic. D correct INC increments an operand arithmetically.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 27 · Q00609
records.text: Q00609 Question 27 COA21 COA11 Which register is a user-accessible register? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A DX B IR C MBR D MDR DX is programmer-accessible. COA21 explicitly identifies DX as programmer-visible and IR/MDR as conceptual internal registers. MBR is the memory-buffer name used for the same data-transfer role as MDR in COA11. The question asks which register is user-accessible in this architectural sense, so the x86 general-purpose register DX is the supported choice. A correct DX belongs to the programmer-visible x86 register set and is usable by ordinary instructions. B incorrect IR is the conceptual internal instruction register, rather than an ordinary programmer-addressable register. C incorrect MBR is the internal memory-buffer/data-transfer register, not a user-visible general-purpose register. D incorrect MDR is the conceptual internal memory-data register, not an ordinary user-accessible execution register.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 28 · Q00614
records.text: Q00614 Question 28 COA21 Which register is found starting from Pentium processor? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A EAX B EIP C R8 D None None was introduced with original Pentium. Reading starting from as introduced with Pentium, COA21 rules out every named register. EAX and EIP already existed with the 80386, while R8 belongs to the later 64-bit extension rather than original Pentium. Therefore none is correct under the introduction-date reading. Simply asking which registers a Pentium contains would be a different question, with EAX and EIP both present. A incorrect EAX existed before Pentium in the 80386; it was not introduced starting with Pentium. B incorrect EIP also existed in the 80386, so Pentium was not its first generation. C incorrect R8 belongs to the later 64-bit extension, not the original Pentium register set. D correct None of the named registers was introduced with original Pentium under the starting-generation reading.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 29 · Q00621
records.text: Q00621 Question 29 COA-S01 How many physical processor cores does the Intel Core i7-920 desktop processor have? Count cores, not hardware threads. Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A 5 B 4 C 6 D 7 4 The supplementary Intel desktop-processor comparison chart specifies four cores and eight threads for the i7-920. The answer is therefore four physical cores. The supplied note provides related background that Core i7 is a family with no single core count, but does not supply this model’s number. Naming the model and consulting Intel supplies that missing fact without implying that every Core i7 has the same configuration. A incorrect Five does not match Intel’s physical-core count for this model. B correct Intel lists four physical cores for the i7-920. C incorrect Six is not the specified model’s physical-core count. D incorrect Seven is not this model’s physical-core count.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 30 · Q00628
records.text: Q00628 Question 30 COA18 A memory operand has effective address EA=A, where A is the address field stored directly in the instruction. Which addressing mode is used? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Direct addressing B Immediate addressing C Register addressing D None Direct addressing In direct addressing, the instruction’s address field is itself the effective address: EA=A, and the operand is M[A]. Immediate addressing uses A as a value rather than a memory address, while register addressing uses a register as the operand source. A transfer’s register and memory endpoints alone do not determine its addressing mode, so the revised question supplies the missing effective-address relationship. A correct EA=A defines direct addressing. B incorrect Immediate addressing uses A as the operand value. C incorrect Register addressing uses a register operand rather than M[A]. D incorrect Direct addressing matches the relationship.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 31 · Q00630
records.text: Q00630 Question 31 COA24 One of the following is not a characteristic of SRAM Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Fast B Expensive C Memory refreshing s D None Memory refreshing s SRAM stores bits in flip-flop state; applying power is sufficient and no refresh is needed (PDF p.81). Fast and relatively expensive are expressly listed, making refreshing the exception. A incorrect Faster than DRAM is stated (p.81). B incorrect More expensive than DRAM is stated (p.81). C correct No need for refreshing is explicit (p.81), so this is the non-characteristic. D incorrect There is a non-characteristic, C.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 32 · Q00632
records.text: Q00632 Question 32 COA33 Which one of the following is analog to digital converter? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A ADC080X B DAC0830 C 82C55 D None ADC080X is the analog-to-digital converter. COA33 defines an ADC as producing a digital code from an analog input and specifically identifies ADC080x as an 8-bit successive-approximation ADC family. DAC0830 performs the reverse conversion. The 82C55 is a programmable parallel I/O interface, not an ADC. The component identifiers therefore resolve this question without inferring capabilities merely from their general interface role. A correct ADC080x is explicitly identified as the analog-to-digital converter family in the note. B incorrect DAC0830 converts digital codes into analog output, which is the reverse direction. C incorrect 82C55 provides programmable parallel I/O; the note explicitly distinguishes it from an ADC. D incorrect ADC080X is a valid analog-to-digital component, so the list is not missing an answer.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 33 · Q00648
records.text: Q00648 Question 33 COA21 Which is NOT an Intel x86 16-bit general-purpose register? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A AX B BP C SI D FLAGS FLAGS Intel’s general-purpose classification includes AX, BP and SI even though these registers have conventional special roles. FLAGS instead reports status conditions and is outside that group. The final option supplies an actual non-general-purpose register rather than incorrectly excluding SP merely because it tracks the stack. This preserves the register-class distinction without inventing a narrower meaning for multipurpose or misrepresenting Intel’s classification. A incorrect AX is a 16-bit general-purpose register. B incorrect BP is general-purpose despite its conventional base-pointer role. C incorrect SI is general-purpose despite its conventional source-index role. D correct FLAGS reports processor status rather than belonging to the general-purpose group.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 34 · Q00689
records.text: Q00689 Question 34 COA01 COA02 Which of the following is a type of computer architecture? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Microarchitecture B Harvard Architecture C Von-Neumann Architecture D All of the mentioned All listed categories are forms of computer design/architecture in the broad wording. COA01 calls microarchitecture the internal processor design, while COA02 contrasts Harvard and Von Neumann memory organizations. The broad phrase type of computer architecture encompasses all three usages, although they describe different abstraction levels. The comprehensive answer is therefore all of the mentioned. No single named option covers the entire set of valid architectural categories. A incorrect Microarchitecture is a valid internal-design category, but this alone omits the two valid memory organizations. B incorrect Harvard is a valid architecture category, but selecting it alone excludes the other valid categories. C incorrect Von Neumann is valid, but the broad question also admits microarchitecture and Harvard organization. D correct All three names describe architectural design categories, though they operate at different abstraction levels.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 35 · Q00690
records.text: Q00690 Question 35 COA05 Which one is not a combinational circuit? Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A Encoder B Decoder C Multiplexer D De-multiplexer E Register Register A register is a group of state-holding flip-flops (PDF p.35). Sequential circuits retain past information (p.15), whereas code/routing combinational circuits transform current inputs (pp.31,33–34). Thus register is the non-combinational choice. A incorrect Encoder maps the active input into a binary code (p.34); no stored state is part of this described mapping. B incorrect Decoder selects an output based on the input pattern (p.33). C incorrect Multiplexer is explicitly combinational (p.31). D incorrect Demultiplexer routes one input to a selected output (p.33), a present-input routing function. E correct Register contains storage flip-flops and retains state (p.35).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 36 · Q00691
records.text: Q00691 Question 36 COA25 In a _________ cache organization, cache permits data to be stored in any cache block. Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Direct Mapped B Set Associativity C Fully Associative D All Fully Associative Associative cache stores an address with each data item and searches by content (PDF p.87), rather than constraining a block to a single index. Set association retains index constraints (p.88). Fully associative is therefore the any-block placement organization. A incorrect Direct mapping has fixed index conflicts (p.88), so does not allow arbitrary block placement. B incorrect Set association allows multiple entries under the same index, not any block anywhere (p.88). C correct Address/content pairs searched associatively permit the unrestricted mapping described (p.87). D incorrect Direct and set mappings are restricted, so not all satisfy the claim.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 37 · Q00692
records.text: Q00692 Question 37 COA27 COA26 Which one used to translate virtual addresses into physical addresses when we are implementing the concept of Virtual memory? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A LRU B FIFO C Memory Management Unit D All Memory Management Unit (MMU). COA27 states that the MMU translates virtual/logical addresses into physical addresses using page tables and often a TLB. LRU and FIFO instead choose replacement victims, as described in COA26. Neither replacement policy performs address translation. Consequently the MMU is the single component matching the requested virtual-memory translation role; the all alternative incorrectly includes two different mechanisms. A incorrect LRU chooses a least-recently-used replacement victim; it does not translate virtual addresses. B incorrect FIFO selects the earliest inserted replacement victim, rather than computing physical addresses. C correct The MMU performs virtual-to-physical address translation using the translation structures described in the note. D incorrect Only the MMU translates addresses; LRU and FIFO are replacement policies.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 38 · Q00693
records.text: Q00693 Question 38 COA12 In a ________ bus, flow is only one-way from the CPU to memory. Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Address Bus B Data Bus C Control Bus D A & C Address Bus In the CPU-master model, CPU address registers identify the memory location (PDF pp.82–83), while data supports reads and writes (p.105) and control/status includes messages from both sides (pp.102–103). This makes A the specific one-way address path. A correct The CPU supplies the memory address (pp.82–83). B incorrect Read and write data travel in opposite directions (p.105). C incorrect Status reports return from I/O modules (p.103), so the whole control/status collection is not only CPU-outward. D incorrect C is not restricted to that one direction, so the conjunction fails.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 39 · Q00694
records.text: Q00694 Question 39 COA23 In memory hierarchy, faster access then_________. Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Greater cost per bit B Greater capacity C Smaller cost per bit D All Greater cost per bit The module states the speed/cost tradeoff directly: faster access has greater cost per bit (PDF p.79). Its separate capacity bullets associate larger capacity with lower cost and slower access, rather than faster access. A correct Exact stated speed/cost relationship (p.79). B incorrect Greater capacity is associated with slower access, not the stated faster tier (p.79). C incorrect Smaller cost per bit is associated with greater capacity, opposite the faster-access bullet (p.79). D incorrect B and C do not match the faster-access relationship.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 40 · Q00695
records.text: Q00695 Question 40 COA13 COA05 Which Shift register type used to act as a delay element? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Serial-In Serial-Out B Parallel-In Serial-Out C Serial-In Parallel-Out D All Serial-In Serial-Out The shift register accepts/transfers data serially and moves each bit one position per clock, emitting the rightmost bit (PDF p.36). With serial input and serial output, an n-stage register delays the stream by n shifts. This derivation identifies SISO under the usual stream-delay meaning. A correct Serial input traverses storage stages to serial output, producing the clock-count delay (p.36). B incorrect Parallel input/serial output serializes a loaded word; it does not preserve the incoming serial stream in the described way. C incorrect Serial input/parallel output exposes the stored bits together rather than the delayed serial stream. D incorrect Not all listed I/O forms implement the same serial-stream delay.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 41 · Q00697
records.text: Q00697 Question 41 COA04 Which one of them is a Universal Logic Gates? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A NAND B Ex-OR C AND D NOT NAND Figure 1.2 on PDF p.7 gives NAND as NOT(A AND B). Tie its inputs to obtain NOT A; NAND followed by that inverter gives AND; applying NAND to inverted inputs gives OR, as can be checked against the same truth tables. Thus NAND alone can build the basic AND/OR/NOT set. A correct NAND supplies inversion by tying inputs and then AND/OR by composition (p.7, Figure 1.2). B incorrect XOR alone maps all-zero inputs to zero; it cannot supply the inverter required by Figure 1.2. C incorrect AND alone also preserves zero and cannot produce NOT using only AND gates. D incorrect NOT only complements one input; it cannot combine independent input variables into AND/OR.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 42 · Q00698
records.text: Q00698 Question 42 COA02 COA01 Which textbook architecture model stores instructions and data in a shared addressed memory system? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Microarchitecture B Harvard Architecture C Von-Neumann Architecture D System Design Von-Neumann Architecture The Von Neumann model uses a shared addressed memory system for instructions and data. Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths. Microarchitecture names an internal implementation, while system design is broader than the particular stored-program memory model requested. The revised stem asks about a defining memory relationship rather than claiming that all modern computers use one exclusive organization. A incorrect Microarchitecture describes internal processor implementation. B incorrect Harvard separates instruction and data memories or paths. C correct Von Neumann uses the described shared addressed memory model. D incorrect System design is broader than this named memory model.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 43 · Q00893
records.text: Q00893 Question 43 COA32 In a design connecting a processor-side bus segment to an unlike peripheral bus segment, which hardware category provides the necessary bridge or interface logic? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SCSI B PCI C Bus bridge/controller logic D Multi bus Bus bridge/controller logic Unlike bus segments need bridge or controller logic to adapt their interfaces and coordinate transfers. PCI names a peripheral expansion interconnect, while SCSI names a storage connection; neither alone identifies the adapting component. Multibus names a bus rather than the requested bridge category. The revised topology and component requirement make the interface-logic choice definite without assuming a particular processor bus or expansion standard. A incorrect SCSI is a storage-connection standard rather than a bridge component. B incorrect PCI names an expansion interconnect rather than the adapting logic. C correct Bridge/controller logic connects unlike bus segments. D incorrect Multibus names a bus rather than the required interface component.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 44 · Q00894
records.text: Q00894 Question 44 COA05 Combinational circuit differ from sequential circuit primarily because Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A Combinational circuit cannot be built using logic circuit B The output of combinational circuit depends only on the present input, not on past output. C . Sequential circuit have no feedback while combinational circuit do D The combinational circuit requires clock signal, but sequential circuit do not The output of combinational circuit depends only on the present input, not on past output. Combinational output depends only on input at the current time (PDF p.10); sequential output also depends on the past and includes memory elements (p.15). This is the primary functional difference, independent of implementation speed. A incorrect The definition explicitly builds a combinational circuit from gates (p.10), contradicting A. B correct B restates the present-input-only definition (p.10). C incorrect Sequential circuits contain memory (p.15); reversing the feedback distinction does not match the combinational definition. D incorrect The module does not make a clock mandatory for combinational logic; it defines direct current-input dependence (p.10).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 45 · Q00909
records.text: Q00909 Question 45 COA15 Which one of the following is the first operation or step in CPU instruction cycle? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Executing the instruction B Handling interrupt C . Decoding the instruction D Fetching the instruction Fetching the instruction The listed cycle begins with fetching an instruction, then decoding, possible indirect-address access, and execution (PDF p.55). In the fetch micro-operations PC first supplies AR and memory then supplies IR. A incorrect Execution follows fetch and decode, rather than initiating the cycle (p.55). B incorrect Interrupt handling is not the first phase in the module’s listed ordinary instruction cycle. C incorrect Decoding is the second listed phase (p.55). D correct Fetching is explicitly phase 1, with register transfers shown on p.55.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 46 · Q00913
records.text: Q00913 Question 46 COA01 COA-S02 Which one of the following is a computer structural component that provides for communication among CPU, main memory and I/O? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A System unit B Computer network C CPU D System interconnection System interconnection The structural-component list defines system interconnection as the mechanism providing communication among CPU, main memory and I/O (PDF p.6). This definition exactly matches the requested role. A incorrect “System unit” is not the named communication component in the list on p.6. B incorrect A network is not the internal mechanism named in this structural definition. C incorrect CPU is one of the three communicating parties, not the interconnection itself (p.6). D correct The definition of system interconnection matches the entire stem (p.6).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 47 · Q00918
records.text: Q00918 Question 47 COA30 is a data transfer method in computer organization and architecture that allows an I/O device to transfer data directly to or from memory without the involvement of the CPU. Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Asynchronous data transfer B Direct Memory Access (DMA) C . Interrupt-driven transfer D Programmed I/O transfer Direct Memory Access (DMA) DMA sends the block directly to/from memory and keeps CPU involvement to setup and completion (PDF pp.107–108). Asynchrony describes timing, whereas interrupt/programmed I/O still make the CPU transfer data. A incorrect Asynchronous transfer describes independent clocks (p.101), not a bypass path. B correct DMA words go directly to or from memory without traversing CPU (p.108). C incorrect The CPU executes transfers under interrupt I/O (p.106). D incorrect Programmed I/O has CPU status checks and data transfer (p.104).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 48 · Q01178
records.text: Q01178 Question 48 COA19 Which instruction class tests a data word or computation status and sets condition information, often without retaining an arithmetic result? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Test instructions B Branch instructions C All of the above D Data-transfer instructions Test instructions TEST/CMP-style instructions examine values and update condition information, often discarding an arithmetic result. Branch instructions use control-flow conditions to choose a target; data-transfer instructions copy values. Those are different roles, so the aggregate alternative cannot identify the testing class. The cleaned question retains the recognizable, image-confirmed test-instruction concept while removing displaced OCR debris. A correct Test instructions examine values and set condition information. B incorrect Branches choose control-flow targets rather than naming the class that establishes the test condition. C incorrect Branch and data-transfer instructions do not both have the specified test role, so the aggregate is false. D incorrect Data-transfer instructions copy values rather than performing the requested condition-setting test.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 49 · Q01179
records.text: Q01179 Question 49 COA19 Branch instructions are used to branch to a different set of instructions depending on the decision made. Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A True B False True A branch changes the ordinary sequential instruction path to the branch address. The module explicitly identifies the actual branch address in a branch instruction (PDF p.72), and visually inspected Table 5-2 (p.52) shows both unconditional branch and conditional skip operations. Interpret “depending on the decision” as conditional branching; it is not true that every branch must be conditional. A correct True under the conditional-branch interpretation: the address field supplies the alternate target (p.72). B incorrect False would deny that conditional transfers select another instruction sequence; the table’s conditional skip examples illustrate such decisions (p.52).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 50 · Q01183
records.text: Q01183 Question 50 COA29 Which of the following is not considered as a peripheral device? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A CPU B Keyboard C Monitor D All of the above CPU Peripherals are external input/output devices such as keyboard and display (PDF p.99). CPU is the central processor structural component (p.6), so it is the only offered non-peripheral. A correct CPU is the processor, distinct from the external I/O devices (p.6). B incorrect Keyboard is explicitly a peripheral (p.99). C incorrect Display/video monitor is explicitly peripheral (p.99). D incorrect Keyboard and monitor are peripherals, so not all choices satisfy the negative stem.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 51 · Q01187
records.text: Q01187 Question 51 COA13 Which one of the following statements is not true about the application of micro-operations? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Selective set operation is implemented using OR micro-operation B Selective clear operation clears to zero the bit in the first operand only where there are corresponding 1's in the logical operand C Clear operation is implemented using Exclusive-OR Micro-operation. D None of the above None of the above Selective set uses A OR B and selective clear zeroes A where B has ones (PDF p.44). For the unqualified clear operation, XOR a register with itself: each bit x XOR x=0, as shown by the equal-input rows of Figure 1.2 on PDF p.7. Thus A–C can all be true and D answers the negative stem. A incorrect The OR expression and example for selective set are explicit (p.44). B incorrect The selective-clear definition exactly states zeroing A at B=1 positions (p.44). C incorrect XOR self-clear is valid because 0 XOR 0 and 1 XOR 1 both equal zero (p.7, visually checked truth table). D correct None of A–C is false under self-XOR clearing, so D is the exception response.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 52 · Q01190
records.text: Q01190 Question 52 COA20 In textbook discussions of richer CISC instructions, which term names the distance between high-level language constructs and machine operations that those instructions may reduce? Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor. A Time delay B Semantic gap C Cost D All of the mentioned Semantic gap The semantic gap is the distance between high-level constructs and machine operations. Richer instructions can reduce that gap by expressing elaborate operations directly. Time and cost are separate design concerns, and neither RISC nor CISC guarantees reductions in them across implementations and workloads. The revised question ties the named gap to the supported richer-instruction discussion instead of asserting one universal purpose shared by both approaches. A incorrect Time delay is a performance measure rather than this conceptual distance. B correct Semantic gap names the high-level-to-machine-operation distance. C incorrect Cost is an implementation measure rather than this gap. D incorrect The question asks for one specific conceptual term.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 53 · Q01248
records.text: Q01248 Question 53 COA14 COA15 Which register identifies the next instruction to fetch, before its address is copied into the address register for a memory access? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Accumulator B Instruction register C Address register D Program counter Program counter The program counter identifies the next instruction to fetch. During fetch, that address can be copied into MAR so memory can perform the access, but MAR’s general role is the address of the current memory operation. IR holds the fetched instruction itself and the accumulator holds operands or results. Specifying next instruction and the point before copying separates PC from the later memory-access address. A incorrect The accumulator holds operands or results. B incorrect IR holds the fetched instruction itself. C incorrect MAR holds the current memory-access address after it is loaded. D correct PC identifies the next instruction to fetch.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 54 · Q01250
records.text: Q01250 Question 54 COA03 Which of the following logic gates has an output value that is identical to its input? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A NAND B NOR C Exclusive-OR D Buffer Buffer The enabled three-state buffer has output Y=A when control C=1 (PDF p.41). Therefore buffer preserves the input logic value. Figure 1.2 on p.7 gives the other gates’ differing two-input truth tables. A incorrect NAND complements AND; it is not an identity function (p.7). B incorrect NOR complements OR; it is not an identity function (p.7). C incorrect XOR depends on both inputs; it equals one input only under an extra fixed-zero assumption (p.7). D correct An enabled buffer explicitly gives Y=A (p.41).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 55 · Q01280
records.text: Q01280 Question 55 COA20 From the labels RISC and CISC alone, which conclusion about processor power efficiency is justified without implementation or workload information? Compare textbook design tendencies without turning them into guarantees about every processor. A RISC B Neither label alone determines power efficiency C IANA D CISC Neither label alone determines power efficiency RISC and CISC describe instruction-set design tendencies, not universal power rankings. Power efficiency depends on implementation and the work being performed, so neither label alone establishes which processor is more efficient. The option states that supported conclusion. RISC and CISC remain unjustified blanket selections, while IANA does not supply the processor implementation or workload needed to resolve the comparison. A incorrect RISC does not guarantee greater power efficiency. B correct The note rejects a guaranteed power ranking from these labels alone. C incorrect This does not provide a relevant processor implementation for the comparison. D incorrect CISC does not guarantee greater power efficiency.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 56 · Q01304
records.text: Q01304 Question 56 COA23 COA24 COA32 Which of the following is not a type of memory used in an operating system? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Cache B RAM C ROM D Ethernet Ethernet is a network connection, not a memory type. COA23 describes cache as copying memory blocks near the CPU, and COA24 describes RAM technologies plus nonvolatile ROM. COA32 explicitly classifies Ethernet as connecting network devices rather than memory. Thus cache, RAM and ROM are memory-related choices, while Ethernet belongs to communications. The phrase used in an operating system does not convert a network technology into storage hardware. A incorrect Cache stores copies of memory blocks and is a genuine level of the memory hierarchy. B incorrect RAM is main-memory storage, not a communication technology excluded from the memory category. C incorrect ROM is nonvolatile memory even though its normal access and modification rules differ from RAM. D correct Ethernet connects network devices and is explicitly distinguished from memory in the note.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 57 · Q01318
records.text: Q01318 Question 57 COA28 Which of the following is not a type of storage device used in an operating system? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Hard disk drive (HDD) B Solid-state drive (SSD) C Tape drive D Ethernet cable Ethernet cable is a communication medium. COA28 describes HDD magnetic storage, SSD nonvolatile semiconductor storage and tape for sequential archives. It then explicitly distinguishes an Ethernet cable as a communication medium rather than a disk or RAM. The question asks for the item outside the storage-device category, so the cable is the supported exclusion regardless of which filesystem or OS uses the other devices. A incorrect An HDD stores persistent magnetic patterns in addressed blocks, so it is a storage device. B incorrect An SSD stores data in nonvolatile semiconductor storage, satisfying the storage-device category. C incorrect A tape drive provides sequential storage suitable for streaming and archives, so it is not excluded. D correct An Ethernet cable carries communication signals rather than functioning as a persistent storage device.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 58 · Q01465
records.text: Q01465 Question 58 COA38 Which generation of computers used vacuum tubes as their primary electronic component? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation First generation: vacuum tubes. Under the familiar generation convention in COA38, vacuum tubes identify the first generation. Transistors belong to the second, integrated circuits to the third, and microprocessor/VLSI-era personal computers to the fourth. This question asks for the defining electronic component in that convention, so the mapping provides a direct answer without needing exact boundary dates for every historical machine. A correct The first generation is the conventional vacuum-tube era specified in the complete note. B incorrect The second generation is associated with transistors rather than vacuum tubes as its defining component. C incorrect The third generation is associated with integrated circuits rather than the vacuum-tube era. D incorrect The fourth generation is associated with microprocessors/VLSI rather than vacuum tubes as its primary component.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 59 · Q01466
records.text: Q01466 Question 59 COA38 Which generation of computers utilized transistors for electronic circuitry? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Second generation: transistors. COA38 maps the second generation to transistor-based circuitry. The surrounding categories distinguish the first vacuum-tube era, third integrated-circuit era and fourth microprocessor/VLSI era. Within this conventional classification, the transistor clue therefore selects the second generation. The answer concerns the defining technology, rather than claiming transistors ceased to exist when integrated circuits appeared. A incorrect The first generation is conventionally identified with vacuum tubes, not transistor-based circuitry. B correct The note explicitly associates transistor circuitry with the second generation of computers. C incorrect Integrated circuits define the third-generation category, rather than the discrete-transistor era requested here. D incorrect Microprocessor/VLSI-era computers define the fourth category, rather than the transistor-generation convention.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 60 · Q01467
records.text: Q01467 Question 60 COA38 Under the course’s conventional generation summary, around the transition into which generation did high-level programming languages become prominent? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Second Generation The course associates high-level languages becoming prominent with the transition into the second generation. That is a conventional historical summary, rather than a claim that every language was first introduced on one sharply defined boundary. The revised verb preserves the generation-history question while avoiding an unsupported universal introduction era. The other options refer to different stages in the familiar circuitry-based chronology. A incorrect The note instead places prominence around the transition into the second era. B correct This matches the explicitly stated historical convention. C incorrect The third era is associated with integrated circuits rather than this transition. D incorrect The fourth era is associated with microprocessor/VLSI personal computers.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 61 · Q01468
records.text: Q01468 Question 61 COA38 Which generation of computers introduced the concept of stored program architecture? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation First generation. COA38 directly places stored-program machines in the first era. The stored-program clue is different from the transistor, integrated-circuit and microprocessor clues defining later generations. Under the historical convention supplied by this note, the concept therefore belongs to the first generation, even though later computers also retained stored-program operation. A correct The note explicitly places the rise of stored-program machines in the first generation. B incorrect The second generation retained stored programs but is not where the note places their introduction. C incorrect The third generation is the integrated-circuit era, later than the stated stored-program introduction. D incorrect The fourth generation is the microprocessor era, much later than the stated first-era development.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 62 · Q01469
records.text: Q01469 Question 62 COA38 Which generation of computers saw the development of integrated circuits? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Third generation: integrated circuits. COA38 associates the third generation with integrated circuits. The first is identified by vacuum tubes, the second by transistors and the fourth by microprocessor/VLSI-era personal computers. Reading development in the question as the conventional adoption/defining-technology category gives third generation; it does not require assuming that every invention date perfectly matches textbook boundaries. A incorrect The first-generation convention identifies vacuum tubes rather than integrated circuits as the defining technology. B incorrect The second-generation convention identifies transistor circuitry, preceding the integrated-circuit generation category. C correct Integrated circuits are the defining third-generation technology in the supplied historical convention. D incorrect The fourth generation is the later microprocessor/VLSI category rather than the initial integrated-circuit category.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 63 · Q01470
records.text: Q01470 Question 63 COA38 A historical computer uses magnetic-core memory and transistor-based circuitry rather than vacuum tubes or integrated circuits. Under the conventional taxonomy, which generation describes its circuitry? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Second Generation Magnetic-core memory alone does not identify a generation because it spanned more than one era. The added circuitry condition supplies the distinguishing feature: the conventional taxonomy associates transistor-based machines with the second generation. Vacuum tubes identify the first era, integrated circuits the third and microprocessor/VLSI personal computers the fourth. This version retains the magnetic-core context and states which technology determines the classification. A incorrect First-generation circuitry uses the vacuum-tube convention. B correct Transistor circuitry identifies the second generation. C incorrect Third-generation circuitry uses the integrated-circuit convention. D incorrect The fourth era is associated with microprocessor/VLSI systems.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 64 · Q01472
records.text: Q01472 Question 64 COA38 Which generation conventionally introduced integrated-circuit circuitry, contributing to improved speed and performance over earlier discrete-transistor systems? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Third Generation Several generations improved speed, so improvement alone is not a unique historical marker. The revised question identifies integrated circuits as the distinguishing technology. Under the stated convention, integrated circuits identify the third generation, following transistor-based second-generation systems. Performance improvement remains a contextual trend rather than a guarantee that every individual later machine outperformed every earlier model. A incorrect The first era is associated with vacuum tubes. B incorrect The second era is associated with discrete transistors. C correct The third era is associated with integrated circuits. D incorrect The fourth era is associated with microprocessor/VLSI systems.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 65 · Q01473
records.text: Q01473 Question 65 COA38 Which generation of computers introduced the use of microprocessors? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Fourth generation: microprocessors. The conventional mapping in COA38 identifies the fourth generation with microprocessor/VLSI-era computers. Vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits identify the preceding first, second and third categories respectively. Thus the microprocessor clue directly selects the fourth generation under the note’s convention; the question does not ask for an exact launch date or individual processor model. A incorrect Vacuum tubes define the first-generation convention, rather than the later microprocessor era. B incorrect The transistor-based second-generation category precedes the note’s microprocessor/VLSI category. C incorrect Third generation denotes integrated-circuit computers; microprocessors identify the subsequent conventional category. D correct The complete note explicitly associates microprocessor/VLSI-era computers with the fourth generation.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 66 · Q01474
records.text: Q01474 Question 66 COA38 Which generation of computers is characterized by the development of personal computers? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A First Generation B Second Generation C Third Generation D Fourth Generation Fourth generation: personal computers. COA38 groups personal computers with the fourth-generation microprocessor/VLSI era. The first three alternatives instead correspond to vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits. The wording characterized by asks for that conventional defining association, so fourth generation is supported without making a universal claim that no personal or individual-use machine could exist in any earlier period. A incorrect The first era is characterized by vacuum tubes in this convention, not microprocessor-based personal computers. B incorrect The second era is the transistor category rather than the personal-computer era identified here. C incorrect The third era is associated with integrated circuits rather than the note’s personal-computer category. D correct The note places microprocessor/VLSI-era personal computers in the fourth-generation historical convention.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 67 · Q01491
records.text: Q01491 Question 67 COA16 COA17 A stack organized computer uses instruction of Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Zero addressing B Two addressing C Index addressing D Indirect addressing Zero addressing For stack arithmetic the operands are implicit on top of stack, so ADD and MUL require no address field (PDF p.69). This is the zero-address organization. PUSH/POP still use explicit addresses; the answer concerns arithmetic operation instructions. A correct Zero-address ADD/MUL is explicit (p.69). B incorrect Two-address instructions instead explicitly name register/memory operands; stack arithmetic does not (pp.67–69). C incorrect Index addressing is an effective-address mechanism, not the stack operand-count format. D incorrect Indirect addressing locates an address through memory (p.72); it is not the stack arithmetic format.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 68 · Q01492
records.text: Q01492 Question 68 COA38 COA12 An n-bit microprocessor has - Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A No answer is correct B n-bit program counter C n-bit address register D n-bit instruction register None of the named register widths necessarily follows. COA38 explicitly states that an n-bit processor label does not force its PC, IR or address register to be n bits. Those widths concern different architectural quantities. Since the stem supplies only the processor-width label and no specific design, none of the three claimed register widths is guaranteed. The no-answer-is-correct alternative is therefore the supported response. A correct None of the three specific register-width claims is implied by the processor-width label alone. B incorrect Program-counter width is not forced to equal the processor’s n-bit label in every architecture. C incorrect Address-register width can differ from processor word width; n bits is not guaranteed. D incorrect Instruction-register width depends on instruction encoding rather than necessarily matching the processor-width label.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 69 · Q01493
records.text: Q01493 Question 69 COA23 In which of the following term the performance of cache memory is measured? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Copy ratio B Data ratio C Hit ratio D Cache ratio Hit ratio Cache performance is explicitly measured by hit ratio, hits/(hits+misses), in PDF p.85. A hit means the requested word is found in cache (p.84), making this a direct measure of cache availability of requested data. A incorrect Copy ratio is not the performance quantity defined on p.85. B incorrect Data ratio is not the named hit/miss measure. C correct Hit ratio and its formula are explicitly provided (p.85). D incorrect “Cache ratio” is not the quantity’s stated name.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 70 · EX2018Q100
records.text: EX2018Q100 Question 70 COA03 Question number 100 What is the name of logic gate based on the following graphical symbol? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A XOR B NOR C NAND D AND NAND The diagram shows an AND-shaped gate with a small output circle. This is a NAND gate; the circle indicates inversion, so F=NOT(A AND B). A incorrect XOR uses the OR-like body with an extra input curve, unlike the source symbol (p.7). B incorrect NOR uses an OR-shaped body with an output circle, not the flat-input AND body (p.7). C correct The AND body plus inversion circle is NAND (p.7). D incorrect AND lacks the output inversion circle visible in the question.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 71 · SM0013
records.text: SM0013 Question 71 COA31 An interface that has multiple lines connecting the input/output module and peripheral device and assures multiple bits to be transferred at the same time is: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Bus interface B Parallel interface C One line interface D Serial interface Parallel interface Parallel registers read/write bits simultaneously (PDF p.35); shift registers transfer serially (p.36), and a common bus supplies a line for each bit (p.40). Multiple lines carrying bits at the same time match a parallel interface by this distinction. A incorrect A bus describes a collection of lines; it does not specify serial versus parallel transfer as precisely as B (p.40). B correct Simultaneous multiple-bit transfer corresponds to the parallel operation defined on p.35. C incorrect One line cannot carry the described multiple separate bit signals simultaneously in this binary-line model. D incorrect Serial shifting transfers the stream sequentially rather than all bits simultaneously (p.36).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 72 · SM0033
records.text: SM0033 Question 72 COA26 Which one of the following is a two-level cache having an internal and external caches? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Multilevel cache B Single level cache C Split cache D Unified cache Multilevel cache. A two-level hierarchy has more than one cache level, so multilevel is the matching category. COA26 distinguishes L1/L2 hierarchy levels from split/unified instruction-data organization and from internal/external placement. Describing one cache as internal and another as external does not make the pair split or unified; those terms answer a different classification question. A correct Two cache levels constitute a multilevel hierarchy, regardless of their internal or external placement. B incorrect Single-level cache contradicts the explicitly stated presence of two cache levels in the hierarchy. C incorrect Split describes separate instruction and data caches, not an internal-plus-external level arrangement. D incorrect Unified describes combined instruction/data caching, not how many internal or external levels exist.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 73 · SM0051
records.text: SM0051 Question 73 COA01 Which statement is NOT correct about computer architecture and organization? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A An architecture can remain for a long time but its organization can change B Manufacturers offer computers with the same architecture but different organization C An architecture can be used for a long time encompassing different computer models D Different organizations cannot implement the same architecture Different organizations cannot implement the same architecture Architecture describes programmer-visible behavior, while organization describes internal implementation. Several internal implementations can preserve the same architecture, allowing it to span models and remain stable while implementation details change. The false statement denies that possibility. The other choices describe compatible consequences of the distinction, without requiring a maximum architecture lifetime or a universal implementation-change rate. A incorrect Implementation can change while architecture stays stable. B incorrect Different organizations can implement one architecture. C incorrect One architecture can encompass different computer models over time. D correct This denies the supported possibility of different implementations of one architecture.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 74 · SM0059
records.text: SM0059 Question 74 COA01 ______ is a set of attributes that can be seen by a program and can have direct impact on the logical execution of a program. Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Arrangement B Organization C Flow control D Architecture Architecture Programmer-visible attributes that directly affect logical execution are the module’s exact definition of computer architecture (PDF p.5). Organization instead comprises operational units and interconnections realizing those specifications. A incorrect Arrangement is not the defined programmer-visible attribute set. B incorrect Organization describes implementation units and interconnections (p.5). C incorrect Flow control is a function, not the definition of this attribute set. D correct Architecture exactly matches the definition and examples (p.5).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 75 · SM0063
records.text: SM0063 Question 75 COA16 What is the purpose of an opcode that is as indicated in the figure below? 4 bits 6 bits 6 bits [opcode] Operant etree [| Opsrand Rates| <_ 16 bits —ccccxxcxor Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A It holds the destination address of an operand B It determines the operation to be done C It holds the source address of an operand D It holds the next instruction reference It determines the operation to be done The inspected diagram divides 16 bits into a 4-bit opcode and two 6-bit operand references. The module defines the operation part as specifying what operation is performed (PDF p.47); reference fields identify operands rather than changing that opcode role. Four opcode bits can distinguish up to 16 operation codes. A incorrect Destination reference belongs to an operand/address field, not the operation field (p.47). B correct Operation selection is the explicit opcode definition (p.47). C incorrect Source reference belongs to an operand/address field. D incorrect The module tracks the next instruction through PC (p.70), not this operation field.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 76 · SM0091
records.text: SM0091 Question 76 COA14 COA15 Which one of the following registers holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched from memory? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Memory address register B Memory buffer register C Program counter D Instruction buffer register Program counter PC holds the address of the instruction to execute next (PDF p.70). During fetch it is copied to AR and the instruction bits then enter IR while PC increments (p.55). Thus PC is the persistent next-instruction tracker. A incorrect MAR can temporarily receive the fetch address, but PC is the register that tracks the next instruction across cycles (p.55). B incorrect The module describes MDR as memory data storage (p.82), not the next-instruction address tracker. C correct Directly matches the PC definition and fetch transfers (pp.55,70). D incorrect An instruction buffer would hold instruction content; the module identifies IR for that role (p.48), not as the next-address tracker.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 77 · SM0201
records.text: SM0201 Question 77 COA29 Which one of the following is NOT an I/O command? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Status command B Output data command C Control command D Issue command Issue command The module enumerates four I/O command kinds: control, test, read and write (PDF pp.104–105). “Status command” is interpreted as the test/status-query kind, and “output data” as write. “Issue” is an action performed by CPU, not one of the four command kinds. A incorrect Status-query corresponds to the test command, which checks status conditions (p.104). B incorrect Output data corresponds to the write command (p.105). C incorrect Control command activates a peripheral and specifies its action (p.104). D correct Issue is not a command category in the four-type list (pp.104–105).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 78 · SM0230
records.text: SM0230 Question 78 COA02 The user who programs a computer in machine or assembly language must be aware of the following EXCEPT: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A The register set B The type of data supported by the instructions C The analysis model D The memory structure The analysis model The machine-language programmer’s architecture includes instruction formats, addressing modes, instruction sets and register organization (PDF p.57); visible data types and memory addressing are also named (p.5). An “analysis model” is not part of that architectural list. A incorrect Register organization is explicitly part of the programmer view (p.57). B incorrect Supported data representation is explicitly architectural (p.5). C correct Analysis model is absent from the programmer-facing attribute list; it is the unmatched option. D incorrect Memory addressing is part of the architecture (p.5), under the intended visible-memory interpretation.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 79 · SM0239
records.text: SM0239 Question 79 COA29 Which part of the computer system is responsible for converting machine-processed data to formats understandable by the user? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Communication components B Output unit C Storage unit D Input unit Output unit Computational results must be recorded/displayed for users (PDF p.99); human-readable screen/display/printer devices provide that communication (p.100). This is the output role. A incorrect Communication devices exchange data with remote devices; the category is not specifically user-readable presentation (p.100). B correct Output devices record/display computed results in meaningful form for users (p.99). C incorrect Storage retains information; it is not the presentation role (p.91). D incorrect Input enters programs/data into the system, the reverse direction (p.99).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 80 · SM0242
records.text: SM0242 Question 80 COA23 In the usual memory hierarchy, which listed tier has the shortest access latency and greatest cost per stored bit? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Register B Magnetic disc C Main memory D Cache memory Register The usual speed and cost-per-bit hierarchy places registers above cache, main RAM and magnetic disk. Registers therefore have the shortest access latency and highest cost per bit among the choices. Faster tiers are generally smaller, so this statement does not compare the total purchase price of a complete device. Cache is fast, but remains below the register tier in this teaching hierarchy. A correct Registers are the fastest and most costly-per-bit tier among these choices. B incorrect Magnetic disk is a slower, high-capacity tier with lower cost per bit. C incorrect Main memory lies below registers and cache in the usual speed/cost hierarchy. D incorrect Cache is fast but below registers in the usual hierarchy.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 81 · SM0277
