records.text: SM0277 Question 81 COA32 For a legacy internal PC disk connection using parallel ATA, which listed interface name matches that connection? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SCSI B iSCSI C IDE D USB IDE The note identifies legacy IDE/PATA as a storage connection, so IDE matches the specified parallel ATA context. SCSI is a different storage interface, iSCSI carries SCSI over IP, and USB commonly connects peripherals including external storage. Naming the legacy internal parallel interface resolves the missing era and connection-role constraints without asserting that one interface is universally standard for all PCs and all storage devices. A incorrect SCSI is a different storage-connection standard. B incorrect iSCSI transports SCSI commands over IP rather than using the specified local parallel interface. C correct IDE corresponds to the stated legacy PATA connection. D incorrect USB is a different peripheral interconnect, not parallel ATA.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 82 · SM0295
records.text: SM0295 Question 82 COA12 In the simple CPU-master memory-bus model, which bus carries the values read from and written to memory? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Control bus B Data bus C Uni-bus D Address bus Data bus The data bus carries memory-transfer values. Reads move values from memory toward the CPU, and writes move values in the opposite direction. Address signals select a location and control signals coordinate timing and read/write operations. The revised stem asks about payload rather than bidirectionality in general, since aggregate control can also contain signals in both directions. Uni-bus names a bus arrangement rather than this payload-signal category. A incorrect Control signals coordinate the transfers rather than carrying their values. B correct The data bus carries read and write values. C incorrect This is not the address/data/control payload-signal category requested. D incorrect Address signals choose the memory location.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 83 · SS077
records.text: SS077 Question 83 COA16 What is the purpose of an opcode that is as indicated in the figure below? 4 bits 6 bits 6 bits <j o bits ——___________» Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A It determines the operation to be done B It holds the destination address of an operand C It holds the next instruction reference D It holds the source address of an operand It determines the operation to be done The instruction has a 4-bit Opcode followed by two 6-bit Operand Reference fields. Opcode selects the operation. A correct Matches the operation-code definition (p.47). B incorrect A destination reference is an operand field, not the opcode. C incorrect Next-instruction location is tracked by PC (p.70), not this operation field. D incorrect Source address belongs to an operand reference, not the operation code (p.47).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 84 · AM0704
records.text: AM0704 Question 84 COA30 COA31 Which of the following is a common way of communicating with I/O devices? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Memory-mapped I/O B Direct memory access (DMA) C Interrupt-driven I/O D All of the above All of the above Memory-mapped I/O shares memory and device address space (PDF p.105); DMA transfers blocks directly (p.107); interrupt I/O requests CPU service when ready (p.106). They are all supported I/O mechanisms, though memory mapping is an addressing choice and the others are transfer/control techniques. A incorrect Memory-mapped I/O is explicitly described (p.105). B incorrect DMA is explicitly described (p.107). C incorrect Interrupt-driven I/O is explicitly described (p.106). D correct All three are legitimate mechanisms under the broad “communicating” wording.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 85 · AM0705
records.text: AM0705 Question 85 COA31 In memory-mapped I/O, I/O devices are mapped into the: Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Main memory address space B Cache memory address space C Virtual memory address space D Secondary memory address space Main memory address space Memory-mapped I/O makes devices and memory share an address space, with I/O treated like memory reads/writes (PDF p.105). The relevant address space is the memory address space, not a separate cache or secondary-storage space. A correct Devices share the memory address space (p.105). B incorrect The module does not map device registers into a separate cache address space. C incorrect The mapping definition does not depend on a process virtual address space. D incorrect Secondary-storage addresses are not the shared CPU memory addresses described on p.105.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 86 · AM0706
records.text: AM0706 Question 86 COA30 COA31 Which technique allows data to be transferred between an I/O device and memory without involving the CPU? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Memory-mapped I/O B Direct memory access (DMA) C Interrupt-driven I/O D I/O polling Direct memory access (DMA) DMA transfers each word directly to/from memory without passing through CPU (PDF p.108). “Without involving” must mean during the actual word transfers, since CPU setup and completion involvement are explicit on the same page. A incorrect Memory mapping specifies how I/O is addressed, not a CPU-bypass data engine (p.105). B correct DMA directly transfers the block with CPU only at beginning/end (p.108). C incorrect The CPU still executes the interrupt-driven data transfer (p.106). D incorrect Polling keeps CPU checking device status and doing transfers (p.104).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 87 · AM0707
records.text: AM0707 Question 87 COA30 COA31 Which method is used to handle I/O operations that require immediate attention from the CPU? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Memory-mapped I/O B Direct memory access (DMA) C Interrupt-driven I/O D I/O polling Interrupt-driven I/O In interrupt-driven I/O the device requests CPU service when ready; CPU can work on other instructions until then (PDF p.106). The priority-interrupt discussion on that page services the higher-priority simultaneous request first. This matches event-driven attention, without guaranteeing zero response latency. A incorrect Memory mapping selects addresses and does not itself notify the CPU (p.105). B incorrect DMA offloads data movement (p.107); it is not the general CPU-service notification technique. C correct The device interrupts CPU requesting service when ready (p.106). D incorrect Polling requires the CPU to discover readiness through repeated checks (p.104).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 88 · AM0708
records.text: AM0708 Question 88 COA30 Which I/O technique involves the CPU continuously checking the status of an I/O device for data transfer completion? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Memory-mapped I/O B Direct memory access (DMA) C Interrupt-driven I/O D I/O polling I/O polling Programmed I/O explicitly makes CPU periodically check I/O status until completion, because the module does not interrupt CPU (PDF p.104). This is the polling behavior described by D. A incorrect Memory mapping is the address arrangement and does not require repeated status checks (p.105). B incorrect DMA permits CPU other work while moving a block (p.108). C incorrect Interrupt I/O notifies CPU when ready instead of requiring periodic checking (p.106). D correct CPU checks status bits periodically until completion (p.104).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 89 · AM0709
records.text: AM0709 Question 89 COA32 Which standard I/O interface is commonly used in UNIX-like operating systems? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A ASCII B USB C RS-232 D POSIX POSIX. COA32 identifies POSIX as a software interface standard with open/read/write/close operations. That is the software I/O interface sense appropriate to UNIX-like operating systems. ASCII is an encoding, while USB and RS-232 describe hardware interconnect/interface roles. Their availability on a UNIX-like machine does not make them the standard OS software interface requested by the alternatives. A incorrect ASCII defines character encoding, not the UNIX-like software interface for opening, reading and writing resources. B incorrect USB is a peripheral interconnect, not the software API standard identified by this OS-level wording. C incorrect RS-232 defines a serial electrical/interface standard rather than the UNIX-like software I/O API. D correct POSIX specifies software interface operations including open, read, write and close for this context.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 90 · AM0710
records.text: AM0710 Question 90 COA32 Which listed interface is a traditional point-to-point serial electrical/interface standard? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A USB B Ethernet C RS-232 D HDMI RS-232 RS-232 specifies a traditional point-to-point serial electrical/interface standard. USB also uses serial communication, so serial alone cannot distinguish them. The revised requirement identifies the traditional point-to-point interface category rather than treating every serial link as equivalent. Ethernet connects network devices and HDMI carries digital audio and video. Their connection roles differ from the interface class requested. A incorrect USB is a serial peripheral interconnect, but not the traditional point-to-point electrical standard requested. B incorrect Ethernet provides networking connectivity. C correct RS-232 matches the traditional point-to-point serial interface category. D incorrect HDMI carries digital audio and video.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 91 · AM0711
records.text: AM0711 Question 91 COA32 Which standard I/O interface is widely used for connecting external storage devices, such as hard drives and flash drives? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SATA B USB C Ethernet D HDMI USB. COA32 explicitly describes USB as a peripheral interconnect used by external storage. This directly matches the stem’s external hard-drive and flash-drive examples. SATA is described more generally as a storage interface, Ethernet connects network devices, and HDMI carries video/audio. The external peripheral examples therefore make USB the supported conventional choice among these options. A incorrect SATA is a storage interface, but USB is the note’s explicit match for the external-peripheral examples. B correct The note explicitly lists external storage among USB peripheral connections, matching the supplied examples. C incorrect Ethernet connects network devices rather than being the named external hard-drive/flash-drive peripheral interconnect. D incorrect HDMI carries digital video and audio, rather than providing the external-storage interface requested.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 92 · AM0712
records.text: AM0712 Question 92 COA32 Which listed interface is specifically a storage-drive interface, rather than a general peripheral interconnect, networking interface or audiovisual link? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SATA B USB C Ethernet D HDMI SATA SATA is specifically a storage interface. USB supplies general peripheral connectivity, Ethernet connects network devices and HDMI carries digital audio/video. The connection role distinguishes these alternatives; a vague high-speed description would not, because several interfaces can be fast in suitable versions. The question therefore asks for a storage-specific interface category without assuming that speed alone uniquely identifies it. A correct SATA is the storage-specific interface in the list. B incorrect USB provides a different peripheral-interconnect role. C incorrect Ethernet serves networking rather than this drive connection. D incorrect HDMI carries audiovisual data rather than this storage link.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 93 · AM0713
records.text: AM0713 Question 93 COA32 Which standard I/O interface is primarily used for audio and video transmission between devices? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SATA B USB C Ethernet D HDMI HDMI. COA32 explicitly identifies HDMI as carrying digital video and audio. That directly matches the primary transmission purpose asked here. SATA serves storage, USB serves general peripherals, and Ethernet serves network connections. Other links can transport encoded media in broader systems, but the stem asks the primary interface role, for which HDMI is the specific supported choice. A incorrect SATA is identified as a storage interface rather than the primary audiovisual connection in this list. B incorrect USB is a general peripheral interconnect; the note specifically assigns the audiovisual role to HDMI. C incorrect Ethernet is a network connection rather than the specifically identified digital audiovisual interface. D correct HDMI is explicitly described as carrying digital video and audio between devices.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 94 · AM0714
records.text: AM0714 Question 94 COA35 COA36 Which technique divides instruction processing into stages so that different stages work on successive instructions during the same cycle? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Branch prediction Pipelining Pipelining overlaps stages of successive instructions: one may be fetched while another is decoded or executed. Superscalar execution instead concerns issuing multiple instructions to functional units in one cycle; it can coexist with a pipeline but is not the definition of the staged organization. Caching supplies nearby copies of memory blocks, and branch prediction guesses future control flow. A correct Pipelining divides processing into stages and overlaps those stages across successive instructions. B incorrect Caching retains memory-block copies; it is not the staged instruction organization described. C incorrect Superscalar architecture provides multiple-issue execution resources rather than defining stage overlap itself. D incorrect Branch prediction guesses direction or targets, rather than dividing instruction processing into pipeline stages.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 95 · AM0715
records.text: AM0715 Question 95 COA23 COA36 Which technique improves the performance of a processor by storing frequently accessed data closer to the processor? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Branch prediction Caching Caching keeps copies of memory blocks near the CPU, exploiting temporal and spatial locality to reduce many memory-access delays. Pipelining overlaps instruction stages, superscalar execution provides multiple-issue resources, and branch prediction guesses control flow. These mechanisms may coexist, but the stated nearby data-copy storage role specifically identifies caching. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps instruction stages rather than creating a data buffer (p.116). B correct Cache is explicitly the fast intermediate RAM buffer that supplies hits (p.84). C incorrect Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to functional units; it is not a memory-copy storage tier. D incorrect Branch prediction guesses control-flow direction or targets; it does not name a nearby memory-block buffer.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 96 · AM0716
records.text: AM0716 Question 96 COA36 COA35 Which architecture allows multiple instructions to be executed in parallel by having multiple execution units? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Branch prediction Superscalar architecture. COA36 defines superscalar execution as issuing multiple instructions to multiple functional units in a cycle when dependencies permit. This matches the multiple execution units in the stem. COA35 distinguishes that multiple-issue capability from ordinary pipelining, which overlaps stages. Caching supplies reused memory data and branch prediction speculates about control flow; neither names the multiple-issue architecture. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps stages but does not by itself provide multiple-instruction issue to several execution units. B incorrect Caching retains nearby copies of memory blocks rather than defining parallel instruction issue. C correct Superscalar execution uses multiple functional units to issue several independent instructions in a cycle. D incorrect Branch prediction guesses future control flow, rather than naming the architecture with multiple execution units.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 97 · AM0717
records.text: AM0717 Question 97 COA36 Which technique predicts the outcome of conditional branches to improve instruction execution in a processor? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Branch prediction Branch prediction. COA36 says branch prediction guesses a branch’s direction/target and continues speculatively, discarding work when the guess is wrong. Predicting the outcome of a conditional branch is exactly that role. Pipelining overlaps processing stages, caching retains reusable data, and superscalar execution issues several instructions; those mechanisms can coexist with prediction but do not replace its definition. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps instruction stages; it does not itself predict the outcome of a conditional branch. B incorrect Caching retains reusable memory contents, rather than selecting the predicted direction of conditional control flow. C incorrect Superscalar execution provides multiple issue; it does not name the conditional-outcome prediction technique. D correct Branch prediction guesses branch direction or target so speculative execution can continue before resolution.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 98 · AM0718
records.text: AM0718 Question 98 COA23 COA27 COA36 Which technique improves memory access performance by organizing memory into hierarchical levels? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Virtual memory Caching Cache is the fast memory-block-copy tier used to reduce the cost of repeated or nearby CPU accesses. Virtual memory instead supplies translated address spaces and can use backing storage for nonresident pages. Pipelining and superscalar execution organize instruction processing, so neither names the memory-hierarchy buffer requested. The answer follows the storage role rather than a general claim that only one mechanism can improve performance. A incorrect Pipelining divides computational tasks into stages (p.116), not memory storage levels. B correct Cache supplies the fast tier in the hierarchy and avoids main-memory access on hits (pp.79,84). C incorrect Superscalar execution concerns multiple instruction issue, not a memory-hierarchy storage tier. D incorrect Virtual memory supplies an apparent larger memory space (p.90), not the fast-cache-hit mechanism.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 99 · AM0719
records.text: AM0719 Question 99 COA36 COA35 Which processor technique issues multiple independent instructions to multiple functional units in one clock cycle, when dependencies permit? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Instruction-level parallelism Superscalar architecture Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions in a cycle when the machine has suitable resources and the instructions’ dependencies permit it. Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions but need not issue several at once. Caching addresses memory access, while instruction-level parallelism is the broader opportunity exploited by several mechanisms. The revised stem asks about multiple issue rather than incorrectly claiming that wider instruction supply necessarily reduces individual memory latency. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps stages but does not by itself require multiple issue. B incorrect Caching retains memory-block copies and is not the multiple-issue technique. C correct Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to multiple units in a cycle. D incorrect Instruction-level parallelism is the broader property exploited rather than this specific issue mechanism.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 100 · AM0720
records.text: AM0720 Question 100 COA02 Which technique translates source or intermediate code into target code during program execution, before the translated portion runs? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Just-in-time (JIT) compilation Just-in-time (JIT) compilation JIT compilation translates code while the program is running, often compiling an intermediate representation before executing that portion. This timing distinguishes it from ahead-of-time translation. Pipelining overlaps processing stages, caching retains copies of data or instructions, and superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to execution resources. Those mechanisms do not name runtime source-to-target compilation. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps stages of executing instructions; it does not translate high-level or intermediate code. B incorrect Caching retains data or instruction copies; it does not perform the compilation described in the stem. C incorrect Superscalar architecture issues multiple instructions; it does not translate a source language into target code. D correct JIT is the only offered compiler; it translates during program execution before the compiled portion executes.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 101 · AM0721
records.text: AM0721 Question 101 COA36 Which technique improves performance by predicting the next set of instructions to be executed based on past execution patterns? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Branch prediction Branch prediction. Predicting which instruction stream follows a branch is the direction/target prediction described in COA36. Using past patterns is consistent with that prediction role, whereas pipeline overlap, cached memory copies and multiple instruction issue address different mechanisms. Prediction remains speculative: a wrong guess discards work rather than changing the program’s required architectural result. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps stages and requires instruction supply, but it is not itself next-path prediction. B incorrect Caching retains copies for reuse; a cached instruction is not a prediction of future control flow. C incorrect Superscalar issue increases concurrent instruction execution rather than identifying the upcoming branch path. D correct Predicting branch direction and targets identifies the likely future instruction stream for speculative execution.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 102 · AM0722
records.text: AM0722 Question 102 COA36 Which technique improves performance by dynamically reordering instructions to maximize instruction-level parallelism? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Out-of-order execution Out-of-order execution. COA36 describes out-of-order execution as scheduling ready operations before stalled older ones while preserving architectural results and exceptions. This is dynamic reordering to exploit instruction-level parallelism. Superscalar issue can provide execution width but does not itself define such reordering. Pipelining overlaps stages and caching improves reuse; neither names the readiness-based dynamic scheduling mechanism. A incorrect Pipelining overlaps stages; dynamic instruction reordering requires an additional readiness-based execution mechanism. B incorrect Caching keeps reusable memory copies and does not itself reorder instruction execution. C incorrect Superscalar issue permits multiple instructions per cycle but does not necessarily require out-of-order scheduling. D correct Out-of-order execution schedules ready instructions around stalled older ones while preserving required results.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 103 · AM0723
records.text: AM0723 Question 103 COA36 Which technique improves performance by dynamically allocating processor resources based on program behavior? Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Pipelining B Caching C Superscalar architecture D Dynamic resource allocation Dynamic resource allocation. COA36 explicitly defines dynamic resource allocation as assigning available internal entries/units at runtime. That definition directly fits the stem’s allocation based on behavior during execution. Pipelining describes overlapping stages, caching describes memory reuse, and superscalar execution describes issuing several instructions. They may use allocated resources, but none is the specific allocation technique named by the question. A incorrect Pipelining defines overlapping instruction stages rather than the general assignment of runtime internal resources. B incorrect Caching retains memory copies; it does not name the runtime assignment of processor entries and units. C incorrect Superscalar execution names multiple issue, rather than the allocation process used to assign available resources. D correct The note explicitly defines this as assigning available internal processor entries and units at runtime.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 104 · AM0724
records.text: AM0724 Question 104 COA01 Which listed item is a fundamental logic building block from which computer hardware is constructed? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A CPU B Memory C Hard disk D Logic gate Logic gate Logic gates perform elementary Boolean functions and are fundamental building blocks of digital hardware. A CPU, memory system and hard disk are larger components built from many lower-level mechanisms. The final option identifies the logic-level building block. The question explicitly states the level of abstraction so that basic does not mean an arbitrary major system component. A incorrect A CPU is a major assembled component rather than a fundamental logic building block. B incorrect Memory is a storage component rather than the requested logic-level building block. C incorrect A hard disk is a complex storage device. D correct A logic gate is the fundamental logic-level building block requested.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 105 · AM0725
records.text: AM0725 Question 105 COA01 COA11 Which component is responsible for executing instructions and performing calculations in a computer? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A CPU B Memory C Hard disk D Motherboard CPU The CPU contains the control unit, ALU and execution registers. Control sequences operations and transfers, while the ALU performs arithmetic and logic, supporting the CPU’s instruction-processing role. Main memory supplies addressed working storage, a hard disk supplies persistent storage, and the motherboard connects components. Those roles distinguish the processing component from the storage and interconnection choices. A correct CPU’s processing/execution function is explicit (pp.6,57). B incorrect Main memory stores data (p.6), rather than being the arithmetic execution unit. C incorrect Disk is secondary storage (p.94), not the processing unit. D incorrect The motherboard physically interconnects components; the CPU carries out the instruction execution and calculations.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 106 · AM0726
records.text: AM0726 Question 106 COA28 COA24 COA05 Which component retains stored data and instructions without power? Here Memory means ordinary volatile main RAM, and CPU excludes separate firmware storage. Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A CPU B Memory C Hard disk D Motherboard Hard disk An HDD preserves magnetic patterns without continuous power, so the hard disk retains the stored data and instructions. The question now restricts Memory to ordinary volatile main RAM, avoiding the broader meaning that would include ROM or flash. CPU and motherboard name processing and interconnection components rather than the persistent storage mechanism sought. These scope conditions make the intended retention comparison definite. A incorrect The CPU is not the specified persistent storage component. B incorrect Ordinary main RAM is volatile under the stated meaning. C correct An HDD retains its stored bits without continuous power. D incorrect The motherboard interconnects components rather than naming the persistent storage mechanism.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 107 · AM0727
records.text: AM0727 Question 107 COA01 The motherboard of a computer is responsible for: Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Executing instructions B Storing data C Connecting different components D Performing calculations Connecting different components. COA01 explicitly states that a motherboard physically connects components. The same section locates the ALU, control unit and registers in the CPU; computation and instruction execution therefore belong to processing components rather than the board’s defining role. Memory provides data storage. The question asks the motherboard’s responsibility, for which physical connection is the specific supported answer. A incorrect Instructions are executed by the CPU; that is distinct from the motherboard’s physical connection role. B incorrect Data storage belongs to memory/storage components, rather than defining what the motherboard itself does. C correct The note explicitly identifies the motherboard as physically connecting the computer’s components. D incorrect Calculations belong to CPU arithmetic/logic hardware rather than the motherboard’s defining connection function.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 108 · AM0728
records.text: AM0728 Question 108 COA02 COA24 COA14 COA28 COA01 Which component supplies the addressable main working store for a running program, distinct from individual CPU execution registers and persistent disk storage? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A CPU B Main memory (RAM) C Hard disk D Motherboard Main memory (RAM) Main RAM holds the addressed working instructions and data used by a running program. CPU registers hold particular fetched instructions, operands or results for immediate execution, and disks retain information persistently. The motherboard connects these components. Specifying the main working-store role prevents the broad temporary-storage description from also fitting CPU registers or cache. A incorrect The CPU executes operations and has immediate registers, but is not the main addressed RAM store requested. B correct Main RAM is the addressable working store for the running program’s instructions and data. C incorrect A hard disk supplies persistent storage rather than the main RAM working store. D incorrect The motherboard provides physical component connections rather than this storage role.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 109 · AM0729
records.text: AM0729 Question 109 COA02 Which type of software controls and manages the hardware resources of a computer? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Operating system B Application software C Programming language D Compiler Operating system. COA02 directly defines the operating system as managing resources and providing services. Applications solve user tasks, and compilers translate source into target code. A programming language is a means of expressing programs rather than the software resource manager. Therefore the operating system is the single option whose stated role matches controlling and managing computer hardware resources. A correct The operating system is explicitly defined as the resource manager and provider of system services. B incorrect Applications solve user tasks using system services rather than serving as the general hardware resource manager. C incorrect A programming language expresses programs; it is not itself the system software managing hardware resources. D incorrect A compiler translates source code into target code rather than performing general OS resource management.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 110 · AM0730
records.text: AM0730 Question 110 COA02 Which software allows users to perform specific tasks or functions on a computer? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Operating system B Application software C Programming language D Compiler Application software. COA02 states that applications solve user tasks. This directly matches software allowing users to perform particular tasks or functions. The operating system instead manages resources and provides services; a compiler translates programs, and a programming language expresses them. These support applications but do not name the general category of user-task software requested here. A incorrect The OS supplies resource management and services rather than naming the category of specific user-task programs. B correct Applications are explicitly described as software solving user tasks, matching the question’s requested category. C incorrect A programming language is a notation for programs, not the category of software performing user tasks. D incorrect A compiler specifically translates code; application software is the general user-task category requested.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 111 · AM0731
records.text: AM0731 Question 111 COA02 COA24 COA14 COA28 Which component provides main working storage for the program’s instructions and data, rather than the CPU’s immediate execution registers or persistent disk storage? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A CPU B Main memory (RAM) C Hard disk D Motherboard Main memory (RAM) Main memory supplies the addressed working storage that holds a program’s instructions and data during operation. CPU registers retain particular fetched instructions, operands and results for immediate execution, while a hard disk supplies persistent storage. The revised stem and expanded memory label distinguish these levels rather than assuming all temporary storage belongs exclusively to one component. A motherboard provides physical interconnection rather than the requested storage role. A incorrect CPU registers serve immediate execution rather than the main working-storage level requested. B correct Main RAM is the addressed working store for program instructions and data. C incorrect A hard disk provides persistent backing storage rather than main working storage. D incorrect The motherboard physically connects components.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 112 · AM0732
records.text: AM0732 Question 112 COA02 Which type of software translates high-level programming languages into machine code? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Operating system B Application software C Programming language D Compiler Compiler A compiler translates source code into target code; in this question the source is a high-level language and the target is machine code. The operating system manages resources, applications solve user tasks, and a programming language is the notation in which a program is expressed. The requested translation function therefore belongs to the compiler category. A incorrect An operating system manages resources and provides services; compiler is the translation category requested. B incorrect Application software solves user tasks rather than naming the general source-to-target translation category. C incorrect The passage distinguishes source high-level language from resulting machine language; a language itself is not the named translating agent (p.77). D correct Compiler support is explicitly tied to high-level-to-machine translation (p.77).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 113 · AM0733
records.text: AM0733 Question 113 COA05 COA34 The system clock in a computer is responsible for: Separate throughput from latency and check which operations overlap or share resources under the stated model. A Controlling the execution speed of instructions B Storing data and instructions C Managing the input/output devices D Connecting different hardware components Controlling the execution speed of instructions Control selections are available at the beginning of a clock cycle and register data are captured on the next clock transition (PDF p.59). Fetch timing likewise advances after each clock pulse (p.55). Thus A is the closest description of clock timing instruction steps; it does not mean frequency alone determines total execution time. A correct Clock transitions time the operations and sequence steps (pp.55,59); this regulates execution pace. B incorrect Registers and memory store bits; the clock times their updates rather than stores the program (p.59). C incorrect I/O management is assigned to interfaces/control mechanisms, not solely the clock (pp.101–102). D incorrect Interconnection provides communication (p.6); the clock provides timing rather than that physical connection.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 114 · AM0734
records.text: AM0734 Question 114 COA15 Which process is responsible for fetching instructions from memory? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Decoding B Execution C Fetching D Storing Fetching The instruction-pipeline list explicitly begins “Fetch the instruction from memory” (PDF p.117), and the fetch micro-operations copy memory into IR (p.55). The question names this retrieval phase, not interpretation or computation. A incorrect Decoding interprets the retrieved instruction after fetching (p.117). B incorrect Execution carries out the operation later in the pipeline (p.117). C correct Fetching is the memory-to-instruction-register retrieval phase (pp.55,117). D incorrect Storing writes the result after execution, the opposite transfer purpose (p.117).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 115 · AM0735
records.text: AM0735 Question 115 COA15 COA16 Which process decodes the fetched instruction and determines the necessary actions? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Decoding B Execution C Fetching D Storing Decoding The module says decoding determines the operation, addressing mode and operand location (PDF p.70). It follows fetch and precedes execution in the instruction phases (p.117). A correct Decoding explicitly determines the required operation and addressing details. B incorrect Execution performs the operation after it has been determined (p.117). C incorrect Fetching retrieves the instruction bits before they are interpreted (p.117). D incorrect Storing writes the computed result, not the operation interpretation (p.117).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 116 · AM0736
records.text: AM0736 Question 116 COA15 Which process carries out the actual operations or calculations specified by the instruction? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Decoding B Execution C Fetching D Storing Execution The instruction stages separate fetch, decode, operand access, execution and result storage (PDF p.117). ALU supplies the required micro-operations for execution (p.57), so actual calculation is execution rather than any transport phase. A incorrect Decoding determines what to do, not the arithmetic itself. B correct Execution is the listed phase that performs the operation (pp.57,117). C incorrect Fetching retrieves the instruction and precedes the calculation (p.117). D incorrect Storing preserves the result after calculation (p.117).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 117 · AM0737
records.text: AM0737 Question 117 COA15 Which process is responsible for storing the results of the executed instruction? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Decoding B Execution C Fetching D Storing Storing The instruction-pipeline sequence ends by storing the result in its proper place (PDF p.117). The RISC variant specifies writing the result into a register (p.118), establishing the result-preservation role of D. A incorrect Decoding interprets operation and addressing fields, before a result exists. B incorrect Execution produces a result; the listed store phase preserves it afterward (p.117). C incorrect Fetching brings in the instruction, not its eventual result (p.117). D correct Store result/write register is the explicit final stage (pp.117–118).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 118 · AM0738
records.text: AM0738 Question 118 COA15 Which unit of the CPU is responsible for fetching instructions and data from memory? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) B Control Unit (CU) C Cache Unit D Register Unit Control Unit (CU) The pipeline description explicitly says the control unit initiates the next fetch when there is buffer space (PDF p.117). CPU control supervises register transfers and ALU work (p.57); the fetch micro-operations transfer address and instruction bits (p.55). This is coordinating responsibility, not a claim the CU physically stores all fetched data. A incorrect ALU performs the arithmetic/logical micro-operations, not the fetch-sequencing role (p.57). B correct CU initiates fetch and supervises the register transfers (pp.57,117). C incorrect Cache supplies stored copies on hits (p.84); it does not decide the instruction-cycle control sequence. D incorrect Registers hold address/data/instruction values, while CU controls their transfers (pp.48,57).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 119 · AM0739
records.text: AM0739 Question 119 COA11 COA01 Which unit of the CPU performs arithmetic and logical operations? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) B Control Unit (CU) C Cache Unit D Register Unit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) ALU is explicitly the CPU part that performs required micro-operations; the module classifies arithmetic and logical manipulation as computational operations (PDF pp.57,74–75). Control selects the operation and registers supply/receive values. A correct ALU performs required arithmetic/logical micro-operations (p.57). B incorrect CU directs transfers and tells ALU which operation to perform (p.57). C incorrect Cache is a fast storage buffer (p.84), not the computation unit. D incorrect Register set stores intermediate data; ALU operates on it (p.57).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 120 · AM0740
records.text: AM0740 Question 120 COA14 Which CPU storage class holds explicit execution operands and results, rather than copies of memory blocks? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) B Control Unit (CU) C Cache Unit D Register Unit Register Unit Registers hold explicit execution operands and results. Cache also stores temporary information, but its role is retaining copies of memory blocks near the processor. The revised question uses that role distinction, so temporary storage alone no longer makes both choices correct. The ALU performs arithmetic and logic, and the control unit coordinates operations rather than being the requested operand-storage class. A incorrect The ALU computes rather than being the operand-storage class. B incorrect The control unit sequences operations rather than holding explicit execution operands as its defining role. C incorrect Cache holds copies of memory blocks. D correct Registers hold explicit execution operands and results.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 121 · AM0741
records.text: AM0741 Question 121 COA11 COA14 Which component of the CPU controls the flow of data and instructions within the CPU? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) B Control Unit (CU) C Cache Unit D Register Unit Control Unit (CU) CU explicitly supervises information transfers among registers and tells ALU what operation to perform (PDF p.57). The bus-control example selects sources, operation and destination (p.59), matching control of internal flow. A incorrect ALU processes operands selected by control (pp.57,59), rather than directs the overall flow. B correct CU selects register sources, destination and ALU operation (p.59). C incorrect Cache stores instruction/data copies (p.84), not the CPU transfer-control sequence. D incorrect Registers hold intermediate data; CU controls their transfers (p.57).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 122 · AM0742
records.text: AM0742 Question 122 COA23 COA14 COA11 Which CPU-near storage component retains copies of memory blocks to speed repeated or nearby memory accesses? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) B Control Unit (CU) C Cache Unit D Register Unit Cache Unit Cache retains copies of memory blocks near the CPU and exploits temporal and spatial locality. Registers instead hold explicit execution operands and results, even though frequently used values may also remain there. The ALU computes values and the control unit sequences operations. The memory-block-copy criterion therefore identifies cache without claiming that no other CPU component can hold useful data. A incorrect The ALU computes arithmetic and logic rather than retaining a memory-block-copy tier. B incorrect The control unit sequences transfers and operations rather than supplying this data-copy storage tier. C correct Cache stores nearby copies of memory blocks for repeated or spatially local accesses. D incorrect Registers hold explicit execution operands/results; that differs from the memory-block-copy cache role.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 123 · AM0743
records.text: AM0743 Question 123 COA15 During a taken branch instruction, which phase computes or applies the branch target to replace the sequential next-PC value? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Decoding B Execution C Fetching D Storing Execution A fetch uses the selected PC to obtain an instruction and can advance it to the sequential address. Executing a taken branch can later replace that sequential value with the branch target. The question now specifically asks about that branch action, rather than the broader process of selecting, reading or advancing a next instruction address. Decode interprets fields and write-back stores results; neither is the conceptual branch-execution role requested. A incorrect Decoding interprets opcode and addressing fields rather than performing the specified branch action. B correct Executing the taken branch replaces the sequential PC with its target. C incorrect Fetching obtains the instruction at the selected address rather than performing this branch action. D incorrect Result storage is not the conceptual branch-target execution phase.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 124 · CS0232
records.text: CS0232 Question 124 COA16 What is the purpose of an opcode in a 16-bit instruction format (4-bit opcode | 6-bit operand ref | 6-bit operand ref)? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A It holds the destination address of an operand B It determines the operation to be done C It holds the source address of an operand D It holds the next instruction reference It determines the operation to be done The stated field widths sum to 16 bits: 4+6+6. Their widths do not change the opcode’s purpose: operation selection (PDF p.47). Operand reference fields identify source/destination values or locations; PC tracks sequence. A incorrect Destination reference is an operand/address field, not the opcode (p.47). B correct Operation selection is the explicit opcode definition (p.47). C incorrect Source reference belongs to the operand/address fields (p.47). D incorrect Next instruction is tracked by PC (p.70), not the opcode.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 125 · CS0234
records.text: CS0234 Question 125 COA23 Which performance metric can be used to measure the time taken to perform a read or write operation? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Transfer rate B Memory cycle time C Fetching time D Access time Access time Access time is the elapsed time from initiation to completion of a memory operation (PDF p.83). Memory cycle time is the minimum separation of successive operations. This distinguishes one read/write duration from transfer throughput or instruction fetching. A incorrect Transfer rate measures an amount per unit time; it is not the single-operation interval defined on p.83. B incorrect Cycle time measures spacing of successive operations, not the requested initiation-to-completion duration (p.83). C incorrect Fetching is one instruction-cycle task, not the general read/write performance metric (p.55). D correct Access time is exactly the operation-duration definition (p.83).

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 126 · CS0235
records.text: CS0235 Question 126 COA28 Under the textbook access-method taxonomy, how is magnetic-disk block access classified when requests identify blocks but mechanical positioning introduces delay? Separate storage role, access timing, placement and power retention; use the specified hierarchy or mapping convention. A Associative B Sequential C Random D Direct Direct The stated textbook taxonomy calls magnetic disk access direct: a request identifies an addressed block, but positioning creates access delay. RAM is classified as random access with broadly address-independent timing, while tape is sequential and associative access matches content. Informal usage may call disks random-access devices too, but the revised question explicitly chooses the textbook classification convention rather than treating the labels as universally exclusive. A incorrect Associative access matches by content rather than addressed disk blocks. B incorrect Tape-like sequential access is not the disk’s required access pattern. C incorrect Random is the RAM category in the explicitly stated textbook taxonomy. D correct Direct is the disk category in that taxonomy.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 127 · CS0236
records.text: CS0236 Question 127 COA38 Which statement reverses the broad integration trend described for computer evolution? Use the stated historical convention or integration trend, rather than assuming every model has identical characteristics. A Increasing component size B Increasing processor speed C Increasing integration density D Increasing memory size Increasing component size The note describes a broad trend toward smaller individual components while density, capacity and processor performance increase. Increasing component size reverses that stated trend. The other alternatives describe growth in performance, integration density or memory capacity and are therefore consistent with it. These are historical tendencies, not guarantees that every later product improves every measured property. A correct The broad trend reduces individual component dimensions, so increasing size reverses it. B incorrect Rising processor performance is consistent with the stated evolutionary tendency. C incorrect Increasing integration density is explicitly part of the stated integration trend. D incorrect Growing storage capacity is consistent with the stated trend even as individual component dimensions shrink.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 128 · CS0237
records.text: CS0237 Question 128 COA02 Which one of the following is NOT correct about Von Neumann's architecture? Identify the role requested and compare it with the definitions and constraints in the cited passages. A Data and instructions are stored separately B Modern computers are based on Von Neumann's architecture C Instruction execution is sequential D Memory content is located by its address Separate instruction and data storage contradicts the textbook Von Neumann model. COA02 defines the textbook Von Neumann model as sharing an addressed memory system between instructions and data, with normally sequential execution unless control flow changes. Thus separate storage is the defining contradiction. The note allows modern machines to retain a unified address-space view while using split caches; ordinary execution and addressed memory remain compatible with that model. A correct Separate instruction/data memories describe Harvard organization rather than the textbook shared-memory Von Neumann model. B incorrect Modern systems can retain a unified address-space view, so this broad conventional association is compatible with the note. C incorrect Normally sequential instruction progression is part of the textbook model, with branches providing explicit control-flow changes. D incorrect The model explicitly uses addressed memory, so locating content by address is a compatible statement.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 129 · CS0238
records.text: CS0238 Question 129 COA19 Which instruction type is used to test the value of a data word or status of a condition? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Data processing instruction B Test instruction C Data movement instruction D Branch instruction Test instruction. COA19 states that TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining an arithmetic result. That exactly matches examining a data word or a condition status. Arithmetic/data processing is a broader computing class, data movement copies values, and branches choose control-flow targets. The named test-instruction category is therefore the direct answer among the options. A incorrect Data processing is a broader computing category; the stem specifically requests the instruction used to test values. B correct TEST/CMP examine values and establish condition information, directly matching the question’s described operation. C incorrect Data movement copies values between locations rather than testing their contents or condition status. D incorrect Branches choose control-flow targets, often using previously established conditions rather than performing the requested test.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 130 · NS0221
records.text: NS0221 Question 130 COA16 What is the purpose of an opcode in a 16-bit instruction format (4-bit opcode | 6-bit operand ref 6-bit operand ref)? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A It holds the destination address of an operand B It determines the operation to be done C It holds the source address of an operand D It holds the next instruction reference The opcode specifies the operation. COA16 defines the opcode as specifying the operation and operand fields as locating data/registers. In the given 16-bit format, the 4-bit opcode therefore selects an operation, while the two 6-bit references identify operands under the machine’s interpretation. The bit widths are not evidence that the opcode stores a source/destination address or next-PC reference. A incorrect A destination operand reference belongs in an operand field, not in the operation-selecting opcode. B correct The opcode determines which operation the processor should perform for this instruction. C incorrect A source operand reference is an operand-field role rather than the opcode’s operation role. D incorrect The next-instruction reference is a control-flow/PC concern, not the general purpose of this opcode field.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 131 · NS0289
records.text: NS0289 Question 131 COA32 A designer adds a PCI expansion card to a processor whose local bus uses a different transfer protocol. The two sides cannot be wired together directly. Which listed hardware category is needed to adapt transfers between the processor bus and the expansion interconnect? Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A SCSI B PCI C Bus bridge/controller logic D Multi bus Bus bridge/controller logic The scenario requires hardware that adapts transfers between unlike bus segments, so bus bridge/controller logic is needed. PCI identifies the expansion interconnect on one side of the connection; merely naming it does not supply the adaptation to the processor bus. SCSI identifies a storage connection and Multibus another bus family. The distinction is between the interconnect being attached and the hardware that enables the attachment. A incorrect SCSI is a storage connection rather than the adapter between these unlike bus segments. B incorrect PCI names the expansion interconnect already present in the scenario, not the adapting component. C correct Bus bridge/controller logic adapts transfers between the unlike processor and expansion bus segments. D incorrect Multibus names a bus family rather than the component needed to adapt this connection.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 132 · NS0290
records.text: NS0290 Question 132 COA05 Combinational circuit differ from sequential circuit primarily because Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A Combinational circuit cannot be built using logic circuit B The output of combinational circuit depends only on the present input, not on past output. C Sequential circuit have no feedback while combinational circuit do D The combinational circuit requires clock signal, but sequential circuit do not Combinational output depends on present inputs rather than stored history. COA05 defines combinational output through present inputs after propagation delay, while sequential output also depends on stored state. B expresses that distinction. Combinational circuits are built from logic, not prohibited from it; the feedback statement reverses the usual state relationship. Nor do combinational circuits inherently require a clock, while clocked sequential circuits update at clock events. A incorrect Combinational circuits are logic circuits; the statement incorrectly denies their ordinary implementation basis. B correct Present inputs determine combinational outputs, whereas sequential circuits additionally depend on retained state. C incorrect This reverses the state/feedback distinction; sequential storage can involve feedback, not its categorical absence. D incorrect Combinational logic does not inherently require a clock; clock events characterize clocked sequential updates.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 133 · NS0304
records.text: NS0304 Question 133 COA15 Which one of the following is the first operation or step in CPU instruction cycle? Identify the register, signal or instruction role and the execution phase; distinguish stored values, addresses and control actions. A Executing the instruction B Handling interrupt C Decoding the instruction D Fetching the instruction Fetch the instruction. COA15 begins the conceptual instruction cycle with fetch, then decode, operand acquisition, execution and any result write-back. Fetch must obtain the instruction before its opcode can be decoded and operation performed. Permitted interrupt checks are a separate stage/transition in that conceptual model, not the first ordinary instruction-processing step among these choices. A incorrect Execution follows obtaining and decoding the instruction, rather than being the cycle’s first conceptual step. B incorrect Interrupt checks/service are distinct from the first ordinary fetch step in the note’s conceptual cycle. C incorrect Decoding requires an already fetched instruction, so it follows rather than precedes fetch. D correct Fetching obtains the instruction and is explicitly first in the conceptual instruction-cycle sequence.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 134 · NS0310
records.text: NS0310 Question 134 COA30 ____________ is a data transfer method in computer organization and architecture that allows an I/O device to transfer data directly to or from memory without the involvement of the CPU. Follow the data path and control responsibility; distinguish the transfer mechanism, address space and interface type. A Asynchronous data transfer B Direct Memory Access (DMA) C Interrupt-driven transfer D Programmed I/O transfer Direct Memory Access (DMA). COA30 says DMA lets a controller transfer a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup. The stem’s without CPU involvement must mean without CPU moving every item, not no configuration/completion involvement whatsoever. Polling and interrupt-driven I/O still require CPU transfer work; asynchronous transfer describes timing coordination rather than this block-moving mechanism. A incorrect Asynchronous transfer describes coordination/timing rather than specifically controller-managed movement directly between device and memory. B correct DMA transfers the block through a controller after CPU setup, avoiding per-item CPU copying. C incorrect Interrupt-driven handlers still consume CPU time to service and move device data in this comparison. D incorrect Programmed I/O repeatedly checks status and has the CPU move each item rather than using DMA.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 135 · NS0367
records.text: NS0367 Question 135 COA03 Which logic gate produces output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A OR gate B AND gate C NAND gate D XOR gate AND gate. COA03 states that AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1. This is exactly the condition in the stem. OR needs any high input, NAND complements AND, and two-input XOR is high when inputs differ. Thus none of the other truth functions has the specified all-high-only output rule. A incorrect OR becomes high when any input is high, so it does not require all inputs to be one. B correct AND outputs one exactly for the all-inputs-one combination required by the stem. C incorrect NAND inverts AND and therefore outputs zero, not one, when all its inputs are one. D incorrect Two-input XOR outputs one when inputs differ, not when both inputs are one.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 136 · NS0368
records.text: NS0368 Question 136 COA-S06 COA03 The Boolean expression F = A⊕B represents which gate? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A XNOR gate B NOR gate C XOR gate D NAND gate XOR gate. The expression A⊕B is the exclusive-OR operation. COA03 defines its two-input output as 1 when the inputs differ and contrasts XNOR as agreement. NOR and NAND complement OR and AND instead. Thus XOR is the operation represented by the given symbol, with no extra circuit diagram or numeric assumption needed. A incorrect XNOR is the complement of XOR, giving one when the two inputs agree. B incorrect NOR complements OR; it is not the exclusive-OR operation denoted by the circled plus. C correct The circled-plus expression denotes exclusive OR, whose output is one for differing inputs. D incorrect NAND complements AND rather than implementing the given exclusive-OR expression.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 137 · NS0369
records.text: NS0369 Question 137 COA04 Which gate is called the 'universal gate' because it can implement any Boolean function? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A AND gate B OR gate C NAND gate D XOR gate NAND, the only universal gate offered. COA04 explicitly states that NAND and NOR are each universal and explains constructing NOT by tying inputs together, then building AND/OR combinations. Of those two universal families, only NAND is offered. AND and OR alone cannot provide inversion under this rule, and XOR is not identified as a universal family. Thus the correct offered gate is NAND. A incorrect AND alone is not the universal family described; it does not supply the required inversion construction. B incorrect OR alone is not the universal family described and cannot generate the stated NOT construction. C correct NAND is explicitly universal and can be combined to construct NOT, AND and OR. D incorrect XOR is not the NAND/NOR universal family; tied inputs produce zero rather than inversion.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 138 · NS0370
records.text: NS0370 Question 138 COA03 For a NOR gate with inputs A=1, B=0, the output F is: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A 0 B 1 C Undefined D Depends on voltage F = 0. COA03 defines OR as high when any input is high and NOR as its complement. At A=1, B=0, the OR value is 1, so NOR produces 0. The input combination is completely specified in ordinary Boolean logic; it is neither undefined nor dependent on an unspecified analog voltage model. A correct OR of 1 and 0 is 1; complementing that for NOR yields zero. B incorrect One is the OR result before inversion, not the NOR output for these inputs. C incorrect The Boolean NOR truth table fully defines this ordinary input combination. D incorrect The stem supplies Boolean input values, so no additional voltage threshold assumption is required.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 139 · NS0371
records.text: NS0371 Question 139 COA04 De Morgan's theorem states that NOT(A·B) equals: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A NOT(A) · NOT(B) B NOT(A) + NOT(B) C A + B D NOT(A+B) NOT(A·B) = NOT(A) + NOT(B). COA04 gives (AB)'=A'+B'. Complementing a product changes AND to OR and complements each operand. B matches that exact transformation. A instead gives the complement of A+B, C omits the operand complements, and D leaves the complement attached to a sum, which represents NOR rather than the requested NAND function. A incorrect The product of complements equals NOT(A+B), rather than the complement of the original product. B correct Complement each operand and change AND to OR, exactly as De Morgan’s product rule states. C incorrect A+B omits both required complements and is not generally equal to NOT(A·B). D incorrect NOT(A+B) is NOR and differs from NOT(A·B), for example when only one input is high.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 140 · NS0372
records.text: NS0372 Question 140 COA04 In Boolean algebra, the expression A + A' (A OR NOT A) always equals: Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A 0 B A C 1 D A' A + A' = 1. COA04 explicitly lists A+A'=1. If A is 0 then A' is 1, and if A is 1 then A' is 0; either way their Boolean OR is 1. Neither A nor A' remains fixed across both assignments, and zero is the product-of-complements result rather than their sum. A incorrect Zero is A AND NOT A; the given operation is OR, so one input is always high. B incorrect A can be zero while the expression remains one, so the identity is not simply A. C correct A bit OR its complement is always one for both possible assignments. D incorrect A complement can be zero while the full expression is one, so it is not the constant result.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 141 · NS0373
records.text: NS0373 Question 141 COA03 How many rows are in the truth table for a Boolean function with 4 input variables? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A 8 B 12 C 16 D 32 16 rows. COA03 gives 2^n rows for n binary inputs. For four independent variables, each has two assignments, so the total combinations are 2×2×2×2=16. The options 8 and 32 correspond to three and five binary variables respectively; 12 does not enumerate all four-variable combinations. A incorrect Eight is 2^3, the number of assignments for three inputs rather than four. B incorrect Twelve omits four of the sixteen possible combinations of four independent binary inputs. C correct Four independent binary inputs yield 2^4=16 distinct truth-table rows. D incorrect Thirty-two is 2^5 and would require five independent binary input variables.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 142 · NS0374
records.text: NS0374 Question 142 COA03 COA04 For the Boolean function F=x+y'z with x=0,y=1,z=1, which options evaluate to the same Boolean value as F under that assignment? Select all that apply. Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A 0 B 1 C x D z 0; x Complement first: y is one, so y-prime is zero. The product y-prime AND z is therefore zero, and OR with x, also zero, leaves F equal to zero. Both the literal zero option and the expression x evaluate to that result under the stated assignment. The literal one and z both evaluate to one. The multiple-selection wording preserves the actual option values rather than arbitrarily rejecting an equivalent expression. A correct The literal zero equals the computed function value. B incorrect One differs from the computed zero. C correct x is assigned zero and therefore equals the function value. D incorrect z is assigned one and differs from the function value.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 143 · NS0375
records.text: NS0375 Question 143 COA-S07 COA05 Which characteristic best describes a flip-flop? Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A A combinational logic circuit B A bistable multivibrator that stores one bit C A 4-bit counter D An arithmetic unit A bistable one-bit storage element. COA05 says a flip-flop stores one bit while powered and classifies flip-flops as sequential circuits with stored state. B is the option describing that storage element. A combinational circuit lacks stored logical state; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state structure, and an arithmetic unit computes rather than defining this one-bit storage component. A incorrect A combinational circuit has no stored logical state, whereas a flip-flop retains a bit. B correct Bistable one-bit storage matches the powered state-retention role of a flip-flop. C incorrect One flip-flop stores one bit; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state organization. D incorrect An arithmetic unit computes values rather than defining the one-bit sequential storage element.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 144 · NS0376
records.text: NS0376 Question 144 COA05 What distinguishes a flip-flop from a simple logic gate in terms of memory? Check whether output depends only on current inputs or also on stored state, and track the stated clock behavior. A Flip-flops use more power B Flip-flops retain state even after inputs change C Flip-flops operate faster D Flip-flops require AC power Flip-flops retain stored state during powered operation. COA05 distinguishes sequential state from combinational outputs determined by present inputs. A flip-flop can retain its bit when inputs change without a qualifying update, giving the memory distinction in B. This does not imply nonvolatile retention after power-off. Power, speed and AC-supply claims are neither the defining property nor guarantees established here. A incorrect Power consumption is implementation-dependent and does not define whether a circuit has logical memory. B correct Stored state persists between valid updates while powered, unlike a purely present-input combinational gate. C incorrect Speed is not the defining memory distinction and is not guaranteed by the flip-flop label. D incorrect The note specifies powered storage, not a requirement for an AC rather than another supply.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 145 · NS0377
records.text: NS0377 Question 145 COA08 What is the decimal equivalent of binary number 1011? Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order. A 9 B 10 C 11 D 13 1011₂ = 11₁₀. Using COA08’s base-position rule, 1011₂ has weights 8, 4, 2 and 1. Its high bits contribute 8+2+1=11, while the 4-place is zero. The note’s worked example confirms the same sum. Nine, ten and thirteen correspond to different low-order bit patterns, not the supplied 1011. A incorrect Nine equals 8+1, corresponding to 1001₂ and omitting the given two-place bit. B incorrect Ten equals 8+2, corresponding to 1010₂ and omitting the given one-place bit. C correct The set bit positions contribute 8+2+1=11 in decimal. D incorrect Thirteen equals 8+4+1, corresponding to 1101₂ rather than the supplied 1011₂.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 146 · NS0378
records.text: NS0378 Question 146 COA08 In hexadecimal, what does the letter 'F' represent in decimal? Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order. A 14 B 15 C 16 D 10 F₁₆ = 15₁₀. COA08 defines hexadecimal digits as 0–9,A–F and explicitly gives F=15. These sixteen symbols represent values zero through fifteen, so sixteen itself requires the two-digit hexadecimal representation 10. Fourteen is E, and ten is A, leaving fifteen as the only value of the single digit F. A incorrect Fourteen corresponds to the preceding hexadecimal digit E, not the final digit F. B correct The note explicitly assigns decimal value fifteen to the hexadecimal digit F. C incorrect Sixteen requires hexadecimal 10; it is outside the value range of a single hexadecimal digit. D incorrect Ten corresponds to hexadecimal A rather than the later digit F.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 147 · NS0379
records.text: NS0379 Question 147 COA08 The octal number system uses a base of: Keep the radix, bit width and representation fixed; evaluate place values or arithmetic steps in order. A 2 B 8 C 10 D 16 Base 8. COA08 gives octal digits 0–7: eight possible digit values, so octal has base eight. Binary has two digits, decimal ten and hexadecimal sixteen. Place weights in octal are therefore powers of eight, not powers of two, ten or sixteen, even though octal digits can be grouped with three binary bits. A incorrect Base two is binary; octal allows eight digit values rather than only zero and one. B correct Octal uses digits zero through seven, giving a base of eight. C incorrect Base ten is decimal, not the eight-digit octal number system. D incorrect Base sixteen is hexadecimal, which uses the additional A–F digits absent from octal.

records.title: Computer Organization and Architecture — Question 148 · NS0380
records.text: NS0380 Question 148 COA08 COA03 Which number system is most fundamental to digital computing and why? Apply the gate truth rules and Boolean identities in the stated input order; distinguish an inversion from the underlying operation. A Decimal, because humans use it B Octal, because it maps to 3 bits C Binary, because digital circuits have two states (on/off) D Hexadecimal, because it is compact Binary matches the two logical states used by digital logic.
