Evidence: PDF 16, 15, 15, 16. A incorrect Session controls dialogs/checkpoints (PDF 16, 15, 15, 16.) B correct Transport explicitly ensures intact and ordered whole-message delivery (PDF 16, 15, 15, 16.) C incorrect Data link controls hop-to-hop frames rather than the entire end-to-end message (PDF 16, 15, 15, 16.) D incorrect Network packets can arrive out of order (PDF 16, 15, 15, 16.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 165 · SS098
records.text: SS098 Question 165 NET25 Which of the following is not a valid host address within the network 172.17.128.0/21 ? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 172.17.128.1/21 B 172.17.135.255 /21 C 172.17.135.0 /21 D 172.17.128.255/21 172.17.135.255/21 is broadcast A /21 groups eight third-octet values, here 128–135. The network is 172.17.128.0 and its broadcast is 172.17.135.255. B sets every host bit to one and cannot be assigned to an ordinary host. The other choices are inside the usable range; ending in .0 or .255 alone does not make an address reserved. A incorrect 172.17.128.1 is one above the network boundary and is a valid usable host. B correct 172.17.135.255 sets all eleven host bits to one and is the subnet broadcast address. C incorrect 172.17.135.0 is inside the /21 block; its host bits are not all zero or all one. D incorrect 172.17.128.255 is an interior host; the .255 ending alone does not make it /21 broadcast.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 166 · SS111
records.text: SS111 Question 166 NET07 NET-S07 Which of the following is not the function of Cross-over UTP cable? Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A To connect router to pc B To connect switch to switch C To connect switch to pc D To connect pc to pc Switch-to-PC normally uses straight-through cable in legacy Ethernet Under the legacy MDI/MDI-X convention, a switch port and PC have unlike roles and use straight-through cable. PCs and router Ethernet endpoints conventionally share the endpoint role, while two switches share the switch role, so those like-role links use crossover. Auto-MDI-X can remove the practical requirement; the question is testing the conventional cable-role distinction. A incorrect A legacy router Ethernet endpoint and PC have like interface roles, so crossover is appropriate. B incorrect Two legacy switch ports have like roles and conventionally require crossover. C correct Switch and PC have unlike legacy interface roles and normally use straight-through cable. D incorrect Two PCs have like legacy interface roles; NET07 explicitly names PC–PC as a crossover example.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 167 · SS126
records.text: SS126 Question 167 NET14 Given a situation two hosts attempt on a half-duplex Ethernet LAN to send data concurrently, resulting in a collision and subsequent to this collision, what will the hosts do? Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A An electrical pulse indicates that the collision has cleared B The router on the segment will signal that the collision has cleared C The jam signal indicates that the collision has been cleared D The hosts will attempt to resume transmission after a time delay has expired Stop and retry after random backoff NET14 gives the collision sequence: detect, jam, stop and retry after random backoff. The jam indicates the collision itself, not that it has cleared. There is no router-coordinated clearance procedure or electrical clearance pulse in the stated rule. Therefore waiting for a delay and attempting transmission again is the supported host behavior. A incorrect The defined procedure uses collision indication and backoff; it does not include a collision-cleared electrical pulse. B incorrect Ethernet collision recovery is performed by the hosts’ MAC procedure, not a router clearance signal. C incorrect A jam announces the collision; it does not certify that the shared medium is clear. D correct After stopping, hosts retry following random backoff, matching a delay before another transmission attempt.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 168 · SS134
records.text: SS134 Question 168 NET10 NET09 Which of the following is true regarding the use of switches and hubs for network connectivity in the network? Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A Switches increase the number of collision domains in the network B Switches take less time to process frames than hubs take C Switches do not forward broadcasts D Hubs can filter frames Switch ports separate collision domains NET10 says each switch port separates collision domains, whereas a half-duplex hub repeats traffic into one shared collision domain. Switches still flood broadcasts within their VLAN, and hubs do not inspect and filter destination frames. The note gives no universal switch-versus-hub processing-time advantage, so A is the supported claim. A correct Replacing a shared hub segment with separate switch ports divides the network into additional collision domains. B incorrect The note establishes no universal lower switch processing time; a hub simply repeats signals. C incorrect Switches flood broadcasts within the VLAN unless another control filters them. D incorrect Hubs repeat physical signals and neither learn MAC destinations nor filter frames.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 169 · SS145
records.text: SS145 Question 169 NET19 NET30 A TCP/IP layer which is responsible for addressing, path selection and routing refers: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Transport Layer B Network Access Layer C Application Layer D Internet Layer Internet Layer The TCP/IP Internet layer corresponds to OSI network and provides IP addressing/source-to-destination transmission with routing. Evidence: PDF 17, 15, 17. A incorrect Transport is process delivery (PDF 17, 15, 17.) B incorrect Network access combines physical/data link (PDF 17, 15, 17.) C incorrect Application combines OSI upper layers (PDF 17, 15, 17.) D correct Internet matches network-layer addressing and routing (PDF 17, 15, 17.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 170 · SS170
records.text: SS170 Question 170 NET12 Which of the following is the correct order of packet data unit as data moved in the OS! reference model from bottom to top? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Segment, packet, frame, bit B Segment, frame, packet, bit C Bit, packet, frame, segment D Bit, frame, packet, segment Bit, frame, packet, segment Moving bottom to top reverses sending encapsulation: physical bits become data-link frames, then network packets, then transport segments. Evidence: PDF 14, 15, 15, 16. A incorrect Starts at transport instead of physical and moves downward B incorrect Starts at transport and misorders frame and packet C incorrect Skips frame before packet D correct Bit, frame, packet, segment follows the upward layer order

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 171 · AM0474
records.text: AM0474 Question 171 NET16 NET14 NET17 Which of the following is not a primary function of the network layer in the OSI model? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Routing B Addressing C Flow control D Fragmentation Flow control is not a primary network-layer duty The network layer supplies logical addressing/routing and, for IPv4, fragmentation when permitted. Flow control instead protects a receiver in transport or hop-local link procedures, as NET14 and NET17 explain. Thus C is not a primary network-layer function in this layer model, without claiming that all control mechanisms belong exclusively to one layer. A incorrect Routing is explicitly a main network-layer duty in the NET12 layer table. B incorrect Logical addressing is explicitly assigned to the network layer. C correct Receiver flow control is described at link and transport scope rather than as a primary network duty. D incorrect NET16 supports IPv4 fragmentation by sources and routers, a network-protocol function.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 172 · AM0475
records.text: AM0475 Question 172 NET20 NET10 NET12 What is the purpose of a MAC address in computer networking? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A To identify a device within a local area network (LAN) B To identify a device within a wide area network (WAN) C To establish a secure connection between two devices D To determine the IP address of a device To identify a device within a local area network (LAN) The module physical MAC address is imprinted on a NIC and used for local physical delivery; it is not encryption or the IP routing address. Evidence: PDF 17, 15. A correct MAC identifies the local physical interface for frame delivery (PDF 17, 15.) B incorrect WAN-wide logical routing uses IP rather than treating MAC as a universal end-to-end address (PDF 17, 15.) C incorrect A physical identifier does not establish encryption/security (PDF 17, 15.) D incorrect ARP starts with IP and resolves MAC; MAC itself is not a rule for determining IP (PDF 17, 15.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 173 · AM0476
records.text: AM0476 Question 173 NET21 Which of the following protocols is used for email transmission? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A FTP (File Transfer Protocol) B SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) C HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) D DNS (Domain Name System) SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) SMTP is explicitly Simple Mail Transfer Protocol in the application list, matching email transmission. Evidence: PDF 18, 28. A incorrect FTP transfers files (PDF 18, 28.) B correct SMTP is the explicitly named mail transfer protocol (PDF 18, 28.) C incorrect HTTP is the web service in the port table (PDF 18, 28.) D incorrect DNS is external naming (PDF 18, 28.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 174 · AM0477
records.text: AM0477 Question 174 NET11 What is the purpose of a firewall in computer networks? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A To encrypt network traffic for secure communication B To manage network resources and allocate bandwidth C To filter and control network traffic based on predefined rules D To connect two separate networks and enable communication between them To filter and control network traffic based on predefined rules The module firewall example permits only authorized systems to access internal computers, supporting selective traffic filtering/control. Evidence: PDF 48, 12, 16. A incorrect Encryption is a distinct presentation function (PDF 48, 12, 16.) B incorrect Bandwidth allocation is not the firewall access-control function described (PDF 48, 12, 16.) C correct Rules permitting authorized access match firewall filtering (PDF 48, 12, 16.) D incorrect Connecting networks is the router/gateway function, not the defining firewall policy (PDF 48, 12, 16.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 175 · AM0478
records.text: AM0478 Question 175 NET08 Which of the following network topologies provides the highest fault tolerance? Draw the links and identify shared components, alternate paths and the effect of the specified failure or growth requirement. A Bus topology B Ring topology C Star topology D Mesh topology Mesh topology Mesh has redundant interconnections and a single link failure does not affect the entire network. Bus backbone, ring break and star center failure are explicit vulnerabilities. Evidence: PDF 23, 24, 23, 23, 23. A incorrect A broken backbone can shut down bus (PDF 23, 24, 23, 23, 23.) B incorrect A break/disabled station can disable a ring (PDF 23, 24, 23, 23, 23.) C incorrect Central device failure can shut down star (PDF 23, 24, 23, 23, 23.) D correct Redundant mesh paths support the strongest listed fault tolerance (PDF 23, 24, 23, 23, 23.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 176 · AM0479
records.text: AM0479 Question 176 NET23 NET28 NET26 Which listed terms describe IPv6’s flexible-prefix addressing or operations supported by that approach? Select all that apply. Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A Classful addressing B Classless addressing C Subnetting D CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) Classless addressing; Subnetting; CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) IPv6 uses flexible network prefixes rather than historical IPv4 address classes. Classless addressing describes this approach, subnetting divides prefixes into smaller networks, and CIDR terminology expresses classless prefixes and aggregation. These are compatible descriptions or operations rather than mutually exclusive schemes. The selection instruction therefore permits all three while excluding the classful A/B/C allocation model associated with historical IPv4. A incorrect Historical classful A/B/C IPv4 defaults are not the IPv6 flexible-prefix scheme. B correct IPv6 uses flexible prefixes rather than fixed historical address classes. C correct IPv6 prefixes can be subdivided into subnets; the term overlaps the broad scheme wording. D correct Classless prefix/CIDR terminology applies to flexible-prefix allocation and routing rather than historical class boundaries.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 177 · AM0480
records.text: AM0480 Question 177 NET20 Which protocol is responsible for translating domain names into IP addresses? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) B DNS (Domain Name System) C ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) D ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) DNS (Domain Name System) DNS is the domain naming service and external name/address service contrasted with hosts entries. Evidence: PDF 18, 65, 28, 17, 17. A incorrect DHCP is named host configuration, not domain naming B correct DNS matches the named domain service C incorrect ARP resolves known IP to MAC D incorrect ICMP reports packet problems

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 178 · AM0481
records.text: AM0481 Question 178 NET29 NET11 NET20 What is the purpose of NAT (Network Address Translation) in computer networks? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A To secure network communications through encryption B To provide redundancy and fault tolerance C To translate private IP addresses to public IP addresses D To manage network resources and allocate bandwidth To translate private IP addresses to public IP addresses NAT explicitly translates an organization private IP address to a public IP address. It is not an encryption, redundancy or bandwidth-allocation mechanism. Evidence: PDF 19, 48, 16. A incorrect Encryption is a separate representation/security transformation (PDF 19, 48, 16.) B incorrect Redundancy is not the address translation definition (PDF 19, 48, 16.) C correct Private-to-public translation is the exact NAT definition (PDF 19, 48, 16.) D incorrect Bandwidth allocation is not the NAT definition (PDF 19, 48, 16.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 179 · AM0482
records.text: AM0482 Question 179 NET17 NET21 Which listed protocol is a connectionless transport-layer protocol, sending independent datagrams without built-in connection setup? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) B UDP (User Datagram Protocol) C HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) D FTP (File Transfer Protocol) UDP (User Datagram Protocol) UDP is a transport protocol that sends independent datagrams without a built-in setup handshake, ordering or retransmission service. TCP instead establishes a connection and supplies an ordered reliable byte stream. HTTP and FTP are application protocols, so they are outside the requested transport-layer category. HTTP being stateless at the application level does not make it a connectionless transport protocol. A incorrect TCP is connection-oriented transport with reliable ordered byte-stream delivery. B correct UDP is the connectionless datagram transport described. C incorrect HTTP is an application protocol; application statelessness is distinct from connectionless transport. D incorrect FTP is an application file-transfer protocol, not a transport protocol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 180 · AM0483
records.text: AM0483 Question 180 NET10 NET09 NET11 Which listed devices ordinarily forward frames at OSI layer 2? Select all that apply. Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Hub B Switch C Router D Bridge Switch; Bridge A bridge and an ordinary Ethernet switch both inspect link-layer frames and use MAC-address information in forwarding. A hub regenerates and repeats physical signals without that address inspection. A router forwards IP packets between networks using network-layer destinations. The explicit multiple-selection instruction preserves both correct layer-2 devices and avoids implying that only one kind of device can operate at a layer. A incorrect A hub repeats layer-1 signals rather than making MAC/frame forwarding decisions. B correct An ordinary Ethernet switch is explicitly a layer-2 forwarding device. C incorrect A router’s defining forwarding function is network-layer IP routing. D correct A bridge is explicitly a layer-2 device, like an ordinary Ethernet switch.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 181 · AM0485
records.text: AM0485 Question 181 NET11 NET09 What is the function of a router in a computer network? Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A To connect multiple networks together B To amplify the strength of network signals C To provide firewall protection D To manage network resources and allocate bandwidth To connect multiple networks together The router definition explicitly interconnects LANs/WANs and determines next paths using routing tables. Firewall functionality may be added, but it is not the primary definition. Evidence: PDF 12, 11, 48. A correct Connecting networks is the explicit router role (PDF 12, 11, 48.) B incorrect Signal regeneration is repeater work (PDF 12, 11, 48.) C incorrect A router can have firewall configuration, but this is optional additional policy (PDF 12, 11, 48.) D incorrect Bandwidth allocation is not the defining routing role (PDF 12, 11, 48.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 182 · AM0486
records.text: AM0486 Question 182 NET09 NET10 NET11 Which of the following is a network device that operates at the Physical layer of the OSI model? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Switch B Hub C Router D Bridge Hub An active hub is explicitly a multiport repeater, and repeaters operate at physical layer. Evidence: PDF 12, 11, 12, 12, 12. A incorrect Switch forwards by MAC at data-link scope (PDF 12, 11, 12, 12, 12.) B correct Active hub repeats physical signals (PDF 12, 11, 12, 12, 12.) C incorrect Router selects IP paths (PDF 12, 11, 12, 12, 12.) D incorrect Bridge filters by MAC (PDF 12, 11, 12, 12, 12.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 183 · AM0487
records.text: AM0487 Question 183 NET11 NET10 Which network component is responsible for converting digital data into analog signals for transmission over telephone lines? Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A Modem B Router C Switch D Firewall Modem The stem asks about conversion for a telephone-line carrier, which is modem modulation. NET11 separates this signal-conversion function from routing IP packets, switching link frames and applying firewall traffic policy. These functions can coexist in one appliance, but the functional component asked for remains the modem. A correct A modem modulates outgoing carrier signals and demodulates incoming ones, supplying the requested conversion. B incorrect A router selects next hops between networks; that role is distinct from telephone-carrier modulation. C incorrect A switch forwards link-layer frames and is not the component defined by carrier modulation. D incorrect A firewall applies security policy to traffic rather than converting data onto a telephone-line carrier.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 184 · AM0488
records.text: AM0488 Question 184 NET21 NET20 Which protocol submits and relays email messages, including acceptance by a receiving mail server? Select one. Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A SMTP B HTTP C FTP D DNS SMTP SMTP is used for mail submission and relay, including a mail server accepting an incoming message. End-user access to stored mail is a separate operation supplied by POP3 or IMAP. HTTP handles web exchanges, FTP transfers files, and DNS resolves records. Specifying server receipt and relay makes the mail-system role clear without assigning mailbox retrieval to the transfer protocol. A correct SMTP submits and relays mail, including server acceptance of incoming messages. B incorrect HTTP defines web request/response exchanges rather than the mail submission and relay protocol requested. C incorrect FTP transfers files and is not the mail submission/relay or mailbox access protocol in the note. D incorrect DNS resolves records; it does not transport or retrieve the user’s messages.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 185 · AM0489
records.text: AM0489 Question 185 NET20 NET11 NET-S02 What is the purpose of DNS (Domain Name System) in computer networks? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A To encrypt network traffic for secure communication B To manage network resources and allocate bandwidth C To convert domain names into IP addresses D To provide firewall protection To convert domain names into IP addresses The domain naming service is contrasted with explicit host-address entries, supporting resolving a name into the corresponding address. Evidence: PDF 18, 65. A incorrect Encryption is not DNS naming (PDF 18, 65.) B incorrect Bandwidth allocation is not DNS naming (PDF 18, 65.) C correct Name-to-address resolution matches Domain Name Service and the hosts-file contrast (PDF 18, 65.) D incorrect Firewall access policy is not DNS naming (PDF 18, 65.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 186 · AM0490
records.text: AM0490 Question 186 NET21 NET17 Which listed application protocol has the name File Transfer Protocol? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A HTTP B FTP C SMTP D TCP FTP FTP is the named application protocol File Transfer Protocol. HTTP also transfers resource bodies and can download files, so generic file transfer alone does not distinguish them. SMTP is a mail-transfer application protocol, while TCP supplies an underlying reliable byte-stream transport. The explicit protocol name identifies the intended service without claiming that FTP is the only way to transfer a file. A incorrect HTTP is Hypertext Transfer Protocol and can carry files, but is not the stated protocol name. B correct FTP expands to File Transfer Protocol. C incorrect SMTP sends and relays email rather than bearing the stated protocol name. D incorrect TCP is a transport protocol, not the named application protocol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 187 · AM0491
records.text: AM0491 Question 187 NET10 NET09 NET11 Which device connects multiple Ethernet LAN endpoints and learns MAC-to-port mappings to forward known unicast frames selectively? Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A Hub B Router C Switch D Modem Switch Both hubs and switches can connect LAN endpoints, but their forwarding behavior differs. A hub repeats incoming signals to its other ports without learning addresses. An ordinary Ethernet switch learns source MAC-to-port mappings and uses the destination MAC address to forward known unicasts. Routers instead forward IP packets between networks, while modems convert carrier signals. The added forwarding requirement distinguishes the intended device. A incorrect A hub connects endpoints but repeats signals without learning MAC-to-port mappings. B incorrect A router’s defining function is connecting/routing between IP networks rather than this shared LAN-device role. C correct A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and forwards known unicasts selectively. D incorrect A modem modulates/demodulates carrier signals rather than providing the offered multiport LAN interconnection function.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 188 · AM0492
records.text: AM0492 Question 188 NET11 NET-S02 NET20 What is the primary function of a firewall in a computer network? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A To manage network resources and allocate bandwidth B To encrypt network traffic for secure communication C To filter and monitor network traffic for security purposes D To convert domain names into IP addresses To filter and monitor network traffic for security purposes The firewall example controls which systems may access internal computers; monitoring/filtering for security is the offered match. Evidence: PDF 48, 16, 18. A incorrect Resource/bandwidth allocation is not the described firewall role (PDF 48, 16, 18.) B incorrect Encryption is a presentation function and distinct from access filtering (PDF 48, 16, 18.) C correct Authorized-access filtering is the module firewall function (PDF 48, 16, 18.) D incorrect DNS is the naming service, not firewall policy (PDF 48, 16, 18.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 189 · AM0493
records.text: AM0493 Question 189 NET20 NET21 Which protocol is responsible for assigning IP addresses to devices on a network automatically? Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A HTTP B DNS C DHCP D FTP DHCP NET20 assigns dynamic address-setting leases to DHCP, whose basic exchange is discover, offer, request and acknowledge. DNS instead resolves names to records. HTTP and FTP are application services for web exchanges and file transfer; neither is the automatic host-address lease protocol. A incorrect HTTP provides web request/response semantics rather than automatic IP-address leases. B incorrect DNS resolves names into records, including addresses, but does not lease the host’s own address. C correct DHCP dynamically leases an IP address and related host-network configuration. D incorrect FTP transfers files; it does not provide the address-assignment exchange described.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 190 · AM0494
records.text: AM0494 Question 190 NET19 NET18 NET14 Which OSI layer establishes and manages application dialogs, including checkpoints for recovery after an interruption? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Physical layer B Data Link layer C Transport layer D Session layer Session layer Session-layer roles include establishing and managing dialogs and coordinating checkpoints so a transfer can resume after an interruption. TCP transport connections are a different form of connection state and do not make every reference to a dialog a transport function. Physical signaling and hop-local link delivery likewise have different scopes. The revised stem identifies dialog and checkpoint management as the lifecycle being classified. A incorrect Physical signaling does not perform application-dialog management or checkpoint coordination. B incorrect Data link handles hop-local frames and link procedures rather than application dialogs and checkpoints. C incorrect Transport handles process delivery and TCP connection state, not the session-dialog role specified. D correct Session manages dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints for recovery.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 191 · AM0495
records.text: AM0495 Question 191 NET17 NET16 NET21 Which protocol is used for reliable data delivery at the transport layer in the TCP/IP protocol suite? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A UDP B IP C FTP D TCP TCP TCP is explicitly reliable and connection-oriented at transport, unlike UDP and network-layer IP. Evidence: PDF 18, 17, 18. A incorrect UDP is explicitly unreliable (PDF 18, 17, 18.) B incorrect IP is network-layer best effort (PDF 18, 17, 18.) C incorrect FTP is application file transfer (PDF 18, 17, 18.) D correct TCP is the explicitly reliable transport protocol (PDF 18, 17, 18.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 192 · AM0496
records.text: AM0496 Question 192 NET30 NET12 NET17 Which layer of the OSI reference model is responsible for addressing and routing data packets across different networks? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Network layer B Data Link layer C Transport layer D Physical layer Network layer Network explicitly adds logical addressing and routes packets from source to destination across intermediate devices. Evidence: PDF 15, 15, 16, 14. A correct Network has addressing and routing responsibilities (PDF 15, 15, 16, 14.) B incorrect Data link handles physical addresses and one-hop frames (PDF 15, 15, 16, 14.) C incorrect Transport delivers to processes with ports (PDF 15, 15, 16, 14.) D incorrect Physical delivers bits/signals (PDF 15, 15, 16, 14.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 193 · AM0497
records.text: AM0497 Question 193 NET14 NET13 NET16 Which OSI layer supplies hop-local frame acknowledgments and retransmission when a reliable-link protocol is used, rather than end-to-end transport recovery? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Network layer B Transport layer C Data Link layer D Application layer Data Link layer Reliable data-link protocols can acknowledge frames and retransmit missing or damaged frames across a single hop. Transport recovery instead covers the end-to-end communication between processes. Network-layer IPv4 includes a header checksum but remains best-effort and does not supply this frame ARQ service. The link-layer role is protocol-dependent: Ethernet error detection alone does not guarantee reliable local delivery. A incorrect IP routing and its header checksum are not the requested hop-local frame ARQ service. B incorrect Transport reliability has end-to-end rather than one-link scope. C correct Data link implements the specified hop-local frame acknowledgment/retransmission procedure. D incorrect Application services are above the specified link-frame recovery mechanism.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 194 · AM0498
records.text: AM0498 Question 194 NET21 NET20 Which protocol submits and relays email messages, including acceptance by a receiving mail server? Select one. Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A SMTP B FTP C HTTP D DNS SMTP SMTP is used for mail submission and relay, including a mail server accepting an incoming message. End-user access to stored mail is a separate operation supplied by POP3 or IMAP. HTTP handles web exchanges, FTP transfers files, and DNS resolves records. Specifying server receipt and relay makes the mail-system role clear without assigning mailbox retrieval to the transfer protocol. A correct SMTP submits and relays mail, including server acceptance of incoming messages. B incorrect FTP transfers files through a separate protocol rather than the mail flow defined here. C incorrect HTTP defines web request/response exchanges rather than the mail submission and relay protocol requested. D incorrect DNS supplies records such as mail-exchanger names rather than delivering or retrieving message contents.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 195 · AM0499
records.text: AM0499 Question 195 NET19 NET09 Which layer of the OSI reference model is responsible for converting data into a format suitable for transmission over a network? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Presentation layer B Session layer C Physical layer D Application layer Presentation layer for representation/format translation The word format identifies representation translation rather than routing or connection management. NET19 assigns encoding translation and other representation work to presentation. Physical signaling maps bits to medium symbols, but does not supply the application-data format translation asked for. Thus A matches the intended formatting responsibility. A correct Presentation translates representations/encodings into suitable data formats. B incorrect Session manages dialogs and checkpoints rather than data representation formats. C incorrect Physical maps bits/symbols to signals, a different responsibility from representation-format translation. D incorrect Application supplies network services to applications rather than the distinct presentation-format function.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 196 · AM0500
records.text: AM0500 Question 196 NET20 NET21 Which protocol is used for translating domain names into IP addresses? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. D incorrect SMTP is mail transfer (PDF 18, 65.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 197 · AM0501
records.text: AM0501 Question 197 NET19 NET18 Which layer of the OSI reference model is responsible for establishing and terminating sessions between applications? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. Evidence: PDF 16, 16, 16, 16. A incorrect Presentation performs representation translation (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) B correct Session establishes and synchronizes dialogs (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) C incorrect Transport connection setup is a different scope from the stated application sessions (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 198 · AM0502
records.text: AM0502 Question 198 NET21 NET17 A file-transfer client uses one connection for protocol commands and a separate connection for file data. Which listed application protocol uses this control/data separation? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A SMTP B HTTP C FTP D TCP FTP FTP separates its control conversation from the data connection used for transfers. That architectural feature distinguishes it from the broad ability to download files, which HTTP also provides. SMTP handles mail submission and relay. TCP is the transport service on which an application protocol can build connections; it does not itself define FTP commands or the application’s separate control and data roles. A incorrect SMTP defines mail transfer, not the described FTP control/data arrangement. B incorrect HTTP can transfer files, but does not define the described separate FTP control and data connections. C correct FTP uses separate control and data connections. D incorrect TCP provides transport connections; the application protocol defines their command/data roles.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 199 · AM0503
records.text: AM0503 Question 199 NET19 NET17 Which layer of the OSI reference model is responsible for providing services directly to the end-user applications? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Presentation layer B Session layer C Transport layer D Application layer Application layer Application explicitly provides user access to network resources; the other layers perform representation, dialog and process-delivery work. Evidence: PDF 16, 16, 16, 16. A incorrect Presentation translates/encrypts/compresses (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) B incorrect Session establishes and synchronizes dialogs (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) C incorrect Transport segments and delivers between processes (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.) D correct Application explicitly exposes network resources to users (PDF 16, 16, 16, 16.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 200 · AM0504
records.text: AM0504 Question 200 NET22 NET24 Which subnet mask represents a Class C network? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 255.0.0.0 B 255.255.0.0 C 255.255.255.0 D 255.255.255.255 255.255.255.0, the historical Class C default In the classful convention requested, Class C has a /24 default. Twenty-four leading one bits give three full 255 octets followed by zero: 255.255.255.0. This is a historical default rather than a restriction that every modern address in that range must use /24; CIDR can specify another prefix. A incorrect 255.0.0.0 is /8, the historical Class A default rather than Class C. B incorrect 255.255.0.0 is /16, the historical Class B default. C correct 255.255.255.0 is /24, matching the historical Class C default prefix. D incorrect 255.255.255.255 is /32, identifying one address rather than the Class C default network.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 201 · AM0505
records.text: AM0505 Question 201 NET25 NET24 What is the maximum number of hosts in a subnet with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.224? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 8 B 16 C 30 D 62 30 usable hosts The mask 255.255.255.224 has 27 one bits and five host bits. Five bits yield 32 total addresses; reserving the subnet identifier and directed broadcast leaves 30 assignable ordinary hosts. This is an ordinary broadcast-subnet calculation, so the special /31 point-to-point exception is not relevant. A incorrect Eight does not equal the usable count from five host bits and two reserved addresses. B incorrect Sixteen is not the /27 usable-host count; this block has 32 total addresses. C correct A /27 has 32 total addresses and 30 ordinary assignable host addresses. D incorrect Sixty-two usable hosts requires six host bits, corresponding to /26 rather than /27.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 202 · AM0506
records.text: AM0506 Question 202 NET23 Which IP address belongs to the loopback network? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 127.0.0.1 B 192.168.0.1 C 10.0.0.1 D 172.16.0.1 127.0.0.1 The module explicitly identifies 127.0.0.1 as localhost for interprocess communication. This supports the loopback instance, without needing an unprovided full 127/8 range rule. Evidence: PDF 65, 19. A correct 127.0.0.1 is explicitly localhost (PDF 65, 19.) B incorrect 192.168.0.1 is not the cited localhost address (PDF 65, 19.) C incorrect 10.0.0.1 is not the cited localhost address (PDF 65, 19.) D incorrect 172.16.0.1 is not the cited localhost address (PDF 65, 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 203 · AM0507
records.text: AM0507 Question 203 NET26 NET22 NET24 How many subnets can be created from a Class B network with a subnet mask of 255.255.240.0? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 8 B 16 C 32 D 64 16 subnets The question explicitly supplies a Class B parent, so use its historical /16. The given mask 255.255.240.0 is /20. Borrowing 20−16=4 bits yields 2^4=16 equal subnets under modern practice. The note says not to subtract two subnets; host capacity is a different calculation. A incorrect Eight subnets would borrow three bits and produce /19 from a /16 parent. B correct The /20 mask borrows four bits from /16, yielding sixteen equal subnets. C incorrect Thirty-two subnets would borrow five bits and require /21 from the Class B parent. D incorrect Sixty-four subnets would borrow six bits and require /22 rather than /20.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 204 · AM0508
records.text: AM0508 Question 204 NET22 NET24 What is the default subnet mask for a Class A network? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 255.0.0.0 B 255.255.0.0 C 255.255.255.0 D 255.255.255.255 255.0.0.0 The historical Class A default is /8. Eight leading mask ones fill only the first octet, giving 255.0.0.0. The other choices correspond to /16, /24 and /32; they can be explicit CIDR prefixes, but they are not the historical default asked for. A correct 255.0.0.0 contains eight leading ones and is the historical Class A default. B incorrect 255.255.0.0 is /16, the historical default for Class B. C incorrect 255.255.255.0 is /24, the historical default for Class C. D incorrect 255.255.255.255 is /32 and describes one address, not the Class A default.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 205 · AM0509
records.text: AM0509 Question 205 NET28 NET24 For a conventional IPv4 link needing two usable endpoints and reserving network/broadcast addresses, which offered mask allocates the smallest sufficient block? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 255.255.255.0 B 255.255.255.128 C 255.255.255.192 D 255.255.255.252 255.255.255.252 The offered masks correspond to /24, /25, /26 and /30 blocks. A conventional /30 contains four addresses, leaving two usable endpoints after reserving network and broadcast addresses. The other choices allocate more addresses than this link needs. Supported /31 point-to-point links are a separate exception, so the question limits the comparison to the conventional model and the masks actually offered. A incorrect /24 is sufficient but allocates 256 addresses, more than the smallest offered sufficient block. B incorrect /25 allocates 128 addresses and is not the smallest sufficient offered block. C incorrect /26 allocates 64 addresses and is not the smallest sufficient offered block. D correct /30 allocates four addresses and two conventional usable endpoints, the smallest sufficient offered block.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 206 · AM0510
records.text: AM0510 Question 206 NET24 NET25 How many bits are in the host portion of an IPv4 address with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.192? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 6 B 8 C 10 D 14 6 192=11000000 leaves six zero mask bits; the full mask is /26. Hence 32-26=6 host bits. Evidence: PDF 18, 19, 19. A correct Six is the calculated count (PDF 18, 19, 19.) B incorrect Eight would correspond to /24 (PDF 18, 19, 19.) C incorrect Ten would correspond to /22 (PDF 18, 19, 19.) D incorrect Fourteen would correspond to /18 (PDF 18, 19, 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 207 · AM0511
records.text: AM0511 Question 207 NET24 NET25 What is the network address for the IP address 192.168.10.25/28? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 192.168.10.0 B 192.168.10.16 C 192.168.10.24 D 192.168.10.25 192.168.10.16 /28 mask last octet is 240. 25=00011001 AND 240=11110000 gives 16=00010000. Therefore network address is 192.168.10.16. Evidence: PDF 18, 19, 19. A incorrect 0 is the preceding /28 block (PDF 18, 19, 19.) B correct 16 is the correct masked boundary (PDF 18, 19, 19.) C incorrect 24 retains host bits and is not a 16-step boundary (PDF 18, 19, 19.) D incorrect 25 is the given host address, not the masked network (PDF 18, 19, 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 208 · AM0512
records.text: AM0512 Question 208 NET25 NET24 How many usable host addresses are available in a subnet with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.224? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 6 B 14 C 30 D 62 30 usable host addresses 224 in the final mask octet is 11100000. That yields /27 and h=5. Computing 2^5−2 gives 30 ordinary usable host addresses after network and directed-broadcast reservations. The distractors correspond to different host-bit counts; none changes the explicit mask in this question. A incorrect Six usable hosts would use three host bits, normally /29 rather than /27. B incorrect Fourteen usable hosts would use four host bits, normally /28. C correct Five host bits give 32 addresses minus two reservations, yielding 30 usable hosts. D incorrect Sixty-two usable hosts would use six host bits and a /26 mask.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 209 · AM0513
records.text: AM0513 Question 209 NET23 NET20 Which address category is defined for internal reuse by RFC1918 rather than global public routing? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A Public IP address B Private IP address C Reserved IP address D Dynamic IP address Private IP address RFC1918 defines private blocks that organizations can reuse internally and that are not globally routed as public destinations. Public addresses can also be used on a LAN when legitimately assigned, so local communication alone would not distinguish the categories. Dynamic describes an assignment method such as a DHCP lease, not an address scope. The revised scope identifies the category by its defined allocation purpose. A incorrect Public addresses are globally allocated unicast space rather than RFC1918 internal-reuse space. B correct Private addresses are the RFC1918 blocks defined for internal reuse. C incorrect Reserved addresses have specific purposes and are not a generic ordinary-LAN host address category. D incorrect Dynamic describes how an address is assigned, not whether it belongs to RFC1918 space.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 210 · AM0514
records.text: AM0514 Question 210 NET22 Which of the following is not a valid IP address? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 192.168.0.1 B 10.0.0.256 C 172.16.0.0 D 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.256 Each IPv4 decimal octet must be 0-255. 10.0.0.256 violates that constraint; the other strings are syntactically valid IPv4 values regardless of host-assignability restrictions. Evidence: PDF 19. A incorrect All four octets satisfy the syntax rule (PDF 19.) B correct 256 exceeds the eight-bit maximum (PDF 19.) C incorrect All octets are syntactically valid; a network-address role is a separate issue (PDF 19.) D incorrect All octets are syntactically valid; use as a mask does not make the bit string invalid (PDF 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 211 · AM0515
records.text: AM0515 Question 211 NET22 NET24 What is the default subnet mask for a Class B IP address? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 255.0.0.0 B 255.255.0.0 C 255.255.255.0 D 255.255.255.255 255.255.0.0 NET22 gives historical Class B a /16 default. The first sixteen mask bits are ones, producing 255.255.0.0. This answers the requested default-mask question; it does not imply that a modern Class B-range address cannot have a different explicit CIDR prefix. A incorrect 255.0.0.0 is /8, the historical default for Class A. B correct 255.255.0.0 has sixteen leading ones and is the historical Class B default. C incorrect 255.255.255.0 is /24, the historical default for Class C. D incorrect 255.255.255.255 is /32, a single-address prefix rather than a Class B default.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 212 · AM0516
records.text: AM0516 Question 212 NET24 NET25 How many bits are used for the host portion of an IP address with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 8 bits B 16 bits C 24 bits D 32 bits 8 bits 255.255.255.0 contains 24 one bits and eight zero host bits. Subtract the 24-bit prefix from the 32-bit address width. Evidence: PDF 18, 19, 19. A correct Eight is 32-24 (PDF 18, 19, 19.) B incorrect Sixteen would require a /16 prefix (PDF 18, 19, 19.) C incorrect Twenty-four is the prefix count, not the host count (PDF 18, 19, 19.) D incorrect Thirty-two is the entire address width (PDF 18, 19, 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 213 · AM0517
records.text: AM0517 Question 213 NET25 NET24 Given a subnet mask of 255.255.255.224, how many host addresses are available in each subnet? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 6 B 14 C 30 D 62 30 host addresses per ordinary subnet The mask 255.255.255.224 is /27, leaving five host bits. A block therefore contains 32 addresses. Because the question asks addresses available to hosts, exclude its network and broadcast addresses, leaving 30. Treating all 32 as usable would confuse block size with conventional broadcast-LAN host capacity. A incorrect Six usable addresses corresponds to /29, not the stated /27 mask. B incorrect Fourteen usable addresses corresponds to /28 and four host bits. C correct The /27 block has five host bits and 32−2=30 conventional usable addresses. D incorrect Sixty-two usable addresses would require /26 and six host bits.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 214 · AM0518
records.text: AM0518 Question 214 NET24 NET25 What is the network address for the IP address 192.168.1.65/26? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 192.168.1.0 B 192.168.1.64 C 192.168.1.65 D 192.168.1.128 192.168.1.64 /26 makes the fourth-octet mask192=11000000. 65=01000001 AND192=11000000 gives64=01000000, so the network is 192.168.1.64. Evidence: PDF 18, 19, 19. A incorrect 0 is the preceding 64-address block (PDF 18, 19, 19.) B correct 64 is the masked network boundary (PDF 18, 19, 19.) C incorrect 65 retains the nonzero host bit (PDF 18, 19, 19.) D incorrect 128 is the next block boundary (PDF 18, 19, 19.)

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 215 · AM0519
records.text: AM0519 Question 215 NET26 NET22 How many subnets can be created from a Class C network with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.192? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 2 B 4 C 8 D 16 4 subnets A historical Class C parent is /24. The supplied 255.255.255.192 mask is /26, borrowing two bits. Modern counting gives 2^2=4 equal subnets, not two: NET26 explicitly rejects subtracting two subnets under modern practice. Here the parent is given, unlike the under-specified standalone-prefix questions. A incorrect Two would incorrectly exclude two subnets under an obsolete unstated convention; modern counting gives four. B correct Borrowing two bits from /24 to /26 produces four equal subnets. C incorrect Eight subnets requires borrowing three bits, producing /27 rather than /26. D incorrect Sixteen subnets requires four borrowed bits and a /28 prefix.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 216 · AM0520
records.text: AM0520 Question 216 NET25 NET24 What is the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to hosts in a subnet with a /27 subnet mask? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 14 B 30 C 62 D 126 30 assignable host IP addresses With /27, 32−27=5 host bits produce 2^5=32 addresses. For an ordinary subnet, network and broadcast are reserved, so 30 can be assigned to hosts. The alternative values are usable-host counts for /28, /26 and /25, rather than the supplied /27. A incorrect Fourteen usable hosts requires /28, leaving only four host bits. B correct A /27 leaves five host bits and therefore 30 assignable ordinary host addresses. C incorrect Sixty-two usable hosts is the /26 result, not /27. D incorrect 126 usable hosts requires /25 and seven host bits.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 217 · AM0521
records.text: AM0521 Question 217 NET23 Which IP address range is reserved for Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA)? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 B 127.0.0.0 - 127.255.255.255 C 169.254.0.0 - 169.254.255.255 D 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 169.254.0.0/16 link-local/APIPA range NET23 assigns link-local/APIPA to 169.254.0.0/16, the range printed in C. That identifies the reserved overall block; the first and last /24 blocks are excluded from normal automatic selection. The private RFC1918 blocks and loopback block offered elsewhere have different purposes and are not the APIPA range. A incorrect 10/8 is RFC1918 private space, not the link-local/APIPA allocation. B incorrect 127/8 is loopback for local protocol access, not automatic link-local addressing. C correct 169.254/16 is the APIPA block; normal automatic host selection excludes its edge /24 blocks. D incorrect 192.168/16 is RFC1918 private space rather than the APIPA block.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 218 · AM0523
records.text: AM0523 Question 218 NET20 NET21 Which of the following protocols is responsible for assigning IP addresses to hosts dynamically? Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A DNS B DHCP C HTTP D FTP DHCP DHCP is the address-configuration service in NET20, dynamically leasing an address together with other settings. DNS resolves names rather than assigning a client’s host address. HTTP and FTP handle web exchanges and file transfers. Therefore B matches dynamic assignment rather than name resolution or application-data transfer. A incorrect DNS resolves names to records and does not perform the dynamic lease assignment asked about. B correct DHCP dynamically leases host addresses and related network configuration. C incorrect HTTP provides web request/response exchanges rather than dynamic IP-address allocation. D incorrect FTP transfers files and is not a host-address lease protocol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 219 · CS0155
records.text: CS0155 Question 219 NET17 NET16 NET03 Which TCP/IP-suite protocols listed below are connectionless? Select all that apply. Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A User Datagram Protocol (UDP) B Internet Protocol C Transmission Control Protocol D The OSI reference protocol User Datagram Protocol (UDP); Internet Protocol UDP sends independent datagrams without built-in connection setup, ordering or retransmission. IP likewise provides connectionless best-effort packet delivery at the network layer. TCP instead establishes transport connection state and supplies a reliable ordered stream. OSI is a reference model rather than a protocol in the TCP/IP suite. The multiple-selection instruction therefore permits both connectionless protocols across the two layers. A correct UDP has no built-in connection setup and treats datagrams independently. B correct IP also supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery at the network layer. C incorrect TCP establishes logical transport connection state before its reliable stream transfer. D incorrect OSI is a reference model, not a connectionless TCP/IP-suite protocol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 220 · CS0156
records.text: CS0156 Question 220 NET23 NET16 Which statements describe capabilities or properties of IPv6? Select all that apply. Encryption support in D means capability, not automatic confidentiality or exclusivity to IPv6. Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A Handle more addresses B Use 128-bits C Route slower and is memory intensive D Support encryptions Handle more addresses; Use 128-bits; Support encryptions IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, giving it a much larger address space than IPv4’s 32-bit addresses. It can support encryption, but that capability does not mean every IPv6 packet is encrypted or that IPv4 cannot support encryption. Routing speed and memory requirements depend on implementation and workload; they are not inherently fixed by the protocol version. Thus the three capability/property statements qualify. A correct A 128-bit address space can represent far more addresses than IPv4’s 32-bit space. B correct NET23 explicitly states that IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits. C incorrect Slower routing and greater memory use are not inherent requirements of every IPv6 implementation. D correct Encryption is supported, but IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic and this is not unique to IPv6.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 221 · CS0157
records.text: CS0157 Question 221 NET23 Which one does NOT describe a loopback address? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A It helps to refer to the host itself B It allows programs to access network protocols for local services C It is an external pseudo address D It is denoted by the IP address: 127.0.0.1 Loopback is local self-reference, not an external address Loopback lets a host address itself and access local services through networking protocols without an external link. NET23 identifies 127/8 and common 127.0.0.1 for that purpose. Describing it as external contradicts this local scope, whereas the remaining choices all describe supported loopback uses or notation. A incorrect Referring to the host itself is precisely the loopback function, so this statement does describe it. B incorrect Local programs can use networking protocols to access local services through loopback. C correct External contradicts loopback’s local self-reference without an external network link. D incorrect 127.0.0.1 is explicitly given as the common IPv4 loopback address.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 222 · CS0164
records.text: CS0164 Question 222 NET05 NET06 In data communication, which of the following is NOT a factor for data rate? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A Travel distance B Bandwidth available C Level of noise D Levels of the signals Travel distance is not explicit in the simplified capacity formulas In the simplified capacity comparison taught in NET05, Nyquist uses bandwidth and signal levels, while Shannon uses bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. Travel distance is not a separate formula parameter, making A the intended choice. The qualification matters: distance can affect attenuation, delay and real achievable rates, so the answer is not physical independence from distance. A correct Travel distance is absent as an independent variable in the taught formulas, despite indirect real-link effects. B incorrect Bandwidth appears directly in both Nyquist and Shannon expressions and limits channel capacity. C incorrect Noise enters Shannon capacity through the signal-to-noise ratio. D incorrect Signal levels enter Nyquist capacity through the number of bits represented per symbol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 223 · NS0334
records.text: NS0334 Question 223 NET12 Which of the following OSI layers is NOT correctly matched to its corresponding data Units (PDU)? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Application layer ---> Data B Transport layer ---> Segment C Physical layer ---> Bit D Network layer ---> Frame Network-layer PDU is packet, not frame The PDUs are: application data, transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits. D assigns the link-layer frame to the network layer, making it the mismatch. Transport segment is appropriate for TCP, so B remains a valid conventional example rather than a claim about every transport protocol. A incorrect Application data is the conventional PDU designation, so this match is valid. B incorrect TCP uses transport segments; this is a valid conventional transport PDU example. C incorrect Bits/symbols belong to physical transport, making this match valid. D correct A frame is link-layer; the network-layer unit is a packet.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 224 · NS0341
records.text: NS0341 Question 224 NET19 NET12 Which of the following layers is responsible for encryption, translation and compression? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Presentation layer B Data link layer C Transport layer D Network layer Presentation layer The three listed operations are representation functions: encoding translation, compression and encryption. NET19 groups them under the OSI presentation role. Link handles frames, transport process delivery and network logical routing; none is the named OSI representation layer. Real implementations may distribute these functions, but the reference-model answer is presentation. A correct Presentation explicitly covers encoding translation, compression and encryption roles. B incorrect Data link handles hop frames/access rather than the OSI representation-function grouping. C incorrect Transport delivers between process endpoints, not the named presentation representation roles. D incorrect Network handles logical addressing/routing rather than compression/encoding translation.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 225 · NS0352
records.text: NS0352 Question 225 NET22 Assume that you have IPv4 addresses in binary notation 11000001 10000011 00011011 11111111 and you are requested to change into dotted decimal notation. What is the equivalent IP address in decimal dotted notation? Sum the eight bit weights in each octet independently, then preserve their order in dotted-decimal notation. A 192.174.27.255 B 192.134.67.254 C 193.130.28.254 D 193.131.27.255 193.131.27.255 Using octet weights 128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1 gives 11000001=193, 10000011=131, 00011011=27 and 11111111=255. Combining the four decimal octets gives 193.131.27.255. This is a notation conversion, not a claim about whether that address is assignable as a host under an unspecified prefix. A incorrect The first octet should be 193 and the second 131, not 192 and 174. B incorrect All four printed octets differ from the binary-derived values 193,131,27,255. C incorrect Only the first octet matches; the correct remaining values are 131,27,255. D correct Each decimal octet matches its eight-bit sum: 193, 131, 27 and 255.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 226 · NS0573
records.text: NS0573 Question 226 NET02 A company has 500 computers distributed across 10 floors of a single building. Which network type BEST describes this setup? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A WAN B MAN C LAN D Internet LAN All computers are in one building, the geographic scope of a LAN in NET02. The count of 500 devices or ten floors does not itself make a MAN/WAN; the note explicitly separates device count from geographic category. No metropolitan or distant-region interconnection is supplied. A incorrect WAN concerns distant regions, not simply many devices on floors of one building. B incorrect MAN requires metropolitan scope rather than a single-building deployment. C correct A single building falls within the LAN scope defined by NET02. D incorrect The Internet is the global network of networks, not the building network described.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 227 · NS0574
records.text: NS0574 Question 227 NET13 NET17 NET16 In which OSI layer does the MAC address operate? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Network Layer (Layer 3) B Physical Layer (Layer 1) C Data Link Layer (Layer 2) D Transport Layer (Layer 4) Data link, layer 2 MAC addressing identifies link-layer frame endpoints and forwarding scope. NET13 assigns medium-dependent addressing/access to MAC in the data-link layer. Physical transports signals, network uses logical IP prefixes and transport identifies process endpoints by ports. The word physical in physical address must not be confused with a layer-1 functional assignment. A incorrect Network-layer addressing uses logical IP addresses rather than the link MAC address. B incorrect Physical transports signals; the conventional physical-address nickname does not move MAC addressing to layer 1. C correct MAC addressing and frame delivery are data-link functions at layer 2. D incorrect Transport identifies process endpoints by ports rather than MAC frame addresses.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 228 · NS0575
records.text: NS0575 Question 228 NET06 NET05 Which of the following correctly describes attenuation in data transmission? Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A The delay caused by different frequencies traveling at different speeds B The loss of signal strength as it travels over a distance C Interference from adjacent communication channels D The maximum data rate of a transmission medium Loss of signal strength NET06 defines attenuation as reduced signal strength. Different delays among frequency components describe distortion, adjacent-channel leakage describes crosstalk and maximum rate concerns capacity. B gives the strength-loss mechanism rather than those separate impairments or performance measures. A incorrect Different component delays change waveform shape, describing distortion rather than attenuation. B correct A reduction in signal strength during propagation is attenuation. C incorrect Adjacent-channel interference is crosstalk, a separate noise source. D incorrect Maximum data rate is channel capacity, not signal-strength loss.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 229 · NS0576
records.text: NS0576 Question 229 NET26 A network administrator wants to divide the Class C network 192.168.10.0 into 6 subnets. What is the minimum number of bits that must be borrowed from the host portion? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 2 bits B 3 bits C 4 bits D 6 bits Borrow 3 bits to obtain at least six equal subnets For equal-sized subnets of a /24 parent, borrowing b bits yields 2^b blocks. Two bits give only four; three give eight, the minimum power-of-two count that accommodates six required subnets. The resulting mask is /27 with 30 conventional hosts per block. Exactly six equal blocks would not fill the parent; two blocks remain unused. A incorrect Two borrowed bits yield only four blocks, fewer than the six required. B correct Three borrowed bits yield eight blocks and are the minimum satisfying at least six. C incorrect Four bits yield sixteen blocks and are not the minimum required. D incorrect Six bits yield sixty-four blocks, substantially more than the minimum.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 230 · NS0577
records.text: NS0577 Question 230 NET08 Which topology provides the HIGHEST level of redundancy? Draw the links and identify shared components, alternate paths and the effect of the specified failure or growth requirement. A Star B Ring C Bus D Mesh Full mesh among the conventional topology choices A full mesh connects every pair of nodes, offering multiple alternate paths compared with the basic star, single ring and shared bus. NET08 explains the additional links/interfaces and improved fault tolerance. D assumes the conventional full-mesh interpretation; actual protected rings or partial mesh designs would require more detail for a quantitative comparison. A incorrect A basic star depends on its central device and lacks the full mesh’s many alternate paths. B incorrect A basic single ring is vulnerable to a break, unlike a full mesh’s multiple paths. C incorrect A shared bus depends on one backbone rather than redundant pairwise paths. D correct A full mesh supplies pairwise links and multiple alternate paths, at increased cable/interface cost.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 231 · NS0578
records.text: NS0578 Question 231 NET24 NET25 What is the broadcast address of the network 192.168.17.0/24? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A 192.168.17.0 B 192.168.17.254 C 192.168.17.255 D 192.168.16.255 192.168.17.255 A /24 prefix fixes the first three octets and leaves eight host bits. Setting them all to one gives final octet 255, so the broadcast is 192.168.17.255. The .0 address is the network boundary and .254 is the last ordinary host; 192.168.16.255 belongs outside the specified /24. A incorrect 192.168.17.0 has all host bits zero and identifies the network, not broadcast. B incorrect 192.168.17.254 is the last ordinary host, one below broadcast. C correct The final eight host bits are all one, giving the /24 broadcast .255. D incorrect The third octet 16 lies outside network 192.168.17.0/24.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 232 · NS0579
records.text: NS0579 Question 232 NET11 NET10 NET09 Which device operates at Layer 3 of the OSI model and uses IP addresses to forward data? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Hub B Bridge C Switch D Router Router IP destination-prefix forwarding between networks is the router function in NET11. Hubs repeat signals and bridges/ordinary switches forward MAC frames at layer 2. Some marketed switches include routing, but the unqualified ordinary switch function in this option set is layer 2; router is the explicit matching device. A incorrect A hub repeats layer-1 signals rather than forwarding on IP prefixes. B incorrect A bridge makes layer-2 frame-forwarding decisions using MAC addresses. C incorrect An ordinary switch is layer 2; a specifically layer-3 switch would require the missing routing qualifier. D correct Routers inspect destination IP prefixes and choose next hops at layer 3.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 233 · NS0580
records.text: NS0580 Question 233 NET17 NET06 UDP is described as a 'connectionless protocol' because it: Identify the requested service or delivery guarantee, then distinguish application roles, transport behavior and address configuration. A Cannot transmit video data B Does not establish a dedicated connection before sending data and provides no delivery guarantee C Only transmits in simplex mode D Operates exclusively at the Network Layer No setup and no built-in delivery guarantee UDP’s connectionlessness means independent datagrams without built-in setup, not an inability to carry video or an enforced physical duplex mode. It is a transport protocol. B correctly combines no connection establishment with absence of built-in reliable delivery; applications may add their own recovery mechanisms. A incorrect UDP can carry live media; connectionlessness does not forbid video data. B correct UDP sends independent datagrams without setup or built-in delivery guarantees. C incorrect UDP does not impose simplex physical transmission; transport service and physical duplex mode are distinct. D incorrect UDP is transport-layer, not exclusively a network-layer protocol.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 234 · NS0581
records.text: NS0581 Question 234 NET22 NET25 Assume historical classful addressing and an ordinary broadcast network. A host has address 185.28.17.9. How many usable host addresses are in its default classful network? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 254 B 65,534 C 16,777,214 D 65,536 65,534 The first octet 185 lies in the historical Class B range, whose default prefix is /16. That leaves sixteen host bits, yielding 2^16 = 65,536 total addresses. Reserving the network and directed-broadcast addresses gives 65,534 usable hosts. The explicit classful assumption permits deriving the default prefix; modern CIDR would require a stated prefix instead of inferring it from the address. A incorrect 254 is the usable count for /24, not the Class B default /16. B correct Class B defaults to /16, giving 2^16−2 = 65,534 usable hosts. C incorrect 16,777,214 belongs to /8 rather than the Class B default. D incorrect 65,536 is the /16 total before network and broadcast reservations.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 235 · NS0582
records.text: NS0582 Question 235 NET06 NET08 Which transmission mode allows simultaneous bidirectional communication? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A Simplex B Half-Duplex C Full-Duplex D Multipoint Full duplex The decisive condition is simultaneous communication in both directions. NET06 defines full duplex exactly that way. Half duplex permits both directions at different times and simplex only one. Multipoint describes sharing a medium among endpoints, not whether two endpoints can send and receive at the same instant. A incorrect Simplex permits communication in one direction only. B incorrect Half duplex alternates directions and does not permit simultaneous transmission both ways. C correct Full duplex supports sending and receiving simultaneously. D incorrect Multipoint describes medium sharing among endpoints rather than a bidirectional timing mode.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 236 · NS0583
records.text: NS0583 Question 236 NET19 NET30 NET12 The OSI Presentation Layer is primarily responsible for: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Routing packets between networks B Establishing and ending communication sessions C Data compression, encryption, and format translation D Physical transmission of raw bits Compression, encryption and representation translation NET19 assigns these three representation functions to the OSI presentation layer. Routing belongs to network, dialogs to session and raw bit signaling to physical. Real software can combine roles, but within the stated OSI model C is the specific matching responsibility set. A incorrect Routing between networks is the network-layer responsibility. B incorrect Session setup/ending belongs to the session role rather than presentation representation handling. C correct Compression, encryption and format translation are the presentation roles explicitly listed in NET19. D incorrect Physical signaling transports bits/symbols rather than translating data representations.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 237 · NS0584
records.text: NS0584 Question 237 NET07 Which statements are not valid universal guarantees for fiber-optic cable? Select all that apply. Interpret B as a capability with suitable optics and installation, and D as a claim of automatic security. Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A Immunity to electromagnetic interference B High bandwidth and long transmission distance C Lower initial cost than copper cables D High data security due to difficulty of tapping Lower initial cost than copper cables; High data security due to difficulty of tapping Fiber guides light, resists electromagnetic interference and can support high capacity over long distances when suitable optics and installation are used. Material alone does not determine a universal installed-cost advantage over copper. Nor does physical tapping difficulty automatically ensure data security: fiber can still be tapped. The selected statements are therefore the unsupported universal guarantees about cost and security, rather than the supported transmission capabilities.
