A incorrect EMI resistance follows from light-guided transmission, so this is not a rejected guarantee under the stated scope. B incorrect With suitable optics and installation, high capacity and long reach are supported capabilities, so this is not selected. C correct Initial cost depends on optics, reach and installation; lower cost than copper is not universal. D correct Fiber can be tapped, so automatic high security does not follow from the medium.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 238 · NS0585
records.text: NS0585 Question 238 NET02 Which option best defines a dedicated server by its primary workload? Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A A server that also acts as a client B A machine whose primary workload is supplying services, even though it may use DNS, backup or update services as a client. C A server that handles only file storage D Any computer in a peer-to-peer network A machine whose primary workload is supplying services, even though it may use DNS, backup or update services as a client. A dedicated server concentrates on supplying services, rather than requiring an absolute prohibition on making any client requests. It may still request DNS resolution, backups or software updates. Merely acting as a client does not define dedication, and dedicated workloads are not limited to file storage. The choice identifies the defining workload while allowing ordinary supporting client activity. A incorrect A dedicated server may act as a DNS/backup client, but that incidental capability is not its defining dedicated workload. B correct Concentration on service workloads is the defining dedicated-server characteristic. C incorrect Dedicated service workloads need not be limited to file storage. D incorrect An arbitrary peer computer is not thereby a dedicated service-workload server.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 239 · NS0586
records.text: NS0586 Question 239 NET20 NET21 Which protocol operates at the Application Layer of the TCP/IP model and is responsible for translating domain names to IP addresses? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A SMTP B FTP C HTTP D DNS DNS DNS is the name-resolution application protocol in NET20. A/AAAA records provide address data for names. SMTP submits/relays mail, FTP transfers files and HTTP serves web requests; none provides the requested general domain-name record service. Its lookup role is separate from DHCP address assignment. A incorrect SMTP submits and relays mail rather than resolving hostnames to addresses. B incorrect FTP transfers files and does not supply the name-resolution record service. C incorrect HTTP defines web exchanges, not the general hostname-to-address service. D correct DNS resolves names into records such as A and AAAA address records.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 240 · NS0587
records.text: NS0587 Question 240 NET06 Crosstalk is best described as: Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A Loss of signal strength over distance B Signals from one communication channel leaking into an adjacent channel C Random electron motion causing electrical noise D Delay caused by varying signal frequencies Leakage from an adjacent communication channel Crosstalk is unwanted coupling from a neighboring communication channel, directly matching B. Strength loss is attenuation, random thermal motion creates thermal noise and differential frequency delay produces distortion. These impairments can coexist but their definitions are distinct, so the question’s mechanism identifies crosstalk specifically. A incorrect Signal-strength loss is attenuation rather than coupling from a neighboring channel. B correct Signals leaking into an adjacent channel are crosstalk. C incorrect Random electron/thermal motion describes thermal noise. D incorrect Different component-frequency delays distort waveform shape rather than defining crosstalk.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 241 · NS0588
records.text: NS0588 Question 241 NET25 How many usable host addresses are available in the subnet 192.168.2.64/26? Convert the mask to a prefix, separate network and host bits, and apply the relevant subnet-count or usable-host rule. A 32 B 64 C 62 D 30 62 usable hosts A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block has 64 addresses. In the specified block, .64 is the network and .127 the broadcast; usable hosts span .65–.126 inclusive, totaling 62. The question asks usable hosts, not block size, and /31 point-to-point exceptions do not apply. A incorrect Thirty-two is not the usable count of this /26 block; /26 has 64 total addresses. B incorrect Sixty-four is the total block size before network/broadcast reservations. C correct Six host bits give 64 total addresses minus two reservations, leaving 62 usable hosts. D incorrect Thirty usable hosts is the /27 result, not /26.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 242 · NS0589
records.text: NS0589 Question 242 NET19 NET18 Which OSI layer is responsible for establishing, maintaining, and ending communication sessions? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Transport Layer B Session Layer C Application Layer D Presentation Layer Session layer The stem explicitly specifies communication sessions, matching the OSI session role rather than merely a TCP connection. NET19 assigns dialog management and checkpoints to that layer. Transport serves process endpoints, application supplies services and presentation handles representations. B is therefore the specific reference-model lifecycle role. A incorrect Transport connection state is distinct from the explicitly named OSI session/dialog lifecycle. B correct Session manages dialogs and their setup, maintenance and recovery/end lifecycle. C incorrect Application supplies user/application network services rather than the distinct session-layer lifecycle. D incorrect Presentation translates/compresses/encrypts representations instead of managing dialogs.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 243 · NS0590
records.text: NS0590 Question 243 NET08 A bus topology network has 20 nodes. If the main cable breaks, what happens? Draw the links and identify shared components, alternate paths and the effect of the specified failure or growth requirement. A Only the two nodes nearest the break are affected B The network continues to function normally C The entire network goes down D Only the node that caused the break is disconnected A main-backbone break can disrupt the whole basic bus segment In the conventional single-backbone bus assumed by these options, a main-cable break disrupts the shared segment, affecting the network rather than just one endpoint. NET08 qualifies the physical mechanism as an unterminated break. Redundant segmentation or protected designs are not specified, so C expresses the standard basic-bus failure consequence. A incorrect A main-backbone fault affects shared signaling, not merely the two closest nodes. B incorrect A broken unterminated backbone does not preserve normal basic-bus operation. C correct The shared basic bus segment can fail as a whole when its main backbone is broken. D incorrect A backbone break differs from an isolated endpoint spur failure and need not be limited to one node.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 244 · NS0591
records.text: NS0591 Question 244 NET06 Synchronous data transmission differs from asynchronous in that synchronous transmission: Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule. A Uses start and stop bits for each data chunk B Sends data continuously with sender and receiver using the same clock C Is always slower than asynchronous D Cannot transmit binary data Ongoing synchronized clock recovery rather than per-character start/stop NET06 contrasts character start/stop framing with ongoing clock recovery in synchronous transmission. B is the intended synchronized-transfer description; “same clock” should mean synchronized timing, not necessarily a single physical clock device. The note gives no universal speed ordering, and both methods can transmit digital/binary data. A incorrect Per-character start/stop bits describe character-oriented asynchronous serial transmission. B correct Synchronous transfer maintains coordinated timing through ongoing clock recovery rather than character start/stop framing. C incorrect No universal slower-than-asynchronous rule follows from the timing method. D incorrect Synchronous framing can carry binary data; the timing convention does not prohibit it.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 245 · NS0592
records.text: NS0592 Question 245 NET11 NET12 NET19 What is the PRIMARY function of the Network Layer (Layer 3)? Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery. A Providing physical transmission of bits B Error detection and MAC addressing C End-to-end routing of data between different networks using IP addresses D Establishing communication sessions between applications Logical IP addressing and routing across networks NET12 gives network-layer logical addressing and routing; NET11 explains forwarding IP packets among networks by destination prefixes. C directly states that responsibility. The other options assign physical signaling, link MAC/error detection and session-dialog management, which belong to different model layers. A incorrect Transporting raw physical bits/symbols is the physical-layer function. B incorrect MAC addressing and hop frame error detection are data-link responsibilities. C correct Network-layer logical addressing and routing carry IP packets between networks. D incorrect Establishing application dialogs is a session-layer role rather than IP routing.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 246 · NS0593
records.text: NS0593 Question 246 NET22 Which of the following IPv4 addresses is INVALID? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 192.168.0.1 B 10.0.0.255 C 172.16.254.1 D 10.256.0.1 10.256.0.1 has an impossible octet An IPv4 decimal octet must fit eight bits, from 0 through 255. D has 256 and is therefore syntactically invalid. A–C each meet that range condition. B’s .255 ending alone does not establish a broadcast without a prefix, so it cannot be rejected merely by its last octet. A incorrect All four octets are within 0–255, so this notation is valid. B incorrect Every octet is valid; a .255 ending alone does not determine broadcast status without a prefix. C incorrect All four values fit eight-bit octets and form valid dotted-decimal notation. D correct The second octet 256 exceeds the maximum representable eight-bit value 255.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 247 · NS0594
records.text: NS0594 Question 247 NET23 NET16 NET-S06 In IPv6, addresses are how many bits long? Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention. A 32 bits B 64 bits C 96 bits D 128 bits 128 bits NET23 explicitly gives IPv6 addresses a 128-bit width. IPv4 uses 32 bits; 64 may describe a common subnet interface boundary but is not the whole IPv6 address length. Ninety-six bits is likewise not the full width. D therefore answers the requested address size. A incorrect Thirty-two bits is the IPv4 address width, not IPv6. B incorrect Sixty-four bits is not the complete IPv6 address width. C incorrect Ninety-six bits does not match the specified 128-bit IPv6 address length. D correct IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits as explicitly stated in NET23.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 248 · NS0595
records.text: NS0595 Question 248 NET10 NET17 NET16 A bridge decides whether to forward a frame to another network segment by examining the: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A IP address in the packet header B Port number in the segment header C Source and destination MAC addresses D TTL (Time to Live) field Learn source MACs and forward according to destination MAC A bridge learns which sources are reachable through each port and consults the destination MAC when forwarding/filtering a frame. C names the relevant link addresses. IP, transport ports and TTL belong to higher-layer packet/segment processing, not the ordinary bridge forwarding decision. Unknown destinations may be flooded, so learning does not imply always-one-port forwarding. A incorrect Destination IP prefixes drive routing, not ordinary layer-2 bridge frame forwarding. B incorrect Transport ports identify process endpoints and are not the bridge MAC-table lookup key. C correct Source MAC informs learning and destination MAC informs forwarding/filtering to the appropriate segment. D incorrect TTL is an IP header field used in routed packet lifetime, not ordinary bridging.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 249 · NS0596
records.text: NS0596 Question 249 NET31 Circuit switching guarantees bandwidth for the duration of a call. What is the main DISADVANTAGE of this? Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions. A High latency during transmission B Bandwidth is wasted when no data is actively being transmitted C Packets may arrive out of order D It cannot support voice communication Reserved bandwidth can be wasted during silence Circuit switching holds resources for the call even while endpoints are silent, so unused reservation cannot be statistically shared as packet traffic would be. B gives that cost. Circuit switching does not inherently deliver packets out of order or prevent voice transmission; traditional telephone calls are a standard example. A incorrect Reserved circuits can offer predictable transfer behavior; setup cost is distinct from universally high transfer latency. B correct Capacity remains reserved during silence and can be wasted when no data is sent. C incorrect Independent out-of-order packet routing is not the defining reserved-circuit disadvantage. D incorrect Traditional telephone calls are the note’s standard circuit-switching example, so voice is supported.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 250 · NS0597
records.text: NS0597 Question 250 NET07 Under the textbook direct line-of-sight wireless-link convention, which option gives the most complete set of listed technologies whose direct path can be blocked by buildings or terrain? Treat radio waves as the broad category rather than assuming every radio propagation mode needs line of sight. Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions. A Radio waves B Microwaves C Infrared D Both B and C Microwave and infrared under the conventional line-of-sight assumption Conventional directional microwave links need suitable path visibility, and infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Obstacles can therefore interrupt the direct links specified here. Both individual technologies fit, so the combined option is the complete response. Radio waves is a broader physical category that includes microwave but also other propagation modes; the question does not assert that all radio links share the same line-of-sight restriction. A incorrect The broad radio category includes propagation modes beyond the specified line-of-sight comparison. B incorrect Microwave fits the stated direct-link case, but this alone omits infrared. C incorrect Infrared fits the stated obstructed-direct-path case, but this alone omits microwave. D correct Both microwave and infrared fit the specified comparison, making this the complete set.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 251 · NS0598
records.text: NS0598 Question 251 NET28 NET26 What does CIDR stand for, and what problem did it solve? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Classless Inter-Domain Routing; it solved address wastage in classful addressing B Classful Internet Domain Routing; it solved packet loss C Centralized IP Domain Routing; it solved routing loops D Classless Internet Data Routing; it solved latency in WANs Classless Inter-Domain Routing; flexible prefixes reduce rigid class allocation waste CIDR replaces rigid class allocation. Flexible prefixes allow blocks sized to requirements and aggregation of aligned blocks, addressing waste from fixed historical class sizes. The other expansions are incorrect and their proposed packet-loss, loop or latency cures are not the defined purpose. A correct This gives the correct expansion and relates flexible prefix allocation to avoiding rigid class-size waste. B incorrect Classful Internet Domain Routing is the wrong expansion, and CIDR is not defined as a packet-loss cure. C incorrect Centralized IP Domain Routing is not the acronym expansion or the stated mechanism. D incorrect Classless Internet Data Routing is incorrect; CIDR is not defined as a general WAN-latency cure.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 252 · NS0599
records.text: NS0599 Question 252 NET26 How many subnets are created when you borrow 5 bits from the host portion of a Class B network? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A 5 B 16 C 32 D 64 32 subnets Borrowing five bits yields 2^5=32 equal subnets under modern counting. The parent Class B /16 would become /21, but the direct subnet count only needs the specified five borrowed bits. NET26 says not to subtract two subnets under modern practice. A incorrect Five is the number of borrowed bits, not the exponential number of resulting subnet combinations. B incorrect Sixteen subnets would use four borrowed bits rather than five. C correct Five borrowed bits have 32 distinct combinations and therefore produce 32 subnets. D incorrect Sixty-four subnets would require six borrowed bits.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 253 · NS0600
records.text: NS0600 Question 253 NET-S06 NET10 The 'forwarding table' in a bridge is also known as the: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Routing table B ARP table C MAC table D IP table MAC table The bridge forwarding database records MAC-to-port associations learned from source addresses and used for destination lookups. MAC table is therefore the matching name. A routing table maps IP prefixes to next hops; ARP associates on-link IPv4 addresses with link addresses. Those are different tables even if one device maintains several of them. A incorrect Routing tables describe destination IP prefixes and next hops rather than bridge MAC-to-port mappings. B incorrect ARP caches associate IPv4 next hops with link addresses, not MAC addresses with bridge ports. C correct The bridge’s learned source-MAC-to-port forwarding database is its MAC table. D incorrect IP table does not name the layer-2 learned MAC forwarding database described in NET10.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 254 · NS0601
records.text: NS0601 Question 254 NET09 NET12 Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for defining voltage levels, cable specifications, and how bits are physically transmitted? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Data Link Layer B Network Layer C Physical Layer D Transport Layer Physical layer Voltage, cable/interface characteristics and signal transport are the physical-layer scope in NET09. Data-link functions operate on frames and MAC access, network handles IP routing and transport handles process delivery. The wording explicitly asks how bits are physically represented and carried, so C is the corresponding layer. A incorrect Data link manages frames/access rather than defining the physical voltage and cable interface. B incorrect Network manages logical addressing/routing rather than electrical signal specifications. C correct Physical-layer specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage and timing. D incorrect Transport supplies process delivery rather than cable and voltage definitions.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 255 · NS0602
records.text: NS0602 Question 255 NET08 In a star topology, what happens if the central hub fails? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Only the hub's nearest neighbor is affected B The entire network fails C The network continues operating in bus mode D Nodes automatically reconnect in ring topology The dependent star loses connectivity when its center fails In a basic star every endpoint depends on the central hub for communication with other endpoints. Failure of that common center therefore affects the whole star. No alternate center or automatic topology reconfiguration is specified; the network does not become a bus or ring merely because the hub stops functioning. A incorrect The center serves all star endpoints, so its failure is not limited to the nearest neighbor. B correct All endpoints depend on the central hub, so the basic star loses inter-endpoint connectivity. C incorrect A hub failure does not physically or logically rewire the star into an operational bus. D incorrect No automatic ring reconnection mechanism follows from the basic star topology.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 256 · NS0603
records.text: NS0603 Question 256 NET06 NET-S07 What type of noise CANNOT be completely eliminated because it is caused by the random motion of electrons due to temperature? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Crosstalk B Impulse noise C Thermal noise D Intermodulation noise Thermal noise The stated cause—random motion associated with temperature—is thermal noise in NET06. Crosstalk is neighboring-channel coupling and impulse noise is a short disturbance. D names a different noise phenomenon not defined by random thermal motion. The cause identifies C without requiring a claim that all other real noise can be perfectly eliminated. A incorrect Crosstalk arises from coupling between nearby communication channels, not the stated thermal-motion cause. B incorrect Impulse noise is a short disturbance rather than persistent random thermal motion. C correct Thermal noise is explicitly caused by random thermal motion, matching the temperature-dependent clue. D incorrect This option does not match the random thermal-motion definition supplied in NET06.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 257 · NS0604
records.text: NS0604 Question 257 NET22 Which IP address class has a first-octet range of 128–191? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Class A B Class B C Class C D Class D Class B NET22 gives first-octet 128–191 for historical Class B, corresponding to leading bits 10. Ordinary Class A is 1–126, Class C is 192–223 and Class D uses leading 1110 for multicast. Since the question explicitly asks classes, the historical categorization is appropriate rather than inferring a current CIDR prefix. A incorrect Ordinary historical Class A uses first octets 1–126 rather than 128–191. B correct Historical Class B spans first octets 128–191, with leading bits 10. C incorrect Historical Class C spans 192–223, above the supplied interval. D incorrect Class D multicast begins with 1110, outside the Class B 128–191 interval.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 258 · NS0605
records.text: NS0605 Question 258 NET19 The Session Layer's 'checkpointing' feature means that it: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Encrypts data to protect it from interception B Compresses data to reduce transmission time C Saves the state of a communication session at regular intervals so it can be resumed after interruption D Translates data between different character encoding formats Checkpoint state supports resuming after interruption A checkpoint records recoverable progress/state so interrupted work can resume from an agreed point. NET19 assigns such coordination to the session role. Encryption, compression and encoding translation belong to representation handling and do not by themselves preserve resumable dialog progress. C matches the checkpoint recovery purpose. A incorrect Encryption conceals content and does not define saving resumable session progress. B incorrect Compression reduces representation size rather than recording recovery checkpoints. C correct Saving agreed progress/state enables continuation after interruption rather than restarting from the beginning. D incorrect Encoding translation changes representation format, not checkpoint recovery state.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 259 · NS0606
records.text: NS0606 Question 259 NET03 Which of the following is a De Jure standard? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A A manufacturer's proprietary cable format adopted industry-wide B A standard officially approved by ISO or IEEE C A standard developed by a single corporation without regulatory approval D A protocol widely used but never formally documented A formally approved standard NET03 defines de jure by formal approval. B directly states official approval, while industry adoption without that approval is de facto. Corporate origin does not alone decide status, but C specifically lacks formal approval and D emphasizes informal use. Therefore B is the option establishing the defining approval condition. A incorrect Widespread adoption alone demonstrates de facto use rather than formal de jure approval. B correct Official approval matches the defining de jure criterion in NET03. C incorrect A corporate format without the stated formal approval does not meet the offered de jure definition. D incorrect Widespread informal use without formal approval is de facto rather than de jure.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 260 · NS0607
records.text: NS0607 Question 260 NET06 Parallel data transmission sends multiple bits simultaneously. Its key DISADVANTAGE compared to serial transmission is: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A It is always slower B It cannot be used for digital data C It requires more transmission lines and can suffer from interference between lines D It only works over fiber-optic cable More conductors and interline impairments Parallel transfer needs several conductors to carry simultaneous bits. Those paths can experience skew and neighboring-channel coupling, as NET06’s impairment definitions explain. C states the extra-line and interference burden. No universal slower-speed claim, inability to carry digital data or fiber-only restriction follows from parallel transmission. A incorrect Parallel is not universally slower; performance depends on implementation, distance and synchronization. B incorrect Parallel transmission can carry digital bits simultaneously, exactly as the stem states. C correct Multiple conductors add wiring and can suffer skew or coupled interference between adjacent lines. D incorrect Parallel transmission is not restricted to fiber and commonly concerns multiple electrical conductors.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 261 · NS0608
records.text: NS0608 Question 261 NET31 NET17 A packet-switching network may be UNSUITABLE for real-time voice communication because: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A It requires a dedicated circuit B Variable latency and possible packet loss can disrupt real-time audio C It cannot carry voice signals D All bandwidth is reserved, leaving none for voice Variable delay and packet loss can disturb real-time audio Real-time audio is sensitive to late or missing data. Packet networks may introduce variable queueing delay and loss, so B gives a plausible suitability issue. Modern voice over packets remains possible with buffering, scheduling and capacity planning; it is not intrinsically prohibited or dependent on reserved circuits. A incorrect Datagram packet switching does not require a dedicated circuit before every communication. B correct Variable queueing latency and loss can make audio arrive late or incomplete. C incorrect NET31 explicitly allows voice over packets with suitable engineering. D incorrect Statistical link sharing differs from reserving all bandwidth for established circuits.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 262 · NS0609
records.text: NS0609 Question 262 NET25 For a Class C network subnetted to /27, how many usable hosts per subnet are available? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A 32 B 30 C 28 D 62 30 usable hosts A /27 leaves five host bits regardless of the historical class of its parent. Those bits provide 32 total addresses. On an ordinary broadcast subnet, network and broadcast reserve two, leaving 30 usable host addresses. Parent classification matters for subnet counting, not this explicit-prefix host calculation. A incorrect Thirty-two is the total address count before reserving network and broadcast. B correct Five host bits give 32−2=30 ordinary usable hosts. C incorrect Twenty-eight does not follow from the stated five host bits and two standard reservations. D incorrect Sixty-two usable hosts corresponds to /26 rather than the supplied /27.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 263 · NS0610
records.text: NS0610 Question 263 NET30 Which routing type sends data to the NEAREST of multiple hosts sharing the same IP address? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Multicast B Broadcast C Unicast D Anycast Anycast Anycast routes to one member of a set sharing the address, typically the nearest by routing metrics. That is not necessarily geographic distance. Multicast targets a subscribed group, broadcast all in scope and ordinary unicast a single designated destination. D uniquely matches the shared-address nearest-member rule. A incorrect Multicast targets a subscribed group rather than selecting only one nearest shared-address member. B incorrect Broadcast targets all destinations within its scope, not the nearest member. C incorrect Ordinary unicast targets one designated destination without the shared-address nearest-member semantics. D correct Anycast selects one shared-address member, normally nearest according to routing metrics.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 264 · NS0611
records.text: NS0611 Question 264 NET07 The term 'coaxial' refers to the fact that the cable's inner conductor and outer shield: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Are made of the same conductive material B Share the same central axis C Carry signals in opposite directions D Are both covered in plastic insulation The conductor and shield share an axis The name coaxial refers to a common geometric axis for the inner conductor and surrounding shield. NET07 states this directly. Neither identical material, opposite signal directions nor a particular insulation covering defines the term; those are separate construction or usage details rather than the shared-axis relationship. A incorrect The definition concerns geometric arrangement, not whether both conductive parts use the same material. B correct The inner conductor and outer shield share a central axis, giving the coaxial name. C incorrect Opposite signal directions are not the defining common-axis geometry. D incorrect Insulation details do not define coaxial; sharing an axis does.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 265 · NS0612
records.text: NS0612 Question 265 NET11 NET10 NET09 Which option best describes a protocol-translating gateway joining unlike networked systems? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A A device that boosts signal strength over long distances B A device that connects networks using the same protocol C A device that connects two or more networks using different protocols, topologies, or architectures D A device that filters traffic based on MAC addresses A device that connects two or more networks using different protocols, topologies, or architectures Gateway has several networking meanings. A default IP gateway is commonly a router, while a protocol gateway translates between unlike protocols or application formats. The question asks for that translating role, so the option joining unlike systems fits. Signal regeneration belongs to repeaters, same-protocol routing does not require translation, and MAC-based filtering describes bridging or switching rather than protocol conversion. A incorrect Signal regeneration/strength extension is a repeater function rather than either gateway meaning defined here. B incorrect Connecting networks using the same protocol describes routing without the required protocol translation. C correct A protocol gateway joins unlike systems through the translation required by the stated scope. D incorrect MAC-address frame filtering describes bridging/switching rather than the gateway distinction in NET11.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 266 · NS0613
records.text: NS0613 Question 266 NET22 NET24 An organization is assigned the Class A IP address 10.200.240.4. What is the network address? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A 10.0.0.0 B 10.200.0.0 C 10.200.240.0 D 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.0 under the explicitly requested Class A default Because the question explicitly assigns Class A, its historical default /8 supplies the intended network/host boundary. Keep first octet 10 and zero the remaining 24 host bits to obtain 10.0.0.0. If a different CIDR prefix were supplied it would override the default, but none is given in this class-specific question. A correct The Class A /8 default keeps first octet 10 and clears the remaining three octets. B incorrect This assumes a /16 boundary instead of the explicitly invoked Class A /8 default. C incorrect This assumes /24, retaining host bits that the Class A default would clear. D incorrect Clearing the network octet too loses the assigned Class A network identifier 10.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 267 · NS0614
records.text: NS0614 Question 267 NET07 NET06 UTP cable is most susceptible to which type of interference? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Thermal noise only B Electromagnetic interference (EMI) and crosstalk C Infrared interference D Gamma radiation EMI and crosstalk UTP is unshielded copper: twisting reduces coupled interference but does not remove all electromagnetic coupling. NET06 identifies crosstalk as leakage from nearby channels. B names the relevant ordinary interference types, whereas thermal-only excludes other sources and infrared/gamma are not the note’s cabling-susceptibility mechanism. A incorrect Thermal noise is not the only impairment; unshielded pairs can experience coupled electromagnetic interference. B correct EMI and adjacent-pair/channel crosstalk are relevant to unshielded copper, though twisting reduces coupling. C incorrect Infrared is an optical/unguided signaling category rather than the stated ordinary copper-coupling issue. D incorrect Gamma radiation is not the interference mechanism identified for UTP in the supplied note.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 268 · NS0615
records.text: NS0615 Question 268 NET10 NET09 NET-S07 For a known unicast whose destination is on a different learned switch port in the same VLAN, what is the main forwarding difference between an active hub and an ordinary Ethernet switch? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Hubs operate at Layer 3; switches operate at Layer 2 B Hubs send data to all connected devices; switches send data only to the intended device C Hubs use IP addresses; switches use MAC addresses D Hubs support fiber-optic; switches do not Hubs send data to all connected devices; switches send data only to the intended device An active hub repeats incoming signals onto its other ports without examining addresses. A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and, for the specified known unicast on another port, forwards the frame only to that destination port. Unknown unicasts and broadcasts are different cases and can be flooded. The scope restriction makes the intended contrast accurate without treating selective forwarding as a universal rule for all switch traffic. A incorrect Hubs are layer-1 repeaters, not layer-3 routers; ordinary switches are layer 2. B correct In this known-unicast case the hub repeats to other ports, while the switch sends only to the learned destination port. C incorrect Hubs do not use IP addresses to decide forwarding; they repeat signals without address inspection. D incorrect Hub versus switch is a signal-repetition versus frame-forwarding distinction; it does not impose the claimed prohibition on optical switch links.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 269 · NS0616
records.text: NS0616 Question 269 NET30 In multicast routing, data is sent to: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A All devices on the network regardless of interest B A single specific destination C The nearest host among multiple hosts sharing an address D Only the devices that have expressed interest in receiving the data A subscribed/interested receiver group NET30 distinguishes multicast group delivery from unicast, broadcast and anycast. Receivers express membership/interest in a group, rather than every network device receiving by definition or only one nearest destination being selected. D matches that destination-set meaning. Delivery still depends on the deployed network’s forwarding and membership mechanisms. A incorrect All devices regardless of interest describes broadcast scope rather than multicast group selection. B incorrect One specific destination is ordinary unicast rather than a receiver group. C incorrect One nearest shared-address member is anycast. D correct Multicast targets a subscribed group of receivers that expressed interest.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 270 · NS0617
records.text: NS0617 Question 270 NET22 What IPv4 address class is designed for multicast addressing? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Class A B Class B C Class C D Class D Class D Historical IPv4 Class D begins with bits 1110 and is designated for multicast. Classes A, B and C describe historical unicast network allocations, with differing default prefixes. The question explicitly asks that historical class designation, so D is supported independently of how modern unicast prefixes are allocated. A incorrect Class A is historical unicast network space rather than the multicast class. B incorrect Class B is historical unicast space with a /16 default, not multicast. C incorrect Class C is historical unicast space with a /24 default. D correct Class D, identified by leading 1110, is designated for IPv4 multicast.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 271 · NS0618
records.text: NS0618 Question 271 NET17 NET14 NET19 Which OSI layer provides sequencing, acknowledgments and receiver flow control for end-to-end reliable process delivery, as in TCP? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Network Layer B Data Link Layer C Transport Layer D Session Layer Transport Layer TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and windows to provide reliable ordered delivery between transport endpoints. Reliable link protocols can use similar mechanisms, but their scope is a single hop. The explicit end-to-end process requirement therefore selects transport. IP supplies best-effort network delivery, while session coordinates dialogs and checkpoints rather than defining TCP’s ordered-byte-stream reliability and receiver flow control. A incorrect IP is best effort and does not supply the listed reliable acknowledgment/retransmission service. B incorrect Data-link reliability is hop-local rather than the required end-to-end process service. C correct Transport supplies TCP’s end-to-end sequencing, acknowledgments and receiver flow control. D incorrect Session manages dialogs/checkpoints rather than the specifically listed link/TCP reliability machinery.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 272 · NS0619
records.text: NS0619 Question 272 NET25 NET24 For the IP address 192.168.2.64/26, what is the broadcast address? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A 192.168.2.65 B 192.168.2.126 C 192.168.2.127 D 192.168.2.255 192.168.2.127 A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses. Starting at .64, this block runs through .127; the final address has all six host bits one and is broadcast. .65 and .126 are ordinary first/last hosts. .255 belongs to another /26 block, so it is not this subnet’s broadcast. A incorrect 192.168.2.65 is the first usable host, not the all-host-bits-one address. B incorrect 192.168.2.126 is the last usable host, one address below broadcast. C correct The .64–.127 /26 block ends at .127, its directed broadcast. D incorrect The .255 address is outside this .64–.127 subnet block.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 273 · NS0620
records.text: NS0620 Question 273 NET21 NET20 Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the role of SMTP? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A Translates domain names to IP addresses B Governs how web pages are requested and delivered C Governs how email messages are sent from a client to a mail server D Enables file transfer between devices over the internet SMTP submits and relays email NET21 assigns SMTP mail submission and relay. A client sending a message to a mail server is therefore a correct SMTP role. DNS resolves names, HTTP serves web requests and FTP transfers files. This does not assign end-user mailbox retrieval to SMTP; POP3/IMAP serve that separate task. A incorrect DNS resolves domain names to address records rather than SMTP. B incorrect HTTP governs web requests/responses, not SMTP. C correct SMTP submits mail from a client to a server and relays messages between mail servers. D incorrect File transfer is the FTP service role in this comparison, not SMTP’s defining mail role.

records.title: Data Communication and Computer Networking — Question 274 · NS0621
records.text: NS0621 Question 274 NET07 An omnidirectional antenna transmits signals in which pattern? Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule. A A narrow beam toward a specific target B Only vertically upward C In all directions simultaneously, creating 360-degree coverage D In a focused line-of-sight path only 360-degree azimuth coverage, with a nonuniform vertical pattern NET07 defines omnidirectional as broad azimuth coverage. C is correct when its 360 degrees refers to the horizontal plane, not equal power in every three-dimensional direction. Directional beams or upward-only radiation do not describe this pattern. Antenna elevation patterns can still have lobes/nulls, so the answer retains that scope qualification. A incorrect A narrow targeted beam is directional rather than omnidirectional azimuth coverage. B incorrect Upward-only radiation does not provide the broad around-the-antenna azimuth pattern. C correct 360-degree azimuth coverage is the intended meaning, without asserting equal power in all three-dimensional directions. D incorrect A single focused path describes a directional antenna pattern.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Course module
records.text: Data Structure and Algorithms

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Study notes
records.text: Data Structure and Algorithms Learn each structure through its rules, representation and operation traces. The seven blueprint items require understanding common structures, implementing searching and sorting, and selecting structures for practical problems. This chapter develops core data structures and algorithms through definitions, traces and cost comparisons. Draw the representation, label indices or pointers, and state the empty/full convention before tracing. Compare costs under the same assumptions: fixed capacity or resizing, balanced or arbitrary tree, expected or worst case. Practise without answer keys, then justify every choice using an invariant or a short calculation.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Practice questions
records.text: Data Structure and Algorithms

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Revision outline
records.text: Data Structure and Algorithms

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Start with the data and the required operations
records.text: An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation. Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack. Abstraction keeps relevant details: patient urgency and arrival order matter for service; hair colour does not. Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections. A record grouping integer, character and floating fields is heterogeneous; an ordinary array has one element type. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting
records.text: For equal-size elements, address(A[i]) = base + i × element_size under zero-based indexing. This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model. A row-major rectangular matrix uses base + (row × columns + column) × element_size. A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed. Inserting in the middle shifts later elements, so it costs linear time. Appending into spare capacity is constant; a resizing append can be linear, though repeated geometric growth gives amortized constant append cost. Example Work it through Insert 9 at index 1 of [2,4,6] with a spare slot: shift 6 then 4 right, giving [2,9,4,6]. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Operations, records and memory ownership
records.text: Traversal processes every item; searching locates a target; insertion and deletion change membership; updating changes a stored value. Sorting reorders items, while merging combines sequences. To merge sorted [1,4] and [2,3], repeatedly emit the smaller front, producing [1,2,3,4]. Destroying a structure releases owned storage. A C struct groups named fields, including arrays and pointers. A singly linked node needs payload plus a same-type link. C fields cannot have initializers inside the type declaration; modern C++ permits default member initializers. In C++, match new with delete and new[] with delete[]. Repair links before freeing a node; never dereference it afterwards. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Algorithm properties are separate obligations
records.text: Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input. Definiteness means each instruction has one interpretation; effectiveness means each step is executable. Correctness means meeting the stated result for every valid input. A finite program can still return the wrong answer. A problem specifies inputs, outputs and assumptions. Language independence concerns the procedure, not its implementation. Efficiency needs a resource model. An unfamiliar characteristic is not false merely because a teaching list omits it. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Measure costs before naming their growth
records.text: Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch. Best, average and worst compare equal-size inputs; average needs a distribution. For m operations each with mean cost f(n), expected total is m f(n), without requiring independence. Exact coefficients depend on which elementary operations count. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Upper, lower and tight bounds
records.text: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions. For n≥1, 3n²+4n+1≤8n²: c=8,k=1 witness O(n²). Constants and lower-order terms disappear from tight polynomial growth. Transitivity multiplies witnesses: f≤c g≤cd h beyond both thresholds. Example Work it through Increasing representative rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2^n, 3^n, n!, n^n. Logarithm bases differ only by a constant factor. Exam tip Exam trap A linear function is also O(n²). MCQs usually intend the tightest listed order; mixed O and Theta options may overlap. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Count loops and account for hidden access costs
records.text: A loop i=1; i<n; i*=2 takes about log₂n iterations. Two independent n-iteration loops nested around constant work take Theta(n²). An n-level ordinary recursion with constant live storage per level needs Theta(n) stack space. Indexed access is not constant for every List implementation. Java LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. Summing get(0), get(2), get(4), … over a length-N list still gives Theta(N²), because a linear number of middle indices each require linear traversal. An iterator scans once in linear time. An exact executable runtime requires valid code and an explicit cost convention. Oracle Java SE 21: LinkedList

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Understand the linked-node chain
records.text: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic. To display or count nodes, follow next from head until null, processing each node. Counting is Theta(n) unless size is maintained. An array-linked list still follows links unless separately position-indexed. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Update links without losing the rest of the list
records.text: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++. Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node. Reverse a chain with prev=null, cur=head: save next=cur.next; set cur.next=prev; advance prev=cur and cur=next; finish with head=prev. This is linear time and constant extra pointers. Example Work it through For 3→7→9, insert 5 after 3: first point 5 at 7, then 3 at 5. Reversing those assignments can lose access to 7→9. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Doubly linked, circular and practical list choices
records.text: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately. Lists suit changing sequences when references to insertion positions are already available. Finding a position is still linear. Lists can hold polynomial terms (coefficient, exponent), directory or block links, child lists in nonbinary trees, and hash chains. Browser history can use a doubly linked cursor. A playlist may be circular; airline seat lookup requires a specified seat-record model, not an automatic linked-list answer. Operation Array Singly linked list Access index i O(1) O(n) worst Insert at front O(n) shifts O(1) Append O(1) with spare capacity O(1) with tail; O(n) head only Delete tail O(1) O(n), predecessor needed Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Implement a stack with one consistent top convention
records.text: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--]. A count-based alternative uses size=0 and A[size++]=x. Do not combine its empty/full tests with the top-index convention. Fixed-array push/pop are constant time. Linked stacks achieve constant time by inserting and deleting at the head; using a singly linked tail for pop would require a predecessor traversal. Exam tip Exam trap Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage. Merely checking isEmpty does not underflow. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Trace stack operations and reversible actions
records.text: Write the stack bottom-to-top after every instruction and record popped values separately. Push 1, push 2, pop emits 2 and leaves [1]. Push 1, push 2, pop, pop, pop then emits 2,1,1; push 2, pop emits 2. The complete output is 2,2,1,1,2. Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Infix, postfix and prefix expressions
records.text: Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses. Prefix places it first; postfix places it last. Their fixed operator arity determines grouping. To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack. Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators. Parentheses temporarily override this order. To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation. Example Work it through A+B*C-D/E becomes ABC*+DE/-. For 8 3 -, pop 3 then 8, producing 5. (A+B)*C becomes AB+C* and prefix *+ABC. Data Structure and Algorithms module University of Manchester: Infix, Postfix and Prefix

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Queues preserve arrival order
records.text: An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail. FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation. Example Work it through Enqueue 4,8; peek is 4, so a conditional removal only if peek>5 does nothing. Enqueue 1,6 then dequeue: [8,1,6]. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots
records.text: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C. Dequeue reads A[front], sets front=(front+1)%C and decreases size. An alternative reserves one unused slot and uses next(rear)==front for full; its empty test and capacity differ. State the convention before tracing. Example Work it through Full capacity-six [11,13,15,17,19,21], front=0: remove 11, then enqueue 9 into slot 0. Physical array: [9,13,15,17,19,21]; logical front-to-rear queue: [13,15,17,19,21,9]. A noncircular version can instead overflow. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Deques, merging and splitting queues
records.text: A deque permits both-end insertion/removal without guaranteeing middle access. Endpoint-linked operations are constant but middle indexing is linear. A circular-array deque may support indexed access. Dequeue names removal; deque names the structure. Merging FIFO queues needs an explicit policy: append one sequence after another or alternate their fronts. Splitting by a predicate preserves each subgroup’s original order if each removed item is appended to its matching output queue. A fixed-capacity buffer also needs a full-policy choice: reject, block or overwrite. Capacity alone does not choose a policy. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Priority queues serve by priority, with an explicit tie rule
records.text: A priority queue returns the smallest or largest priority key under its convention. Urgent patients may precede earlier arrivals. Insertions and extractions can interleave. Binary heaps support constant peek and logarithmic insert/extract. Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter). Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing. Exam tip Exam trap FIFO ordering among equal priorities requires an explicit stability policy. That is an additional policy, not a universal priority-queue rule. Sedgewick and Wayne: Priority Queues

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes
records.text: A rooted tree has one parentless root and one parent per other node. It is connected and acyclic, has n-1 edges, and one path between any pair. Depth counts root-to-node edges; height is maximum depth. A single-node tree therefore has height zero. Leaves have no children. Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — BST search follows a global ordering invariant
records.text: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy. Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it. Standard optimal-BST dynamic programming tries each possible root for each key interval: O(n²) intervals times O(n) roots gives O(n³) construction. It minimizes probability-weighted search depth, not necessarily worst-case height. Example Work it through Insert 40,20,50,10,30,60: root children are 20 and 50; 20 has 10,30; 50 has right child 60. Height is two edges. Sorted insertions 1,2,3,4,5 instead form a right chain. Data Structure and Algorithms module University of Freiburg: Optimal Binary Search Trees

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Tree traversal is a rule you can execute
records.text: Preorder visits node,left,right; inorder left,node,right; postorder left,right,node. Apply recursively; null children do nothing. Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST. Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue. For root 4, children 2 and 6, and leaves 1,3,5,7: preorder is 4,2,1,3,6,5,7; inorder is 1,2,3,4,5,6,7; postorder is 1,3,2,5,7,6,4. Level order is 4,2,6,1,3,5,7. Randomized visitation is possible; it is simply not one of these standard named depth-first orders. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — BST deletion preserves every subtree restriction
records.text: A leaf can be detached by clearing its parent link. For one child, make the parent bypass the node and point to the child. For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location. That second deletion has at most one child. Deletion by merging is another approach. Promote the right subtree and attach the entire old left subtree to the minimum node in the promoted right subtree; or use the symmetric left promotion. Update root itself when deleting root. Copying values and reconnecting subtrees can yield different valid shapes, so a trace must name its deletion method. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Balanced trees prevent the sorted-input chain
records.text: AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order. Inserting 30,20,10 triggers LL repair: 20 becomes root with children 10,30. Red-black colouring rules provide another logarithmic-height discipline. Both prevent linear worst-case search; balanced trees also support ordered ranges unlike ordinary hashing. Sedgewick and Wayne: Balanced Search Trees

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering
records.text: A binary max-heap is complete with each parent at least its children; a min-heap reverses this order. Unlike BSTs, heaps do not order entire subtrees. The root is maximum. If all keys are distinct, the second largest is a root child. With duplicate maxima, the second largest distinct value may be deeper: [9,9,9,8,7,6,5] is a valid max-heap and that value is 8 at index 3. The minimum may be any leaf, requiring linear worst-case scanning. Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0. One-based representation uses children 2i,2i+1 and parent floor(i/2). A child exists only if its index is inside the current heap size. Exam tip Exam trap The right-child formula 2i+1 assumes one-based indexing. For zero-based indexing with the root at index 0, the right-child formula is 2i+2. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Restore a heap after insertion or removal
records.text: Insert at the next complete-tree position and swap upward while parent order is violated. To remove the root, move the final element to root, reduce heap size, then swap downward with the more dominant child until order holds. Each path has logarithmic length. Building bottom-up by sinking internal nodes takes linear total time; repeated independent insertions give an O(n log n) construction bound. Example Work it through Max-heap [10,8,6,2,1,4,5]: remove 10, move 5 to root and sink, giving [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8, move 4 up then exchange with 6: [6,5,4,2,1]. Data Structure and Algorithms module Sedgewick and Wayne: Priority Queues

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice
records.text: Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity. With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position. Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly. Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup. Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions. MIT 6.006: Recitation4 Hashing

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Resolve collisions and watch the load factor
records.text: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found. Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely. At h(k)=3 in a seven-slot linear-probing table, addresses wrap 3,4,5,6,0,1,2. A home address is not guaranteed to remain the final slot. Sedgewick and Wayne: Hash Tables

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts
records.text: A map associates unique keys with values; different keys may share values, and entries can be traversed. A set forbids duplicate elements. Null and iteration-order policies depend on implementation. Lists preserve positions and generally allow duplicates; Java LinkedList also permits null. A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements. Oracle Java SE 21: Map Oracle Java SE 21: Set Oracle Java SE 21: LinkedList Oracle Java SE 21: LinkedHashMap

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Linear search: a scan with an early stop
records.text: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear. For a single unsorted query, sorting first is rarely justified. Small lists may favour scanning because setup matters. Sorting does not avoid examining all values for mean, variance or arbitrary parity counts. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval
records.text: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement. Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality. Example Work it through Find 19 in [11,13,15,17,19,21]: mid=2 gives 15; search indices 3..5; mid=4 gives 19. Binary debugging needs an ordered good/bad boundary, not arbitrary fault locations. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Search variants need their own assumptions
records.text: Interpolation search estimates the index from numeric values: lo+(hi-lo)×(key-A[lo])/(A[hi]-A[lo]), rounded to a valid index. Guard equal endpoints and out-of-range targets. On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time. Binary search gives a logarithmic worst bound without that distribution assumption. Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic. Jump search probes block boundaries then scans within a block. Regular intervals could mean unit-step scanning or larger jumps. Interpolation also needs sortedness, so prerequisite questions can overlap binary search. University of Waterloo, Douglas Harder: Interpolation Search University of Massachusetts: Running Time lecture University of Waterloo, Douglas Harder: Jump Search

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Compare sorting rules, not just algorithm names
records.text: Stable sorting preserves the input order of equal keys. An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested. There is no single algorithm identified by stable or in-place alone. State the implementation, input case and resource being compared. Method Best / average / worst time Extra storage; usual stability Bubble with early stop n / n² / n² constant; stable Selection n² / n² / n² constant; unstable Insertion n / n² / n² constant; stable Quicksort n log n / n log n / n² stack usually log n average, n worst; unstable Ordinary array mergesort n log n in all cases linear; stable with left-first ties Heapsort O(n log n) bound in all cases constant with iterative sink; unstable Exam tip Exam trap Big-O bounds can overlap. n log(n²)=2n log n, so it has the same growth as n log n, unlike n(log n)². Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes
records.text: For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons. Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic. Strict swaps preserve equal-key order. Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps. Example Work it through [4,1,3,2] → [1,4,3,2] → [1,3,4,2] → [1,3,2,4] after the first pass. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons
records.text: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls. Selection suits expensive record moves with cheap key comparisons, not every large dataset. It is unstable: exchanging first 2a with 1 in [2a,2b,1] gives [1,2b,2a]. Constant extra element storage is shared by several sorts. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix
records.text: Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap. That gives n-1 insertion passes. On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time. Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time. Few inversions mean few shifts, favouring insertion for nearly sorted or small arrays. Shift only strictly larger keys for stability. A linked implementation saves array shifts but still must locate each insertion position. Example Work it through Insert 2 into prefix [1,4,7]: save 2, move 7 then 4 right, and write 2 after 1. The sorted prefix becomes [1,2,4,7]. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Shell sort: insertion across decreasing gaps
records.text: Choose a sequence of positive gaps ending at 1. For each gap h, insertion-sort each subsequence of positions h apart. The final h=1 pass finishes ordinary sorting after earlier long moves have reduced disorder. An h-sorted array satisfies A[j]≤A[j+h] wherever both indices exist. The O(n^(3/2)) bound depends on gaps; Knuth increments 1,4,13,… have that worst order. Shell sort is generally unstable because distant moves can reorder ties; extra element storage is constant. Example Work it through For [5,4,3,2,1], gap 3 sorts positions (0,3) and (1,4), giving [2,1,3,5,4]. Gap 1 then produces [1,2,3,4,5]. Data Structure and Algorithms module Sedgewick and Wayne: Shell.java

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces
records.text: Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces. Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work. Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model. Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best. In the ten-distinct-value example, a final pivot 5 has five smaller values before it and four larger after it. Internal orders depend on the partition algorithm; several candidate arrays can satisfy the invariant. State the algorithm before predicting one exact array. Quicksort normally rearranges in the same array but recursive storage can be linear in the worst case. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Merge sort and internal versus external sorting
records.text: Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front. With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order. Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer. There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges. Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons. Data Structure and Algorithms module Virginia Tech OpenDSA: External Sorting

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Heapsort: repeatedly place the extreme at the end
records.text: For ascending in-place heapsort, build a max-heap over the array. Exchange root with the final active element, shrink the active heap, and sink the new root. The removed maximum now belongs in the sorted suffix. Repeat until one active item remains. Building with bottom-up sinking is linear; repeated extraction gives O(n log n) worst time. Iterative sinking needs constant auxiliary storage. The method is generally unstable because long root-to-end exchanges can reorder equal keys. It is not uniquely the method for sorting by priorities: any comparison sort can compare a priority field. Heap extraction is its distinctive mechanism. Data Structure and Algorithms module
