records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Radix sorting uses key digits, not arbitrary magic
records.text: LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left. Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits. With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage. MSD begins at leading digits and subdivides equal-prefix groups. Strings are lexicographically comparable. Radix methods require accessible digits and length/signed-value conventions, not arbitrary unstructured keys. Large radix, long keys or small n may favour comparison sorting. Sedgewick and Wayne: LSD.java

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Graphs: represent the relationships you actually need
records.text: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles. A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup. Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours. Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts. Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — BFS: discover one distance layer at a time
records.text: Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers. BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths. With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²). To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex. Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances. Example Work it through Edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D; alphabetical neighbours: queue [A] → [B,C] → [C,D] → [D] → []. Discovery order A,B,C,D; D has distance two. Sedgewick and Wayne: Undirected Graphs

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — DFS: finish a branch before returning
records.text: Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles. Using the same graph and alphabetical neighbours, recursive DFS can discover A,B,D,C. Its path is a valid reachability witness but not necessarily shortest. Adjacency-list cost is O(V+E), with O(V) visited state and possible stack depth. DFS supports cycle and connectivity analysis; a directed cycle test distinguishes active recursion vertices from already completed ones. Data Structure and Algorithms module

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives
records.text: For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford. An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected. An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs. Example Work it through Triangle weights AB=1, BC=2, AC=10: Prim or Kruskal selects AB,BC, total 3. Dijkstra from A gets B=1 and improves C from 10 to 3 through B. Sedgewick and Wayne: Shortest Paths Sedgewick and Wayne: Minimum Spanning Trees

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules
records.text: Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray. For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending). It is linear time with constant working storage. Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case. Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text. Preprocess the pattern’s longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. After mismatch, fall back using those prefix lengths rather than restarting comparisons from the beginning; the text pointer need not move backward. Pattern preprocessing plus scanning takes O(pattern length+text length). Example Work it through For [-2,3,-1,4,-5], Kadane ending values are -2,3,2,6,1, so best is 6 from [3,-1,4]. Pattern ABAB has prefix lengths [0,0,1,2]. University of Alberta: Advanced Algorithms Lecture2 Jayadev Misra, University of Texas: Knuth-Morris-Pratt Algorithm

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — State trace data and representation assumptions
records.text: A trace needs the complete operation sequence, initial state, capacity and output orientation. State these assumptions before calculating. Evaluate all choices against the rules; a selected answer does not make other valid choices false. Specify whether a question asks which structure can implement something or which is best under stated costs. ADTs do not force one representation, and serial-access memory is not inherently LIFO. A heap file is an unordered database record file, unrelated to a binary heap: insertion uses available space, scanning can find records, and ordered output requires sorting or an index. It need not insert at the beginning. Data Structure and Algorithms module UC Berkeley CS186: Disk and Files

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Best, average and worst compare equal-size inputs
records.text: Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. Average-case cost averages costs using a stated input distribution. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation. For successful binary search with all stored positions equally likely, average probes have order Theta(log n). The probe decisions form a binary tree: only a bounded number of positions occur in shallow levels, while a constant fraction require logarithmic depth. Interval halving also gives the logarithmic upper bound. A distribution concentrating on an immediate midpoint hit would give a different average. NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Best case NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Worst case NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Average case Sedgewick and Wayne — Algorithms, binary-search symbol-table average costs

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Queues for deferred interrupt work
records.text: An interrupt service routine may need to record work quickly and defer its completion. Operating systems can queue that deferred work for later processing; Windows deferred procedure calls are one concrete example. This is a queue application, but it does not imply that every interrupt system uses a single FIFO service policy. Microsoft — Introduction to DPC objects

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Linked nodes and multiway tree branching
records.text: A linked binary-tree node stores a payload and two child pointers, one for the left child and one for the right child. A null child pointer means that child is absent; a root pointer gives access to the whole tree. In a dynamically allocated version, insertion can allocate a node and attach it through the appropriate child link. A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree. Its allowed branching factor can exceed two, so a general B-tree is not the binary-tree family. Balanced describes a height discipline; it does not by itself restrict every node to two children. Data Structure and Algorithms module · page 9 Data Structure and Algorithms module · page 5 NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — B-tree

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Recognize recursive divide-and-conquer structure
records.text: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 1 · Q00012
records.text: Q00012 Question 1 DSA25 When we use a hash table data structure, our hash function should map the expected inputs (keys) as evenly as possible over its output range(indexes). This property of good hash function is known as______. Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout. A Uniformity B Determinism C Continuity D Data normalization Uniformity DSA25 defines uniformity as spreading expected keys evenly among addresses. That directly matches the question’s wording. Determinism is a different obligation: repeated equal keys receive the same address for the chosen function. Continuity and data normalization do not name this distribution property, so only Uniformity answers the literal stem. A correct Uniformity describes spreading expected input keys evenly across the output address range, exactly as the stem requires. B incorrect Determinism requires repeated equal keys to map identically; it does not require an even address distribution. C incorrect Continuity is not the key-distribution property defined for hash functions in DSA25. D incorrect Data normalization does not name the even-distribution requirement of a hash function.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 2 · Q00013
records.text: Q00013 Question 2 DSA23 In a one-based array representation of a binary heap, the root is at index 1. If a node at index i has a right child, at which index is that child stored? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A 2*i+1 B i/2 C (i+1)/2 D 2*i A. 2*i+1 Heap child formulas depend on whether indexing begins at zero or one. With the explicitly stated one-based convention, the two children of node i occupy positions 2i and 2i+1. The latter is the right child. Integer division by two instead identifies a parent in this convention. The existence condition matters because an index computed beyond the current heap size does not designate an actual child. A correct 2i+1 is the one-based right-child index. B incorrect floor(i/2) computes the parent for nonroot nodes. C incorrect (i+1)/2 does not compute the right child. D incorrect 2i is the one-based left child.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 3 · Q00014
records.text: Q00014 Question 3 DSA28 DSA29 Use iterative sequential search and iterative binary search on random-access arrays, with constant-size indices. For binary search, reverse comparisons on descending arrays. Compare tight asymptotic auxiliary space and worst-case element probes as n grows. Which statement is false? Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Binary searching algorithm can work on list of data which is stored in descending order B Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency C Sequential searching algorithm can work on sorted and unsorted list of data D Binary search has a smaller tight worst-case probe order than sequential search on sorted random-access arrays. B. Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency Both iterative algorithms keep only a fixed number of indices and temporary values, giving constant auxiliary space. Their worst-case probe counts differ: sequential search can inspect every element, whereas binary search halves the ordered interval each time. Binary search can also handle descending order with reversed comparisons, and sequential search does not require sorted input. Under these specified implementations, the unequal-memory claim is the false statement. A incorrect Descending binary search works with reversed comparisons. B correct Both iterative implementations use constant auxiliary space, so this inequality claim is false. C incorrect A sequential scan works with either input ordering. D incorrect Binary search has logarithmic rather than linear worst-case probes.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 4 · Q00045
records.text: Q00045 Question 4 DSA37 DSA34 DSA33 DSA36 For ordinary array sorting implementations, which listed algorithm uses a temporary element buffer proportional to n rather than only a fixed number of saved elements? Count recursive call frames separately from auxiliary element storage. Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Insertion sort B Selection sort C Merge sort D Quick sort C. Merge sort Ordinary array mergesort merges two sorted halves through a temporary buffer that can hold a number of elements proportional to n. Insertion sort retains one item while shifting, and selection sort needs fixed temporary storage for a minimum position and an exchange. Ordinary quicksort partitions inside the original array. Its recursive stack is counted separately here, so the linear element-buffer requirement uniquely identifies mergesort. A incorrect Insertion saves one item and shifts within the same array. B incorrect Selection retains a minimum position and a fixed-size swap temporary. C correct Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary element buffer. D incorrect In-array partitioning needs no full merge buffer; recursive frames are excluded by the stated convention.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 5 · Q00066

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 6 · Q00076
records.text: Q00076 Question 6 DSA14 Which one of the following is true about Queue data structure? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Queue data structure applies first come first served policy B Queue data structure uses last in first out rule C Queue data structure does not have efficient basic operations D Queue data structure cannot be implemented using linked list Queue data structure applies first come first served policy FIFO serves the first arrival first; the module also explicitly gives linked-list enqueue and dequeue. Therefore A is true and the supplied D key contradicts page 8. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 8. A correct First come first served is stated under queue applications. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8. B incorrect LIFO describes the stack, whereas queue deletion is at the front. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8. C incorrect A blanket inefficiency claim is unsupported; front removal and rear insertion can use fixed pointer updates. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8. D incorrect The module expressly implements the queue as a linked list. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 7 · Q00148
records.text: Q00148 Question 7 DSA09 An unsorted singly linked list maintains only its head pointer. Which option gives the complete set of listed operations with tight worst-case constant time? There is no cached tail, predecessor index or positional index. Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Insertion at the front of the linked list B Insertion at the end of the linked list C Deletion of the front node of the linked list D Deletion of the last node of the linked list E A&C E. A&C Inserting at the head links the new node to the old head and updates head. Deleting the head advances head and releases one node. Both use constant work. Appending requires traversal to find the tail, and deleting the tail requires its predecessor, also found by traversal. The complete constant-time set is therefore insertion at the front together with deletion of the front, which is option E. A incorrect Front insertion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front deletion. B incorrect Head-only append traverses the list to find its tail. C incorrect Front deletion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front insertion. D incorrect Tail deletion must locate its predecessor by traversal. E correct This combines exactly the two listed constant-time operations.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 11 · Q00153
records.text: Q00153 Question 11 DSA15 A capacity-six circular queue uses all six slots with front=0 and size=6. Its physical array is [11,13,15,17,19,21]. After dequeue() and enqueue(9), what is the logical front-to-rear sequence? Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout. A 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 B 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9 C 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 9 D Queue overflow B. 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9 The initial front element is 11, so dequeue removes it and advances front to the slot containing 13. The queue now has five items. Circular insertion reuses the freed physical slot zero for 9 and restores size six. Reading from the new front around to the rear gives 13,15,17,19,21,9. Physical slot order differs from this requested logical service order. A incorrect This would remove 21 and prepend 9 rather than remove the front. B correct This is the front-to-rear order after removing 11 and appending 9. C incorrect This incorrectly retains 11 and removes the rear 21. D incorrect Circular reuse makes room for the insertion after the removal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 12 · Q00154
records.text: Q00154 Question 12 DSA15 A circular queue has capacity six, front=0 and size=6, using physical slots [11,13,15,17,19,21]. It can use all six slots. After dequeue() and enqueue(9), list the physical array in index order 0 through 5. Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout. A 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 B 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9 C 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 9 D 9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21 D. 9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21 Dequeue reads 11 at index zero, advances front to index one and reduces size to five. The count-based insertion formula then gives (front+size)%6=(1+5)%6=0. Enqueue therefore writes 9 into the freed slot zero. All other physical slots retain their old values. The logical service order begins at 13, but the requested physical index order begins at the newly stored 9. A incorrect This drops 21 and retains the removed 11. B incorrect This is logical front-to-rear order, not physical index order. C incorrect This overwrites 21 instead of reusing slot zero. D correct Slot zero receives 9 and slots 1–5 remain unchanged.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 13 · Q00171
records.text: Q00171 Question 13 DSA41 The data structure used in the standard implementation of Breadth First Search is ? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Stack B Array C Linked List D Queue Queue Breadth-first search repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues its undiscovered neighbors. FIFO ordering ensures earlier distance layers are processed before later ones. Arrays or linked nodes can store this frontier, but Queue names its required access discipline. A stack instead serves latest pending work. A incorrect A stack serves the latest pending vertex first and does not preserve BFS distance-layer order. B incorrect An array can store a queue, but an array alone specifies no FIFO frontier discipline. C incorrect Linked nodes can represent a queue, but Linked List alone does not specify breadth-first processing. D correct A FIFO queue processes discovered vertices by distance layer, the standard BFS frontier rule.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 14 · Q00214
records.text: Q00214 Question 14 DSA07 Suppose we define a static method totalEvenLoc() that returns the total for even-index items of an integer list as shown, on the right, below. What is the Big O running time of the method if lst is a LinkedList of size N? public static int totalEvenLoc(List<Integer> lst) { int sum = 0; for(int i = 0; i < lst.size(); i += 2) sum += lst.get(i); return sum; } Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A O(N) B O(1) C O(N^2) D O(logN) E O(NlogN) O(N²), tightly Θ(N²) The loop visits about N/2 even indices, but LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. A linear number of those indices lie near the middle, each requiring linear traversal. DSA07 analyzes exactly this access pattern and obtains Θ(N²) total work. Incrementing by two changes a constant factor, not the quadratic order. A incorrect O(N) would require constant-cost indexed access; LinkedList.get(i) instead traverses nodes. B incorrect A growing number of accesses and additions prevents a constant bound on total work. C correct A linear number of middle-index accesses each traverse a linear number of nodes, yielding quadratic time. D incorrect Neither the iteration count nor the accumulated linked-node traversal has logarithmic growth. E incorrect Quadratic traversal grows faster than N log N, so this is not a valid upper bound.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 15 · Q00215
records.text: Q00215 Question 15 DSA24 The array 10, 8, 6, 2, 1, 4, 5 is organized into a full heap (heap and full BT). Which array represents the heap after the first and second biggest elements are removed? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A 6 5 4 2 1 B 6 4 5 2 1 C 6 4 5 1 2 D 6 5 4 1 2 6 5 4 2 1 Remove 10 by moving 5 to root and adjusting: [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8 by moving 4 to root and adjusting through child 6: [6,5,4,2,1]. These are standard root-last swaps and downward heap restoration. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 11. A correct Matches both root deletions and adjustment steps. See assigned PDF 11. B incorrect A valid max heap, but not the result of these root-last adjustments. See assigned PDF 11. C incorrect Changes the lower pair 2,1 as well as giving a different adjustment history. See assigned PDF 11. D incorrect Reverses the unchanged lower pair 2,1. See assigned PDF 11.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 16 · Q00216
records.text: Q00216 Question 16 DSA14 Think of a reference implementation of a classical queue with front and rear pointing to the appropriate locations in the queue. Which of these references will change during an insertion into a possibly empty queue? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Neither change B Only front changes C None of the choices is correct D Both may change. E Only rear changes Both may change. Insertion into an empty linked queue makes the new node both front and rear. Insertion into a nonempty queue changes rear while front remains. Consequently both references may change across the allowed cases. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 8, 5. A incorrect Insertion must update at least rear to include the new node. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 5. B incorrect Rear changes too; front alone is insufficient. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 5. C incorrect D describes the empty-queue case correctly. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 5. D correct Both change when the first node is inserted. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 5. E incorrect Rear alone changes only in the nonempty case. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 5.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 17 · Q00217
records.text: Q00217 Question 17 DSA29 Binary search is to operate on an already ordered sequence of comparable keys through an indexed-access interface. Which listed property is required of its search domain, rather than being a particular physical array representation or allocation policy? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A The array must hold elements of the same data type. B All are additional requirements. C The array must be contiguous. D The search interval must have valid finite bounds. E The array must fix its size a prior to population. F None is an additional requirement. D. The search interval must have valid finite bounds. Binary search maintains an interval of candidate indices and repeatedly shrinks it until a match or an empty interval is obtained. That operation requires valid finite bounds. Homogeneous physical storage and contiguity are properties of ordinary array representations, rather than requirements of the abstract interval-halving procedure. Fixing capacity before population is unnecessary: a resizable sequence can be populated first and searched afterward. Hence not all listed properties are requirements. A incorrect Comparable keys are assumed; identical physical data types are not the abstract domain requirement. B incorrect All fails because prior fixed allocation is unnecessary. C incorrect Contiguity is a representation choice rather than the abstract search-domain requirement. D correct The candidate index domain needs valid finite bounds. E incorrect A resizable sequence may be populated before searching. F incorrect Valid finite bounds are a required condition among these choices.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 18 · Q00218
records.text: Q00218 Question 18 DSA14 What will be the content of the queue (shown from queue front on the left to queue rear on the right), after the given sequence of operations shown below? Queue q = new Queue(); q.enqueue(4); q.enqueue(8); if(q.peek() > 5) q.dequeue(); q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(6); q.dequeue(); Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout. A 4, 6 B 4, 8, 1 C 8, 1, 6 D 8, 6 E 4, 1 8, 1, 6 After enqueues the queue is [4,8]. Peek examines the front 4, so 4>5 is false and the conditional dequeue does not execute. Enqueues give [4,8,1,6]; the final dequeue removes 4, leaving [8,1,6]. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 6. A incorrect Drops 8 and 1 without corresponding deletions. See assigned PDF 7, 6. B incorrect Leaves the removed 4 and omits the enqueued 6. See assigned PDF 7, 6. C correct Matches the final FIFO sequence. See assigned PDF 7, 6. D incorrect Incorrectly removes 1 as well as 4. See assigned PDF 7, 6. E incorrect Drops 8 and 6 and retains the removed 4. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 19 · Q00286
records.text: Q00286 Question 19 DSA19 What is the tightest listed worst-case time bound for constructing an optimal binary search tree using the standard interval dynamic program that tries every key as root of every interval? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A O(n) B O(n³) C O(logn) D O (n!) B. O(n³) This asks about constructing an optimal BST, rather than searching a tree after construction. The standard dynamic program considers quadratically many key intervals. For each interval it tries up to a linear number of candidate roots, combining the relevant subproblem costs. Multiplying those counts gives cubic construction time. The cubic option states that bound; the linear, logarithmic and factorial alternatives do not give the tight construction order. A incorrect Linear time does not cover all intervals and root candidates. B correct Quadratic intervals times linear root trials give cubic time. C incorrect Logarithmic time concerns balanced search paths, not this construction. D incorrect Factorial is a loose upper bound rather than the tight listed order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 20 · Q00288
records.text: Q00288 Question 20 DSA28 Which of the following is the best case time complexity of linear search algorithm? Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A O(n'2) B O(n) C O(1) D O(log n) O(1) A match at the very first inspected element ends scanning after one comparison, independent of n. Interpret the options as tight growth orders rather than arbitrary loose Big-O upper bounds. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect Quadratic is not the tight best-case count. See assigned PDF 3. B incorrect Linear is the complete-scan bound, not the immediate-match cost. See assigned PDF 3. C correct One first-element comparison is constant. See assigned PDF 3. D incorrect Logarithmic describes halving, not immediate linear-search success. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 21 · Q00289
records.text: Q00289 Question 21 DSA14 If the elements '1', '2', '3' and '4' are inserted in a queue, what would be order for the removal? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A 4321 B 3241 C 1234 D None of the above 1234 FIFO removes the four insertions in their original order: 1 then 2 then 3 then 4. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7. A incorrect 4321 reverses arrival order. See assigned PDF 7. B incorrect 3241 puts later arrivals before 1 and 2. See assigned PDF 7. C correct 1234 preserves insertion order. See assigned PDF 7. D incorrect C already supplies the FIFO result. See assigned PDF 7.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 22 · Q00290
records.text: Q00290 Question 22 DSA02 What is the disadvantage of array data structure? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A The amount of memory to be allocated should be known beforehand. B Elements of an array can be accessed in constant time. C Elements are stored in contiguous memory blocks. D Multiple other data structures can be implemented using arrays. The amount of memory to be allocated should be known beforehand. The module calls array storage static and contrasts it with dynamically allocated nodes. A fixed array requires a capacity in advance; constant access and reuse as a storage implementation are benefits, while contiguous storage alone is not the capacity drawback. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6, 7, 5. A correct Preallocated fixed capacity is the disadvantage illustrated by static array implementations. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 5. B incorrect Constant indexed access is an advantage, not a disadvantage. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 5. C incorrect Contiguity itself does not state the capacity limitation. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 5. D incorrect Supporting other structures is useful rather than a disadvantage. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 5.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 23 · Q00291
records.text: Q00291 Question 23 DSA33 For selection sort on n elements, n>=2, count only exchanges between distinct positions and omit the final one-element suffix. What is the maximum number of swaps? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A n - 1 B 1 C n D n - 2 A. n - 1 Selection sort places the minimum remaining element into each successive position. After n-1 such placements, the last position is determined automatically. Each placement needs at most one exchange between distinct positions, so the maximum is n-1. This count excludes self-swaps and the redundant final-position call that some implementations include. The choice of input can require an exchange on every one of those meaningful passes. A correct There are n-1 meaningful placements, each requiring at most one exchange. B incorrect More than one exchange can be needed for larger n. C incorrect n counts an extra redundant final swap call under another convention. D incorrect n-2 omits a possible exchange on a meaningful pass.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 24 · Q00293
records.text: Q00293 Question 24 DSA11 DSA13 In an infix-to-prefix conversion algorithm that temporarily holds pending operators and parentheses using last-in, first-out access, which abstract data type supplies that access discipline? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Stack B Queue C Binary tree D Linked list A. Stack Pending operators must be retrieved in reverse order when grouping or precedence requires them to be emitted. A stack provides that last-in, first-out discipline. An expression tree is another possible representation for conversion, but it is not the requested pending-operator ADT in this specified algorithm. A queue retrieves the oldest entry first, while a linked list alone describes storage links without prescribing the needed access policy. A correct A stack retrieves the latest pending operator first. B incorrect A queue uses first-in, first-out access. C incorrect An expression tree can support another conversion method but is not this pending-operator ADT. D incorrect A linked list can implement storage but alone does not specify LIFO behavior.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 25 · Q00294
records.text: Q00294 Question 25 DSA11 Which one of the following is the process of inserting an element in the stack? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Insert B Add C Push D None of the above Push The stack terminology explicitly names adding an element Push. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A incorrect Insert is a generic action rather than the given operation name. See assigned PDF 6. B incorrect Add is descriptive rather than the module stack name. See assigned PDF 6. C correct Push is defined as adding an element to the stack. See assigned PDF 6. D incorrect C is explicitly defined, so none is false. See assigned PDF 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 26 · Q00371
records.text: Q00371 Question 26 DSA-S01 How many cases are there, which are used to compare various data structure's execution time in a relative manner? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A 2 B 3 C 4 D 5 Three: best, average, worst. DSA05 names best, average, and worst as the ordinary cases for comparing costs on inputs of equal size. Average additionally needs an input distribution. Counting these cases gives three. This is a classification of input cases, rather than a count of resources, data structures, or asymptotic bound notations. A incorrect Two omits one of the three named categories: best, average, and worst case. B correct The note lists three ordinary fixed-size input cases: best, average, and worst. C incorrect Four does not match the three ordinary input-case categories listed in DSA05. D incorrect Five adds categories outside the stated best, average, and worst input-case classification.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 27 · Q00372
records.text: Q00372 Question 27 DSA-S01 Which case of data structure operation takes maximum time? Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Worst Case B Average Case C Best Case D None of the above Worst case DSA05 distinguishes best, average, and worst over inputs of the same size. Worst selects the largest runtime; best selects the smallest, while average takes an expectation under a distribution. Therefore Worst Case directly matches maximum time. This input-case distinction is independent of whether the resulting cost function is described with O, Ω, or Θ notation. A correct Worst case takes the maximum operation cost over valid inputs of the same size. B incorrect Average case computes an expected cost under a distribution instead of selecting the maximum. C incorrect Best case selects the minimum cost, the opposite extremum from the question. D incorrect Worst Case is offered and directly identifies the requested maximum-time input case.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 28 · Q00375
records.text: Q00375 Question 28 DSA18 DSA04 DSA05 Which listed characteristic is a binary-tree shape condition rather than a general functional-correctness or resource-cost criterion for arbitrary data-structure operations? Interpret completeness as the complete-tree shape property. Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Completeness B Correctness C Time Complexity D Space Complexity A. Completeness Correctness asks whether operations produce their specified results. Time and space complexity measure operation counts and memory use under a resource model. Completeness, under the explicit meaning supplied here, instead describes how a binary tree’s levels are filled: earlier levels are full and the last fills from the left. It is a particular shape condition, rather than a universal assessment criterion for every data structure. A correct Completeness describes a particular binary-tree shape. B incorrect Correctness assesses whether an operation meets its specification. C incorrect Time complexity assesses operation cost. D incorrect Space complexity assesses memory cost.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 29 · Q00377
records.text: Q00377 Question 29 DSA14 DSA16 Which abstract data types permit deleting an element at the front and inserting an element at the rear? Include types that also permit additional endpoint operations. Select all that apply. Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Stacks B Queues C Deques D Binary search tree B. Queues; C. Deques An ordinary queue supplies exactly the stated FIFO operations: insertion at the rear and removal at the front. A deque allows insertion and removal at both ends, which includes those same two operations as a subset. The question explicitly includes types with additional endpoint capabilities, so both qualify. A stack exposes a single LIFO top, and a BST organizes access by keys rather than front and rear. A incorrect A stack exposes a single LIFO top rather than these FIFO endpoints. B correct A queue enqueues at rear and dequeues at front. C correct A deque includes both requested operations among its endpoint capabilities. D incorrect A BST uses key-based tree operations rather than front/rear endpoints.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 30 · Q00379
records.text: Q00379 Question 30 DSA34 DSA36 DSA37 DSA39 Which algorithms have tight worst-case time Theta(n²)? Use ordinary array comparison-sort implementations; radix sort uses counting-based passes with fixed digit count and fixed radix. Select all that apply. Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Merge sort B Insertion sort C Quick sort D Radix sort B. Insertion sort; C. Quick sort Insertion sort on reverse input shifts a growing sorted prefix, totaling quadratic work. Quicksort repeatedly choosing an extreme pivot also accumulates quadratic partition work. Ordinary merge sort instead performs linear work at logarithmically many levels. Under the explicitly fixed digit count and radix, radix sorting is linear in n. Tight bounds distinguish these actual growth rates from the looser quadratic upper bounds that faster algorithms also satisfy. A incorrect Ordinary merge sort has tight n log n worst time. B correct Reverse-order insertion gives quadratic shifts. C correct Repeated extreme quicksort pivots give quadratic work. D incorrect Fixed-width, fixed-radix counting passes give linear time.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 31 · Q00380
records.text: Q00380 Question 31 DSA32 DSA33 DSA34 In which sorting algorithm does the largest element "bubble" to the end of the list at each pass? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Insertion sort D Heap sort Bubble sort Repeated adjacent out-of-order swaps push the largest item toward the final position in a left-to-right pass. This is exactly the bubble-sort mechanism. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 4, 3, 11. A correct Adjacent comparisons bubble the largest to its proper end. See assigned PDF 4, 3, 3, 11. B incorrect Selection finds a minimum and swaps it into position rather than bubbling through adjacent pairs. See assigned PDF 4, 3, 3, 11. C incorrect Insertion inserts each new element into a sorted prefix. See assigned PDF 4, 3, 3, 11. D incorrect Heap sort removes a root maximum using tree adjustment. See assigned PDF 4, 3, 3, 11.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 32 · Q00381
records.text: Q00381 Question 32 DSA32 DSA34 DSA36 DSA37 DSA33 Which algorithms have tight best-case time Theta(n)? Use early-exit bubble sort, ordinary quicksort, ordinary array mergesort without merge-skipping, and standard insertion sort. Select all that apply. Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort A. Bubble sort; D. Insertion sort Early-exit bubble sort terminates after one complete no-swap pass on already sorted input, so its best case is linear. Insertion sort also checks each new item once without shifting it on sorted input. Ordinary quicksort still partitions across logarithmically many balanced levels in its best case, and ordinary mergesort still performs its merges. Thus exactly the bubble and insertion implementations have the requested linear best case. A correct The no-swap early exit gives a linear sorted-input pass. B incorrect Ordinary quicksort has n log n best growth. C incorrect Without merge-skipping, mergesort still uses n log n work. D correct Sorted input needs one ordering check per insertion pass.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 33 · Q00382
records.text: Q00382 Question 33 DSA32 DSA34 DSA33 DSA37 Which ordinary iterative array sorting implementations use constant auxiliary element storage? Use buffered mergesort for C. Select all that apply. Apply the naming, type and syntax rules before deciding whether an option can be used as stated. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort A. Bubble sort; B. Selection sort; D. Insertion sort Bubble sort reuses one temporary element for each adjacent swap. Selection sort retains the minimum position while scanning, then exchanges elements using the same fixed-size temporary storage. Insertion sort saves one item and shifts preceding entries within the original array before filling the gap. The indices and saved elements stay fixed in number as n grows, giving constant auxiliary storage for A, B and D. Buffered mergesort instead needs a linear auxiliary buffer. A correct Adjacent swaps reuse a single temporary element and a fixed number of indices. B correct The suffix scan retains a minimum index; the exchange needs only fixed-size temporary storage. C incorrect The specified buffered array mergesort allocates a linear auxiliary merge buffer. D correct One saved item and fixed-size indices suffice while larger entries shift within the original array.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 34 · Q00383
records.text: Q00383 Question 34 DSA36 DSA32 DSA34 Which sorting algorithm uses a pivot element to partition the list into two sublists? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Quick sort D Insertion sort Quick sort The source quicksort procedure chooses a pivot and partitions around it before recursively sorting both sides. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 11, 4, 3. A incorrect Bubble uses adjacent exchanges without a pivot partition. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. B incorrect Selection chooses the minimum for its next position. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. C correct Quicksort explicitly chooses and positions a pivot. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. D incorrect Insertion extends a sorted prefix rather than partitioning by a pivot. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 35 · Q00384
records.text: Q00384 Question 35 DSA32 DSA37 DSA33 DSA31 Which sorting implementations preserve the relative input order of equal keys? Use bubble sort with strict adjacent swaps, standard exchange-based selection sort, ordinary in-place quicksort, and mergesort with left-first tie handling. Select all that apply. Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Quick sort D Merge sort A. Bubble sort; D. Merge sort Strict bubble swaps never exchange equal adjacent keys, so equal records retain their input order. Left-first handling during merging likewise preserves the order of ties from the left and right runs. Standard selection sort can reverse ties through a distant minimum exchange, and ordinary quicksort partitioning does not guarantee stable order. The specified implementation details therefore make bubble and merge the two stable choices. A correct Strict adjacent swaps preserve equal-key order. B incorrect A distant minimum exchange can reverse equal records. C incorrect Ordinary in-place partitioning does not guarantee stability. D correct Taking the left run first on ties preserves equal-key order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 36 · Q00385
records.text: Q00385 Question 36 DSA37 DSA39 DSA32 DSA33 DSA34 Which algorithm has tight Theta(n log n) time in both the average and worst cases? Use ordinary array implementations; radix sort uses fixed digit count and fixed radix. Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Merge sort D Radix sort C. Merge sort Ordinary mergesort performs linear merging at each of logarithmically many levels, giving n log n work regardless of input order. Bubble and selection have quadratic average and worst time. Fixed-width, fixed-radix counting passes instead give radix sort linear time, so radix does not have the requested tight n log n growth. Specifying tight bounds excludes faster methods that would also satisfy the looser Big-O upper bound. A incorrect Bubble has quadratic average and worst time. B incorrect Selection makes quadratic comparisons in every order. C correct Ordinary mergesort has tight n log n average and worst time. D incorrect With fixed digits and radix, radix sorting has tight linear time.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 37 · Q00386
records.text: Q00386 Question 37 DSA39 DSA32 DSA34 DSA33 For a large array of nonnegative integer keys with fixed digit count and fixed radix, which listed ordinary algorithm can achieve linear time using counting-based digit passes and O(n+r) auxiliary storage? Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Radix sort D Insertion sort C. Radix sort With digit count d and radix r fixed, the radix cost O(d(n+r)) reduces to linear growth in n. Its counting-based stable passes use auxiliary storage for output and digit counts. The key assumptions make this an eligible radix-sorting workload rather than an unspecified large-list claim. Bubble, selection and insertion use constant extra element storage in their ordinary forms and can require quadratic work. A incorrect Bubble uses adjacent comparisons and can require quadratic work. B incorrect Selection uses quadratic comparisons and constant extra element storage. C correct Radix uses the stated digit passes and auxiliary storage. D incorrect Insertion uses prefix shifts and can require quadratic work.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 38 · Q00387
records.text: Q00387 Question 38 DSA39 DSA32 DSA33 DSA37 Which listed sorting algorithm orders fixed-length strings by stably processing individual character positions, without using whole-string comparison operations? Assume an ordered finite character alphabet and LSD passes. Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Merge sort D Radix sort D. Radix sort Strings can be compared lexicographically, but the stated question asks for a digit-based mechanism rather than whole-key comparisons. LSD radix sorting treats each character position as a digit, stably sorting from the last position toward the first. Stability retains the ordering established by earlier passes. Bubble, selection and merge use comparisons between keys in their ordinary forms, so they do not implement this specified character-pass mechanism. A incorrect Ordinary bubble sort compares adjacent whole keys. B incorrect Ordinary selection chooses a minimum through key comparisons. C incorrect Ordinary merge compares the fronts of sorted key runs. D correct LSD radix uses stable character-position passes from least significant to most significant.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 39 · Q00388
records.text: Q00388 Question 39 DSA34 How many passes does an insertion sort algorithm consist of? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A N B N-1 C N+1 D N2 N-1 The first element is already a sorted prefix. Each of the remaining N-1 elements is inserted once: the source starts with the first two, then adds the third, and so on. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect N counts the initial singleton as an insertion pass. See assigned PDF 3. B correct There is one insertion for each position 2 through N. See assigned PDF 3. C incorrect N+1 adds two passes with no corresponding elements. See assigned PDF 3. D incorrect N squared is a work bound, not the count of outer passes. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 40 · Q00389
records.text: Q00389 Question 40 DSA34 What is the running time of an insertion sort algorithm if the input is pre-sorted? Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage. A O(N2) B O(N log N) C O(N) D O(M log N) O(N) For sorted input every new item already belongs after its predecessor. Each of N-1 prefix extensions needs constant comparison work and no shifts, giving Theta(N). Big-O choices are interpreted as tight orders. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect Quadratic is the adverse-input bound, not the tight sorted-input cost. See assigned PDF 3. B incorrect N log N adds work not performed by this insertion process. See assigned PDF 3. C correct One constant check per extension gives linear work. See assigned PDF 3. D incorrect M is undefined and no M-dependent process is given. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 41 · Q00390
records.text: Q00390 Question 41 DSA34 Which of the following examples represent the worst case input for an insertion sort? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A array in sorted order B array sorted in reverse order C normal unsorted array D large array array sorted in reverse order Reverse order forces each inserted item to move through the whole preceding prefix. The movement total 1+2+...+(n-1)=n(n-1)/2 is quadratic. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect Sorted input needs no shifts. See assigned PDF 3. B correct Each next element is smaller than every element in the prefix. See assigned PDF 3. C incorrect An arbitrary unsorted array need not maximize all insertion distances. See assigned PDF 3. D incorrect Large size alone does not determine relative ordering or maximal shifts. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 42 · Q00391
records.text: Q00391 Question 42 DSA33 Which scenario specifically favors selection sort’s small number of record exchanges, when records themselves are moved and comparisons are cheap? Interpret large values as large records and small keys as inexpensive comparison keys. Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A The input is already sorted B A large file has to be sorted C Large values need to be sorted with small keys D Small values need to be sorted with large keys C. Large values need to be sorted with small keys Selection sort scans suffixes and makes quadratic comparisons regardless of the initial order, but it performs at most one meaningful exchange per placement. That tradeoff can be useful when physically moving a large record is expensive while comparing its small key is cheap. A large file or sorted input alone does not offer this advantage. Expensive large-key comparisons instead make selection’s many comparisons less attractive. A incorrect Sorted order does not reduce selection’s quadratic comparison count. B incorrect Large file size alone does not identify the expensive-move advantage. C correct Large records with cheap keys match the many-comparisons/few-exchanges tradeoff. D incorrect Expensive comparisons with cheap moves do not favor that tradeoff.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 43 · Q00392
records.text: Q00392 Question 43 DSA33 What is the advantage of selection sort over other sorting techniques? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A It requires no additional storage space B It is scalable C It works best for inputs which are already sorted D It is faster than any other sorting technique Constant extra element storage, conventionally called in-place sorting. DSA33 says selection uses constant extra element storage, which is the conventional meaning of A’s no-additional-storage phrasing. It still needs a few temporary values, so literally zero bytes would be inaccurate. Its quadratic comparisons do not improve on already sorted input, and the note gives no universal scalability or fastest-algorithm claim. A names the valid conventional benefit. A correct Interpreted conventionally as in-place, selection uses constant extra element storage rather than an auxiliary array. B incorrect Quadratic comparisons do not provide an unqualified scalability advantage for growing datasets. C incorrect Selection makes the same quadratic comparisons even on already sorted input. D incorrect No universal fastest claim follows; selection trades few moves for many comparisons.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 44 · Q00393
records.text: Q00393 Question 44 DSA37 What is an external sorting algorithm? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A Algorithm that uses tape or disk during the sort B Algorithm that uses main memory during the sort C Algorithm that involves swapping D Algorithm that are considered 'in place' Sorting using external storage such as disk or tape. DSA37 defines external sorting through datasets beyond main memory and buffered disk runs. Option A captures this distinguishing external-storage use. Main memory may still hold buffers, but using it alone does not define external sorting. Swapping and being in place are separate implementation properties and do not identify whether the working dataset resides externally. A correct Tape or disk stores external runs when the working dataset does not fit wholly in main memory. B incorrect Main-memory use alone does not distinguish external sorting; external algorithms also use memory for buffers. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 74 · Q00424
records.text: Q00424 Question 74 DSA11 DSA45 A serial-storage interface restricts insertion and removal to the same current end: an item must be removed before any item stored earlier beneath it can be removed. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 87 · Q00714
records.text: Q00714 Question 87 DSA19 During ordinary lookup in a binary search tree with distinct keys and strict left-smaller/right-larger ordering, which rule correctly chooses the next subtree or recognizes a match? Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option. A If the searched key is less than the root, go to left. B If the searched key is larger than the root, go to left. C If the searched key is equal to the root, go to left. D None. A. If the searched key is less than the root, go to left. The BST invariant puts every key in the current node’s left subtree below that node’s key and every right-subtree key above it. A target smaller than the current key must therefore be sought on the left. A larger target belongs on the right, while equality finishes the lookup at the current node. This directional rule relies on BST ordering, not merely on having a binary shape. A correct A smaller target follows the left subtree under the BST invariant. B incorrect A larger target follows right, not left. C incorrect Equality is a successful match rather than a reason to continue left. D incorrect A supplies a valid search rule.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 103 · Q01204
records.text: Q01204 Question 103 DSA12 DSA14 Which task requires FIFO service rather than the LIFO service of a stack used as the sole pending-item ADT? In D, asynchronous transfer must deliver buffered items in arrival order. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A String reversal B Recursion C Backtracking D Asynchronous buffered transfer with mandatory arrival-order delivery D. Asynchronous buffered transfer with mandatory arrival-order delivery Stacks support reversal by popping items in reverse insertion order. They also manage nested recursive calls and backtracking through the most recent pending context or choice. The stated asynchronous-transfer contract instead requires older buffered items to be delivered before newer arrivals. That is FIFO service, so an ordinary queue supplies the needed ordering. A single stack’s LIFO removal rule does not meet this explicitly ordered buffering contract. A incorrect Reversal uses the stack’s reverse insertion order. B incorrect Nested recursive calls return most-recent-first. C incorrect Backtracking resumes the latest pending choice. D correct Arrival-order delivery requires FIFO rather than a single stack’s LIFO.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 111 · Q01578
records.text: Q01578 Question 111 DSA03 DSA09 An owning dynamically allocated linked-list API must provide item search, insertion and removal. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 112 · Q01579
records.text: Q01579 Question 112 DSA23 DSA18 Consider a max-heap of n>=3 distinct keys, stored in ordinary level-order array form. Its binary tree is full: every internal node has two children. Which statement is false? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A The root is the biggest element. B The second biggest element is necessarily found at depth 1 (root is at depth 0) C The search for the smallest element can be accomplished in O(log n) time (worst case) D The last element of the array is necessarily the right most child on the lowest level. C is false: finding the minimum can require Theta(n) time. The root contains the maximum key. With distinct keys, the second largest must be one of its children, since a deeper key has a larger ancestor above it. Completeness places the final occupied array slot at the rightmost occupied position of the lowest level. The minimum can occur at any leaf, however, so finding it may require a linear scan rather than logarithmic worst-case time. C is therefore false. A incorrect The max-heap order makes the root the largest key, so this is true rather than the requested false statement. B incorrect Distinct keys ensure the second largest is a root child, so this is true. C correct The minimum may require scanning linearly many leaves; the logarithmic worst-case claim is false. D incorrect Level-order storage of a complete heap ends at the rightmost occupied position on the lowest level.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 113 · Q01580
records.text: Q01580 Question 113 DSA37 For ordinary top-down array mergesort on n=8 items with left-first ties and no merge-skipping, which description alone guarantees the maximum possible number of key comparisons across the merges? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A When the list is initially sorted in the "reverse" order B When the list is already sorted in the "right" order C When the list contains all similar elements D When the list contains all distinct elements E None of the choices is correct E. None of the choices is correct Maximum merge comparisons depend on the interleaving of the sorted runs, rather than merely on a broad input label. Sorted or reverse-sorted input produces separated runs, and equal keys let left-first merging exhaust a run early. Distinct keys permit a worst interleaving but do not force one; already sorted distinct keys are a counterexample. None of A–D therefore guarantees the requested exact maximum. A incorrect Reverse order alone does not force worst interleavings. B incorrect Sorted runs can be merged with an early exhaustion of one side. C incorrect Left-first equal keys exhaust a run without maximum interleaving. D incorrect Distinct keys can already be sorted, so distinctness is insufficient. E correct No preceding description alone guarantees the exact maximum comparison count.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 114 · Q01618
records.text: Q01618 Question 114 DSA29 If a sorted list contains 100 elements, what is the maximum number of comparisons to make to search for an element using binary searching algorithm? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A None of the choices are correct B 100 C 10 D 7 E 50 7 With one midpoint-key comparison per visited node, the maximum probes are floor(log2 100)+1=7, since 64<=100<128. Equivalently seven binary levels can distinguish up to 127 keys. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect Seven is present as D. See assigned PDF 3. B incorrect 100 is a complete linear scan. See assigned PDF 3. C incorrect 10 exceeds the needed halving depth. See assigned PDF 3. D correct Seven midpoint probes suffice in the worst case. See assigned PDF 3. E incorrect 50 counts only the first halving, not the number of probes. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 115 · Q01619
records.text: Q01619 Question 115 DSA02 DSA08 DSA10 For ordinary representations without an extra positional index, which listed structure guarantees O(1) worst-case access to an arbitrary valid logical position as its length grows? Use fixed-size elements and unit-cost address arithmetic. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Singly linked list B Doubly linked list C Every listed linked structure guarantees constant-time access to an arbitrary logical position. D Circular linked list E Array E. Array An array computes an element address from its base address, the requested index and the fixed element size, giving constant-time access. Ordinary singly, doubly and circular linked lists instead follow links to reach a logical position; even starting from the nearer endpoint leaves linear worst-case traversal. The replacement aggregate claim is false because those linked structures lack a direct positional index. Array is therefore the unique matching choice. A incorrect A singly linked list may traverse linearly many successor links. B incorrect A doubly linked list still has linear worst-case access to middle positions. C incorrect The listed linked structures do not all have constant-time arbitrary positional lookup. D incorrect Circularity changes how a chain ends, not how a logical position is located. E correct An array computes the address directly with fixed-size element arithmetic.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 116 · Q01620
records.text: Q01620 Question 116 DSA19 DSA29 DSA23 Which listed representations guarantee O(log n) worst-case arbitrary-key lookup under these implementations? Use a height-balanced BST for A, an ordinary singly linked list for C, an ordinary binary heap for D, and a sorted random-access array with binary search for E. Select all that apply. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Height-balanced BST B A and C C Singly linked list D Heap E Sorted random-access array with binary search A. Height-balanced BST; E. Sorted random-access array with binary search A height-balanced BST has logarithmic height, so following its ordered search path takes logarithmic worst-case time. A sorted random-access array supports logarithmic binary-search probes. An ordinary singly linked list must traverse links, and a heap does not order entire subtrees by arbitrary search keys. Thus the combined A-and-C claim fails because C lacks the guarantee, while A and E independently meet it. A correct Balance bounds the BST search path logarithmically. B incorrect C lacks the logarithmic guarantee, so A and C is false. C incorrect Singly linked lookup may scan all nodes. D incorrect Heap order privileges the extreme but not arbitrary-key lookup. E correct Binary search on a sorted random-access array is logarithmic.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 117 · Q00426B
records.text: Q00426B Question 117 DSA14 A queue is a ? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A FIFO (First In First Out) list B LIFO (Last In First Out) list C Ordered array D Linear tree FIFO (First In First Out) list The source expressly calls queues First in First out lists. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7. A correct FIFO preserves arrival order. See assigned PDF 7. B incorrect LIFO names a stack. See assigned PDF 7. C incorrect An ordered array is one possible storage form, not the abstract queue rule. See assigned PDF 7. D incorrect Linear tree is not the source queue definition. See assigned PDF 7.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 118 · Q00394
records.text: Q00394 Question 118 DSA37 What is an internal sorting algorithm? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Algorithm that uses tape or disk during the sort B Algorithm that uses main memory during the sort C Algorithm that involves swapping D Algorithm that are considered 'in place' Sorting whose working dataset fits in main memory. DSA37 defines internal sorting by fitting the working dataset in memory. Option B expresses that main-memory setting. In contrast, external sorting handles disk-backed runs when data exceeds memory. Swapping is an operation used by some algorithms, and in-place describes auxiliary storage; neither determines whether a sort is internal. A incorrect Tape or disk working data characterizes external sorting rather than the main-memory internal setting. B correct Internal sorting keeps its working dataset in main memory, matching the definition in DSA37. C incorrect Swapping is an implementation operation and does not define the location of the working dataset. D incorrect In-place concerns auxiliary element storage; an internal sort may still use a separate memory buffer.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 119 · SM0008
records.text: SM0008 Question 119 DSA29 What is the time complexity order of binary searching algorithm? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A O(n^3) B O(n) C O(log n) D O(1) O(log n) The stated time is proportional to log2 n because each midpoint decision discards half the remaining ordered interval. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3. A incorrect Cubic does not match repeated halving. See assigned PDF 3. B incorrect Linear is the source sequential-search order. See assigned PDF 3. C correct Logarithmic is the explicit binary-search order. See assigned PDF 3. D incorrect Constant time occurs for an immediate match, not a general search bound. See assigned PDF 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 120 · SM0016
records.text: SM0016 Question 120 DSA36 What is the tightest listed worst-case time bound for ordinary quicksort when each partition may choose an extreme pivot? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A O(n) B O(n^2) C O(2^n) D O(n log n) B. O(n^2) An extreme pivot leaves one empty part and one part with only a single element removed. Repeating that pattern makes partition work proportional to n+(n-1)+… rather than distributing it across balanced levels. The sum is quadratic. Balanced partitions explain the n log n alternative, but they are not guaranteed in this worst case. Exponential time is a looser upper bound, not the tightest listed one. A incorrect Linear time does not cover repeated partition scans. B correct Repeated extreme pivots produce quadratic total work. C incorrect Exponential is a much looser upper bound. D incorrect n log n requires suitably balanced or expected partitions.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 121 · SM0043
records.text: SM0043 Question 121 DSA25 Under universal hashing, one random family member is chosen for a table independently of a fixed key set. Which claims are false? Interpret C as an unconditional superiority claim. Select all that apply. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A In universal hashing a hash function is selected randomly from a set of hash functions for each key B In universal hashing a hash function is selected from a set of hash functions independent of keys C A single fixed hash function is always better than universal hashing at reducing collisions. D Universal hashing controls collision probability without guaranteeing zero collisions. A. In universal hashing a hash function is selected randomly from a set of hash functions for each key; C. A single fixed hash function is always better than universal hashing at reducing collisions. Universal hashing chooses one random function for the table and then uses it consistently, rather than selecting an unrelated function afresh for each key. Its purpose is to control collision probability for a fixed key set. It does not establish that a single fixed function is always better for avoiding collisions. Thus A and C are false, while independent table-level choice and probability control are the valid principles. A correct The chosen function is reused for the table rather than chosen afresh per key. B incorrect Independence from the fixed key set is the stated selection principle. C correct Unconditional fixed-function superiority does not follow and contradicts the randomized collision-control purpose. D incorrect Universal choice controls collision probability without promising no collisions.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 122 · SM0050

Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. See assigned PDF 9. C incorrect External nodes are defined by having no child. See assigned PDF 9. D incorrect Internal nodes have at least one child, which does not imply parentlessness. See assigned PDF 9.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 123 · SM0053
records.text: SM0053 Question 123 DSA08 Linked list data structure is ____________ type of data structure. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.
