records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 124 · SM0064
records.text: SM0064 Question 124 DSA17 Assume there is a line of patients waiting for service from a clinic. Seriously sick patients should get service first. Which data structure is the most appropriate for this real-world problem? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Tree B Queue C Stack D Priority Queue Priority Queue Give each patient a key representing medical urgency and serve by that priority. This adapts the module associated-key priority queue to the stated urgency rule. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 8, 7. A incorrect A tree alone does not define urgency-based service. See assigned PDF 8, 7. B incorrect A plain FIFO queue serves arrival order rather than illness severity. See assigned PDF 8, 7. C incorrect A stack gives recent arrivals precedence, regardless of severity. See assigned PDF 8, 7. D correct Associated priority keys represent how urgently each patient needs service. See assigned PDF 8, 7.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 125 · SM0076
records.text: SM0076 Question 125 DSA42 For an input graph, Depth First Traversal (DFT) algorithm uses ________ data structure to traverse. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Priority queue B Tree C Queue D Stack Stack DSA42 says DFS recursively explores an unvisited neighbor to completion before returning. The recursive call stack stores return points; an explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work-first order. A queue would change that discipline, while a priority queue or tree alone does not encode the required depth-first frontier behavior. A incorrect Priority service follows priority keys and does not guarantee finishing the latest active branch first. B incorrect A tree may represent traversal results, but it does not identify the standard DFS pending-work discipline. C incorrect FIFO queue order produces breadth-first pending work rather than the required latest-pending-work behavior. D correct A stack, explicit or supplied by recursion, preserves return points and latest-pending-work-first order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 126 · SM0082
records.text: SM0082 Question 126 DSA11 Which statement is true about the pop() operation of Stack data structures? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A pop() returns the end/top element but it doesn't delete that element B pop() removes the end/top element from the stack C pop() inserts a new element at the middle of stack D pop() inserts a new element at the beginning/bottom of stack pop() removes the end/top element from the stack The pop pseudocode reads the current top and decrements top, so the element is logically removed. Merely inspecting without deletion is peek. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A incorrect This describes peek, not pop. See assigned PDF 6, 6. B correct Pop removes the current top by decreasing top. See assigned PDF 6, 6. C incorrect Pop does not insert, and stack insertion is only at top. See assigned PDF 6, 6. D incorrect Pop is removal, not bottom insertion. See assigned PDF 6, 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 127 · SM0210
records.text: SM0210 Question 127 DSA09 DSA06 A singly linked list of n nodes maintains only its head; there is no tail pointer or index. Appending traverses to the last node before linking a new node. Which listed bounds hold for its worst-case time? Select all that apply. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A O(n) B Theta(1) C Theta(n) D O(1) A. O(n); C. Theta(n) The append operation begins at the head and must follow the chain to locate its final node. That requires linear traversal, followed by a constant amount of link work. Its tight worst-case bound is therefore Theta(n), which also implies the upper bound O(n). Neither constant-time choice holds as the list grows. Maintaining a separate tail would change the operation cost, but that representation is explicitly excluded. A correct O(n) is a valid upper bound on the traversal. B incorrect The growing traversal prevents a constant tight bound. C correct Theta(n) is the tight traversal bound. D incorrect O(1) does not bound arbitrary head-only append traversal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 128 · SM0213
records.text: SM0213 Question 128 DSA29 DSA28 DSA25 DSA42 Which ordinary search method requires its input key sequence to be sorted before using comparisons to discard the half that cannot contain a target? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Hash search B Depth-first search C Binary search D Linear search C. Binary search Binary search compares a target with the midpoint of an ordered interval, then safely discards one half. That elimination depends on sorted order. Linear search can scan unsorted values, hashing selects addresses from keys rather than sorted positions, and depth-first search follows graph adjacency. The revised alternatives therefore have clear operational meanings, and Binary search uniquely matches the stated ordered-half-elimination requirement. A incorrect Hash lookup uses computed addresses rather than a sorted input interval. B incorrect Depth-first search follows adjacency, not ordered-array halves. C correct Binary search needs ordering to safely discard a comparison-selected half. D incorrect Linear scanning permits unsorted input.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 129 · SM0229
records.text: SM0229 Question 129 DSA19 DSA20 Given a binary search tree, which traversal type would print the values in the nodes in sorted order? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Pre-order B Pre-order and Post-order C In-order D Post-order In-order All left-subtree keys precede the root, and all right-subtree keys follow it. Recursively visiting left, parent, right therefore emits increasing keys. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9. A incorrect Preorder prints root before smaller left keys. See assigned PDF 9, 9. B incorrect Including preorder cannot guarantee increasing order. See assigned PDF 9, 9. C correct Inorder matches left keys < root < right keys recursively. See assigned PDF 9, 9. D incorrect Postorder prints the root after larger right keys. See assigned PDF 9, 9.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 130 · SM0240
records.text: SM0240 Question 130 DSA11 DSA12 If a sequence of operations: push(1), push(2), pop, push(1), push(2), pop, pop, pop, push(2), pop are performed on a stack, the sequence of popped values is: Trace the initial state and update only the fields affected by each permitted operation. A 2,1,2,2,1 B 2,2,1,1,2 C 2,1,2,2,2 D 2,2,1,2,2 2,2,1,1,2 Trace bottom-to-top: [1], [1,2], pop 2; [1,1], [1,1,2], pop 2; pop 1; pop 1; [2], pop 2. Popped sequence is 2,2,1,1,2. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A incorrect The second pop is 2, not 1. See assigned PDF 6. B correct Exactly matches all five top removals. See assigned PDF 6. C incorrect The second pop is again 2, not 1. See assigned PDF 6. D incorrect The fourth pop removes the original bottom 1, not 2. See assigned PDF 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 131 · SM0279
records.text: SM0279 Question 131 DSA18 DSA01 Which of the following is FALSE in Data Structures and Algorithms? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A A tree contains a cycle B Tree is a non-linear data structure C A tree is a connected graph D A tree with n nodes contains (n-1) edges A tree contains a cycle Unique root paths and one parent per nonroot node exclude cycles. The n-1 nonroot nodes each contribute one parent edge, making the rooted tree connected with n-1 edges. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9, 2. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 132 · SM0282
records.text: SM0282 Question 132 DSA15 A fixed-capacity circular array queue uses front and size indices, modulo slot reuse, and no shifting or resizing. Under unit-cost index arithmetic, what is the tightest listed worst-case pair for enqueue and dequeue, including full/empty checks? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A O(n), O(1) B O(1), O(n) C O(1), O(1) D O(n), O(n) C. O(1), O(1) Enqueue computes a slot from front and size, writes one item and updates the count. Dequeue reads the front slot, advances front modulo capacity and decreases the count. Full or empty checks also inspect only constant-size state. No operation shifts or resizes the array, so each uses constant work in the stated model. The linear alternatives are looser bounds rather than the requested tight pair. A incorrect Linear enqueue is looser than the constant cost of this implementation. B incorrect Linear dequeue is looser than its constant index update cost. C correct Both endpoint operations use constant work. D incorrect Both linear bounds are looser than the requested tight pair.

A Queues B Linked-list C Tree D Stack Tree The module classifies trees as nonlinear, while queues and stacks are linear sequences and a linked list is a next-pointer chain. See assigned PDF 2, 4, 6. C correct Tree is an explicit nonlinear example. See assigned PDF 2, 4, 6. D incorrect Stack is an explicit linear example. See assigned PDF 2, 4, 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 134 · SS149
records.text: SS149 Question 134 DSA41 DSA14 For this question, an indirect queue application means using FIFO as auxiliary storage inside a graph traversal algorithm, rather than directly modeling a waiting line or scheduling service. Which listed description fits? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Operating systems schedule jobs (with equal priority) in the order of arrival (e.g., a print queue). B Simulation of real-world queues such as lines at a ticket counter or any other first-come first-served scenario requires a queue. C Auxiliary data structure for algorithms D Multiprogramming C. Auxiliary data structure for algorithms The supplied convention distinguishes an algorithm’s internal work storage from a real-world waiting-line model. BFS uses a queue to hold its discovered but not yet explored vertices, so auxiliary algorithm storage is the matching category. Equal-priority job scheduling and ticket-line simulation directly model service waiting. Multiprogramming is a broader operating-system setting and does not specifically name the internal graph-traversal role requested here. A incorrect Arrival-order print scheduling directly models a service queue. B incorrect Ticket-line simulation directly models real-world waiting. C correct An algorithmic frontier queue is auxiliary storage inside graph traversal. D incorrect Multiprogramming is a broad execution setting, not the specified internal traversal role.

records.text: SS158 Question 135 DSA11 A queue in which the item most recently added is always the first one out refers to: Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A FIFO queue B Real time queue C Priority queue D LIFO queue LIFO queue Most recently added first removed is LIFO by definition. The name LIFO queue here describes stack discipline rather than the ordinary FIFO queue. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6, 7, 8. A incorrect FIFO removes the earliest insertion. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 8. B incorrect Real time alone does not specify last-in removal. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 8. C incorrect Priority depends on keys, not necessarily insertion recency. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 8. D correct LIFO exactly names last-in-first-out service. See assigned PDF 6, 7, 8.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 136 · AM0394

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 137 · AM0395
records.text: AM0395 Question 137 DSA14 Which data structure follows the FIFO (First-In-First-Out) principle? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree Queue FIFO is explicitly the queue policy: enqueue at rear and dequeue at front. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 6. A incorrect Stack is LIFO. See assigned PDF 7, 6. B correct Queue preserves insertion order for removal. See assigned PDF 7, 6. C incorrect A linked list can implement a queue but does not inherently impose FIFO. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 138 · AM0396
records.text: AM0396 Question 138 DSA10 DSA11 Which listed representation permits insertion and removal at either endpoint in constant time? Use ordinary stack and FIFO queue interfaces, and interpret C as a doubly linked list maintaining both head and tail. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Doubly linked list with head and tail D Binary tree C. Doubly linked list with head and tail A doubly linked list stores predecessor and successor links, while head and tail provide direct access to both endpoints. Inserting or removing there updates a fixed number of links, including the empty and singleton cases. Ordinary stack and FIFO queue interfaces expose fewer endpoint operations, and a binary tree has no corresponding two-end sequence guarantee. The explicit linked-list variant is essential because singly linked tail deletion needs a predecessor traversal. A incorrect A stack exposes insertion/removal at one top only. B incorrect An ordinary FIFO queue does not permit all four endpoint operations. C correct A doubly linked list with both endpoint pointers supports constant-time operations at each end. D incorrect A binary tree has no two-end sequence-operation guarantee.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 140 · AM0398
records.text: AM0398 Question 140 DSA12 Which data structure is best suited for implementing a backtracking algorithm? See assigned PDF 7, 6. C incorrect A generic linked list does not prescribe backtracking order. See assigned PDF 7, 6. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 141 · AM0399
records.text: AM0399 Question 141 DSA10 DSA14 A dispatcher keeps pending jobs in a sequence. Urgent jobs are added at the front, ordinary jobs at the back; serving removes the front job, and cancellation removes the last job. Which listed representation supports every operation in worst-case constant time as the sequence grows? Use ordinary stack and FIFO queue interfaces, with no additional indexes or auxiliary structures. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Doubly linked list with head and tail D Binary tree C. Doubly linked list with head and tail Urgent arrival inserts at the head, ordinary arrival appends at the tail, service removes the head, and cancellation removes the tail. A doubly linked list with both endpoint pointers updates a fixed number of links for each action; its prev link identifies the predecessor needed for tail removal. A stack exposes only one top, a FIFO queue lacks last-job cancellation and front insertion, and a generic binary tree provides no such endpoint-cost guarantee. A incorrect One stack top cannot directly supply both service-at-front and cancellation-at-back operations. B incorrect An ordinary FIFO queue permits rear insertion and front removal, but not urgent front insertion or last-job removal. C correct Head and tail permit direct endpoint access, and prev links make last-job removal constant time. D incorrect A generic binary tree has no guarantee for all four ordered-sequence endpoint updates.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 142 · AM0400
records.text: AM0400 Question 142 DSA01 DSA14 DSA15 DSA08 DSA23 DSA-S03 Which listed structures admit both array-based and linked-node representations? Links may be array indices or pointers, and binary-tree representations include the complete binary-tree case. Select all that apply. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree A. Stack; B. Queue; C. Linked list; D. Binary tree Stacks and queues have both array and linked-node implementations. A linked list can store its next links as indices into an array or as pointers between allocated nodes. A binary tree can use linked child references, while the complete binary-tree case has the indexed heap representation. The question concerns possible representations, so all four qualify without requiring one universal layout for every instance. A correct A stack can use an array top or a linked head. B correct A queue can use circular slots or linked endpoint nodes. C correct List links may be indices or node references. D correct Binary trees have linked-node forms and indexed complete-tree forms.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 143 · AM0401
records.text: AM0401 Question 143 DSA12 DSA11 DSA14 DSA45 A character reader supplies a word from left to right. After reading finishes, an output routine must remove one character at a time from a single auxiliary ADT to display the word right to left. It may use only the ADT’s standard insertion/removal interface and must preserve the original input. Which ADT directly supplies the needed removal order? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree A. Stack Insert the characters in the order they are read. The required output starts with the last character inserted, then continues toward the earliest one, so a stack’s LIFO interface directly supplies the reversal. A queue would preserve the original order. A linked list could represent a stack, but its storage links alone do not prescribe LIFO; a generic tree likewise has no matching removal contract. A correct Repeated stack removals produce the characters in reverse insertion order. B incorrect FIFO removal would reproduce the original character order. C incorrect A list is a possible representation but does not itself prescribe the required removal policy. D incorrect A generic tree does not define the requested reverse-insertion removal contract.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 144 · AM0402
records.text: AM0402 Question 144 DSA12 Which data structure is commonly used for implementing function call stacks in programming languages? Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree Stack The source explicitly states that a memory stack is used in function calls including recursion, keeping the most recent active call on top. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A correct Nested calls return in LIFO order through a stack. See assigned PDF 6, 6. B incorrect Queue FIFO order would not reflect nested returns. See assigned PDF 6, 6. C incorrect Linked nodes can store frames but the controlling ADT is still a stack. See assigned PDF 6, 6. D incorrect A binary tree does not provide the specified call-return discipline. See assigned PDF 6, 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 148 · AM0406
records.text: AM0406 Question 148 DSA-S03 DSA08 DSA11 DSA14 Which listed structures can create nodes using dynamic memory allocation in a linked-node implementation? Select all that apply. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 149 · AM0407
records.text: AM0407 Question 149 DSA11 DSA15 DSA08 DSA23 Which structures admit an array-based representation? Array slots may contain payloads and integer links; for binary trees include complete trees stored with child-index formulas. Select all that apply. B correct Modulo-indexed slots implement a circular queue. C correct Array indices can encode list links. D correct Complete binary trees use the indexed heap layout.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 150 · AM0408
records.text: AM0408 Question 150 DSA10 DSA08 Which listed representation provides direct next and previous links for walking a linear sequence forward and backward without retracing from its head? Use ordinary stack/queue interfaces and a binary tree without parent or traversal-thread links. Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option. A incorrect A stack interface exposes its top, not a bidirectional traversal. B incorrect A queue interface exposes FIFO endpoints, not neighboring prev/next traversal. C correct Doubly linked nodes provide next and prev links. D incorrect The specified child-only tree lacks the requested linear previous/next links.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 151 · AM0409
records.text: AM0409 Question 151 DSA14 DSA10 DSA11 DSA-S03 Which specified representations provide direct constant-time inspection of both first and last items in a nonempty sequence? A is a head-only linked stack, B a linked queue with front and rear pointers, C a linked list with head and tail, and D a child-linked binary tree with no cached endpoints. Select all that apply. A head-only linked stack must follow links to reach its oldest item, and a generic child-linked tree without endpoint caches supplies no direct first/last guarantee. The answer follows the representations, not the generic names alone. A incorrect A head-only stack lacks a direct reference to its oldest node. B correct Front and rear pointers directly expose both endpoint items. C correct Head and tail pointers directly expose both endpoint items. D incorrect The unaugmented tree has no cached traversal endpoints.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 152 · AM0410
records.text: AM0410 Question 152 DSA12 Which data structure can be efficiently used for implementing undo and redo functionality in applications? records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 153 · AM0411
records.text: AM0411 Question 153 DSA12 DSA11 A forward-only input sequence must be emitted in reverse order after all input is read, using one auxiliary ADT through its standard insertion/removal interface. Which ADT directly reverses the order without modifying the input links or adding a separate reversal algorithm? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree A. A generic linked list or binary tree does not itself specify the required removal discipline; reversing existing links would be a separate algorithm excluded by this question. C incorrect A generic list has no inherent reverse-removal contract without an added algorithm or stack policy. D incorrect A generic tree supplies no required reverse-sequence service.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 154 · AM0412
records.text: AM0412 Question 154 DSA42 Which abstract frontier service policy directly implements the latest-pending-work-first behavior of depth-first search? Choose the ADT, rather than a storage representation that could be given that policy. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree A. Stack DFS finishes the most recently entered unfinished branch before returning to older pending work. A stack directly supplies this latest-pending-work-first rule. A queue would instead remove older pending items first, producing a breadth-first discipline under ordinary graph traversal. A linked list may implement a stack, but its links alone do not prescribe the frontier policy. A binary tree describes possible input relationships rather than the required pending-work ADT. A correct A stack directly supplies latest-pending-work-first service. B incorrect A FIFO queue retrieves older pending work first. C incorrect Linked-list storage alone does not specify a frontier service policy. D incorrect A binary tree is not the latest-pending-work service ADT.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 155 · AM0413
records.text: AM0413 Question 155 DSA17 Which listed representations can implement a priority queue without retaining an unmodified LIFO or FIFO removal contract? Interpret D as a binary heap and C as an ordered or unordered list using extremum selection. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree organized as a binary heap C. Linked list; D. Binary tree organized as a binary heap A priority queue removes an item with an extreme priority key. An unordered list can scan for that extremum, while an ordered list maintains the relevant order during insertion. A binary heap supplies the same priority contract through heap order and logarithmic insertion/extraction. An unmodified stack or FIFO queue removes according to arrival position rather than priority. Thus the list and heap-shaped binary tree qualify under the stated algorithms. A incorrect An unmodified stack removes by recency rather than priority. B incorrect An unmodified FIFO queue removes by arrival order rather than priority. C correct Ordered or scanned lists can select the extreme priority. D correct A binary heap implements priority selection through heap order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 156 · AM0416
records.text: AM0416 Question 156 DSA14 DSA11 Which ordinary ADT restricts insertion to the rear and removal or peek to the front, preserving arrival order? Assume standard ADT interfaces rather than additional traversal operations. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree B. Queue The ordinary queue inserts new items at its rear and removes or observes the front item. These restrictions produce FIFO service: earlier arrivals are removed before later arrivals. A stack uses a single top and LIFO order. A general linked list permits operations beyond these restricted endpoints, while a binary tree organizes hierarchical relationships. Specifying the exact operations resolves the original vague use of access. A incorrect A stack operates at one top using LIFO. B correct A queue has rear insertion and front removal/peek. C incorrect A general list does not restrict access to those two operations. D incorrect A binary tree does not have this FIFO endpoint contract.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 157 · AM0417
records.text: AM0417 Question 157 DSA-S03 DSA01 DSA14 DSA08 Which structures can use nodes connected by pointers in a linked implementation? Do not require that every implementation use pointers. Queue; C. Linked list; D. Binary tree Pointer links can connect the nodes of several structures. A pointer-based binary tree instead links child nodes along branches. All four therefore admit a node-and-pointer representation. Their alternative array layouts do not invalidate this existence claim about linked implementations. A correct A linked stack connects nodes through head-chain links. B correct A linked queue connects nodes and retains endpoint pointers. C correct A linked list directly uses node links. D correct A pointer-based tree links its child nodes.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 159 · AM0420
records.text: AM0420 Question 159 DSA11 DSA14 DSA17 Which ADTs impose an item-removal order through their ordinary service contract? Use LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, and smallest-priority-first with FIFO ties for priority queues. A generic binary tree has no specified traversal. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Priority queue D Binary tree A. Stack; B. Queue; C. Priority queue Stacks impose reverse arrival order and queues impose arrival order. A priority queue also imposes an order once the priority direction and tie rule are supplied; this version chooses the smallest priority and serves equal priorities FIFO. A generic binary tree supplies a shape with several possible traversals rather than a single inherent removal order. Consequently the three service ADTs qualify and the unspecified tree does not. A correct A stack imposes LIFO removal. B correct A queue imposes FIFO removal. C correct The stated priority and tie rules define priority-queue removal order. D incorrect A generic tree without a traversal has no single inherent removal order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 160 · AM0421
records.text: AM0421 Question 160 DSA19 DSA22 DSA-S03 Which is the most general listed binary-tree family defined by the following distinct-key invariant alone, without an additional balancing discipline: every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller, and every key in its right subtree is larger? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A AVL tree B Binary search tree C Red-black tree D B-tree B. Binary search tree The global left-smaller/right-larger invariant defines the binary search tree family. It applies to every descendant in each subtree, not only immediate children. AVL and red-black trees satisfy that ordering but impose additional balancing disciplines, so they are more specialized than the family requested. The binary-tree restriction also excludes a general B-tree. Asking for the most general family prevents those BST subclasses from becoming competing selections. A incorrect AVL adds balance requirements beyond the stated invariant. B correct BST is the general family defined by the strict subtree ordering alone. C incorrect Red-black trees add a balancing discipline beyond the stated invariant. D incorrect A general B-tree is not the requested binary-tree family.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 161 · AM0422

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 163 · AM0425
records.text: AM0425 Question 163 DSA12 DSA11 Which data structure uses the concept of "first in, last out" to handle function calls and recursion? records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 164 · AM0427
records.text: AM0427 Question 164 DSA42 Which data structure is suitable for implementing depth-first search (DFS) algorithm? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree Stack DSA42 describes recursively finishing an unvisited neighbor before returning to the parent. Explicit stack storage or the runtime call stack preserves this latest-pending-work-first behavior. A FIFO queue changes the exploration order. Linked lists can store frames but do not themselves define stack order, and a binary tree alone is not a frontier policy. A correct A stack stores pending frames or vertices so the latest unfinished branch is resumed first. B incorrect A queue serves the oldest pending work and changes the depth-first exploration discipline. C incorrect A linked list may store a stack, but its name alone supplies no depth-first service order. D incorrect A binary tree is not the standard pending-work ADT needed to preserve DFS return points.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 165 · AM0428
records.text: AM0428 Question 165 DSA27 A capacity-limited cache evicts entries strictly in insertion order; cache hits do not change that order. Which ADT should maintain its eviction order? Ask for the service policy rather than a possible storage implementation. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree B. Queue The earliest inserted resident entry must be evicted first, and hits do not move it. This is FIFO order, which a queue directly maintains through rear insertion and front removal. A linked list could be used to implement that queue but does not independently prescribe the eviction discipline. A stack reverses insertion order, and a generic binary tree provides no FIFO eviction contract. A incorrect LIFO would evict the most recent insertion rather than the oldest. B correct FIFO queue service matches insertion-order eviction. C incorrect A linked list is a possible representation but does not itself prescribe FIFO service. D incorrect A generic binary tree does not prescribe insertion-order eviction.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 166 · AM0429
records.text: AM0429 Question 166 DSA12 Which data structure is commonly used for implementing undo-redo functionality in text editors? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 6. A correct Two stacks implement the required action reversal and restoration ordering. See assigned PDF 7, 6. B incorrect FIFO would undo actions in their original order. See assigned PDF 7, 6. C incorrect A linked list can store history but needs an added stack discipline. See assigned PDF 7, 6. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 167 · AM0430
records.text: AM0430 Question 167 DSA11 Which data structure allows easy traversal in a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order? A stack pops the most recently pushed remaining element first. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A correct Stack expressly enforces last-in-first-out. See assigned PDF 6. B incorrect Queue expressly enforces first-in-first-out. See assigned PDF 6. C incorrect A linked list can emulate LIFO only after choosing an endpoint policy. See assigned PDF 6. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 168 · AM0431
records.text: AM0431 Question 168 DSA16 DSA15 DSA02 Which specified representation supports constant-time insertion/deletion at either endpoint and constant-time indexed access to the logical middle item? Assume fixed capacity, no shifting or resizing, spare space for insertion, and a nonempty sequence for access. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Fixed-capacity circular-array deque D Binary tree C. Fixed-capacity circular-array deque A circular-array deque maps logical position k to a slot by adding the front index and reducing modulo capacity. That makes the middle item directly indexable. Endpoint insertions and deletions change only a slot and constant-size indices when no resize or shift occurs. A linked deque would not provide this indexing guarantee, so the array representation is explicit. The other ordinary ADT interfaces lack the combined operation set. A incorrect A stack does not expose both-end updates and middle indexing. B incorrect An ordinary queue does not expose all four endpoint operations or arbitrary middle access. C correct The fixed circular-array deque supplies endpoint updates and indexed middle access. D incorrect A generic binary tree lacks constant-time access by middle sequence position.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 169 · AM0432
records.text: AM0432 Question 169 DSA12 Which data structure is commonly used for implementing the undo operation in a text editor? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Binary tree Stack The latest action must be reversed first, matching LIFO and the source backtracking application. Pushing action records and popping the latest implements that order. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6, 7. A correct Top holds the latest pending action to undo. See assigned PDF 6, 7. B incorrect FIFO selects the oldest pending action instead. See assigned PDF 6, 7. C incorrect A generic linked list needs a chosen stack discipline to implement undo. See assigned PDF 6, 7. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 170 · AM0433
records.text: AM0433 Question 170 DSA15 DSA16 A bounded FIFO buffer must reuse freed array slots by wrapping indices modulo its fixed capacity, without shifting items. New insertions are rejected while full. Which listed term specifically names this storage representation? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Stack B Queue C Linked list D Circular buffer D. Circular buffer A circular buffer reuses its fixed slots by wrapping indices modulo capacity, so released positions can be used again without moving surviving items. The FIFO order is tracked logically rather than by requiring the front to remain at physical slot zero. Queue names the service ADT and can have other representations; it does not specifically identify this layout. Stack and linked list likewise do not name the stated circular-array representation. A incorrect A stack names LIFO service rather than the specified FIFO ring storage. B incorrect Queue names the FIFO ADT but does not specifically identify its storage layout. C incorrect A linked list does not name modulo-indexed circular array slots. D correct Circular buffer specifically names the stated fixed-slot wraparound representation.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 171 · AM0434
records.text: AM0434 Question 171 DSA36 DSA34 DSA37 DSA38 DSA32 Which ordinary array sorting algorithms have tight worst-case time Theta(n²)? Select all that apply. Use buffered mergesort, ordinary quicksort, standard insertion sort and iterative heapsort. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Merge sort B Quick sort C Insertion sort D Heap sort B. Quick sort; C. Insertion sort Repeated extreme partitions make ordinary quicksort accumulate quadratic work. Insertion sort on reverse input similarly accumulates quadratic prefix shifts. Buffered mergesort and iterative heapsort have n log n worst-case bounds instead, so they are not tightly quadratic even though quadratic is a valid looser upper bound. The explicit tight-bound question therefore selects quicksort and insertion alone in this primary option set. A incorrect Buffered mergesort has n log n worst growth. B correct Extreme quicksort partitions give tight quadratic worst growth. C correct Reverse-order insertion gives tight quadratic worst growth. D incorrect Iterative heapsort has an n log n worst bound.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 172 · AM0435
records.text: AM0435 Question 172 DSA-S04 DSA39 DSA36 DSA37 DSA34 Which sorting algorithm uses the divide-and-conquer strategy? Use ordinary array implementations, with radix sorting specifically meaning iterative least-significant-digit passes. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Merge sort D Radix sort C. Merge sort Mergesort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them and merges their results, so it uses divide and conquer. Ordinary bubble sort uses adjacent passes and selection sort repeatedly selects a suffix minimum. The explicitly specified LSD radix method performs stable digit passes rather than recursive subproblem decomposition. This convention removes the possible confusion with MSD radix grouping while retaining the original primary answer. A incorrect Ordinary bubble sort uses adjacent passes rather than recursive decomposition. B incorrect Ordinary selection sort repeatedly places one suffix minimum. C correct Mergesort recursively solves smaller halves and combines their results. D incorrect The specified iterative LSD form uses digit passes rather than recursive divide and conquer.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 173 · AM0436
records.text: AM0436 Question 173 DSA39 DSA37 DSA38 DSA31 Which specified sorting implementations preserve the relative order of equal full keys? Use ordinary in-place quicksort, ordinary heapsort, LSD radix with stable digit passes, and mergesort with left-first ties. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Quick sort B Heap sort C Radix sort D Merge sort C. Radix sort; D. Merge sort Stable LSD radix passes preserve the ordering already established by less significant digits. Equal full keys remain tied on every pass, so their relative order remains unchanged. Mergesort with left-first ties also preserves equal-key order while combining runs. Ordinary in-place quicksort and heapsort do not guarantee that stability because distant exchanges can reorder equal records. Hence both radix and merge qualify under the specified implementations. A incorrect Ordinary quicksort does not guarantee equal-key stability. B incorrect Long heap exchanges can reorder equal records. C correct Stable digit passes preserve the order of equal full keys. D correct Left-first merge ties preserve equal-key order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 174 · AM0437
records.text: AM0437 Question 174 DSA36 Which sorting algorithm uses a pivot element to partition the array into two subarrays? A Bubble sort B Selection sort C Quick sort D Insertion sort Quick sort The module quicksort explicitly selects a pivot and partitions values below/above it before recursion. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 11, 4, 3. A incorrect Bubble uses adjacent comparisons and swaps. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. B incorrect Selection chooses the minimum for the next output slot. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. C correct Pivot partitioning is the stated quicksort procedure. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3. D incorrect Insertion puts each item into a sorted prefix. See assigned PDF 11, 4, 3, 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 175 · AM0439
records.text: AM0439 Question 175 DSA29 DSA30 Which searching algorithm is based on comparing the target value with elements at midpoints of the array? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Interpolation search D Depth-first search Binary search DSA29 computes the midpoint of the current ordered interval, compares it with the target, and discards the half that cannot contain the target. That is exactly the midpoint-based procedure in the stem. Linear search scans successive elements, interpolation estimates a position from values, and DFS follows graph branches rather than ordered-array midpoints. A incorrect Linear search compares successive elements rather than repeatedly choosing the midpoint of a shrinking ordered interval. B correct Binary search explicitly compares the target with the current interval midpoint and keeps one half. C incorrect Interpolation search estimates a probe from numeric values and their distribution, rather than always using the midpoint. D incorrect Depth-first search explores graph neighbors and branches, not ordered-array midpoint intervals.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 176 · AM0440
records.text: AM0440 Question 176 DSA29 DSA30 DSA28 Which ordinary array-search algorithms require sorted input? For interpolation search also assume comparable numeric values and appropriate endpoint guards. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Interpolation search D Depth-first search B. Binary search; C. Interpolation search Binary search relies on order to discard half the remaining candidate interval after a comparison. Interpolation search also relies on sorted numeric values when estimating a candidate position from endpoint values. Both therefore require sorted input, although their further assumptions differ. Linear search simply scans and permits unsorted data. DFS follows graph adjacency rather than relying on a sorted array-search interval. A incorrect Linear scanning permits unsorted data. B correct Binary interval elimination needs sorted order. C correct Interpolation index estimation also needs sorted input. D incorrect DFS follows graph connections and has no sorted-array requirement.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 177 · AM0441
records.text: AM0441 Question 177 DSA28 DSA29 DSA30 DSA42 Which searching algorithm works by comparing the target value with elements from the beginning of the array until a match is found? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Interpolation search D Depth-first search A. Linear search Linear search starts at the beginning and compares successive elements until a match or exhaustion. Binary search instead chooses a midpoint of an ordered interval, and interpolation search estimates a position from endpoint key values. Depth-first search follows an unvisited graph branch before returning. These positive procedural differences classify the alternatives without any appeal to an old module’s omissions, so A remains the definite matching choice. A correct Linear search compares successive elements from the beginning. B incorrect Binary search probes a midpoint rather than scanning every successive position. C incorrect Interpolation search estimates a probe position from endpoint values. D incorrect DFS follows graph adjacency and unfinished branches rather than a beginning-to-end array scan.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 178 · AM0442
records.text: AM0442 Question 178 DSA30 Which searching algorithm is more efficient for uniformly distributed data in a sorted array? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Interpolation search D Depth-first search Interpolation search under the stated uniform-data model. DSA30 gives interpolation search expected O(log log n) probes on sorted, suitably uniform numeric data. Binary search has logarithmic worst-case probes without that distribution assumption, while linear search scans. The stem supplies the distribution and sortedness conditions that motivate interpolation. The expected advantage does not promise faster finite runs or logarithmic worst-case behavior on arbitrary distributions. A incorrect Linear search still examines successive elements and does not exploit uniform numeric distribution for sublinear expected probing. B incorrect Binary search gives logarithmic worst-case probing, but does not exploit uniform values for the stated expected advantage. C correct Interpolation estimates positions from uniformly distributed sorted numeric values, supporting the note’s expected O(log log n) probes. D incorrect DFS explores graph or tree branches and is not the distribution-based ordered-array search described here.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 179 · AM0443
records.text: AM0443 Question 179 DSA41 DSA42 Which named algorithms explore a graph or tree by following adjacency links to unvisited vertices, using branch-first or distance-layer-first traversal? Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Depth-first search D Breadth-first search C. Depth-first search; D. Breadth-first search DFS explores an unvisited branch before returning to later neighbors, using recursion or a stack. BFS instead processes a FIFO frontier so successive distance layers are explored in order. Both follow adjacency relationships and apply to trees as well as general graphs. Linear sequence scanning and binary interval search are different algorithms and do not implement these two adjacency-frontier traversal disciplines. A incorrect Linear sequence search does not implement the specified adjacency-frontier traversal. B incorrect Binary search eliminates ordered interval halves rather than following arbitrary adjacency. C correct DFS is branch-first adjacency traversal. D correct BFS is distance-layer-first adjacency traversal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 180 · AM0446
records.text: AM0446 Question 180 DSA31 DSA37 Under a uniform random permutation of distinct keys, which ordinary sorting algorithms have tight average time Theta(n log n)? Use fixed-position-pivot quicksort, buffered mergesort without merge-skipping, and standard bubble/insertion implementations. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort The random-order model supplies the average-case assumption needed for ordinary quicksort’s expected n log n work. Buffered mergesort performs n log n work across input orders, so its average has the same order. Bubble and insertion have quadratic ordinary average behavior under this random permutation model. Tight bounds and the stated distribution make quicksort and mergesort the complete selection, rather than leaving average cost unspecified. The DSA31 comparison table supplies the average-case entries used in this comparison. A incorrect Ordinary bubble sorting has quadratic random-order average work. B correct The stated random-input model gives quicksort expected n log n work. C correct Buffered mergesort has n log n work in every input order. D incorrect Ordinary insertion has quadratic random-order average work.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 181 · AM0447
records.text: AM0447 Question 181 DSA33 Which sorting algorithm works by repeatedly selecting the smallest element from the unsorted portion and placing it at the beginning? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Selection sort D Insertion sort Selection sort The source selection sort scans for the smallest remaining element and swaps it with the current first unsorted position. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3, 4, 11. A incorrect Bubble pushes elements through adjacent swaps. See assigned PDF 3, 4, 11, 3. B incorrect Quicksort partitions by a pivot, not necessarily the minimum. See assigned PDF 3, 4, 11, 3. C correct Exactly the minimum-selection and placement procedure given. See assigned PDF 3, 4, 11, 3. D incorrect Insertion places the next encountered element into a sorted prefix. See assigned PDF 3, 4, 11, 3.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 182 · AM0448
records.text: AM0448 Question 182 DSA32 DSA34 DSA36 DSA37 Which ordinary array sorting algorithms are comparison sorts that use constant extra element storage inside the original array? Count recursive call stacks separately from element storage; use buffered mergesort for C. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort A. Bubble sort; B. Quick sort; D. Insertion sort Bubble sort swaps adjacent keys and insertion sort shifts a prefix while retaining one saved key. Quicksort partitions within the same array using constant extra element storage. Its recursive frames are counted separately under the explicitly stated convention. Buffered mergesort instead allocates a linear merge buffer. Therefore bubble, quick and insertion meet the element-storage definition, while a total-auxiliary-space question would need to account for quicksort’s stack as well. A correct Bubble compares and swaps within the original array. B correct Quicksort partitions in the array; its recursive stack is separately counted. C incorrect Buffered mergesort needs linear extra element storage. D correct Insertion compares and shifts within the original array with one saved key.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 183 · AM0449
records.text: AM0449 Question 183 DSA29 DSA25 Which searching algorithm requires the input array to be sorted? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search Binary search DSA29 defines binary search over an ascending random-access sequence and reverses comparisons for descending data. Sortedness makes the half-elimination step sound. Linear scanning works without order; hashing needs a built table rather than sorted positions; DFS follows adjacency. Only Binary search among this option set requires a sorted input sequence for its ordinary operation. A incorrect Linear search explicitly permits unsorted data and compares items one after another. B correct Binary search relies on ordered values to determine which half can still contain the target. C incorrect Hash lookup needs a hash-table organization, not values arranged in sorted-array order. D incorrect Depth-first search follows graph or tree adjacency and does not require a sorted input array.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 184 · AM0450
records.text: AM0450 Question 184 DSA29 DSA28 DSA26 Which searching algorithm has a worst-case time complexity of O(log n)? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search Binary search has logarithmic worst-case time. DSA29 bounds binary-search probes by floor(log₂n)+1 on nonempty random-access input. This supplies logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost comparisons. Linear search may scan all items; adverse hash collisions may require linear work; DFS can inspect all vertices and edges. Their ordinary worst cases do not share binary search’s logarithmic bound. A incorrect Linear search can inspect every item when the target is absent or last, giving linear worst-case time. B correct Each comparison discards about half the ordered interval, giving logarithmic worst-case probes. C incorrect Ordinary hash lookup can degrade to linear time under adverse collisions, despite expected constant-time performance. D incorrect DFS may visit all graph vertices and edges, rather than guarantee logarithmic worst-case work.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 185 · AM0451
records.text: AM0451 Question 185 DSA28 DSA25 Which search compares a target with consecutive sequence elements at a fixed stride of one, stopping at the first match or after exhausting the sequence? No hashing or other preprocessing is used. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search A. Linear search The stated unit stride means the algorithm inspects successive elements in order. It stops early when a comparison matches or reports failure after the sequence is exhausted, which is linear search. Binary search uses a shrinking midpoint interval rather than consecutive positions. Hash search starts from computed addresses, and DFS follows graph adjacency. Specifying stride one distinguishes ordinary scanning from larger-step jump-search interpretations. A correct Linear search compares successive elements until a match or exhaustion. B incorrect Binary search chooses midpoints rather than every consecutive element. C incorrect Hash search uses computed addresses rather than the stated scan. D incorrect DFS follows graph adjacency rather than consecutive sequence positions.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 186 · AM0452
records.text: AM0452 Question 186 DSA28 DSA29 DSA25 Which searching algorithm is suitable for unsorted arrays or lists? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search Linear search directly searches an unsorted sequence. DSA28 explicitly allows unsorted data for linear search: compare successive elements until the target is found or the sequence ends. Binary search requires sortedness. Hash lookup can be useful after building a table, but it does not directly search the supplied ordinary list without that preprocessing. DFS presumes graph or tree adjacency rather than a simple sequence query. A correct Linear search can inspect an unsorted array or list directly without sorting or building another structure. B incorrect Binary search needs ordering to safely eliminate half the remaining candidate positions. C incorrect Hash search needs a constructed hash table; the stem supplies an ordinary unsorted array or list. D incorrect DFS explores graph or tree adjacency and is not the direct unsorted-sequence scan described here.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 187 · AM0453
records.text: AM0453 Question 187 DSA42 Which searching algorithm is commonly used for traversing graphs or trees? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search Depth-first search DSA42 describes marking a vertex and recursively visiting each unmarked neighbor before resuming later neighbors. That procedure is standard depth-first traversal and applies to graphs and trees. Linear search scans a sequence, binary search uses an ordered interval, and hash search queries table addresses. None of those alternatives names the adjacency-following traversal in this option set. A incorrect Linear search scans sequence elements and is not the named adjacency-following graph/tree traversal. B incorrect Binary search reduces an ordered interval rather than visiting arbitrary graph or tree connections. C incorrect Hash search probes key-derived table addresses rather than traversing graph or tree edges. D correct DFS follows unvisited neighbors recursively or through an explicit stack, providing a standard traversal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 188 · AM0455
records.text: AM0455 Question 188 DSA32 DSA34 DSA37 DSA31 Which specified sorting implementations are stable? Use strict adjacent swaps for bubble, ordinary in-place quicksort, left-first merge ties, and insertion shifts of strictly larger keys only. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort A. Bubble sort; C. Merge sort; D. Insertion sort Bubble sort’s strict adjacent swaps do not exchange equal keys. Mergesort preserves ties by taking an equal key from the left run first. Insertion sort shifts only strictly larger keys, leaving equal earlier keys ahead of the inserted one. Those three mechanisms preserve relative equal-key order. Ordinary in-place quicksort does not guarantee it because partition exchanges can move equal records past one another. A correct Strict adjacent swaps preserve ties. B incorrect Ordinary quicksort does not guarantee equal-key order. C correct Left-first equal-key merging preserves ties. D correct Shifting only larger keys leaves equal earlier keys in place.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 189 · AM0456
records.text: AM0456 Question 189 DSA34 Which sorting algorithm is commonly used for small input sizes or partially sorted arrays? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort Insertion sort DSA34 explicitly favors insertion for small arrays or few inversions. Each inversion corresponds to shifting work, so nearly sorted data requires few shifts; sorted input is linear. This low-setup incremental algorithm is the conventional match among the choices. The other algorithms can sort these inputs, but their mere applicability does not identify the specific use case emphasized in the note. A incorrect Bubble can exploit early stopping but is not the note’s specific small-array/few-inversions recommendation. B incorrect Quicksort incurs partition and recursive setup and is not the cited small-subarray method. C incorrect Ordinary merge sorting uses its merge levels and buffer even on nearly sorted input. D correct Insertion has low setup and few shifts on nearly sorted or small arrays.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 190 · AM0457
records.text: AM0457 Question 190 DSA30 Which searching algorithm divides the search space into three parts at each step? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Ternary search D Depth-first search Ternary search DSA30 explicitly describes sorted-array ternary search as comparing two split points and retaining the relevant third. The three candidate regions give the technique its name. Binary search uses one midpoint and two regions, linear search scans successively, and DFS explores graph branches. Thus Ternary search uniquely matches the described three-part split. A incorrect Linear search advances through successive items and does not divide the remaining interval into thirds. B incorrect Binary search uses one midpoint and retains one of two halves, not one of three regions. C correct Ternary search uses two split points to divide the ordered search interval into three candidate parts. D incorrect DFS explores graph or tree branches rather than repeatedly trisecting an ordered search interval.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 191 · AM0458
records.text: AM0458 Question 191 DSA32 DSA34 DSA31 DSA37 Which ordinary array sorting implementations use O(1) total auxiliary space in both best and average cases? Count live recursive frames; use recursive quicksort without tail-call elimination and buffered mergesort. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort A. Bubble sort; D. Insertion sort The DSA31 table gives bubble and insertion constant extra storage across input cases. Their iterative forms retain only a fixed number of indices and temporaries, so total auxiliary space stays constant. The same table gives ordinary recursive quicksort a logarithmic average stack, and buffered mergesort needs a linear auxiliary array. Counting all live frames and buffers therefore leaves exactly bubble and insertion as the qualifying choices. A correct Bubble uses fixed temporary storage across cases. B incorrect The recursive quicksort stack is not constant in its ordinary average case. C incorrect Buffered mergesort uses linear auxiliary storage. D correct Insertion needs a saved key and fixed-size indices.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 192 · AM0459
records.text: AM0459 Question 192 DSA-S04 DSA29 Which searching algorithm is based on the principle of divide-and-conquer? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search Binary search DSA29 compares the middle value with the target and continues only in the half that can contain it. This solves a smaller instance of the same ordered-search problem and is the divide-and-conquer reduction intended here. Linear scanning removes one candidate at a time, hashing computes addresses, and DFS follows adjacency without this ordered half-elimination rule. A incorrect Linear search scans successive candidates rather than repeatedly solving a half-size ordered-search instance. B correct Binary search divides the ordered interval and continues in the only half that can contain the target. C incorrect Hash search derives an address and resolves collisions rather than recursively dividing an ordered problem. D incorrect DFS follows adjacency branches and does not inherently apply the ordered half-elimination strategy described here.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 193 · AM0460
records.text: AM0460 Question 193 DSA37 DSA36 DSA34 DSA32 Which sorting algorithm has the worst-case time complexity of O(n log n)? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort Merge sort Ordinary merge combines n items over log n levels, giving n log n even in the worst case. The other offered algorithms have quadratic adverse-input work. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 4, 11, 3. A incorrect Bubble can perform quadratic passes/exchanges. See assigned PDF 4, 11, 11, 3. B incorrect Quicksort is explicitly quadratic in the worst case. See assigned PDF 4, 11, 11, 3. C correct Merge is explicitly n log n. See assigned PDF 4, 11, 11, 3. records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 194 · AM0461
records.text: AM0461 Question 194 DSA37 Which sorting algorithm is efficient for sorting data in external memory (hard disks)? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort Merge sort using buffered external runs. DSA37 describes external sorting by building sorted runs and merging buffered disk streams to reduce I/O. Merge sort naturally supports that strategy even when the whole dataset does not fit RAM. Bubble and insertion sorting repeatedly move local data, while ordinary quicksort assumes partition access rather than the external sequential-run pattern specified here. A incorrect Bubble sort’s repeated adjacent passes do not provide the buffered sorted-run strategy used for efficient external sorting. B incorrect Ordinary quicksort partitioning is not the sequential buffered-run merging strategy identified for external data here. C correct Merge sorting combines buffered sorted runs sequentially and is directly suited to disk-backed external sorting. D incorrect Insertion sort’s repeated local insertion work does not provide the note’s efficient external-run merging mechanism.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 195 · AM0462
records.text: AM0462 Question 195 DSA26 DSA27 A large dataset has an equality-key index implemented by a hash table with suitable key distribution and bounded load. No ordered or range queries are needed. Which listed search uses this index for expected constant-time lookup? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Linear search B Binary search C Hash search D Depth-first search C. Hash search Hash lookup computes a bucket or probe start from the key and uses the existing index to locate an equality match. With suitable distribution and bounded load, the note gives expected constant lookup. The important assumptions are the index and workload, rather than dataset size alone. Linear scanning ignores the index, binary search needs an ordered interval, and DFS follows graph relationships instead of this equality-key access structure. A incorrect A scan can inspect linearly many records and does not use the hash index. B incorrect Binary search uses an ordered interval rather than this index. C correct Hash search uses the stated index with expected constant lookup. D incorrect DFS follows graph connections rather than the equality-key index.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 196 · AM0463
records.text: AM0463 Question 196 DSA31 DSA37 For a uniform random permutation of distinct keys, which listed ordinary algorithms have the smallest tight average-case growth order? Use fixed-position-pivot quicksort, buffered mergesort without merge-skipping, and standard bubble/insertion. Select all algorithms tied for the smallest order. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Insertion sort B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort Under the stated random-input model, ordinary quicksort has expected n log n work. Buffered mergesort performs n log n work in every order, so its average shares that order. Bubble and insertion have quadratic average work on random permutations. Quicksort and mergesort therefore tie for the smallest asymptotic average order among these options; the question does not ask for a measured running-time ranking between the tied methods. The DSA31 comparison table supplies the average-case entries used in this comparison. A incorrect Quadratic average growth is larger than n log n. B correct Expected n log n ties for the smallest listed average growth. C correct n log n across orders ties for the smallest listed average growth. D incorrect Quadratic average growth is larger than n log n.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 197 · AM0464
records.text: AM0464 Question 197 DSA26 DSA27 Which data structure is best suited for implementing a dictionary with fast lookup and insertion? Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Array B Linked list C Hash table D Stack Hash table for expected fast dictionary lookup and insertion. DSA27 explicitly names hashing as a dictionary implementation with expected constant lookup. DSA26 qualifies this by a suitable distribution and controlled load; insertion is likewise expected fast under those conditions. Arrays and linked lists lack the same ordinary key-lookup performance, while a stack specifies LIFO access. This is an expected-performance recommendation, not a universal worst-case guarantee. A incorrect An ordinary array lacks key-derived lookup and may require scanning or maintaining a sorted order with costly insertions. B incorrect An ordinary linked list needs traversal to locate an arbitrary dictionary key, giving linear worst-case lookup. C correct A well-sized hash table offers expected fast key lookup and insertion under suitable hashing and load assumptions. D incorrect A stack exposes LIFO top operations and does not directly provide efficient arbitrary-key dictionary lookup.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 198 · AM0465
records.text: AM0465 Question 198 DSA43 DSA41 Which listed algorithm guarantees shortest paths from one source to all reachable vertices for arbitrary graphs with nonnegative edge weights that may differ? Compare the standard forms of the listed algorithms. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Depth-first search B Breadth-first search C Dijkstra's algorithm D Prim's algorithm C. Dijkstra's algorithm Standard Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edge weights justify this shortest-path procedure even when different edges have different costs. BFS minimizes edge count and is sufficient when edge costs are equal, which is weaker than the stated guarantee. DFS supplies reachability paths, while Prim minimizes total spanning-tree cost rather than source-to-vertex route lengths. A incorrect A DFS path need not have minimum total weight. B incorrect BFS minimizes edge count and does not guarantee minimum weight for arbitrary differing costs. C correct Dijkstra guarantees source shortest paths under nonnegative weights. D incorrect Prim solves the spanning-tree objective rather than source shortest paths.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 199 · AM0466
records.text: AM0466 Question 199 DSA11 DSA01 Which listed standard representations directly implement stack push/pop at an array top or linked-chain head, without simulating LIFO through another ADT? Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Array B Linked list C Queue D Tree A. Array; B. Linked list The array representation maintains a top index and changes it when pushing or popping. The linked representation inserts and removes at the chain head, so the latest node is also the next one removed. Both directly implement LIFO with ordinary constant endpoint operations. A queue has FIFO service, while a generic tree has no stack-top contract; emulations through those ADTs are outside this representation question. A correct An array with a top index directly implements stack operations. B correct A linked chain with head insertion/removal directly implements stack operations. C incorrect An ordinary FIFO queue is not a direct stack representation. D incorrect A generic tree does not supply the specified stack-top representation.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 200 · AM0467
records.text: AM0467 Question 200 DSA38 Given a consistent comparator on a priority field, which listed comparison sorting algorithms can sort records by that field? No particular extraction mechanism or equal-priority stability is required. Select all that apply. Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question. A Bubble sort B Quick sort C Merge sort D Heap sort A. Bubble sort; B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort; D. Heap sort Priority is a key field that any comparison sort can use through a consistent comparator. Bubble compares neighboring priorities, quicksort partitions by priority, mergesort combines priority-ordered runs, and heapsort repeatedly places a priority extreme. Since no heap-extraction mechanism or tie-stability condition is required, every listed algorithm can produce the requested priority ordering. Priorities alone do not identify one unique sorting method. A correct Bubble can compare adjacent priority fields. B correct Quicksort can partition with the priority comparator. C correct Mergesort can merge runs by the priority field. D correct Heapsort can extract priority extremes.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 201 · AM0468
records.text: AM0468 Question 201 DSA27 DSA10 An LRU cache already has hash lookup that returns a reference to the matching entry. Which listed representation should maintain recency order so a known entry can be removed and moved to the recent end in constant time, with eviction at the least-recent end? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. A Array B Doubly linked list with head and tail C Hash table D Queue B. Doubly linked list with head and tail The hash index handles locating an entry, while the recency component must unlink a known entry and reconnect it at the recent end. A doubly linked list supplies both neighboring links for that constant-time removal and maintains endpoints for movement and eviction. An array would generally shift entries, a bare hash table does not supply recency order, and an ordinary FIFO queue cannot remove an arbitrary known interior entry. A incorrect Maintaining array recency order generally requires shifts. B correct A doubly linked recency list supports unlinking a known node and endpoint updates. C incorrect The existing hash index handles lookup but does not itself maintain LRU order. D incorrect An ordinary queue lacks arbitrary known-interior-node removal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 202 · AM0469
records.text: AM0469 Question 202 DSA44 Which algorithm is used to find the maximum subarray sum in an array? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Binary search B Quick sort C Merge sort D Kadane's algorithm Kadane’s algorithm DSA44 directly identifies Kadane as the contiguous maximum-sum-subarray algorithm. It updates the best sum ending at the current item and the best sum seen overall, using linear time and constant working storage. Binary search does not optimize contiguous sums, and quicksort or merge sort reorder values rather than preserve the original adjacency needed by this problem. A incorrect Binary search locates targets or ordered boundaries; it does not compute a contiguous maximum-sum subarray. B incorrect Quicksort reorders values and does not preserve the original adjacency required for maximum subarray sum. C incorrect Merge sort orders values; the named sorting algorithm is not the maximum-subarray recurrence. D correct Kadane maintains the best sum ending here and the best anywhere, directly solving the stated problem.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 203 · AM0470
records.text: AM0470 Question 203 DSA40 Which data structure is commonly used to implement a graph? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Array B Linked list C Hash table D Adjacency list Adjacency list DSA40 describes adjacency lists as storing each vertex’s neighbors in Θ(V+E) space. This names a complete graph representation among the choices. Arrays, linked lists, or maps may store parts of a representation, but those container names alone do not specify how vertices and their edges are encoded. The answer identifies the graph-specific organization. A incorrect An array can store a matrix or adjacency containers, but its name alone does not specify a graph representation. B incorrect A linked list can hold neighbor records, but alone does not describe the vertex-to-neighbor organization. C incorrect Hash tables may index vertices or neighbors, but do not by themselves name the graph representation supplied here. D correct An adjacency list explicitly associates vertices with their neighbors and is a standard graph representation.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 204 · AM0471
records.text: AM0471 Question 204 DSA43 Which algorithm is used to find the minimum spanning tree in a graph? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Depth-first search B Breadth-first search C Dijkstra's algorithm D Prim's algorithm Prim’s algorithm DSA43 defines an MST as a minimum-total-cost connection of all vertices in a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Dijkstra minimizes source-path distances instead, while BFS and DFS are traversals without a general minimum-weight spanning-tree guarantee. Thus Prim is the listed MST algorithm. A incorrect DFS can produce a spanning tree but does not generally minimize total edge weight. B incorrect BFS produces minimum-edge source layers in unweighted graphs, not a general minimum-weight spanning tree. C incorrect Dijkstra minimizes source-to-vertex distances, a different objective from total spanning-tree connection cost. D correct Prim grows a spanning tree by repeatedly choosing a cheapest edge crossing to an outside vertex.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 205 · AM0472
records.text: AM0472 Question 205 DSA17 A priority queue needs O(1) peek and O(log n) worst-case insertion and extraction for an interleaved workload.
