Compare ordinary sorted/unsorted array and linked-list implementations, a binary heap, and an unmodified FIFO queue; exclude representations with extra search indexes. Which meets all requirements? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Array B Linked list C Binary heap D Queue C. Binary heap A binary heap exposes the extreme key at its root, so peek is constant, and insertion or extraction restores order along a logarithmic-height path. Ordinary unordered arrays or lists need a linear search for an extreme, while ordered versions pay linear insertion in the general case. An unmodified FIFO queue follows arrival order rather than priority. The stated operation bounds make the heap the unique matching standard representation. A incorrect Ordinary ordered/unsorted arrays trade linear insertion against linear extremum selection. B incorrect Ordinary lists likewise have a linear cost in one required operation. C correct A binary heap provides constant peek and logarithmic insertion/extraction. D incorrect An unmodified queue serves FIFO rather than priority order.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 206 · AM0473
records.text: AM0473 Question 206 DSA44 Which algorithm is commonly used for pattern matching in strings? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Depth-first search B Breadth-first search C Dijkstra's algorithm D Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm Knuth–Morris–Pratt DSA44 explicitly defines KMP as finding a pattern inside text. It preprocesses longest proper prefix/suffix lengths and uses them to avoid restarting comparisons after mismatch, giving linear combined pattern-and-text work. DFS, BFS, and Dijkstra concern graph exploration or paths, rather than this specialized substring-matching mechanism. KMP uniquely matches the question among these choices. A incorrect DFS explores graph or tree branches; it is not the substring-pattern algorithm identified in DSA44. B incorrect BFS explores graph distance layers rather than applying prefix/suffix reuse for text matching. C incorrect Dijkstra computes nonnegative weighted shortest paths, not substring pattern occurrences. D correct KMP is the pattern-matching algorithm using preprocessed prefix/suffix lengths to avoid repeated text comparisons.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 207 · CS0122
records.text: CS0122 Question 207 DSA25 Assume a very large finite key universe U but only n stored keys, with n much smaller than |U|. A hash table uses capacity proportional to n. Compare allocated storage, rather than unconditional speed. Which statement is false? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A For n much smaller than |U|, the specified hash table uses less allocated storage than direct addressing. B Direct Address table doesn't use hash function to map keys C Hash table allocates one separate memory slot for each key in the universe U D There is one-to-one correspondence between keys in universe U and memory slots in the Direct Address table C. Hash table allocates one separate memory slot for each key in the universe U Direct addressing reserves a distinct slot for every possible key in the universe, whether present or absent, so its storage is proportional to |U|. The specified hash table stores the actual entries plus capacity proportional to n. For this sparse-universe storage comparison, hashing uses less space. C incorrectly attributes the direct-address allocation rule to hashing, while direct key-to-slot mapping and separate universe slots accurately describe direct addressing. A incorrect Under the sparse-universe storage assumptions, the hash table uses fewer allocated slots. B incorrect Direct addressing maps directly to a key’s universe slot without compressive hashing. C correct One slot for every possible key describes direct addressing, not the specified hash table. D incorrect Each universe key has a separate direct-address slot.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 208 · CS0131
records.text: CS0131 Question 208 DSA11 What is the time complexity order of push() operation of Stack data structure implemented using array? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. A O(n) B O(log n) C O(n^2) D O(1) O(1) The fixed-array push checks fullness, increments top and stores one item. A bounded number of unit-cost operations independent of n gives O(1). Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6. A incorrect Linear would require scanning or copying that the given push does not do. See assigned PDF 6. B incorrect Logarithmic would require a search/adjustment absent from push. See assigned PDF 6. C incorrect Quadratic has no nested work in this code. See assigned PDF 6. D correct Only a fullness test, index increment and one assignment are performed. See assigned PDF 6.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 209 · CS0132
records.text: CS0132 Question 209 DSA25 A zero-based six-slot hash table uses h(key)=key%6. What home index does it compute for key 36, before any collision resolution? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A At index 35 B At index 1 C At index 6 D At index 0 D. At index 0 The home address is obtained by applying the stated remainder function. Since 36 is exactly divisible by 6, the remainder is zero and the home index is 0. The question stops before collision resolution, so occupied slots cannot change this computed address. Index 1 could be a displaced location under some probing state, but it is not the function’s output; indices 6 and 35 are outside the table. A incorrect 35 is outside the valid zero-based range 0–5. B incorrect 1 is not the remainder of 36 divided by 6. C incorrect 6 is outside the valid range and is not a possible remainder modulo 6. D correct 36%6 equals 0.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 210 · CS0133
records.text: CS0133 Question 210 DSA26 Which method can resolve collision in hashed files by proceeding from the occupied position specified by the hash address and checking subsequent positions until an empty position is found? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Open addressing B Multiple hashing C Chaining D Cluster indexing Open addressing, specifically linear probing. DSA26 defines open addressing as keeping entries within the array and probing until an available slot is found. Checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. Multiple hashing changes probe steps, chaining stores collisions in bucket lists, and cluster indexing is not this insertion procedure. Therefore Open addressing is the matching general method among the options. A correct Open addressing searches alternative table positions; checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. B incorrect Multiple or double hashing derives another probe step rather than the stated simple successive-slot scan. C incorrect Chaining puts colliding entries in a bucket list instead of searching successive array slots. D incorrect Cluster indexing does not name the collision insertion strategy described by the successive-position probing rule.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 211 · CS0134
records.text: CS0134 Question 211 DSA18 Which one of the following is true about tree data structure? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Tree is a static data structure B Tree is a linear data structure C Tree forms a cycle — in other words tree is a cyclic data structure D There is only one unique path when we traverse from one node to another node in a tree There is only one unique path when we traverse from one node to another node in a tree A rooted tree gives every nonroot node exactly one parent and a unique root path. Between any two nodes, ascend to their common ancestor and descend; a second distinct path would create a cycle and violate the parent/path hierarchy. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9, 2. A incorrect The pointer-based tree representation does not require static size. See assigned PDF 9, 2, 9. B incorrect The source explicitly classifies trees as nonlinear. See assigned PDF 9, 2, 9. C incorrect A cycle contradicts the unique-path hierarchy. See assigned PDF 9, 2, 9. D correct The rooted hierarchy gives one unique connecting path for every node pair. See assigned PDF 9, 2, 9.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 212 · CS0135
records.text: CS0135 Question 212 DSA45 For an unordered heap record file without an ordered index or a maintained sorted copy, which statement is not correct? Ordinary insertion uses available storage rather than maintaining field order. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Sorting is required to read records in particular field order B Linear search can be used to search a necessary record C Record insertion is efficient D New records are inserted at the beginning of the file D. New records are inserted at the beginning of the file A heap file does not maintain record order by a chosen field. With no ordered index or sorted copy, ordered output therefore requires sorting; an ordinary scan can locate a record, and insertion can place a record in available storage. Nothing requires new records to be inserted at the beginning of the file. D is the incorrect claim, while the explicit no-index scope makes A’s ordering requirement appropriate. A incorrect Under the specified no-index/no-sorted-copy scope, field-ordered output requires ordering the records. B incorrect A linear scan can search unordered records. C incorrect Using available storage avoids maintaining a sorted record sequence during insertion. D correct Heap-file insertion is not required to place every new record at the beginning.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 213 · NS0298
records.text: NS0298 Question 213 DSA01 Which listed structures are linear in the course classification? Select all that apply. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Tree B Array C Queue D Linked list B. Array; C. Queue; D. Linked list A linear structure arranges items along a sequence rather than through hierarchical branching. The note explicitly includes arrays, queues and linked lists in that category, giving three valid selections. A tree instead models a hierarchy and is classified as nonlinear. The select-all instruction allows every listed member of the linear category to be recognized rather than forcing an arbitrary single choice. A incorrect Trees model hierarchy rather than a linear sequence. B correct Arrays are classified as linear. C correct Queues are classified as linear. D correct Linked lists are classified as linear.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 214 · NS0319
records.text: NS0319 Question 214 DSA11 DSA14 Which abbreviations name the stack service policy? Select all that apply. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A LIFO B FIFO C FILO D FCFS A. LIFO; C. FILO The most recently pushed item is removed first by a stack. This is last in, first out, abbreviated LIFO. Equivalently, the first item inserted remains until later items have been removed, making it first in, last out or FILO. FIFO and FCFS instead preserve arrival order in ordinary queue service. Both A and C therefore name the same stack discipline. A correct LIFO means last in, first out. B incorrect FIFO means first in, first out, an ordinary queue policy. C correct FILO is the equivalent first in, last out view of a stack. D incorrect FCFS describes arrival-order service rather than stack service.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 215 · NS0337
records.text: NS0337 Question 215 DSA29 DSA06 For ordinary binary search on a sorted random-access array of n elements, what is the tightest listed worst-case time bound? Count each indexed probe as constant work. State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. A O(n (log n)²) B O(n²) C O(n) D O(log n) D. O(log n) Binary search repeatedly removes roughly half of the remaining candidate interval. The note bounds its worst probes by floor(log₂n)+1 for nonempty input, giving logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost indexing. The linear, quadratic and n-times-squared-log options all grow faster and are looser upper bounds. Explicitly asking for the tightest bound selects the logarithmic alternative rather than treating every valid Big-O upper bound as equally responsive. A incorrect n(log n)² is a much looser upper bound. B incorrect Quadratic is a looser upper bound. C incorrect Linear is a looser upper bound. D correct Logarithmic matches the interval-halving probe growth.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 216 · NS0351
records.text: NS0351 Question 216 DSA32 Which sorting algorithm compares each pair of adjacent elements from the beginning of an array and, if they are in reversed order, swaps them; if at least one swaps has been done, repeat step 1. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Insertion sort B Bubble sort C Selection sort D Shell sort Bubble sort with early stopping DSA32 describes adjacent comparisons, swapping strict inversions, and repeating passes until a pass performs no swaps. That matches every part of the stem, including its stopping condition. Insertion grows a sorted prefix, selection chooses a suffix minimum, and Shell uses separated gap subsequences, so none has this exact adjacent full-pass mechanism. A incorrect Insertion places each next value into a sorted prefix rather than repeating full adjacent passes. B correct Adjacent inversion swaps and repetition until no swaps identify optimized bubble sort. C incorrect Selection finds a suffix minimum and exchanges it with the prefix boundary. D incorrect Shell sorts gap-separated subsequences before its final gap-one insertion pass.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 217 · NS0354
records.text: NS0354 Question 217 DSA42 DSA14 DSA-S02 Among the following one is NOT the application of queue in the real world. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A It is used in operating systems for handling interrupts. B It is used to maintain the play list in media players in order C It is used in Depth First search D It is widely used as waiting lists for a single shared resource Depth-first search uses stack discipline rather than the ordinary queue. DSA42 finishes a branch using a stack or recursion and explicitly says a queue changes that discipline. DSA14 gives FIFO waiting, play sequences, and asynchronous buffering as queue uses. Interrupt work can also be buffered pending service. Thus the standard DFS claim is the non-queue application among the offered ordinary examples. A incorrect Pending interrupts can be buffered for later service; queue use need not imply one universal interrupt priority policy. B incorrect A FIFO play queue can preserve the order of media items. C correct Standard DFS uses latest-pending-work-first stack or recursion rather than FIFO queue service. D incorrect Waiting for one shared resource is a direct FIFO queue application.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 218 · NS0519
records.text: NS0519 Question 218 DSA11 DSA01 Which data structure uses LIFO? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Queue B Array C Stack D Linked List Stack DSA11 explicitly assigns LIFO to a stack. Arrays and linked lists can represent that stack, but neither storage structure inherently fixes its removal order. A queue instead supplies FIFO. The question asks for the service-policy ADT, so Stack is the specific answer rather than one of the possible underlying representations. A incorrect A queue follows FIFO, not the latest-in-first-out order requested. B incorrect An array is a representation and does not inherently impose LIFO service. C correct A stack is explicitly defined by LIFO, equivalently FILO. D incorrect A linked list can implement several policies and does not inherently require LIFO.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 219 · NS0520
records.text: NS0520 Question 219 DSA02 DSA08 What distinguishes a dynamic data structure from a static one? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Dynamic structures can change size at runtime; static structures have fixed capacity. DSA02 distinguishes fixed arrays from resizable arrays, and DSA08 allocates linked nodes as needed. Runtime growth or shrinkage is the key distinction; fixed capacity need not mean compile-time allocation.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 220 · NS0521
records.text: NS0521 Question 220 DSA01 Which classification includes both Trees and Graphs? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Linear B Homogeneous C Non-linear D Static Non-linear DSA01 treats arrays, lists, stacks, and queues as linear sequences, trees as hierarchies, and graphs as general connections. Trees and graphs therefore belong to the nonlinear relationship category. Homogeneity describes element types and static describes storage capacity; neither classifies both by their branching relationship structure. C is the appropriate shared category. A incorrect Linear describes sequence-like structures rather than branching trees and general graphs. B incorrect Homogeneous concerns uniform element types and does not identify their relationship structure. C correct Trees and graphs are nonlinear relationship structures, unlike the listed linear sequences. D incorrect Static concerns storage or capacity decisions, not whether connections branch.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 221 · NS0522
records.text: NS0522 Question 221 DSA01 In an ADT, what two components are always defined? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. An ADT defines its values/data and permitted operations. DSA01 explicitly defines an abstract data type through values and operations, leaving representation to the implementation. The same LIFO stack can therefore use arrays or linked nodes without changing its contract.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 222 · NS0523
records.text: NS0523 Question 222 DSA01 A structure in C that groups int, char, and float is an example of: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Homogeneous B Non-homogeneous C Linear D Static Non-homogeneous, or heterogeneous DSA01 directly identifies a record grouping integer, character, and floating fields as heterogeneous. The different field types distinguish it from an ordinary same-element-type array. Linear describes relationships, and static describes storage behavior, neither of which follows merely from the field types. Thus Non-homogeneous is the requested classification. A incorrect Homogeneous would mean a uniform element type, contrary to the mixed int, char, and float fields. B correct The record combines different field types and is therefore heterogeneous or non-homogeneous. C incorrect Linear concerns relationships or order, not the mixed-type classification asked here. D incorrect Static concerns allocation or lifetime and is not established merely by these field types.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 223 · NS0524
records.text: NS0524 Question 223 DSA01 What does abstraction in algorithms allow programmers to do? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Abstraction preserves relevant behavior and hides irrelevant implementation detail. DSA01 illustrates abstraction using patient urgency and arrival order while ignoring hair colour. Programmers retain the data and operations needed for the task and separate that contract from representation details. This supports the substantive answer without additional facts.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 224 · NS0525
records.text: NS0525 Question 224 DSA03 DSA27 Which operation involves combining elements from two sorted sets into one sorted set? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Merging DSA03 calls combining sequences merging and works through sorted inputs by repeatedly emitting the smaller current front. Advancing only the selected sequence preserves sorted output until the remaining suffix is appended. For mathematical sets, duplicate handling additionally follows the set contract.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 225 · NS0526
records.text: NS0526 Question 225 DSA03 DSA09 What is the term for the operation that releases memory when a data structure is no longer needed? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Destruction or deallocation of owned storage. DSA03 says destroying a structure releases owned storage. In a linked chain, DSA09 visits and releases each owned node; C++ allocation forms must be matched to their deletion forms, and freed nodes must not be dereferenced.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 226 · NS0527
records.text: NS0527 Question 226 DSA06 Given T(n) = 6n + 4, what is the Big-O complexity? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. O(n), tightly Θ(n). For n≥1, 6n+4≤10n, while 6n+4≥6n. These constant upper and lower multiples establish linear growth by DSA06. O(n) is the natural tightest-order response, though larger upper bounds also exist.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 227 · NS0528
records.text: NS0528 Question 227 DSA06 Show why f(n) = 3n² + 4n + 1 is O(n²). What are the values of c and k? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. One valid witness pair is c=8, k=1. For every n≥1, 4n≤4n² and 1≤n², so 3n²+4n+1≤8n². DSA06 supplies the same inequality, proving the required eventual upper bound with c=8 and k=1. Other larger constants may also work.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 228 · NS0529
records.text: NS0529 Question 228 DSA04 Which property of an algorithm ensures it terminates after a finite number of steps? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Finiteness DSA04 defines finiteness as terminating after finitely many steps for every valid input. It is distinct from definiteness, executable instructions, or correctness: a terminating procedure can still return a wrong answer. The required concept is directly covered.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 229 · NS0530
records.text: NS0530 Question 229 DSA07 DSA05 An algorithm has exactly two independent nested loops. Each executes n iterations, and the innermost body performs constant work. Loop-control operations are constant time, with no early exits or hidden nonconstant operations. What is the tight time complexity as n grows? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Theta(n²) time. For each of the n outer iterations, the inner loop executes n times, so the constant-cost body runs n×n=n² times. Outer-loop overhead is linear and inner-loop control is also bounded by a constant per body execution. Those contributions do not change the dominant quadratic growth. Under the stated independence, fixed loop count and body-cost assumptions, the tight time complexity is Theta(n²).

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 230 · NS0531
records.text: NS0531 Question 230 DSA06 Big-Theta (Θ) notation represents: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. A Upper bound only B Lower bound only C Both upper and lower bound D Average case only Both upper and lower asymptotic bounds. DSA06 defines Big-O as an eventual upper bound, Omega as the reverse bound, and Theta as requiring both. Thus Theta expresses a tight growth class up to positive constants. It is independent of choosing best, average, or worst input cases; Average case only confuses the bound relation with an input-distribution choice. A incorrect An upper bound alone is Big-O and does not supply Theta’s lower requirement. B incorrect A lower bound alone is Omega and does not supply Theta’s upper requirement. C correct Theta requires simultaneous eventual upper and lower constant-factor bounds. D incorrect Theta can describe any case or resource function, not only an average case.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 231 · NS0532
records.text: NS0532 Question 231 DSA06 Which grows faster asymptotically: O(n log n) or O(n)? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Representative n log n grows faster than n; Big-O classes themselves overlap. DSA06 orders representative rates with n before n log n. Their ratio is log n, which grows without bound, so the representative n log n rate grows faster. However an O(n) function is also O(n log n), so membership alone does not compare actual runtimes.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 232 · NS0533
records.text: NS0533 Question 232 DSA05 What is the running time contribution of a single assignment statement according to analysis rules? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. One constant time unit in the elementary-operation model. DSA05 explicitly treats a single assignment as one unit in an elementary model, not one physical second. The convention abstracts hardware and requires that evaluating the assigned expression itself be constant cost; complicated expressions need their own accounting.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 233 · NS0534
records.text: NS0534 Question 233 DSA06 State the Transitivity theorem of Big-O. Why is it useful? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), then f∈O(h); this composes upper bounds. DSA06 composes the eventual inequalities f≤c g and g≤d h to obtain f≤cd h beyond both thresholds. Choose the larger threshold and multiply the positive witness constants. This lets a complicated bound pass through a simpler intermediate function.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 234 · NS0535
records.text: NS0535 Question 234 DSA06 Rank from slowest to fastest growing: O(n²), O(1), O(2ⁿ), O(log n), O(n) State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Increasing representative growth: 1, log n, n, n², 2^n. DSA06 gives the standard growth ordering, with constants below logarithms, then linear and quadratic functions, then exponential. The ranking compares representative rates, not disjoint Big-O classes, since loose upper bounds overlap.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 235 · NS0536
records.text: NS0536 Question 235 DSA05 What are the three main resources considered in algorithm analysis? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Time, memory space, and—in distributed settings—communication volume. DSA05 measures operation counts and live memory, and adds communication volume for distributed algorithms. Thus the third resource is context-dependent rather than a universal resource needed by every local algorithm. These are the three supported categories in the note.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 236 · NS0537
records.text: NS0537 Question 236 DSA28 What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search and when does it occur? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Θ(n) worst time, when absent or at the last position. DSA28 scans until equality or exhaustion. An absent target or one in the final position requires all n comparisons, giving linear worst time; a first-position match instead takes constant time. The operation and cases are directly supported.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 237 · NS0538
records.text: NS0538 Question 237 DSA29 Binary Search requires the list to be: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A Unsorted B Sorted C Circular D Linked Sorted DSA29 eliminates half an ordered interval according to the midpoint comparison. That elimination is valid only when comparable values follow a consistent order; descending input works with reversed comparisons. Circularity and links are representation properties, not substitutes for sortedness. An unsorted sequence gives no safe smaller-half decision. Therefore Sorted is the required prerequisite. A incorrect Without order, a midpoint comparison cannot safely eliminate either half. B correct Consistent sorted order supports the midpoint half-elimination invariant. C incorrect Circular storage does not establish the value ordering needed by binary search. D incorrect Linked storage does not imply sortedness and also changes midpoint-access costs.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 238 · NS0539
records.text: NS0539 Question 238 DSA29 How many steps does Binary Search take for a list of 1,000,000 elements (approximately)? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. About 20 worst-case midpoint probes. DSA29 gives floor(log₂n)+1 probes for n>0. Since 2^19=524288 and 2^20=1048576, one million lies between them, so the worst probe count is twenty under the ordinary interval algorithm. A root/midpoint hit can finish earlier.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 239 · NS0540
records.text: NS0540 Question 239 DSA32 What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort and why? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Worst and usual average Θ(n²); early-stop best Θ(n). DSA32 sums repeated adjacent passes to at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons, yielding quadratic worst and ordinary average work. A no-swap early-stop pass makes sorted input linear, while a fixed pass schedule remains quadratic. The answer needs these implementation and case distinctions.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 240 · NS0541
records.text: NS0541 Question 240 DSA33 In Selection Sort, what does each pass through the unsorted subarray accomplish? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Select the remaining minimum and put it at the next prefix position. DSA33 scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and exchanges it with A[i]. After each meaningful pass, the sorted prefix grows by one and contains the smallest keys placed so far. This differs from inserting the next encountered item into a prefix.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 241 · NS0542
records.text: NS0542 Question 241 DSA33 DSA34 How does Insertion Sort differ from Selection Sort conceptually? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Selection finds a suffix minimum; insertion places the next item into a sorted prefix. DSA33 chooses the globally smallest remaining key for each next output position. DSA34 instead takes the next input item, shifts larger prefix values, and inserts it into their gap. Both grow sorted prefixes, but choose their next item differently.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 242 · NS0543
records.text: NS0543 Question 242 DSA32 What is the best-case scenario for Bubble Sort and what is its complexity in that case? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Already sorted input; Θ(n) with no-swap early stopping. DSA32 performs one pass over an already sorted array, makes no swaps, and stops when early-exit detection is enabled. That is linear best work. A fixed-pass implementation still executes its quadratic comparison schedule even on the same input.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 243 · NS0544
records.text: NS0544 Question 243 DSA08 What are the two components of each node in a singly linked list? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Payload/data and a next-node link. DSA08 defines a singly linked node as data plus next. The head reference points to the first node, and a null next terminates an ordinary noncircular chain. Head is a list-level reference rather than a second payload field inside every node.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 244 · NS0545
records.text: NS0545 Question 244 DSA10 DSA08 How does a circular linked list differ from a singly linked list? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A circular tail links back to head instead of ending at null. DSA10 defines circularity by the tail-to-head link and stops traversal after returning to the start. This is independent of singly versus doubly linked: a singly linked list can itself be circular. Compared with the ordinary noncircular singly linked chain, termination changes from null to return-to-start.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 245 · NS0546
records.text: NS0546 Question 245 DSA09 To delete a node from the front of a singly linked list, what single update is needed? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Advance head to the old head’s next link, then reclaim the old node. DSA09 saves old=head, sets head=head.next, and releases old in an owned C++ chain. The essential link update is advancing head; check empty before dereferencing, and clear tail too if the only node was removed. This answers the operation without hiding ownership work.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 246 · NS0547
records.text: NS0547 Question 246 DSA10 What extra pointer does each node in a doubly linked list have compared to a singly linked list? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. A prev link to the predecessor. DSA10 says doubly linked nodes add prev alongside next. That extra link permits backward traversal and supports endpoint updates when head and tail are maintained. It does not automatically give constant arbitrary positional access, which may still need traversal.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 247 · NS0548
records.text: NS0548 Question 247 DSA02 DSA08 Why do linked lists have slower access times than arrays? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Arrays compute addresses directly; linked positional access follows a chain. DSA02 computes an element address from base, index, and element size in constant time. DSA08’s chain lacks direct index arithmetic, so reaching an arbitrary position may traverse linearly many links. This comparison concerns positional access rather than every operation: a known-head update can be constant.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 248 · NS0549
records.text: NS0549 Question 248 DSA13 Convert the infix expression A + B * C - D / E to postfix. Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. ABC*+DE/- DSA13 works the exact expression. Multiplication groups B*C and division groups D/E before addition and subtraction. Emit A, then B C *, then +, then D E /, then −, producing ABC*+DE/-.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 249 · NS0550
records.text: NS0550 Question 249 DSA11 What condition causes stack overflow in an array-implemented stack? Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations. Attempting push when the fixed array is full. DSA11 distinguishes full storage from the overflow attempt. Under zero-based top-as-last-occupied convention, full means top=C−1; a count convention uses size=C. A push must check this before writing beyond capacity.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 250 · NS0551
records.text: NS0551 Question 250 DSA11 What are the three main operations of a Stack and their time complexities? State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question. Push, pop, and peek are O(1) for fixed-array or head-linked stacks. DSA11 defines push insertion, pop removal/return, and peek observation at top. Fixed-array indexing and linked-head updates take constant work. A resizing append or singly linked tail-pop implementation can change the cost, so the guarantee needs the stated representations.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 251 · NS0552
records.text: NS0552 Question 251 DSA13 In postfix notation, why are parentheses unnecessary? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Operator position and known arity determine grouping. DSA13 places postfix operators after their operands. During stack evaluation, each binary operator consumes the two latest operand values in right-then-left order and pushes their result. The sequence therefore encodes grouping without precedence parentheses.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 252 · NS0553
records.text: NS0553 Question 252 DSA15 What is the difference between a simple array queue and a circular queue? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Circular wraparound reuses freed front slots; a simple noncircular queue may not. DSA15 distinguishes a rear index reaching the array end from circular modulo arithmetic. A circular queue can insert into positions freed at the front, while a simple noncircular version may report overflow despite those gaps. Capacity and empty/full conventions still must be consistent.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 253 · NS0554
records.text: NS0554 Question 253 DSA17 A stable priority queue serves smaller numeric priority keys first and compares equal priorities by an increasing arrival counter, also smallest first. If two tasks have equal priority, in what order are they served? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. FIFO among equal priorities: the task that arrived earlier is served first. The priority comparison ties, so the specified comparator proceeds to the arrival counter. An increasing counter gives the earlier arrival the smaller secondary key, causing it to be removed first. Equal-priority tasks are therefore served FIFO under this stable policy. That result follows from the explicitly chosen tie rule; an ordinary priority queue without a stability or comparator rule would not inherently guarantee arrival-order service.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 254 · NS0555
records.text: NS0555 Question 254 DSA11 DSA15 What causes queue underflow and what does it indicate? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Dequeue on an empty queue causes underflow. DSA11 defines underflow as attempted removal from empty storage; DSA15’s count convention detects empty using size==0. This indicates that no item exists to return, not that the array is full or that an ordinary emptiness test itself failed.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 255 · NS0556
records.text: NS0556 Question 255 DSA12 Name three real-world applications of stacks. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Runtime call frames, undo/redo history, and string or sequence reversal. DSA12 gives nested calls latest-first returns, moving latest actions between undo and redo stacks, and reversing input by pushing then popping. Each example uses the same latest-pending-item discipline. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 256 · NS0557
records.text: NS0557 Question 256 DSA19 What property must hold at every node of a Binary Search Tree? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger, for distinct keys. DSA19 imposes this invariant over entire subtrees at every node, not only immediate children. A descendant can satisfy its parent comparison yet violate an ancestor bound. Duplicate keys require an explicit count or placement policy instead of silently weakening the distinct-key rule.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 257 · NS0558
records.text: NS0558 Question 257 DSA20 DSA19 List the order of nodes visited in Inorder traversal of BST: root=4, left subtree has 1,2,3, right has 5,6,7. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 DSA20 visits left subtree, node, then right subtree for inorder, and says BST inorder returns sorted keys. The supplied seven distinct keys therefore appear in increasing order even though the internal child shapes are not fully specified. Shape would matter to preorder or postorder.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 258 · NS0559
records.text: NS0559 Question 258 DSA21 When deleting a BST node with two children, what are the two valid replacement choices? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Inorder predecessor or inorder successor. DSA21 identifies the maximum key in the left subtree and minimum key in the right subtree as valid replacement values. Copy one into the deleted node, then remove that value’s original node, which has at most one child. These preserve the subtree order invariant.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 259 · NS0560
records.text: NS0560 Question 259 DSA19 DSA22 What is the time complexity of BST search in the best case vs worst case? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Best successful search Θ(1); arbitrary BST worst Θ(n), balanced worst Θ(log n). DSA19 gives a constant root hit and O(height) search. A chain has linear height, producing linear worst work; logarithmic height disciplines in DSA22 improve that worst bound. Calling every BST logarithmic would incorrectly assume balance.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 260 · NS0561
records.text: NS0561 Question 260 DSA41 DSA42 What is the key difference between BFS and DFS graph traversal? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. BFS explores distance layers with FIFO; DFS finishes branches with a stack or recursion. DSA41 enqueues discoveries in layer order, while DSA42 resumes the latest unfinished branch before later neighbors. Both can traverse all reachable vertices, but their pending-work discipline and visitation order differ. BFS also has the unweighted minimum-edge guarantee.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 261 · NS0562
records.text: NS0562 Question 261 DSA40 A directed graph has edges with direction; an undirected graph does not. Give one real-world example of each. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Directed: following accounts; undirected: a mutual friendship relationship. DSA40 gives following as directed because u following v need not imply v following u. It gives mutual friendship as undirected, representing a symmetric connection. The examples concern relation semantics rather than whether lines happen to be drawn with arrows.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 262 · NS0563
records.text: NS0563 Question 262 DSA40 DSA41 Why is a dense graph more computationally expensive to process than a sparse graph? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Edge-processing algorithms do more work when E is larger. DSA40 says dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts and adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space. Traversals or algorithms inspecting every edge therefore require more work as density increases. This is not universal: a vertex-only operation need not inspect edges.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 263 · NS0564
records.text: NS0564 Question 263 DSA18 In a full binary tree, every node has either 0 or 2 children. How does this differ from a complete binary tree? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Full restricts each node to zero or two children; complete restricts level filling. DSA18 defines full by each node’s child count and complete by filled earlier levels plus left-filled final level. Those are distinct conditions: completeness can allow one child at the boundary, while fullness alone need not keep every level filled.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 264 · NS0565
records.text: NS0565 Question 264 DSA40 DSA43 What distinguishes a weighted graph from an unweighted graph, and when would you prefer weighted? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Weighted edges carry differing costs; use them when edge costs matter. DSA40 assigns costs to weighted edges and says unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. Distances or travel costs can therefore justify weights when fewer edges is not the true objective. DSA43 then distinguishes weighted shortest paths from unweighted BFS.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 265 · NS0566
records.text: NS0566 Question 265 DSA19 If a BST receives keys in sorted order (1,2,3,4,5), what shape does the tree take and what is the search complexity? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. An ordinary unbalanced insertion forms a right chain; worst search is Θ(n). DSA19 explicitly traces sorted insertion 1,2,3,4,5 into a right chain. Each new larger key follows right links to the tail, making the height linear. Worst search follows that chain, while a root hit remains constant. Balanced insertion would rotate and is a different assumption.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 266 · NS0567
records.text: NS0567 Question 266 DSA10 DSA02 When would you choose a linked list over an array? Give a specific scenario. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Choose links for frequent known-location updates, such as a doubly linked history cursor. DSA10 gives browser history with a doubly linked cursor as an application. With references to current insertion or removal positions, link changes avoid shifting an array’s later elements; arbitrary positional lookup can still be linear. This concrete scenario supports the choice without claiming universal superiority.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 267 · NS0568
records.text: NS0568 Question 267 DSA11 DSA14 DSA12 How does a stack differ from a queue? Give an application for each. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Stack: LIFO for undo; queue: FIFO for equal-priority printer jobs. DSA11 gives latest-first stack service and DSA12 applies it to undoing the latest edit. DSA14 gives arrival-order queues for equal-priority printing. Both ADTs may use arrays or nodes; their service order, not that representation, is the distinction.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 268 · NS0569
records.text: NS0569 Question 268 DSA22 DSA19 Why is a balanced BST (like AVL) preferred over a regular BST? Explain the worst-case scenario. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Balance prevents linear-height chains and guarantees logarithmic worst search. DSA22 maintains AVL balance factors through rotations that preserve inorder. DSA19 shows ordinary sorted insertion producing a chain, where a search can traverse all nodes. Maintaining logarithmic height prevents that worst degradation, though root-hit best time remains constant.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 269 · NS0570
records.text: NS0570 Question 269 DSA26 What is a hash collision? Name two methods to resolve collisions and compare them. Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. A collision maps different keys to one home address; compare chaining and open addressing. DSA26 stores colliding entries in bucket lists for chaining, whereas open addressing probes other array slots. Chaining uses link or bucket overhead and expected O(1+α) work; probing keeps entries inside the table and requires careful load and deletion policies. Neither prevents all collisions.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 270 · NS0571
records.text: NS0571 Question 270 DSA41 DSA42 DSA43 What is the difference between BFS and DFS? Which finds the shortest path? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. BFS uses FIFO layers and finds shortest unweighted paths; DFS uses branch-first stack order. DSA41 guarantees minimum-edge paths for BFS on unweighted graphs. DSA42 says DFS paths are reachability witnesses but need not be shortest. Differing edge weights require an appropriate weighted-path algorithm, such as Dijkstra under nonnegative weights.

records.title: Data Structure and Algorithms — Question 271 · NS0572
records.text: NS0572 Question 271 DSA12 A text editor needs to implement multi-level undo. Which data structure is most appropriate and why? Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result. Use an undo stack, with a second redo stack if needed. DSA12 moves the latest action from undo to redo and reverses that movement for redo. Pushing each new edit and popping for undo naturally matches the most-recent-edit-first requirement. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

records.title: Web Programming — Course module
records.text: Web Programming

records.title: Web Programming — Study notes
records.text: Web Programming Build a connected model of browser markup, CSS, JavaScript, server processing and persistent data. Read code literally before tracing it. Unless a section explicitly discusses legacy syntax, JavaScript means modern ECMAScript in a browser and PHP means PHP 8.x; database examples use MySQLi or PDO with a configured MySQL connection. Trace input → request → server validation → database → response → DOM update, including failures and permissions. Practise CSS winner/box calculations and small JS/PHP traces; record values and types after every statement. Compare GET/POST, browser/server state, callbacks/concurrency and parameterization/output encoding. Check task assumptions and code validity before selecting an answer.

records.title: Web Programming — Practice questions
records.text: Web Programming

records.title: Web Programming — Revision outline
records.text: Web Programming

records.title: Web Programming — Browser, server and technology roles
records.text: The Internet connects networks; the Web is a resource system commonly using HTTP. A browser/user agent requests resources and renders HTML/CSS, then runs permitted JavaScript. A web/HTTP server receives requests and returns representations, sometimes invoking application code. Client and server are roles and can run on the same machine. HTML supplies structure/meaning; CSS controls presentation; JavaScript supplies programmable interactivity. PHP, Python, JSP/Java and ASP.NET applications generate server responses and access databases; C# is commonly used with ASP.NET. Node.js is a JavaScript runtime, not a separate language. JavaScript can run on either side. Browser scripts are sandboxed, but may access selected files/devices through permission-based APIs. They are not inherently limited to trivial programs, nor can they freely access arbitrary client hardware. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Hosting, URLs and static versus dynamic content
records.text: Hosting supplies an environment where a site is served; domain registration reserves a name, and DNS maps names to network records. An ISP provides connectivity. A URL identifies scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment; the host identifies the machine/service name, while a fragment selects a local document location. A basic static server returns stored files; dynamic processing constructs a representation from logic, requests or data. Static pages can still run interactive browser scripts, and dynamic generation need not change visible text every time. A website groups resources; a page is one document/resource. Open standards do not guarantee identical support for every feature in every browser. Historical editor-name items refer to Microsoft FrontPage and Macromedia HomeSite5, not languages or required modern tools. Web Programming module Adobe/Macromedia HomeSite support archive Microsoft IE5 Corporate Deployment Guide

records.title: Web Programming — Read an HTTP/1.1 exchange
records.text: An HTTP/1.1 request begins with method, request-target and version, followed by header fields, a blank line, and an optional body. For example, GET /courses?id=7 HTTP/1.1 followed by Host: example.edu and a terminating blank line can have no body. A response begins with version, status code and optional reason phrase, then headers, blank line and permitted content. Request lines are not response status lines. Content-Type describes representation format; Content-Length or transfer framing establishes message boundaries when applicable. HTTP is stateless in its request semantics, but applications maintain state through sessions/databases. HTTP2/3 encode messages differently; a textual request-line description applies to HTTP/1.x. Asynchronous use is a client programming choice, not proof that HTTP has no responses. IETF RFC 9112

records.title: Web Programming — Methods, status and GET/POST reasoning
records.text: GET retrieves a representation with safe semantics; do not implement an intentional state-changing action as a GET link. POST asks the target to process supplied content. PUT creates/replaces the identified resource representation; DELETE requests removal of its association. Safe describes intended state effects; idempotent means repeating the same request has the same intended effect, not necessarily the same response. GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent; arbitrary POST is not. 200 indicates success, 201 creation, 204 success without content, 301 permanent redirection, 400 malformed request, 401 missing/invalid authentication, 403 refusal, 404 unavailable/not found, and 500 an unexpected server failure. GET forms usually put name/value pairs in the URL query; POST forms put them in the body. Neither method encrypts data. POST bodies are visible to developer tools and subject to server/configured size limits. IETF RFC 9110

records.title: Web Programming — HTTPS and resource-oriented APIs
records.text: HTTPS uses HTTP over TLS, protecting channel confidentiality/integrity and authenticating the server under certificate checks. It does not make unvalidated input safe or guarantee a trustworthy merchant. A RESTful API follows constraints such as client/server separation, stateless requests, cacheability and a uniform resource interface. Resources have identifiers and representations; JSON is common but not required. Merely returning JSON does not prove REST. For a resource /students/7, GET reads it, PUT can replace it, and DELETE requests removal, subject to authentication/authorization and validation. Represent errors consistently and evaluate retry safety before repeating a request. Store durable application facts server-side; stateless API requests can still operate on persistent database state. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — HTML document, text and metadata
records.text: HTML means HyperText Markup Language. selects modern standards mode; is the document root, holds metadata, and contains document content. supplies the page/tab title. Meta charset declares encoding; description summarizes the page; viewport controls mobile viewport behavior. Heading levels h1–h6 express hierarchy, with h6 conventionally smallest in default styling, not a mandatory CSS size. <p> marks paragraphs; <br> is a line break and <hr> a thematic break. <pre> preserves source whitespace; <code> marks code. <strong> indicates importance and <em> stress; <b>/<i> have other text semantics and are not identical to importance/emphasis. <sub>/<sup> mark sub/superscripts. <!-- comment --> is not displayed but remains visible in source. Entities include ©, <, > and &. Tags mark boundaries; an element includes content and attributes, or is a void element such as img. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Links, images and accessible meaning
records.text: Use Read for a link; href is the destination, not url/link. A fragment such as href="#details" links to an element with id="details". target="_self" uses the current context, _blank a new context, _parent its parent and _top the top-level context. Browser preferences determine tab versus window. supplies source and alternative text. Use empty alt for purely decorative images; informative images need meaningful alternatives. Width/height reserve dimensions; title is not a replacement for alt. An anchor may wrap an image. Give controls programmatic labels, clear link text and keyboard access; visual styling alone does not establish accessibility. Attributes belong in opening tags, with unique IDs when used for document identification. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Lists, tables and navigation
records.text: Unordered <ul> and ordered <ol> contain <li> items. Ordered lists can specify start and numbering type; use CSS list-style-type for presentation. A definition list uses <dl>, <dt> terms and <dd> descriptions. Navigation can be a semantic <nav> containing a list of links. <table> contains rows <tr>, header cells <th> and data cells <td>; a td is not the table itself. colspan spans columns; rowspan spans rows. Account for occupied cells before placing the next cell, and use header associations for accessible data. CSS handles borders, background, cell padding and collapsed borders; legacy bgcolor/bordercolor are not preferred styling. Resetting nav ul with list-style-type:none; margin:0; padding:0 removes bullets and default spacing only; it does not itself arrange links horizontally or create a dropdown. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Form controls and successful submission
records.text: A form’s action identifies its processing URL, method its submission method, and enctype its encoding. The default method is GET. Named enabled successful controls contribute values: unchecked checkboxes/radios are usually absent. A label’s for matches the control’s id; name identifies its submitted field. Same-name radio buttons form a single-choice group; checkboxes permit independent selections. <select> contains <option>; textarea accepts multiple lines. For a text input, size indicates approximate visible width, whereas maxlength limits entered text length. Neither means a server security bound. type="password" masks display but does not encrypt. submit submits; button has no submission action by itself. type=email/required give browser validation feedback; arbitrary clients can bypass it. No GET/POST method universally means “parse one element at a time.” Web Programming module WHATWG HTML input standard

records.title: Web Programming — Frames, media and graphics
records.text: Legacy frameset/frame divides a window into separate documents; frameset replaced body in old frameset documents. Named targets controlled which frame changed; independent scrolling could leave other frames stationary. These elements are obsolete in modern HTML. An iframe embeds a document within an ordinary page and needs appropriate permissions/sandboxing for untrusted content. Modern audio/video elements embed supported media, often with controls and fallback content; embed/object can also embed supported resources. Several tags can embed supported video resources; distinguish their semantics and browser support. Old bgsound or Flash examples do not imply current browser support. Canvas provides script-driven bitmap drawing via a context; SVG describes scalable shapes in the DOM. For a simple canvas task, obtain getContext("2d"), then use fillRect(x,y,w,h); line/path methods require beginPath/moveTo/lineTo/stroke. Preserve a text alternative where graphics convey information. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — CSS attachment and selector meaning
records.text: An external sheet uses <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in head; an internal sheet uses style; an inline declaration uses an element’s style attribute. External CSS promotes reuse, consistent design and caching; it does not guarantee that every page becomes smaller or accessible. A rule is selector { property: value; }. Comments use /* ... */. Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID, h1,h2 groups selectors, nav ul selects descendants and nav>ul direct children. Attribute selectors match properties such as [type="email"], pseudo-classes states such as :hover/:focus, and pseudo-elements parts such as ::before. A selector chooses where declarations apply; it is not itself the property that sets a color. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Resolve cascade, specificity and inheritance
records.text:
First compare applicable declarations in their cascade origin, importance and layer context; then compare specificity and order within the relevant context. In an ordinary same-origin/same-layer author example, an ID outweighs class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, which outweigh type/pseudo-element selectors. Compare counts lexicographically, not as an unlimited base-ten total. Equally specific applicable rules use later source order. An important declaration outranks a competing normal declaration in that context. For

, #intro{color:blue} beats .note{color:red}. A competing p{color:green!important} beats those normal declarations. Inherited color/fonts apply when the element lacks a stronger specified value; margin/padding/borders do not normally inherit. :not() contributes the specificity of its argument rather than universally zero. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN specificity

records.title: Web Programming — Style properties and box calculations
records.text: color sets text color; background-color sets background; font-size size, font-family face, font-style italic, font-weight weight, text-align inline-content alignment, and text-decoration effects such as underline. Margin lies outside the border; padding lies inside; border surrounds content/padding. With content-box width200px, horizontal padding10px and borders2px, border-box width is224px, excluding margins. With border-box width200px, content width is176px. Shorthand values follow top/right/bottom/left: one applies everywhere, two vertical/horizontal, three top/horizontal/bottom, four each side. Adjacent vertical block margins can collapse rather than add; padding does not collapse. Non-replaced inline elements do not obey width/height like blocks. A 1rem length uses root font size; font-size in em uses parent font size, whereas many other em lengths use the element’s computed font size. In historical markup, the body text attribute controlled default text color, while bgcolor controlled background. Current CSS uses color and background-color instead. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Layout, alignment and responsive design
records.text: Normal flow lays out blocks/inlines. Flexbox arranges direct children on a main axis; justify-content follows that axis, align-items the cross axis. With row direction in ordinary horizontal writing, cross-axis alignment is vertical. Grid organizes rows and columns with explicit tracks, such as grid-template-columns:1fr 2fr. vertical-align applies to inline/table-cell contexts and does not center every block. align-content distributes tracks/lines when there is applicable extra space, not arbitrary single-child centering. Relative positioning offsets a box while retaining its flow space; absolute removes it and uses its containing block, often established by a positioned ancestor; fixed commonly uses the viewport. Responsive design combines flexible layout, images, viewport metadata and media queries, for example @media(max-width:600px){.cards{grid-template-columns:1fr}}. A min-width768px query targets wider viewports, not mobile alone. Browser compatibility requires feature testing and fallbacks; responsive size handling is a different issue. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — JavaScript syntax, inclusion and declarations
records.text: Use <script src="app.js"></script> for an external .js file; script content has no HTML closing-tag syntax inside its JavaScript source. A deferred script runs after parsing and before DOMContentLoaded. JavaScript originated at Netscape; it is distinct from Java and supports sophisticated applications through prototype-based objects and first-class functions. Identifiers are case-sensitive and may start with letters, underscore or $, not digits or spaces. var has function/global scope; let/const are block-scoped. const prevents rebinding but not mutation of an object’s contents. // comments end at line end; /* */ span a block. Semicolons delimit statements, although automatic insertion exists. Whitespace usually separates tokens but newlines can affect parsing, especially after return. “use strict” is a directive string, not a reserved statement keyword. Parse syntax before computing outputs. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Types, conversions and missing values
records.text: JavaScript primitives are undefined, null, Boolean, Number, BigInt, String and Symbol; objects include arrays, functions and dates. Float is not a separate Number primitive type. Arrays are objects, even though informal texts call them an array data type. typeof new Date() is "object"; typeof null is historically "object". An unassigned declared variable or missing ordinary object property evaluates to undefined; directly reading an undeclared variable usually throws ReferenceError. Strings use either quote style, with appropriate escaping. + can concatenate when a string is involved; arithmetic / converts ordinary numeric strings. "abc"/"def" produces NaN; nonzero Number divided by zero produces signed Infinity, while 0/0 produces NaN. parseInt("12.8",10) reads12, stopping at the dot; this is parsing, not rounding. Global isNaN converts first; Number.isNaN does not. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN JavaScript data structures

records.title: Web Programming — Trace assignments, comparisons and postfix updates
records.text: Evaluate operators in their specified order and write down both value and type. JavaScript has ==/!= with coercion and ===/!== without coercion; strict operators do not replace or remove the loose ones. A condition ? x : y chooses one branch. var a="20"; var b=a=30; assigns Number 30 to both, so a+b is 60, not 50. "1 plus 1 is "+1+1 concatenates left to right to "1 plus 1 is 11". Postfix a++ yields the old value and then increments a. If a=10, a==a++ compares10 with10, then the body sees11. With a=1, printing a-- then a prints10. These JS evaluation rules are not portable to C/C++ expressions with unsequenced modifications. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN equality comparisons Mozilla MDN increment operator

records.title: Web Programming — Math, string and array API microtraces
records.text: Math.abs(-9)=9, Math.floor(5.9)=5, and Math.sqrt(36)=6. A JS string’s substring(start,end) includes start and excludes end: "exitexam".substring(2,6) is "itex". Indexes start at zero. Array push/pop add/remove at the end; unshift/shift act at the beginning. slice returns a selected shallow copy; splice(start,deleteCount,...items) mutates by removal/insertion. reverse reverses in place. reduce combines sequentially from left to right; reduceRight combines sequentially from right to left with an accumulator, not simultaneous parallel execution. For [1,2,3].reduceRight((a,v)=>a-v,0), accumulator values are -3,-5,-6. An absent initial value uses the last present item first; an empty array without one throws. Method spelling and case matter. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN reduceRight Mozilla MDN Math Mozilla MDN substring

records.title: Web Programming — Control flow, functions and errors
records.text: for(initialization;test;update) initializes once, checks before each iteration, then updates after each body. while checks before its body; do...while executes at least once. break exits and continue advances to the next iteration. A loop from n=1 while n<7 prints a message only at n=5 when testing n%5==0. function f(x){return x*2;} has a parameter and returns a value; functions can be passed/stored like other values. Arrow syntax is compact but differs in this/constructor behavior. Runtime argument limits mean “no limit whatsoever” is too absolute. try/catch handles thrown errors during execution; throw signals one; finally runs cleanup. Parse-time syntax errors and logical errors are different. bool ans=true is not JavaScript declaration syntax; use let ans=true. A literal type of expression is not the typeof operator. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — DOM selection, creation and safe updates
records.text: The DOM is a hierarchy of nodes representing the document. document.getElementById("x") returns the matching element or null; querySelector(".item") returns the first match, and querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList. Other plural lookup methods can return live collections. Guard missing elements and run code after the relevant markup exists. To add a div: const el=document.createElement("div"); el.textContent="Hello"; document.body.appendChild(el);. Creation alone does not insert it. createTextNode makes text; appendChild attaches an existing node. innerHTML parses/replaces descendants, so += reparses/replaces the prior descendant content too and can destroy listeners/state. Use textContent for untrusted plain text. element.style.backgroundColor sets a style property; classList.add changes a class. getElementByld with a lowercase l replacing I is a different, nonexistent method. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Events and validated submission
records.text: An event handler runs when an event occurs: click, input, keydown, mouseover, submit and load are examples. addEventListener("click",handler) registers a function without calling it immediately. Multiple listeners may coexist; once removes one after use, capture selects an earlier propagation phase and passive promises no default cancellation. Event bubbling is distinct from the browser’s default action. For submission, form.addEventListener("submit",e=>{if(!valid()){e.preventDefault();}}) stops the default only on failure. Returning false from an addEventListener callback does not cancel it; return false works in an appropriate inline/onsubmit property handler whose caller uses that return. For cancelable keyboard defaults, call preventDefault rather than assuming a different key event itself disappears. Browser checks improve feedback; repeat validation and authorization on the server. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN addEventListener

records.title: Web Programming — Window, dialogs and browser properties
records.text: In a normal browser page, window exposes the browsing context and document is its document property. alert displays information, confirm returns a Boolean, and prompt requests text or returns null on cancellation. console.log logs diagnostics. location.reload() reloads the current page. screen.availHeight, screen.availWidth and screen.colorDepth have exact camelCase spelling; ColorsDepth is not the property. window.onload is a handler property for the load event, typically after dependent resources finish. Global let/const are not window properties like classic top-level var bindings. document.write is a method/function property; writing after document load can replace the document. document.bgColor is a legacy property; Document.bgcolor has wrong object/case. Use document.body.style.backgroundColor for current styling. Browser workers support concurrent computation, but DOM access normally remains on the page’s main thread. Web Programming module Mozilla MDN Screen

records.title: Web Programming — PHP syntax, names and types
records.text: PHP means PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. Use <?php ... ?> in a .php file; a closing tag can be omitted at file end. It can emit ordinary text and HTML. PHP8 no longer accepts historical <script language="PHP"> delimiters; short <? depends on configuration, so use the full form. A stray >> is not a closing PHP tag. Variables begin with $, then a letter/underscore and subsequent letters/digits/underscores; $AGE18 works but $18AGE does not. Names are case-sensitive. Dynamic typing permits values of different types without a preceding type declaration, though optional declarations can constrain them. Scalars include int,float,string,bool; arrays/objects are structured values and null means no value. var_dump displays type and value. Constants cannot normally be redefined during execution. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — PHP output, strings and comparisons
records.text:
echo is a language construct with no return value and can emit comma-separated expressions. print takes one expression and returns1. They are two basic output constructs, not the only output mechanisms; printf, print_r and others exist. Neither automatically inserts spaces/newlines. Two prints of5 emit55; "I"."am" emitsIam. Dot concatenates; + is arithmetic. Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and escapes such as \n; single quotes normally preserve dollar names literally. To emit literal $lfc use echo '$lfc'; or escape the dollar in double quotes. String offsets start at zero: "maroon"[2] is r when the surrounding PHP is valid. strlen counts bytes; strpos can return integer0 or false, requiring ===false for failure. strrev reverses bytes and str_replace replaces matching content. PHP 8==8.0 is true, but 8===8.0 is false because types differ; echo false emits an empty string, echo true emits1. PHP sends markup as response characters; a browser then interprets it. echo "A
B" emits a tag in raw output but normally displays two text lines. The invalid
markup depends on HTML error recovery, so specify raw versus rendered output. Web Programming module PHP manual: strings PHP manual: echo

records.title: Web Programming — PHP scope, parameters and persistent locals
records.text: A variable outside a function has global scope. A function’s locals and by-value parameters are separate bindings; use global $x or $GLOBALS["x"] to refer to a global explicitly. Superglobals are available across scopes. A static local retains its value across calls during the execution lifecycle; static storage is not simply another visibility scope. An uninitialized static local begins as null, so echo emits no characters. If global $i=10 and sample($i) increments/prints its by-value parameter, the caller’s $i stays10. Printing before, during and after gives10,11,10 when commas are written by the source. A global statement outside the function does not turn its value parameter into a reference. Common “three scopes” teaching counts local, global and static, but state the taxonomy. A static counter initialized0 then incremented on each call emits1 then2. Web Programming module PHP manual: variable scope

records.title: Web Programming — PHP arrays, loops and callable behavior
records.text: PHP arrays map integer/string keys to values. Numeric arrays start at index0 unless keys are supplied: [20,12,23,19,18] has19 at index3. Associative syntax uses a contiguous => operator: ["top"=>"black"] stores black under key"top". Splitting it as = > is a parse error, not valid array syntax. foreach($items as $key=>$value) iterates entries; for and while use tests/updates much like the corresponding JS forms. $sub-=$sub is $sub=$sub-$sub, not decrement. For $sum=0; foreach([2,4] as $v){$sum+=$v;} the result is6. A function can receive arguments, return a value, or produce output; classes/objects/variables also support server processing, so no single one of these mechanisms alone defines “dynamic PHP.” Use braces to make nesting explicit. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Request data, server validation and injection
records.text: $_GET contains query parameters; $_POST contains supported form POST data; $_FILES upload metadata; $_SERVER request/environment details; $_COOKIE cookie values; $_SESSION session data after startup. $GLOBALS is the actual global-symbol array; $_GLOBAL is not the built-in name. $_REQUEST may combine GET/POST/cookie data according to configuration; it is not a database interface and has ambiguous precedence, so prefer the intended source. isset tests existence and non-null, not truth or valid syntax. Read input, check required fields/type/length/range, authenticate and authorize, then process. Bind SQL parameters to keep values separate from commands. Encode output for HTML/attribute/JS context; textContent handles plain browser text. A security test can detect SQL injection or XSS but does not itself fix either. Client validation, encryption and a database connection do not replace these controls. Web Programming module

records.title: Web Programming — Cookies and browser storage
records.text: Cookies are browser-held name/value data automatically attached to matching requests subject to domain, path, expiry, Secure and SameSite rules. HttpOnly restricts script access; Secure requires secure transport. They are not attached to every site indiscriminately.
