records.title: Web Programming — Question 260 · NS0804
records.text: NS0804 Question 260 WEB06 What is the highest-level heading tag in HTML? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A <h6> B <heading> C <h0> D <h1> <h1> WEB06 defines heading levels h1 through h6 as a hierarchy. h1 is the highest level and h6 the lowest, regardless of CSS choices that can change their visual size. heading and h0 are not the defined heading-level tags. The answer is semantic rank, not whichever text happens to be styled largest. A incorrect h6 is the lowest of the defined heading levels, not the highest. B incorrect heading is not one of the defined h1–h6 heading-level tags. C incorrect h0 is outside the defined heading levels in WEB06. records.title: Web Programming — Question 261 · NS0805
records.text: NS0805 Question 261 WEB06 Which element is the root element of an HTML page? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A <head> B <body> C <html> D <root> <html> WEB06 explicitly identifies html as the document root, with head holding metadata and body containing document content. Those two elements are inside the document rather than replacing its root. root is not the HTML tag used for this role. Thus the root-element question directly selects C. A incorrect head holds metadata and is not the document root. B incorrect body holds document content but is not the document’s root element. C correct html is explicitly defined as the document root in WEB06. D incorrect root is not the HTML root tag given here.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 262 · NS0806
records.text: NS0806 Question 262 WEB07 Which attribute provides alternative text for an image? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A title B src C alt D caption alt WEB07 gives img a src for its resource and alt for alternative text. Informative images need meaningful alternatives; decorative ones use empty alt. A title is not a replacement for alt, and a caption is separate visible context rather than the requested attribute. Therefore C names the accessibility text attribute. A incorrect title is not a replacement for the image’s alternative-text attribute. B incorrect src identifies the image resource rather than its alternative text. C correct alt supplies the image’s alternative text, or an empty value for purely decorative images. D incorrect caption is not the requested image alternative-text attribute.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 263 · NS0807
records.text: NS0807 Question 263 WEB07 What does target="_blank" do in a link? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A Opens the link in the same window B Opens the link in a new tab or window C Closes the current window D Opens the link in a parent frame Open a new browsing context, commonly a new tab or window. WEB07 maps _blank to a new context, _self to current, and _parent to parent. Browser preferences decide tab versus window, so B correctly allows either. The target does not close the current window or select the parent frame. This is a browsing-context request rather than a guaranteed window-management UI behavior. A incorrect The current context is selected by _self rather than _blank. B correct _blank requests a new context, with tab versus window determined by browser behavior. C incorrect The target does not request that the current window be closed. D incorrect The parent context is selected by _parent rather than _blank.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 264 · NS0808
records.text: NS0808 Question 264 WEB08 Which HTML tag is used for an unordered list? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A <ol> B <li> C <ul> D <list> <ul> WEB08 defines ul as unordered and ol as ordered, with li items inside either. C therefore supplies the requested container. li is only an item, and list is not the defined HTML list-container name. Presentation of markers can be changed with CSS without changing whether the element is the unordered-list structure. A incorrect ol is an ordered-list container, not the unordered-list container requested. B incorrect li marks an item inside a list rather than the list container itself. C correct ul is explicitly the unordered-list container in WEB08. D incorrect list is not the unordered-list element spelling defined here.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 265 · NS0809
records.text: NS0809 Question 265 WEB08 What HTML tag defines a table row? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A <td> B <th> C <table> D <tr> <tr> WEB08 distinguishes the table element, row elements, and header/data cells. tr defines one row, while th and td are cells placed within rows. table contains the complete tabular structure. Therefore D is the row tag, independent of how many columns or spans the cells in that row occupy. A incorrect td defines a data cell, not the containing row. B incorrect th defines a header cell, not the containing row. C incorrect table defines the whole table rather than one row. D correct tr is the table-row element explicitly identified in WEB08.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 266 · NS0810
records.text: NS0810 Question 266 WEB08 What does the colspan attribute do in a table? Use the element or attribute meaning and document structure, rather than appearance or a similar-looking name. A Sets the column color B Merges cells across multiple columns C Sets the column width D Merges cells across multiple rows Make one cell span multiple columns. WEB08 explicitly distinguishes colspan from rowspan. colspan allocates a cell across columns, often described informally as merging cells horizontally; it does not change a column’s color or width rule. rowspan is the vertical counterpart across rows. B therefore matches, while actual placement must still account for positions already occupied by spans. A incorrect Column color is a styling concern rather than the colspan structural span. B correct colspan makes one cell occupy positions across multiple columns. C incorrect Column width is not the meaning of the colspan count. D incorrect Spanning rows is rowspan, not colspan.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 267 · NS0811
records.text: NS0811 Question 267 WEB06 WEB14 WEB-S12 Which meta tag is used for responsive design on mobile devices? Identify the requested presentation effect and layout context before matching the property or rule. A <meta name="keywords"> B <meta name="robots"> C <meta name="description"> D <meta name="viewport"> <meta name="viewport"> WEB06 gives viewport metadata control over mobile viewport behavior, and WEB14 includes it alongside flexible layout and media queries for responsive design. Keywords and description concern metadata for content/discoverability, while robots concerns crawler directives. The viewport entry is the relevant mobile-layout metadata; it does not replace responsive CSS by itself. A incorrect Keywords metadata does not configure the mobile viewport used for responsive layout. B incorrect Robots metadata concerns crawler handling rather than the mobile viewport. C incorrect Description summarizes the page rather than controlling mobile viewport behavior. D correct Viewport metadata configures mobile viewport behavior as part of responsive design.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 268 · NS0812
records.text: NS0812 Question 268 WEB11 Which CSS selector targets an element with id="logo"? Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax. A .logo B logo C *logo D #logo #logo WEB11 explicitly uses #logo as an ID selector and .notice as a class selector. Thus an element whose id is logo is targeted with #logo. A bare logo would be a type selector for an element named logo, while the starred concatenation is not the stated ID syntax. D is the correct selector. A incorrect .logo targets a class named logo rather than id="logo". B incorrect Bare logo is a type selector, not the ID selector requested. C incorrect *logo is not the defined CSS ID-selector syntax. D correct #logo is the explicit ID-selector pattern supplied in WEB11.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 269 · NS0813
records.text: NS0813 Question 269 WEB11 Which CSS selector targets all elements with class="highlight"? Identify which elements a rule targets and distinguish selector syntax from declaration syntax. A #highlight B .highlight C *highlight D highlight .highlight WEB11 gives a dot-prefixed name as a class selector and a hash-prefixed name as an ID selector. Applying that rule to highlight yields .highlight. A bare word selects element type, and *highlight is not the supported class syntax. The class rule can match every element carrying that class, rather than only one unique ID. A incorrect #highlight selects an ID rather than elements with the highlight class. B correct .highlight is the dot-prefixed class selector matching the requested class. C incorrect *highlight is not the defined class-selector syntax. B correct It generates numeric values commonly used for row identifiers; gaps and explicit values remain possible. C incorrect It does not automatically delete old rows. D incorrect It does not perform database backups.

records.title: Web Programming — Question 305 · NS0849
records.text: NS0849 Question 305 WEB32 Which PHP function closes a MySQL database connection? Identify the API and operation first, then distinguish connection setup, statement execution and result processing. A mysqli_end() B mysqli_disconnect() C mysqli_close() D db_close() mysqli_close($conn) WEB32 explicitly gives mysqli_close as closing a connection. C names that MySQLi API; the procedural form uses the connection argument in real code. Closing a connection is separate from ending a query or deleting stored data, and the other offered function names are not the standard one identified here. A incorrect mysqli_end() is not the connection-closing function named in WEB32. B incorrect mysqli_disconnect() is not the API identified here for this operation. C correct mysqli_close closes the MySQLi connection, using its connection argument in procedural code. D incorrect db_close() is not the standard MySQLi function named in the supplied note.

records.text: Operating System

records.title: Operating System — Study notes
records.text: Operating System An OS controls resource sharing, protects programs and provides convenient services. Learn the state changes and algorithms behind each term. Scheduling and deadlock questions require explicit assumptions; a policy name alone does not establish a universal performance ranking. Draw process-state transitions and a Gantt chart before calculating scheduling metrics. Record arrivals, burst lengths, priority convention, quantum and switch cost. For deadlock, identify held resources and directed waits; distinguish prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery. CPU preemption is not the same as resource preemption. Trace address translation, page replacement and file-block lookup with small numbers. Compare convenience, efficiency and ability to evolve using concrete mechanisms.

records.title: Operating System — Practice questions
records.text: Operating System

records.title: Operating System — Revision outline
records.text: Operating System

records.title: Operating System — Objectives, resource management and evolution
records.text: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function. Ability to evolve means adding hardware support, features and repairs through maintainable interfaces/modules. Backward compatibility preserves supported older application behavior; it is not a promise that every old binary works. Scalability means handling greater workload/resources; portability means adapting to other platforms. Fault tolerance continues correct service despite specified failures; recovery restores service afterward. Updates and monitoring help administration, but automatic updates are not a defining property of every OS. Operating System module Oracle Solaris 11

records.title: Operating System — Batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing and real time
records.text: Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices. Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users. A single CPU interleaves execution; multiple CPUs can execute work truly in parallel. Shared-memory multiprocessors do not require each CPU to have private main memory. Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications. Network systems expose remote services; distributed systems coordinate work across machines, sometimes hiding location. Real-time correctness includes timing: hard deadlines must be met, while soft deadline misses degrade service. “Real time” does not simply mean fast. Spooling and multitasking are mechanisms, not proof of a particular OS generation. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Kernel, shell, privilege and boot
records.text: The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling. A shell reads/interprets user commands; a GUI is another interface. Browsers, office tools and editors are applications. Device drivers are commonly kernel components, although user-space drivers also exist. Kernel mode has privileged operations; supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode, so offering both as exclusive answers is ambiguous. Firmware/bootloader stages execute before transferring control to a kernel loaded into RAM. The kernel is the first core OS component, not the first program ever executed at power-on. Loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel; “kernel modules cannot be loaded while running” is false in modular systems. A resident kernel remains active through the session. Utilities such as antivirus and disk tools can combine user processes with privileged components. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — APIs, system calls and virtualization
records.text: A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket. A user-facing API/library may wrap that request; not every library function enters the kernel. Distinguish the application API from the direct user/kernel boundary when describing access to OS services. Process control, file/device management, information retrieval and communication are service categories. Video editing and a database-specific write_database() are application operations, not standard generic syscall categories/names. Virtualization presents a virtual machine environment, often allowing guest operating systems on one host through a hypervisor. It differs from virtual memory, which translates a process’s addresses. Kernel, shell, API and VM are not interchangeable labels. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Programs, processes and PCB contents
records.text: A program is stored instructions; a process is an executing instance with address space and resources. A process does not universally “manage applications” or “provide a user interface.” The PCB records identity, state, PC/registers, scheduling information, memory/accounting details and I/O/open-resource state. A saved PC identifies where execution resumes. A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead. An interrupt or system call can switch privilege without switching process. Task is OS-specific terminology: it may mean process, thread or schedulable entity. No universal process-versus-task distinction follows from the word alone. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Process states, queues and schedulers
records.text: New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state. The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests. The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission. Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work. The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection. A bare “priority” causes running→ready only if a preemptive policy chooses another process. Operating System module UIC CPU Scheduling

records.title: Operating System — Creation, fork/exec and termination
records.text: Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call. In POSIX-style systems fork() creates a child: zero is returned in the child and the child PID in the parent on success. The two have distinct address spaces, although resources may be shared through explicit mechanisms. exec replaces the current process image; it does not itself create another process. Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary. exit() terminates normally through the runtime; abort() requests abnormal termination. A reference to nonexistent/protected memory is a fatal fault, unlike an application deciding to exit after bad input. “Terminate exit” is not a precise standard category. Parent termination does not universally kill all descendants. Linux man-pages fork(2) Linux man-pages execve(2)

records.title: Operating System — Threads and mapping models
records.text: A thread has its own PC, registers and stack. Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources. A process can contain many threads; a thread belongs to one process at a time. Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially. Independent processes can exist; cooperating ones communicate/share data. User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS. In many-to-one mapping, a blocking kernel call can block all user threads and one kernel execution context cannot use multiple CPUs simultaneously. One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks. Many-to-many multiplexes user threads over several kernel threads. Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither. Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — IPC and blocking semantics
records.text: Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates. Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations. Pipes provide streams; message queues preserve messages; sockets connect endpoints; RPC requests a remote operation. HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.” Blocking send waits for the required handoff/buffering/receipt condition defined by its API. Blocking receive waits for a message. Nonblocking operations return promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. “Sender blocked until received” identifies blocking send under rendezvous semantics. File locks coordinate access rather than transfer arbitrary payloads, though locking is synchronization within IPC. Do not equate asynchronous messaging with no synchronization ever. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Races, critical sections and correctness
records.text: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself. A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions. Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures. Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection. A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization. Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent. Example Worked microexample Two threads read counter=0, each computes 1 and each stores 1. Two increments produce 1 instead of 2. Protecting the entire read-modify-write with one lock prevents that lost update. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Semaphores and resource-count traces
records.text: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter. Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model. A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks. Example Worked microexample Initialize a mutex semaphore to 1. Each thread does wait(m); critical work; signal(m). For a buffer of N slots use empty=N, full=0 and mutex=1: producer waits empty then mutex, inserts, unlocks then signals full. Waiting for empty while already holding mutex can prevent the consumer from freeing a slot. Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP Semaphores

records.title: Operating System — Turn variables and atomic primitives
records.text: Strict alternation uses turn=0/1: process i waits while turn≠i, then enters and sets turn to the other process on leaving. It enforces turns but can violate progress if the other process stays outside its critical region. A naive lock-variable test followed by a separate set races because both processes can observe free before either sets it. Test-and-set and compare-and-swap combine checking/updating atomically; ordinary check-then-write does not. Peterson’s classic algorithm uses flags plus turn for two processes under its memory-model assumptions; a semaphore can coordinate more than two. Disabling local interrupts does not exclude other CPUs and is not a general user-space locking solution. Interrupts can notify/synchronize events, so they cannot be universally excluded from every synchronization-related classification. UIC Process Synchronization

records.title: Operating System — Scheduling metrics and calculation method
records.text: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting. Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time. Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization. First construct a time line with arrivals, idle gaps, preemptions and overhead, then calculate per-process values before averages. Do not confuse first response with final completion. Example Worked microexample A job arrives at 2, starts at 5, uses 4 CPU units without interruption and finishes at 9: response=3, turnaround=7, waiting=3. Six completions in two hours means throughput=3 jobs/hour. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Preemptive versus non-preemptive decisions
records.text: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release. CPU preemption saves a context and reallocates processing time; taking an occupied printer or lock may be unsafe. This is why time-slicing does not automatically remove the no-resource-preemption condition for deadlock. Frequent switches have cost; non-preemptive policies can delay interactive work behind long bursts. Operating System module UIC CPU Scheduling

records.title: Operating System — FCFS and the convoy effect
records.text: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect. A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large. FCFS does not universally have the worst turnaround for every possible workload. Example Worked microexample All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3. Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17. Turnarounds 24,27,30 average to 27. If arrivals are not simultaneous, recompute using their actual times. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — SJF/SJN and shortest remaining time
records.text: Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt. Future burst lengths normally need estimates. SJF minimizes average waiting for the usual fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no preemption/switch cost; that theorem is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy. Repeated short arrivals can starve a long job. The shortest total original burst is not necessarily the shortest remaining burst after execution has begun. Example Worked microexample P1 arrives 0 with burst 8; P2 arrives 1 with burst 2. SRTF runs P1 0–1, P2 1–3, P1 3–10. P1 waiting=2 and P2 waiting=0. Non-preemptive SJF cannot interrupt P1 once it has started. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Priority, starvation and aging
records.text: Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job. Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority. State whether a high-priority arrival preempts. Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load. SJF can also starve long jobs; starvation is not exclusive to fixed-priority scheduling. Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit. It is not a deadlock cure. Priority inversion occurs when urgent work waits on a resource held by lower-priority work; priority inheritance can temporarily raise the holder’s priority. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Round Robin, quantum and bounded turns
records.text: RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave. Specify how arrivals at a quantum boundary enter the queue. A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead. RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths. With n continuously ready jobs, no priority bypass and zero overhead, a just-requeued job waits at most (n−1)q for its next turn. This bounds one interval, not total lifetime waiting when arrivals or blocking are unrestricted. Include context-switch costs if given. Example Worked microexample P1=5,P2=3, both arrive 0, q=2: P1 0–2,P2 2–4,P1 4–6,P2 6–7,P1 7–8. Completions 8,7; waiting=8−5=3 and 7−3=4; average 3.5. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Multilevel queues and feedback
records.text: A multilevel queue separates classes, such as foreground interactive and background batch, and chooses both between queues and within them. Fixed interqueue priority may starve lower queues; allocating time shares between classes can avoid this. A multilevel feedback queue allows movement according to observed behavior, commonly demoting CPU-intensive jobs and periodically boosting priority. Do not infer movement from a simple multilevel-queue label. State initial class, quantum per level, promotion/demotion rules and interqueue policy before tracing. A binary search tree is a data structure that might implement a queue; it is not itself a CPU selection policy. “Infinite” is not a standard scheduling-policy category. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Fair-share, proportional shares and guarantees
records.text: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal. Lottery scheduling assigns tickets and selects a winning ticket each turn. With weights 3:1, expected shares are 75% and 25%; short-run results vary and this is not a deterministic no-starvation deadline. Stride-style scheduling tracks progress toward shares deterministically. Any “guaranteed scheduling” answer needs the actual guarantee and assumptions; finite FCFS and RR can also avoid indefinite postponement. Example Worked microexample If user A runs four ready tasks and B runs one, plain RR gives A about 80% overall. A policy granting each user half the CPU instead gives A’s tasks about 12.5% each and B’s task 50%. Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP Proportional Share Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — How to evaluate scheduling claims
records.text: There is no universally best policy for response, waiting, fairness and throughput simultaneously. State the workload and objective, apply the algorithm and compare measured results. Maximum waiting at submission is not determined from burst times alone if future arrivals, priorities or overhead are unconstrained. Known finite workloads are different from an open stream with potential starvation. An item asking for one non-preemptive algorithm while offering FCFS and SJN has multiple answers. Equal share needs a process/user/group definition. “Highest average turnaround” requires a concrete workload; do not memorize FCFS as an absolute. RR is a conventional interactive choice because turns improve responsiveness, subject to quantum and overhead. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Deadlock and its four necessary conditions
records.text: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide. Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies. Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits. All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests. Preventing any one condition prevents that class of deadlock. A preemptive CPU scheduler can coexist with deadlocked locks. Example Worked microexample P1 holds lock A and requests B; P2 holds B and requests A. Neither releases before acquiring the other: nonshareable locks, retained holdings, no forced release and a cycle all occur. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Resource graphs and missing-diagram limits
records.text: In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment. Follow these directions to form waits. No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion. A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q. For a complete single-instance example, suppose P0 holds R0 and requests R1, while P1 holds R1 and requests R0. The wait-for edges P0→P1 and P1→P0 form a cycle, so neither can proceed. With multiple resource instances, inspect all assignments and available instances before concluding that a cycle is a deadlock. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Prevention: identify the condition removed
records.text: Prevention constrains how requests are made. Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait. Not every physical resource is shareable or safely preemptable. “If waiting, release all held resources and try again” removes simultaneous holding while waiting. Distinguish voluntary resource release from forced preemption when describing resource reclamation. Prevention can waste utilization or cause starvation; avoiding deadlock is not the same as treating every process fairly. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Avoidance and the Banker safety test
records.text: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe. Banker requires maximum claims. Compute Need=Max−Allocation. Set Work=Available and repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need≤Work componentwise; simulate completion by adding its Allocation to Work. Finishing all gives a safe sequence. Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds. Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked. Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition. Example Worked microexample One resource type: Available=1; P1 holds 1 and needs 1 more; P2 holds 2 and needs 2 more. P1 can finish, returning its allocation so Work becomes 2; P2 can then finish. Safe order P1,P2. A maximum claim must be known before testing. University of Illinois Chicago, Deadlocks

records.title: Operating System — Detection, recovery and intentional ignoring
records.text: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible recovery tools; choose according to the resource and process conditions. Repeatedly sacrificing the same victim can cause starvation. Checking on every request versus periodically trades overhead against detection delay; no universal best interval exists. Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks. “Deadlock acceptance” can mean intentional ignoring, not necessarily an invalid approach. A detection graph, avoidance safety graph and ordinary scheduling queue solve different problems. University of Illinois Chicago, Deadlocks

records.title: Operating System — Address binding, dynamic loading and linking
records.text: Compile-time binding uses absolute addresses if placement is known. Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory. Execution-time binding translates while running and permits movement with hardware support. Logical/virtual addresses are generated for a process; physical addresses select RAM. An MMU translates logical addresses to physical addresses, not the reverse. Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed. Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable. Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages. These differ from a context switch, which primarily changes execution state. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Contiguous allocation and fit policies
records.text: A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region. In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length. Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset. The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base. If limit instead means last valid offset, the inequality changes; specify the convention. First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest. No policy universally optimizes both search time and future storage utilization. Binary-fit is not one of these standard names. Example Worked microexample Holes 100,500,200,300 and request 180: first-fit selects 500, best-fit 200, worst-fit 500. For base=4000,length=100, logical offset 99 maps to 4099; offset 100 traps. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Internal and external fragmentation
records.text: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation. Coalescing joins adjacent free holes; compaction moves allocated regions to consolidate free space and requires relocation support. Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally. Variable-length segmentation/contiguous partitions can fragment externally. This is not a statement that every allocator inside a paging OS is fragmentation-free. Track units and round allocations up rather than assuming all requests exactly fill blocks. Example Worked microexample A 10 KiB object in 4 KiB pages needs ceil(10/4)=3 pages: 12 KiB allocated and 2 KiB unused. Two 3 KiB free holes cannot serve one contiguous 5 KiB request although 6 KiB is free. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Paging, page tables and TLB
records.text: Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags. Physical address=frame×P+offset. A TLB caches translations; a TLB miss may require a table walk while the page is already resident. Table size depends on the number of virtual pages and entry size, not just physical RAM. Protection and present bits must be checked before access. A page-table lookup is not a CPU scheduling operation. Example Worked microexample Page size 1024, v=2053: page 2, offset 5. If page 2 maps to frame 7, physical address=7173. With 16-bit virtual addresses and 1 KiB pages, there are 64 virtual pages and a 6-bit page number. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Segmentation and contrasts with paging
records.text: Segmentation uses logical variable-length units such as code, stack and arrays. A segment-table entry provides base, limit and permissions. For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset. An out-of-range offset traps; it must not spill into the next segment. Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally. Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications. Apply all three contrasts when comparing paging and segmentation. Example Worked microexample Segment 1 has base 8000 and length 500. Offset 120 maps to 8120; offset 500 is invalid under the length convention. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Virtual memory and page-fault handling
records.text: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage. It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints. Demand paging brings a page in when accessed. On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart. Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings. An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded. Excessive active-page demand can cause thrashing: repeated faults dominate useful computation. Reducing active load or adding suitable memory can help. Example Worked microexample If access costs 100 ns and an additional page-in costs 5 ms, a fault probability of 10^−4 adds roughly 500 ns per access; rare long delays still matter. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Replacement-policy traces
records.text: Replacement chooses a victim when no suitable free frame is available. FIFO evicts the earliest loaded page; a hit does not refresh insertion time. LRU evicts the least recently accessed and updates recency on every access. Optimal evicts the page used farthest in the future, serving as an offline lower bound. LFU uses reference counts and needs tie/aging rules. Write a row per reference, identify hits before evicting, and count initial loads as faults. FIFO may exhibit Belady’s anomaly when more frames cause more faults; LRU and optimal have the stack property. Page buffering retains useful free/modified pages to reduce effective fault cost. Example Worked microexample Three empty frames, references 1,2,3,1,4,1: FIFO faults at 1,2,3,4 and the last 1: five faults. LRU updates page 1 on its hit, evicts 2 for 4, and ends with a hit on 1: four faults. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Device controllers, drivers and I/O services
records.text: A controller is device hardware exposing status, control and data registers. A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations. Device independence and uniform naming hide brand-specific details; error handling reports/retries supported failures. Polling checks readiness repeatedly; interrupts request CPU attention; DMA transfers blocks after setup without CPU work for every byte. Both the kernel and drivers participate in I/O; specify the abstraction level being discussed. Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver. Input/output/storage/NIC devices are OS-managed hardware; user accounts are identities. Printer-paper and network errors can be handled/reported, but continued operation during total power loss requires hardware support, not OS software alone. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Buffering, caching, spooling and clocks
records.text: Buffering temporarily holds data in transit to absorb speed/transfer-size differences. Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse. Spooling queues jobs for a device such as a printer, usually on disk, so producers need not own it throughout job creation. These have different purposes even if one implementation combines them. The clock/timer supports timekeeping, timeouts, accounting and preemptive scheduling. A system monitor reports CPU, memory, storage and network usage; it measures rather than directly creating more resources. Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors. A broad “OS does all disk functions” claim needs these responsibility boundaries. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Files, descriptors and ordinary operations
records.text: A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name. A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode. Descriptor and offset are not synonyms. Read advances the offset on seekable files and may return fewer bytes than requested; zero normally indicates end-of-file. Sockets also support ordinary read/write, alongside socket/connect/send operations, so read is not uniquely “not a network call.” FAT32, NTFS and ext4 are filesystem formats; HTTP is an application communication protocol. Operating System module Linux man-pages read(2)

records.title: Operating System — Directories, mounting and links
records.text: A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace. Two-level directories separate users. A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs. Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements. A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling. Removing one hard link does not erase content while other names/open references retain it. Mounting attaches a filesystem at a mount point; it does not format the device. NFS provides remote filesystem access; FTP transfers files rather than itself mounting a local filesystem. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Contiguous, linked and indexed file allocation
records.text: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping. Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead. A Unix inode can combine direct pointers with indirect levels. Check pointer size, block size, index capacity and whether metadata reads are cached. Example Worked microexample A 1024-byte index block with 4-byte pointers holds 256 block addresses. With 1024-byte data blocks, one such index level addresses 256 KiB of file data, excluding metadata and any reserved entries. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Protection, authentication and threats
records.text: Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations. An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model, not universal defaults granting all owners full access or everyone read. Read, write, execute, append and delete are different rights, with filesystem-specific rules. Least privilege limits damage. Password hashing verifies secrets without storing plaintext; one-time passwords expire after use. Encryption protects confidentiality under correct key use but does not automatically provide integrity. Trojans masquerade as useful software, worms propagate independently and viruses attach to hosts; denial of service harms availability. Modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, but support/configuration depends on product. CLI, GUI, speech/natural language and VR are possible interfaces, not a closed list excluding the last two. Operating System module

records.title: Operating System — Linux, Android and product-history limits
records.text: Linux is a Unix-compatible kernel written from scratch by Linus Torvalds; a distribution combines it with userland, libraries and tools. Android’s base kernel layer is Linux; its framework and applications are higher layers. AOSP is open source, while a shipped device can include proprietary applications/services. Windows and macOS are both proprietary products, although macOS contains open-source components, so “which is not open source?” offering both is ambiguous. Microsoft Office is an application suite. Windows is the Microsoft family commonly described as succeeding the MS-DOS desktop era; Solaris originated at Sun. “First widely used OS,” “first multitasking OS,” and generation/function pairings require a definition and historical evidence; UNIX was not the first system ever to multitask. “Most mobile devices” needs a population and date; architecture facts do not prove market share. records.text: Check whether the stated conditions support one answer or several before selecting a response. A general system-call purpose should say requesting a kernel service; a process purpose should say executing a program. CPU, memory and I/O management span multiple managers; device, process, file and security management describe particular responsibilities. Virtual memory provides isolation and translated space; it does not remove every memory constraint. Specify the OS/API, scheduling variant, arrivals/quantum, exact graph, base-limit convention or scope of comparison needed to answer the question. Support the answer with the relevant operating-system rule and stated assumptions. A process/resource graph question requires its actual edges; theory alone cannot reconstruct a missing diagram. records.title: Operating System — UNIX origins and the first four historical generations
records.text: UNIX development began at Bell Labs in 1969, led by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie with other collaborators. Ritchie is therefore a co-creator, not the sole inventor of the first operating system. The later UNIX time-sharing system described by Ritchie and Thompson is multiuser and interactive and supports asynchronous processes. Its later versions incorporated multiprogramming. This history does not make UNIX the first system ever to multitask. In the first four generations of the cited NYU teaching taxonomy, the first generation uses vacuum tubes and manual single-user operation without a separate resident OS. The second generation pairs transistors with uniprogrammed batch systems; the resident OS starts successive jobs without being reloaded for every job. The third generation pairs integrated circuits with multiprogramming. The fourth emphasizes personal computers. These are characteristic-era associations, not claims that each feature existed exclusively in one era. records.title: Operating System — Thread management costs and execution privilege
records.text: In the conventional library-thread comparison, user-level thread creation and switching can avoid entering the kernel. Kernel-managed thread creation and management commonly incur additional kernel work and are therefore generally slower to create and manage in this comparison. This is a typical comparison, not a universal speed or reliability guarantee. Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations. records.title: Operating System — Memory allocation and page-policy decisions
records.text: Memory management tracks which primary-memory regions are free or in use, assigns memory to processes and data, and deallocates it when no longer needed or when a process terminates. Allocation and deallocation concern memory ownership; CPU selection belongs to scheduling. A buddy allocator manages power-of-two block sizes. It takes a smallest sufficient block, splitting larger blocks when necessary, and can merge a freed block with its free buddy. This is not the worst-fit rule of selecting the largest arbitrary hole. A fetch policy decides when contents are brought into memory; demand paging fetches a valid nonresident page when it is accessed. A cleaning policy concerns writing modified contents to backing storage. A replacement policy chooses which resident page to evict. These decisions can cooperate during one page fault, but they are different decisions. records.title: Operating System — Communication endpoints and timed I/O events
records.text: In the descriptor-based socket API, socket() creates a communication endpoint and returns its descriptor. connect() associates the socket with the requested peer address; send() transmits data to another socket. Receiving through read() uses the ordinary descriptor-input interface described in the file-services lesson. IRQ means interrupt request. A controller can raise an interrupt to request CPU attention. In a clock-tick scheduler, the scheduler initializes a running process’s quantum counter; each clock interrupt decrements it, and reaching zero triggers scheduling. Clock support also maintains time of day and usage accounting. Direct message communication names the receiving process explicitly. Indirect communication uses a mailbox or port. This naming distinction is independent of whether a send or receive blocks: naming a destination does not determine synchronization semantics. records.title: Operating System — Compilation versus operating-system execution services
records.text: A compiler translates source code toward an executable representation. For example, the conventional GCC toolchain distinguishes preprocessing, compilation proper, assembly and linking. A compiler uses operating-system services as a development tool; it is not the runtime kernel component that selects ready processes, manages memory or handles protected service requests. records.title: Operating System — Filesystem links in Linux
records.text: Linux provides link() to create another hard-link name for an existing file. The old and new names identify the same file, so hard links are not a Windows-only facility. unlink() removes a filesystem name; when that name is a symbolic link, it removes the link itself. Removing a name and erasing the target’s contents are different operations. Linux man-pages · link(2) Linux man-pages · unlink(2)

records.text: Missing or multiple answer concepts Requested concept omitted Several valid examples: reject uniqueness System call: kernel-service request Process: executing program CPU/memory/I/O: multiple managers Device/process/file/security choices: missing umbrella Virtual memory: isolation, translated space Virtual memory ≠ unlimited memory Minimal wording repairs Specify OS versus API Scheduling variant Arrivals and quantum Exact process/resource graph Base-limit convention Comparison scope Marked answer ≠ evidence Missing edges: unrecoverable from theory

records.title: Operating System — Question 1 · Q00023
records.text: Q00023 Question 1 OS12 OS10 Which mutual exclusion mechanism keeps track of turns to enter the critical region using an integer variable, which is initially-0, and another process waits until it turns to 1? Track who may enter and distinguish separate tests and updates from atomic operations. A Lock variable B Disabling interrupts C Strict alteration D Race condition Strict alternation (option misspells it as alteration). OS12 defines strict alternation using turn=0/1: each process waits until turn equals its identifier and passes the turn on leaving. That directly matches the described integer ownership variable. A naive lock variable instead records availability and can race during separate test/set operations. Disabling interrupts and a race condition do not implement the described turn-taking algorithm. A incorrect A naive lock variable records free/busy status rather than assigning alternating ownership to process 0 or 1. B incorrect Disabling interrupts does not implement the integer turn-owner protocol described in the stem. C correct Strict alternation uses a turn variable initialized to one process and passed to the other. D incorrect A race condition is a concurrency failure, not a mechanism providing the described alternating access.

records.title: Operating System — Question 2 · Q00031
records.text: Q00031 Question 2 OS09 Which one of the following messaging communication best explains the statement: "Until the message is received, the sending process is blocked'"? Identify how data moves, which participant waits and what event allows the operation to continue. A Blocking receive B Non-block receive C Non-block sending D Blocking send Blocking send. OS09 explicitly identifies a sender blocked until receipt as blocking send under rendezvous semantics. The stem describes the sending process waiting, not a receiver awaiting an incoming message. Nonblocking sending returns promptly rather than waiting for receipt, and receive modes describe the other side. The receipt condition here supplies the relevant API assumption. A incorrect Blocking receive waits on the receiving side, whereas the stem explicitly blocks the sender. B incorrect Nonblocking receive returns promptly on the receiving side and does not describe sender waiting. C incorrect Nonblocking sending returns promptly rather than keeping the sender blocked until the handoff completes. D correct Under the stated rendezvous condition, waiting until message receipt is blocking-send behavior.

records.title: Operating System — Question 3 · Q00034
records.text: Q00034 Question 3 OS06 OS01 OS09 _______is the component of the operating system that is responsible to decide which process to run first among ready processes. Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Memory manager B Inter process communication C Disk manager D Scheduler Scheduler The CPU scheduler selects among ready processes and allocates the CPU (PDF p20). This is precisely the selection task in the stem. A incorrect Memory allocation is a separate function (p5). B incorrect Process data exchange (p11) is not selection of the next CPU user. C incorrect Device allocation (p6) does not decide CPU order. D correct CPU scheduling selects ready processes (p20).

records.title: Operating System — Question 4 · Q00092
records.text: Q00092 Question 4 OS03 Which one of the following is not true? Distinguish command interfaces, privileged core services and the stages of booting. A kernel is the program that constitutes the central core of the operating system B kernel is the first part of operating system to load into memory during booting C kernel is made of various modules which cannot be loaded in running operating system D kernel remains in the memory during the entire computer session The claim that kernel modules cannot load while running is false. OS03 states that loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel, directly contradicting option C’s absolute prohibition. It describes the kernel as the core OS component and resident through the session. Option B is read as the first core OS component, rather than the first code executed at power-on: firmware and bootloader stages precede it. A incorrect The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling, so this statement is true. B incorrect As the first core OS component, the kernel is loaded at boot; firmware/bootloader execution precedes that OS boundary. C correct Modular kernels permit runtime module loading, directly refuting the statement that it cannot occur. D incorrect A resident kernel remains active throughout the session, matching the note’s ordinary kernel model.

records.title: Operating System — Question 5 · Q00164
records.text: Q00164 Question 5 OS34 OS35 One is not the goal of I/O software Separate device hardware, device-specific software and general event or transfer mechanisms. A Buffering B Device independence C Uniform naming D Error handling E None of the above None: all four are I/O-software goals or supporting functions. OS34 identifies device independence, uniform naming and error handling as I/O services. OS35 explains buffering as holding in-transit data to absorb speed/size differences. Each listed feature therefore supports I/O software, so none is an exclusion. Calling buffering a supporting mechanism rather than a high-level objective does not make it unrelated to I/O software’s goals. A incorrect Buffering absorbs transfer-speed and size differences, directly supporting reliable and efficient I/O software. B incorrect Device independence is an explicit I/O service that hides device-specific details from higher layers. C incorrect Uniform naming is explicitly included among the I/O services described here. D incorrect Reporting or retrying supported device failures is the error-handling responsibility of I/O software. E correct All four listed functions support I/O software, leaving no listed function to exclude.

records.title: Operating System — Question 6 · Q00165
records.text: Q00165 Question 6 OS27 OS28 OS34 OS35 OS-S04 Which hardware unit translates a process’s logical/virtual addresses to physical memory addresses during execution? Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation. A MMU B IRQ C DMA D Cache E Relocation Register MMU The MMU performs execution-time translation from a process’s logical or virtual address to a physical RAM address. A relocation register can supply a base used in a simple translation, but it is a register rather than the complete translating unit. IRQ concerns interrupts, DMA moves data, and a cache stores reusable information. The corrected direction therefore identifies the MMU uniquely. A correct The MMU is the hardware unit performing logical-to-physical translation. B incorrect An IRQ signals an interrupt rather than translating process addresses. C incorrect DMA transfers data between devices and memory after setup. D incorrect A cache retains reusable contents; it is not the general address-translating unit. E incorrect A relocation register holds a base parameter used by translation hardware.

records.title: Operating System — Question 7 · Q00166
records.text: Q00166 Question 7 OS28 For holes of sizes 100, 500, 200 and 300 in that scan order and a request of size 180, which policy is better at minimizing this request’s leftover space in its selected hole? Ignore search cost and future requests. Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention. A First fit algorithm is better B Best fit algorithm is better C Worst fit algorithm is better D All of the above Best fit algorithm is better Best-fit chooses the smallest hole large enough for the request: 200, leaving 20 unused units. First-fit stops at 500 and leaves 320 units; worst-fit also chooses 500. Under the stated objective, best-fit gives the smallest remainder for this allocation. This calculation says nothing about future fragmentation or overall search speed, which require a broader workload. A incorrect First-fit selects 500 in this scan order, leaving 320 rather than the minimum remainder. B correct Best-fit selects 200 and leaves only 20 units. C incorrect Worst-fit selects 500 and leaves 320 units. D incorrect The policies do not tie: only best-fit minimizes this request’s leftover space.

records.title: Operating System — Question 8 · Q00167
records.text: Q00167 Question 8 OS13 OS16 OS17 OS18 All jobs arrive together at submission, have known finite CPU bursts, perform no I/O, and no further jobs arrive. Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, known fixed priorities (smaller value is higher; non-preemptive priority), a known positive RR quantum, and listed order for ties. For which listed algorithms can each job’s total waiting time be computed at submission? Choose the most complete answer. Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures. A Shortest job first B Shortest remaining time C Priority based D Round Robin E All of the above All of the above The closed workload and explicit policy parameters determine each scheduling timeline. SJF orders known bursts, SRTF uses remaining bursts, priority uses the supplied fixed order, and RR uses its quantum and ready queue. Completion minus arrival minus burst then gives waiting time. Each named algorithm is individually computable, so the aggregate option is the most complete answer under these assumptions. A incorrect SJF waiting is computable, but this option omits the other computable policies. B incorrect SRTF waiting is computable for the known closed workload, but this is incomplete. C incorrect Fixed-priority waiting is computable with the supplied priorities and tie rule, but this is incomplete. D incorrect RR waiting is computable with the known quantum and queue order, but this is incomplete. E correct All four schedules and their total waiting times can be computed from the fully specified finite workload.

records.title: Operating System — Question 9 · Q00168
records.text: Q00168 Question 9 OS10 OS22 One is not a problem caused by concurrency of processes Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required. A Race condition B Starvation C Deadlock D Mutual exclusion E None Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property. OS10 explicitly contrasts mutual exclusion, a desired safety property, with race conditions, starvation and deadlock as possible failures. Although a badly designed locking scheme can introduce deadlock, that does not turn the mutual-exclusion requirement itself into a concurrency failure. Therefore it is the single option that is not a problem in the sense used by the list. A incorrect A race is a concurrency failure caused by uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. B incorrect Starvation is a possible indefinite-delay failure of concurrent scheduling or resource competition. C incorrect Deadlock is a possible failure in which blocked participants cannot supply one another’s required events. D correct Mutual exclusion is a correctness property protecting shared state, rather than a failure to be avoided. E incorrect Mutual exclusion provides a clear non-failure option, so none of the choices is not appropriate.

records.title: Operating System — Question 10 · Q00169
records.text: Q00169 Question 10 OS26 OS22 Which methods can participate in recovery after deadlock has been detected? Assume checkpoints and safe resource reclamation are available where needed. Select all that apply. Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking. A Kill the process B Rollback C Non-preempt the resource D Lock the process Kill the process; Rollback Terminating a selected process can release resources and break the dependency cycle. Recovery may instead reclaim safely preemptable resources and restore affected work to a checkpoint, so rollback can also participate. Merely preserving non-preemption or locking a process does not remove the deadlocked dependencies. With checkpoint and reclamation support stated, both termination and rollback are valid recovery tools. A correct Killing a selected victim can release resources and break the deadlock. B correct Rollback can restore affected work after safe resource reclamation. C incorrect Non-preemption preserves a deadlock-enabling restriction rather than recovering the processes. D incorrect Locking a blocked process does not release resources or restore progress.

records.title: Operating System — Question 11 · Q00170
records.text: Q00170 Question 11 OS24 One deadlock prevention method says, "if a process must wait for a needed resource, it drops all of its previously held resources and tries to acquire all resources gain." These attacks Identify the resource-request restriction and which necessary condition it removes. A Circular wait condition B No preemption conditions C Mutual exclusion condition D Hold and wait condition E None of the above The policy removes hold-and-wait. Under this policy, a process releases all previously held resources when it must wait. Releasing all resources before retrying removes simultaneous holding while waiting. The stem describes voluntary dropping, not forced withdrawal by another agent, so hold-and-wait is the directly attacked condition. It supplies no global ordering or resource-sharing rule. A incorrect The policy does not impose a global acquisition order, which is the direct circular-wait prevention method. B incorrect The stem specifies the process dropping resources, not a general rule permitting forced resource preemption. C incorrect Resources may remain nonshareable; releasing holdings does not remove mutual-exclusion requirements. D correct A process no longer retains allocated resources while waiting to acquire the rest. E incorrect Hold-and-wait is explicitly removed by the release-all-before-waiting rule, so an identified condition fits.

records.title: Operating System — Question 12 · Q00229
records.text: Q00229 Question 12 OS10 OS17 OS36 Which statements are false? Interpret aging under a priority scheme and workload where increasing waiting jobs’ priority prevents indefinite postponement. Select all that apply. Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required. A File system standards of various OS is the same. B SJF may cause starvation. C Aging is the solution of the starvation problem in the case of priority scheduling. D Critical section is a resource that cannot be accessed by multiple processes concurrently. File system standards of various OS is the same.; Critical section is a resource that cannot be accessed by multiple processes concurrently. Filesystems are not governed by one identical format across all operating systems; the notes distinguish FAT32, NTFS and ext4. A critical section is code that accesses shared state, not the resource itself. SJF can starve a long job when short work continues arriving. Aging addresses priority starvation under the stated policy assumptions, so those latter two statements are true. A correct The universal sameness claim is false; different filesystem formats exist. B incorrect SJF may starve long work under repeated short arrivals, so this statement is true. C incorrect Aging raises effective priority and addresses starvation under the specified conditions, so this statement is true. D correct A critical section is protected code rather than the shared resource, making this statement false.

records.title: Operating System — Question 13 · Q00230
records.text: Q00230 Question 13 OS07 One of the following system calls is used to create a new process. Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause. A Fork() B exit() C abort() D exec() fork(). OS07 states that fork() creates a child in POSIX-style systems, returning zero in the child and its PID in the parent on success. exec replaces the current process image and does not itself create another process. exit and abort terminate execution normally and abnormally respectively. Creation therefore corresponds to fork among the literal listed calls. A correct fork creates a child process rather than replacing or terminating the existing process image. B incorrect exit terminates normally through the runtime rather than creating a new process. C incorrect abort requests abnormal termination rather than allocating a new child execution instance. D incorrect exec replaces the current process image; it does not itself create another process.

records.title: Operating System — Question 14 · Q00232
records.text: Q00232 Question 14 OS16 OS15 OS17 OS18 Which of the following process scheduling algorithms select the next process to be executed based on each process burst time? Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule. A FCFS B Shortest Job First C Round robin D Priority scheduling algorithm Shortest Job First SJF requires knowing how long a process will take (PDF p23); that is the burst-length selection described. Priority may use time as one possible priority input (p24), but its general rule is highest assigned priority. A incorrect FCFS orders arrival (p23), not burst length. B correct SJF chooses short work based on execution duration (p23). C incorrect RR assigns a fixed quantum (p25). D incorrect Priority selects assigned priority; time requirements are only one possible input (p24).

records.title: Operating System — Question 15 · Q00233
records.text: Q00233 Question 15 OS11 OS12 __________ is a software solution of a critical section problem if the number of instances and processes are more than two. Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model. A Semaphore B Compare and swap C Peterson D Test set Semaphore. OS12 explicitly says a semaphore can coordinate more than two processes, while classic Peterson’s algorithm is for two under its memory-model assumptions. OS11 explains counting semaphores as tracking several permits, fitting multiple resource instances. Compare-and-swap and test-and-set are atomic primitives rather than the named software coordination abstraction requested by the stem. A correct Counting semaphores track multiple permits and coordinate more than two participating processes. B incorrect Compare-and-swap is an atomic checking/updating primitive, rather than the requested software semaphore abstraction. C incorrect Classic Peterson’s algorithm solves the two-process case, not the stated more-than-two configuration. D incorrect Test-and-set is an atomic primitive; the software multiple-permit coordination mechanism here is a semaphore.

records.title: Operating System — Question 16 · Q00359
records.text: Q00359 Question 16 OS07 A process can be terminated due to: Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause. A killed by another process B normal exit C all of the mentioned D fatal error All listed causes can terminate a process. OS07 distinguishes voluntary normal completion from involuntary faults or being killed. Each named cause is therefore a genuine termination cause, although the causes differ in who initiates them and whether completion is normal. The aggregate choice includes all three. Selecting only one named cause would omit other valid termination paths supported by the complete note. A incorrect Being killed can terminate a process, but this alone omits normal completion and fatal faults. B incorrect Normal exit is valid, but it is only one of the three supported termination causes. C correct Being killed, normal exit and fatal error all provide legitimate process-termination causes. D incorrect A fatal error can terminate execution, but the other two named causes are also valid.

records.title: Operating System — Question 17 · Q00360
records.text: Q00360 Question 17 OS04 Which named interface directly requests protected operating-system services across the user/kernel boundary, rather than merely providing application-facing wrappers? Identify the abstraction layer and separate a protected service request from an application task. A library B system calls C assembly instructions D API system calls A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as process creation or file access. An application may call an API implemented by a library, but that wrapper is distinct from the direct user/kernel service boundary. Assembly can encode the machine instructions used to enter that boundary without being its general interface name. The requested abstraction is therefore system calls. A incorrect A library can wrap system calls but is not itself the direct kernel-service boundary. B correct System calls directly request protected kernel services. C incorrect Assembly instructions are a programming representation, not the named service-interface abstraction. D incorrect An API is the application-facing interface and may wrap the direct system-call request.

records.title: Operating System — Question 18 · Q00361
records.text: Q00361 Question 18 OS06 OS05 OS34 Which module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Interrupt B Dispatcher C Scheduler D none of the mentioned Dispatcher The module uses overlapping terminology: it calls the short-term scheduler dispatcher on PDF p20, and describes the dispatcher selecting execution on p19. Under the conventional selection-versus-handoff reading requested by the stem, B is the matching term; p21 explains the handoff state work. A incorrect Interrupts trigger handling, not the named CPU-handoff module (p45). B correct Dispatcher is the execution-transfer role described on p19, with state switching on p21. C incorrect The stem already assigns selection to the scheduler; note that p20 loosely equates it with dispatcher. D incorrect The module explicitly names a dispatcher, so none is not appropriate.

records.title: Operating System — Question 19 · Q00362
records.text: Q00362 Question 19 OS22 Which of the following condition is required for deadlock to be possible? Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock. A mutual exclusion B all of the mentioned C a process may hold allocated resources while awaiting assignment of other resources D no resource can be forcibly removed from a process holding it All named conditions are necessary conditions. OS22 lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. The three substantive choices name the first three, so all of the mentioned is the comprehensive option. Circular wait is also required despite being omitted from the list. Having these policies does not prove a particular current allocation is already deadlocked. A incorrect Mutual exclusion is necessary, but selecting it alone omits the other two necessary conditions offered. B correct Each substantive option names a standard necessary deadlock condition; the aggregate includes all offered conditions. C incorrect Retaining resources while requesting more is hold-and-wait, one valid condition among the three offered. D incorrect No forced removal is no-preemption, which is necessary but does not exclude the other valid conditions.

records.title: Operating System — Question 20 · Q00363
records.text: Q00363 Question 20 OS15 OS16 OS17 Which scheduling algorithm allocates the CPU first to the process that requests the CPU first? Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time. A first-come, first-served scheduling B priority scheduling C shortest job scheduling D none of the mentioned first-come, first-served scheduling Jobs execute first come, first served on PDF p23. The first CPU requester is consequently the first served in the FCFS queue. A correct Directly matches the arrival-order rule (p23). B incorrect Uses highest priority (p24). C incorrect Uses execution-length information (p23). D incorrect An offered policy already matches the rule.

records.title: Operating System — Question 21 · Q00607
