That can prevent entry into a deadlocked state in the broad everyday sense used by can help prevent, although its technical category is avoidance rather than condition-breaking prevention. FCFS, RR and SJN are CPU scheduling policies and do not themselves test resource-allocation safety. A incorrect FCFS orders CPU bursts by arrival rather than testing maximum resource claims and safe allocations. B incorrect RR schedules CPU turns; time slicing does not establish safe allocation of locks or other resources. C incorrect SJN selects shortest next CPU bursts rather than performing a resource-state safety test. D correct Banker admits resource requests only when the resulting state is safe; its strict classification is avoidance.

records.title: Operating System — Question 156 · AM0683
records.text: AM0683 Question 156 OS25 OS24 OS26 What is the purpose of the Banker's Algorithm in deadlock avoidance? Compute remaining needs and simulate feasible completions before deciding whether an allocation is safe. A To break the hold and wait condition. B To allocate resources in a fair and equitable manner. C To detect deadlocked processes and recover from deadlock. D To ensure that resource requests will not lead to an unsafe state. Ensure each granted request preserves a safe state. Banker’s algorithm checks whether a tentative resource grant preserves a safe state. It computes remaining needs and simulates an order in which all processes can finish, granting only requests within the declared need and available resources that pass this safety test. It is an avoidance policy, not a fairness guarantee, an already-deadlocked-state detector, or prevention by eliminating hold-and-wait. A incorrect Banker does not require removing hold-and-wait; it checks whether tentative allocation remains safe. B incorrect Its safety criterion is not a guarantee of fair or equal allocation among processes. C incorrect Detection and recovery address actual deadlock, whereas Banker checks safety before granting a request. D correct Preserving a safe state after each grant is the purpose of the Banker avoidance test.

records.title: Operating System — Question 157 · AM0684
records.text: AM0684 Question 157 OS14 OS15 Which of the following is a characteristic of preemptive scheduling? Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking. A Tasks cannot be interrupted once started. B Tasks are allowed to complete their execution. C Tasks can be interrupted and rescheduled. D Tasks are scheduled based on their arrival time. Tasks can be interrupted and rescheduled. PDF p25 explicitly preempts a process after its quantum; p19 returns forcibly removed work to the ready queue. C states interrupting and rescheduling that work. A incorrect Contradicts the explicit forced removal/preemption on pp19,25. B incorrect Tasks can eventually complete, but permission to finish does not distinguish preemptive scheduling. C correct Matches the interruption/rescheduling mechanism. D incorrect Arrival ordering defines FCFS (p23), not preemption.

records.title: Operating System — Question 158 · AM0685
records.text: AM0685 Question 158 OS14 OS17 Which listed scheduling policies are non-preemptive? SJN means non-preemptive shortest-next-burst scheduling; D specifically uses immediate preemption for a higher-priority arrival. Select all that apply. Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Preemptive Priority Scheduling First-Come, First-Served (FCFS); Shortest Job Next (SJN) FCFS ordinarily serves each ready burst in arrival order without forcibly taking the CPU away. SJN, as explicitly defined, chooses the shortest ready burst and then lets it continue non-preemptively. RR can interrupt a burst at its quantum boundary, while the stated priority variant interrupts for a higher-priority arrival. Thus FCFS and SJN are the two non-preemptive policies in this list. A incorrect RR uses quantum expiry to preempt unfinished work. B correct FCFS ordinarily lets the selected burst continue without forced preemption. C correct SJN is explicitly the non-preemptive shortest-next-burst policy. D incorrect This option explicitly preempts for a higher-priority arrival.

records.title: Operating System — Question 159 · AM0686
records.text: AM0686 Question 159 OS17 OS18 OS15 OS16 Which scheduling algorithm is based on the priority assigned to each task? Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Priority Scheduling PDF p24 assigns a priority to each process and executes the highest priority first. That is D; other policies use quantum, arrival or execution length. A incorrect RR uses fixed quantum (p25). B incorrect FCFS follows arrival order (p23). C incorrect SJN uses job length (p23). D correct Assigned priority is the explicit selection rule (p24).

records.title: Operating System — Question 160 · AM0687
records.text: AM0687 Question 160 OS20 User A has four continuously ready tasks and user B has one. The policy goal is equal aggregate CPU entitlement for each user, independent of task count. Which listed policy directly implements that goal when configured with equal per-user weights? Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Fair-Share Scheduling Fair-Share Scheduling Equal-turn RR gives each of the five tasks roughly one fifth of CPU service, so user A receives about 80 percent and B about 20 percent. Equal per-user fair-share instead gives each user half, dividing A’s half among its four tasks. FCFS and SJN do not enforce that user entitlement. The explicitly defined participant scope makes fair-share the unique matching policy. A incorrect Per-task RR gives A four fifths of service rather than equal per-user shares. B incorrect FCFS orders bursts by arrival and does not enforce per-user entitlements. C incorrect SJN favors short bursts and does not allocate equal user shares. D correct Equal per-user fair-share weights directly implement the stated half-and-half goal.

records.title: Operating System — Question 161 · AM0688
records.text: AM0688 Question 161 OS15 OS18 OS17 A ready target has finitely many jobs ahead, all CPU bursts and RR quanta are finite and positive, context overhead is finite, and later arrivals join the tail without bypassing existing peers. Infinitely many later short or high-priority jobs may arrive over time. Which policies prevent that target from being postponed forever by later arrivals? D uses fixed priorities without aging. Select all that apply. Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Fixed-priority scheduling without aging Round Robin; First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) RR gives the target a turn after the finite work ahead has received bounded turns. FCFS serves the finite earlier bursts before later arrivals, so the target eventually starts. SJN can repeatedly prefer later short jobs, and fixed priority can repeatedly prefer later high-priority jobs. The assumptions distinguish guaranteed eventual service from policies that permit an endless stream to bypass the target. A correct RR’s finite cyclic turns reach the target without later-arrival bypass. B correct FCFS drains the finite predecessor work before serving later arrivals. C incorrect An endless sequence of short arrivals can keep a long target waiting under SJN. D incorrect An endless sequence of higher-priority arrivals can starve a low-priority target without aging.

records.title: Operating System — Question 162 · AM0689
records.text: AM0689 Question 162 OS16 Which scheduling algorithm is based on the estimated remaining time required for each task? Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). OS16 says SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work. This matches the estimated remaining-time criterion in the stem. SJN chooses the shortest next burst non-preemptively, while RR uses cyclic quanta and FCFS arrival order. The distinction matters after execution has begun: the originally shortest burst need not be the currently shortest remaining job. A incorrect RR rotates bounded turns rather than selecting the job with the smallest estimated remaining execution. B incorrect FCFS follows arrival order rather than comparing estimated remaining CPU work. C incorrect Non-preemptive SJN compares next burst lengths when selecting, not continuously reconsidered remaining work. D correct SRTF explicitly selects the shortest remaining work and can preempt on a shorter arrival.

records.title: Operating System — Question 163 · AM0690
records.text: AM0690 Question 163 OS17 OS15 OS18 Which policies can starve a ready job through repeated preference for later arrivals? Assume correct implementations, finite bursts, ordinary RR with a positive quantum, FCFS without bypass, non-preemptive SJN, and fixed-priority scheduling without aging. Select all that apply. Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Shortest Job Next (SJN); Priority Scheduling SJN can continually choose newly arrived short bursts while an older long job remains ready. Fixed priority without aging can likewise keep choosing high-priority arrivals over a low-priority target. Ordinary RR cycles peers, and FCFS does not let later arrivals overtake a finite set of predecessors. Thus the preference rules of SJN and fixed priority create the two stated starvation risks. A incorrect Ordinary RR returns ready jobs to recurring turns rather than repeatedly bypassing a peer. B incorrect FCFS preserves arrival order, so later arrivals do not overtake the target. C correct Repeated short arrivals can starve an older long SJN job. D correct Continued high-priority arrivals can starve a low-priority job without aging.

records.title: Operating System — Question 164 · AM0691
records.text: AM0691 Question 164 OS18 OS15 OS16 OS17 Which scheduling algorithm uses time slices to allocate CPU time to tasks? Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Round Robin Each RR process receives a fixed time quantum (PDF p25); it is preempted when that period expires. A is the direct time-slice mechanism. A correct Exactly the fixed-quantum rule (p25). B incorrect Arrival-order service does not itself define repeated time slices (p23). C incorrect SJN bases selection on execution duration (p23). D incorrect Priority bases selection on assigned rank (p24); it need not use a quantum.

records.title: Operating System — Question 165 · AM0692
records.text: AM0692 Question 165 OS16 OS13 OS14 For a fixed finite set of simultaneous ready jobs with known CPU bursts, no I/O and zero switch cost, which listed non-preemptive policy minimizes average waiting over all possible execution orders for arbitrary burst lengths? Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) Shortest Job Next (SJN) For the simultaneous known-burst workload, shortest-job order minimizes total waiting. Consider adjacent bursts L>S after an elapsed prefix T. Long then short gives waits T and T+L; short then long gives T and T+S, reducing their sum by L−S. Jobs outside the pair are unaffected. Repeatedly removing inversions gives SJN order. FCFS does not enforce it, while RR and SRTF are preemptive policies. A incorrect RR is preemptive and is outside the requested non-preemptive policy class. B incorrect FCFS can tie on favorable orders but does not minimize waiting for arbitrary burst orders. C correct SJN selects the shortest ready bursts and gives the standard minimum-average-waiting order. D incorrect SRTF is the preemptive remaining-time policy rather than the requested non-preemptive one.

records.title: Operating System — Question 166 · AM0693
records.text: AM0693 Question 166 OS18 OS21 Which scheduling algorithm provides better response time for interactive tasks? Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals. A Round Robin B First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Round Robin Time-sharing seeks short response by giving users short CPU bursts (PDF p7). RR implements fixed quantum turns (p25), so A is a well-supported interactive choice with a suitably short quantum. A correct Repeated short quanta implement the p7 interactive strategy. B incorrect Arrival-order long work can delay later interactive work (p23). C incorrect SJN needs duration estimates (p23), not a guaranteed prompt periodic turn. D incorrect Priority may help selected interactive jobs, but depends on assigned ranks rather than the general time-sharing mechanism.

records.title: Operating System — Question 167 · AM0694
records.text: AM0694 Question 167 OS14 Which listed policy is preemptive? SJN denotes non-preemptive shortest-job-next, and D specifically keeps the running burst until completion, blocking or voluntary release. Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Non-preemptive Priority Scheduling Round Robin RR limits a turn to a quantum and can return an unfinished runnable job to the ready queue. That is preemption. FCFS and the stated SJN variant keep a selected burst until it ends or blocks. The priority option is explicitly non-preemptive, so a higher-priority arrival does not interrupt its current burst. RR is therefore the unique preemptive policy in this list. A incorrect FCFS ordinarily does not forcibly interrupt the selected burst. B correct RR preempts unfinished work at quantum expiry. C incorrect SJN is explicitly the non-preemptive shortest-job policy. D incorrect The stated priority variant is explicitly non-preemptive.

records.title: Operating System — Question 168 · AM0695
records.text: AM0695 Question 168 OS20 OS15 OS16 OS17 Which listed policy allocates CPU according to declared user/group entitlement weights, so fairness can mean unequal proportional shares rather than arrival order? Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Shortest Job Next (SJN) C Priority Scheduling D Fair-Share Scheduling Fair-Share Scheduling Fair-share scheduling allocates service according to stated weights, which may apply to users or groups rather than individual processes. That directly implements proportional entitlement. FCFS respects arrival order, SJN chooses shorter bursts, and priority chooses a ranking; those rules do not themselves specify weighted user/group shares. The revised fairness criterion therefore identifies fair-share without implying every fair policy must use equal shares. A incorrect FCFS provides arrival ordering rather than declared weighted entitlements. B incorrect SJN selects by burst length rather than entitlement weights. C incorrect Priority ranking does not itself implement proportional user/group shares. D correct Fair-share scheduling allocates according to declared weights and participant scope.

records.title: Operating System — Question 169 · AM0696
records.text: AM0696 Question 169 OS16 OS15 OS18 OS17 Which algorithm gives priority to the tasks with the shortest burst time? Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Shortest Job Next (SJN) SJF on PDF p23 requires knowing how long a process will take and favors shortest jobs. C uses the synonymous SJN label. Priority can incorporate time requirements, but does not necessarily rank by shortest burst. A incorrect FCFS chooses order of arrival (p23). B incorrect RR chooses fixed turns (p25). C correct Shortest-job selection uses the known execution duration (p23). D incorrect Assigned priorities can reflect many requirements, not necessarily shortest burst (p24).

records.title: Operating System — Question 170 · AM0698
records.text: AM0698 Question 170 OS02 OS18 Which scheduling algorithm is most suitable for time-sharing systems? Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Round Robin PDF p7 describes time-sharing as short bursts/quantums for many users, seeking fast response. RR’s fixed quantum and preemption (p25) directly implement that pattern, making B the matching policy. A incorrect A long early FCFS job can delay other users, unlike repeated short turns. B correct Fixed quantum sharing directly implements p7’s time-sharing pattern. C incorrect SJN requires knowing lengths, not a periodic-turn guarantee. D incorrect Priority ordering alone does not guarantee each user a quantum.

records.title: Operating System — Question 171 · AM0699
records.text: AM0699 Question 171 OS17 OS15 OS18 Which correctly implemented policies can still cause starvation under an ongoing stream of preferred arrivals? Assume finite bursts, ordinary RR with tail insertion, FCFS without bypass, non-preemptive SJN, and fixed priority without aging. Select all that apply. Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Shortest Job Next (SJN); Priority Scheduling Starvation can arise from the policy even when its implementation is correct. SJN repeatedly favors short arrivals over an older long burst, while fixed priority can repeatedly favor high-priority arrivals over low-priority work. FCFS preserves arrival order, and RR provides recurring turns under the stated finite-work assumptions. Thus SJN and fixed priority are the two policies with the specified inherent bypass risk. A incorrect FCFS later arrivals cannot bypass a target with finite predecessor work. B incorrect Ordinary RR returns peers to recurring turns rather than favoring newcomers indefinitely. C correct Repeated shorter arrivals can indefinitely postpone a long SJN job. D correct Continued higher-priority arrivals can indefinitely postpone low-priority work without aging.

records.title: Operating System — Question 172 · AM0701
records.text: AM0701 Question 172 OS18 OS05 Which scheduling algorithm has the potential for higher overhead due to frequent context switches? Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling Round Robin Each RR quantum expiration preempts and saves state (PDF p25). PDF p21 calls context-switch time pure overhead, so frequent short quanta create the overhead risk described. A incorrect FCFS need not switch after every short quantum. B correct Repeated quantum expiration creates frequent context saves; p21 identifies their cost. C incorrect Whole-job SJN does not inherently expire a quantum repeatedly. D incorrect Priority can preempt frequently under some arrivals, but that is not inherent in its p24 ranking rule.

records.title: Operating System — Question 173 · AM0702
records.text: AM0702 Question 173 OS20 OS18 OS15 OS16 Two continuously ready user groups have declared CPU entitlements of 3:1, independent of how many tasks each launches. Which listed policy is designed to enforce those unequal per-group shares over time? Identify the allocation entity, entitlement weights and whether the guarantee is probabilistic. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Fair-Share Scheduling Fair-Share Scheduling A fair-share policy allocates CPU according to declared weights and participant scope. Weights of 3:1 give intended group shares of 75 and 25 percent. Plain RR supplies equal turns to processes and does not implement those unequal group entitlements independently of task count. FCFS and SJN also lack that share rule. The question asks for the policy design rather than a universal finite-time deadline. A incorrect FCFS orders bursts by arrival rather than enforcing weighted group service. B incorrect Plain per-task RR does not enforce unequal group weights independent of task count. C incorrect SJN selects short bursts rather than proportional group entitlements. D correct Configured fair-share scheduling implements the declared group-weight allocation.

records.title: Operating System — Question 174 · AM0703
records.text: AM0703 Question 174 OS13 OS15 OS16 OS17 OS18 Three jobs all arrive at time 0 in listed order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts 24, 3, 3 and priorities 2, 1, 3 (smaller number is higher). There is no I/O or overhead. Compare FCFS, RR with quantum 4, non-preemptive SJN, and non-preemptive priority; use listed order for ties. Which has the highest average turnaround for this workload? Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures. A First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) B Round Robin C Shortest Job Next (SJN) D Priority Scheduling First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) FCFS completes P1, P2, P3 at 24, 27 and 30, giving average turnaround 27. RR completes them at 30, 7 and 10, averaging 47/3. SJN completes short jobs at 3 and 6, then P1 at 30, averaging 13. Priority runs P2, P1, P3 and averages 20. FCFS is uniquely highest for this specified workload, without a universal worst-policy claim. A correct FCFS average turnaround is (24+27+30)/3=27, the largest. B incorrect RR average turnaround is (30+7+10)/3=47/3, below 27. C incorrect SJN average turnaround is (3+6+30)/3=13. D incorrect Priority average turnaround is (3+27+30)/3=20.

records.title: Operating System — Question 175 · CS0218
records.text: CS0218 Question 175 OS07 Which one of the following is a voluntary termination of a process? Separate creation, image replacement and termination; classify termination by its cause. A Error exit B Killed by another process C Terminated by another process D Fatal exit Error exit, when the program detects an error and chooses to terminate. OS07 explicitly classifies program-detected error exits as voluntary. Being killed or terminated by another process is imposed, and a fatal unrecoverable fault is involuntary. The distinction is the termination decision’s origin, not whether the run succeeded: a program can voluntarily exit because its input is invalid or it detects another handled error. A correct A program-detected error exit is a deliberate voluntary termination path, even though execution was unsuccessful. B incorrect Being killed by another process is imposed externally and is therefore involuntary. C incorrect Termination by another process is external rather than a voluntary exit chosen by the program. D incorrect A fatal unrecoverable fault causes involuntary termination rather than a deliberate program error exit.

records.title: Operating System — Question 176 · CS0219
records.text: CS0219 Question 176 OS08 OS07 Which statements are false in a system with one-to-one kernel-supported threads? In A, “children” means a process may create another process and a running thread may invoke a thread-creation operation; it does not require an OS thread-parent hierarchy. In B, “execute sequentially” means threads are required to finish one after another without interleaving. Select all that apply. Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping. A Both can create children B Threads within a process execute sequentially C Processes are not independent of one another D If one thread is blocked, another thread can run Threads within a process execute sequentially; Processes are not independent of one another Threads within one process need not finish sequentially; their execution may interleave or run on multiple CPUs. Independent processes can also exist, so C’s universal dependence claim is false. The defined creation operations make A true without imposing a thread-parent hierarchy. Under one-to-one mapping, one blocked thread need not block every other thread, making D a valid possibility rather than a false statement. A incorrect The defined process and thread creation operations are allowed, so A is true. B correct Mandatory finish-before-next sequential execution is false; threads can interleave or run in parallel. C correct Universal process dependence is false because independent processes can exist. D incorrect One-to-one mapping permits another runnable thread to execute when one blocks, so D is true.

records.title: Operating System — Question 177 · CS0220
records.text: CS0220 Question 177 OS02 Which statements are false under a classification based on simultaneous users? A single user may run multiple applications, and B means concurrent database accesses by those applications, not by additional users. In C, “at most one” describes the system’s supported capacity. Select all that apply. Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model. A In single user systems many users can login simultaneously B Single user systems can allow concurrent access to the database C Multiuser system can allow at most one user at a time D In Multiuser system many users can access the system concurrently In single user systems many users can login simultaneously; Multiuser system can allow at most one user at a time Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access rather than application count. A therefore contradicts single-user status, and C contradicts the supported multiple-user capacity. One user may still run several applications accessing a database concurrently, which is the explicit meaning of B here. D states the multiuser capability correctly. The selected false statements are A and C. A correct Many simultaneous logged-in users contradict the single-user definition. B incorrect Concurrent applications belonging to one user do not violate single-user status, so B is true. C correct A capacity of at most one user contradicts the multiuser definition. D incorrect Supporting concurrent access by many users is the multiuser capability, so D is true.

records.title: Operating System — Question 178 · CS0221
records.text: CS0221 Question 178 OS10 OS06 OS22 When a process executes code that possibly changes the value of shared data, its execution has to be mutually exclusive. Therefore, the process is in: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required. A Deadlock B Terminated C Critical section D Blocked Critical section. OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state that needs protection. The stem describes execution that may change shared data and therefore requires mutual exclusion, directly matching that definition. Deadlock and blocking are waiting states or failures, while termination means execution has ended. None identifies the protected shared-state code currently being executed. A incorrect Deadlock involves blocked dependencies, whereas the stem describes protected code actively accessing shared data. B incorrect A terminated process has ended execution, contradicting the stem’s currently executing shared-data operation. C correct Code that accesses shared data and requires mutual exclusion is a critical section. D incorrect A blocked process cannot proceed pending an event; the stem instead identifies the code requiring protection.

records.title: Operating System — Question 179 · NS0308
records.text: NS0308 Question 179 OS06 OS-S03 OS01 Which one of the following function of operating system is categorized under process management? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Allocates the device in the efficient way B De-allocates memory when a process releases it. C Allocates the memory when the process requests it to do so. D Allocates the processor (CPU) to a process Allocate the CPU to a process. Allocating the CPU to a ready process is the scheduling role within process management. Device allocation belongs to device management. Allocating requested memory and reclaiming memory that has been released belong to memory management. Specifying the resource in the deallocation option removes its former overlap with several managers and leaves processor allocation as the distinct process-management function. A incorrect Allocating a device is a device-management responsibility. B incorrect Reclaiming released memory is a memory-management responsibility under the stated resource classification. C incorrect Allocating requested memory belongs to memory management. D correct Selecting a ready process to receive the CPU is the process-scheduling responsibility.

records.title: Operating System — Question 180 · NS0316
records.text: NS0316 Question 180 OS01 What is the primary function of an operating system? Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications. A To connect to the internet B To create documents and spreadsheets C To design computer hardware D To act as an intermediary between users and computer hardware Act as the service/resource intermediary between users/programs and hardware. OS01 describes the OS allocating hardware resources and providing program services, with convenient interfaces and abstractions. D captures that intermediary role. Internet connectivity and document creation are narrower tasks, and hardware design is not a runtime OS service. The answer combines convenience and resource control rather than reducing the OS to one application or device function. A incorrect Internet access is one supported communication activity rather than the general purpose of an operating system. B incorrect Document and spreadsheet creation are application tasks that use OS services rather than define the OS. C incorrect Designing hardware is not the runtime resource/service function described for an operating system. D correct The OS provides interfaces and controlled resource services linking users/programs to the underlying hardware.

records.title: Operating System — Question 181 · NS0323
records.text: NS0323 Question 181 OS34 A user installs a new printer. The OS automatically detects and configures it. This is an example of: Separate device hardware, device-specific software and general event or transfer mechanisms. A Plug-and-play functionality B Manual driver installation C Manual hardware management D Resource allocation Plug-and-play functionality. OS34 defines plug-and-play as discovering/configuring compatible new hardware, which directly matches automatic printer setup. A driver may still be needed, so automatic configuration does not imply driver-free operation. Manual driver installation and hardware management contradict the scenario’s automatic action. Resource allocation may occur during setup but is broader than the specific feature named. A correct Automatic detection and configuration of the printer is the note’s plug-and-play behavior. B incorrect The stem specifies automatic setup, not user-performed manual installation of a driver. C incorrect Manual hardware management does not match the automatic discovery/configuration described in the scenario. D incorrect Allocation can be part of setup, but it does not specifically name automatic device discovery/configuration.

records.title: Operating System — Question 182 · NS0330
records.text: NS0330 Question 182 OS22 In a system, resources cannot be forcibly taken from processes; they must be released voluntarily. Which deadlock condition does this represent? Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock. A No Preemption B Hold and Wait C Mutual Exclusion D Circular Wait No preemption. OS22 defines no resource preemption as voluntary release by the current holder. The stem repeats that resources cannot be forcibly taken, giving a direct match. Holding while requesting another resource, one-at-a-time ownership and a closed chain of waits are separate conditions and do not by themselves express the withdrawal restriction. A correct The holder must release voluntarily, so the system cannot forcibly preempt the resource. B incorrect Hold-and-wait concerns retaining one resource while requesting another rather than whether withdrawal is allowed. C incorrect Mutual exclusion limits simultaneous ownership, not whether allocated resources can be forcibly reclaimed. D incorrect Circular wait concerns a closed dependency chain, not the resource-release rule specified here.

records.title: Operating System — Question 183 · NS0359
records.text: NS0359 Question 183 OS02 OS20 How does an operating system improve efficiency in a multi-user environment? Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model. A By allowing only one user to access the system at a time B By disabling all background services C By using time-sharing and process scheduling to allocate CPU time fairly among users and processes D By requiring manual intervention for each task Time-sharing and scheduling distribute CPU service among users/processes. OS02 describes time-sharing as rapid scheduling/preemption supporting interactive users. OS20 explains that fair allocation needs a share policy and may operate per user/group. C describes those relevant mechanisms rather than disabling services or requiring manual intervention. Its fairly should be understood under a specified policy, not as an automatic equality guarantee from time-sharing alone. A incorrect Restricting access to one user contradicts the multiuser setting rather than explaining its efficient sharing. B incorrect Disabling every background service is neither required nor the time-sharing/resource-allocation mechanism described. C correct Scheduling/time-sharing interleave useful work and can allocate service according to the system’s fairness policy. D incorrect Manual intervention for each task adds administration rather than explaining efficient automatic CPU allocation.

records.title: Operating System — Question 184 · NS0684
records.text: NS0684 Question 184 OS01 What is the primary role of an Operating System? Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications. A Run application software only B Manage hardware and software resources and act as interface between user and hardware C Provide internet connectivity D Store user files permanently Manage resources and provide interfaces/services. OS01 defines both allocation of CPU/memory/storage/devices/communications and services to programs, while describing convenient interfaces. B combines those core responsibilities. Running applications only, providing connectivity only or permanently storing files each captures a narrower task and omits the overall system-management role. The primary role is therefore the resource/interface combination, not a single service. A incorrect Application execution is supported, but only excludes the OS’s other essential resource and service duties. B correct Resource management plus user/program interfaces matches the combined OS role defined here. C incorrect Internet connectivity is one communication service rather than the complete primary OS role. D incorrect Permanent file storage is a storage-device/filesystem service and not the complete operating-system purpose.

records.title: Operating System — Question 185 · NS0685
records.text: NS0685 Question 185 OS02 Which type of OS is designed to process large numbers of similar jobs without user interaction during execution? Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model. A Real-Time OS B Time-Sharing OS C Batch System D Single-User OS Batch system. OS02 defines batch jobs as running with little interaction after submission. That matches processing submitted similar jobs without user interaction during execution. Time-sharing targets interactive users, real-time targets timing correctness, and single-user classifies concurrent access rather than job interaction. The job-processing clue therefore selects batch rather than a user-count or deadline category. A incorrect Real-time classification concerns meeting deadlines rather than the absence of user interaction during submitted job processing. B incorrect Time-sharing supports interactive users through rapid scheduling, unlike the noninteractive batch description. C correct Batch processing runs submitted jobs with little interaction, directly matching the scenario. D incorrect Single-user describes concurrent user access, not whether a workload is submitted and processed as batches.

records.title: Operating System — Question 186 · NS0686
records.text: NS0686 Question 186 OS05 In a Process Control Block (PCB), what does the Program Counter store? Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state. A The process priority level B The address of the next instruction to be executed for that process C The amount of CPU time used D The list of open files The saved next-instruction position for resuming the process. OS05 says the PCB records PC/registers alongside scheduling, memory/accounting and I/O information, and a saved PC identifies where execution resumes. Thus B describes its specific field role. Priority, CPU usage and open files can be other PCB information, but they are not the program-counter value. The question requires distinguishing fields within one record rather than excluding them from the PCB entirely. A incorrect Priority is scheduling information in the PCB, not the saved next-instruction position held by PC. B correct The saved PC records the instruction position at which the process will resume execution. C incorrect CPU time consumed is accounting information rather than the program-counter address. D incorrect Open files belong to I/O/open-resource state, not to the saved instruction-pointer field.

records.title: Operating System — Question 187 · NS0687
records.text: NS0687 Question 187 OS06 Which process state indicates that a process is waiting for an I/O event to complete? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Ready B Running C Waiting D Terminated Waiting/blocked. OS06 defines waiting/blocked as unable to proceed until an event and maps blocking I/O from running to waiting. Therefore a process waiting for I/O completion is in Waiting. It is not ready while the event prevents progress, not running during the wait, and not terminated merely because its request is outstanding. Completion normally makes it ready afterward. A incorrect Ready means eligible for CPU immediately; the outstanding blocking I/O prevents that eligibility. B incorrect Running means currently using a CPU, unlike the blocked interval awaiting I/O completion. C correct Waiting/blocked is the state for a process that cannot proceed until its I/O event completes. D incorrect Terminated means execution has ended, not temporarily paused pending completion of an I/O request.

records.title: Operating System — Question 188 · NS0688
records.text: NS0688 Question 188 OS05 What is the primary purpose of a Context Switch? Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state. A To permanently stop a process B To save the state of the current process and restore the state of the next scheduled process C To allocate more memory to a process D To terminate a low-priority process Save one execution context and restore another. OS05 directly defines a context switch as saving one execution context and restoring another, with overhead interrupting useful application work. B matches. A process may later resume, so switching does not permanently stop or kill it. Allocating memory is another management operation, and a privilege transition alone need not switch processes. A incorrect The outgoing process can resume later; permanent stopping is termination rather than context switching. B correct Saving current state and restoring the selected execution context is the defined context-switch purpose. C incorrect Memory allocation changes resource assignment, not the saved/restored execution context defining a switch. D incorrect A context switch need not terminate any process, regardless of priority.

records.title: Operating System — Question 189 · NS0689
records.text: NS0689 Question 189 OS06 Which scheduler is responsible for selecting which process from the ready queue should be executed next on the CPU? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Long-Term Scheduler B Medium-Term Scheduler C Short-Term (CPU) Scheduler D I/O Scheduler Short-term (CPU) scheduler. OS06 assigns admission to the long-term scheduler, suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler and ready-work selection to the short-term scheduler. The question specifically asks which ready process receives the CPU next, so C is exact. The dispatcher then performs the handoff; that is distinct from selecting the ready process. Device request ordering is not CPU ready-queue selection. A incorrect The long-term scheduler admits jobs rather than making each immediate ready-queue CPU selection. B incorrect The medium-term scheduler suspends/swaps work rather than choosing the next CPU-ready process. C correct The short-term CPU scheduler selects the next eligible process from ready work. D incorrect An I/O scheduler orders device work rather than selecting the next process for the CPU.

records.title: Operating System — Question 190 · NS0690
records.text: NS0690 Question 190 OS06 OS27 OS34 What is the role of the Medium-Term Scheduler? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Decide which jobs enter the system B Pick the next process for the CPU C Swap processes between main memory and secondary storage to manage memory D Handle device driver requests Suspend/swap processes between resident and backing-store states. OS06 explicitly assigns suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler. OS27 distinguishes traditional whole-process swapping to backing storage from page movement. Thus C is the matching memory/load-control role. Admitting jobs belongs to long-term scheduling, picking the next ready process to short-term scheduling, and servicing drivers to device-management paths. A incorrect Deciding admission into the system is the long-term scheduler’s role in the supplied model. B incorrect Selecting the next CPU process belongs to the short-term scheduler, not the medium-term one. C correct Medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps processes to control resident load and memory use. D incorrect Device-driver requests concern I/O service rather than the scheduler’s suspension/swapping function.

records.title: Operating System — Question 191 · NS0691
records.text: NS0691 Question 191 OS10 A Race Condition occurs when: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required. A Two processes finish execution at the same time B Multiple processes access shared resources simultaneously without proper synchronization, causing unpredictable results C A high-priority process always runs before a low-priority one D A process is preempted by the OS scheduler Uncoordinated conflicting shared accesses make results depend on interleaving. OS10 defines a race by results depending on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. B is the intended match, with shared access understood to include a conflict such as an update; simultaneous read-only access alone is insufficient. Coincident completion, ordinary priority selection and preemption do not by themselves establish a shared-state race. A incorrect Two completions at the same time need not involve conflicting shared accesses or interleaving-dependent results. B correct Unsynchronized conflicting shared accesses can make results depend on execution interleaving, which is the race condition. C incorrect Priority order alone is a scheduling choice and does not establish a conflicting shared-data race. D incorrect Preemption can expose a race but is not itself sufficient without conflicting unprotected accesses.

records.title: Operating System — Question 192 · NS0692
records.text: NS0692 Question 192 OS22 Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock? Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock. A Mutual Exclusion B Hold and Wait C Preemption D Circular Wait Preemption is not a necessary condition; no-preemption is. OS22 names mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as the necessary set. The option Preemption reverses one of those conditions. Therefore C is the exception, while the other three are genuine members. This resource-preemption rule is separate from whether CPU scheduling uses timer preemption. A incorrect Mutual exclusion is explicitly one of the four necessary conditions in the standard resource model. B incorrect Hold-and-wait is explicitly necessary: a process retains a resource while requesting another. C correct The required condition is no-preemption; permitting preemption is not one of the necessary conditions. D incorrect Circular wait is explicitly a required closed dependency chain in the standard model.

records.title: Operating System — Question 193 · NS0693
records.text: NS0693 Question 193 OS15 OS13 All three processes arrive at time 0 and are ready immediately. Their CPU burst times are P1 = 24 ms, P2 = 3 ms and P3 = 3 ms. Using non-preemptive FCFS with tie order P1, P2, P3, and ignoring context-switch overhead, what is the average waiting time? Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time. A 3 ms B 9 ms C 17 ms D 27 ms 17 ms. FCFS runs P1 from 0 to 24 ms, P2 from 24 to 27 ms, and P3 from 27 to 30 ms. Because every process arrives at 0, their waiting times are 0, 24 and 27 ms. The average is (0+24+27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms, so C is correct. The average turnaround is a different quantity: (24+27+30)/3 = 27 ms. A incorrect 3 ms is the burst time of P2 or P3, not the average ready-queue wait. B incorrect The three waits total 51 ms, so dividing by three cannot give 9 ms. C correct The waits 0, 24 and 27 ms average to 17 ms. D incorrect 27 ms is the average turnaround time in this example, not the average waiting time.

records.title: Operating System — Question 194 · NS0694
records.text: NS0694 Question 194 OS17 OS10 OS29 What problem does the 'Aging' technique solve in Priority Scheduling? Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank. A Deadlock B Starvation of low-priority processes C Race conditions D Memory fragmentation Starvation of low-priority processes. OS17 defines aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement under suitable rules/workloads. Thus B names the problem it addresses. It does not remove a deadlock dependency cycle, coordinate conflicting memory updates or consolidate fragmented memory. The result still depends on the priority/aging policy; naming aging alone does not provide an unconditional deadline guarantee. A incorrect Aging changes priority rather than breaking the blocked resource dependencies of a deadlock. B correct Increasing effective priority of waiting low-priority jobs addresses their starvation under sustained higher-priority load. C incorrect Races require shared-access synchronization; priority aging is not a mutual-exclusion mechanism. D incorrect Memory fragmentation concerns allocation layout rather than the priority of waiting CPU jobs.

records.title: Operating System — Question 195 · NS0695
records.text: NS0695 Question 195 OS16 OS18 OS15 Which scheduling algorithm is known as preemptive SJF? Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule. A Round Robin B FCFS C Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) D Priority Scheduling Shortest Remaining Time First. OS16 distinguishes non-preemptive SJF/SJN from SRTF, which reconsiders at arrivals and can preempt for shorter remaining work. Therefore SRTF is the preemptive SJF variant. RR uses fixed cyclic turns, FCFS arrival order and generic priority an independently defined ranking. The original burst length and the remaining length must not be confused after a job has executed. A incorrect RR selects cyclic quantum turns rather than the shortest remaining CPU work. B incorrect FCFS follows arrival order and is ordinarily non-preemptive rather than preemptive shortest-job scheduling. C correct SRTF chooses minimum remaining work and can interrupt a running job for a shorter arrival. D incorrect Generic priority scheduling does not specifically rank by remaining burst length and can be either variant.

records.title: Operating System — Question 196 · NS0696
records.text: NS0696 Question 196 OS18 In Round Robin scheduling, what is the key challenge? Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals. A Managing priority levels B Determining the appropriate time quantum length C Avoiding deadlocks D Allocating memory to processes Choose an appropriate time quantum. OS18 says a large RR quantum approaches FCFS, while tiny quanta increase context-switch overhead. Selecting q therefore trades responsiveness against overhead, matching B. Priority management, deadlock policy and memory allocation are separate concerns rather than the defining parameter-selection challenge of ordinary Round Robin. The useful quantum depends on workloads and switching cost. A incorrect Basic RR uses cyclic ready-queue turns rather than requiring a hierarchy of priority levels. B correct Quantum length controls responsiveness and switching overhead, creating RR’s characteristic tuning tradeoff. C incorrect Deadlock avoidance concerns resources and dependencies, not the defining RR quantum parameter. D incorrect Memory allocation is a separate management problem rather than the Round Robin selection rule’s main parameter.

records.title: Operating System — Question 197 · NS0697
records.text: NS0697 Question 197 OS11 OS15 OS28 OS38 What is a Semaphore? Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model. A A scheduling algorithm B A memory management technique C A synchronization variable that controls access to shared resources in a multi-process environment D A type of file allocation method A synchronization variable with atomic wait and signal operations. OS11 defines a semaphore through atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Tokens control whether participants can proceed with shared resource work, with binary or counting forms. C identifies that synchronization role. Scheduling, memory-management and file-allocation policies solve different resource-selection/layout problems and do not define semaphore semantics. A incorrect A semaphore synchronizes participants; it is not itself a CPU-selection scheduling algorithm. B incorrect It controls coordination through permits, rather than choosing memory locations or translation layouts. C correct Atomic wait/signal on a synchronization variable controls permits for concurrent shared-resource operations. D incorrect File allocation chooses storage-block layout; that is separate from semaphore synchronization semantics.

records.title: Operating System — Question 198 · NS0698
records.text: NS0698 Question 198 OS11 What is the difference between a Binary Semaphore and a Counting Semaphore? Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model. A Binary semaphores are faster B Binary semaphores have only two states (0 or 1), while counting semaphores track available resources up to a maximum count C Counting semaphores are used only for deadlock prevention D There is no difference Binary tracks one permit; counting tracks several. OS11 defines a binary semaphore as one permit and a counting semaphore as several, under the nonnegative-token model. Thus binary availability is 0/1 while a resource pool can have a larger count. B states this logical distinction. Internal negative-waiter encodings are implementation details, not a reason to claim speed guarantees, deadlock-only usage or no difference. A incorrect The note gives no universal relative-speed guarantee; permit capacity is the defining distinction. B correct In the nonnegative-token model, binary availability is zero/one while counting semaphores track several available permits. C incorrect Counting semaphores coordinate resource pools and are not limited to preventing deadlock. D incorrect The allowed permit count is a substantive difference explicitly stated here.

records.title: Operating System — Question 199 · NS0699
records.text: NS0699 Question 199 OS22 What must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur? Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock. A Only Mutual Exclusion and Circular Wait B Any two of the four conditions C All four necessary conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait D Only Circular Wait All four standard necessary conditions. OS22 says all four conditions are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. C names that full set. Any two or a cycle alone does not state the complete conjunction. This is a necessary-condition answer, not an assertion that merely allowing all four policies proves a deadlock already exists in a particular allocation state. A incorrect It omits hold-and-wait and no-preemption, both necessary in the stated standard resource model. B incorrect An arbitrary pair does not supply all four necessary restrictions for the standard deadlock model. C correct This option lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait together. D incorrect A cycle alone omits other necessary restrictions; it is not the complete standard condition set.

records.title: Operating System — Question 200 · NS0700
records.text: NS0700 Question 200 OS23 In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), what does a cycle with single-instance resources indicate? Follow request and assignment arrows and check how many instances each resource has. A Potential deadlock only B No deadlock possible C Definite deadlock D High CPU utilization Definite deadlock under single-instance resource assumptions. OS23 says a cycle implies deadlock when every resource type has one instance. The stem supplies that decisive assumption, so C follows. With multiple instances a cycle would indicate only a possibility, but importing that different model would ignore the literal question. A graph cycle also says nothing by itself about high CPU utilization. A incorrect Potential-only applies to the more general multiple-instance caveat, not the supplied single-instance case. B incorrect A cycle in the stated single-instance model establishes deadlock rather than excluding it. C correct The note explicitly gives cycle implies deadlock for a graph with one instance per resource type. D incorrect Resource dependency cycles do not measure CPU busy time or establish high processor utilization.

records.title: Operating System — Question 201 · NS0701
records.text: NS0701 Question 201 OS26 OS24 OS25 Which deadlock handling method allows deadlock to occur but then recovers from it? Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking. A Deadlock Prevention B Deadlock Ignorance C Deadlock Recovery D Deadlock Avoidance Deadlock recovery. OS26 describes recovery through terminating selected processes or safely reclaiming resources and rolling work back after deadlock is detected. That matches allowing occurrence and then resolving it. Prevention removes a necessary condition, avoidance preserves safety before granting, and ignoring accepts risk without committing to recovery. The complete handling strategy is detection plus recovery; C is the offered recovery component. A incorrect Prevention constrains requests so the targeted deadlock class cannot arise rather than accepting occurrence first. B incorrect Ignoring rare deadlock does not define active detection and subsequent recovery. C correct Recovery acts on an actual detected deadlock using termination, reclamation or rollback as appropriate. D incorrect Avoidance checks safe states before grants rather than deliberately permitting deadlock and then repairing it.

records.title: Operating System — Question 202 · NS0702
records.text: NS0702 Question 202 OS27 What is Address Binding at 'Load Time'? Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation. A Addresses are fixed by the compiler before execution B Addresses are determined while the program executes C Final memory addresses are assigned when the program is loaded into memory (since addresses are unknown at compile time) D Addresses are stored on the hard disk Relocate addresses when the program is loaded. OS27 defines load-time binding as relocation when placed into memory. That matches C’s final-address assignment at load when placement was unknown at compile time. Fixing absolute addresses during compilation is compile-time binding; translating while running is execution-time binding. Merely storing address bytes on a disk describes neither the placement decision nor its timing. A incorrect Fixing absolute addresses in the compiler is compile-time binding, not relocation on loading. B incorrect Translation during execution is execution-time binding rather than assignment during loading. C correct The loader resolves placement-dependent addresses when placing the program into memory. D incorrect Storing address information on disk does not define when placement-dependent address binding occurs.

records.title: Operating System — Question 203 · NS0703
records.text: NS0703 Question 203 OS31 OS30 Under basic page-frame allocation and variable-segment allocation, which statement correctly contrasts allocation-unit size and external fragmentation? Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location. A Paging uses variable-sized blocks; segmentation uses fixed-sized blocks B Paging divides memory into fixed-sized pages eliminating external fragmentation; segmentation uses variable-sized logical segments but can cause external fragmentation C Segmentation is used only in virtual memory D Paging requires no hardware support Fixed-size paging avoids external page-frame fragmentation; variable segments can fragment externally. Paging maps fixed-size pages into equal-size frames, avoiding external fragmentation of frame allocation, although internal waste can remain. Segmentation uses variable-length logical regions and can leave external holes. This is the unit-size and fragmentation contrast in B. A reverses the sizes. C does not supply that contrast, and D substitutes a hardware-support claim for it; page translation still requires mappings and checks. A incorrect The sizes are reversed: pages are fixed-size units and segments are variable-length regions. B correct This gives the required fixed-page versus variable-segment size and external-fragmentation contrast. C incorrect An exclusive-use statement does not compare allocation-unit sizes or external fragmentation as requested. D incorrect This does not give the requested size/fragmentation contrast; paging also uses translation mappings and checks.

records.title: Operating System — Question 204 · NS0704
records.text: NS0704 Question 204 OS29 What causes External Fragmentation in memory management? Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space. A Allocated memory blocks being larger than needed B Free memory being scattered in small non-contiguous pieces making it impossible to satisfy large allocation requests C Processes using too much CPU time D Too many open files in the directory Free capacity is split across holes too small for a required contiguous allocation. OS29 defines external fragmentation as sufficient total free space split into holes unable to satisfy a contiguous allocation. B matches that definition, with large requests understood to require one continuous region. A instead describes internal fragmentation. CPU time and open-file counts may create other pressures but do not define the spatial fragmentation of free memory. A incorrect Unused space within an oversized allocated block is internal fragmentation, not external free-hole fragmentation. B correct Noncontiguous small holes can have enough total capacity yet fail to satisfy one contiguous request. C incorrect CPU execution time does not define the spatial layout of free memory holes. D incorrect Open-file count is a resource-use limit rather than the definition of external memory fragmentation.

records.title: Operating System — Question 205 · NS0705
records.text: NS0705 Question 205 OS30 OS36 What is the purpose of the Page Table in Paging? Split the address into page and offset, then apply the mapping and access checks. A To allocate CPU time to processes B To map logical page numbers to physical frame numbers in memory C To store file access permissions D To manage disk I/O operations Map virtual/logical pages to physical frames. OS30 says the page table maps each virtual page to a frame with protection/status flags. B directly states the primary translation role. CPU time allocation belongs to scheduling; file permissions belong to filesystem metadata, despite page tables also having memory-protection bits. Disk I/O may service nonresident pages but does not define the page table’s mapping purpose. A incorrect CPU time allocation is scheduling, not the page-to-frame translation recorded by a page table. B correct The table identifies the physical frame corresponding to each virtual page and records relevant flags. C incorrect Memory access-protection flags differ from filesystem file-access permissions; file permissions are not the page table’s purpose. D incorrect Page faults may cause I/O, but general disk-operation management is not the table’s translation role.

records.title: Operating System — Question 206 · NS0706
records.text: NS0706 Question 206 OS31 OS30 In Segmentation, how is a physical address calculated? Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location. A Page number x frame size B Base address of segment + offset C Logical address - limit register D Frame number + page offset Physical address = segment base + valid offset. OS31 gives segment-table base, limit and permissions, then validates (segment,offset) and adds base+offset. B matches, conditional on the offset passing the bound/protection checks. A and D mix in paging components and omit required scaling or displacement, while subtracting a limit is not the segment translation formula. An invalid offset traps rather than spilling into another segment. A incorrect Page number times frame size is not the segment base-plus-offset translation and omits required mapping. B correct After segment and bound checks, add the selected segment’s physical base to the offset. C incorrect The limit is a bound for validation, not a number subtracted to form the physical address. D incorrect Frame terminology belongs to paging, and adding an unscaled frame number is not the segmentation formula.

records.title: Operating System — Question 207 · NS0707
records.text: NS0707 Question 207 OS32 OS35 What is Virtual Memory? Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps. A Extra RAM chips added to a computer B A technique using hard disk space as an extension of physical memory, allowing programs larger than physical memory to execute C The memory inside the CPU cache D Memory used only by the operating system Translated protected address spaces can use backing storage for nonresident portions. OS32 describes virtual memory as protected translated address spaces with nonresident program portions backed by storage. B gives the disk-backed extension aspect and can allow programs exceeding resident physical memory to execute. It is not a complete definition of virtual memory, nor does it eliminate finite capacity constraints. The other alternatives confuse RAM installation, cache or an OS-only restriction. A incorrect Installing RAM chips adds physical capacity; virtual-memory translation is a different mechanism. B correct Backing storage holds nonresident portions, permitting a program’s address space to exceed its currently resident physical memory. C incorrect CPU cache retains copied memory blocks and is not the virtual-address/backing-store mechanism. D incorrect Processes receive virtual address spaces; virtual memory is not restricted to storage used only by the OS.

records.title: Operating System — Question 208 · NS0708
records.text: NS0708 Question 208 OS32 In demand paging, assume the accessed virtual page is valid, permitted and backed by disk, but its contents are not resident and must be read from disk. What event is the page fault in this scenario? Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps. A A hardware memory error B When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk C An error in the page table D When a process exceeds its allocated memory When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk A valid nonresident access traps so the OS can obtain the page contents, update the mapping and restart the access. The specified page is disk-backed and requires a read, making B accurate for this scenario. Page faults in general need not read disk; zero-fill and shared mappings are other cases. Nothing here requires hardware failure, table corruption or exceeding the permitted address range. A incorrect The trap does not imply damaged memory hardware. B correct The valid disk-backed page is nonresident, so this access requires the stated page-in. C incorrect A correct table may intentionally mark a valid page nonresident. D incorrect The page is explicitly within the valid permitted mapping, so no allocation violation is implied.

records.title: Operating System — Question 209 · NS0709
records.text: NS0709 Question 209 OS32 OS27 OS28 What is Demand Paging? Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps. A Loading the entire program into memory before execution B Loading only the pages that are actually needed during program execution, keeping others on disk until required C Allocating memory in fixed partitions D Swapping entire processes between memory and disk Bring a page into memory when it is needed/accessed. OS32 defines demand paging as bringing a page in when accessed. B matches loading only the pages demanded during execution, with disk backing for the described stored portions. Not all pages must literally originate on disk because zero-fill/shared cases exist. Whole-program loading, fixed contiguous partitions and whole-process swapping do not name this per-page demand policy. A incorrect Loading the entire program before execution is eager loading rather than fetching pages on demand. B correct Pages are brought in as execution needs them; disk backing is the described common stored-page case. C incorrect Fixed partitions are a contiguous-allocation arrangement rather than the page-access-triggered loading policy. D incorrect Moving an entire process is traditional swapping, not the individual-page demand mechanism.

records.title: Operating System — Question 210 · NS0710
records.text: NS0710 Question 210 OS29 What is the difference between Internal and External Fragmentation? Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space. A Both are the same type of memory waste B Internal fragmentation wastes space inside allocated partitions (allocated > needed); external fragmentation wastes space between allocations C External fragmentation occurs in paging systems D Internal fragmentation only occurs in virtual memory Internal waste is inside allocations; external holes are between them. OS29 defines internal fragmentation as unused space inside an allocated unit and external fragmentation as free holes unable to serve a required contiguous request. B states the location distinction. C is not the general definition and needs allocator scope; D adds an unsupported virtual-memory-only restriction. These wastes can arise from allocation geometry rather than the program’s CPU behavior. A incorrect The note explicitly distinguishes internal unused allocation space from external free-hole fragmentation. B correct Internal space is wasted within an allocation; external waste is free space split between allocations. C incorrect This does not define the contrast; basic page-frame allocation avoids external fragmentation, though other allocators may differ. D incorrect Unused space within an allocated unit is not limited by definition to virtual-memory systems.

records.title: Operating System — Question 211 · NS0711
records.text: NS0711 Question 211 OS28 Which memory allocation strategy picks the first hole large enough to accommodate a process? Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention. A Best-Fit B Worst-Fit C First-Fit D Next-Fit First-fit. OS28 defines first-fit as selecting the first adequate hole. This is exactly the stem’s first hole large enough. Best-fit searches for the smallest adequate hole, worst-fit for the largest, and next-fit resumes from a prior search position. The explicit first-hole condition selects first-fit without any numeric hole trace. A incorrect Best-fit minimizes adequate hole size rather than stopping at the first adequate hole. B incorrect Worst-fit selects the largest available hole rather than the first adequate one encountered. C correct First-fit stops at the first hole that can accommodate the requested allocation. D incorrect Next-fit continues from the previous search position; the stem gives the ordinary first-fit criterion.

records.title: Operating System — Question 212 · NS0712
records.text: NS0712 Question 212 OS27 OS05 What is Swapping in OS memory management? Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation. A Exchanging CPU registers between processes B Temporarily moving an entire process from main memory to a backing store (disk) to free memory for other processes C Copying files between directories D Replacing old CPU instructions with new ones Temporarily move a whole process to backing store. OS27 explicitly distinguishes traditional swapping of a whole process to backing store from paging individual pages and context switching execution state. B describes the whole-process memory-management operation. Saving registers is a context-switch task, file copying is a filesystem operation, and replacing instruction contents does not define swapping’s residence change. A incorrect Saving/restoring CPU register contexts is context switching rather than moving a whole process out of RAM. B correct Traditional swapping moves a process image to backing storage to free resident memory. C incorrect Copying files changes directory/storage contents rather than a process image’s memory residence. D incorrect Replacing instruction contents is not the defined transfer of a whole process between RAM and backing store.

records.title: Operating System — Question 213 · NS0713
records.text: NS0713 Question 213 OS27 OS32 OS17 What is Dynamic Loading? Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation. A Loading the entire program into memory at startup B Loading routines from disk into memory only when they are actually called during execution C Dynamically changing the priority of a process D Moving pages between RAM and disk automatically Load a routine only when needed. OS27 directly defines dynamic loading as bringing a routine in when needed. B states the routine-on-call form of that rule. Eager startup loading is the opposite, priority changes are scheduling, and automatic page movement is a virtual-memory mechanism at a different granularity. Dynamic loading concerns when code routines become resident, not which process gets CPU priority. A incorrect Loading all routines at startup is eager loading rather than bringing them in only on demand. B correct A routine is loaded when execution actually calls or needs it, matching dynamic loading. C incorrect Changing priority affects scheduling and does not load a routine’s code into memory. D incorrect Paging moves pages by virtual-memory demand, whereas dynamic loading names demand-driven routine loading.

records.title: Operating System — Question 214 · NS0714
records.text: NS0714 Question 214 OS08 OS-S02 What is the key management-layer distinction between user-level threads and kernel-level threads, without assuming universal speed or reliability advantages? Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping. A User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS B Kernel-level threads are always faster C User-level threads can access hardware directly D There is no practical difference between them User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS User-level threads are managed by a library, while kernel threads are execution contexts known to the OS. Their mapping affects blocking behavior and use of multiple CPUs. The management layer alone does not guarantee faster creation, faster execution or greater stability; those depend on implementation. It also does not grant user code privileged hardware access. The option keeps the supported management distinction. A correct This states library management versus OS-known kernel threads. B incorrect No management layer guarantees that kernel threads are always faster. C incorrect User-level thread management does not grant direct privileged hardware access. D incorrect Blocking and CPU-use differences show that the distinction has practical effects.

records.title: Operating System — Question 215 · NS0715
records.text: NS0715 Question 215 OS09 What is IPC (Inter-Process Communication)? Identify how data moves, which participant waits and what event allows the operation to continue. A A CPU scheduling algorithm B Mechanisms allowing processes to exchange information, synchronize, and coordinate activities C A method for allocating memory between processes D A file system operation Mechanisms for exchanging information and coordinating processes. OS09 describes shared-memory communication, send/receive, pipes, queues, sockets and RPC, including synchronization for conflicting updates. B summarizes the exchange and coordination role. IPC is not a CPU selection algorithm or a particular memory-allocation/file operation, even though shared memory and file-based mechanisms may be used to implement it. A incorrect CPU scheduling selects execution opportunities, rather than defining communication and coordination among processes. B correct Exchanging information with appropriate synchronization/coordination captures the IPC mechanisms described here. C incorrect Shared memory can implement IPC, but memory allocation alone does not define interprocess communication. D incorrect Files can participate in communication, but IPC is not restricted to one filesystem operation.

records.title: Operating System — Question 216 · NS0716
records.text: NS0716 Question 216 OS10 What is the Critical Section problem concerned with? Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required. A Preventing processes from using too much CPU B Ensuring that no two processes are executing their critical sections (code accessing shared resources) simultaneously C Managing disk I/O operations D Scheduling processes in real-time systems Mutually exclude conflicting critical-region execution. OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state needing protection and lists mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting as requirements. B states the exclusion aspect for critical sections protecting the same conflicting resource. The problem also includes progress/fair-waiting requirements, so exclusion is not its entire specification. CPU quotas, disk management and real-time scheduling are different topics. A incorrect CPU consumption limits are not the shared-access exclusion problem defining critical sections. B correct Conflicting critical regions must not execute simultaneously; this is the mutual-exclusion part of the correctness requirements. C incorrect Disk I/O can involve shared state, but managing it generally is not the critical-section problem definition. D incorrect Real-time selection addresses timing/scheduling, not the core shared-state exclusion requirement requested.

records.title: Operating System — Question 217 · NS0717
records.text: NS0717 Question 217 OS13 For a general process that may perform I/O, which formula defines turnaround time from event timestamps? Waiting means time in the ready queue; burst means total CPU service. The formula must remain valid for nonzero arrival times and blocked intervals. Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures. A Burst Time - Waiting Time B Completion Time - Arrival Time C Start Time + Burst Time D Waiting Time + Burst Time Completion Time - Arrival Time Turnaround is completion time minus arrival time, including CPU execution, ready-queue waiting and blocked intervals. Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked time when I/O occurs. Start plus burst may resemble a completion timestamp for uninterrupted work, but it is not elapsed turnaround and does not subtract arrival. Burst minus waiting has no general elapsed-time interpretation. Only B remains valid in the full stated model. A incorrect Subtracting ready waiting from CPU service is not turnaround. B correct Completion minus arrival includes the entire elapsed lifetime. C incorrect Start plus burst is not generally completion with I/O and does not subtract arrival. D incorrect Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked intervals.

records.title: Operating System — Question 218 · NS0718
records.text: NS0718 Question 218 OS15 OS18 OS08 What is the Convoy Effect in FCFS scheduling? Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.
