A High-priority processes always complete first B All processes receive equal CPU time C Short processes get stuck waiting behind one very long process, causing high average waiting times D Multiple processes share the same memory space Short jobs wait behind a long FCFS burst. OS15 describes the convoy effect as long CPU-bound work making many short jobs wait under non-preemptive FCFS. C directly states that queueing effect and its high waiting-time consequence. FCFS does not use priority order or grant equal total CPU, and shared address space is unrelated to the arrival-order delay. The effect depends on a long burst preceding shorter ones. A incorrect Priority order does not define FCFS, which follows arrival order rather than high-priority completion. B incorrect FCFS serves entire bursts of possibly different lengths rather than enforcing equal CPU shares. C correct Short jobs are delayed behind the long non-preempted burst, producing the FCFS convoy effect. D incorrect Shared memory concerns address-space organization rather than the scheduling delay called a convoy.

records.title: Operating System — Question 219 · NS0719
records.text: NS0719 Question 219 OS14 OS21 What is Cooperative (Non-Preemptive) vs Preemptive Scheduling? Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking. A They are the same thing B Non-preemptive: process runs until it voluntarily releases CPU; Preemptive: OS can forcibly take CPU from a running process for another C Preemptive scheduling never interrupts processes D Non-preemptive scheduling always gives better performance Voluntary release versus possible forced CPU preemption. OS14 says non-preemptive scheduling retains the CPU until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding, while preemptive scheduling may return running work to ready. B captures the voluntary-versus-forced distinction, with completion/blocking included among natural release events. C contradicts preemption, D claims an unsupported universal performance ranking, and A erases the defining difference. A incorrect The policies differ in whether a running CPU burst can be forcibly interrupted for another process. B correct Non-preemptive work releases naturally/voluntarily; preemptive policy may forcibly reassign CPU execution time. C incorrect Forcibly interrupting running work is exactly what preemptive scheduling permits. D incorrect No policy universally performs better for all workloads and objectives, so the absolute performance claim fails.

records.title: Operating System — Question 220 · NS0720
records.text: NS0720 Question 220 OS13 Which scheduling criterion measures the number of processes completed per unit of time? Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures. A CPU Utilization B Response Time C Throughput D Turnaround Time Throughput. OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. That exactly matches the stem’s process-completion rate. CPU utilization is busy-time fraction; response measures delay to first start, and turnaround delay to completion. The units therefore distinguish throughput from the other criteria without requiring a scheduling example. A incorrect CPU utilization measures busy-time fraction, not how many processes finish per unit time. B incorrect Response measures first-service delay for a process rather than a completion-count rate. C correct Throughput is explicitly the number of completed jobs divided by elapsed time. D incorrect Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion elapsed duration rather than completed jobs per time.

records.title: Operating System — Question 221 · NS0721
records.text: NS0721 Question 221 OS06 What does the Job Queue contain? Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role. A Only processes currently running on the CPU B All processes currently in the system, including those not yet admitted to memory C Only processes waiting for I/O devices D Processes that have already terminated All processes in the broad textbook system/job-queue sense. OS06 explicitly defines the broad textbook job queue as processes in the system and distinguishes a narrower admission queue awaiting memory. B matches that broad usage, including not-yet-admitted jobs. Ready/running or I/O-blocked work are subsets, not the whole category; already-ended processes are not the intended current job population. The answer retains the note’s terminology qualification. A incorrect Currently running work is only a subset, not the broad population represented by the textbook job queue. B correct The broad textbook usage includes system processes/jobs, including those awaiting memory admission. C incorrect I/O waiting belongs to device queues and does not exhaust the broad job-queue population. D incorrect Already-terminated work is not the current job population intended here’s broad system queue.

records.title: Operating System — Question 222 · NS0722
records.text: NS0722 Question 222 OS36 In an open seekable file’s state, what does its current file-offset field (the file-position pointer, rather than the descriptor handle) track? Distinguish a file operation, a resource handle, an offset and file metadata. A The physical location of the file on disk B The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation C The owner's access permissions D The file's creation timestamp The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation The current offset records the logical position used for the next read or write on a seekable open file. A descriptor is instead a process-local integer handle referring to open-file state. Physical disk-block locations, permissions and creation timestamps describe other mapping or metadata information. By asking specifically about the position field, the revised stem makes B precise without conflating a descriptor with an offset. A incorrect Physical disk location is separate from the current logical I/O offset. B correct The file-offset field records the position for the next read or write. C incorrect Owner permissions are access-control metadata rather than the current position. D incorrect Creation time is metadata rather than the current I/O offset.

records.title: Operating System — Question 223 · NS0723
records.text: NS0723 Question 223 OS39 OS29 OS06 What is the purpose of an Access Control List (ACL) in file protection? Distinguish identity checks, permission checks and the particular security property at issue. A To track disk space usage B To specify exactly which users/groups have which types of access (read, write, execute) to each file C To manage disk fragmentation D To schedule file I/O operations Specify principals and permitted access rights. OS39 defines an ACL as listing principals and rights. B states that users/groups can receive different read/write/execute permissions for a file. Authentication verifies identity first; authorization uses these permitted operations. Space accounting, fragmentation and I/O ordering do not define an access-control list. The answer does not assume universal default rights or that every filesystem uses exactly the same permission model. A incorrect Disk-space usage is storage accounting, not the list of principals and allowed operations. B correct An ACL associates users/groups or other principals with specified access rights on the resource. C incorrect Fragmentation concerns block placement and free-space layout rather than authorization entries. D incorrect Scheduling I/O requests controls service order, not which principal is authorized to access a file.

records.title: Operating System — Question 224 · NS0724
records.text: NS0724 Question 224 OS38 OS30 What is Contiguous Allocation of disk space? Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata. A Files are stored in scattered blocks linked by pointers B Each file occupies a continuous set of consecutive disk blocks, enabling fast sequential and direct access C Files are indexed using a separate index block D Files are allocated in fixed-size frames A file occupies consecutive disk blocks. OS38 defines contiguous allocation through consecutive blocks, with logical block i at start+i. This permits sequential and direct access without following a chain. B matches. Scattered pointers describe linked allocation, a separate index describes indexed allocation, and fixed physical memory frames belong to paging rather than file-contiguity organization. Growth and external fragmentation remain drawbacks. A incorrect Scattered blocks linked by pointers describe linked allocation rather than one consecutive run. B correct A consecutive block run supports start-plus-index lookup and sequential/direct file access. C incorrect A separate block-pointer index describes indexed allocation, not contiguous placement itself. D incorrect Physical memory frames are paging units rather than the disk-block contiguity rule for a file.

records.title: Operating System — Question 225 · NS0725
records.text: NS0725 Question 225 OS38 OS29 What problem does Linked Allocation solve compared to Contiguous Allocation? Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata. A It speeds up random access B It eliminates external fragmentation and pre-known file size requirements since blocks can be scattered and linked anywhere C It reduces internal fragmentation D It requires less memory for storing file metadata Linked blocks permit growth without reserving a full contiguous run. OS38 says linked allocation supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file. Since successive blocks can occupy separate free locations, it removes the external-contiguity problem and the need to reserve the final length beforehand. B captures that advantage. Random access still requires traversing earlier links, internal last-block waste may remain, and no universal smaller-metadata claim follows. A incorrect Locating a later linked block requires traversal, so faster random access is not its general advantage. B correct Separate linked blocks allow incremental growth without a single reserved contiguous region or preknown final length. C incorrect A partially used final block can still waste space internally; linking does not specifically remove that waste. D incorrect Pointers add metadata, and the note gives no universal less-memory guarantee over contiguous allocation.

records.title: Operating System — Question 226 · NS0726
records.text: NS0726 Question 226 OS38 In Indexed Allocation, what is the Index Block? Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata. A A pointer stored in each data block to the next block B A dedicated block containing all the disk-block addresses (pointers to data blocks) for a specific file C A table stored at the beginning of the disk for all files D A block that stores file metadata like size and timestamps A per-file block of data-block pointers in the simple indexed model. OS38 defines indexed allocation through a per-file array/tree of block pointers and gives an index-block capacity example. B describes the simple single-index-block form. Large files may need multiple index levels, so all addresses in one block is model-dependent rather than universal. A is linked allocation, C a global-table description, and D ordinary metadata without the defining data-block pointers. A incorrect A next pointer in each data block describes linked allocation rather than a separate per-file index. B correct In the simple indexed model, a dedicated per-file index contains pointers to the file’s data blocks. C incorrect A global table for all files is not the per-file index block described by indexed allocation. D incorrect Size/timestamps alone do not provide the data-block address index that defines this allocation structure.

records.title: Operating System — Question 227 · NS0727
records.text: NS0727 Question 227 OS38 What is the difference between Sequential Access and Direct Access for files? Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata. A They are identical access methods B Sequential access reads/writes records in order; direct access allows jumping to any block/record position by specifying its block number C Direct access is only possible for text files D Sequential access requires more disk space Sequential access proceeds in order; direct access selects a position. OS38 contrasts linked traversal of preceding blocks with contiguous start+i and indexed direct lookup. These illustrate the access distinction in B: sequential progression versus selecting a numbered position without reading every preceding record. Nothing restricts direct access to text or requires sequential files to occupy more disk space merely because of their access method. A incorrect Order-dependent traversal and direct selection are different access behaviors, not identical methods. B correct Sequential access advances through records; direct access identifies a chosen block/position for access. C incorrect The direct block-lookup rule does not impose a text-file-only restriction. D incorrect Access order alone does not determine a greater storage-space requirement for sequential files.

records.title: Operating System — Question 228 · NS0728
records.text: NS0728 Question 228 OS37 What is a Tree-Structured Directory? Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems. A A directory where all files are in one flat list B A hierarchical directory organization with a root directory from which subdirectories and files branch out, each file having a unique path C A directory shared among multiple users D A temporary directory deleted on reboot A rooted hierarchy of nested directories and files. OS37 says a tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths. In the pure tree model, each entry has a path from the root, matching B. Flat lists instead describe single-level organization; sharing among users and deletion at reboot do not define tree structure. Links can add graph relationships, but that is an extension beyond the pure tree premise. A incorrect One flat file list is single-level organization rather than nested branches from a root. B correct A root with nested subdirectories and paths is the tree hierarchy described here. C incorrect Multiple users sharing a directory does not by itself define its structural hierarchy. D incorrect Deletion on reboot is a lifetime policy rather than the rooted directory-tree organization.

records.title: Operating System — Question 229 · NS0729
records.text: NS0729 Question 229 OS37 OS-S06 What is the difference between Hard Links and Symbolic Links in file systems? Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems. A Hard links can span different file systems; symbolic links cannot B Hard links create multiple directory entries pointing to the same file's data blocks; symbolic links are special files containing the path to another file C Symbolic links cannot be deleted D Hard links are only supported in Windows Hard links name one file object; symbolic links store a pathname. A hard link supplies another name for the same underlying file object; a symbolic link stores a pathname. Symbolic links can cross filesystems and may dangle, whereas ordinary hard links stay within a filesystem. Linux’s link operation supplies a direct counterexample to the Windows-only claim. unlink can remove a symbolic-link name, so the link is not undeletable. B states the correct distinction. A incorrect The boundary is reversed: symbolic links may cross filesystems, while ordinary hard links remain within one. B correct Both hard-link names identify the same underlying file; a symbolic link contains a pathname to resolve. C incorrect A symbolic-link name can be removed with unlink; removing it does not erase the target’s contents. D incorrect Linux provides hard links through link(), so they are not supported only in Windows.

records.title: Operating System — Question 230 · NS0730
records.text: NS0730 Question 230 OS37 OS35 What is File System Mounting? Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems. A Creating a new file system B The process of attaching a file system to a specific location in the existing directory tree, making it accessible C Deleting old files to free disk space D Formatting a disk partition Attach a filesystem at a mount point. OS37 explicitly defines mounting as attaching a filesystem at a mount point and distinguishes it from formatting. B states that integration into the existing namespace. Creation/formatting establish a filesystem’s on-device structure; deleting files frees content space. None of those is the namespace attachment operation requested by mounting. A incorrect Creating a new filesystem establishes storage structure rather than attaching it to an existing namespace. B correct Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a chosen point in the directory hierarchy. C incorrect Deleting files changes contents/free space rather than attaching a filesystem to the namespace. D incorrect Formatting is explicitly distinguished from mounting in the supplied note.

records.title: Operating System — Question 231 · NS0731
records.text: NS0731 Question 231 OS26 In the context of deadlock recovery, what is 'Rollback'? Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking. A Restarting the entire operating system B Returning a preempted process to a safe previous state after resources are taken back from it during deadlock resolution C Deleting all processes involved in a deadlock D Rebooting the computer to free all resources Restore an affected process to a prior checkpoint after reclaiming resources. OS26 describes reclaiming safely preemptable resources and rolling affected work back to a checkpoint. B states that restoration to a safe prior state after resources are withdrawn. Restarting the entire OS/computer and killing all involved processes are different coarse recovery actions, not the meaning of rollback. Safe checkpoints/restart semantics are required to make withdrawal and restoration coherent. A incorrect Restarting the whole OS is not the checkpoint restoration of affected work that defines rollback. B correct Rollback restores an affected process to a previous recoverable state after safe resource reclamation. C incorrect Terminating processes is a separate recovery tool rather than restoring their earlier execution state. D incorrect Rebooting frees broad machine state but is not the process-checkpoint restoration definition of rollback.

records.title: Operating System — Question 232 · NS0732
records.text: NS0732 Question 232 OS28 OS30 What is the purpose of relocation/base and limit registers in the standard contiguous single-process-region memory model? The limit denotes the permitted region length. Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention. A They speed up CPU scheduling decisions B The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base C They track file system locations on disk D They manage virtual memory page tables The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base In the standard base/limit model, the base identifies the process’s physical starting address and the limit gives its permitted length. Hardware checks that the logical offset is nonnegative and smaller than the limit, then computes base plus offset. This protects accesses to the assigned region. The registers do not describe the OS base and size, schedule CPU work, track disk files or manage page tables. A incorrect These registers check memory accesses rather than schedule CPU work. B correct The option states the process base, length bound and checked translation. C incorrect Disk-block locations are not the purpose of RAM base/limit registers. D incorrect Simple contiguous base/limit translation does not manage page-table mappings.

records.title: Operating System — Question 233 · NS0733
records.text: NS0733 Question 233 OS27 OS30 In Dynamic Linking, what is a key advantage over Static Linking? Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation. A Programs run faster with dynamic linking B Multiple programs share one copy of library code in memory rather than each program embedding its own copy, saving memory C Dynamic linking eliminates the need for a page table D Dynamically linked programs cannot have bugs Share suitable library code pages across programs. OS27 says dynamic linking resolves external-library references at load/runtime and allows suitable library code pages to be shared, whereas static linking copies selected code into the executable. B captures the potential memory saving. It is not an unconditional speed guarantee, does not remove address translation/page tables and cannot eliminate programming bugs. Only shareable code/pages are implied, not arbitrary writable library state. A incorrect Dynamic resolution/sharing does not guarantee faster execution for every program or workload. B correct Several processes can share suitable library code pages rather than each embedding a separate static copy. C incorrect Library linking does not remove virtual-address translation or its page-table requirements. D incorrect Choosing dynamic rather than static linking cannot guarantee the absence of programming errors.

records.title: Software Engineering — Course module
records.text: Software Engineering

records.title: Software Engineering — Study notes
records.text: Software Engineering Apply requirements, models, design and testing as one connected engineering workflow. The official blueprint allocates six items; this chapter covers software development, management, architecture and testing. Classify the actual scenario before choosing a process, requirement type, model or test level. Broad labels often overlap. Write one use case with an exception flow, derive boundary/control/entity objects and a service contract, then derive tests from those obligations. Draw dependency networks and calculate times before inspecting choices; state any missing assumptions.

records.title: Software Engineering — Practice questions
records.text: Software Engineering

records.title: Software Engineering — Revision outline
records.text: Software Engineering

records.title: Software Engineering — Software engineering, processes and work products
records.text: Software engineering applies systematic methods to development, operation and maintenance. A software product includes executable code and relevant requirements, designs, test assets, configuration and user documentation. A process defines activities, ordering, roles, products and entry/exit conditions. Its four broad activities are specification, design/implementation, validation and evolution. Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior. Either can use iterative or sequential development. OOP does not automatically shorten every project. Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex. Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Lifecycle phases and model selection
records.text: A common lifecycle names requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Analysis clarifies the problem; system design chooses architecture; object/detail design specifies interfaces and algorithms; implementation writes code; testing evaluates behavior; deployment puts it into service. These activities may overlap and repeat. Select a process using requirement stability, technical risk, delivery urgency, stakeholder availability, team skills and assurance needs. “Team has little experience” alone does not uniquely identify a process. A risk-driven cycle, prototype or carefully planned staged process may each help, depending on the actual uncertainty. No process eliminates the need for testing or documentation. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Waterfall and the V-model
records.text: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables. It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly. It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback. Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions. The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels. Requirements inform acceptance tests; system design informs system tests; component/detail design informs integration/unit tests. Coding lies at the bottom. Test planning starts early. Stable requirements and strong assurance may favor this organization, but neither a V shape nor waterfall guarantees safety or correctness. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Iteration, increments and early delivery
records.text: Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both. Delivering registration first, then payments, then reporting is incremental; revising a registration prototype after feedback is iterative. Each increment still needs design, implementation and testing. Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early. Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning. Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules. Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Agile values, stories and Scrum
records.text: Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans. The latter still have value. Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation. A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work. Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done. Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope. Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal. Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable. Software Engineering module Agile Manifesto Scrum Guide

records.title: Software Engineering — Spiral development and risk
records.text: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment. A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment. The amount and type of work depend on the risks. Use risk emphasis to distinguish spiral from a generic changing-requirements scenario. Spiral can incorporate incremental, prototyping or sequential activities, but calling it the uniquely “most general” process is a textbook convention rather than a universal theorem. Risk analysis requires skill and may impose excessive overhead on a small low-risk project. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Prototypes, RAD and reuse-oriented development
records.text: A prototype explores requirements, usability or technical feasibility. A throwaway prototype is discarded after learning; an evolutionary prototype is deliberately refined toward production. A quick prototype may omit robustness, security or architecture, so do not deploy it unchanged without evaluation. Coding may occur during prototyping even if a diagram labels that activity construction rather than coding. RAD uses rapid construction, timeboxing, user participation and often reusable components; it requires available users and skilled designers/developers. Reuse-oriented development searches components, evaluates fit, may adjust requirements, designs around interfaces and builds missing parts. Product-line assets may include requirements, architecture, components and tests; all are potentially reusable. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Feasibility and levels of requirements
records.text: Feasibility asks whether a proposal is worth doing and can be delivered within technical, economic, operational and schedule constraints. Examine existing limitations, organizational impacts, benefits, cost, available skills and integration risk. System analysis studies the problem and needed behavior in more detail; the activities inform each other. Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals. User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements. A natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Functional requirements include prohibited behavior
records.text: A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions. “When the sensor detects intrusion, send an alert” is functional. “Only a manager may approve refunds” also specifies permitted/prohibited behavior. A negative statement is not automatically nonfunctional. Write one clear obligation with an actor/trigger, action and observable result. “The system shall generate a PDF report” is functional. “The system shall not reveal another customer’s balance” can be a security-related functional rule. Security as a broad quality goal and the functions implementing it must be distinguished. Words such as must, should and not work do not by themselves determine a requirement’s classification. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Nonfunctional qualities and measurable constraints
records.text: Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints. Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning. Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution. “Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint. Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category. Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Validate requirements and maintain traceability
records.text: Correct requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs. Complete requirements address the agreed scope, normal and exceptional behavior. Consistency excludes contradictions. Clarity/unambiguity gives one intended interpretation; feasibility/realism means achievable within constraints. Verifiability means objective evidence can check fulfillment. Replace “fast for most users” with a defined metric, workload and threshold. Trace each requirement backward to its source/rationale and forward to design, code and tests. Record dependencies among requirements. A traceability matrix links these artifacts and helps impact analysis; it is not just a cost/schedule ledger. Stakeholders must negotiate conflicting requirements rather than independently approving incompatible demands. Scope, understanding and volatility are distinct elicitation difficulties. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Elicitation techniques, FAST and QFD
records.text: Interviews ask stakeholders about needs; document analysis examines manuals, contracts and current records; observation/ethnography studies actual daily work. Prototypes reveal tacit expectations. Workshops/JAD bring users, managers and developers together with a facilitator and recorder to build consensus. Use several sources and check assumptions against observed work. In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications. QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit. Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — From scenarios to analysis objects
records.text: A scenario is one concrete execution; a use case abstracts the related successful and alternative scenarios. Analysis integrates functional (use cases/scenarios), structural/object (classes) and dynamic (states/interactions) models. Entity objects represent domain information such as Incident; boundary objects mediate interaction, such as ReportForm; control objects coordinate a use case. A UI form is normally boundary, not entity. Use nouns as candidate objects, possessive descriptions as candidate attributes, and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations. These are heuristics, not automatic parsing rules. CRC means Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. A control per use case or participating actor can be a useful starting point, not a mandatory UML rule or fixed object lifetime. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Actors, use cases and scope
records.text: An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system. A person may play several roles, and several people may play one role. A primary actor seeks a goal; a supporting actor provides a service. Ask which user groups perform main functions, administer or maintain the system, and which external systems exchange information. Draw actors outside the system boundary rectangle and use-case ovals inside. Name a goal with a verb and noun. The diagram shows roles, goals and relationships, not the full detailed algorithm or UI layout. Being an internal component is different from being an external actor; the chosen boundary determines which role applies. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Write a complete use case with alternatives
records.text: Record name/goal, actors, trigger, preconditions, main success flow, alternatives/exceptions and postconditions. Use active subject–verb steps at one abstraction level; separate errors from the normal flow. Example: Submit Incident. Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID. Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing. Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record. An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure. Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Include, extend, generalization and abstract use cases
records.text: Include factors required reused behavior: Submit Order includes Validate Order, with the dashed arrow from the including/base use case to the included one. Extend adds conditional behavior at extension points: Apply Discount extends Checkout, with the arrow from the extension to the base. The base is meaningful independently. For an extension, draw the arrow from the extending use case to the base use case. Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element. An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case. It is not defined merely by reuse or lack of a direct actor line. Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Class diagrams, visibility and multiplicity
records.text: A class box lists name, attributes and operations; + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility. A class diagram shows static types and relationships, while an object diagram shows particular instances/links. UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process. Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements. Multiplicity at one end counts how many objects there may correspond to one object at the opposite end: 1 exactly one, 0..1 optional, 0..* any nonnegative number, 1..* at least one. A one-to-many association does not automatically mean composition. Read each end separately before choosing cardinality. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Association, aggregation, composition and generalization
records.text: Association connects related instances. A dashed dependency arrow means a client uses a supplier. Generalization uses a solid line and hollow triangle pointing to the superclass/general element. Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond at the whole end and weak whole-part meaning; it does not by itself define a detailed lifecycle policy. Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite. Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification. For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise. The Car–Engine example describes composition. Software Engineering module OMG UML2.5.1

records.title: Software Engineering — Sequence diagrams and the emergency-report example
records.text: Sequence diagrams show interactions across lifelines, with order/time generally downward. Messages cross between participants; activation rectangles show execution. A creation message starts a lifeline; an X marks modeled destruction, not a guarantee about when a garbage collector runs. Synchronous calls wait for completion; asynchronous messages permit the sender to proceed. One interaction-diagram layout heuristic puts the initiating actor first, boundary second, control third, then entities. This is not a required UML column order. In ReportEmergency, FieldOfficer activates ReportEmergencyButton, enters details through EmergencyReportForm, and later sees AcknowledgmentNotice; DispatcherStation belongs to the dispatcher side. Choose the button for initiating this particular scenario. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Activity, state and data-flow models
records.text: An activity diagram models workflow: filled circle start, rounded actions, guarded decision diamond, thick fork/join bars and partitions/swimlanes for responsibility. A diamond can also merge alternative flows; a join synchronizes concurrent flows. A state machine models states and transitions triggered by events, often with guards/actions, for one object’s lifecycle. Choose a sequence diagram for message order between participants, a state machine for event-dependent state changes, and activity for workflow. Both sequence and state diagrams describe behavior over time. State machines are useful for objects with significant states, whether entity or control. A DFD shows data stores/flows and transformations from inputs to outputs; it is not a UML diagram. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Design and subsystem decomposition
records.text: System design turns the analysis model into architecture: design goals, subsystem responsibilities, dependencies, hardware mapping, data management, access control, control flow and startup/shutdown/error policies. Detail/object design refines APIs, parameter/return types, exceptions, component choices and algorithms. A subsystem is a manageable logical collection with services and an interface; it need not be a physical replaceable artifact. Group closely related objects and functionality, minimize associations crossing boundaries, and isolate communication infrastructure where useful. User workflows inform decomposition but do not alone dictate the internal structure. Analysis describes domain needs; subsystem decomposition is principally a design result. Architecture documentation supports communication and records major decisions, not every source-level execution step. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Cohesion, coupling, modularity and refactoring
records.text: Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling. Information hiding exposes stable operations while concealing changeable decisions. Logical cohesion groups similar-category operations, often selected by a flag; temporal cohesion groups operations done at the same time; functional cohesion focuses on one task. Splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity. If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers. Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Layers, tiers and architecture views
records.text: A layer is a logical abstraction level; a tier is a deployment separation. A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping. For top-to-bottom A,B,C,D, A→B obeys closed layering, A→C skips, and lower-to-upper calls violate the simple dependency rule unless explicitly mediated by a defined mechanism. A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects. Module structures show code organization, component-and-connector structures runtime interaction, and allocation structures map software to hardware, teams or environment. Processes/threads belong in concurrency views. Evaluate architectures against quality attributes and scenarios; processor allocation, decomposition and style selection can all be architectural concerns. Software Engineering module Rose-Hulman: What is software architecture

records.title: Software Engineering — Architecture styles and integration boundaries
records.text: Repository style shares central data, simplifying common access but creating bottleneck/schema dependencies. MVC separates domain model, display view and interaction controller. Client–server separates requesters from service providers; peer-to-peer permits both roles. Pipe-and-filter applies successive transformations to data streams. Three-tier separates presentation, application logic and storage; some four-tier variants split presentation client/server. An API gateway presents one entry point and routes/combines calls to services, hiding service boundaries from clients. It can centralize policies but also become a bottleneck. A component diagram shows components/interfaces/dependencies; a deployment diagram places software artifacts on nodes. Choose the style for the required interactions and qualities rather than selecting a universally best architecture. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Design principles and operation contracts
records.text: Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities. Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components. A hybrid combines both. SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations. DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work. A contract states preconditions, postconditions and invariants. For withdraw(amount): require amount>0 and amount<=balance; ensure balance=oldBalance-amount; preserve balance>=0. Validation checks inputs; implementation enforces the transition. A complete feature needs both UI/API and persisted behavior, not only a diagram. Software Engineering module University of Washington: Software Design and Style

records.title: Software Engineering — A small analysis-to-implementation example
records.text: For Submit Incident, let a boundary read input, a service validate and coordinate, and a repository save an Incident entity. Pseudocode: submit(input){require authenticated; if missing(location) return validationError; incident=new Incident(input); repository.save(incident); return incident.id;}. Save and ID assignment must succeed together, or roll back. Derive tests from the model: missing location saves nothing; valid input returns a saved ID; a storage failure yields an error without a partial record; unauthorized input is rejected. Trace requirement→use-case step→service operation→repository effect→test. Use the implementation exercise to connect analysis and design tools to working code. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Patterns, variability and testability
records.text: Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors. A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method. Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. The pattern name is Memento, not Momento. Variability can use selectable features, omission/inclusion and extension points; overloading supplies alternate signatures in code but is not every variability mechanism. Testability improves with controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity. A sandbox can isolate execution. Assess each design claim independently before evaluating a combined statement. Software Engineering module Design Patterns introduction, university-hosted author text

records.title: Software Engineering — Planning, WBS, estimation and tools
records.text: Planning is continuous: identify scope/deliverables, decompose work, estimate effort/duration/cost, assign resources, sequence dependencies and revise as evidence changes. A WBS is hierarchical and covers project scope without adding unrelated work. Tools help coordinate ownership, dependencies and progress; they do not replace judgment or automatically fix bugs. Function points estimate functional size using inputs, outputs, inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files, weighted under the chosen method. They are not just lines of code and are not a direct exact measure of complexity. Git tracks versions; issue trackers such as Jira track work/defects; CI tools such as Jenkins automate checks; Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Critical path: forward and backward passes
records.text: In a dependency network, ES=max predecessor EF and EF=ES+duration; start tasks have ES=0 unless another constraint applies. Project earliest finish is the maximum terminal EF. Backward, LF=min successor LS and LS=LF-duration, starting from the required finish. Total float/slack=LS-ES=LF-EF. A critical path has the longest total duration and normally zero float in an unconstrained schedule. If A takes 5 days and B=3,C=4 both follow A, project duration is 5+max(3,4)=9 days. B finishes at 8, but the project waits for C at 9. If paths B5+C6 and D8+E3 share a zero-duration start/end, both total 11; there are two critical paths, not one. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Slack assumptions and PERT calculations
records.text: Early start/finish values alone do not determine slack without successor relationships and the project completion constraint. If C3→D6 is a complete path parallel to A4→B5 and both finish at day9, C has zero float. That network cannot be silently inferred from four unrelated ES/EF rows. Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2. For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days². Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average. These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times. Software Engineering module PMI: PERT estimation

records.title: Software Engineering — Business value, risks and resource optimization
records.text: With benefits and costs already discounted to a common date, ROI=(benefits-costs)/costs*100%. Birr120000 benefits and Birr100000 costs give 20%, not 120%. Identify project risks to resources/schedule, product risks to quality, and business risks to the organization. Analyze likelihood and impact, plan responses and monitor. Avoidance changes the plan to remove a risk, mitigation reduces likelihood/impact, transfer assigns consequences contractually, and retention/acceptance keeps the risk; passive acceptance may take no action. Resource leveling adjusts dates to respect resource availability and can change project finish; smoothing uses available float within schedule constraints. Neither magically creates extra staff. Software Engineering module PMI Lexicon of Project Management Terms

records.title: Software Engineering — Team organization, development and maturity
records.text: Functional organizations group specialists by discipline; project organizations group people around projects. Functional specialization helps staffing and knowledge continuity but may create handoff barriers. Democratic teams share decisions; chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination. These are different classification dimensions. Tuckman’s sequence is forming→storming→norming→performing→adjourning: orientation, conflict, norms, effective work and closure. Historical Software CMM levels are 1 Initial, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed, 5 Optimizing. Level2 establishes basic project discipline including requirements management, project planning, quality assurance and configuration management. These historical labels must not be silently replaced by modern CMMI terminology. A maturity model concerns process capability, not a guarantee that every product is defect free. Software Engineering module SEI: Software CMM v1.1 UC Berkeley Team Building Toolkit

records.title: Software Engineering — Configuration, change control and version control
records.text: Configuration management identifies controlled items, versions/baselines, change procedures, status and audits. Items may include source code, requirements, manuals, test plans, environments and build configurations. A team’s ordinary browser is usually a tool rather than product CI, but a controlled test-browser version may be an environment CI. Change management handles request, impact assessment, decision/prioritization, implementation and validation; configuration management keeps all affected versions consistent. Distributed Git gives each clone local history and supports independent branches followed by merging; it does not eliminate merge conflicts or approvals. Plan test configuration management early and apply it throughout testing, not at just one exclusive phase. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Quality assurance, verification and validation
records.text: Quality assurance establishes and checks processes/standards; quality control evaluates work products. An SQA plan identifies standards, responsibilities, evaluations, reviews, audits and assurance records. Quality of conformance means following the design/specification; a product can conform to a poor specification. Verification asks whether specified obligations are implemented correctly; validation asks whether the product meets intended stakeholder needs. Both can use reviews, analysis or execution, so “human-only versus computer-only” is false. A fault/defect is an underlying problem; an error may be an incorrect internal state; a failure is an externally observed departure from required service. Reliability is a product quality attribute; low cost or short development time are project outcomes. Tests increase confidence and reveal defects but cannot generally guarantee correctness over every possible input. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Testing levels and acceptance
records.text: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks; a driver invokes the unit and a stub substitutes a called dependency. Integration testing exercises interfaces and interactions among combined parts. System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment. Acceptance testing supports the customer/user’s acceptance decision against agreed needs and criteria. Alpha typically happens in a controlled developer setting with selected users; beta uses external users in their environments. None of these levels is universally the longest. Unit is a level, while white-box is a technique; a unit can be tested using black-box cases too. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Test types, regression and exploratory work
records.text: Functional tests check required behavior against the SRS and acceptance criteria. Performance tests assess speed, throughput and resources under a specified workload; load uses expected demands and stress exceeds normal limits. Usability, security, compatibility and reliability tests target their respective qualities. “Normal operating conditions” alone does not distinguish functional from performance testing. Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change; confirmation testing checks the particular defect repair. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution and is experience based. Manual/automated describe execution support, not a compulsory black-/white-box classification. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Equivalence, boundaries and decision tables
records.text: Equivalence partitioning groups inputs expected to behave alike, then samples valid and invalid groups. For allowed age18..60, useful partitions are below18,18..60,above60. Boundary tests target edges and neighbors, such as 17,18,19,59,60,61, with the exact set chosen under the stated coverage scheme. A decision table lists condition combinations and resulting actions. For validCard and enoughFunds, enumerate TT,TF,FT,FF; specify dispense only for TT and the proper rejection for others. Cover feasible rules rather than blindly using every impossible combination. These are specification-based techniques. Test requirements can also define state-transition cases, such as rejecting dispatch from an already closed incident. Software Engineering module ISTQB CTFL4.0.1 syllabus

records.title: Software Engineering — Statement, decision and branch coverage
records.text: Statement coverage is the number of distinct executable statements exercised divided by the total executable statements in the declared test scope. Unreachable statements can prevent100%; any justified exclusions must be documented with the adjusted scope. Decision coverage counts decision outcomes; branch coverage counts control-flow edges, including unconditional edges under the stated convention. Testing both true and false of each decision may need more than two overall test cases when branches nest. Coverage is evidence of exercised structure, not proof of all behavior. In the width/length/height program, the outer if has separate inner decisions in each branch. Need outer true with inner true and false, and outer false with its inner true and false: four tests, for example (w,l,h)=(3,2,4),(3,2,1),(2,3,4),(2,3,1). One run cannot exercise both outer branches. All paths may be infeasible or infinite with loops; specify the chosen coverage target. Software Engineering module ISTQB CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, sections 4.3.1–4.3.2

records.title: Software Engineering — Test process, plans and defect reports
records.text: Plan objectives, scope, resources, schedule, risks and entry/exit criteria. Analyze the test basis for testable features and defects; design cases/expected results; implement data, scripts and environment; execute and compare; report defects; evaluate completion. Analysis asks what to test and assesses testability; design asks how. Monitoring/control run across these activities. A test plan describes intended work; incident/defect reports are normally execution outputs. A defect report should identify build/environment, steps, expected versus actual behavior, evidence and severity. Anyone finding a fault should record it; testers often coordinate reporting, but it is not their exclusive permission. Configuration control makes the tested version reproducible. Software Engineering module ISTQB CTFL4.0.1 syllabus

records.title: Software Engineering — Maintenance and software evolution
records.text: Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code. Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work. Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost. A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release. Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity. Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description. Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Apply network calculations and compare design claims
records.text: The earliest-finish example yields 9 days. Zero slack follows only from an explicit completion-path assumption when latest times or the full network are unavailable. In the path-duration example, two paths each total 11 days. Use the network rules to justify the calculation before comparing it with an answer key. Evaluate descriptions of architectural structures and views separately; both can be true. Evaluate the individual claims before considering a combined option, especially if the option refers to itself. Requirements, tests and architecture can all be reusable product-line assets. When several choices satisfy the rules, identify the needed distinction rather than selecting a false rule. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Context-dependent claims and model limitations
records.text: Context matters: no test level is always most time consuming; no process is determined by team inexperience alone; no waterfall rule makes every later change impossible. Requirements may describe required and prohibited behavior, including interface functions as well as usability qualities. Identify an interface requirement’s exact obligation before classifying it as functional or nonfunctional. Sequence/state diagrams both show dynamic behavior. Composition needs the diamond’s placement and ownership semantics. “Agile least suitable for safety-critical government work” assumes a particular lightweight process without required assurance; it is not universally true. Treat the guide’s conventions as scenario hints and keep the stronger engineering rules explicit. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Design choices, evidence and economical improvement
records.text: Choose designs by their effect on stated goals. Fine-grained self-contained components, separation of producers/consumers and limited shared mutable data often improve maintainability. Trade-offs remain: interfaces can add latency, isolation can complicate transactions, and global state can simplify one operation while coupling many others. Prefer measurable quality scenarios to counting components alone. Pareto’s 80/20 rule is a prioritization heuristic: a small subset of causes may account for much of the observed impact. It does not guarantee 80% of defects can be fixed with exactly 20% effort. Refactor to preserve behavior while improving structure; optimize only against measured needs; record rationale and update traceability and regression evidence after change. Software Engineering module

records.title: Software Engineering — Scope, understanding and changing requirements
records.text: Elicitation difficulties have several distinct sources. Scope problems concern agreeing on system boundaries and the appropriate level of detail. Understanding problems arise when stakeholders and analysts have different domain knowledge, omit tacit needs or communicate conflicting interpretations. Volatility means that requirements change as circumstances and understanding develop. These difficulties call for repeated communication, explicit boundaries, negotiated meanings and controlled revision. They can occur together; resolving one does not automatically remove the others. CMU SEI — Issues in Requirements Elicitation

records.title: Software Engineering — Objects, shared models and specialization
records.text: An object-oriented approach can use a consistent vocabulary of objects, classes and relationships across analysis, design and implementation. Models are refined for different purposes rather than being identical artifacts. This continuity can reduce translation errors and effort; reusable classes can shorten suitable projects, but neither shorter duration nor good design is guaranteed. Generalization places common concepts in a more general superclass and specialized concepts in subclasses. Available inherited attributes and operations are shared by subclasses, which may extend or override behavior. Defining common features once can reduce duplicated maintenance. The top of the hierarchy is more general, not more specialized. Encapsulation groups state with operations and hides representation behind an interface. Polymorphism permits different object types to respond differently through a common operation or interface. Abstraction exposes the relevant contract while omitting unnecessary detail. Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in new contexts rather than writing them again. These ideas support each other but name different properties. records.title: Software Engineering — Modeling categories and data diagrams
records.text: In the course’s UML building-block terminology, structural things describe static conceptual or physical elements. Behavioral things describe dynamic interactions and state behavior. Grouping things organize model elements into packages. Annotational things attach explanatory remarks or constraints, usually as notes. An entity–relationship diagram models entity types, their attributes and the relationships between them, commonly for data design. Its focus differs from a use-case diagram of external roles and goals, a class diagram of classes and their features, or a deployment diagram mapping artifacts to execution nodes. Software Engineering module · page 45 Software Engineering module · page 46 IBM — Entity relationship diagrams

records.title: Software Engineering — Plan-driven and adaptive planning
records.text: In a plan-driven process, activities are planned in advance and progress is assessed against that plan. Agile planning is incremental and adapts to changing needs. This distinction concerns planning strategy; a process can combine advance planning with staged deliveries and feedback. Software Engineering module · page 13

records.title: Software Engineering — Exploration artifacts and collaborative implementation
records.text: A storyboard sketches a sequence of moments in a proposed interaction, helping people explore how a concept would be used. A wireframe sketches interface structure and the arrangement of content or controls. Both can inform requirements, but neither automatically supplies a complete use-case description with actors, preconditions, flows and postconditions. Pair programming is a way for two programmers to work together on the same implementation task, commonly sharing a workstation with complementary writing and reviewing roles. It is an implementation collaboration practice rather than a replacement for modeling a user goal. IDEO Design Kit — Storyboard IBM Enterprise Design Thinking Toolkit — Wireframes Agile Alliance — Pair programming Software Engineering module · page 70

records.title: Software Engineering — Distinguish a requirements specification from neighboring terms
records.text: A Software Requirements Specification records agreed software services and constraints. A Capability Development Document is a defense capability-requirements artifact describing needed capability characteristics and performance parameters; its specialized acquisition context differs from the ordinary software SRS. Domain-driven design is an approach that organizes software models around the business domain, not the name of an agreed requirements specification. Software Engineering module · page 62 U.S. Army — Getting Requirements Right Microsoft — Designing a DDD-oriented microservice

records.title: Software Engineering — Scalability and robustness are different qualities
records.text: Scalability is the ability to accommodate additional workload while maintaining the required service, often by increasing available resources. It concerns growth in demand. Compatibility concerns supported cooperating environments, such as browsers and devices; usability concerns successful and learnable user tasks. Robustness concerns reliable operation across varied or difficult operating conditions and controlled failure outside the supported range. It is different from usability, which concerns people successfully learning and carrying out tasks. Improving an interface’s task success does not by itself establish robustness under adverse conditions. Microsoft — Scaling cloud-native applications NIST CSRC Glossary — Robustness
