C incorrect Validation checks the changed product against needs rather than naming ongoing adaptation itself. D correct Evolution updates existing software as stakeholder needs and operating conditions change.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 232 · NS0748
records.text: NS0748 Question 232 SE-S04 A software process that plans all activities in advance and measures progress against that plan is classified as: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Agile Process B Plan-Driven Process C Incremental Process D Evolutionary Process Plan-driven process. The stem defines up-front planning and measurement against that plan. B names the plan-driven organization, illustrated by SE03’s planned phases and reviewed deliverables. Incremental delivery and evolution describe how results grow or change and can coexist with planning. Agile also plans, but it emphasizes adaptation rather than defining all activity commitments in advance as stated here. A incorrect Agile uses planning but adapts content as feedback arrives rather than defining this fixed up-front emphasis. B correct Plan-driven explicitly organizes activities and progress measurement around an advance plan. C incorrect Incremental describes staged capability delivery and does not alone specify up-front planning commitments. D incorrect Evolutionary describes progressive change rather than necessarily advance planning of all activities.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 233 · NS0749
records.text: NS0749 Question 233 SE08 In requirement elicitation, the document created to describe what the system should do — agreed upon by clients and developers — is called: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Analysis Model B Use Case Diagram C Requirements Specification D Design Document Requirements Specification. SE08 states that the Software Requirements Specification organizes agreed requirements. That is the artifact describing what the system should do for client/developer agreement. Analysis models support technical discussion, a use-case diagram captures only selected goals/relationships and a design document describes solution decisions. None replaces the overall agreed requirements specification. A incorrect Analysis models formalize selected aspects for discussion rather than replacing the full agreed requirements document. B incorrect A use-case diagram shows goals and roles but not the complete requirements specification. C correct The requirements specification organizes the agreed services and constraints the system must satisfy. D incorrect A design document describes how the solution is organized rather than the complete statement of required behavior.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 234 · NS0750
records.text: NS0750 Question 234 SE08 What is the key distinction between a Requirements Specification and an Analysis Model? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A The specification uses diagrams; the model uses natural language B The specification uses natural language; the model uses symbols and diagrams C Both use the same representation but serve different purposes D The analysis model is only for developers; specification is for testing In the taught convention, natural-language client specification versus symbolic/diagrammatic analysis models. SE08 explicitly describes natural-language specification for clients and analysis models that formalize it for technical discussion. B matches that teaching convention. This is not a universal ban on diagrams in an SRS: the note immediately allows them in real specifications. The other choices reverse the convention or impose unsupported exclusive audiences and purposes. A incorrect It reverses the natural-language specification versus formalized-model convention taught in the note. B correct This matches the taught convention, while real requirements specifications can also include diagrams. C incorrect The taught distinction does use different representation emphases rather than identical forms. D incorrect Neither artifact has the exclusive audience or testing-only purpose asserted here.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 235 · NS0751
records.text: NS0751 Question 235 SE14 In use case modeling, actors can be defined as: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Only human users who interact with the system B People, machines, or external systems that interact with the system C Only primary users who need system assistance D Software components within the system boundary External interacting roles played by people, devices or other systems. SE14 explicitly permits a person, device or other system to play an external actor role. B is the only option including those categories. Actors are not restricted to primary users or humans, and internal components are inside the chosen system boundary rather than external roles. One person may play several actors, so actor instances should not be confused with individual people. A incorrect Actors can be devices or external systems as well as human users. B correct People, devices and external systems can play roles interacting across the system boundary. C incorrect Supporting and administrative external roles can be actors, not only primary goal-seeking users. D incorrect Internal components are not external actor roles under the chosen system boundary.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 236 · NS0752
records.text: NS0752 Question 236 SE10 Which type of requirement specifies that 'the system must respond within 1 second'? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Functional Requirement B System Constraint C Non-Functional Requirement D Domain Requirement Nonfunctional performance requirement. SE10 identifies response time as a performance quality. A one-second threshold constrains how well a service responds rather than naming the service itself, so C is the appropriate category. A complete measurable requirement should also define the operation, load and timing conditions. Those omissions affect test precision, not the underlying classification of the stated response-time target. A incorrect The statement constrains response speed rather than specifying which service is performed. B incorrect The specific quality is performance; this is not primarily a technology or implementation constraint. C correct The one-second limit is a nonfunctional response-time/performance target. D incorrect No domain-specific business rule is stated; the obligation concerns a general performance quality.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 237 · NS0753
records.text: NS0753 Question 237 SE10 When technology constraints are separated from quality attributes, what is the most specific category for “the system must be built using Java”? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Functional Requirement B Non-Functional Requirement C System/Constraint Requirement D Quality Requirement System/Constraint Requirement The statement prescribes an implementation technology rather than an externally observable service or a measurable product quality. In the course’s explicit separation of quality attributes from technology constraints, the specific category is a system or constraint requirement. A broad requirements taxonomy can place constraints under nonfunctional requirements, but the question asks for the more specific category. No performance, reliability or usability threshold is supplied by merely naming Java. A incorrect The statement prescribes technology rather than an observable service. B incorrect This is a broader umbrella in some taxonomies; it is incomplete when the specific constraint category is offered. C correct A required implementation language is a technology or system constraint. D incorrect No measurable quality attribute is specified merely by requiring Java.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 238 · NS0754
records.text: NS0754 Question 238 SE10 SE-S07 Which nonfunctional requirement category addresses the ability of the system to work across different web browsers and devices? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Reliability B Scalability C Usability D Compatibility Compatibility. SE10 distinguishes compatibility, which concerns cooperating environments, from portability, which concerns moving environments. Supporting different browsers and devices in the question is the offered compatibility category. Reliability concerns failure-free service, scalability concerns growth and usability concerns task success/ease of learning. None of those names the stated cross-environment cooperation requirement as directly. A incorrect Reliability concerns failure-free service rather than which browsers and devices can cooperate with the system. B incorrect Scalability concerns handling increased workload rather than cross-browser/device compatibility. C incorrect Usability concerns ease of learning and successful tasks, not the supported environment set itself. D correct Compatibility addresses operating/cooperating across the specified browsers and device environments.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 239 · NS0755
records.text: NS0755 Question 239 SE10 SE-S07 Dependability in software engineering is a broader concept that includes all of the following EXCEPT: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Reliability B Robustness C Safety D Portability Portability is the exception to the usual central dependability categories. SE10 explicitly includes reliability, safety and robustness in dependability and says portability is not its usual central category. Portability instead concerns moving environments. Thus D is the listed exception. The distinction does not imply portability never affects practical service outcomes, only that it is a different quality category from the taught dependability grouping. A incorrect Reliability is explicitly included in the taught dependability grouping. B incorrect Robustness is explicitly included in the broader dependability concept. C incorrect Safety is explicitly included among dependability concerns. D correct Portability concerns moving environments rather than the usual central dependability categories.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 240 · NS0756
records.text: NS0756 Question 240 SE13 In requirements elicitation activities, which step involves formalizing scenarios into structured descriptions of system interactions? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Identifying Actors B Identifying Use Cases C Identifying Scenarios D Refining Use Cases Identifying use cases by abstracting concrete scenarios. SE13 calls a scenario one concrete execution and a use case an abstraction of related success and alternative scenarios. Formalizing those interactions into the more general use-case description therefore identifies use cases. Identifying actors establishes external roles, identifying scenarios captures individual executions and later refinement adds detail to an already identified use case. A incorrect Actor identification establishes external roles rather than generalizing scenario executions into interaction descriptions. B correct Use cases abstract related concrete scenarios into structured goal-oriented interaction descriptions. C incorrect Scenario identification captures concrete executions rather than their use-case abstraction. D incorrect Refinement elaborates an existing use case; the scenario-to-use-case abstraction is the identification step asked here.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 241 · NS0757
records.text: NS0757 Question 241 SE15 According to the Simple Use Case Writing Guide, which of the following is CORRECT practice? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Use passive voice so responsibility is unclear B Describe user interface elements in detail C Document exceptions separately from the main flow D Combine multiple tasks into one use case for brevity Document exceptions separately from the main success flow. SE15 instructs writers to use active subject–verb steps and separate errors from normal flow. C follows that rule directly. Passive voice hides responsibility, detailed UI design distracts from goal-level behavior, and combining unrelated tasks does not produce a clear use case. The distinction concerns organizing scenarios rather than omitting exception handling. A incorrect Passive voice makes responsibility less clear, contrary to the active subject–verb guideline. B incorrect Detailed UI elements are not the goal-level behavior and flow structure emphasized by the guide. C correct Separating exception behavior keeps the main success flow clear while still documenting failures. D incorrect Combining multiple unrelated tasks sacrifices a coherent goal and consistent abstraction level.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 242 · NS0758
records.text: NS0758 Question 242 SE12 In the FAST (Facilitated Application Specification Technique), participants are initially asked to individually create lists of three item categories. Which is NOT one of them? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Things that are part of the environment surrounding the system B Things the system produces or outputs C Technical risks and constraints D Things the system uses or takes as inputs Technical risks and constraints are not one of the three initial FAST lists. SE12 explicitly lists environment elements, outputs and inputs as the initial participant categories. A, B and D match them. Technical risks and constraints can matter elsewhere in engineering, but they are not one of those three named initial FAST lists. The negative question asks about that procedure, not whether risk information is ever useful. A incorrect Environment elements are explicitly one of the initial FAST categories. B incorrect System outputs are explicitly included in the three initial lists. C correct Risks and constraints are not one of the specified environment/output/input categories. D incorrect Inputs and things the system uses are part of the stated initial categories.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 243 · NS0759
records.text: NS0759 Question 243 SE12 In Quality Function Deployment (QFD), which category of requirements represents features that go beyond customer expectations and provide great satisfaction? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Normal Requirements B Expected Requirements C Exciting Requirements D Implicit Requirements Exciting requirements. SE12 distinguishes explicitly stated normal needs, assumed expected needs and exciting needs that bring unanticipated benefit. Features exceeding expectations and producing additional satisfaction match the exciting category. Calling them merely implicit would confuse customer assumptions with unexpected added value rather than identify the QFD term. A incorrect Normal requirements are explicitly stated needs rather than unexpected extra benefits. B incorrect Expected requirements are assumed by customers and do not denote surprising added satisfaction. C correct Exciting requirements deliver unanticipated benefit beyond the customer’s expectations. D incorrect Implicit describes assumed needs more generally, not the QFD category for unanticipated benefits.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 244 · NS0760
records.text: NS0760 Question 244 SE11 Which validation property ensures that the requirements specification does not contain contradictory statements? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Completeness B Consistency C Clarity D Correctness Consistency. SE11 directly defines consistency as excluding contradictions. Completeness covers agreed scope, clarity gives one intended interpretation, and correctness reflects stakeholder needs. A specification can be complete yet inconsistent, or clear yet wrong, so these properties cannot substitute for the precise no-contradictions condition. A incorrect Completeness concerns covering scope and behavior, not whether requirements contradict each other. B correct Consistency requires the specification’s statements to coexist without contradiction. C incorrect Clarity addresses interpretive ambiguity rather than logical compatibility between requirements. D incorrect Correctness concerns actual stakeholder needs, a different validation property.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 245 · NS0761
records.text: NS0761 Question 245 SE03 The Waterfall model is MOST appropriate when: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Requirements are expected to change frequently during development B The project is large and complex with evolving needs C Requirements are constant, the project is short, and technology is stable D The team needs to deliver working software in small increments Stable requirements and familiar, stable technology. SE03 says classical waterfall fits well-understood stable requirements and familiar technology, directly supporting C among these alternatives. Frequent change, evolving needs and early small deliveries call for feedback or incremental capability rather than waterfall’s late feedback. Short duration alone is not a proof, but C also supplies the decisive stability conditions stated in the note. A incorrect Frequent requirement changes make late-feedback sequential planning a poor fit. B incorrect Large evolving needs do not establish the stable requirements that favor classical waterfall. C correct Constant requirements and stable technology match the note’s stated waterfall selection conditions. D incorrect Prioritized usable small deliveries are the rationale for incremental delivery rather than a single sequential release.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 246 · NS0762
records.text: NS0762 Question 246 SE03 Which is a characteristic drawback of classical waterfall compared with approaches that seek repeated early feedback? Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Requires skilled developers B Late feedback can make requirement changes costly through rework of earlier phase deliverables. C No clear project milestones D Does not support documentation Late feedback can make requirement changes costly through rework of earlier phase deliverables. Classical waterfall separates planned phases and may receive important feedback late. Correcting earlier assumptions can then require costly rework across completed deliverables, which is its characteristic drawback here. Changes are still possible under control. Skilled developers are needed across approaches, and waterfall provides milestone visibility and documentation, so the other alternatives do not identify the stated comparative disadvantage. A incorrect Skill requirements are not unique to waterfall. B correct Late feedback can make requirement changes costly after earlier phases. C incorrect Waterfall provides clear reviewed milestones. D incorrect Waterfall supports planned documentation.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 247 · NS0763
records.text: NS0763 Question 247 SE04 What is the key conceptual distinction between iteration and incremental delivery, even when a process combines both? Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Iterative adds new features each cycle; Incremental refines the same set repeatedly B Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. C They are identical; the terms are interchangeable D Incremental involves risk analysis; Iterative does not Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. Iteration revisits and improves a solution, while an increment adds usable functionality. A process can refine existing capability and add new capability in the same cycle, so the concepts are compatible but not identical. Neither requires rebuilding the entire system or making every increment completely independent. Risk analysis is a separate concern rather than the structural distinction defining these two terms. A incorrect This reverses refinement and added functionality. B correct Iteration refines; increments add usable capability. C incorrect The terms differ even when combined in one process. D incorrect Risk analysis does not define their distinction.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 248 · NS0764
records.text: NS0764 Question 248 SE04 SE02 A large application already has its core capabilities. The main development goal is to revisit and improve that existing solution repeatedly as feedback and future changes arrive, rather than primarily add new capability in each delivery. Which concept most directly names that emphasis? Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Waterfall Model B V-Model C Iterative Model D Incremental Model Iterative Model The stated emphasis is iterative: revisiting and improving an existing solution in response to feedback. Incremental development names the addition of usable functionality, which is not the primary goal specified, although both can coexist. Classical waterfall’s stable staged planning and the V-model’s paired assurance structure do not directly name this refinement emphasis. Large size and anticipated change alone would not have selected a unique model. A incorrect Classical waterfall does not directly name repeated refinement as the organizing emphasis. B incorrect The V-model emphasizes paired development and tests. C correct Iteration directly names revisiting and improving the existing solution. D incorrect Incremental describes added functionality rather than the specified primary emphasis.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 249 · NS0765
records.text: NS0765 Question 249 SE05 In the Agile SDLC, small units of functionality that the software needs to deliver are called: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Sprints B Iterations C User Stories D Epics User stories. SE05 defines a user story as a small user need and value supported by acceptance criteria. Sprints and iterations name cycles or timeboxes, not the need itself. An epic groups broader work. C therefore names the small functional work unit intended here, without claiming that Agile requirements consist only of story text. A incorrect A Sprint is a timeboxed development interval rather than the individual user need. B incorrect An iteration is a cycle of work or refinement, not a small functional requirement. C correct A user story states a small user need and its value with acceptance criteria. D incorrect An epic groups broader work rather than naming the smaller story-sized need.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 250 · NS0766
records.text: NS0766 Question 250 SE06 The Spiral Model distinguishes itself from other models primarily through its emphasis on: Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Sequential phase completion B Risk Analysis at every cycle C Customer delivery at the end of the project D Strict adherence to initial requirements Risk analysis and reduction in every spiral cycle. SE06 defines spiral development as risk driven, with each cycle identifying objectives and alternatives, assessing and reducing risks, producing a result and planning commitment. That emphasis distinguishes it from merely repeating phases or delivering only at the end. It can adapt requirements and combine other activities rather than enforcing an unchangeable initial specification. A incorrect A spiral can contain staged work, but sequential completion is not its defining driver. B correct Risk assessment and reduction guide each cycle’s work and further commitment. C incorrect Only delivering at the end is not the distinguishing spiral principle. D incorrect A risk-driven cycle can revise plans and requirements rather than rigidly freeze them.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 251 · NS0767
records.text: NS0767 Question 251 SE03 The V-Model derives its name from its shape. What does the BOTTOM of the 'V' represent? Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Requirements Gathering B Deployment C Coding/Implementation D Maintenance Coding/implementation. SE03 explicitly places coding at the bottom of the V while specification and design stages correspond to later testing levels. Requirements therefore begin the development side rather than occupy the bottom; deployment and maintenance are not that connecting implementation activity. This is a model-diagram convention, not a claim that all real work follows a perfect geometric sequence. A incorrect Requirements occur on the specification side, not at the coding bottom of the V. B incorrect Deployment is not the implementation activity joining the V-model’s sides. C correct The note explicitly identifies coding as the bottom of the V. D incorrect Maintenance occurs in lifecycle evolution rather than at this implementation point.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 252 · NS0768
records.text: NS0768 Question 252 SE17 Which organization standardizes and maintains UML as a modeling language? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A IEEE B ISO C Object Management Group (OMG) D W3C Object Management Group (OMG) The note identifies the Object Management Group as UML’s standardizing and maintaining organization. UML is a modeling language rather than a software lifecycle process. This stewardship question does not claim that the organization originally invented every contributing notation. IEEE, ISO and W3C are not the organization to which the supplied note attributes this particular standardization and maintenance role. A incorrect IEEE is not the attributed UML steward. B incorrect ISO is not the organization attributed this role in the note. C correct OMG is the stated standardizing and maintaining organization. D incorrect W3C is not the attributed UML steward.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 253 · NS0769
records.text: NS0769 Question 253 SE14 In a UML Use Case Diagram, the rectangle enclosing all use cases is called: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A System Context B System Boundary Box C Package Container D Module Frame The system boundary box. SE14 says actors are outside the system-boundary rectangle and use-case ovals are inside. The enclosing rectangle therefore marks the modeled system’s boundary. A context may be communicated by the diagram, but it is not the specific box name requested; packages and modules serve different grouping roles rather than defining this external actor boundary. A incorrect System context is broader information, not the specific name of this enclosing boundary rectangle. B correct The rectangle separates the modeled system’s use cases from external actor roles. C incorrect A package groups modeling elements but is not the stated system/actor boundary. D incorrect Module frame is not the use-case system-boundary term defined in SE14.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 254 · NS0770
records.text: NS0770 Question 254 SE16 When execution reaches an include relationship’s inclusion point in a base use case, what does include require? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Optional behavior that may be added to the base use case B The included behavior is required whenever execution reaches the inclusion point. C An inheritance relationship between two use cases D A timing constraint between two use cases The included behavior is required whenever execution reaches the inclusion point. Include factors required reused behavior into another use case. When the base reaches the inclusion point, the included behavior is incorporated and performed as specified. This does not imply that every possible conditional branch of the base reaches that point. Optional conditional additions correspond to extend, specialization to generalization, and timing constraints are separate from the inclusion relationship. A incorrect Conditional optional added behavior describes extend. B correct The included behavior is required when its inclusion point is reached. C incorrect Specialization is generalization rather than include. D incorrect Include is not a timing constraint.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 255 · NS0771
records.text: NS0771 Question 255 SE17 In a UML class diagram, visibility marked with '#' indicates: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Public access B Private access C Protected access D Package-level access Protected visibility. SE17 lists + public, - private, # protected and ~ package. The requested hash marker therefore means protected access. These symbols indicate visibility of a class member; they do not express object multiplicity, inheritance direction or class ownership, and the other choices correspond to different explicit markers. A incorrect Public visibility is marked with + rather than #. B incorrect Private visibility is marked with - rather than #. C correct The note explicitly assigns # to protected visibility. D incorrect Package visibility uses ~ rather than the protected # marker.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 256 · NS0772
records.text: NS0772 Question 256 SE18 In UML, which relationship is represented by a HOLLOW diamond shape pointing toward the 'whole' class? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Composition B Dependency C Aggregation D Generalization Shared aggregation. SE18 defines shared aggregation with a hollow diamond at the whole end. Composition instead uses a filled diamond; dependency is a dashed arrow and generalization uses a hollow triangle. The question’s whole-end description is consistent with the notation, so the hollow shape uniquely identifies aggregation among these alternatives. A incorrect Composition uses a filled diamond, not the specified hollow diamond. B incorrect Dependency is represented by a dashed arrow rather than a whole-part diamond. C correct Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond placed at the whole end. D incorrect Generalization uses a hollow triangle toward the general element rather than a diamond.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 257 · NS0773
records.text: NS0773 Question 257 SE18 Which statement accurately distinguishes UML composition from shared aggregation while allowing model-defined detachment or transfer? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Aggregation is for classes; Composition is for interfaces B Composition has exclusive composite ownership at a time and destroys still-owned parts with the whole; shared aggregation gives weaker whole-part meaning. C Aggregation implies inheritance; Composition does not D They are synonymous in modern UML Composition has exclusive composite ownership at a time and destroys still-owned parts with the whole; shared aggregation gives weaker whole-part meaning. Composition gives strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and still-owned parts are destroyed with that composite. Shared aggregation indicates weaker whole-part meaning without that detailed lifecycle policy. A model can permit detachment or transfer, so permanent inability to exist independently is too strong. Neither relationship is inheritance, and composition is not restricted to interfaces. A incorrect Composition is not restricted to interfaces. B correct This states strong ownership and destruction of still-owned parts, unlike weak shared aggregation. C incorrect Aggregation is not inheritance; generalization is separate. D incorrect The ownership meanings differ, so they are not synonyms.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 258 · NS0774
records.text: NS0774 Question 258 SE19 Under the course’s sequence-diagram layout heuristic—rather than a mandatory UML column rule—which participant belongs in the second column? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A The control object managing the use case B The actor who initiated the use case C A boundary object the actor used to start the use case D An entity object central to the use case A boundary object the actor used to start the use case The course’s heuristic places the initiating actor first, the boundary object second, the control object third and entity objects afterward. The boundary used by the actor therefore occupies the second column under that convention. UML itself does not mandate this column order; lifeline semantics come from the modeled participants and messages rather than their horizontal position alone. A incorrect The heuristic places control third. B incorrect The initiating actor is first. C correct The actor-facing boundary is second under the specified heuristic. D incorrect Entities follow the boundary and control in this heuristic.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 259 · NS0775
records.text: NS0775 Question 259 SE20 In a UML Activity Diagram, a diamond shape is used to represent: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Initial State B Final State C Action Box D Decision Box A decision node, also usable as a merge node in the appropriate flow. SE20 names the guarded decision diamond and separately notes that the same shape can merge alternative flows. D is therefore a correct use of the shape, without claiming decision is its only role. Initial nodes are filled circles, actions are rounded, and final-state notation is not the diamond described. A incorrect The initial node is a filled circle rather than a diamond. B incorrect The diamond is not the standard final-state marker in the described notation. C incorrect Actions are rounded nodes rather than guarded-flow diamonds. D correct A diamond can represent a guarded decision; it can also merge alternative flows.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 260 · NS0776
records.text: NS0776 Question 260 SE22 In system design, 'coupling' between subsystems refers to: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits. A How well objects within a subsystem work toward a common goal B The number of operations a subsystem exposes C The degree of dependency between two subsystems D The architectural pattern chosen for the system The degree of dependency between subsystems. SE22 explicitly distinguishes cohesion within a module from coupling between modules. A describes cohesion; C describes coupling. Interface operation count can affect design complexity but is not the definition of dependence, and an architectural pattern may influence coupling without being the relationship measure itself. The goal is usually low coupling with high cohesion. A incorrect Related purpose inside a subsystem defines cohesion rather than between-subsystem coupling. B incorrect Operation count alone does not measure the actual dependencies between subsystems. C correct Coupling is the degree of dependency between modules or subsystems. D incorrect An architectural style can affect coupling but is not its definition.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 261 · NS0777
records.text: NS0777 Question 261 SE23 In architectural design, a 'closed architecture' in a layered system means: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits. A No external access to any layer is allowed B A layer can access any layer at deeper levels freely C A layer can only call the layer immediately below it D All layers communicate through a central repository Calls are restricted to the immediately lower layer. SE23 defines a closed layered architecture as allowing calls only to the immediately lower layer. Open layering may permit approved skipping, so B describes a different policy. Closed does not mean no external access or a shared repository; it concerns permitted dependencies between layers rather than the system’s exposure or storage organization. A incorrect Closed layering restricts interlayer calls, not every form of external access. B incorrect Skipping freely to deeper layers contradicts the immediate-lower-layer restriction. C correct A layer calls only the immediately lower layer in the defined closed architecture. D incorrect A central repository is another architectural arrangement and does not define closed layering.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 262 · NS0778
records.text: NS0778 Question 262 SE24 Which architectural style divides subsystems into Model, View, and Controller components? Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits. A Repository Style B Client/Server Style C Peer-to-Peer Style D Model-View-Controller Style Model–View–Controller. SE24 explicitly defines MVC as separating a domain model, display view and interaction controller. D names that exact style. Repository, client–server and peer-to-peer organize central data or interacting roles differently; any may be combined with MVC, but none is the name of this particular three-responsibility separation. A incorrect Repository style centers shared data rather than the specific model/view/controller separation. B incorrect Client–server separates requesters and service providers, not these three presentation-interaction responsibilities. C incorrect Peer-to-peer allows participants to play requester and provider roles rather than defining MVC components. D correct Model–View–Controller explicitly names the three responsibilities in the question.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 263 · NS0779
records.text: NS0779 Question 263 SE24 SE23 In the Three-Tier architectural style, which layer handles 'storing, retrieving, and querying persistent data'? Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits. A Interface Layer B Application Logic Layer C Storage Layer D Presentation Layer The storage layer/tier. SE24 separates three-tier presentation, application logic and storage. Persistent data storage and retrieval belong to the storage responsibility, whereas presentation handles interaction and application logic coordinates domain behavior. The question uses layer for a tier-style role; that terminology does not change which responsibility owns persistence. A incorrect The interface responsibility handles interaction rather than persistent storage and querying. B incorrect Application logic coordinates domain operations but delegates persistence to the storage responsibility. C correct The storage role handles persistent data, including retrieval and queries. D incorrect Presentation formats user interaction and output rather than owning persistent data storage.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 264 · NS0780
records.text: NS0780 Question 264 SE13 In the analysis model, which type of object represents the bridges between the system and the actors? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Entity Objects B Control Objects C Boundary Objects D Interface Objects Boundary objects. SE13 defines boundary objects as mediating interaction, with ReportForm as an example. That is the bridge between external actors and the system. Entity objects hold domain information, while controls coordinate use cases. Interface objects is a generic descriptive phrase, but boundary is the explicitly defined analysis-category name requested among these choices. A incorrect Entity objects represent domain information rather than the actor-facing interaction bridge. B incorrect Control objects coordinate use-case behavior rather than primarily mediate actor interaction. C correct Boundary objects are explicitly defined as mediating system–actor interaction. D incorrect Interface objects is not the named entity/boundary/control category specified here’s analysis model.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 265 · NS0781
records.text: NS0781 Question 265 SE13 Which heuristic rule states that there should be 'one control object per actor' in a use case? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A CRC Card Heuristic B Control Object Identification Heuristic C Boundary Object Heuristic D Sequence Diagram Column Rule The control-object identification heuristic. SE13 permits one control per use case or participating actor as a useful starting point, while denying a mandatory UML rule. The stem already asks for a heuristic, so B correctly identifies the control-object selection guideline. CRC, boundary identification and column layout concern different tasks; none makes the count a required lifetime or architecture constraint. A incorrect CRC records class responsibilities and collaborators rather than prescribing this candidate-control count. B correct This is the heuristic for identifying candidate use-case control objects, not a universal UML constraint. C incorrect Boundary heuristics identify interaction-facing objects rather than coordinating controls. D incorrect Sequence-column layout orders participants visually and does not define candidate control-object counts.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 266 · NS0782
records.text: NS0782 Question 266 SE13 CRC cards stand for: Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Class, Requirements, Conditions B Component, Relationship, Constraints C Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators D Control, Reuse, Composition Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. SE13 expands CRC directly as Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. The card identifies the class, what it must do or know, and which other objects help fulfill those responsibilities. The distractors replace these terms with requirements, components or unrelated design concepts and therefore do not preserve the stated expansion. A incorrect Requirements and Conditions are not the R and final C in the stated expansion. B incorrect Component, Relationship and Constraints do not match the class-card terminology. C correct This is the exact CRC expansion supplied in SE13. D incorrect Control, Reuse and Composition are different concepts rather than the CRC card fields.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 267 · NS0783
records.text: NS0783 Question 267 SE17 In UML association multiplicity, what does '0..*' mean? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Exactly one instance B Zero or exactly one instance C Zero or more instances D One or more instances Zero or more instances. SE17 defines 0..* as any nonnegative number. Zero is allowed and the star places no finite upper bound, so C fits. The alternatives correspond to 1, 0..1 and 1..* respectively. Multiplicity at one end is interpreted relative to one object at the opposite end, not as a whole-system object count. A incorrect Exactly one corresponds to multiplicity 1 rather than 0..*. B incorrect Optional single-valued multiplicity is 0..1, not an unbounded star. C correct Zero is permitted and the upper star allows any number of related instances. D incorrect One or more requires lower bound 1, written 1..*.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 268 · NS0784
records.text: NS0784 Question 268 SE13 In Abbott's heuristics for identifying associations, which phrase pattern most directly suggests a relationship between classes? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Look for adjective phrases describing class properties B Examine verb phrases like 'has', 'is part of', 'manages', 'reports to' C Find all nouns that appear more than twice D Identify all user interface terms Verb phrases expressing relationships, such as manages or reports to. SE13 recommends nouns as candidate objects and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations. B is the relationship-phrase option. Adjectives generally describe properties, repeated nouns do not automatically imply an association, and UI terms suggest boundary concerns. These are candidate-identification heuristics rather than a proof that every verb must become a modeled link. A incorrect Property descriptions suggest attributes rather than directly identifying links between classes. B correct Relationship verbs are the note’s direct heuristic for candidate associations. C incorrect Noun frequency is not the stated association-identification rule; nouns instead suggest candidate objects. D incorrect UI terminology may suggest boundaries but does not directly establish an association between domain classes.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 269 · NS0785
records.text: NS0785 Question 269 SE36 In software testing, which type of testing evaluates the software's behavior WITHOUT knowledge of its internal code structure? Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking. A White Box Testing B Grey Box Testing C Black Box Testing D Structural Testing Black-box testing. SE36 contrasts black-box cases derived from required behavior with white-box cases derived from implementation structure. Grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. The question excludes internal-code knowledge, so black-box is the appropriate technique. Structural testing instead refers to the very internal paths or statements that this scenario does not inspect. A incorrect White-box testing explicitly uses internal implementation structure to derive cases. B incorrect Grey-box testing uses partial internal knowledge rather than excluding it. C correct Black-box testing derives cases from externally specified behavior without needing code structure. D incorrect Structural testing is based on internal control or code structure, contrary to the stem.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 270 · NS0786
records.text: NS0786 Question 270 SE35 Which type of functional testing verifies that individual components work correctly in ISOLATION? Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking. A System Testing B Integration Testing C Regression Testing D Unit Testing Unit testing. SE35 defines unit testing as isolating a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs or mocks. Integration checks combined interactions and system testing evaluates the whole system. Regression describes testing after changes and can occur at different levels, so it is not the isolation level named by the question. A incorrect System testing evaluates the complete integrated system rather than an isolated component. B incorrect Integration testing focuses on interactions among combined parts, not isolation. C incorrect Regression checks unintended effects after change and is not inherently a component-isolation level. D correct Unit testing evaluates a small component in isolation, with dependencies replaceable by test doubles.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 271 · NS0787
records.text: NS0787 Question 271 SE36 Non-functional testing that evaluates how the system behaves under expected workloads and measures response speed is called: Separate testing scope, technique and purpose. Use the stated workload, observable result or coverage target rather than a universal ranking. A Usability Testing B Reliability Testing C Performance Testing D Compatibility Testing Performance testing, specifically load-oriented testing under expected demand. SE36 defines performance tests as assessing speed, throughput and resource use under a specified workload and distinguishes expected load from stress beyond normal limits. The stem explicitly adds workload and response speed, so it supports performance testing rather than merely a vague normal-condition test. Usability, reliability and compatibility target different quality questions. A incorrect Usability focuses on task success and ease of use rather than response-speed measurements under load. B incorrect Reliability concerns failure-free service, not primarily the stated response-time criterion. C correct Speed under an expected workload is performance/load testing as defined in SE36. D incorrect Compatibility examines cooperating environments rather than the specified speed-under-load behavior.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 272 · NS0788
records.text: NS0788 Question 272 SE13 In the analysis phase, which model type uses use cases and scenarios to describe what the software should do? Distinguish observable services, measurable qualities and implementation constraints. Check scope, stakeholder meaning and the requested level of specificity. A Dynamic Model B Analysis Object Model C Functional Model D Structural Model The functional model. SE13 explicitly associates use cases and scenarios with functional modeling, classes with structural/object modeling, and states/interactions with dynamic modeling. Thus C names the requested description of what the system should do. The alternatives describe state-dependent behavior or static object structure rather than this user-goal and scenario view. A incorrect Dynamic models emphasize states and interactions rather than the named use-case/scenario category. B incorrect The analysis object model captures classes and relationships rather than the functional use-case view. C correct Use cases and scenarios are explicitly the functional analysis model. D incorrect Structural modeling describes static classes and links rather than required user-goal flows.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 273 · NS0789
records.text: NS0789 Question 273 SE20 SE13 In an analysis model, an object coordinates a use case and moves among Idle, WaitingForReply and Completing states as events arrive. Domain entities are passive records and the form has no persistent modes in this scenario. Which object category is the direct state-machine target described? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Entity Objects B Boundary Objects C Control Objects D All objects equally Control Objects A control object coordinates a use case, and the described coordinator has significant event-dependent states. A state machine is therefore directly useful for that control object in this scenario. Entities and boundaries can also have meaningful lifecycles in other systems, but here their stated behavior does not supply the modeled states. Suitability follows from responsibilities and lifecycle behavior, not equal need across all objects. A incorrect The scenario’s entities are passive records rather than the stated coordinator. B incorrect The form has no persistent modes and is not the use-case coordinator. C correct The stateful coordinator is a control object. D incorrect The need depends on significant state behavior, not equality across every object.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 274 · NS0790
records.text: NS0790 Question 274 SE19 In the ReportEmergency use case example, which boundary object allows the FieldOfficer to initiate the reporting process? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A EmergencyReportForm B AcknowledgmentNotice C ReportEmergencyButton D DispatcherStation ReportEmergencyButton. SE19 explicitly says FieldOfficer activates ReportEmergencyButton, supplies details through EmergencyReportForm and later sees AcknowledgmentNotice. DispatcherStation belongs to the dispatcher side. Therefore the button initiates this particular scenario; the form handles later input and the notice reports completion. This is grounded in the named example rather than a generic rule that every use case starts with a button. A incorrect The form receives incident details after initiation rather than starting the documented scenario. B incorrect The acknowledgment is seen later as feedback, not used to initiate reporting. C correct The note explicitly identifies this button as the FieldOfficer’s initiating boundary object. D incorrect DispatcherStation is on the dispatcher side rather than the FieldOfficer’s initiation interface.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 275 · NS0791
records.text: NS0791 Question 275 SE18 SE16 Generalization in UML modeling is best described as: Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A Dividing a class into multiple subclasses with no shared properties B Identifying a general concept where other concepts are more specific versions of it C Creating interfaces for external system communication D Grouping unrelated classes into a package for organization A general concept with more-specific specializations. SE16 relates a specialized actor or use case to a more general one; SE18 gives the corresponding class generalization toward a superclass. B expresses that abstraction/specialization relationship. It does not merely package unrelated classes, create an external interface or split classes while denying shared general properties. A incorrect Specialization is related through a general concept rather than requiring no shared properties. B correct Generalization identifies the common general element of which other concepts are more specific versions. C incorrect External communication interfaces do not by themselves define a generalization relationship. D incorrect Packaging unrelated classes is organizational grouping rather than specialization of a shared general concept.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 276 · NS0792
records.text: NS0792 Question 276 SE22 The 'high cohesion, low coupling' principle in subsystem design means: Separate responsibilities inside a component from dependencies across boundaries. Evaluate the stated structure, change and reuse goals without assuming guaranteed benefits. A Subsystems should be tightly interconnected for maximum communication efficiency B Objects within a subsystem should be closely related, while subsystems themselves should be mostly independent C Each subsystem should have minimal internal functionality to reduce complexity D All subsystems should share a single central data repository Related responsibilities within a subsystem, limited dependencies between subsystems. SE22 defines cohesion as related purpose within a module and coupling as dependency across modules, then recommends high cohesion and low coupling. B states both dimensions. It does not require minimal functionality, tight cross-connections or one shared repository; those choices can undermine coherent responsibilities or increase dependency rather than establish the principle. A incorrect Tight interconnection increases coupling rather than meeting the low-coupling goal. B correct Closely related internal responsibilities and limited external dependencies express both parts of the principle. C incorrect Cohesion concerns related purpose, not simply having as little functionality as possible. D incorrect A shared repository is a style choice and can create dependencies; it does not define cohesion or coupling.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 277 · NS0793
records.text: NS0793 Question 277 SE05 SE03 A safety-critical contract requires traceable assurance records and reviewed verification before release. Waterfall, V-model and spiral proposals include those obligations; the proposed lightweight Agile variant supplies working code but omits the required assurance records. Which proposal is least appropriate as specified? Identify whether the scenario prioritizes delivery, learning, adaptation or risk reduction. Several processes can share individual practices, so compare their defining emphasis. A Waterfall Model B V-Model C Agile Model D Spiral Model Agile Model The specified Agile proposal omits mandatory assurance records, so it cannot satisfy the stated contract without modification. The other proposals include those obligations and are not excluded on that ground. This is a judgment about the supplied lightweight variant, not Agile in general: the note explicitly allows Agile to incorporate required documentation and assurance. Stable requirements alone would not establish a universal ranking. A incorrect This proposal includes the required reviewed deliverables. B incorrect This proposal includes the required assurance obligations. C correct The specified lightweight variant omits mandatory records and is therefore least suitable as proposed. D incorrect This proposal includes the stated assurance obligations.

records.title: Software Engineering — Question 278 · NS0794
records.text: NS0794 Question 278 SE19 In a sequence diagram, what does an 'X' (cross) at the end of a lifeline dashed line indicate? Match the information to be represented with each model’s purpose. Read relationship direction, boundary and ownership conditions before classifying it. A The object is temporarily inactive B The object is waiting for a message C The object ceases to exist at that point D The object is calling itself recursively Modeled destruction of the object at that point. SE19 explicitly identifies X as modeled destruction, so C is correct in UML diagram semantics. Temporary inactivity and waiting do not end an object’s modeled existence, and a recursive message is represented by an interaction rather than destruction. The marker does not guarantee the runtime moment at which a garbage collector reclaims memory. A incorrect Temporary inactivity does not terminate the object’s lifeline. B incorrect Waiting for a message does not mean the modeled object has been destroyed. C correct X marks the object’s modeled destruction at that point, not necessarily immediate memory reclamation. D incorrect A recursive call is an interaction message and does not use the destruction marker.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Course module
records.text: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Study notes
records.text: Design and Analysis of Algorithms Design an algorithm by specifying its states, choices and correctness argument, then count its work and peak storage. A familiar strategy name is not enough: independent subproblems, reuse, safe local choices, feasibility pruning and objective bounds lead to different methods. For cost questions fix input size, case, primitive operation and arithmetic model. Write the sum or recurrence before selecting an asymptotic bound. For each design technique practice a small trace and explain why its discarded alternatives cannot improve the required answer. Distinguish an exact algorithm from a heuristic, a decision problem from an optimization problem, and a tight bound from a merely valid upper bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Practice questions
records.text: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Revision outline
records.text: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Specify the problem and prove correctness
records.text: State inputs, output, constraints and empty-solution policy. Algorithms are finite, definite executable methods independent of source language; feasible satisfies constraints, optimal is best feasible. Conditional branches are legitimate control flow. Prove an invariant initially, after each step and at termination; for recursion prove base cases and the inductive reduction. Testing finds failures but finite tests do not prove correctness for all inputs. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Cost model, experiments and input size
records.text: Analysis counts operations and storage as functions of input size: array length n, graph vertices V/edges E, or the number of bits in integers. A RAM model commonly gives constant cost to bounded-word arithmetic/access. Arbitrarily large integer arithmetic and printing long outputs need their own costs. Elapsed measurements also depend on hardware, compiler, cache, I/O and competing load. Experimental/dynamic measurement observes actual runs; asymptotic analysis abstracts growth; probabilistic analysis studies expectations. There is no universal taxonomy proving “graph analysis” or “dynamic analysis” is invalid. Auxiliary space excludes input; I/O complexity counts transfers. Representation affects costs; “data type complexity” is not a standard metric name. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Input cases and bound notation are independent
records.text: At fixed size n, best case minimizes cost, worst case maximizes it, and average case takes an expectation under a specified input distribution. Randomized expected cost may average internal choices for one fixed input. Smallest input size is not best case. O/Ω/Θ bound functions independently of case or resource. A worst-case upper bound covers every size-n input, but O does not mean worst case. Constant best case and quadratic worst case are not universal. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Formal asymptotic bounds and constants
records.text: For eventually nonnegative f, g, f∈O(g) means f(n)≤c·g(n) for all n≥n 0, with fixed c>0. Ω reverses that inequality; Θ requires both bounds. Little-o means f/g→0, and little-ω means f/g→∞ where the ratio exists. Θ specifies growth up to constant factors, not exact seconds or identical best/worst cases. Prove the inequality for the whole tail, not selected values. Transitivity allows chained upper bounds; sums are dominated by the largest nonnegative growth term. Example Worked microexample 10n+5≤15n for n≥1, so c=15,n 0=1 works. Also 3n²+4n+1≤8n² for n≥1. The inequality 7n²+3n+5≤8n² is false at n=1; c=15 works for all n≥1. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Growth ordering and loose bounds
records.text: Representative growth is 1,log n,n,n log n,n²,n³,…,b^n,n! for fixed b>1. Log bases differ by a constant. Both n log n and n² are superlinear; log n is sublinear. Polynomial growth has a fixed exponent in input size. O(n²) also implies O(n³): upper bounds need not be tight. Several asymptotic bounds can hold simultaneously for the same function. Neither representative growth ordering nor Big-O labels alone determine finite-input speed. Example Worked microexample For f=4n² and g=8n, f/g=n/2→∞. Therefore f∈Ω(g) and evenω(g), while f is neither O(g) nor Θ(g). Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Loops, exact counts and additive costs
records.text: Sequential costs add; independent nested loop counts multiply. A dependent loop requires summation. n iterations of a constant body give Θ(n); ∑i=1.. n i=n(n+1)/2 gives Θ(n²). Doubling i=1,2,4,… until i≥n takes ceil(log 2 n) iterations for n>1. A 10n loop is linear under constant-cost output. If m operations each have expected cost f(n) at the same fixed size, expected total is m f(n), by linearity of expectation; independence is unnecessary. If sizes change, sum f(n_i). Exact coefficients depend on whether tests, increments, arithmetic and assignments count separately. Example Worked microexample For sum=0; for(i=1;i<=n;i++) sum=sum+1; return sum: counting two initializations, n+1 tests, n increments,2n body operations and one return gives 4n+4. A different primitive-cost convention changes this exact expression, not Θ(n). Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Analyze conditional nested loops and code validity
records.text: For the loop i=0.. n−1, j=i.. i²−1, and k=0.. j−1 only when j%i==0, i=0 and 1 have empty j ranges, so no remainder by zero is evaluated. For i≥2, successful j values are i,2i,…,(i−1)i. The inner work is i∑m=1.. i−1 m=i²(i−1)/2=Θ(i³). Summing over i gives Θ(n⁴); condition checks add only Θ(n³). Neither n⁵ nor n⁷ is tight for this loop, though both are valid Big-O upper bounds. This assumes mathematical integers and constant-cost output; literal signed C++ overflow in i*i is undefined, and executable runtime analysis requires valid syntax in a specified language. Redeclaring parameter n and using return @;3 are syntax errors; neither establishes logarithmic complexity. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Peak storage and recursion stacks
records.text: Space complexity measures peak simultaneously live storage, not the sum of every allocation ever made. Count input, auxiliary structures and stack according to the requested convention. n active recursion levels with constant-size frames need Θ(n) stack; depth log n with constant frames needs Θ(log n). The number of total calls does not determine peak depth. Slicing/copying arrays can add storage omitted by an index-based pseudocode analysis. Tail-call elimination is language/runtime-dependent and cannot be assumed for ordinary C++/Java recursion. Resource tradeoffs include caching subproblem results to save time while consuming memory. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Recurrences: substitution and expansion
records.text: Include every recursive call, nonrecursive work and base case. Expansion gives T(n)=T(n−1)+Θ(1)→Θ(n), and T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1)→Θ(log n). For 2T(n/2)+Θ(n), logarithmically many levels each cost Θ(n), giving Θ(n log n). Substitution guesses a bound and proves it inductively with constants/base cases; a lower-order correction may close the induction. Unequal/decrementing recurrences need separate analysis. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Recursion trees and the Master theorem
records.text: For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), a≥1, b>1, let p=log_b a. Level i has a^i nodes of size n/b^i. Compare f with n^p: a polynomial gap below gives Θ(n^p); f=Θ(n^p) gives Θ(n^p log n); a polynomial gap above gives Θ(f(n)) if a f(n/b)≤c f(n) for fixed c<1. The third case needs this regularity condition. A log-factor boundary may need an extended theorem or explicit summation. State base work and include leaves. This version does not apply to T(n)=T(n−1)+n or unequal-split quicksort. Example Worked microexample 4T(n/2)+n gives Θ(n²);2T(n/2)+n gives Θ(n log n); T(n/2)+n² gives Θ(n²). Each follows a different case. Also 4T(n/2)+n² gives Θ(n² log n), case 2. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module MIT6.006 Recitation3

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Comparison sorting lower bounds
records.text: A comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves for distinct-key orderings. Height h allows at most 2^h leaves, so h≥log 2(n!)=Ω(n log n); merge sort matches this worst-case bound. Array indexing is not forbidden. Counting/radix sorting exploits structured keys outside the comparison-only model. Recurrences analyze particular algorithms; this decision tree bounds the entire comparison class. Assess a lower-bound argument by its computational model and reasoning rather than by a technique label alone. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module Virginia Tech OpenDSA, Sorting Lower Bound

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Choose a design from structural conditions
records.text: Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines results. DP reuses a defined set of subproblem states. Greedy commits to a feasible local choice only when a safety argument supports it. Backtracking grows/retracts candidates when constraints fail; branch and bound also rejects candidates whose best possible objective cannot beat an incumbent. “Breaks into subproblems,” “sequence of choices,” “incremental,” or “optimization” alone describes several strategies. Exponential runtime is an outcome, not enough information to select a method. Specify overlap, local-choice safety, revisability, exactness and usable bounds. Ordinary selection sort repeatedly selects one minimum; it is not a divide-and-conquer algorithm. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Binary search and simultaneous minimum/maximum
records.text: Binary search requires sorted random-access data. Maintain inclusive low/high bounds, compute mid=low+(high−low)//2, and replace high with mid−1 or low with mid+1 according to the comparison. Stop when found or low>high. T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1): worst Θ(log n), best Θ(1); iterative auxiliary space Θ(1), recursive Θ(log n). Finding both extrema by two unconditional comparisons per element costs 2n−2 comparisons, regardless of order. Pair elements first, compare within each pair, then compare the smaller with minimum and larger with maximum: even n uses 3n/2−2 comparisons. A balanced recursive version has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(1)=Θ(n). An unconditional two-if scan does not have an n−1-comparison best case. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Merge sort: invariant, trace and costs
records.text: Split by indices, recursively sort each half, then repeatedly copy the smaller remaining front element into a temporary result. The merge invariant says the output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest elements already consumed. Append the unexhausted suffix. Equal keys must be taken from the left half first to preserve stability. Ordinary array merge sort has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n) across input orders, Θ(n) auxiliary buffer and Θ(log n) recursion depth. A written +O(n) recurrence alone establishes an upper bound; the tight result also uses linear merge work. Empty/singleton subarrays are base cases. Example Worked microexample [4,1,3,2] splits into[4,1] and[3,2], which sort to[1,4] and[2,3]. Merge selects 1,2,3 and appends 4. No assumption that the original array is already sorted is needed. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Quicksort: partition variants and worst cases
records.text: Choose a pivot, partition, then sort the resulting smaller ranges. In a two-pointer scheme, advance i while values are below pivot and j while above; when i≤j, swap and advance both. Bound the scans and ensure progress on equal values. Recurse on the resulting ranges. Hoare-style partition boundaries need not put the pivot at its final position; Lomuto-style partition commonly does. Do not mix their return conventions. Balanced splits give Θ(n log n); repeatedly highly unbalanced splits give Θ(n²). Random pivots give expected Θ(n log n), not a deterministic guarantee. Median-of-three does not eliminate adversarial cases; three-way partitioning helps repeated keys. Standard quicksort is unstable, uses expected Θ(log n) stack but worst Θ(n); recursing on the smaller side and iterating on the larger bounds stack by O(log n). Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Sorting choices and comparison costs
records.text: Insertion shifts larger sorted-prefix keys: stable with strict comparisons, Θ(n) best and Θ(n²) worst. Optimized bubble sort swaps adjacent inversions and stops after a no-swap pass: stable, Θ(n) best, Θ(n²) worst. Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum: Θ(n²) comparisons in every order, normally unstable. These use Θ(1) auxiliary array space. Heap sort builds a max-heap in Θ(n), then extracts/restores in O(log n) per item: O(n log n) total, Θ(1) auxiliary space, ordinarily unstable. It is not standard D&C. Merge sort offers stability/worst-case guarantees; quicksort’s practical advantage depends on implementation/workload. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Strassen multiplication and divide/combine tradeoffs
records.text: Ordinary n×n multiplication computes n products/sums per output entry: Θ(n³). Eight half-size block products still give 8T(n/2)+Θ(n²)=Θ(n³). Strassen uses seven products plus block sums/differences:7T(n/2)+Θ(n²)=Θ(n^log 2 7)≈Θ(n^2.807). Zero-padding preserves the required product. The smaller exponent trades extra additions/temporary storage and possible numerical issues against multiplication work. Use an ordinary base case for small matrices and specify exact versus floating-point arithmetic. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Maximum contiguous subarray: two valid strategies
records.text: A maximum subarray is contiguous; it is not an arbitrary subsequence. Divide-and-conquer compares the best left, best right and best crossing result. The crossing result is the best suffix of the left half plus best prefix of the right, found in Θ(n). This yields 2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n). Kadane’s DP keeps the best sum ending at i: end[i]=max(A[i], end[i−1]+A[i]); keep the largest end seen. This is Θ(n) time and Θ(1) extra space. For a required nonempty subarray initialize from A[0], not zero; all-negative input then returns its largest element. Empty-allowed variants may return zero. Both D&C and DP can solve the maximum-subarray problem; specify the algorithm before assigning its complexity. Example Worked microexample For[−2,3,−1,4,−5], ending sums are−2,3,2,6,1; optimum 6 comes from[3,−1,4]. For[−4,−2], a nonempty answer is−2. University of Alberta CMPUT498/501 Lecture2

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Greedy correctness, limits and counterexamples
records.text: A greedy algorithm repeatedly selects a locally attractive feasible option without later undoing it. Optimal substructure alone does not prove this safe. An exchange proof inserts the greedy choice into an optimum without worsening cost; recurse. MST cut proofs use this exchange. Advantages are often simple decisions and low overhead; limitations are irrevocable errors and problem-specific applicability. A heuristic has no approximation guarantee merely because it is greedy. For coins{1,3,4} and target 6, largest-first gives 4+1+1 while 3+3 uses fewer coins. Activity selection instead has a safe earliest-finish rule for maximizing the number of nonoverlapping unweighted intervals; replacing the first chosen activity in an optimum with an earlier-finishing one leaves at least as much room. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Fractional knapsack versus indivisible items
records.text: For positive weights/profits and divisible items, sort by decreasing value/weight, take complete items while they fit, then the fitting fraction of the next. The exchange argument replaces lower-density selected weight by available higher-density weight; value cannot decrease. Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by a linear scan. Handle zero-weight beneficial items separately rather than divide by zero. This proof depends on divisibility. With capacity 10 and items(6,12),(5,8),(5,8), ratio-greedy chooses value 12; the two weight 5 items give 16 under 0/1 rules. Specify whether the knapsack problem is fractional,0/1 or unbounded. Feasibility alone does not guarantee optimality. Example Worked microexample Weights 15,10,18 and values 24,15,25 with capacity 20: take the weight 15 item and half the weight 10 item. Value 24+7.5=31.5; initial remaining capacity must be 20, not the number of items. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Unit-time job sequencing with deadlines
records.text: Assume one machine, initially available jobs, unit durations, integer deadlines and profit only for on-time completion. Process nonnegative-profit jobs by decreasing profit; place each in the latest free slot finishing by its deadline, or reject it. Latest placement preserves earlier slots for tighter deadlines; feasible unit-job sets support profit-first exchange. Sorting plus slot scans costs O(n log n+nD), with D capped at n.
