Equal-profit order is arbitrary; earlier deadline is optional. Variable durations/release times invalidate this rule. Example Worked microexample Slots finishing 1…5 contain J 2,J 4,J 3,J 5,J 1. Profits 180+300+190+120+200=990; deadlines hold. J 6 cannot finish by 2. The five largest profits sum to 990, giving a matching upper bound. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Optimal merge patterns and Huffman coding
records.text: Combine the two smallest weights, add their sum to total cost, and reinsert it. A min-heap gives O(n log n) time/O(n) space. Cost p+q counts moved records; worst-case comparisons are p+q−1 for nonempty lists, and actual comparisons may be fewer. Huffman uses frequencies as weights and 0/1 branches to leaf symbols, making a prefix-free code. Cost is∑frequency×depth. An exchange makes the two least frequencies deepest siblings; contract them and induct. Ties can change codes without changing optimal cost. Header overhead can outweigh tiny-file savings. Example Worked microexample For weights 2,3,5,6: merge 2+3=5, then 5+5=10, then 10+6=16. Total weighted merge cost 31; the same tree construction minimizes weighted prefix-code length. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — MSTs: Prim, Kruskal and the cut proof
records.text: For a connected weighted undirected graph, an MST spans every vertex without cycles and minimizes total edge weight; it has V−1 edges. Negative edges are allowed. Equal weights may yield multiple MSTs; distinct weights suffice for uniqueness. A tree is itself a graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal sorts edges globally, accepting one only when union-find says its endpoints are in different components. The cut proof exchanges a light crossing edge into some optimum without raising its weight. Matrix Prim costs O(V²); binary-heap Prim O(E log V), and Kruskal O(E log E). Dense-graph comparisons depend on these implementations. Disconnected input gives a minimum spanning forest. Example Worked microexample Triangle AB=1,BC=2,AC=4: Kruskal accepts AB and BC for cost 3. If every edge is 1, any two edges give an MST, so uniqueness fails. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Dijkstra: relaxation and the nonnegative condition
records.text: Initialize dist[source]=0, others∞ and predecessors unset. Repeatedly extract the unsettled vertex u of minimum distance; relax each edge by dist[v]=min(dist[v], dist[u]+w(u, v)), updating predecessors when improved. Once the minimum is∞, remaining vertices are unreachable. A destination may be finalized before stopping, not merely discovered. Nonnegative edges ensure a later path through unsettled vertices cannot improve a finalized distance. With s→a=2, s→b=5, b→a=−4, finalizing a at 2 misses the later distance 1. Binary-heap/list implementation costs O((V+E)log V), matrix scanning O(V²). An MST minimizes total connection cost; Dijkstra minimizes each source-path distance, a different objective. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — DP states, optimal substructure and proof
records.text: Define state meaning, choices, recurrence, bases and dependency order. Prove replacing a subsolution by a better one improves the full solution; otherwise state information may be missing. Show the recurrence covers all legal final choices and generates feasible candidates, then induct in dependency order. Store choices for reconstruction. Overlapping states motivate reuse; optimal substructure supports optimization. These are textbook signatures, not requirements that every DP problem optimize or every state have multiple users. DP also counts/decides. Cost=states×work per state and can remain exponential. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Memoization, tabulation and Fibonacci
records.text: Memoization recursively checks a cache before solving a state and stores its result. Tabulation orders dependencies explicitly; chosen domains may exclude irrelevant states. Cache keys include all relevant parameters; recursion/locality/sparsity affect implementation cost. Naive Fibonacci recomputes F(n−2) across branches: call count is Θ(φ^n), with O(2^n) a valid loose upper bound. F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(i)=F(i−1)+F(i−2) yield Θ(n) unit-cost additions with memoization/tabulation. Keeping only two recent values uses Θ(1) machine words; arbitrary-precision output needs growing bit storage. This naive overlapping recursion is not the independent-subproblem ideal of D&C. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Multistage/DAG paths and Bellman–Ford
records.text: For a DAG or multistage graph, compute cost-to-go in reverse topological order: F(t)=0 and F(u)=min over outgoing(u, v) of[w(u, v)+F(v)]. Missing routes have∞. Record the minimizing next vertex. Equivalently propagate source distances forward. Complexity is Θ(V+E) with adjacency lists; negative edges are harmless without cycles. Follow the recurrence’s dependencies when choosing the evaluation direction. For a general graph, Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges for up to V−1 passes and tests an additional pass for a reachable negative cycle: O(VE). Thus “single-source shortest path” does not uniquely imply greedy; graph assumptions determine the algorithm. Example Worked microexample s→a=2,s→b=5,a→t=4,b→t=−1 gives F(a)=4,F(b)=−1 and F(s)=min(6,4)=4 via b. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Floyd–Warshall, reachability and negative cycles
records.text: For all-pairs distances initialize D[i, i]=0, D[i, j] to the minimum direct edge weight, and missing edges to∞. Preserve a negative self-loop by taking min(0, its weight). For k outermost, update D[i, j]=min(D[i, j], D[i, k]+D[k, j]); before phase k, intermediates are restricted to earlier vertices. Guard unreachable sums and numeric overflow. Three loops give Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage. A negative diagonal afterward identifies a negative cycle; pairs able to traverse it have no finite minimum walk distance. Warshall reachability replaces min/+ by OR/AND. Floyd’s cost is not a universal best-achievable bound for all APSP settings; sparse nonnegative graphs permit repeated Dijkstra and other models permit other methods. Example Worked microexample If D[a,b]=4,D[b,c]=2,D[a,c]=11, phase b reduces D[a,c] to 6. Later phases must retain that improvement rather than restoring 11. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — 0/1 knapsack DP and dominance
records.text: For integer capacity W, K[i, w] is maximum value using the first i items within capacity w. Initialize K[0, w]=0. If weight_i>w, use K[i−1, w]; otherwise take max(K[i−1, w], value_i+K[i−1, w−weight_i]). The previous-row reference ensures each item is used at most once. Backtrack changed values to recover chosen items. Time O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial because W takes only O(log W) binary input bits. Storage can be O(W); update capacities downward for 0/1 selection. Upward iteration allows reuse and solves an unbounded variant. In sparse(weight, profit) states, discard an option dominated by another with no greater weight and no smaller profit, provided both have the same remaining items. Example Worked microexample Weights 2,3,4, values 1,2,5 and W=6 yield value 6 by choosing weights 2+4. A state(weight 5,profit 3) is dominated by(weight 4,profit 5). Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — LCS: prefix states and reconstruction
records.text: A subsequence preserves order but need not be contiguous. For prefixes of lengths i, j define L[i, j]. Empty-prefix rows/columns are 0. If X[i−1]=Y[j−1], set L[i, j]=1+L[i−1, j−1]; otherwise use max(L[i−1, j], L[i, j−1]). Keep prefix lengths i and j distinct from the zero-based character indices i−1 and j−1. Fill rows/columns in increasing order. Reconstruct by taking matching characters diagonally or following a neighbor with the same optimal value; ties may produce different LCSs. Time Θ(mn), table storage Θ(mn); two rows reduce value-only storage to O(min(m, n)), while ordinary reconstruction needs retained decisions or another technique. Example Worked microexample X=ABC,Y=AC: LCS is AC, length 2. Contiguous-substring matching would require a different recurrence, resetting a mismatch to zero. MIT6.006 Lecture16

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Interval DP: matrix chains and optimal BSTs
records.text: For matrix A_i of size p[i−1]×p[i], M[i, i]=0 and M[i, j]=min over i≤k<j of(M[i, k]+M[k+1, j]+p[i−1]p[k]p[j]). Fill by increasing interval length and store the split. Three matrices 10×30,30×5,5×60 cost 4500 under(AB)C versus 27000 under A(BC). Time O(n³), space O(n²); multiplication order stays fixed while parentheses change. For an OBST use sorted-key success weights p_i and gap failure weights q_i. Let W(i, j)=∑p_i.. p_j+∑q_(i−1).. q_j. Under the comparison-count convention, C(i, i−1)=0 and C(i, j)=W(i, j)+min_r(C(i, r−1)+C(r+1, j)); store r. CLRS-style dummy-node depths instead initialize empty cost to q_(i−1); final values differ by the fixed total gap weight. Basic time O(n³), space O(n²). Design and Analysis of Algorithms module Stony Brook University, Dynamic Programming

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Reliability design under a budget
records.text: Assume independent device failures. With m_i parallel copies of stage i, each reliability r_i, stage reliability is φ_i(m_i)=1−(1−r_i)^m_i. Series stages multiply: total∏φ_i. Choose integers m_i≥1 with∑m_i c_i≤B; extra copies improve reliability but consume budget. Correlated failures invalidate the simple independence formula. Let R[i, b] be best reliability for the first i stages within budget b. Base R[0, b]=1; maximize R[i−1, b−m c_i]φ_i(m) over feasible m≥1. Empty candidate sets give 0. Time is O(stages×budget×maximum copies), with O(budget) value storage; reconstruct retained copy counts. Example Worked microexample For costs 30,15,20, reliabilities 0.9,0.8,0.5 and budget 105, copy counts(1,2,2) cost 100 and yield 0.9×0.96×0.75=0.648. Three copies of the weak last stage with the others single cost 105 but yield only 0.63. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Exact TSP with subset DP
records.text: TSP asks for a minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex once and returning to its start; a shortest path need not visit all vertices or return. Fix start s. Let F(S, j) be minimum cost from s through exactly S, ending at j∈S. Base F({s}, s)=0. Transition F(S, j)=min_i∈S−{j}[F(S−{j}, i)+w(i, j)]. Finish with min_j≠s[F(V, j)+w(j, s)]. Missing edges cost∞. Store predecessor choices to reconstruct a tour. Held–Karp uses O(V²2^V) time and O(V 2^V) space, improving factorial enumeration but remaining exponential. Greedy nearest-neighbor is a heuristic without a general exactness guarantee; backtracking and branch and bound can also solve exact TSP. Specify the problem variant and algorithm before choosing a solution method. For Held–Karp, S contains the start s. Initialize F({s},s)=0 and impossible states to infinity; for larger sets, evaluate endpoints j other than s. These boundary cases prevent using a nonexistent predecessor state. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — BFS, DFS and graph representation
records.text: BFS marks a vertex when enqueued, explores neighbors with a FIFO queue and records predecessor/level. Levels give shortest paths by edge count in unweighted/equal-weight graphs. DFS marks on entry, recursively or iteratively explores an unvisited neighbor to completion, then resumes the parent. Run from each unvisited vertex for a full disconnected traversal. Adjacency lists give O(V+E) traversal time and O(V) auxiliary visited/queue/stack space; adjacency matrices give O(V²) scanning. State neighbor order before requesting one exact traversal sequence. Reverse DFS finish order gives a topological order only for DAGs. BFS/DFS being printed under a DP unit does not make ordinary traversal a DP optimization algorithm. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Articulation points and biconnected components
records.text: An articulation vertex increases the number of connected components when removed. In an undirected DFS, disc[u] is discovery time and low[u] is the smallest discovery number reachable from u’s subtree using downward tree edges and at most one back edge. Update low from children and nonparent back edges. A root is articulation if it has at least two DFS children; a nonroot u is articulation if some child v has low[v]≥disc[u]. Such a child cannot reach an ancestor of u without u. A bridge has the stricter condition low[v]>disc[u]. An edge stack can output a vertex-biconnected block when low[v]≥disc[u], popping through edge(u, v). With adjacency lists these checks cost O(V+E). Distinguish vertex-biconnectivity from strong connectivity in directed graphs. For a simple undirected graph initialize disc[u]=low[u]=++time on entry. For an unvisited neighbor v, push tree edge(u,v), DFS(v), then low[u]=min(low[u],low[v]). For a visited nonparent ancestor v, push the back edge once when disc[v]<disc[u] and use low[u]=min(low[u],disc[v]). After a child returns with low[v]>=disc[u], pop through(u,v) to output one block. Keep the separate root-child articulation rule and bridge test low[v]>disc[u]. Restart DFS at each unvisited vertex. For multigraphs skip the parent edge by identity rather than skipping every edge to the parent. Example A small procedure check Two triangles A-B-C-A and C-D-E-C, DFS order A,B,C,D,E: disc=(1,2,3,4,5), low=(1,1,1,3,3). Only C is articulation; no edge is a bridge; stack yields blocks{A-B,B-C,C-A} and{C-D,D-E,E-C}. low[D]=disc[C] shows why articulation uses>= but bridge uses>. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module IARCS, Articulation Points CMU15-451: Undirected DFS and Biconnected Components

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Backtracking template and safe pruning
records.text: Represent a partial assignment x[1.. k]. For each allowed next choice: assign it, test whether an extension remains possible, recurse if promising, and undo the assignment on return. Report complete feasible candidates; stop after one only if the task requests existence/a single answer. Explicit constraints restrict each variable’s domain; implicit constraints relate choices. Correctness requires exhaustive consideration of every feasible extension and pruning only impossible branches. Merely disliking a partial objective is not enough. DFS recursion uses space proportional to search depth, while total search can remain exponential. Memoizing equivalent states or stronger constraints can reduce work, but branch count depends on actual choices/tests. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — N-queens: row, column and diagonal tests
records.text: Use x[r]=column for one queen per row. Reject against earlier row i when x[r]=x[i] or |x[r]−x[i]|=|r−i|; distinct rows are built into the representation. Recurse after legal placement and remove it on return. Column and r−column/r+column sets permit constant-time conflict tests. Distinct columns leave at most n! complete permutations plus partial-node work; pruning does not guarantee polynomial time. Placement/conflict storage is O(n). Boards 2 and 3 have no solutions; state empty-board conventions. Example Worked microexample For n=4, column vector(2,4,1,3) is valid. Rows 1 and 2 with columns 2 and 3 would share a diagonal because both differences are 1, so that partial branch is rejected. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Subset sum: include/exclude and admissible bounds
records.text: Include/exclude each item while tracking current sum s and remaining sum R. For nonnegative weights prune s>target or s+R<target. On equality report the subset, considering zero-weight extensions if all subsets are needed. Sorting positive weights can strengthen tests but cannot force inclusion of the next item. With negative values, s>target may recover later; use valid attainable-range bounds. There are up to 2^n subsets and O(n) recursion depth. Define whether duplicate-valued items count by index. Example Worked microexample For{3,4,5,6}, target 13, subset{3,4,6} succeeds. At s=9 with remaining total 3, s+R=12<13 proves failure. At s=9 with remaining 4, equality can still be reached. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Graph coloring: feasibility versus minimum colors
records.text: For a fixed m, assign colors 1…m to vertices, rejecting a color used by an already colored neighbor. Backtrack when all colors fail. At most m^V complete assignments exist, with additional checking cost; a simple O(V)-per-test implementation gives an exponential bound. A self-loop makes proper coloring impossible. The decision question asks whether m colors suffice; optimization asks for the chromatic number. Trying increasing m with a complete decision search finds the minimum. Greedy coloring chooses a color by vertex order and may use too many; it is not a general optimum proof. An odd cycle needs 3 colors; an edge-containing bipartite graph needs 2, and an edgeless nonempty graph needs 1. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Hamiltonian cycles and permutation search
records.text: Fix a start vertex to avoid rotational duplicates. Extend a path with an unused vertex adjacent to its current end. At V vertices require an edge back to the start; otherwise backtrack. A Hamiltonian cycle visits vertices once, while an Euler cycle concerns visiting edges. Fixing the start leaves up to(V−1)! candidate permutations, with polynomial checking overhead. For a simple undirected graph with at least 3 vertices, a degree 1 vertex or articulation point rules out a Hamiltonian cycle, but their absence does not prove one exists. TSP optimizes a weighted Hamiltonian tour; the decision existence search alone does not minimize its cost. Reversed undirected tours may be equivalent if enumerating unique cycles. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Branch and bound: node states and bound direction
records.text: A live node is generated and still eligible for expansion; the E-node is currently expanded; a dead node is finished or pruned. FIFO selects live nodes by queue order, LIFO by stack order, and least-cost/best-bound uses a priority queue. Selection changes work/storage; valid bounds preserve exactness. For minimization, an incumbent feasible solution supplies an upper bound U; a partial node supplies a lower bound L on every completion. Prune if L≥U when only one optimum/value is needed. For maximization, feasible profit is a lower bound and an optimistic completion estimate is an upper bound; prune if upper≤incumbent. Keep equality branches when all optimal solutions must be enumerated. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Knapsack branch and bound
records.text: Sort positive-weight/value items by decreasing density and branch include/exclude. Reject overweight nodes. To bound a node’s possible profit, fill its remaining capacity fractionally from remaining items; this relaxation can only improve on 0/1 feasibility, so its value is an upper bound. A whole-item feasible completion updates the incumbent; the fractional result itself is not a legal 0/1 answer. With capacity 10 and items(6,12),(5,8),(5,8), the root fractional bound is 18.4: take the first and 4/5 of the second. The first-item-in branch has whole-item value 12; excluding it permits the two other items, value 16. Continue until every live upper bound is≤16 to certify optimality. Avoid downward floating-point rounding that could invalidate the bound; worst-case search remains exponential. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — TSP branch and bound by matrix reduction
records.text: For directed TSP, set diagonal/forbidden entries to∞. Subtract each finite row minimum, then each finite column minimum, accumulating reductions. Every tour uses one entry per row/column, so their sum is a lower bound; the relaxed assignment may contain disjoint subtours. When including edge i→j, remove its used row/column, prevent premature subtours, reduce again and add the selected reduced-edge cost and new reductions to the parent bound. Compare bounds with the best complete tour and expand a promising live node. Never treat a reduced matrix’s zeros as proof of a complete valid tour. Branch on an undecided edge i->j. The include child deletes row i/column j and adds its selected reduced cost plus new reductions to the parent bound. The exclude child sets that entry to infinity and adds only new reductions. Keep forced in/out-degree at most one. Track each forced path from head h to tail t and forbid t->h until the path contains every vertex; this blocks premature cycles. A required residual row/column with no finite choice is infeasible and pruned. Accept only one complete cycle through every vertex, not a set of disjoint cycles. Example A small procedure check For four cities, cheap forced edges1->2,2->1 and3->4,4->3 satisfy one incoming/outgoing edge per city but are two disjoint2-cycles, not a tour. Once forced path1->2 is formed, forbid2->1 while fewer than4 vertices are in the path. Preserve the existing3-city reduction example: bound25 equals tour cost25. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module BYU CS312: TSP Branch and Bound

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — P, NP, reductions and encoding size
records.text: P contains decision problems solvable deterministically in polynomial input-bit time. NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine. NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains open. A polynomial many-one reduction A≤p B transforms each A-instance into a B-instance preserving yes/no. To prove B NP-hard, reduce a known hard A to B, not the reverse. NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP; optimization TSP is normally called NP-hard, while its bounded-tour decision form is NP-complete. A valid proposed tour and its cost are easy to check, but certifying global optimality is another task. Pseudo-polynomial O(nW) knapsack is not polynomial in the bit length of W. University of Waterloo CS365, P versus NP UC Davis ECS120, NP-Completeness and Reductions

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Check algorithm specifications and cost assumptions
records.text: For p=10,n=5, if(n>p) cout<<(n+p) skips output and terminates. Skipping this output does not by itself violate feasibility, finiteness or control flow. Efficiency or a missing required output needs a specification. A precise degree for 3n?+7n+12 requires the missing exponent; fixed nonnegative integer exponents still give polynomials. Use valid declarations rather than ini/inl or a redeclared n; exact counts also need a primitive-cost model. Justify the result from the specification, valid code and cost assumptions. Design and Analysis of Algorithms module

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Problem specification and correctness

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 1 · Q00065
records.text: Q00065 Question 1 DAA12 DAA16 Which one of the following is not an example of divide and conquer algorithm? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Quick sort B Binary searching C Merge sort D Heap sort Heap sort DAA16 explicitly classifies heap sort as outside standard divide and conquer: it builds a heap and repeatedly extracts its maximum. Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts ranges; merge sort recursively sorts halves; binary search recursively or iteratively reduces to a smaller half. Thus heap sort is the single exclusion among the listed algorithms. A incorrect Quicksort partitions its input and recursively sorts the resulting smaller ranges, a standard divide-and-conquer pattern. B incorrect Binary search repeatedly reduces a sorted search interval to one half; the note treats this as divide-and-conquer. C incorrect Merge sort divides into halves, sorts each recursively, and combines them by merging. D correct Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly restores it after extraction, rather than independently sorting and combining subinstances.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 2 · Q00149
records.text: Q00149 Question 2 DAA06 DAA02 For n≥2, determine the tight asymptotic running time of this syntax-repaired C++-style pseudocode under mathematical-integer, unit-cost arithmetic and output: function(n) { a=0; print("Enter a positive integer"); for(i=1; i<n; i*=2) a=i; return 0; } Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Θ(n log n) B Θ(n²) C Θ(log n) D Θ(n) Θ(log n) The loop visits i=1,2,4,… while i<n, so it executes ceil(log₂n) iterations. Each iteration has constant work under the stated arithmetic and output model, and initialization, the fixed prompt and return add constant overhead. The total is therefore Θ(log n). A incorrect n log n grows faster and is not the tight order. B incorrect Quadratic grows faster and is not the tight order. C correct The doubling loop takes logarithmically many constant-cost iterations. D incorrect Linear is a looser upper bound rather than the tight order.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 3 · Q00173
records.text: Q00173 Question 3 DAA09 DAA01 Recursion is a method in which the solution of a problem depends on: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Larger instances of the same problem B Smaller instances of the same problem C Larger instances of different problems D Smaller instances of different problems Smaller instances of the same problem Recursion reduces a problem to simpler instances of that same problem (PDF p.14). Thus smaller same-problem instances, with a terminating base case, match the definition. A incorrect Larger instances do not implement the reducing step on p.14. B correct Smaller instances preserve the problem while reducing its size (p.14). C incorrect Changing both size upward and problem identity fails the recursive reduction (p.14). D incorrect Smaller instances of a different problem are not the same-problem recursion described on p.14.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 4 · Q00175
records.text: Q00175 Question 4 DAA25 DAA19 If an optimal solution can be created for a problem by constructing optimal solutions for its subproblems, the problem possesses property. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Overlapping subproblems B Optimal substructure C Memoization D Greedy Optimal substructure Optimal substructure means an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems (PDF p.28). The principle of optimality on p.49 expresses exactly the construction in the stem. A incorrect Overlap concerns repeated subproblems, not optimality of their solutions (pp.28,49). B correct This is the named property defined on p.28. C incorrect Memoization stores computed answers; it is not the optimality property (p.49). D incorrect Greedy is a design strategy requiring additional choice conditions (p.28).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 5 · Q00176
records.text: Q00176 Question 5 DAA25 DAA26 If a problem can be broken into subproblems that are reused several times, the problem possesses property. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Overlapping subproblems B Optimal substructure C Memoization D Greedy Overlapping subproblems Reusing a subproblem several times means subproblems share sub-subproblems, the contrast made on PDF p.48. This is overlapping subproblems; storing an answer is a response to that property, not the property itself. A correct Shared sub-subproblems and repeated work are described on p.48. B incorrect Optimal substructure concerns optimal solutions rather than repetition (p.28). C incorrect Saving results in a table addresses repeated work; it is not the reuse property (p.48). D incorrect A greedy choice is unrelated to whether subproblems recur (pp.28,48).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 6 · Q00177
records.text: Q00177 Question 6 DAA12 If a problem can be solved by combining optimal solutions to non-overlapping sub-problems, the strategy is called _______. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Dynamic programming B Divide and Conquer C Recursion D Greedy Divide and Conquer PDF p.48 explicitly contrasts independent subproblems in divide and conquer with shared sub-subproblems in dynamic programming. Combining independent solutions therefore identifies divide and conquer; optimality alone does not identify greedy. A incorrect Dynamic programming is motivated by non-independent shared subproblems (p.48). B correct Independent subproblems are recursively solved and combined (pp.17,48). C incorrect Recursion is a mechanism; the more specific independent-split-and-combine strategy is given on p.48. D incorrect Greedy needs a locally justified choice, which this stem does not specify (p.48 contrast).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 7 · Q00283
records.text: Q00283 Question 7 DAA08 Suppose we want to determine the efficiency of the algorithm, then how we can measure the space factor Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A To count the maximum memory required by the algorithm B To count the average memory required by the algorithm C To count the minimum memory required by the algorithm D To count the maximum disk space needed by the algorithm To count the maximum memory required by the algorithm Space needed to run to completion must allow the program to finish without exhausting memory (PDF p.6). Hence the required allocation is peak simultaneously needed memory for that execution; average or minimum use may underallocate. A correct Maximum simultaneously required memory supports completion (p.6). B incorrect Average use can fall below a later peak and cannot guarantee enough memory (p.6). C incorrect Minimum use cannot supply the full execution requirement (p.6). D incorrect Disk capacity alone does not measure the program memory requirement defined on p.6.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 8 · Q00284
records.text: Q00284 Question 8 DAA02 Two main measures for the efficiency of an algorithm are Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Processor and memory B Data and space C Complexity and capacity D Time and space Time and space Performance is stated in computer memory and time (PDF p.4), and complexity is expressed as space and time (p.6). The pair is therefore time and space. A incorrect Processor is a device, not the time measure paired with memory (p.4). B incorrect Data is the problem content, not one of the two resource measures (p.6). C incorrect Complexity and capacity are not the stated two measures (p.6). D correct Time and space are explicitly named on p.6.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 9 · Q00285
records.text: Q00285 Question 9 DAA28 For the standard Floyd–Warshall implementation on an n-vertex weighted graph, using constant-time distance arithmetic and the full k,i,j loops, what is the tight running-time bound? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Θ(n²) B Θ(n³) C Θ(n) D Θ(n⁴) Θ(n³) Floyd–Warshall considers each intermediate vertex k and updates every ordered pair i,j. The three independent n-sized loop ranges perform Θ(n³) constant-cost updates. The n² output table explains storage, not the time of this implementation. Other graph assumptions can support different algorithms, so this is the cost of the explicitly named method rather than a universal best-achievable APSP bound. A incorrect Quadratic counts pair storage but misses the intermediate-vertex loop. B correct Three full n-sized loops give cubic time. C incorrect Linear is too small even for the explicit pair table. D incorrect Quartic is a loose upper bound rather than the tight cost.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 10 · Q00287
records.text: Q00287 Question 10 DAA08 A recursive execution has n simultaneously active call levels, each retaining Theta(1) storage. Count only live call-frame storage. What is the tightest listed asymptotic upper bound on its peak space? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(n'2) B O(n) C O(1) D O(log n) B. O(n) All n call frames are live at the deepest point. Each frame retains a fixed positive amount of storage, so their combined peak space is proportional to n. This gives Theta(n) space and makes O(n) the tightest listed upper bound. O(n²) is a looser valid upper bound, while constant and logarithmic space cannot hold for n simultaneously live constant-size frames. A incorrect Quadratic is a valid but looser upper bound than the requested tightest one. B correct Linear space tightly bounds n live constant-size frames. C incorrect Constant space cannot hold as the number of live frames grows. D incorrect Logarithmic space cannot hold for n live constant-size frames.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 11 · Q00295
records.text: Q00295 Question 11 DAA14 DAA16 Which of the following is a Divide and Conquer algorithm? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Merge Sort B Heap Sort C Selection Sort D Bubble Sort Merge sort DAA14 splits into halves, recursively sorts each, and merges the results, directly implementing divide and conquer. DAA16 excludes standard heap sort from that category and describes selection’s repeated minimum and bubble’s adjacent passes. Only Merge Sort among these options has the specified independent recursive decomposition and combination mechanism. A correct Merge sort recursively solves halves and combines them through a merge. B incorrect Standard heapsort builds and repeatedly restores a heap rather than applying the standard independent-subproblem decomposition. C incorrect Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum instead of recursively sorting halves. D incorrect Bubble repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions instead of recursively decomposing subinstances.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 12 · Q00373
records.text: Q00373 Question 12 DAA06 In Average case, if operation takes ƒ(n) time in execution, then m operations will take? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A ƒ(n) B f(m) C mf(n) D nf(m) mf(n) Adding m execution costs each with mean f(n) gives mean total m*f(n) by the consecutive-block addition rule (PDF p.12), using the average-case meaning on p.14. This assumes n is fixed and each of the m operations has the stated mean; no independence is needed to add expected costs. A incorrect f(n) counts only one mean execution cost (pp.12,14). B incorrect f(m) changes the argument instead of adding m costs (p.12). C correct m equal mean costs sum to m*f(n) (p.12). D incorrect n*f(m) swaps operation count and input size without justification (p.12).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 13 · Q00376
records.text: Q00376 Question 13 DAA04 DAA05 O(1) means computing time is __________________ Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Constant B Quadratic C Linear D Cubic Constant O(1) is a bounded constant upper growth rate independent of input size. The related PDF p.3 visually orders constant K before log n, n, n log n and n^2; the assigned PDF p.14 explains comparison by growth rate. A correct A constant bound does not increase with n (cross-module p.3 growth diagram). B incorrect Quadratic corresponds to n squared, which grows with n (assigned p.14). C incorrect Linear is proportional to n, unlike 1 (assigned p.14). D incorrect Cubic is proportional to n cubed, unlike 1 (assigned p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 14 · Q00378
records.text: Q00378 Question 14 DAA15 DAA16 Which of the following sorting algorithm is of divide-and-conquer type? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Bubble sort B Insertion sort C Quick sort D Selection sort Quicksort DAA15 partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts smaller ranges, which is the divide-and-conquer strategy. The other ordinary methods in DAA16 use adjacent passes, sorted-prefix insertion, or repeated suffix-minimum selection. They do not use the same recursive partition decomposition. Thus Quick sort is the unique matching main choice. A incorrect Bubble uses repeated adjacent comparisons rather than recursive partitioning. B incorrect Insertion grows a sorted prefix by shifting larger preceding values. C correct Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting smaller ranges. D incorrect Selection repeatedly picks a suffix minimum rather than recursively partitioning and combining.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 15 · Q00718
records.text: Q00718 Question 15 DAA02 DAA04 of an algorithm refers to defining the mathematical bound/framing of its run-time performance? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Space complexity B Asymptotic analysis C Time complexity D none of the above Asymptotic analysis Asymptotic analysis studies the limiting growth of running time with input size and groups functions by growth bounds (PDF p.14). Time complexity is the resource function being studied; the bounding analysis is asymptotic analysis. A incorrect Space concerns memory, not bounding the stated runtime (p.14). B correct The growth-rate and bounding analysis is explicitly titled Asymptotic Analysis (p.14). C incorrect Time complexity describes runtime; asymptotic analysis classifies its growth as asked (p.14). D incorrect The bounding concept is provided by the p.14 section, so “none” fails.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 16 · Q00719
records.text: Q00719 Question 16 DAA12 DAA27 DAA24 Which described implementation uses dynamic programming through stored dependent subproblem values? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Multistage DAG shortest paths using stored reverse-topological cost-to-go values B Single-source shortest paths by Dijkstra on nonnegative edges C Merge sort D Chess game-tree search without cached subproblem values Multistage DAG shortest paths using stored reverse-topological cost-to-go values Multistage DAG paths can be solved by storing the best cost-to-go for each vertex and evaluating vertices in reverse topological order. Each value combines outgoing-edge costs with already solved successor values, which is dynamic programming. The specified Dijkstra implementation uses greedy finalization, merge sort uses independent halves, and uncached chess tree search does not reuse stored subproblem values as described. A correct The reverse-topological cost recurrence reuses solved successor values. B incorrect Dijkstra uses greedy minimum-distance finalization under nonnegative weights. C incorrect Merge sort divides into independent halves and merges them. D incorrect The stipulated uncached search does not reuse solved state values.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 17 · Q00720
records.text: Q00720 Question 17 DAA22 DAA19 Optimal merge pattern is an example of _________ Algorithm design Approach Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Dynamic Programming B Divide and Conquered C Greedy D Back tracking Greedy The optimal-merge construction explicitly chooses the two smallest files at each step (PDF p.43). That repeated local selection is called a greedy attempt on the page and gives the listed example an optimal merge pattern. A incorrect No table of overlapping subproblems drives the p.43 construction. B incorrect The pairing order is chosen by repeated smallest-file selection, not a predetermined independent split (p.43). C correct The module explicitly calls this selection rule greedy (p.43). D incorrect The described rule does not backtrack over earlier pairings (p.43).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 18 · Q00898
records.text: Q00898 Question 18 DAA03 For each input length n, a report records the smallest number of comparisons attained over all legal inputs of that length. Which case-analysis function is the report recording? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Average time B Small time C . Worst time D Best time D. Best time At each fixed length n, the report selects the legal input with the smallest comparison count. This records best-case time under a comparison-count model. Worst case would record the largest count, and average case would take an expectation under a specified distribution. Comparing different input lengths is a separate growth analysis, so the application preserves the fixed-size meaning of Best time. A incorrect Average time is an expectation, not the minimum. B incorrect Small time is not the standard case-analysis term. C incorrect Worst time is the maximum over inputs of the fixed size. D correct Best time is the minimum over legal inputs of that fixed size.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 19 · Q00925
records.text: Q00925 Question 19 DAA11 Which statement about proving worst-case lower bounds for all comparison-based sorting algorithms is FALSE? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A A comparison decision tree must distinguish n! possible orders of distinct keys. B Solving a recurrence for one chosen sorting algorithm, by itself, proves a lower bound for every algorithm in the comparison class. C Suppressing constant factors in asymptotic notation does not by itself invalidate a lower-bound proof. D A decision-tree argument can establish an Ω(n log n) worst-case comparison bound even when array indexing is allowed. B. A single algorithm’s recurrence alone does not prove a class-wide lower bound. A recurrence describes the running time of the particular algorithm it models. An upper or tight bound for that algorithm does not exclude a different comparison algorithm using fewer operations, so B is false. The class-wide decision-tree argument instead distinguishes n! orders of distinct keys and needs height at least log₂(n!), giving Ω(n log n). Ignoring constants and allowing ordinary array access do not defeat that comparison-count argument. A incorrect This is a true premise of the comparison decision-tree lower-bound argument, so it is not the requested false statement. B correct This is false: a recurrence for one algorithm does not lower-bound every other algorithm. C incorrect This is true: asymptotic lower bounds intentionally disregard constant factors. D incorrect This is true: the bound concerns comparisons, not a prohibition on array indexing.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 20 · Q00929
records.text: Q00929 Question 20 DAA06 For integer n≥0, treat the code below as mathematical-integer RAM pseudocode: arithmetic is exact and unit-cost, with no overflow. Charge 1 unit for each initialization, comparison, loop increment and return; charge 1 for the addition and 1 for assignment in sum=sum+1. Ignore declarations, parameter passing and function-call overhead. What is T(n)? total(n) { sum=0; for(i=1;i<=n;i++) sum=sum+1; return sum; } Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A 5n+5 B 4n²+4 C 6n+2 D 4n+4 4n+4 In this exact-integer model, the two initializations cost 2 units. The test i<=n runs n+1 times, the increment runs n times, and addition plus assignment costs 2n units. The return costs one unit. Thus T(n)=2+(n+1)+n+2n+1=4n+4, including n=0. Unbounded mathematical arithmetic keeps the final increment defined throughout the stated domain. A incorrect 5n+5 does not match the specified operation counts. B incorrect Quadratic growth does not match a single n-iteration constant-body loop. C incorrect 6n+2 charges operations differently from the stated model. D correct The complete count is 2+(n+1)+n+2n+1=4n+4.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 21 · Q01211
records.text: Q01211 Question 21 DAA02 Which option most completely covers the listed factors that affect a program’s exact elapsed running time, including its workload and execution environment? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Processor speed B Current processor load C Input size of the given algorithm D All All listed factors affect observed runtime. Input size influences how many operations the algorithm performs. Processor speed influences how quickly that work executes, and competing processor load influences the resources available during the run. All three can therefore affect exact elapsed time. Each individual factor is true but incomplete as an answer to the combined-factor question; D includes the whole set without confusing elapsed measurements with an abstract operation-count bound. A incorrect True but incomplete: processor speed matters, but it omits current load and input size. B incorrect True but incomplete: competing load matters, but it omits processor speed and input size. C incorrect True but incomplete: input size matters, but it omits the execution-environment factors. D correct All three listed factors contribute to exact elapsed time.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 22 · Q01230
records.text: Q01230 Question 22 DAA29 DAA34 Which of the following is an example of a Dynamic Programming algorithm? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Breadth First Search B Depth First Search C Dijkstra's Algorithm D Knapsack Problem Knapsack Problem The module develops 0/1 knapsack in the dynamic-programming unit (PDF p.71; application list p.49), with alternatives of including or excluding an item. Dijkstra is placed in the greedy unit (p.46). BFS and DFS are traversal techniques, rather than the shared-subproblem optimization example intended here (p.85). A incorrect Breadth-first search is a traversal; p.85 separates graph search from the knapsack optimization example. B incorrect Depth-first search is a traversal; the dynamic-programming item-selection example is p.71. C incorrect Dijkstra appears under the greedy unit on p.46, not as the intended dynamic-programming example. D correct The 0/1 knapsack variant is explicitly developed in the dynamic-programming unit on p.71.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 23 · Q01232
records.text: Q01232 Question 23 DAA01 DAA02 When designing an algorithm for a specified implementation environment, which option most completely covers the listed resource, correctness and alternative-method considerations? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Whether the method respects the chosen hardware/resource cost model. B Whether the software implementation correctly realizes the specified method. C If there is more than one way to solve the problem. D All of the above All of the above Algorithm design starts with inputs, outputs, constraints and correctness, then evaluates resource use under a stated model. For an implementation, respecting the selected hardware/resource assumptions and ensuring the program implements the method correctly both matter. Comparing alternative solution methods is also legitimate. Thus the all-of-the-above option combines all three considerations; none of the individual choices alone covers the entire set. A incorrect Respecting the resource model matters but is only one consideration. B incorrect Implementation correctness matters but is only one consideration. C incorrect Comparing alternatives matters but is only one consideration. D correct All three stated considerations belong in the implementation-aware design.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 24 · SM0007
records.text: SM0007 Question 24 DAA01 DAA23 Assume you have a weighted graph G with a set of vertices V and set of edges E. Which one of the following is an optimization problem on the graph? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Traverse all vertices in graph G B Is vertex p in V reachable from vertex q in V in graph G C Find minimum spanning tree from graph G D How many cycles are there in graph G Find minimum spanning tree from graph G An optimization problem seeks a feasible solution minimizing or maximizing an objective (PDF p.27). The minimum spanning tree minimizes total edge weight while connecting every vertex (p.36); the other tasks ask for traversal, a yes/no fact or a count. A incorrect Traversal asks to visit vertices rather than optimize a weight (pp.27,36). B incorrect Reachability is a decision question rather than minimization (pp.27,85). C correct Minimum total tree weight is the optimization objective (p.36). D incorrect Counting cycles asks for a number, with no minimization or maximization criterion (p.27).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 25 · SM0031
records.text: SM0031 Question 25 DAA03 DAA04 For an average-cost function f(n)=E[T(n)] under a specified input distribution, which notation expresses a tight constant-factor growth bound relative to g(n)? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A f(n)∈Ω(g(n)) B f(n)∈O(g(n)) C f(n)∈ω(g(n)) D f(n)∈Θ(g(n)) f(n)∈Θ(g(n)) Average case first takes an expectation under the specified distribution. A tight growth relation for that resulting function requires both an eventual upper and lower constant-factor bound relative to g, which is Θ. Big-O supplies only an upper bound, Ω only a lower bound, and little-ω a strict asymptotic lower relation. None of the symbols intrinsically means average case. A incorrect Ω supplies a lower bound without the matching upper bound. B incorrect O supplies an upper bound without the matching lower bound. C incorrect Little-ω means f/g tends to infinity rather than constant-factor equivalence. D correct Θ states both constant-factor upper and lower bounds.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 26 · SM0065
records.text: SM0065 Question 26 DAA22 DAA16 DAA23 DAA14 Size of large data files can be reduced to save storage disk space. Which algorithm is appropriate to reduce the size of large files? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Heap sort algorithm B Prim's algorithm C Merge sort algorithm D Huffman encoding algorithm D. Huffman encoding algorithm Huffman coding assigns prefix-free bit strings to symbols using their frequencies, minimizing the weighted code length in its model. It can therefore reduce the storage required for data represented with those codes. Heap sort and merge sort instead reorder items, while Prim builds a minimum spanning tree of a weighted graph. Those other objectives do not encode file contents more compactly. Metadata overhead still prevents a universal compression guarantee for every file. A incorrect Heap sort reorders items by repeatedly extracting a heap extreme; it does not encode file symbols. B incorrect Prim minimizes graph-connection weight, not encoded file length. C incorrect Merge sort orders records by recursively sorting and merging, rather than encoding symbols. D correct Huffman builds a frequency-based prefix code minimizing its weighted length.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 27 · SM0083
records.text: SM0083 Question 27 DAA03 DAA04 For the worst-cost function f(n)=max over size-n inputs T(input), which notation expresses a tight constant-factor bound relative to g(n)? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A f(n)∈ω(g(n)) B f(n)∈Θ(g(n)) C f(n)∈o(g(n)) D f(n)∈Ω(g(n)) f(n)∈Θ(g(n)) Worst case maximizes cost over all inputs of a fixed size. Once that function is defined, Θ expresses matching constant-factor upper and lower bounds relative to g. Little-o and little-ω describe strict asymptotic relations, and Ω alone supplies only a lower bound. The answer concerns tightness of the bound, not a claim that any notation inherently selects the worst input case. A incorrect Little-ω gives a strict lower-growth relation. B correct Θ gives matching constant-factor upper and lower bounds. C incorrect Little-o gives a strict upper-growth relation. D incorrect Ω alone lacks the required upper bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 28 · SM0087
records.text: SM0087 Question 28 DAA23 Which one of the following algorithms can be used to extract a Minimum Spanning Tree from an input graph? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Prim's algorithm B Huffman encoding algorithm C Dijkstra's algorithm D Merge sort algorithm Prim's algorithm The module explicitly names Prim among the two minimum-cost spanning-tree methods (PDF p.37). Huffman codes optimize expected message length (p.45), Dijkstra is single-source path search (p.46), and merge sort orders arrays (p.21). A correct Prim is explicitly a minimum-cost spanning-tree method (p.37). B incorrect Huffman builds codes, not a spanning tree of the input graph (p.45). C incorrect Dijkstra targets source-to-vertex paths, a different objective (p.46). D incorrect Merge sort combines sorted sequences, not graph edges (p.21).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 29 · SM0214
records.text: SM0214 Question 29 DAA03 Which analysis case calculates the upper bound on running time of an algorithm? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Optimal case B Best case C Average case D Worst case Worst case Worst-case time is the maximum time over the inputs under consideration and therefore bounds all their runtimes (PDF p.14). This is the case-analysis upper bound, distinct from the separate question of an asymptotic bound on that maximum. A incorrect Optimal case is not a defined case function on p.14. B incorrect Best case minimizes rather than bounds all runtime values from above (p.14). C incorrect An average need not exceed every observation (p.14). D correct Worst case supplies the all-input bound explicitly described on p.14.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 30 · SM0249
records.text: SM0249 Question 30 DAA05 An algorithm has unit-cost running-time function T(n)=3nᵏ+7n+12, where k is a fixed integer with k≥2 independent of n. Which listed growth class describes it? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Linear B Polynomial C Constant D Exponential Polynomial A fixed exponent k≥2 makes the leading term 3nᵏ dominate 7n+12. The resulting function has Θ(nᵏ) growth, which is polynomial. It is not linear because k exceeds one, and the positive growing terms exclude constant growth. Exponential growth would instead put the input in an exponent of a fixed base, a different form from the fixed-degree polynomial here. A incorrect k≥2 prevents linear growth. B correct A fixed degree k gives polynomial growth. C incorrect The positive n-dependent terms prevent constant growth. D incorrect A fixed-degree power is not exponential growth.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 31 · SM0302
records.text: SM0302 Question 31 DAA08 The amount of memory needed to run an algorithm to completion is known as: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Space complexity B Time complexity C Worst case D Best case Space complexity Space complexity is explicitly defined as the memory needed to run to completion (PDF p.6). This is a resource quantity, not an input-case category. A correct This is the exact definition on p.6. B incorrect Time measures duration rather than memory (p.6 contrast). C incorrect Worst case selects inputs; it is not the memory-resource name (p.6). D incorrect Best case selects inputs; it is not the memory-resource name (p.6).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 32 · SS116
records.text: SS116 Question 32 DAA07 Interpret the following as mathematical-integer pseudocode with constant-cost arithmetic and print operations. Which offered Big-O upper bounds on the full running time are valid? Select all that apply; the bounds need not be tight. for i=0,...,n−1: for j=i,...,i²−1: if j mod i == 0: for k=0,...,j−1: print("*") An upper limit below the lower limit makes an empty loop. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(n⁵) B O(n⁷) C O(n log n) D O(n²) O(n⁵); O(n⁷) For i=0 and i=1 the j loop is empty, so no division by zero occurs. For i≥2, successful j values are i,2i,…,(i−1)i. Their k-loop work totals i²(i−1)/2=Θ(i³), and summing over i yields Θ(n⁴). Consequently both O(n⁵) and O(n⁷) are valid loose upper bounds, while the two smaller offered rates cannot bound the work. A correct A quartic function is also O(n⁵). B correct A quartic function is also O(n⁷). C incorrect n log n is too small to upper-bound quartic work. D incorrect n² is too small to upper-bound quartic work.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 33 · SS120
records.text: SS120 Question 33 DAA01 DAA02 Which claims about abstract algorithms are NOT true? Select all that apply. In C, platform considerations mean choosing realistic resource constraints, not making source language part of the definition. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Is step wise logical description of how to solve the problem B ls equivalent to the programming language code C Should be developed by considering the platforms on which it runs D Its abstract definition requires the details of a particular programming language. ls equivalent to the programming language code; Its abstract definition requires the details of a particular programming language. An algorithm is a definite executable method independent of a particular source language. Equating it with programming-language code, or making that language’s details essential to its abstract definition, is therefore false. A stepwise logical description is appropriate. Resource constraints and a platform-aware cost model can legitimately inform implementation choices without changing the underlying method’s language independence. Thus B and D are the false claims. A incorrect A stepwise logical description is compatible with an algorithm. B correct The abstract method is not identical to a source-language implementation. C incorrect Realistic resource constraints may inform design, so C is not selected. D correct Programming-language details are not essential to the abstract method.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 34 · SS132
records.text: SS132 Question 34 DAA06 For integer n>=0, determine the tightest listed growth bound for this mathematical-integer pseudocode. Arithmetic, loop-control operations and each print operation have unit cost; ignore output-digit length. function someFunction(n) { for (i=0; i<10*n; i=i+1) { print(n); } } Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(n) B O(n²) C O(log n) D O(log(2n)) A. O(n) The loop body runs 10n times. Each iteration performs a constant amount of loop-control work and one unit-cost print, while initialization and the final failed condition check contribute only constant additional work. The total therefore has linear growth. Quadratic is a looser upper bound, while logarithmic growth is too small. The explicit mathematical and output-cost model avoids syntax and representation-cost distractions. A correct A constant multiple of n iterations gives the tight linear bound. B incorrect Quadratic is a looser bound rather than the requested tightest one. C incorrect Logarithmic growth is too small for 10n body executions. D incorrect log(2n) differs from log n only by a constant and is also too small.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 35 · SS141
records.text: SS141 Question 35 DAA03 Which of the following analysis mechanism defines the input for which the algorithm takes the least time (fastest time to complete)? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Standard Case B Average case C Worst case D Best case Best case The least runtime among inputs of a fixed size is best-case time, the fastest case in the p.14 three-case classification. It is not the average or worst case. A incorrect Standard case is not a defined category on p.14. B incorrect Average case concerns a distribution or average set, not a minimum (p.14). C incorrect Worst case takes the slowest input (p.14). D correct Best case is the minimum-time case intended by p.14.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 36 · AM0344
records.text: AM0344 Question 36 DAA02 Which described activity is outside analysis of an algorithm’s resource costs? Interpret dynamic analysis as measuring executed operations or storage. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Asymptotic analysis B Experimental analysis C Dynamic analysis D Graph connectivity analysis of the input data, without examining algorithm resource costs Graph connectivity analysis of the input data, without examining algorithm resource costs Asymptotic analysis studies resource growth, experimental analysis measures runs, and dynamic observation can measure executed operations or storage. The graph alternative asks only a mathematical connectivity question about input data, expressly without examining algorithm costs. It is outside the resource-analysis task as described, although graph-based representations can certainly support valid resource analysis in other contexts. This scope avoids an unsupported universal taxonomy. A incorrect Asymptotic analysis studies resource growth. B incorrect Experimental analysis measures resource costs of actual runs. C incorrect The stipulated dynamic analysis observes executed costs. D correct The stated connectivity-only task does not examine algorithm resource costs.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 37 · AM0345
records.text: AM0345 Question 37 DAA02 DAA03 What is the primary growth-related purpose of asymptotic analysis? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A To measure the actual running time of an algorithm B To determine the best-case scenario for an algorithm C To analyze the behavior of an algorithm as the input size increases D To evaluate the correctness of an algorithm To analyze the behavior of an algorithm as the input size increases Asymptotic analysis abstracts how resource use grows with input size. It can analyze best-, average- or worst-cost functions, but does not itself choose one input case or measure actual elapsed seconds. Those measurements depend on environment and workload. Correctness is a separate obligation to meet the specification. Hence C states the primary growth-related purpose among these choices. A incorrect Actual elapsed-time measurement is experimental. B incorrect Asymptotic analysis is not restricted to the best case. C correct It analyzes resource behavior as input size grows. D incorrect Growth bounds do not prove correctness.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 38 · AM0346
records.text: AM0346 Question 38 DAA04 DAA16 Which notation expresses a general asymptotic upper bound on an algorithm’s worst-cost function, allowing equality up to constant factors and not requiring a matching lower bound? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Big O notation (O) B Theta notation (Θ) C Omega notation (Ω) D Small o notation (o) Big O notation (O) Big-O states an eventual constant-factor upper bound and allows the bounded function to have the same order as its comparator. Θ additionally requires a lower bound, Ω is a lower-bound relation, and little-o requires strictly slower growth. The worst-case function is selected separately by maximizing over equal-size inputs; Big-O itself does not mean worst case. The explicit upper-bound requirement uniquely identifies A. A correct O gives the requested non-strict upper bound. B incorrect Θ requires a matching lower bound as well. C incorrect Ω gives a lower bound. D incorrect Little-o requires strictly slower growth.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 39 · AM0347
records.text: AM0347 Question 39 DAA13 For binary search on a nonempty sorted random-access array, what is the tight best-case time when the key may be at the initial midpoint? Use constant-time comparisons. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Θ(1) B Θ(log n) C Θ(n) D Θ(n²) Θ(1) If the sought key is at the first midpoint, binary search finds it after one constant-time comparison and returns. This is Θ(1) best-case time, regardless of the array length. The logarithmic bound describes its worst case, not this fastest legal input at fixed size. The linear and quadratic alternatives are likewise not tight for the midpoint-match case. A correct An initial midpoint match takes constant work. B incorrect Logarithmic describes worst-case search depth, not the tight best case. C incorrect Linear is not tight for a one-comparison match. D incorrect Quadratic is not tight for a one-comparison match.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 40 · AM0348
records.text: AM0348 Question 40 DAA16 DAA06 For ordinary array insertion sort on n distinct keys, with constant-time comparisons and shifts, what is the tight worst-case running time? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Θ(log n) B Θ(n) C Θ(n log n) D Θ(n²) Θ(n²) A descending input makes each inserted key move across every earlier key in the sorted prefix. The work sums as 1+2+⋯+(n−1), which is Θ(n²). This establishes the tight worst case for the specified insertion-sort implementation. The smaller alternatives cannot upper-bound that quadratic work, and the answer is not a general claim about worst-case complexity of every algorithm. A incorrect Logarithmic is too small for the summed shifts. B incorrect Linear is too small for the summed shifts. C incorrect n log n is too small for quadratic worst-case shifts. D correct The sum of prefix lengths gives quadratic work.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 41 · AM0349
records.text: AM0349 Question 41 DAA05 Which of the following time complexities represents an algorithm with logarithmic growth? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(1) B O(log n) C O(n) D O(n^2) O(log n) Binary search takes time proportional to log_2 n. B matches logarithmic growth. A incorrect 1 is a constant, not a logarithm (p.14 growth comparison). B correct log n is the logarithmic class named on p.14 and instantiated in cross-module p.3. C incorrect n is linear rather than logarithmic (p.14). D incorrect n^2 is quadratic rather than logarithmic (p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 42 · AM0350
records.text: AM0350 Question 42 DAA05 DAA06 Which of the following time complexities represents an algorithm with linear growth? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(1) B O(log n) C O(n) D O(n^2) O(n) Linear growth means work proportional to input size n; sequential search takes O(n) time. The growth classes n, log n and n^2 are distinct. A incorrect 1 stays bounded instead of increasing proportionally to n (p.14). B incorrect log n increases more slowly than n (p.14 growth classes). C correct O(n) is the linear class illustrated by sequential search (cross-module p.3). D incorrect n^2 scales with the square rather than the first power (p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 43 · AM0351
records.text: AM0351 Question 43 DAA05 Which tight running-time growth rates are strictly superlinear, meaning f(n)/n→∞? Select all that apply. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Θ(log n) B Θ(n) C Θ(n log n) D Θ(n²) Θ(n log n); Θ(n²) For n log n, dividing by n gives log n, which grows without bound. For n², the ratio is n, also unbounded. Both are therefore superlinear. The logarithmic representative is sublinear and n itself has constant ratio one, so neither meets the strict condition. Using tight rates prevents a loose upper-bound label from being mistaken for an algorithm’s actual growth. A incorrect log n grows more slowly than n. B incorrect n is linear, with ratio one. C correct The ratio to n is log n and diverges. D correct The ratio to n is n and diverges.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 44 · AM0352
records.text: AM0352 Question 44 DAA02 What is the purpose of experimental analysis in algorithm analysis? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A To measure the actual running time of an algorithm B To determine the best-case scenario for an algorithm C To analyze the behavior of an algorithm as the input size increases D To evaluate the correctness of an algorithm To measure the actual running time of an algorithm The module distinguishes analytical performance analysis from conducting experiments for performance measurement (PDF p.4). Experimental analysis therefore measures actual performance on chosen executions rather than deriving a limiting rate or proving correctness. A correct Direct runtime measurement is the performance-measurement purpose (p.4). B incorrect An experiment might include favorable inputs but does not inherently determine a universal best case (p.4). C incorrect Growth analysis is analytical; experiments can sample sizes but are not the defining limiting argument (p.4). D incorrect Correctness tests can accompany experiments, but the stated performance-measurement purpose is separate (p.4).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 45 · AM0353
records.text: AM0353 Question 45 DAA02 Which offered phrase is not a standard resource-metric name in the course’s time/space/I-O cost model? This does not ask whether representation affects cost. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Space complexity B Auxiliary space C Input-output complexity D Data type complexity Data type complexity Space complexity measures storage, auxiliary space isolates additional storage beyond input, and I/O complexity counts transfers. These are resource metrics in the stated model. Data type complexity is not the standard metric name used for representation effects; those effects are accounted for through arithmetic, storage or bit-operation costs. Therefore D is the terminology exception without asserting that data representation is irrelevant. A incorrect Space complexity is a standard storage metric. B incorrect Auxiliary space is a standard additional-storage metric. C incorrect I/O complexity is a standard transfer metric. D correct Data type complexity is not the standard metric name in this model.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 46 · AM0354
records.text: AM0354 Question 46 DAA02 What is the purpose of algorithm analysis in computer science? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A To design algorithms for specific problems B To implement algorithms using programming languages C To analyze the efficiency and performance of algorithms D To test algorithms for correctness To analyze the efficiency and performance of algorithms Performance analysis estimates computer memory and time requirements (PDF p.4), and studying those requirements helps choose between algorithms (p.6). Thus efficiency/performance is the direct purpose asked for. A incorrect Design creates a method; p.4 analysis estimates resources of a method. B incorrect Implementation expresses a method in code; p.4 analysis estimates performance. C correct This directly matches the memory-and-time performance definition (p.4). D incorrect Correctness is necessary but is distinct from the p.4 performance analysis objective.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 47 · AM0355
records.text: AM0355 Question 47 DAA02 DAA03 Which can be legitimate techniques for analyzing algorithm resource costs? Select all that apply. Dynamic means observing actual executions; empirical means measuring runs. Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A Asymptotic analysis B Empirical analysis C Dynamic analysis D Probabilistic analysis Asymptotic analysis; Empirical analysis; Dynamic analysis; Probabilistic analysis Asymptotic reasoning studies growth, empirical measurements observe actual runs, and dynamic analysis under the stated meaning also observes execution costs. Probabilistic analysis studies expected cost under a distribution or internal randomness. All four can therefore be legitimate resource-analysis techniques. Empirical and dynamic may overlap; they do not have to be disjoint categories for their methods to be useful. A correct Asymptotic analysis studies cost growth. B correct Empirical analysis measures actual runs. C correct Dynamic observation measures actual execution costs under the given definition. D correct Probabilistic analysis studies expectations.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 48 · AM0358
records.text: AM0358 Question 48 DAA04 DAA05 What does a time complexity of O(1) indicate? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A The algorithm runs in constant time. B The algorithm runs in logarithmic time. C The algorithm runs in linear time. D The algorithm runs in quadratic time. The algorithm runs in constant time. A constant upper bound O(1) does not grow with input size; it is the constant K at the start of the visually inspected growth ordering in Data Structures and Algorithms PDF p.3. The assigned PDF p.14 motivates classifying by growth rather than exact operation count. A correct Constant time has a fixed upper bound independent of n (cross-module p.3). B incorrect Logarithmic time grows with n, unlike 1 (assigned p.14). C incorrect Linear time grows proportionally to n (assigned p.14). D incorrect Quadratic time grows as n^2 (assigned p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 49 · AM0359
records.text: AM0359 Question 49 DAA05 Which of the following time complexities indicates the most efficient algorithm? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A O(1) B O(log n) C O(n) D O(n^2) O(1) When comparing the listed representative growth rates for the same task and cost model as n becomes large, constant growth is smallest. The visually inspected related-module PDF p.3 ordering places K before log n, n and n^2; assigned p.14 focuses on large-input growth. This is not a guarantee about clock time for every finite input. A correct Constant is the smallest representative listed growth (cross-module p.3 diagram). B incorrect log n grows beyond any fixed constant (p.14 growth interpretation). C incorrect n grows faster than constant and logarithmic rates (p.14). D incorrect n^2 grows fastest among these listed rates (p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 50 · AM0360
records.text: AM0360 Question 50 DAA04 DAA05 What does a time complexity of O(n^2) signify? Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule. A The algorithm runs in linear time. B The algorithm runs in logarithmic time. C The algorithm runs in quadratic time. D The algorithm runs in exponential time. The algorithm runs in quadratic time. The exponent 2 identifies the quadratic representative growth class n^2, listed on PDF p.14. Strictly O(n^2) is an upper bound (cross-module p.3), so it does not prove that an algorithm actually requires quadratic time. C is the conventional class-name answer. A incorrect Linear is the n class, not the name of n^2 (p.14). B incorrect Logarithmic is the log n class, distinct from n^2 (p.14). C correct Quadratic names the squared-input growth class (p.14). D incorrect Exponential uses a growing exponent, such as 2^n, separately listed on p.14.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 51 · AM0363
records.text: AM0363 Question 51 DAA02 In fixed unit-cost RAM analysis of operation count and storage as functions of input size, which factor is abstracted away rather than being a parameter of the analysis? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Time complexity B Space complexity C Input size D Hardware configuration Hardware configuration The fixed RAM model counts operations and storage relative to input size. Time complexity, space complexity and input size are therefore central to the analysis. The particular hardware configuration is abstracted away by the stipulated unit costs. It would matter for actual elapsed measurements, alongside compiler, cache, I/O and load, but that is a different analysis setting from the one explicitly requested.
