A incorrect Operation-count time complexity is a central resource. B incorrect Space complexity is a central resource. C incorrect Costs are expressed as functions of input size. D correct The fixed unit-cost abstraction hides the specific hardware configuration.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 52 · AM0364
records.text: AM0364 Question 52 DAA12 Which technique solves smaller largely independent instances recursively and then combines their results, without relying on reuse of overlapping states? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer Divide and conquer separates a problem into smaller largely independent instances, solves them and combines the results. Dynamic programming instead emphasizes defined reusable states when subproblems overlap. Greedy commits to safe local choices, while backtracking explores and retracts partial candidates. The independence and combination conditions distinguish the requested technique from these other ways of reducing or extending a problem. A correct Independent recursive subinstances and combination define divide and conquer. B incorrect Greedy is defined by safe irrevocable local choices. C incorrect DP emphasizes reusable subproblem states rather than this independent structure. D incorrect Backtracking is defined by candidate extension and retraction.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 53 · AM0365
records.text: AM0365 Question 53 DAA19 Which algorithm design technique guarantees finding the optimal solution at each step but may not lead to the overall optimal solution? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Greedy algorithm B Divide and conquer C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Greedy algorithm Greedy makes the best available local choice based on current information (PDF p.27), and the module explicitly warns that such choices can fail to yield a global optimum (p.30). “Optimal at each step” must mean locally best, not globally guaranteed. A correct Local short-sighted choices and possible global failure match pp.27,30. B incorrect Independent splitting and combining does not define a locally best choice (p.27 contrast). C incorrect Dynamic programming retains subproblem alternatives rather than irrevocably picking only the local best (p.30 contrast). D incorrect Backtracking revisits choices, unlike non-recoverable greedy choices on p.30.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 54 · AM0366
records.text: AM0366 Question 54 DAA36 Which algorithm design technique is used to solve problems by exploring all possible solutions? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Backtracking Backtracking generates solution tuples and explores choices with constraints, returning to earlier positions when needed (PDF pp.95–96). It can enumerate all valid solutions while pruning branches proved unpromising, so “all possible solutions” should not be read as requiring every invalid tuple to be visited. A incorrect Divide and conquer combines independent solved parts rather than enumerating candidate tuples (pp.95–96 contrast). B incorrect Greedy follows one selection sequence rather than revisiting alternatives (pp.95–96 contrast). C incorrect Dynamic programming caches subproblems rather than being the tuple-enumeration method shown on p.96. D correct The p.96 schema generates all solutions and backtracks over choices.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 55 · AM0367
records.text: AM0367 Question 55 DAA25 DAA26 Which algorithm design technique is suitable for problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming Shared sub-subproblems motivate saving results once (PDF p.48); optimal substructure makes an optimal solution a combination of optimal subsolutions (pp.28,49). Together these are the properties for the module’s dynamic-programming optimization method. A incorrect Independent subproblems distinguish divide and conquer in p.48. B incorrect Optimal substructure alone does not prove the greedy-choice property (pp.28,49). C correct Caching shared subproblem solutions with optimal substructure is exactly the method on pp.48–49. D incorrect Backtracking searches constrained tuples; it need not exploit repeated subproblems via a table (p.48 contrast).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 56 · AM0368
records.text: AM0368 Question 56 DAA19 Which technique builds an optimum by repeatedly making a locally attractive feasible choice, never undoing it, when an exchange or safety proof justifies each commitment? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Greedy algorithm Greedy algorithms repeatedly commit to locally attractive feasible choices without later undoing them. An exchange or related safety proof is needed to show that these commitments can form an optimum. Dynamic programming compares reusable states, backtracking revises candidates, and divide and conquer combines independent subinstances. The explicit safety and irrevocability conditions distinguish greedy from the broad idea of an optimal choice sequence. A incorrect Divide and conquer relies on independent decomposition and combination. B correct Safe irrevocable local commitments define greedy. C incorrect DP evaluates state alternatives rather than requiring irrevocable local choices. D incorrect Backtracking undoes choices, contrary to the stated rule.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 57 · AM0369
records.text: AM0369 Question 57 DAA12 DAA19 Which algorithm design technique is suitable for solving problems with optimal substructure but does not involve overlapping subproblems? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer is the supported independent-subproblem strategy. DAA12 characterizes divide and conquer by smaller largely independent instances. The stated absence of overlapping subproblems fits that structure. Optimal substructure alone does not establish greedy safety, as DAA19 warns, while DP’s main reuse motivation is overlap. Backtracking needs a candidate-and-constraint search description absent here. A is therefore the supported textbook structural match, rather than a proof that only it can ever apply. A correct Independent smaller instances with combinable optimal results fit divide and conquer. B incorrect Optimal substructure alone does not prove a safe greedy local choice. C incorrect Without overlapping states, the stated premise does not motivate DP reuse. D incorrect No candidate retraction or constraint-based enumeration is specified to identify backtracking.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 58 · AM0370
records.text: AM0370 Question 58 DAA36 Which technique explores a series of candidate choices, retracting a choice when constraints show that its partial candidate cannot extend to a solution? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Backtracking Backtracking extends a partial assignment, tests whether a feasible completion remains possible, and undoes the assignment when returning to try alternatives. That matches the stated constraint-driven retraction. Greedy keeps its choices, DP stores reusable state values, and divide and conquer combines independent instances. Merely having a series of choices would not distinguish them; the explicit undo-and-retry mechanism does. A incorrect Independent decomposition is not the described candidate retraction. B incorrect Greedy does not undo committed choices. C incorrect DP is characterized by reuse of states rather than this search rule. D correct Backtracking extends, checks, retracts and tries alternatives.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 59 · AM0371
records.text: AM0371 Question 59 DAA18 DAA20 DAA29 DAA33 Which listed techniques can support exact optimization when their required structural or exhaustive-search conditions hold? Select all that apply; consider maximum subarray, fractional knapsack, 0/1 knapsack and complete tour enumeration as examples. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer; Greedy algorithm; Dynamic programming; Backtracking Divide and conquer optimizes maximum subarray by comparing left, right and crossing results. Greedy optimizes fractional knapsack under divisibility, DP optimizes 0/1 knapsack states, and complete backtracking can enumerate tours and retain the cheapest. All four techniques therefore have exact optimization applications under their own conditions. None becomes universally appropriate merely because the task asks for an optimum. A correct Maximum-subarray divide and conquer is an exact optimizer. B correct Density-greedy is exact for divisible fractional knapsack. C correct 0/1 knapsack DP computes an exact optimum. D correct Complete tour enumeration can retain the exact minimum.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 60 · AM0372
records.text: AM0372 Question 60 DAA25 DAA26 An exponential recursive optimization repeatedly solves the same well-defined states. Optimal substructure holds and there are only polynomially many distinct states with polynomial work per state. Which technique avoids the repeated work by storing state results? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming Dynamic programming stores the result for each distinct state, through memoization or tabulation, and reuses it instead of repeating equivalent recursive work. With the stated polynomial state count and polynomial work per state, this yields polynomial total work. Greedy needs an additional local-choice safety argument, divide and conquer targets independent instances, and plain backtracking does not provide the specified reuse. A incorrect Independent subproblem decomposition does not address the stated repeated states. B incorrect No safe irrevocable local-choice rule is supplied. C correct DP stores and reuses the repeated state results. D incorrect Plain candidate backtracking does not supply the requested cache reuse.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 61 · AM0373
records.text: AM0373 Question 61 DAA25 DAA26 Which technique combines solutions of overlapping subproblems using a defined state recurrence and reuses each solved state rather than solving it repeatedly? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming Dynamic programming defines states and a recurrence, solves dependencies in a valid order and reuses the resulting values. Combining those values forms larger solutions without repeating the same state work. Divide and conquer combines largely independent instances instead, greedy keeps safe local commitments, and backtracking grows and retracts candidates. The explicit overlap and reuse conditions make DP the specific match. A incorrect Divide and conquer emphasizes independent instances rather than reused overlapping states. B incorrect Greedy is defined by safe local commitments. C correct DP combines stored dependent state values. D incorrect Backtracking is defined by candidate search and retraction.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 62 · AM0374
records.text: AM0374 Question 62 DAA24 DAA19 For nonnegative weighted edges, an algorithm repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with minimum current source distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. Which design technique describes this Dijkstra procedure? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Greedy algorithm Dijkstra chooses the unsettled vertex of minimum distance and commits to its finalized value. Nonnegative edges ensure that a later path through other unsettled vertices cannot improve it. That safe irrevocable minimum choice is greedy. DP methods also solve other shortest-path settings, but they are not the explicitly described finalization procedure; independent decomposition and retracting path search are likewise different designs. A incorrect The procedure does not solve independent graph subinstances and combine them. B correct Safe minimum-distance finalization is a greedy choice. C incorrect A DP path recurrence is a different method from the specified Dijkstra procedure. D incorrect The algorithm finalizes distances rather than retracting path candidates.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 63 · AM0375
records.text: AM0375 Question 63 DAA14 DAA15 Which algorithm design technique is commonly used for sorting algorithms? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer Merge sort splits into independent halves and merges (PDF p.21), and quick sort partitions into independently sorted subarrays (p.23). These provide the concrete common sorting examples for divide and conquer. The answer is about those taught examples, not a claim that every sort uses this technique. A correct Both merge sort and quick sort are explicitly divide and conquer (pp.21,23). B incorrect No greedy-choice sorting construction is the taught example in pp.21–23. C incorrect No tabulated shared-subproblem sorting construction is presented in pp.21–23. D incorrect No candidate-solution backtracking sort is the taught example in pp.21–23.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 64 · AM0376
records.text: AM0376 Question 64 DAA25 DAA26 A sequence-decision problem has overlapping state subproblems and optimal substructure. Which technique evaluates all legal next choices through a recurrence and stores the best value for each state for reuse? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming Dynamic programming defines enough state to summarize the remaining decision problem, evaluates all legal choices and stores the best resulting value. Optimal substructure justifies using the stored optimal subsolutions, and overlap makes reuse useful. A mere decision sequence would not identify a technique; the explicit recurrence and reuse distinguish DP from greedy commitments, independent divide-and-conquer instances and backtracking without cached state values. A incorrect Independent decomposition does not describe the stated state reuse. B incorrect Greedy does not generally evaluate all choices through cached state recurrences. C correct DP evaluates and reuses best state values. D incorrect Backtracking without state caching revisits candidate choices rather than implementing this reuse rule.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 65 · AM0377
records.text: AM0377 Question 65 DAA36 Which technique builds a candidate incrementally, checks constraints after each addition and undoes the last addition when it cannot lead to a complete feasible solution? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Backtracking Backtracking keeps a partial candidate, adds a choice, checks whether completion remains possible, and recursively explores promising extensions. On return it undoes the choice so other alternatives can be tried. Greedy also grows solutions but does not undo committed choices; DP builds reusable states rather than this candidate stack. Independent divide-and-conquer combination does not describe the specified constraint-search mechanism. A incorrect Independent subinstance combination is a different mechanism. B incorrect Greedy keeps rather than undoes its commitments. C incorrect DP is defined by state reuse rather than this candidate undo rule. D correct Constraint checks and undoing partial choices are backtracking.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 66 · AM0379
records.text: AM0379 Question 66 DAA18 Which technique finds maximum contiguous subarray by recursively comparing the best left-half, right-half and crossing subarray, with a linear-time crossing computation? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer The stated construction splits the array, recursively solves each half and combines those results with the best crossing interval. This is divide and conquer, with recurrence 2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n). Kadane also solves the same problem, but uses a best-sum-ending-at-index DP recurrence rather than this construction. Greedy commitments and extend/retract search do not describe the specified three-way comparison. A correct Independent halves plus the crossing combination define divide and conquer. B incorrect No irrevocable local-choice rule defines this construction. C incorrect Kadane is DP, but it is not the described left/right/crossing algorithm. D incorrect The construction does not extend and retract candidate assignments.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 67 · AM0380
records.text: AM0380 Question 67 DAA33 DAA36 Which listed techniques describe exact TSP algorithms using either (i) cached subset-and-endpoint states or (ii) complete extend-and-retract enumeration of feasible tours while retaining the cheapest? Select all that apply. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming; Backtracking Held–Karp stores the best cost for a visited subset and endpoint, which is dynamic programming. Complete backtracking extends feasible tours, retracts choices and retains the least-cost complete tour. Both are exact constructions described by the stem. Greedy nearest-neighbor can produce a tour but has no general optimality guarantee, while independent divide-and-conquer combination is not either specified construction. A incorrect Neither specified construction is independent divide-and-conquer combination. B incorrect A greedy tour heuristic is not a general exact optimizer. C correct Cached subset-and-endpoint states form Held–Karp DP. D correct Complete extend-and-retract tour search is backtracking.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 68 · AM0381
records.text: AM0381 Question 68 DAA19 Which algorithm design technique is used for solving problems that can be solved by making the best local choice at each step? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Greedy algorithm The greedy-choice property selects a local optimum, and the method uses immediately available information (PDF p.27). The stem’s best local choice identifies greedy. PDF p.30 warns that this is not automatically a global optimality proof. A incorrect Independent splitting is not the p.27 local-choice criterion. B correct Greedy directly matches the p.27 short-sighted local-selection description. C incorrect Dynamic programming compares subproblem solutions rather than committing solely to the best current choice (p.30 contrast). D incorrect Backtracking revisits choices rather than making the non-recoverable choices described on p.30.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 69 · AM0382
records.text: AM0382 Question 69 DAA30 Which algorithm design technique is used for finding the longest common subsequence between two sequences? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Dynamic programming using prefix-pair states. DAA30 defines a state for each pair of prefix lengths. A match extends a diagonal state; a mismatch takes the larger of two neighboring prefix solutions. Filling states in dependency order avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems and gives Θ(mn) time. This is the note’s dynamic-programming solution; no greedy safety rule or backtracking enumeration is supplied. A incorrect The given LCS construction reuses overlapping prefix states rather than only independently solving and combining disjoint pieces. B incorrect No rule for committing to a locally best character is justified; prefix alternatives must be compared. C correct The prefix-pair table and recurrence reuse optimal subproblem lengths, exactly the dynamic-programming technique described. D incorrect The note computes stored prefix states instead of exhaustively extending and undoing candidate subsequences.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 70 · AM0383
records.text: AM0383 Question 70 DAA12 Which algorithm design technique is used for solving problems that can be divided into smaller independent subproblems? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Divide and conquer B Greedy algorithm C Dynamic programming D Backtracking Divide and conquer PDF p.48 explicitly describes divide and conquer as partitioning into independent subproblems, solving recursively, and combining solutions. The independence qualification makes this stem more specific than merely saying “subproblems.” A correct A directly matches independent partitioning and recursive solution (pp.17,48). B incorrect Greedy is distinguished by local feasible selection, not independent recursive partitioning (p.48 contrast). C incorrect Dynamic programming is motivated by subproblems sharing sub-subproblems (p.48). D incorrect Backtracking searches constrained assignments rather than the independent partition framework (p.48).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 71 · AM0384
records.text: AM0384 Question 71 DAA02 Which term refers to the amount of resources, such as time and memory, required by an algorithm to solve a problem? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Efficiency B Complexity C Optimality D Completeness Complexity Complexity expresses algorithm requirements in time and space (PDF p.6), with performance defined as needed computer memory and time (p.4). Efficiency is an evaluation of those requirements; complexity names the resource requirement being quantified. A incorrect Efficiency evaluates how economically resources are used, while p.6 calls their expression complexity. B correct Complexity is explicitly expressed in time and space requirements (p.6). C incorrect Optimality concerns the objective value of a solution, not the resources used to find it (p.6 contrast). D incorrect Completeness concerns fully solving a problem, not its memory/time quantity (p.4 context).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 72 · AM0385
records.text: AM0385 Question 72 DAA02 What is the purpose of analyzing the computational complexity of algorithms? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A To determine the correctness of an algorithm B To measure the size of the input data C To evaluate the performance of an algorithm D To compare different programming languages To evaluate the performance of an algorithm Analysis estimates memory and time needed to solve an input problem (PDF p.4); these estimates help select between possible algorithms (p.6). Evaluating performance is therefore the direct purpose. A incorrect Correctness concerns whether the result is right; the p.4 performance definition concerns resources. B incorrect Input size is an argument of the analysis, not the ultimate performance-evaluation purpose (pp.4,6). C correct Evaluating resource performance directly matches pp.4,6. D incorrect The comparison is between algorithms and their requirements, not primarily programming languages (p.6).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 73 · AM0387
records.text: AM0387 Question 73 DAA04 DAA03 What does f(n)∈O(g(n)) mean, independently of whether f measures best, average, worst or space cost? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A The best-case time complexity of an algorithm B The average-case time complexity of an algorithm C An eventual constant-factor upper bound: f(n)≤c·g(n) for fixed c>0 and all sufficiently large n. D The space complexity of an algorithm An eventual constant-factor upper bound: f(n)≤c·g(n) for fixed c>0 and all sufficiently large n. Big-O gives an eventual constant-factor upper bound: for some fixed c>0 and n₀, f(n)≤c·g(n) whenever n≥n₀. It does not choose best, average or worst inputs, nor does it specify time rather than space. Those choices determine the function being bounded. Option C states the general mathematical relation that applies across all of those analyses. A incorrect Best case is a way to define f, not the meaning of Big-O. B incorrect Average case defines an expectation, not the bound relation. C correct The eventual upper inequality is the definition of Big-O. D incorrect Space is one possible resource for f, not the definition of the notation.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 74 · AM0388
records.text: AM0388 Question 74 DAA04 DAA05 Which time complexity indicates an algorithm that executes in constant time regardless of the input size? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A O(1) B O(n) C O(log n) D O(n^2) O(1) A bound independent of input size is constant O(1). This is the constant K in the visually inspected related-module p.3 growth diagram and agrees with classifying growth rather than exact operation count on assigned PDF p.14. A correct 1 is independent of n and gives the constant upper bound (cross-module p.3). B incorrect n grows as the input increases, unlike a constant (assigned p.14). C incorrect log n still grows, though slowly (assigned p.14). D incorrect n^2 increases quadratically rather than staying fixed (assigned p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 75 · AM0389
records.text: AM0389 Question 75 DAA08 Which term describes the amount of memory required by an algorithm to solve a problem? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Time complexity B Space complexity C Computational complexity D Algorithmic complexity Space complexity PDF p.6 explicitly defines space complexity as the amount of memory space needed to run a program to completion. B is the specific resource name, while the other complexity terms are broader or refer to duration. A incorrect Time complexity measures time rather than memory (p.6). B correct Space complexity is the precise definition on p.6. C incorrect Computational complexity is broader than the memory-specific measure asked for (p.6 distinguishes resources). D incorrect Algorithmic complexity is broader; p.6 names the particular memory measure space complexity.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 76 · AM0390
records.text: AM0390 Question 76 DAA03 What does the term "worst-case analysis" refer to in computational complexity? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Analyzing the best-case performance of an algorithm B Analyzing the average-case performance of an algorithm C Analyzing the worst possible input for an algorithm D Analyzing the expected performance of an algorithm Analyzing the worst possible input for an algorithm Worst-case analysis considers the worst possible input among inputs of a fixed size, giving a bound covering all their runtimes (PDF p.14). C describes that selection; average and expected costs answer different questions. A incorrect Best case considers the fastest rather than slowest input (p.14). B incorrect Average case uses an average input rather than the maximizing one (p.14). C correct The worst possible input is precisely the p.14 definition. D incorrect Expected performance requires averaging rather than selecting the slowest input (p.14).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 77 · AM0391
records.text: AM0391 Question 77 DAA05 What is the significance of logarithmic time complexity, such as O(log n)? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A It indicates linear time complexity. B It indicates constant time complexity. C It indicates exponential time complexity. D It indicates sublinear time complexity. It indicates sublinear time complexity. For increasing positive n, log n grows more slowly than n: repeated halving reaches unit size in only log_2 n stages, as illustrated by binary search (Data Structures and Algorithms PDF p.3). Assigned PDF p.14 separately lists logarithmic and linear classes. Therefore logarithmic growth is sublinear. A incorrect Linear is proportional to n, faster than log n (cross-module p.3 search comparison). B incorrect Logarithms remain unbounded, so they are not constant (assigned p.14). C incorrect Exponential growth is represented by 2^n, not log n (assigned p.14). D correct Log n grows slower than n, so it is sublinear (cross-module p.3 search comparison).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 78 · AM0392
records.text: AM0392 Question 78 DAA44 What does the term "P versus NP problem" refer to in computational complexity theory? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A The problem of distinguishing between parallel and non-parallel algorithms. B The problem of determining the runtime of algorithms. C The problem of comparing the efficiency of programming languages. D The problem of determining if certain types of problems have efficient algorithms. Whether efficiently verifiable decision problems also have efficient solving algorithms. DAA44 defines P by deterministic polynomial-time decision solving and NP by polynomial-time certificate verification, equivalently nondeterministic polynomial solving. The P-versus-NP problem asks whether these classes coincide. Option D captures the question of efficient algorithms for this particular class of problems, although its wording is broad. It does not concern parallelism, language comparisons, or timing one program. A incorrect P and NP refer to polynomial solving and verification classes, not parallel versus non-parallel execution. B incorrect The question concerns equality of decision-problem classes, not merely determining a particular algorithm runtime. C incorrect Programming-language efficiency is unrelated to whether polynomial-time solvability and verifiability coincide. D correct This broadly expresses whether NP problems have deterministic polynomial-time solving algorithms, the P-versus-NP question.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 79 · AM0393
records.text: AM0393 Question 79 DAA44 Which complexity class includes problems that can be solved by a non-deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A P B NP C NP-complete D Exponential NP DAA44 identifies NP with decision problems solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine. P is a contained class defined using deterministic machines; NP-complete adds hardness, which the stem never requires. Exponential is a time-growth description rather than the requested definition. The alternate set replaces Exponential with NP-hard, which likewise does not change the defining NP answer. A incorrect P is defined through deterministic polynomial time; it is contained in NP but does not name the full defined class. B correct NP exactly names decision problems solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. C incorrect NP-complete requires both NP membership and NP-hardness; hardness is absent from the stem. D incorrect Exponential describes time growth, not the class defined by nondeterministic polynomial-time computation.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 80 · CS0114
records.text: CS0114 Question 80 DAA45 DAA01 For p=10 and n=5, execute if(n>p){print(n+p);}. Treat the comparison, branch and possible output as executable constant-cost operations. Which assessment is correct without adding an unstated output requirement? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Feasibility is violated. B Finiteness is violated. C Sequential control flow is violated. D No violation is demonstrated by this fragment. No violation is demonstrated by this fragment. The condition 5>10 is false, so the print is skipped and the fragment terminates after constant work. Its operations are executable and its conditional control flow is legitimate. Nothing in this specified fragment violates feasibility or finiteness, and an unrequired output is not a correctness obligation. Thus the accurate assessment is that no property violation is demonstrated by this fragment. A incorrect The specified operations are executable, so feasibility is satisfied. B incorrect The fragment terminates, so finiteness is satisfied. C incorrect A conditional branch is legitimate algorithmic control flow. D correct The false branch skips output and terminates without the claimed property violations.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 81 · CS0115
records.text: CS0115 Question 81 DAA04 DAA05 Assume it is given that f(n) = 4n^2, g(n) = 8n. Which asymptotic notation is correct? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A f(n) = Big-Oh(g(n)) B f(n) = Little-Oh(g(n)) C f(n) = Big-Omega(g(n)) D f(n) = Theta(g(n)) f(n) = Big-Omega(g(n)) Compare f/g=(4n^2)/(8n)=n/2, which grows without bound. Thus f eventually exceeds a constant multiple of g, establishing Omega(g) and excluding O(g), little-o(g) and Theta(g). The assigned PDF p.14 introduces growth comparison; the precise upper/lower/tight definitions are in Data Structures and Algorithms PDF p.3. For example n>=2 gives f>=g. A incorrect O(g) requires an eventual constant upper multiple; n/2 is unbounded, so it fails (cross-module p.3). B incorrect Little-o(g) requires slower growth; the ratio instead grows without bound (cross-module p.3). C correct Omega(g) is a lower growth bound; f>=g for every n>=2 establishes it (cross-module p.3). D incorrect Theta(g) requires the same growth rate; quadratic and linear differ by unbounded n/2 (cross-module p.3).

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 82 · CS0116
records.text: CS0116 Question 82 DAA23 For a connected weighted undirected graph, which statements about its minimum spanning trees are true? Select all that apply; weights may tie. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Minimum spanning tree contains all vertices from an input graph B We can have only one unique minimum spanning tree for a graph C Minimum spanning trees are graphs D Minimum spanning trees form a cycle Minimum spanning tree contains all vertices from an input graph; Minimum spanning trees are graphs An MST contains every vertex and is a tree, hence is itself a graph. It is acyclic and has V−1 edges. Equal edge weights may permit multiple different MSTs, so uniqueness is not guaranteed. These properties make A and C true, while B’s universal uniqueness claim and D’s cycle claim are false. Distinct edge weights would be a sufficient additional uniqueness condition. A correct Spanning includes every input vertex. B incorrect Tied weights may yield multiple MSTs. C correct A tree is a particular kind of graph. D incorrect An MST is acyclic.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 83 · NS0294
records.text: NS0294 Question 83 DAA03 At a fixed input size n, what is the minimum running time over all legal inputs of that size called? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Average time B Small time C Worst time D Best time Best time Best-case time is the minimum cost among legal inputs of a fixed size. Worst case takes the maximum, and average case takes an expectation under a specified distribution. Choosing a smaller input size would ask a different question and would not define best case. The revised wording explicitly holds n fixed, making best time the unique standard case term. A incorrect Average time takes an expectation rather than a minimum. B incorrect Small time is not the defined input-case category. C incorrect Worst time takes the maximum at fixed size. D correct Best time takes the minimum at fixed size.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 84 · NS0314
records.text: NS0314 Question 84 DAA11 DAA14 A researcher solves mergesort’s recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n), obtaining Θ(n log n), and claims that this calculation alone proves every comparison-based sorting algorithm requires Ω(n log n) worst-case time. What is the flaw in that reasoning? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A The proof fails because comparison decision trees allow only array indexing. B The recurrence describes one algorithm; a separate argument is needed to lower-bound the whole comparison class. C The proof fails only because Θ notation ignores constant factors. D There is no flaw: any upper bound for one comparison sort automatically lower-bounds all comparison sorts. B. One algorithm’s recurrence is not a universal lower-bound argument. Solving the given recurrence establishes mergesort’s Θ(n log n) running time, but it does not rule out a different comparison algorithm with less work. The unsupported step is extending one algorithm’s recurrence to a lower bound for the whole class. A separate decision-tree argument supplies the universal result: n! possible orders require height at least log₂(n!). Discarding constants and permitting array indexing do not invalidate that argument. A incorrect The comparison model does not impose the stated array-indexing-only restriction. B correct The recurrence bounds mergesort; the n!-leaf decision-tree argument is what supplies a class-wide lower bound. C incorrect Ignoring constants is not the logical error; the unsupported extension from one algorithm to every algorithm is. D incorrect An upper bound for one available algorithm does not exclude a faster different algorithm, so it is not automatically a universal lower bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 85 · NS0317
records.text: NS0317 Question 85 DAA06 DAA02 A routine sums the integers from n down to 1. For integer n≥0, use mathematical-integer RAM pseudocode with exact unit-cost arithmetic and no overflow. Charge 1 unit for each initialization, comparison, compound decrement i-- and return; charge 1 for addition and 1 for assignment in sum=sum+i. Ignore declarations, parameter passing and function-call overhead. What is T(n)? total(n) { sum=0; for(i=n;i>0;i--) sum=sum+i; return sum; } Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A 5n+5 B 4n²+4 C 6n+2 D 4n+4 4n+4 The descending loop executes n times. Initializing sum and i costs 2 units; i>0 is tested n+1 times; the compound decrement costs n units; and adding i then assigning the result costs 2n. One return gives T(n)=2+(n+1)+n+2n+1=4n+4. Although the returned sum grows quadratically with n, the number of unit-cost operations grows linearly. Exact mathematical integers prevent accumulator or loop-control overflow. A incorrect This overcounts the specified model by one unit per iteration and one fixed unit. B incorrect The numeric sum grows quadratically, but there are only n constant-cost loop iterations. C incorrect The stated iteration has one test, one compound decrement and two accumulator operations, not six units of iteration work. D correct Two initializations, n+1 tests, n decrements, 2n body units and one return total 4n+4.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 86 · NS0468
records.text: NS0468 Question 86 DAA12 Which strategy breaks a problem into smaller largely independent subinstances, solves them recursively and combines their results, without caching repeated overlapping states? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A Greedy B Backtracking C Divide and Conquer D Dynamic Programming Divide and Conquer Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines their results into the original solution. Dynamic programming can also recurse and combine values, but its distinguishing mechanism is reusable state values when subproblems overlap. Greedy is defined by safe irrevocable local choices, and backtracking by revising partial candidates. Independence and the lack of overlap-based caching resolve the original broad decomposition wording. A incorrect Greedy is defined by safe local choices. B incorrect Backtracking extends and retracts candidates. C correct Independent recursive subinstances and combination define divide and conquer. D incorrect The specified independence excludes the overlapping-state reuse emphasized by DP.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 87 · NS0469
records.text: NS0469 Question 87 DAA04 What is the formal definition of Big-O notation? State the roles of constants c and k. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. f∈O(g) iff ∃c>0,k such that 0≤f(n)≤c g(n) for all n≥k. DAA04 requires one fixed positive multiplier and one threshold covering the entire tail of the eventually nonnegative functions. c permits constant-factor scaling; k excludes a finite initial prefix. Neither may be chosen anew for each n. This defines an eventual upper bound, independently of input case or whether the resource is time or space.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 88 · NS0470
records.text: NS0470 Question 88 DAA04 Show that f(n) = 10n + 5 is O(n). What values of c and k satisfy the definition? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. c=15 and k=1 work. For every n≥1, 5≤5n, so 10n+5≤15n. Choosing c=15 and k=1 therefore satisfies the Big-O upper inequality for the whole tail. DAA04 gives this exact worked example. These witnesses need not be unique; the goal is one valid fixed constant and threshold, not the smallest pair.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 89 · NS0471
records.text: NS0471 Question 89 DAA04 Show that f(n) = 3n² + 4n + 1 is O(n²). What are the constants? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. c=8 and k=1 work. For n≥1, replace 4n by at most 4n² and 1 by at most n². The sum is then at most 8n², satisfying DAA04’s upper-bound definition. Thus c=8 and k=1 are valid witnesses. They are not uniquely required constants; larger multipliers or thresholds can also satisfy the inequality.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 90 · NS0472
records.text: NS0472 Question 90 DAA05 Rank these complexity classes from slowest to fastest growing: O(n!), O(n²), O(log n), O(2ⁿ), O(n log n) Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Increasing representative growth: log n, n log n, n², 2^n, n!. DAA05 orders logarithmic, polynomial, exponential, and factorial rates. A log factor above n is still dominated by n²; fixed-base exponential eventually exceeds any fixed polynomial, and factorial exceeds fixed-base exponential. This ranks representative functions, not mutually exclusive Big-O sets, since a slower function can also satisfy a looser larger upper bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 91 · NS0473
records.text: NS0473 Question 91 DAA04 Big-Theta Θ(h(n)) provides what kind of bound on an algorithm's complexity? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. A tight asymptotic bound: both upper and lower constant-factor bounds. DAA04 requires positive constants c1,c2 and a threshold k with c1 h(n)≤f(n)≤c2 h(n) for all n≥k. Theta therefore specifies growth up to constant factors, not exact seconds. It can describe best, average, worst, or space functions; choosing Theta does not itself choose an input case.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 92 · NS0474
records.text: NS0474 Question 92 DAA04 What does Big-Omega Ω(g(n)) represent and how does it differ from Big-O? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Ω is an eventual lower bound; O is an eventual upper bound. DAA04 gives f∈Ω(g) when f(n)≥c g(n) beyond a fixed threshold for some c>0, reversing the Big-O inequality. The relations describe functions independently of best or worst case. A function may satisfy both, giving Theta, or only one for a particular comparator; they are not literal fastest-versus-slowest input labels.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 93 · NS0475
records.text: NS0475 Question 93 DAA04 State the Transitivity Theorem of Big-O and explain why it is useful. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), then f∈O(h). DAA04 permits chained upper bounds. If f≤c g past k1 and g≤d h past k2, then f≤cd h for every n beyond max(k1,k2). Multiplying constants and combining thresholds proves transitivity. It is useful for replacing a complicated intermediate expression by a simpler known bound without redoing the entire comparison.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 94 · NS0476
records.text: NS0476 Question 94 DAA05 According to Big-O Theorem 6, order the following correctly: n!, 2ⁿ, n², n log n, n, log n, constant k Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Increasing growth: k, log n, n, n log n, n², 2^n, n!. For fixed positive k, DAA05 places constant growth first, followed by logarithmic and linear rates, then n log n, quadratic, exponential, and factorial growth. The ordering is eventual, not a promise of speed for every small input. It concerns representative functions; Big-O memberships can overlap when upper bounds are loose.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 95 · NS0477
records.text: NS0477 Question 95 DAA01 DAA02 How is algorithm validation different from algorithm analysis? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Validation checks required behavior; analysis measures resource costs. DAA01 specifies legal inputs, required outputs, and correctness proof through invariants or recursive induction. DAA02 counts operations and storage as input size grows. A procedure can be fast yet incorrect, or correct yet expensive. Testing can reveal failures but finite tests do not prove correctness for all inputs, so resource analysis does not replace validation.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 96 · NS0478
records.text: NS0478 Question 96 DAA10 What is the general recurrence equation for a divide-and-conquer algorithm? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. For equal-size splits, T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), with an explicit base case. DAA10 uses a recursive subcalls of size n/b and f(n) nonrecursive divide/combine work, with a≥1 and b>1. Include a base such as T(1)=Θ(1). Unequal or decrementing subproblems require a more general sum of subproblem costs; the equal-split form is a common model, not every possible divide-and-conquer recurrence.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 97 · NS0479
records.text: NS0479 Question 97 DAA14 What is the time complexity of Merge Sort and how is it derived? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Ordinary array merge sort is Θ(n log n). DAA14 gives T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n): two half-size sorts and linear merging. There are logarithmically many levels, each totaling linear merge work, with linear total leaf work. Therefore the tight result is n log n across input orders, assuming the ordinary algorithm rather than a variant that skips already ordered merges.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 98 · NS0480
records.text: NS0480 Question 98 DAA14 Explain the three steps of Merge Sort in order. Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Split into halves, recursively sort each half, then merge the sorted halves. DAA14 stops at empty or singleton ranges. During combination it repeatedly takes the smaller remaining front item, then appends the unexhausted suffix. Left-first equal-key selection preserves stability. These steps separate division, recursive solution, and combination; the merge assumes each half is already sorted rather than that the original full array was sorted.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 99 · NS0481
records.text: NS0481 Question 99 DAA14 What property makes Merge Sort a 'stable' sorting algorithm? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Take equal keys from the left half first while merging. DAA14 explicitly requires left-first equal-key handling for stability. Recursive halves retain their internal equal-key order, and choosing a left equal before a right equal preserves their original cross-half order. Inductively the entire output retains the relative order of equal-key records. Choosing the right equal first can break that property.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 100 · NS0482
records.text: NS0482 Question 100 DAA15 What is the average and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort, and when does the worst case occur? Match the defining mechanism and its assumptions to the required claim; keep resource bounds separate from correctness. Expected average Θ(n log n); worst Θ(n²) from repeated highly unbalanced partitions. DAA15 gives logarithmic partition depth when splits are balanced and expected n log n with random pivots. Repeated extreme pivots leave sizes n−1,n−2,…, causing n+(n−1)+… work. Sorted input can trigger this with certain fixed endpoint pivots, but input order alone is not a universal worst-case characterization across partition rules.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 101 · NS0483
records.text: NS0483 Question 101 DAA15 Describe the partitioning step of Quick Sort using indices i and j. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Advance i over values below the pivot and j over values above; swap while i≤j, then advance both. DAA15’s two-pointer partition bounds its scans and ensures progress even on equal values. After pointers cross, recurse on the resulting smaller ranges. Hoare-style boundaries need not put the pivot in its final position, whereas Lomuto commonly does. The chosen return convention and recursion ranges must match; mixing them can miss elements or fail to terminate.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 102 · NS0484
records.text: NS0484 Question 102 DAA14 DAA15 Compare Merge Sort and Quick Sort on: stability, worst-case complexity, and space usage. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Merge: stable, Θ(n log n) worst, Θ(n) buffer. Quick: unstable, Θ(n²) worst, expected Θ(log n) and worst Θ(n) stack. DAA14 provides merge’s linear buffer and logarithmic recursion depth, with left-first ties for stability. DAA15 gives quicksort’s in-array partitioning but nonconstant recursive storage and potentially linear depth. Recursing only on the smaller side can bound that stack logarithmically. These describe ordinary implementations; ignoring recursive frames would misstate total auxiliary space.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 103 · NS0485
records.text: NS0485 Question 103 DAA13 DAA12 Why is Binary Search classified as a Divide and Conquer algorithm? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Each midpoint comparison reduces the ordered-search instance to one half. DAA13 maintains sorted low/high bounds and excludes the half that cannot contain the target. The recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1) gives logarithmic worst work. Unlike sorting two halves, binary search solves only one surviving subinstance and requires no substantial combination step; this is the common divide-and-conquer or decrease-by-factor classification.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 104 · NS0486
records.text: NS0486 Question 104 DAA19 What is the core principle of the Greedy algorithmic paradigm? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Repeatedly make a locally attractive feasible choice and keep it. DAA19 defines greedy decisions as irrevocable rather than exploring and undoing alternatives. To obtain a global optimum, the local choice needs a problem-specific safety argument, often an exchange proof. Optimal substructure alone is insufficient. Thus local attractiveness is the mechanism, while global optimality is a separate correctness obligation rather than an automatic consequence.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 105 · NS0487
records.text: NS0487 Question 105 DAA01 DAA19 What is the difference between a feasible solution and an optimal solution in the context of Greedy algorithms? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Feasible satisfies constraints; optimal is best among feasible solutions. DAA01 separates constraint satisfaction from objective quality. For example, a legal set of knapsack items may fit capacity but have less value than another legal set. DAA19 warns that greedy choices require a safety proof to reach an optimum; constructing a feasible result alone does not prove global optimality.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 106 · NS0488
records.text: NS0488 Question 106 DAA19 Name two advantages and two disadvantages of Greedy algorithms. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Advantages: simple choices and low overhead. Disadvantages: irrevocable mistakes and problem-specific applicability. DAA19 identifies these benefits and limitations. Greedy can avoid maintaining a large state table, but a locally attractive choice can prevent an optimum and cannot later be undone within the paradigm. An exchange or other safety proof is therefore essential. A greedy heuristic has no approximation guarantee solely because it uses local choices.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 107 · NS0489
records.text: NS0489 Question 107 DAA21 In the Job Sequencing with Deadlines algorithm, why are jobs sorted in decreasing order of profit first? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Profit-first gives high-value feasible jobs priority under the unit-duration scheduling assumptions. DAA21 processes nonnegative-profit jobs in decreasing profit and places each in its latest free slot meeting its deadline. This preserves earlier slots for tighter deadlines, while an exchange argument supports profit-first selection for feasible unit-job sets. The rule needs one machine, initially available unit jobs, and on-time profit; variable durations can invalidate it.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 108 · NS0490
records.text: NS0490 Question 108 DAA21 Given jobs J4(deadline=2, profit=300), J1(deadline=5, profit=200), J3(deadline=3, profit=190), J2(deadline=3, profit=180), J5(deadline=4, profit=120), J6(deadline=2, profit=100) — what is the optimal schedule and maximum profit? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Slots 1–5: J2,J4,J3,J5,J1; maximum profit 990. DAA21’s greedy placement gives J4 at slot2, J1 at5, J3 at3, J2 at1, and J5 at4; J6 cannot fit before deadline2. Every accepted deadline holds. Their profits sum to 180+300+190+120+200=990. Since these are the five largest profits and only five slots exist, 990 also matches an upper bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 109 · NS0491
records.text: NS0491 Question 109 DAA22 What is the Optimal Merge Pattern and what greedy strategy does it apply? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Repeatedly merge the two smallest files or weights, reinsert their sum, and minimize total merge cost. DAA22 charges p+q for combining file sizes p and q, adds that charge to total cost, and returns the merged size to a min-heap. Combining small weights early avoids repeatedly charging large weights at deep levels. The min-heap implementation costs O(n log n); actual comparison counts are a distinct cost model.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 110 · NS0492
records.text: NS0492 Question 110 DAA23 What is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) and what problem does it solve? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. An MST connects all vertices without cycles using minimum total edge weight. DAA23 assumes a connected undirected weighted graph and gives an MST V−1 edges. It minimizes total connection cost, not every source-to-vertex route. Prim and Kruskal find such trees through safe light edges. Equal weights can allow several optima, and disconnected input instead yields a minimum spanning forest rather than one spanning tree.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 111 · NS0493
records.text: NS0493 Question 111 DAA23 Compare Prim's Algorithm and Kruskal's Algorithm: approach, edge selection, and best use case. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Prim grows one tree across a cut; Kruskal accepts globally light edges joining distinct components. DAA23 gives matrix Prim O(V²), heap/list Prim O(E log V), and edge-sorting Kruskal O(E log E). Matrix Prim can favor dense graphs because it avoids sorting quadratically many edges; Kruskal naturally uses an edge list and union-find. Best use depends on representation and implementation, not a universal measured-speed ranking.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 112 · NS0494
records.text: NS0494 Question 112 DAA23 How does Kruskal's Algorithm detect and avoid cycles when building the MST? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Use union-find: reject an edge if its endpoints already belong to the same component. DAA23 processes edges globally in increasing weight. If the endpoint representatives differ, the edge joins components without creating a cycle, so accept it and union the sets. If they match, a path already connects the endpoints and adding the edge would close a cycle. The light-edge exchange property supports minimum total weight.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 113 · NS0495
records.text: NS0495 Question 113 DAA24 What is Dijkstra's Algorithm used for and what is its key limitation? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Single-source shortest paths with nonnegative edge weights; negative edges break its general guarantee. DAA24 finalizes the least unsettled tentative distance and relaxes outgoing edges. Nonnegative weights ensure a later route through unsettled vertices cannot improve a finalized distance. A negative edge can violate that proof even without a negative cycle. This differs from MST construction, and unreachable vertices retain infinite distance.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 114 · NS0496
records.text: NS0496 Question 114 DAA24 List the steps of Dijkstra's Algorithm in order. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Initialize distances; repeatedly finalize the smallest unsettled distance and relax its outgoing edges. DAA24 starts source at zero, all others at infinity, with predecessors unset. Extract the minimum unsettled vertex; update dist[v] and its predecessor when dist[u]+w(u,v) improves it. Stop when none remain or the minimum is infinite. For an early destination stop, finalize it first rather than stopping merely on discovery.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 115 · NS0497
records.text: NS0497 Question 115 DAA23 DAA24 What is the difference between MST (Minimum Spanning Tree) and SSSP (Single-Source Shortest Path)? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. MST minimizes total connection weight; SSSP minimizes each source-to-vertex path distance. DAA23’s spanning tree connects every vertex with minimum sum of selected edge weights. DAA24’s source shortest paths optimize a different objective for a designated source and can choose a different tree. An MST need not contain shortest source routes. Standard MST permits negative weights, while Dijkstra’s particular SSSP algorithm needs nonnegative weights.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 116 · NS0498
records.text: NS0498 Question 116 DAA25 Which two textbook structural properties justify and motivate the usual dynamic-programming approach to optimization? Explain their different roles rather than treating them as universal requirements for every use of DP. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems: the first justifies composing optimal subsolutions, while the second motivates reusing stored state results. Optimal substructure means an optimal solution can be built using appropriate optimal subsolutions. Overlap means the same state problem occurs repeatedly, making saved results useful. These properties justify and motivate the familiar optimization pattern, provided the state captures all relevant information and the recurrence is correct. DP can also count or decide, so the two properties are not stated here as universal necessities for every DP computation.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 117 · NS0499
records.text: NS0499 Question 117 DAA12 DAA25 How does Dynamic Programming differ from Divide and Conquer? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Divide and conquer solves largely independent instances; DP reuses dependent or overlapping states. DAA12 distinguishes independent recursive decomposition and combination from a defined set of reused states. DP requires state meaning, transitions, bases, and dependency order so each needed state is computed without redundant recomputation. Divide and conquer usually does not need a shared-state cache. Merely splitting a problem into smaller parts is common to both and does not distinguish them.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 118 · NS0500
records.text: NS0500 Question 118 DAA19 DAA25 How does Dynamic Programming differ from the Greedy approach? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Greedy commits to a proved-safe local choice; DP compares stored subproblem alternatives. DAA19 makes greedy choices irrevocable and requires a safety argument. DAA25 defines states and recurrence choices, then computes optimal state values in dependency order. DP can retain alternatives that a greedy rule would discard. Optimal substructure does not itself make greedy safe, and neither approach is universally preferable without the problem’s structural conditions.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 119 · NS0501
records.text: NS0501 Question 119 DAA25 What are the four development steps of a Dynamic Programming algorithm? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Define and justify optimal states; derive recurrence and bases; compute dependencies once; reconstruct retained choices. DAA25 first requires a state meaning and legal choices, then a correctness argument for the recurrence and feasible candidates. Evaluate states in dependency order, accounting for states times work per state. Store decisions so the chosen solution can be reconstructed afterward. These provide the requested four development stages without assuming DP is automatically polynomial.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 120 · NS0502
records.text: NS0502 Question 120 DAA26 Explain memoization and tabulation — the two DP implementation strategies. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Memoization solves requested states recursively with a cache; tabulation fills states in explicit dependency order. DAA26 checks the cache before recursively solving a memoized state and stores its result. Tabulation schedules prerequisite states first without that demand-driven recursion. Keys must include all relevant parameters, and chosen domains may avoid irrelevant states. Both reuse results, but sparsity, recursion overhead, and locality can affect which implementation is preferable.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 121 · NS0503
records.text: NS0503 Question 121 DAA26 In the Fibonacci sequence, why is naive recursion inefficient and how does DP improve it? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Naive recursion repeats Fibonacci states; DP computes each required state once. DAA26 shows that F(n−2) reappears across recursion branches, causing Θ(φ^n) calls, with O(2^n) a valid loose bound. Memoization or tabulation uses the two preceding values and only Θ(n) unit-cost additions. Two rolling values reduce working machine words to constant, though arbitrary-precision values require growing bit costs.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 122 · NS0504
records.text: NS0504 Question 122 DAA29 DAA20 What is the 0/1 knapsack optimization problem with positive integer weights, nonnegative values and integer capacity W, and why does its item-and-capacity state formulation suit dynamic programming? Each item may be chosen at most once. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Choose a subset with total weight at most W and maximum total value. DP compares excluding each item with including it once and reuses item/capacity state results. Define K[i,w] as the best value using the first i items within capacity w. An item that fits can be excluded or included with its value added to K[i-1,w-weight_i]; taking the larger value gives the recurrence. The previous-row reference enforces at-most-once use, and repeated states are reused. The O(nW) running time is pseudo-polynomial in binary-encoded capacity, unlike the separate fractional-knapsack greedy method.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 123 · NS0505
records.text: NS0505 Question 123 DAA28 What is the All Pairs Shortest Path (APSP) problem and which algorithm solves it? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. APSP finds shortest distances for every ordered vertex pair; Floyd–Warshall is one DP algorithm. DAA28 initializes direct-edge costs and progressively allows each vertex as an intermediate. Its min-plus recurrence gives Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage. Negative cycles make affected pair distances lack a finite minimum; Floyd detects them through negative diagonals. Its cost is a taught solution rather than a universal best-achievable APSP bound.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 124 · NS0506
records.text: NS0506 Question 124 DAA28 Describe the APSP initialization step. What values fill the matrix initially? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Initialize D[i,i]=0, direct pairs to minimum edge weights, and missing edges to infinity. DAA28 uses zero for the empty self-path, but preserves a negative self-loop by taking min(0, its weight). Parallel direct edges use their minimum. Infinity denotes no known route, so later arithmetic must guard unreachable sums and overflow. This is Floyd’s initialization before intermediate vertices are considered, not an adjacency-only final answer.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 125 · NS0507
records.text: NS0507 Question 125 DAA28 What is the DP update rule used in the APSP algorithm for each intermediate vertex k? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. D[i,j] ← min(D[i,j], D[i,k]+D[k,j]), with k outermost. DAA28’s phase invariant permits only earlier vertices as intermediates before phase k. Each pair then compares its current route with a route through k. Guard infinite operands and overflow rather than adding unreachable values blindly. Keeping k as the outer phase index is essential to the stated dependency proof.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 126 · NS0508
records.text: NS0508 Question 126 DAA36 Which design strategy explores ALL possible solutions by incrementally building candidates and abandoning invalid ones? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Backtracking DAA36 assigns the next choice, checks whether a feasible extension remains possible, recurses, and undoes the choice on return. A complete search reports every required candidate while pruning only impossible branches. Stop after one solution only if the task asks for existence or a single solution; otherwise early stopping would fail the ALL requirement.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 127 · NS0509
records.text: NS0509 Question 127 DAA19 Explain why Greedy algorithms are not guaranteed to give a globally optimal solution, with an example. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. A locally attractive choice can block the optimum; coins {1,3,4} for target 6 are a counterexample. DAA19’s largest-first choice produces 4+1+1, using three coins, while 3+3 uses two. Once the greedy method keeps 4, it cannot repair the earlier choice within its irrevocable policy. Therefore local feasibility and attractiveness do not prove global optimality; a problem-specific exchange or safety proof is needed.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 128 · NS0510
records.text: NS0510 Question 128 DAA15 For ordinary array quicksort, what partition pattern causes quadratic worst-case time, and how can randomized pivot selection or three-way partitioning mitigate relevant workloads? Distinguish expected-time improvements from worst-case and stack-space guarantees. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Repeated very unbalanced partitions cause quadratic work. Random pivots give expected Theta(n log n) time; three-way partitioning helps repeated keys, and smaller-side recursion can limit stack space. Extreme pivots can leave subproblems of sizes n-1,n-2 and so on, giving quadratic total partition work. Random pivots improve expected time to Theta(n log n) but do not remove quadratic possible executions. Three-way partitioning helps repeated keys, while median-of-three still admits adversarial inputs. Recursing only on the smaller side and iterating on the larger separately bounds stack depth by O(log n). No universal rarity claim is needed.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 129 · NS0511
records.text: NS0511 Question 129 DAA21 For the Job Sequencing algorithm, if two jobs have the same profit, how should ties be broken? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Equal-profit jobs may be processed in any order under the stated unit-job assumptions. DAA21 explicitly permits arbitrary equal-profit ordering; earlier deadline is an optional tie convention rather than a correctness requirement. Each accepted job still goes into its latest free slot finishing by its deadline. The freedom relies on the one-machine, initially available unit-duration model and does not automatically extend to variable durations or release times.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 130 · NS0512
records.text: NS0512 Question 130 DAA23 Using the note’s worst-case bounds, compare matrix-based Prim with Kruskal that comparison-sorts all edges on a dense simple undirected graph, where E=Theta(V²). Why can this implementation pairing favor Prim asymptotically? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Matrix Prim has O(V²) time; edge-sorting Kruskal has O(E log E)=O(V² log V). The matrix implementation avoids the all-edge sorting factor. The matrix-based Prim implementation scans vertex connections in O(V²) time. Kruskal’s stated bound includes sorting all E edges, giving O(E log E). For dense simple graphs E has order V², so that expression becomes O(V² log V), whereas matrix Prim retains its quadratic bound. This explains the advantage of the specified implementations and does not claim that every version of Prim is always faster in measured runtime.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 131 · NS0513
records.text: NS0513 Question 131 DAA24 DAA27 Can Dijkstra's Algorithm be applied to a graph with negative edge weights? Why or why not? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Standard Dijkstra is not generally correct with negative edges. DAA24’s example s→a=2, s→b=5, b→a=−4 finalizes a at 2 but a later route improves it to 1. That violates the nonnegative-edge finalization proof even without a negative cycle. Some instances may happen to work, but no general guarantee remains. Bellman–Ford or DAG DP supplies an appropriate alternative under its assumptions.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 132 · NS0514
records.text: NS0514 Question 132 DAA28 What is the time complexity of APSP using the Floyd-Warshall approach and why? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) distance storage. DAA28 runs one intermediate-vertex phase for every k and examines every ordered pair i,j during each phase. V phases times V² constant-cost relaxations gives cubic time. The matrix has V² entries. These bounds assume bounded-cost arithmetic and do not claim that Floyd is universally optimal among all APSP algorithms or models.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 133 · NS0515
records.text: NS0515 Question 133 DAA26 DAA12 Explain the difference between 'Divide and Conquer' and 'Dynamic Programming' using the Fibonacci problem. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Naive Fibonacci has overlapping recursive calls; DP reuses them instead of treating them as independent. DAA26 explicitly says naive Fibonacci is not the independent-subproblem ideal of divide and conquer. Both branches recompute states such as F(n−2), causing exponential calls. A cache or increasing-index table computes each state once, giving linear unit-cost additions.
