Recursion alone therefore does not establish a well-structured independent divide-and-conquer algorithm.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 134 · NS0516
records.text: NS0516 Question 134 DAA14 What does the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) represent and what is its solution? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Two half-size recursive calls plus at most linear combine work; O(n log n), tight Θ(n log n) if combine work is Θ(n). DAA14 warns that a written +O(n) term alone gives an upper bound rather than a matching lower bound. Expanding logarithmically many levels with at most linear aggregate work gives O(n log n). Ordinary merging actually costs Θ(n), supplying the tight result, but a cheaper unspecified combine function need not do so.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 135 · NS0517
records.text: NS0517 Question 135 DAA22 How does the Optimal Merge Pattern relate to Huffman Coding? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Both repeatedly combine the two smallest weights; Huffman interprets the resulting tree as a prefix code. DAA22 uses file sizes as merge weights and frequencies as Huffman weights. Reinsert each combined weight so large values avoid unnecessary depth. In Huffman the weighted path length is ∑frequency×depth, the same merge-tree objective. Equal-weight choices can change codewords without changing the optimal total cost.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 136 · NS0518
records.text: NS0518 Question 136 DAA25 DAA27 In Dynamic Programming, what is 'optimal substructure' and give one example. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. An optimal solution contains suitable optimal subsolutions; a DAG shortest path has an optimal suffix. DAA25 justifies replacing a subsolution with a better one without breaking feasibility. For DAA27’s DAG cost-to-go, if a chosen u→v route used a nonoptimal v-to-target suffix, replacing it with the cheaper suffix would improve the whole route, contradicting optimality. The state must retain enough information for this replacement argument to be valid.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 137 · NS0622
records.text: NS0622 Question 137 DAA04 DAA05 What is the difference between Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notation? Provide examples. State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. O is an eventual upper bound, Ω a lower bound, and Θ both. DAA04 defines the relations by fixed constant-factor inequalities beyond a threshold. For f=3n²+4n+1 and n≥1, 3n²≤f≤8n², so f∈Θ(n²), and consequently both O(n²) and Ω(n²). It is also O(n³), showing that upper bounds need not be tight or name an input case.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 138 · NS0623
records.text: NS0623 Question 138 DAA14 DAA15 Why is Merge Sort Θ(n log n) in all cases while Quick Sort can be O(n²)? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Merge has balanced halves with linear merging per level; quicksort can repeatedly keep an n−1 side. DAA14 yields logarithmically many full linear-work merge levels across input orders. DAA15 allows extreme pivots creating the sum n+(n−1)+… and quadratic work. Random pivots improve expected quicksort performance without a worst-case guarantee. The comparison concerns ordinary merge sorting; optimizations that skip merges require their own best-case analysis.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 139 · NS0624
records.text: NS0624 Question 139 DAA19 When would you choose a greedy algorithm over dynamic programming? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Choose greedy when a local-choice safety proof exists and its lower overhead meets the task. DAA19 supports exchange arguments that insert the greedy choice into some optimum without worsening it. With that proof, irrevocable decisions can avoid a DP table and simplify implementation. If local safety is absent but a correct reusable-state recurrence exists, DP is a stronger candidate. Optimal substructure alone is not enough to justify greedy.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 140 · NS0625
records.text: NS0625 Question 140 DAA26 Why is naive recursive Fibonacci O(2ⁿ) while DP Fibonacci is O(n)? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Naive recursion repeats states exponentially; DP computes n states once. DAA26 gives tight naive call growth Θ(φ^n), so O(2^n) is a valid loose upper bound rather than the exact rate. Memoization or tabulation needs Θ(n) unit-cost additions and can keep two rolling values for value-only output. Arbitrary-precision arithmetic grows with output bit length and is not truly constant cost per addition.

records.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms — Question 141 · NS0626
records.text: NS0626 Question 141 DAA10 Apply the Master Theorem to T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n². What is the solution? State the model and invariant, then derive the result from the cited procedure or recurrence, checking base cases and limitations. Θ(n² log n) DAA10 has a=4, b=2, so n^(log_b a)=n². The additive f(n)=n² matches that power, selecting the balanced second case. Its logarithmically many levels each contribute Θ(n²), including the appropriate base work, so the total is Θ(n² log n). The polynomial-gap regularity condition belongs to the larger-f third case and is unnecessary here.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Study notes
records.text: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence Study intelligent agents, search and games, knowledge and reasoning, learning, and perception as connected ways to choose actions. For each problem identify the available information, objective, assumptions, and evidence of success before choosing a technique. Give this course its official six-item priority. Learn the comparisons, then practise applying them rather than memorizing option letters. Trace frontier order, path costs, quantifier scope, learning feedback, and evaluation splits on paper. State the conditions behind completeness and optimality. Use the question reference index to revisit weak concepts. Check notation and assumptions carefully when several choices appear valid.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Practice questions
records.text: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Revision outline
records.text: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — AI capabilities and scope
records.text: Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence: reasoning, learning, planning, perception and language. Applied AI builds useful solutions; cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence. A model should be compared with human behavior or experimental observations before claiming it explains human thought. Narrow or weak AI addresses bounded tasks, such as face recognition, spam filtering or a voice assistant. General AI denotes broad competence transferable across domains; strong AI also has a philosophical meaning involving actual understanding. Do not equate a humanoid body, autonomous vehicle, or many features with general intelligence. Exam tip Exam trap Data analysis overlaps AI when it uses learning or inference. It is not categorically excluded from AI. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Four approaches and the Turing test
records.text: Thinking humanly models human mental processes; thinking rationally derives conclusions by valid logic. Acting humanly seeks humanlike behavior; acting rationally selects actions expected to achieve objectives. Thought processes and observed behavior are different evaluation targets. The conversational Turing test asks whether a judge can reliably distinguish a machine from a human through their dialogue. It requires language use, knowledge, reasoning and often learning. It tests an operational behavior criterion, not proof of consciousness. Cognitive models can be tested against response times, errors and psychological experiments. Example Choose the approach Finding a best action sequence to a goal fits acting rationally. Explaining human errors with a computational model fits thinking humanly. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Agents, percepts and action
records.text: An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts through actuators or effectors. Cameras sense; motors move. Software sensors may be incoming messages and software actions may be API requests. Humans are agents but are not artificial agents. A percept is one observation; a percept sequence is the entire observation history. An agent function maps percept sequences to actions: f:P*→A. An agent program implements that mapping on an architecture; agent = architecture + program. Environment means the setting in which it senses and acts, not merely the search space. Autonomy means relying substantially on experience rather than only a designer’s prior instructions. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Rationality and performance
records.text: A performance measure defines success externally: safety, useful deliveries, elapsed time, or cost. Rationality depends on that measure, prior knowledge, percept history, and available actions. A rational agent selects the action with the best expected performance given its information. Omniscience would mean knowing actual action outcomes in advance. Rationality does not require omniscience or guaranteed success. Even complete outcome knowledge cannot create a successful action when every available action fails. Information gathering and exploration may therefore be rational actions. Example Uncertain route A route with expected travel time 20 minutes can be the rational choice even if an unforeseen closure makes it take 40 minutes. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Specify the task with PEAS
records.text: PEAS means Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. Specify all four before designing an agent. For a taxi: performance includes safety and travel time; environment includes roads, traffic and passengers; actuators include steering, brakes and displays; sensors include cameras, positioning and speed readings. A sensor is not an actuator just because it influences a decision. The performance measure is not the percept sequence: one defines success, the other supplies evidence. Separate what the agent can observe from what a designer knows about the world. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Simple and model-based reflex agents
records.text: A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean. It has no persistent world-state memory. This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions. A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects. It then applies rules to that state. Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them. Example Remember a hidden room Remembering that a room was cleaned after it leaves sensor range requires internal state. Merely detecting current dirt does not. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Goals, utility and model updates
records.text: A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state. A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s). Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes. Updating an internal state after selecting an action predicts the action’s effect; it does not itself modify the external environment. A stored variable named goal is insufficient to prove a goal-based policy if BEST_ACTION never uses it. Model-based, goal-based, utility-based and learning capabilities can coexist. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Learning-agent components
records.text: The performance element selects actions. The learning element changes the agent to improve future performance. The critic evaluates behavior against a performance standard and supplies feedback. The problem generator suggests exploratory actions likely to yield useful experience. Learning is improvement on task T, measured by P, through experience E. For spam filtering, T is classifying email, E is past labeled messages, and P might be recall at a required precision. Exploration trades immediate reward for information; exploitation uses the best action currently known. Learning can improve reflex, goal-based or utility-based agents. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Environment dimensions
records.text: Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy. Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness. Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness. Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations. Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do. A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic. Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges. Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability. Example Classify examples Chess is sequential, discrete and deterministic given both players’ chosen moves; untimed chess is static, timed chess semidynamic. A fixed crossword is static. Driving is partially observable, sequential, dynamic and partly continuous. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Single-state, multiple-state and contingency problems
records.text: With a known deterministic model and full observation, a single current state can be used. Without observation but with known deterministic transitions, a sensorless or multiple-state problem tracks a belief state: a set of possible states. Nondeterminism or partial observation may require a contingency plan with branches based on later percepts. Exploration or online search is required when the state space or transition model is unknown; observation alone does not identify this category. These classifications can overlap. A pairing based only on “partially observable, deterministic” cannot distinguish a known sensorless problem from an unknown exploration problem. Russell and Norvig, problem-solving slides

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Formulate before searching
records.text: First formulate the goal; then formulate the problem by specifying initial state, legal actions, transition model, goal test, and action costs. Search selects a sequence; execution applies it. A state abstracts away irrelevant world details. In route finding, states are cities, actions are roads, successors are neighboring cities, and path cost is accumulated distance or time. A solution is a legal path ending at a goal; an optimal solution has minimum cost. Automatic programming or program synthesis searches for a program satisfying a specification; conditional plans and loops require richer representations than a fixed action list. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Frontiers and evaluation criteria
records.text: A search node records a state plus parent, action, depth and path cost. Expanding a node generates its successors. OPEN or frontier stores discovered candidates awaiting expansion; CLOSED records expanded states. Reaching the same state through different paths does not imply the same node or cost. Completeness means finding a solution if one exists under stated assumptions; optimality means returning the best solution. Time counts work, often generated nodes; space counts simultaneous storage. Let b be branching factor, d shallowest goal depth, m maximum search depth, and ℓ a depth limit. Graph-search bounds in vertices V and edges E differ from implicit-tree bounds. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Breadth-first search
records.text: BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs. The tree contains 1+b+…+b^d nodes through depth d, giving O(b^d) under generation-time goal testing. Expanding depth-d nodes before testing can generate depth d+1 and yields O(b^(d+1)); specify the convention. Explicit finite graph traversal with visited-state tracking takes O(V+E) time and O(V) space. Example Trace a queue If S has children A,B and A has C,D, BFS removal order starts S,A,B,C,D, assuming that child order. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Depth-first search
records.text: DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first. Implicit-tree worst-case time is O(b^m), and space is O(bm) when pending siblings are stored, or O(m) for path-only recursive generation. DFS is not generally optimal and can fail on infinite paths or cycles. On a finite graph, visited-state tracking makes traversal complete but needs O(V) storage. Do not confuse the O(b^m) worst-case time bound with the DFS space bounds above. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra
records.text: UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n). Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated. Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent. With finite branching and each step at least ε>0, UCS is complete and optimal. Finite graphs permit nonnegative edges with proper duplicate handling. Dijkstra uses the same minimum-distance principle, often computing all reachable distances; UCS commonly stops at a goal and generates states on demand. Queue initialization is an implementation choice, not a fundamental distinction. Negative edges invalidate the usual finalized-distance argument. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions
records.text: DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level. Bidirectional search grows from start and goal until frontiers connect. With suitable reverse actions, meeting tests and equal-cost BFS, time and space may fall to O(b^(d/2)). Weighted variants require a sound stopping bound; the first intersection need not be cheapest. IDA* deepens an f=g+h threshold rather than only a depth limit. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Heuristics and greedy best-first search
records.text: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g. Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m). Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Admissibility, consistency and A*
records.text: A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path. Admissibility suffices for optimal A* tree search; graph search that never reopens CLOSED states normally requires consistency. With an admissible inconsistent heuristic, reopen states when g improves. Test a goal when removed at minimum f. Completeness also needs finite branching and positive lower-bounded costs in infinite spaces. Worst-case time and memory can be exponential; no heuristic universally guarantees speed. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module UC Berkeley CS188, Search Note 1

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Work a heuristic-search example
records.text: For S→A cost 2, S→B cost 1, A→G cost 2, B→G cost 10, set h(A)=2, h(B)=1, h(G)=0. After expanding S, greedy chooses B because 1<2 and can then choose G, returning cost 11. A* compares A:f=2+2=4 and B:f=1+1=2; after B, its G entry costs 11. It next expands A and replaces G with cost 4, which is removed and accepted. For a sliding puzzle with unit moves, misplaced-tile count and summed Manhattan distances excluding the blank are lower bounds. Straight-line distance is a lower bound on road distance; it is not automatically a lower bound on travel time without conversion using a valid speed bound. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Local optimization and evolutionary search
records.text: Local search keeps a complete candidate configuration and improves its objective; the path may be irrelevant. Hill climbing chooses better neighbors. First-improvement accepts the first improvement; steepest-ascent examines all neighbors; stochastic variants choose among improvements. Local maxima, plateaus and ridges can stop progress. Random restarts or limited sideways steps can help without guaranteeing success. A genetic algorithm maintains a population, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and repeats replacement. It searches without guaranteeing global optimality. Means–ends analysis selects a difference between current and goal states, chooses an operator reducing it, and recursively solves its preconditions. Neither method is simply A* running backward. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Constraint satisfaction
records.text: A CSP specifies variables X, domains D, and constraints C. A solution assigns every variable a value and satisfies every constraint. Complete means all variables assigned; consistent means no violated constraint. A complete assignment can still be inconsistent. Backtracking assigns a variable, tries a legal value, and undoes the choice on failure. Choose the variable with fewest remaining values; break ties by degree; try values that rule out fewest neighbor choices. Forward checking removes incompatible neighbor values. Arc consistency removes a value when a binary constraint offers it no support in the other domain. CSP is a problem framework using search and propagation, not a universal fourth uninformed traversal. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Games and minimax
records.text: Adversarial search models agents with competing objectives. A game specifies states, player to move, legal actions, successor function, terminal test and utility. Perfect information means previous moves and current state are visible; it does not reveal future choices or imply absence of chance. Zero-sum utility makes one player’s gain the other’s loss. Minimax assigns terminal utilities, takes minima at MIN nodes and maxima at MAX nodes, then chooses a maximum-valued root action. It gives the best guaranteed outcome against optimal opposition within the modeled tree. For stochastic outcomes add chance nodes weighted by probabilities. Example Back up leaves If two MIN children have leaves [3,5] and [2,9], their values are 3 and 2. MAX chooses the first branch with value 3. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Alpha–beta and game evaluation
records.text: Alpha is MAX’s best lower bound; beta is MIN’s best upper bound. Pass bounds down, update alpha at MAX and beta at MIN, and prune when alpha≥beta. Pruning preserves the minimax value for the same searched tree. Good move ordering increases pruning: worst-case O(b^m), ideal ordering about O(b^(m/2)). At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions. These are different features, often combined. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Represent knowledge for inference
records.text: Knowledge representation encodes facts, objects, relations, events and rules so a machine can use them. Syntax defines legal expressions; semantics defines their meaning. A knowledge base stores assertions; an inference system derives consequences. Declarative knowledge says what is true; procedural knowledge specifies how to act. A semantic network connects concept nodes by labeled relations such as is-a. Frames describe stereotyped entities through slots, values and defaults. Production systems use IF conditions THEN conclusions or actions, matching rules against working memory and selecting among applicable rules. A graph suits relationships such as frequently bought together; frames suit attributes. No representation is always best for recommendation without task requirements. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Propositional logic and models
records.text: Propositional atoms represent whole true-or-false claims. ¬P negates; P∧Q requires both; P∨Q requires at least one; P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; P↔Q requires matching truth values. Thus P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q. De Morgan gives ¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q. A model is an interpretation making a sentence true. Valid means true in every interpretation; satisfiable means true in at least one; unsatisfiable means true in none. Invalid means not valid, and may still be satisfiable. P∨¬P is valid; P is satisfiable but not valid; P∧¬P is unsatisfiable. Entailment KB⊨α means every model of KB also satisfies α. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — First-order logic and quantifier scope
records.text: First-order logic adds objects, predicates, functions and quantified object variables. Human(a) is a property; Likes(a,b) a relation; father(a) a function term. Propositional logic has no object quantifiers, but its truth still depends on the assigned atom values. Use ∀x(Human(x)→Mortal(x)) for all humans, and ∃x(Student(x)∧Tall(x)) for at least one tall student. These are useful translation patterns, not rules forbidding other connectives. ∀x∃y Likes(x,y) allows a different y for each x; ∃y∀x Likes(x,y) requires one shared y. Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x). Only occurrences within the correct quantifier’s scope are bound. Example Someone at the door ∃x(StandingAt(x,door)∧Tall(x)) requires one individual satisfying both predicates. Using implication instead allows an unrelated individual to satisfy it vacuously. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Inference, unification and chaining
records.text: Modus ponens derives Q from P and P→Q; modus tollens derives ¬P from P→Q and ¬Q. Affirming Q does not prove P. Universal instantiation substitutes an object for a universally quantified variable. Unification finds a consistent substitution: Knows(x,Ada) and Knows(Ben,y) unify with x=Ben,y=Ada. Distinct constants cannot be unified by renaming them. Resolution combines clauses P∨Q and ¬P∨R into Q∨R. To prove α, add ¬α to KB in clause form and derive contradiction. Forward chaining starts with facts and fires rules; backward chaining starts with a query and proves required premises. Sound inference preserves truth; completeness means finding all entailed conclusions in its specified setting. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Deduction, induction and abduction
records.text: Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal. Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it. Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations. Classical logical entailment is monotonic: adding premises preserves previous consequences. Default reasoning can be nonmonotonic: infer a bird usually flies, then withdraw this when told it is a penguin. Common-sense defaults are useful with incomplete knowledge, but are not guaranteed truths. Blind search is a search strategy, not a definition of reasoning. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Probability and uncertain models
records.text: Probability describes uncertainty about events. P(¬A)=1−P(A); P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes gives P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E): posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence probability. For mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses, P(E)=ΣiP(E|Hi)P(Hi). A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with conditional probability tables; its joint distribution factors as the product of each node’s probability given its parents. A Markov model assumes the next state depends on the current state rather than the entire past. These represent uncertainty; fuzzy membership represents a different issue. Example Update a hypothesis If P(H)=0.1, P(E|H)=0.8 and P(E|¬H)=0.2, then P(E)=0.26 and P(H|E)=0.08/0.26≈0.308. Likelihood 0.8 is not the posterior. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Fuzzy logic and vague categories
records.text: Fuzzy sets assign graded membership μ(x) between 0 and 1 to concepts such as warm or tall. A temperature can belong to warm with degree 0.7. This is not a 70% probability that an otherwise crisp warm proposition is true. Boolean logic uses only true and false; probability describes uncertainty about events. A fuzzy controller fuzzifies measurements, applies graded IF–THEN rules, combines outputs and often defuzzifies to a numerical action. Fuzzy control suits linguistic rules about degrees; reinforcement learning suits reward-based adaptation. Merely saying an environment is complex or uncertain does not uniquely select either method. James Brule, Fuzzy Systems tutorial, CMU archive

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Supervised learning and prediction
records.text: Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method. A decision tree tests an attribute at each internal node, follows the corresponding branch and predicts at a leaf. ID3 chooses high information gain: H(S)=−Σpᵢlog₂pᵢ; gain is parent entropy minus weighted child entropy. Gini impurity is 1−Σpᵢ², zero for a pure class. Pruning limits overfitting. Neural networks, support-vector machines and trees can all be supervised. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning
records.text: Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates. Semi-supervised learning combines some labels with additional unlabeled data. Active learning chooses informative cases for an oracle to label; it still uses labels. “Exploratory learning” is not an exclusive standard synonym: it can mean unsupervised exploration or active data acquisition, so define the feedback. A task named summarization or time-series analysis is not automatically supervised; its training targets determine that. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module Burr Settles, From Theories to Queries

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Reinforcement learning
records.text: An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward. An illustrative discounted return is Gt=rt+1+γrt+2+γ²rt+3+…, with 0≤γ<1. The policy maps states or histories to action choices. Exploration gathers information; exploitation pursues currently estimated reward. RL is part of machine learning, which is part of AI. “No labels” alone fits both unsupervised learning and RL; reward-driven interaction distinguishes RL. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Neural networks and deep learning
records.text: A neuron computes z=Σiwixi+b and output a=φ(z). For x=(2,1), w=(0.5,−1), b=0.2, z=0.2. Linear activation returns z; sigmoid returns 1/(1+e^(−z)); tanh is bipolar; ReLU returns max(0,z). Nonlinearities let multiple layers represent nonlinear relationships. Feedforward networks pass signals toward outputs without recurrent state loops; recurrent networks carry state across sequence steps. Training adjusts weights, often through gradients and backpropagation. Backpropagation is not the same as a recurrent connection. Deep learning uses multiple representation layers and can learn features from images, sound and text. CNNs share filters across image locations. ANN is a brain-inspired abstraction, not a literal brain simulation; DL⊂ML⊂AI. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Generalization and validation
records.text: Overfitting means fitting training-specific details so performance drops on unseen data; underfitting means the model is too limited or poorly fitted even on training data. A learning curve plots performance against training size or training progress. Complexity control, regularization, pruning and more representative data can help. Train data fits parameters; validation data selects models or settings; a held-out test set estimates final performance. In k-fold validation, train k models, each on k−1 folds and evaluate on the remaining fold, then average scores. Stratification approximately preserves label proportions. Fit preprocessing within each training fold. Time-ordered data needs splits respecting time; repeated tuning on the final test set leaks information. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module scikit-learn, Cross-validation

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Measure the right errors
records.text: With a fixed positive class, TP means true positives, FP false positive predictions, FN missed positives, TN true negatives. Accuracy=(TP+TN)/N; precision=TP/(TP+FP); recall=TP/(TP+FN); F1=2PR/(P+R). State the averaging and zero-denominator convention when relevant. For TP=30, FP=10, FN=20, TN=40, accuracy=70%, precision=75%, recall=60%, and F1≈66.7%. Accuracy can hide failure on a rare class. Choose recall when missed positives matter; choose precision when false alarms are costly. Regression errors include MAE=mean|y−ŷ| and MSE=mean(y−ŷ)²; squared error penalizes large misses more strongly. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Language processing tasks
records.text: NLP interprets and generates human language: translation, dialogue, summarization, question answering and text generation. Speech recognition converts audio to text; speech synthesis generates speech. They overlap language processing but solve different input/output tasks. Tokenization divides text into processing units; tokens may be words, punctuation or subwords. POS tagging assigns grammatical roles; named-entity recognition identifies people, organizations and locations. Parsing identifies grammatical structure; semantics concerns meaning; discourse links sentences; pragmatics uses context and speaker intent. Sentiment analysis predicts evaluative tone. Ambiguity can occur at every level: “bank” has multiple senses, and “I saw the man with a telescope” has multiple attachments. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Morphology, sounds and prosody
records.text: Morphology studies meaningful word parts: un-happi-ness contains a prefix, stem and suffix; cats contains cat and plural -s. It differs from tokenization, which identifies processing boundaries. Phonetics studies physical speech sounds; phonology studies a language’s sound patterns and contrasts. Prosody concerns stress, rhythm, timing, prominence and intonation across syllables and phrases. A pitch rise can help signal a question; shifting stress can change emphasis. These cues assist dialogue and speech processing. Pragmatics concerns intended meaning in context, not the internal components of words. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, phonetics chapter

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Perception, vision and robotics
records.text: Computer vision interprets images or video: classification names image content, detection locates objects, segmentation labels pixels, and recognition identifies objects or people. Occlusion, lighting change, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context make open-world perception difficult even when a face detector works well. Robotics combines mechanical, electrical, control and computing systems to sense, plan and act physically. Components include sensors, controller, power supply, actuators and an end effector. Locomotion may be legged, wheeled or tracked, with trade-offs in terrain, stability and efficiency. Software can act autonomously without being a robot. Humanoid shape is not evidence of general intelligence. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Expert systems and choosing methods
records.text: An expert system applies specialized knowledge to a domain such as equipment diagnosis. The domain expert supplies expertise; the knowledge engineer elicits and encodes it; the inference engine reasons over a knowledge base and working facts. The user interface handles interaction; an explanation facility presents why or how a conclusion was reached. Rules offer inspectable domain reasoning but can be brittle and costly to maintain. Learned models handle data-rich patterns but depend on representative data and validation. Search suits explicit action alternatives; probabilistic models suit uncertain evidence. Bias in data or evaluation can create unfair outcomes. Evaluate errors across relevant groups, robustness, privacy and human oversight rather than assuming automation is always beneficial. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Clarify search and logic questions
records.text: A* is forward best-first search combining actual past cost with estimated future cost; it does not inherently run a backward frontier. Both A* and IDA* can have exponential worst cases and optimality under their conditions. “Minimum heuristic” and “estimated closest” describe the same greedy choice. LIFO and FILO are synonyms. Using information from the current state alone does not establish that a search uses a heuristic. Ask whether remaining cost is estimated. Both “invalid iff unsatisfiable” and “satisfiable implies valid” are false in general; distinguish validity from satisfiability. Evaluate each validity claim separately, or identify all false statements when several are offered. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module UC Berkeley CS188, Search Note 1

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Distinguish agent categories and components
records.text: The common teaching list contains five agent classes when learning agents are included, or four decision architectures before learning is added. State the convention when counting agent types. “Target-based” can mean goal-based; “unity-based” is not utility-based. A generic rule does not distinguish simple from model-based reflex without specifying memory. A goal declaration unused by the action policy does not establish goal-based behavior. “Sensors and effectors” describes interaction, not omniscience or intelligence by itself. Define the mechanical distinction when comparing effectors and actuators as acting components. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Clarify overlapping learning and AI labels
records.text: ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives. Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised. To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure. Face recognition is both an applied task and a narrow capability. Broad machine-intelligence goals can include emulating human intelligence and building systems that learn. Humanlike problem-solving alone does not uniquely select expert systems. Python is widely used, but C++ and Java also implement AI; “commonly used” does not isolate one language. McCarthy is associated with naming AI, not its sole invention. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Interpret quantified statements and search assumptions
records.text: The formula ∀x∃y∃t¬F(x,y,t) means that for each person there is a person and time at which fooling fails. By quantifier negation this is ¬∃x∀y∀t F(x,y,t), so nobody fools everybody all the time. Forbidding every successful instance is a much stronger claim than this formula. Preserve the quantifiers and negation when translating between a formula and a verbal statement. Compare Dijkstra and uniform-cost search under stated implementations rather than treating queue initialization as an intrinsic difference. For chess, specify the unit of decision: moves within a match are sequential; independently reset matches can be episodes. Select a recommendation design from explicit requirements; graph relationships can support a choice without excluding other designs. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Programmed computation and learned patterns
records.text: A conventional computer manipulates digital information according to a program or sequence of instructions. Programs can implement storage, retrieval and learning operations. Neural networks can learn pattern recognition from examples, so executing instructions and learning patterns are not mutually exclusive descriptions. This provides no universal claim that every machine is better or worse than every human at completing missing information. AI algorithms are not exclusive to one programming language. Rumale is a Ruby machine-learning library with classification and clustering implementations, demonstrating that Ruby can implement learning algorithms as well as the general-purpose languages already discussed. Language choice and learning regime are different decisions. NIST glossary — Computer Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module · page 71 Rumale — official project README

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal
records.text: Binary search exploits the order of a sorted sequence: a comparison narrows the remaining candidate interval instead of exploring arbitrary successor states. Array bisection therefore differs from breadth-first or depth-first traversal of a general state-space graph. A storage container such as an array does not by itself specify FIFO or LIFO frontier behavior. Python documentation — Array bisection and searching sorted lists Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module · page 18

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Agent task models and practical planning
records.text: An AI task is modeled as an agent interacting with its environment: observations enter through sensors and selected actions affect the environment through actuators. This task-level description differs from an agent implementation, which combines a program with a computing architecture. In ordinary usage, rationality means reasonable, sensible judgment. For an AI agent, the operational criterion is the action with the best expected performance given its percept history and available knowledge, rather than guaranteed success or knowledge of the actual future. Planning constructs actions to reach a goal. Scheduling additionally assigns activities to times and resources while respecting constraints such as resource conflicts and precedence. It is an AI application when search or constraint reasoning chooses feasible or useful assignments; automated telescope experiment scheduling is an example. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module · page 11 Introduction to Artificial Intelligence module · page 7

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Attributing the name of artificial intelligence
records.text: John McCarthy is credited with coining the term artificial intelligence in the 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth summer research project. The Dartmouth workshop took place in 1956 and helped establish the field. Naming the field does not mean that one person invented all its ideas or methods. Stanford HAI — What is Artificial Intelligence? Dartmouth — Artificial Intelligence Coined at Dartmouth

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Related search and game-evaluation methods
records.text: Simulated annealing follows a current candidate and randomly samples a neighboring move. It accepts improvements and sometimes accepts worse moves according to a temperature that decreases over time. Unlike genetic search, its defining mechanism is not a population undergoing parent selection, crossover and mutation. For two admissible heuristics, h₂ dominates h₁ when h₂(n)≥h₁(n) for every node. Dominance compares estimates; it is not itself a condition ensuring that an arbitrary heuristic never overestimates. Both estimates must separately satisfy the relevant admissibility assumptions. A Monte Carlo game simulation samples possible continuations and uses their outcomes to estimate position value. An evaluation function is the scoring mapping itself; sampling is one way of obtaining an estimate, while minimax backs values up and alpha–beta removes branches that cannot affect that backed-up decision. Russell and Norvig — Informed Search and Exploration Silver et al. — Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Prediction, transfer and explicit representations
records.text: Transfer learning reuses representations or a model learned on an earlier task for a new task, for example adapting pretrained image features to new image classes. This is a reuse strategy, not a specification that the new task has no labels or rewards. Support-vector machines include supervised classification and regression methods. They use support vectors in their decision function rather than being defined by a next-state conditional-dependence assumption. In estimation, variance measures how predictions change across different training samples; overfitting instead names poor generalization caused by fitting training-specific details. An ontology describes entities or individuals, classes and properties and may state logical relationships and restrictions. It organizes explicit conceptual knowledge. Conditional probability tables and a probabilistic factorization are additional modeling commitments, not inherent in the word ontology. An application programming interface (API) exposes defined operations through which software requests functionality. It can be an interface used by an agent, but the interface alone is not the general entity that perceives an environment and selects actions. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Behavior tests, understanding and software tests
records.text: Searle’s Chinese-room argument challenges whether executing formal symbol-manipulation rules is sufficient for understanding. It is a philosophical argument about understanding, not the conversational judge-and-hidden-participant procedure of the Turing test. Black-box software testing examines externally visible functionality without inspecting implementation internals. A specification may concern any software behavior; this testing method does not by itself require conversational indistinguishability from a human. John Searle — Minds, Brains, and Programs (author draft) NIST glossary — Black box testing

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 3 · Q00028
records.text: Q00028 Question 3 AI10 Assume the entire state space and transition model are known for every task below, despite any hidden current state. Which problem/environment coupling is incorrect? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Contingency problem -> partially observable, non-deterministic B Multiple state problem deterministic, partially observable C Exploration problem -> partially observable, deterministic D Single state problem-> fully observable, deterministic Exploration problem -> partially observable, deterministic A known deterministic model with incomplete observation can be handled by a belief state representing several possible current states. Unknown state spaces or transition models create the need for exploration; partial observability alone does not. Nondeterministic partial observation can require contingency branches, while full observation with known deterministic transitions supports a single-state formulation. The explicit knowledge assumption therefore makes the exploration pairing the incorrect one. A incorrect This is a valid coupling: partial observation and nondeterminism can require contingency branches, so it is not the incorrect pairing. B incorrect This is valid under the known-model assumption: incomplete observation can require a belief state, so it is not selected. C correct This is the incorrect coupling: hidden state with a known deterministic model does not by itself require exploration. D incorrect This is valid: full observation and known deterministic transitions support a single current state.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 4 · Q00033
records.text: Q00033 Question 4 AI26 AI25 Which one of the following is correct first order logic for the statement "There is someone standing at the door and is tall"? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A ∀x (StandingAt (x; door ) B ∀x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x)) C ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x)) D ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door ) -> toll(x)) ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x)) “There is someone” requires ∃x, and “standing ... and ... tall” requires StandingAt(x,door) ∧ tall(x), so C asserts one witness with both properties (PDF pp. 46, 49). An implication does not assert its antecedent and therefore cannot assert that anyone is at the door. A incorrect Incomplete formula with a universal quantifier and no tall predicate. See PDF p. 49, 46. B incorrect Claims everyone has both properties rather than at least one person. See PDF p. 49, 46. C correct Existentially binds the same x in both conjuncts. See PDF p. 49, 46. D incorrect Uses implication instead of conjunction and also spells the predicate toll. See PDF p. 49, 46.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 5 · Q00057
records.text: Q00057 Question 5 AI04 Which statements are incorrect? Interpret rational action as maximizing expected performance given available information; do not assume a successful action always exists. Select all that apply. Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A A rational agent know the result of its action, but unrealistic B Rational agent take action but not 100% sure of success C Rational agent act to achieve utmost success based on information D An omniscience agent takes actions for 100% sure of success A rational agent know the result of its action, but unrealistic; An omniscience agent takes actions for 100% sure of success Rationality concerns choosing the action with the best expected performance given the agent’s information. It does not mean knowing actual outcomes in advance, so the first claim incorrectly attributes omniscience to a rational agent. Even omniscience would not ensure success if all available actions fail. The remaining statements correctly allow uncertainty while requiring the best expected choice under the available evidence. A correct This is false: rationality does not imply knowing actual action outcomes in advance. B incorrect This is true: a rational action need not guarantee success. C incorrect This is true when utmost success means best expected performance given the available information. D correct This is false: complete outcome knowledge cannot guarantee that a successful action exists.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 6 · Q00059
records.text: Q00059 Question 6 AI15 AI13 AI16 ________ finds the shortest path to the goal based on cost. Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Depth first search B Iterative deepening C Uniform cost search D Breath first search Uniform cost search Uniform-cost search explicitly seeks the goal path with lowest cumulative cost and uses a priority queue (PDF p. 21). “Shortest” here means minimum cost, under the usual nonnegative-cost setting; minimum depth alone is not sufficient when edge costs vary. A incorrect Follows depth and is explicitly nonoptimal on p. 19. See PDF p. 21, 21. B incorrect Increases depth limits, not cumulative-cost priority. See PDF p. 21, 21. C correct Directly minimizes cumulative path cost. See PDF p. 21, 21. D incorrect Minimizes steps; equivalent to UCS only when all edge costs are equal. See PDF p. 21, 21.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 8 · Q00178
records.text: Q00178 Question 8 AI22 AI23 Among the following, which kind of algorithm is used in the Game tree to make decisions of Win/Lose? D incorrect Chooses local heuristic promise rather than alternating MAX/MIN decisions. See PDF p. 33, 34.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 12 · Q00182
records.text: Q00182 Question 12 AI32 AI33 Here “exploratory learning” means discovering structure in data without target labels, oracle labeling or reward-driven interaction. Which learning regime is meant? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Supervised learning B Active learning C Unsupervised learning D Reinforcement learning E None of the Above Unsupervised learning Unsupervised learning seeks patterns such as clusters or associations without target labels. Active learning asks an oracle to label selected cases, supervised learning fits labeled input-target examples, and reinforcement learning improves behavior from reward-driven interaction. Specifying the feedback makes the intended use of exploratory precise. The term alone would have several usages, but the stated unlabeled structure-discovery task identifies a definite learning regime. A incorrect Supervised learning uses labeled targets, excluded by the stem. B incorrect Active learning obtains oracle labels, excluded by the stem. C correct Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels. D incorrect Reinforcement learning uses reward-driven interaction, excluded here. E incorrect The specified regime is present among the choices.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 13 · Q00183
records.text: Q00183 Question 13 AI26 AI44 Let F(x,y,t) mean that person x can fool person y at time t. Over nonempty person and time domains, which statement is equivalent to ∀x∃y∃t ¬F(x,y,t)? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Everyone can fool some person at some time B Every person has someone whom they cannot fool at any time. C No person can fool any person at any time. D No one can fool everyone all the time No one can fool everyone all the time For each person x, the formula requires a person y and a time t for which fooling fails. Moving negation across the quantifiers gives ¬∃x∀y∀t F(x,y,t): nobody can fool everyone all the time. The witness and time can depend on x. Requiring failure at every time, or forbidding all fooling events, would be stronger claims. A incorrect This asserts a successful fooling event for each person, rather than an unsuccessful event. B incorrect This requires one witness person who cannot be fooled at every time, a stronger time scope than the formula requires. C incorrect This forbids all fooling events, much stronger than requiring one unsuccessful event for each person. D correct Negating someone fooling everyone at every time yields, for each person, someone and some time when fooling fails.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 14 · Q00184
records.text: Q00184 Question 14 AI37 A language system must decide which interpretation is intended when a sentence permits more than one meaning or grammatical attachment. Which NLP challenge does this describe? Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task. A Handling Tokenization B Handling Ambiguity of Sentences C Handling POS-Tagging D Handling Semantics of Sentences E All of the mentioned Handling Ambiguity of Sentences The difficulty described is ambiguity: a word or sentence can permit multiple meanings or structural attachments. Tokenization creates units, POS tagging assigns grammatical roles, and semantic analysis concerns meaning. These tasks can help resolve ambiguity, but they are not synonymous with the particular obstacle. The question therefore asks for the named challenge rather than ranking all NLP difficulties. A incorrect Tokenization decides processing units; it does not name the existence of multiple interpretations. B correct Ambiguity means that more than one interpretation is possible. C incorrect POS tagging assigns grammatical categories rather than naming the competing interpretations. D incorrect Semantics studies meaning generally; the specific obstacle described is multiplicity of interpretations. E incorrect This includes tokenization, tagging and semantic analysis in general, which do not all name the specific multiple-interpretation obstacle.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 15 · Q00199
records.text: Q00199 Question 15 AI17 AI-S02 A goal-directed search strategy uses a problem-specific estimate of remaining cost to order current frontier candidates. Which category is it? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Uninformed search B Informed search C Circular traversal without heuristic estimates D Binary search Informed search Informed search uses problem-specific heuristic information to estimate remaining cost or promise. Merely retaining the current state would not establish that category, because uninformed search also uses states, successors and known costs. The revised stem supplies the missing estimate. Binary search concerns an ordered interval rather than this state-space frontier, and circular traversal does not identify the heuristic-informed category being tested. A incorrect Uninformed search lacks the extra remaining-cost heuristic specified here. B correct Informed search uses problem-specific heuristic estimates to guide the frontier. C incorrect Traversal without heuristic estimates does not meet the specified remaining-cost-guided strategy. D incorrect Binary search needs an ordered search interval, not merely goal-directed state exploration.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 16 · Q00200
records.text: Q00200 Question 16 AI09 An agent’s actions affect later decisions; identical state-action pairs can have different outcomes; and the world changes while the agent deliberates. Which list describes these three properties? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Deterministic, fully observable, static B Fully observable, sequential, deterministic C Partially observable, static, continuous D Sequential, non-deterministic, dynamic Sequential, non-deterministic, dynamic The scenario establishes three independent dimensions. Earlier actions affect later decisions, so it is sequential. Outcomes are not fixed by the state-action pair, so it is non-deterministic. Change during deliberation makes it dynamic. It gives no complete observation or continuity specification. Classifying the stated properties avoids an unsupported universal ranking of how difficult different environments must be. A incorrect Determinism and a static world contradict the uncertain outcomes and ongoing change. B incorrect Sequential fits, but deterministic outcomes contradict the scenario. C incorrect A static environment cannot change while the agent deliberates; this list also omits the stated action dependence. D correct Sequential captures dependent decisions, non-deterministic captures uncertain outcomes, and dynamic captures change during deliberation.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 18 · Q00202
records.text: Q00202 Question 18 AI35 An evaluation technique of classifier accuracy where we randomly partition the data into k mutually exclusive subsets, each approximately equal size and, use Di as test set and others as training set at i-th iteration is ______. Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Random sampling B Cross-validation C Stratified cross-validation D Holdout method k-fold cross-validation. AI35 describes exactly the rotation in the stem: build k models, each trained on all folds except one, evaluate on that held-out fold, then average the scores. The stem does not say class proportions are preserved, so stratification is not established. A single holdout split or generic random sampling does not specify this complete rotation. A incorrect Random sampling alone does not specify the disjoint k-fold rotation of training and test subsets. B correct The described repeated use of each fold as the held-out subset is k-fold cross-validation. C incorrect Stratification additionally preserves label proportions, a condition not supplied by equal fold sizes alone. D incorrect A holdout method uses a fixed split rather than rotating through all k disjoint test folds.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 31 · Q00600
records.text: Q00600 Question 31 AI38 Which types of rule used in phonology to interpretation of the fluctuation in stress and intonation across the sentences? Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task. A Phonetic rule B Phonemic rule C Prosodic rule D Morpheme rule Prosodic rules. AI38 identifies stress and intonation as prosodic phenomena, alongside rhythm, timing and prominence. That directly matches the sentence-level variations in the question. Physical sound production and phonemic contrasts describe other aspects of speech; morphemes are meaningful word parts. The phrase phonology in the stem does not change the specific prosodic level requested. A incorrect Phonetic rules concern physical speech sounds, while the stated stress and intonation patterns are specifically prosodic. B incorrect Phonemic contrasts distinguish sound categories; they are not the specific stress-and-intonation rule category requested. C correct Prosodic rules address stress, prominence, rhythm and intonation across syllables and phrases. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 39 · Q00655
records.text: Q00655 Question 39 AI26 AI25 Which statement correctly distinguishes propositional logic from first-order logic? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A It evaluates whole propositions using a truth assignment, without quantifying over objects in a domain. B It is predicate logic C It assigns truth to open predicates without assigning values to their object variables. D It contains quantifier It evaluates whole propositions using a truth assignment, without quantifying over objects in a domain. Propositional logic treats atoms as whole true-or-false claims and evaluates compound formulas from a truth assignment. It does not quantify over individual objects. First-order logic adds predicates, object variables, interpretations and quantifiers. The distinction does not mean that propositional truth needs no assignment: the truth values of its atoms still matter. A correct Propositional evaluation uses atom truth values rather than object-domain quantification. B incorrect Propositional logic is not identical to first-order predicate logic. C incorrect Open predicates need interpretation and variable assignments; this is not a propositional truth rule. D incorrect Object quantifiers belong to first-order logic, not propositional syntax.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 47 · Q00961
records.text: Q00961 Question 47 AI39 AI01 Why is perception still a challenge for AI—even though systems can recognize faces? Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task. A Because perception is unrelated to reasoning B Because AI lacks actuators C Because open-world inputs may contain occlusion, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context. D Because sensors are too expensive Because open-world inputs may contain occlusion, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context. Recognizing faces in some settings does not solve all perception problems. Occlusion can hide relevant features, noise can corrupt observations, and unfamiliar conditions or missing context can make an interpretation unreliable. These are difficulties in interpreting sensory information. They do not require every perception task to use natural-language understanding, and they are distinct from actuator availability or sensor price. A incorrect Perception can use context and support reasoning; it is not unrelated to it. B incorrect Actuators implement actions, while the question concerns difficulty interpreting sensory input. C correct Occlusion, noise and unfamiliar or incomplete context can defeat otherwise successful recognition systems. D incorrect Cost is not the conceptual reason that open-world interpretation remains difficult.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 63 · Q01020
records.text: Q01020 Question 63 AI30 AI20 AI33 AI34 Which approach represents imprecise linguistic categories such as warm by graded membership between zero and one, rather than treating membership as strictly true or false? A Genetic algorithms B Fuzzy logic C Neural networks D Reinforcement learning Fuzzy logic Fuzzy logic represents imprecise categories through graded membership, so an input can belong to a category to a degree rather than only completely or not at all. This differs from uncertainty about whether an event occurs. Genetic search, neural networks and reinforcement learning can be combined with fuzzy methods, but their defining mechanisms do not supply this membership interpretation. Artificial intelligence therefore also contains reinforcement learning, but it is the broader ancestor rather than the immediate parent requested. Data analytics is an application context rather than the stated parent field. The explicit hierarchy makes the nearer containing field the unique taxonomic selection. A incorrect AI contains RL indirectly through machine learning, but is not the immediate parent requested. B incorrect Data analytics is not the stated parent-field classification of RL in the note. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 102 · Q01060
records.text: Q01060 Question 102 AI14 For DFS on an implicit tree with branching factor b and maximum depth m, storing pending siblings, which expression gives the standard worst-case space bound? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A b B b^2 C b^b D O(bm) O(bm) Depth-first search retains the active branch and pending alternatives rather than an entire breadth frontier. With up to b pending entries per level over depth m, the standard stored-frontier space bound is O(bm). Path-only on-demand generation can use O(m), but that is a different implementation convention. The expression gives the depth-dependent storage bound rather than an exponential time bound. A incorrect b omits growth with search depth m in the general DFS storage bound. B incorrect b² is not the stated depth-dependent worst-case DFS storage expression. C incorrect b^b is neither of the note’s DFS space bounds. D correct With pending siblings, at most a branching-factor-sized set per depth gives the standard O(bm) space bound.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 103 · Q01061
records.text: Q01061 Question 103 AI13 For BFS on an implicit tree with branching factor b>1 and shallowest goal depth d, using generation-time goal testing, which expression gives the standard worst-case generated-node order? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A b B b^d C b^2 D b^b b^d BFS generates levels in order. Under generation-time goal testing, the generated nodes through the shallowest goal depth d are bounded by the geometric sum 1+b+…+b^d, whose dominant term is b^d when b>1. Testing only after expanding deeper nodes can change the conventional bound by another factor of b, so the question states the goal-test convention. A incorrect b counts one level and does not account for arbitrary goal depth. B correct The sum 1+b+…+b^d has order b^d for b>1. C incorrect b² only describes a fixed depth-two case rather than general depth d. D incorrect b^b wrongly replaces solution depth d with the branching factor.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 104 · Q01062
records.text: Q01062 Question 104 AI14 AI13 Which labels describe the recursive DFS stack’s removal order? Select all that apply. Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A LIFO B LILO C FIFO D FILO LIFO; FILO Recursive depth-first search returns first from the most recently entered unfinished call. That is last-in-first-out stack order, also called first-in-last-out. The two labels are synonyms rather than distinct data structures. FIFO or LILO describes the opposite end-to-end order and does not characterize the DFS call stack. The multiple-selection instruction therefore retains both correct names for the same discipline. A correct LIFO is the stack order used by recursion and depth-first exploration. B incorrect LILO does not express the required last-in-first-out removal order. C incorrect FIFO is queue order, associated with breadth-first rather than depth-first selection. D correct FILO is another name for LIFO and therefore also describes the DFS stack.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 107 · Q01065
records.text: Q01065 Question 107 AI17 What is the heuristic function of greedy best-first search? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A f(n) != h(n) B f(n) < h(n) C f(n) = h(n) D f(n) > h(n) f(n) = h(n) The operational rule removes the node with lowest h(n), so the greedy evaluation is f(n)=h(n).
