records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 108 · Q01066
records.text: Q01066 Question 108 AI17 AI13 AI14 Greedy best-first search selects which descriptions of the next node? Interpret “closest” as estimated remaining cost h, not actual distance. Select all that apply. Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Shallowest B Deepest C The one closest to the goal node D Minimum heuristic cost The one closest to the goal node; Minimum heuristic cost Greedy best-first search orders the frontier by h alone, choosing the smallest estimated remaining cost and ignoring cost already paid. Under the explicit interpretation, estimated closest to the goal and minimum heuristic cost express that same rule. Shallowest-first uses depth as in breadth-first search, while deepest-first follows depth-first ordering. Both heuristic descriptions are therefore valid and neither depth description is selected. A incorrect Shallowest-first is BFS-style depth ordering rather than greedy heuristic selection. B incorrect Deepest-first is DFS-style selection rather than minimum estimated remaining cost. C correct Read closest as estimated by h; it is the same greedy criterion as minimum heuristic cost. D correct Greedy best-first selects a node with minimum h, ignoring already-paid path cost.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 109 · Q01067
records.text: Q01067 Question 109 AI18 AI15 AI17 AI13 AI14 Which general search family contains A* because it selects frontier nodes by a minimum evaluation value? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Breadth-First-Search B Depth-First-Search C Uniform Cost Search D Best-First-Search Best-First-Search Best-first search is the general family that selects a frontier node according to an evaluation value. A* is one member, using f=g+h. Uniform-cost search is another member, using g alone. Breadth-first and depth-first names describe depth-oriented selection disciplines. The question asks for the containing family rather than claiming A* is identical to one simpler algorithm. A incorrect BFS selects by depth/FIFO order rather than the general evaluation-priority family. B incorrect DFS follows stack/deepest-branch order rather than minimum evaluation priority. C incorrect UCS is another best-first method using g alone; it is not the general family containing A*. D correct Best-first search is the family that selects by an evaluation, with A* using g+h.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 110 · Q01188
records.text: Q01188 Question 110 AI07 AI06 Function MY_AGENT (PERCEPT) return action static state, a description of the current world state goal, a description of the goal to achieve may be in terms of state state ← UPDATE_STATE(state, percept) actionSet ← POSSIBLE_ACTIONS(state) action ← BEST_ACTION(actionSet) state ← UPDATE_STATE(state, action) return action What is the purpose of the final instruction state ← UPDATE_STATE(state, action), after BEST_ACTION has selected an action? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Modify the state of the environment if necessary B Update the state information to be like the one after executing the best action chosen C Update the environment so that the agent can perceive the next percept D Modify the state of the environment once the decision of which action to choose is made. Update the state information to be like the one after executing the best action chosen The final update uses the chosen action to predict what the agent’s internal state representation should look like after that action. It is distinct from the earlier update using the current percept. Updating memory does not execute an actuator or directly modify the external environment. Naming the exact instruction resolves the missing referent while preserving the model-update interpretation of the original prototype. A incorrect Updating an internal state representation does not itself modify the external environment. B correct The final call predicts and records the internal state after the selected action. C incorrect Neither internal update executes an environmental action or produces the next percept. D incorrect Selecting an action and updating memory are distinct from changing the external world through execution.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 111 · Q01194
records.text: Q01194 Question 111 AI17 AI15 AI13 AI14 To implement greedy best-first search, let the evaluation be the estimated remaining cost h(n). Which OPEN-list insertion policy supplies its node-selection order? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Append newly generated nodes at the beginning of the open list B Append newly generated nodes at the end of the open list C Insert newly generated nodes in the open list according to their path cost (lowest values first) D Insert newly generated nodes in the open list according to their evaluation function (lowest values first) Insert newly generated nodes in the open list according to their evaluation function (lowest values first) Greedy best-first search orders its frontier by h alone, the estimate of remaining cost. A priority-ordered OPEN list with the smallest evaluation first therefore implements the rule when that evaluation is h. Ordering by g would instead implement uniform-cost search. Unconditionally prepending or appending nodes gives stack-like or FIFO behavior without the required heuristic ranking. A incorrect Prepending every new node gives a stack-like policy rather than ordering by remaining-cost estimates. B incorrect Appending every new node gives FIFO breadth order rather than heuristic priority. C incorrect Ordering by accumulated path cost g implements uniform-cost selection, not greedy h-only selection. D correct Ordering by the stated evaluation h puts the smallest estimated remaining cost first.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 112 · Q01199
records.text: Q01199 Question 112 AI25 In classical propositional logic over a nonempty set of interpretations, which statements are false? In D, “models” means all interpretations. Select all that apply. Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A A sentence is said to be invalid iff it is unsatisfiable. B A sentence is valid if it is satisfiable. C A sentence which is not invalid is satisfiable. D A sentence is unsatisfiable if it is false in all models. A sentence is said to be invalid iff it is unsatisfiable.; A sentence is valid if it is satisfiable. Validity requires truth in every interpretation, while satisfiability requires truth in at least one. A contingent atom can therefore be satisfiable and invalid, refuting both the proposed invalid-unsatisfiable equivalence and the claim that satisfiability implies validity. Not invalid means valid and hence satisfiable in the stated nonempty setting. Unsatisfiable means false in every interpretation, so the remaining two statements are true. A correct False: a satisfiable contingent sentence can be invalid without being unsatisfiable. B correct False: truth in one interpretation does not imply truth in every interpretation. C incorrect True: not invalid means valid, which entails satisfiability in the ordinary model setting. D incorrect True: unsatisfiable means there is no interpretation making the sentence true.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 113 · Q01202
records.text: Q01202 Question 113 AI07 AI06 Consider this agent prototype: Function MY_AGENT(percept) returns action static state, goal state ← UPDATE_STATE(state, percept) actionSet ← POSSIBLE_ACTIONS(state) action ← BEST_ACTION(actionSet, state, goal) state ← UPDATE_STATE(state, action) return action BEST_ACTION uses lookahead over future action sequences and chooses by whether the specified desired state is reached; it does not rank successful outcomes by utility or learn from experience. Which category best describes this action-selection criterion? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Goal based B Model based reflex C Simple reflex D Utility based Goal based The action selector explicitly consults the desired state and looks ahead over sequences that can reach it. That is the defining goal-based decision criterion. Persistent state also gives the agent a model-based capability, but memory alone does not identify its selection policy. A reflex policy would apply condition-action rules instead of goal-directed lookahead, and utility-based choice would rank degrees of desirability among outcomes. A correct Goal-directed lookahead chooses sequences reaching a desired state, matching goal-based action selection. B incorrect The agent maintains a model, but the stated policy uses goal-directed lookahead rather than reflex rules. C incorrect Persistent state and future-sequence evaluation contradict a current-percept-only reflex policy. D incorrect No utility ranking is used; the selector evaluates attainment of the desired state.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 114 · Q01220
records.text: Q01220 Question 114 AI03 AI42 AI39 Which are general terms for the components through which an arbitrary AI agent acts on its environment, rather than sensing components or one particular robot subtype? The scope allows the two synonymous general terms without incorrectly denying that robotic manipulators can carry out actions. C correct Actuators are the note’s equivalent general term for acting components. D incorrect A manipulator is a particular physical device, not the general acting-interface term requested.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 115 · Q01252
records.text: Q01252 Question 115 AI09 A control agent has incomplete observations, uncertain transition outcomes, actions that affect later decisions, a world that changes during deliberation, and real-valued measurements and controls. Which list matches all these properties? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. Incomplete observations give partial observability; uncertain outcomes give non-determinism; effects on later decisions give sequentiality; ongoing change gives dynamics; and real-valued quantities give continuity. Only one list matches the whole combination. This classification avoids claiming that these dimensions establish a universal numerical ranking of task difficulty. A incorrect Full observability, episodic independence and a static discrete setting contradict the scenario. B incorrect Partial observability and continuity fit, but static and episodic do not. C correct Partial observability, non-determinism, sequentiality, dynamics and continuity all match. D incorrect The other stated properties fit, but determinism contradicts uncertain transition outcomes.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 120 · Q01569
records.text: Q01569 Question 120 AI35 AI-S06 A problem in supervised machine learning model due to too much attention to the particular data set it is trained on, causing it to perform poorly on unseen data is ____ Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Under fitting B Over fitting C Learning curve D Variance Overfitting. Underfitting is insufficient fit even on training data; a learning curve is a plot used to inspect performance. Variance may describe sensitivity but does not name the training-versus-generalization failure asked for. A incorrect Underfitting means the model is too limited or poorly fitted even on the training data. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 121 · Q01570
records.text: Q01570 Question 121 AI17 AI-S02 Which general AI search category uses the problem definition and known costs without a problem-specific estimate of remaining cost to a goal? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. Informed methods add such guidance, and greedy best-first uses it directly as h. Binary search is a different ordered-lookup algorithm for sorted sequences. The formerly undefined circular-search distractor is replaced with a meaningful search method. A incorrect Informed search adds problem-specific guidance beyond the basic problem definition. B correct Uninformed search uses the problem definition without a heuristic estimate of remaining cost. C incorrect Greedy best-first explicitly uses h, an estimate of remaining cost. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 122 · Q01571
records.text: Q01571 Question 122 AI02 AI-S07 Which named test uses a judge’s inability to distinguish a machine from a human through conversation as its operational criterion? A The Chinese room B A psychological response-time experiment C Turing test D Black box testing Turing test The conversational Turing test evaluates whether a judge can reliably distinguish a machine’s dialogue from a human’s. Those are different questions or procedures. A incorrect The Chinese-room argument concerns whether formal symbol manipulation suffices for understanding; it is not the judge-and-conversation test. B incorrect A response-time experiment evaluates a cognitive model against human measurements rather than applying conversational indistinguishability. C correct The conversational Turing test uses this judge-and-hidden-participant criterion. D incorrect Black-box testing checks external software functionality without inspecting internals; it does not inherently require humanlike conversation.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 128 · SM0037
records.text: SM0037 Question 128 AI11 Which one of the following is a step in problem solving that lists the actions and states that the agent has to consider provided a goal? A Problem formulation B Execute C Search D Goal formulation Problem formulation. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 129 · SM0061

Replacing the overly broad perception option supplies the precise established term without changing the agent-history concept. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 130 · SM0211
records.text: SM0211 Question 130 AI31 AI32 AI33 Every training example has an input and its desired target output; there is no extra unlabeled training pool or interaction reward. Which learning regime fits this setup? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Semi-supervised learning B Unsupervised learning C Supervised learning D Reinforcement learning Supervised learning The training data consist entirely of input–target pairs, so the task is supervised learning. The desired target provides the learning signal. Semi-supervised learning would add an unlabeled pool, unsupervised learning would seek structure without targets, and reinforcement learning would use rewards from interaction. Stating the complete data setup distinguishes the regimes without implying that any use of labels excludes semi-supervised methods. A incorrect Semi-supervised learning requires additional unlabeled training data alongside labeled examples, absent here. B incorrect Unsupervised learning discovers structure without the supplied target labels. C correct Supervised learning fits the mapping from the labeled input–target pairs described. D incorrect Reinforcement learning uses evaluative interaction rewards, not the described desired-output pairs.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 132 · SM0253
records.text: SM0253 Question 132 AI24 AI17 Which statement is not a correct characterization of reasoning? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Using knowledge to derive conclusions that can guide what a system does. B A process of thinking, logically arguing, and drawing inference C Theory of blind searching D The act of deriving a conclusion from certain premises using a given methodology Theory of blind searching Reasoning uses knowledge and a specified methodology to derive conclusions from premises. Logical argument and inference are therefore appropriate descriptions. Blind search is instead a search strategy that explores alternatives without heuristic guidance; it does not define reasoning as a whole. Clarifying the incomplete knowledge-system option into a claim about deriving conclusions leaves the intended search-versus-inference distinction as the unique exception. A incorrect Using knowledge to derive conclusions is a valid characterization, so it is not the exception. B incorrect Logical argument and drawing inferences describe reasoning, so this is not a false characterization for the negative question. C correct Blind search is one search strategy rather than a definition of reasoning. D incorrect Deriving a conclusion from premises using a methodology describes reasoning and does not satisfy the negative question.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 133 · SM0261
records.text: SM0261 Question 133 AI28 Which reasoning technique applies valid inference rules so that true premises guarantee a true conclusion? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Abductive reasoning B Analogical reasoning C Deductive reasoning D Inductive reasoning Deductive reasoning Deductive reasoning uses truth-preserving inference: when the premises are true and the rule is valid, the conclusion must be true. Rules in a broad sense are not sufficient to identify deduction, since many reasoning methods use procedures. Induction generalizes from cases, abduction proposes explanations, and analogy transfers conclusions across similarities; these do not supply the stated logical guarantee. A incorrect Abduction proposes plausible explanatory hypotheses that can still be false. B incorrect Analogy transfers a conclusion from a similar case without a truth-preservation guarantee. C correct Valid deductive inference preserves truth from premises to conclusion. D incorrect Induction generalizes beyond the observed cases and remains revisable.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 134 · SM0269
records.text: SM0269 Question 134 AI18 For A* tree search with an admissible heuristic and positive step costs, what is the intended benefit of using the heuristic alongside accumulated edge costs? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A To seek a least-cost path while potentially reducing expansions through heuristic guidance. B To find the path with the maximum distance from the start to the goal node C To find paths with non-optimal searches from node to the goal node D To find the path with the maximum cost from the start to the goal node To seek a least-cost path while potentially reducing expansions through heuristic guidance. A* adds accumulated cost g to an admissible remaining-cost estimate h. Under the stated tree-search conditions, this supports least-cost solutions, while useful heuristic guidance can reduce expansions. It does not guarantee a speed improvement for every problem or heuristic. Maximizing distance or cost is a different objective, and deliberately seeking nonoptimal paths is not the benefit described. A correct An admissible remaining-cost estimate supports optimal tree search and can guide exploration toward useful candidates. B incorrect A* minimizes total path cost; it does not seek maximum path length. C incorrect Nonoptimality is not the purpose of admissible A* tree search. D incorrect A* seeks minimum, not maximum, total cost.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 136 · SS100
records.text: SS100 Question 136 AI18 AI16 AI17 AI15 An informed search keeps one priority frontier ordered by g(n)+h(n), permanently closes states, and tests goals on removal. With a consistent heuristic, finite branching and positive lower-bounded step costs, which algorithm is this? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Iterative Deepening A* Search B Greedy Best-First Search C Uniform Cost Search D A* Search A* Search A* uses a best-first priority frontier ordered by g+h. Consistency provides the standard guarantee for graph search that permanently closes states, with the stated cost and goal-test conditions. IDA* also uses f values but organizes repeated depth-first threshold searches instead. Greedy search omits g, and UCS omits h. The frontier organization distinguishes the algorithms rather than a worst-case complexity shared by several methods. A incorrect IDA* repeats depth-first searches under increasing f thresholds rather than retaining this single priority frontier. B incorrect Greedy best-first uses h alone and does not have the stated cost-aware priority. C incorrect UCS uses g alone, without the heuristic term. D correct A* uses g+h; consistency supports optimality when graph states are closed without reopening.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 138 · SS171
records.text: SS171 Question 138 AI32 AI31 AI33 AI-S06 A new dataset has no target labels. The objective is to discover its groups or structure, with neither interaction rewards nor reuse of a pretrained model. Which learning regime applies? records.text: AM0626 Question 143 AI24 AI29 AI34 Which representation system matches IF-THEN production rules against working memory and applies a selected rule to derive a conclusion or action? records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 147 · AM0630
records.text: AM0630 Question 147 AI29 AI31 AI33 AI-S06 Which model family assumes that the distribution of the next state depends on the current state rather than the entire earlier history? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Decision trees B Markov models C Support vector machines D Reinforcement learning Markov models The Markov assumption makes the current state sufficient for the next-state distribution, rather than requiring the full preceding history. That identifies the model family. Decision trees and support-vector machines are prediction methods with other defining structures. Reinforcement learning is a reward-based learning framework that can use a Markov model, but it is not itself the particular conditional-dependence assumption. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 148 · AM0631
records.text: AM0631 Question 148 AI33 AI43 AI20 AI32 Which learning regime is defined by an agent trying actions, receiving environmental rewards and improving a policy to maximize expected cumulative return? C incorrect Deep learning specifies multilayer neural representations and can be used within several learning regimes. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 157 · AM0640

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Admissible heuristic B Consistent heuristic C Informed heuristic D Dominance comparison between heuristics Informed heuristic Informed search adds problem-specific knowledge to guide exploration, often through a remaining-cost estimate. That general characterization does not guarantee admissibility or consistency, which impose additional mathematical conditions. Dominance instead compares two estimates pointwise. The question asks for the broad knowledge-use property rather than one of those stronger conditions or comparisons. A incorrect Admissibility adds a non-overestimation bound, stronger than the general knowledge-use characterization requested. B incorrect Consistency adds an edge-by-edge inequality, stronger than the general property requested. C correct Informed heuristic guidance uses problem-specific knowledge to estimate remaining cost or promise. D incorrect Dominance compares the numerical estimates of two heuristics rather than naming general use of problem knowledge.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 164 · AM0647
records.text: AM0647 Question 164 AI18 AI-S05 Which term names the heuristic property defined by 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), where h*(n) is the true cheapest remaining cost? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Admissible heuristic B Consistent heuristic C Informed heuristic D Dominance comparison between heuristics Admissible heuristic The displayed non-overestimation inequality defines admissibility. Consistency is a different edge condition; with the usual nonnegative heuristic estimates and a zero goal estimate, it implies admissibility for states with a goal path. Thus a consistent heuristic can also satisfy the bound, but consistency is not the name of the property being defined. Informedness and dominance do not independently establish the bound. A correct Admissibility is exactly the non-overestimation property stated by this inequality. B incorrect Consistency is an edge-by-edge inequality with goal normalization, rather than the name of the displayed non-overestimation bound. C incorrect Being informed only means using problem knowledge and does not impose this bound. D incorrect Dominance compares two heuristic estimates and does not by itself bound either one by the true remaining cost.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 165 · AM0648
records.text: AM0648 Question 165 AI18 AI13 AI14 AI20 Which forward best-first algorithm ranks frontier nodes by accumulated path cost plus a heuristic estimate of remaining cost? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Depth-first search B Breadth-first search C A* search algorithm D Hill climbing algorithm A* search algorithm A* orders frontier nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost still needed. Estimating future cost is not a backward search frontier. DFS and BFS use depth-related removal orders, while hill climbing improves neighboring complete candidates. Replacing the mistaken backward-search phrase preserves the intended heuristic-and-cost algorithm identification. A incorrect DFS follows a stack order and does not inherently combine a heuristic with backward search. B incorrect BFS uses breadth order without requiring heuristics or a backward frontier. C correct A* is forward best-first search using f = g + h. D incorrect Hill climbing selects improving neighbors rather than ordering a frontier by accumulated plus remaining path cost.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 166 · AM0649
records.text: AM0649 Question 166 AI23 AI22 What is the main advantage of using heuristics in game playing AI systems? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A They guarantee victory in every game. B They make the game unpredictable and exciting. C They allow the AI to learn from its opponents. D They improve the AI's decision-making and gameplay. They improve the AI's decision-making and gameplay. Game search computes candidate moves with a heuristic and chooses the best backed-up outcome, supporting improved decision quality rather than automatic victory or learning. Evidence: PDF 33, 34. A incorrect Optimal opponent may prevent a win. See PDF p. 33, 34. B incorrect Unpredictability is not the stated purpose. See PDF p. 33, 34. C incorrect Heuristic evaluation is not necessarily learning. See PDF p. 33, 34. D correct Matches heuristic move evaluation and selection. See PDF p. 33, 34.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 167 · AM0650
records.text: AM0650 Question 167 AI23 AI22 AI-S05 Which component is the scoring mapping that assigns a heuristic desirability value to a game state, rather than a search, pruning or sampling procedure? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Minimax algorithm B Alpha-beta pruning C Monte Carlo simulation D Evaluation function Evaluation function An evaluation function assigns a desirability score to a game state, especially when search stops at a depth cutoff. Minimax uses scores to choose moves, and alpha–beta avoids branches that cannot alter the backed-up result. Monte Carlo sampling can estimate values from possible continuations, but the sampling procedure is distinct from the mapping whose output is a state score. A incorrect Minimax backs values up through competing choices; it uses state scores rather than being the score mapping itself. B incorrect Alpha–beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect a minimax decision; it is not the scoring mapping. C incorrect Monte Carlo simulation samples continuations whose outcomes may estimate value; sampling is a procedure, not the score mapping itself. D correct An evaluation function maps a state to its estimated desirability score.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 168 · AM0651
records.text: AM0651 Question 168 AI23 What is the purpose of using heuristics in game tree search algorithms? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A To guarantee a win in every game. B To eliminate the need for search algorithms. C To reduce the search space and improve efficiency. D To ensure a systematic exploration of the search tree. To reduce the search space and improve efficiency. Pruning removes nodes that cannot affect the decision and speeds game search; heuristic domain-informed ordering improves pruning effectiveness. This supports efficiency, not guaranteed wins or eliminating search. Evidence: PDF 35, 35. A incorrect A better search can still lose to stronger positions. See PDF p. 35, 35. B incorrect Pruning/search guidance still requires search. See PDF p. 35, 35. C correct Matches reducing irrelevant exploration. See PDF p. 35, 35. D incorrect Systematic traversal does not describe the efficiency purpose. See PDF p. 35, 35.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 169 · AM0652
records.text: AM0652 Question 169 AI23 Which game-state heuristic evaluates the weighted number and value of pieces held by each player, rather than legal move count or controlled territory? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Material heuristic B Mobility heuristic C Distance heuristic D Tactical heuristic Material heuristic Material evaluation counts pieces with weights reflecting their values. Mobility instead measures legal options, while territory evaluates controlled regions. Restricting the stem to weighted pieces removes the original conflation of material and territory. Distance and tactical features may inform other evaluations, but they do not name the weighted piece-count feature requested. The distinction concerns what the evaluator measures. A correct Material is the weighted piece-count/value feature. B incorrect Mobility measures available legal moves rather than the amount of material or territory controlled. C incorrect Distance evaluates spatial separation, not the piece-count or controlled-region feature stated here. D incorrect This does not name weighted piece holdings; the feature described is material evaluation.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 170 · AM0653
records.text: AM0653 Question 170 AI23 Which heuristic evaluates a game state by considering the available moves and options for each player? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Material heuristic B Mobility heuristic C Distance heuristic D Tactical heuristic The mobility heuristic. AI23 explicitly says mobility counts legal options. Available moves and options for each player are exactly that feature, making mobility the supported answer. Material measures weighted pieces, while distance and tactics refer to different aspects of a position. The heuristic may be combined with other features, but the specific feature requested is unambiguous. A incorrect Material evaluates the amount or value of pieces, not the number of available moves. B correct Mobility directly counts or scores the legal move options available to a player. C incorrect Distance concerns separation or proximity, not the legal-option count described in the question. D incorrect Tactical evaluation concerns concrete threats or sequences rather than the specific mobility feature requested.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 174 · CS0203
records.text: CS0203 Question 174 AI17 Which one of the following searching strategies best explains: 'The searching agent is based on problem-specific knowledge and the agent knows how far away a different state is from the goal'? records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 175 · NS0001
records.text: NS0001 Question 175 AI01 AI08 AI40 Which type of AI is capable of performing any intellectual task that a human can do? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Narrow AI B General AI C Machine Learning D Expert Systems General AI. AI01 defines general AI by broad competence transferable across domains, matching the hypothetical ability to perform any human intellectual task. Narrow AI is bounded; machine learning names a family of methods and expert systems supply specialized domain knowledge. Neither automatically gives universal intellectual capability. The statement describes a category, not a claim that such a system presently exists. A incorrect Narrow AI is limited to bounded tasks rather than broad intellectual transfer. B correct General AI is the broad cross-domain competence category described. C incorrect Machine learning is a method family and does not itself imply general intellectual competence. D incorrect Expert systems apply specialized domain knowledge, not arbitrary human intellectual capability.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 176 · NS0002
records.text: NS0002 Question 176 AI08 AI-S01 What is the primary goal of Machine Learning? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A To hard-code rules into a machine B To allow systems to learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed C To simulate physical environments D To build robotic hardware Improve task performance through experience. AI08 defines learning as improvement on a task, measured by performance, through experience. B captures that adaptive objective; without explicitly programmed means the learned behavior is not simply an exhaustive hand-coded rule list, not that no algorithm is programmed. Simulation and robot construction can use ML but do not define its primary goal. A incorrect Hard-coding all task rules is not the experience-based improvement defining machine learning. B correct The system improves measured task performance from experience rather than only fixed task rules. C incorrect Physical simulation is one application context, not the definition or primary learning objective. D incorrect Building hardware is not required for machine learning, which also operates in software.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 177 · NS0003
records.text: NS0003 Question 177 AI28 AI29 Which reasoning type guarantees that if premises are true, the conclusion is also true? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Inductive Reasoning B Abductive Reasoning C Deductive Reasoning D Probabilistic Reasoning Deductive reasoning. AI28 defines deduction by truth-preserving rules and contrasts induction’s revisable generalizations and abduction’s plausible explanations. With valid deductive inference and true premises, the conclusion must be true. Probabilistic support expresses uncertainty rather than this logical guarantee, so deductive is the relevant reasoning type. A incorrect Induction generalizes beyond observations and can be overturned by new examples. B incorrect Abduction proposes plausible explanations without guaranteeing that they are true. C correct Valid deductive rules preserve truth from true premises to the conclusion. D incorrect Probability can quantify uncertain conclusions rather than provide the stated deductive guarantee.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 178 · NS0004
records.text: NS0004 Question 178 AI09 A self-driving car's environment is best classified as: Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Fully Observable, Deterministic, Static B Partially Observable, Stochastic, Dynamic C Fully Observable, Stochastic, Static D Partially Observable, Deterministic, Dynamic Partially observable, stochastic and dynamic. AI09 describes driving as partially observable, sequential and dynamic. Traffic participants and noisy observations make outcomes uncertain rather than fully determined by the car’s chosen action. B matches that ordinary driving setting. Neither full visibility nor a static world fits roads whose relevant conditions change while the agent deliberates. A incorrect Driving has hidden/noisy information and a changing world rather than full observability and static conditions. B correct Hidden state, uncertain outcomes and ongoing traffic changes fit the ordinary driving task. C incorrect Full observability and static conditions do not fit the stated driving environment. D incorrect Partial observation and dynamics fit, but deterministic outcomes ignore the uncertainty in ordinary driving.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 179 · NS0005
records.text: NS0005 Question 179 AI18 AI15 AI17 In the A* algorithm, what does the evaluation function f(n) represent? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Only the heuristic cost to goal B Only the cost from start to node n C The sum of cost from start to n (g(n)) and estimated cost from n to goal (h(n)) D The product of g(n) and h(n) f(n)=g(n)+h(n). AI18 directly defines A* evaluation as actual start-to-node cost g plus estimated node-to-goal cost h. This estimates a solution cost through the node. Using only h is greedy best-first, using only g is uniform-cost selection, and multiplication is not the A* rule. A incorrect Using h alone is greedy best-first rather than A* evaluation. B incorrect Using g alone is uniform-cost ordering and omits the remaining-cost estimate. C correct A* adds the accumulated path cost and estimated remaining cost. D incorrect The defined evaluation is a sum, not a product.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 180 · NS0006
records.text: NS0006 Question 180 AI06 AI07 AI08 Which reflex architecture maintains an internal world state and applies condition–action rules to that modeled state, rather than using only the current percept? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Simple Reflex Agent B Goal-Based Agent C Model-Based Reflex Agent D Learning Agent Model-Based Reflex Agent Model-based reflex agents update internal state from previous state, action and current observation, using models of world change and action effects. They then apply rules to that modeled state. Simple reflex agents lack persistent world-state memory. Goal-based and learning capabilities may coexist with a model, but the question specifically asks for the reflex architecture defined by state maintenance and rule application. A incorrect Simple reflex uses only the current percept without persistent world-state memory. B incorrect Goal-based choice uses future sequences reaching desired states, whereas the requested architecture applies reflex rules to modeled state. C correct Model-based reflex maintains internal state and applies rules to that state. D incorrect Learning concerns improving the agent from experience rather than naming this reflex architecture.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 181 · NS0007
records.text: NS0007 Question 181 AI04 What distinguishes a Rational Agent from an Omniscient Agent? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Rational agents always make perfect decisions B Rational agents act on best available information but can make mistakes; omniscient agents know all outcomes C Omniscient agents are a common AI type D Rational agents do not use information Rational choice uses available information; omniscience knows actual outcomes. AI04 defines rationality by best expected performance using information available, while omniscience means knowing actual outcomes in advance. Rational actions can fail and do not require perfect predictions. The contrast is epistemic, not whether an agent uses any information or whether omniscient systems are common implementations. A incorrect Rationality does not guarantee perfect outcomes or foreknowledge. B correct This distinguishes information-conditioned expected performance from knowing actual outcomes. C incorrect The note treats omniscience as an idealized outcome-knowledge condition, not a common AI implementation. D incorrect Rationality explicitly depends on percepts, prior knowledge and available actions.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 182 · NS0008
records.text: NS0008 Question 182 AI13 AI14 AI16 Which search algorithm is guaranteed to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Depth-First Search B Depth-Limited Search C Breadth-First Search D Best-First Search Breadth-first search. AI13 says BFS explores levels in increasing depth and minimizes the number of edges. An unweighted graph gives equal step costs, making that shortest-path property applicable with visited-state tracking. DFS or a fixed depth limit does not guarantee minimum depth, and generic best-first needs its evaluation rule specified. A incorrect DFS can reach a longer path first and is not generally optimal. B incorrect A depth limit can miss a solution or return a nonshortest path within its bound. C correct BFS explores increasing edge counts and finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph. D incorrect Best-first is a family; an unspecified evaluation rule does not guarantee shortest paths.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 183 · NS0009
records.text: NS0009 Question 183 AI15 AI17 Why is Uniform Cost Search (UCS) NOT considered a heuristic approach? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It doesn't consider costs B It uses cost as a known factor but employs no domain-specific knowledge or estimates C It uses heuristic functions D It only works on trees, not graphs UCS uses known accumulated cost without a heuristic estimate. AI15 orders UCS by actual path cost g, and AI17 explicitly calls it uninformed despite using g. Known action costs come from the problem definition; a heuristic adds an estimate of future cost. UCS can operate on graphs with duplicate handling, so neither ignoring costs nor tree-only operation explains the distinction. A incorrect UCS explicitly orders its frontier by accumulated path cost. B correct Known costs are used, but no problem-specific estimate of remaining cost is required. C incorrect UCS does not require an h estimate; g is actual accumulated cost. D incorrect UCS works on graphs with proper relaxation and duplicate handling.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 184 · NS0010
records.text: NS0010 Question 184 AI14 AI13 AI15 Which data structure supplies the defining next-node removal order of a depth-first search frontier? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Queue (FIFO) B Stack (LIFO) C Priority Queue D Hash Table Stack (LIFO) DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. That removal discipline distinguishes it from breadth-first FIFO selection and cost- or heuristic-priority selection. A hash table can still be used alongside DFS to record visited states. The question therefore specifies frontier removal rather than broadly asking which structures may track nodes. A incorrect A FIFO queue removes the oldest entry, giving breadth-first rather than depth-first frontier order. B correct A LIFO stack processes the most recently pending branch first, implementing DFS. C incorrect A priority queue removes according to a key rather than the defining DFS LIFO order. D incorrect A hash table may store visited states, but does not supply the frontier’s next-node removal order.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 185 · NS0011
records.text: NS0011 Question 185 AI14 What is the main limitation of Depth-First Search regarding completeness? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It uses too much memory B It can get stuck in cycles or infinite paths and fail to find a solution C It always finds suboptimal solutions D It only works for trees Cycles or infinite branches can prevent finding an existing solution. AI14 says DFS can fail on infinite paths or cycles and is not generally optimal. Without suitable restrictions or duplicate handling, it may never return to a pending branch containing a goal. Finite visited-state graph traversal changes that result; the limitation is therefore not that DFS only works on trees or always returns a bad path. A incorrect DFS is usually memory-efficient; excess storage is not its defining completeness failure. B correct It may follow an infinite branch or cycle indefinitely while a solution waits elsewhere. C incorrect A returned path can be optimal by coincidence; always suboptimal is too strong. D incorrect DFS also traverses graphs, especially with visited-state tracking.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 186 · NS0012
records.text: NS0012 Question 186 AI31 AI32 AI33 AI43 Which options can be used without a training set of labeled input–target examples? Select all that apply. For D, consider whether some deep-learning objectives permit unlabeled or reward feedback. Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Supervised Learning B Reinforcement Learning C Unsupervised Learning D Deep Learning Reinforcement Learning; Unsupervised Learning; Deep Learning Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels. Reinforcement learning can learn from rewards rather than correct-action target examples. Deep learning is an architecture family and can be trained with unsupervised or reinforcement objectives, so it also need not require labeled input-target data. Supervised learning is specifically defined by those labeled pairs. The capability wording permits both regimes and architecture families to be judged accurately. A incorrect Supervised learning uses labeled examples by definition. B correct RL learns through rewards and interaction, without requiring labeled correct actions. C correct Unsupervised learning explicitly seeks structure without target labels. D correct Deep learning can use unlabeled or reward objectives, so labels are not inherently required.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 187 · NS0013
records.text: NS0013 Question 187 AI18 For A* tree search with finite branching, step costs bounded below by a positive constant, goal testing on removal and h(goal)=0, which listed heuristic condition is the weakest sufficient guarantee of optimality? Treat monotone as synonymous with consistent. Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Consistent B Admissible (never overestimates the actual cost) C Monotone D Domain-independent Admissible (never overestimates the actual cost) Admissibility requires that a heuristic never overestimate the true cheapest remaining cost. It suffices for optimal A* tree search under the stated cost and goal-testing assumptions. Consistency, also called monotonicity here, is stronger and is particularly important when graph search permanently closes states. Domain independence is unrelated to the optimality condition. Asking for the weakest sufficient listed condition distinguishes admissibility from the stronger alternatives. A incorrect Consistency is sufficient but stronger than the weakest listed condition for tree A*. B correct Admissibility is sufficient for optimal tree A* under the stated assumptions. C incorrect Monotonicity is consistency here and is stronger than necessary for the tree-search guarantee. D incorrect Domain independence is not a heuristic optimality condition.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 188 · NS0014
records.text: NS0014 Question 188 AI16 AI13 AI14 Iterative Deepening Search (IDS) combines the advantages of which two algorithms? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A UCS and A* B BFS and DFS C Greedy Search and BFS D DLS and UCS Breadth-first solution depth with depth-first memory use. AI16 defines IDS as DLS runs at limits 0,1,2,…, finding the shallowest solution under finite branching with O(bd) frontier space. It obtains BFS’s shallow-solution behavior and DFS-style memory use. It does not combine UCS priorities, greedy ordering or A* cost thresholds; IDA* is a separate threshold-based variant. A incorrect IDS does not combine UCS costs with A* evaluation. B correct It obtains breadth-first shallow-solution behavior through repeated depth-first limited searches. C incorrect No greedy heuristic ordering is required for IDS. D incorrect DLS is used, but UCS ordering is not part of standard iterative deepening.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 189 · NS0015
records.text: NS0015 Question 189 AI23 A zero-sum game evaluator measures a position from the designated MAX player’s perspective. What does a positive evaluation value indicate? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A A draw or neutral position. B An estimated advantage for the designated MAX player. C An estimated advantage for the opposing MIN player. D An invalid game state. An estimated advantage for the designated MAX player. Under this convention, positive values estimate an advantage for MAX, negative values favor MIN, and zero is neutral. A positive heuristic score does not guarantee an eventual win, because it may be only an estimate at a search cutoff. The reference player must be specified before a sign can be interpreted; player names alone do not determine the convention. A incorrect A neutral result is represented by zero under the stated sign convention. B correct A positive value favors the designated MAX player under this convention. C incorrect An advantage for MIN would have a negative sign under this convention. D incorrect The sign estimates desirability, not whether the position is legally valid.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 190 · NS0016
records.text: NS0016 Question 190 AI24 AI29 Which knowledge representation technique uses interconnected nodes and arcs to show concept relationships? A Frames B Logic C Semantic Networks D Probabilistic Models Semantic networks. AI24 defines semantic networks using concept nodes and labeled relations such as is-a. That matches the node/arc representation in the stem. Frames organize slots, logic uses formal sentences and probabilistic models attach uncertainty; those may have related graph forms, but the specific concept-relationship network term is semantic network. B incorrect Logic represents claims with formal expressions, not specifically the node/arc scheme described. C correct Semantic networks connect concept nodes with labeled relationship arcs. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 191 · NS0017
records.text: NS0017 Question 191 AI34 AI35 Which listed group comprises unstructured input modalities from which deep neural models can learn hierarchical features? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Tabular numerical data only B Structured relational data C Unstructured data like images, sound, and text D Small labeled datasets Unstructured data like images, sound, and text Deep learning uses multiple representation layers and can learn features from images, sound and text. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 192 · NS0018
records.text: NS0018 Question 192 AI08 Which agent type improves its performance over time through experience and feedback? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Simple Reflex Agent B Model-Based Reflex Agent C Goal-Based Agent D Learning Agent A learning agent. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 193 · NS0019
records.text: NS0019 Question 193 AI28 AI29 What is abductive reasoning best described as? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Drawing certain conclusions from known facts B Making educated guesses from patterns C Finding the best explanation for a set of observations D Using probability to decide outcomes Finding a plausible best explanation for observations. AI28 illustrates abduction with wet ground suggesting rain while allowing sprinklers as another cause. It proposes an explanatory hypothesis rather than guaranteeing truth or merely generalizing a pattern. C gives that explanatory role. Probability may rank hypotheses, but numerical probability alone is not the definition of abductive reasoning. A incorrect Certain truth-preserving conclusions describe valid deduction rather than explanatory abduction. B incorrect Pattern-based generalization is closer to induction and omits the explanatory-hypothesis requirement. C correct Abduction seeks a plausible explanation for observed evidence without guaranteeing that explanation. D incorrect Probability can support a diagnosis but does not itself define the explanatory reasoning form.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 194 · NS0020
records.text: NS0020 Question 194 AI09 How is ordinary untimed chess classified with respect to transition outcomes, change during deliberation and state/action values? Assume both players’ moves are specified when evaluating a transition. Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A Stochastic, Dynamic, Continuous B Deterministic, Static, Discrete C Stochastic, Static, Discrete D Deterministic, Dynamic, Continuous Deterministic, Static, Discrete Chess has discrete positions and legal moves. Given the selected move, the resulting position is determined by the rules rather than random outcome sampling. In untimed play, the environment does not change while the player deliberates, so the relevant classification is static. Opponent choice is strategic uncertainty rather than dice-like stochasticity. Specifying untimed play excludes the semidynamic effect of a score-affecting clock. A incorrect Chess moves are discrete, and opponent strategy is not dice-like stochasticity. B correct Untimed chess is deterministic given chosen moves, static while deliberating and discrete. C incorrect Ordinary chess transition outcomes are deterministic given chosen moves rather than stochastic. D incorrect Chess is discrete rather than continuous, and a clock gives semidynamic rather than this classification.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 195 · NS0021

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 196 · NS0022
records.text: NS0022 Question 196 AI17 AI15 Which search strategy is called 'blind search' because it uses no extra problem knowledge? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Informed Search B Heuristic Search C Uninformed Search D Best-First Search Uninformed search. AI17 says uninformed methods use the problem definition and known costs without a problem-specific remaining-cost estimate. This is the usual blind-search meaning. Informed or heuristic search explicitly adds such estimates, and best-first is a broad ordering family that may use heuristic information rather than naming the blind category. A incorrect Informed search adds problem-specific guidance beyond the basic problem definition. B incorrect Heuristic search uses the extra estimate excluded by the stem. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 197 · NS0023
records.text: NS0023 Question 197 AI33 AI31 In Reinforcement Learning, what guides an agent to improve its behavior? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Labeled training examples B Hard-coded rules C Rewards and penalties from environment interactions D Pre-trained heuristic functions Reward feedback from interactions. AI33 describes an agent acting, receiving reward and a new observation, and improving its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards may be positive or negative and delayed; they need not name the correct action. Labeled examples, fixed rules and predefined heuristics do not provide this distinctive reinforcement feedback mechanism. A incorrect Correct target labels characterize supervised learning rather than reinforcement feedback. B incorrect Fixed rules alone do not provide the reward-based adaptation defining RL. C correct Rewards and penalties evaluate outcomes and guide improvement of expected cumulative return. D incorrect A pretrained heuristic may help implementation but is not the defining RL feedback signal.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 198 · NS0024
records.text: NS0024 Question 198 AI17 For greedy best-first search on an implicit finite tree with branching factor b and maximum depth m, what is the standard worst-case node-count time bound? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A O(m) B O(b*m) C O(b^m) D O(log m) O(b^m) Greedy best-first ordering can be misled by a heuristic and may need to explore an exponentially large portion of the finite search tree. With branching factor b and depth m, the standard worst-case generated-node bound is O(b^m). This is a node-count convention rather than a claim about every priority-queue implementation or all best-first algorithms. The explicit algorithm and tree model determine the bound. A incorrect A misleading heuristic can force exponentially many nodes, so a bound merely linear in maximum depth m is insufficient. B incorrect O(bm) is a familiar DFS storage form, not this generic search-time guarantee. C correct The specified implicit finite-tree worst case can require O(b^m) nodes. D incorrect A logarithmic-in-depth bound is insufficient when the search can explore an exponential number of tree nodes.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 199 · NS0025

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 201 · NS0027
records.text: NS0027 Question 201 AI31 AI32 AI28 Which listed term is a reasoning method rather than one of the common learning regimes classified by availability of target labels? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Supervised Learning B Unsupervised Learning C Deductive reasoning D Semi-supervised Learning Deductive reasoning Supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised learning differ in the target labels available during training. Deductive reasoning instead derives consequences from premises using truth-preserving rules. Deduction can be used inside a learning system, so the distinction is not that the two can never coexist. The question separates a reasoning method from the conventional label-availability taxonomy. A incorrect Supervised learning uses labeled input–target pairs, so it is a label-availability learning regime. B incorrect Unsupervised learning has no supplied targets and discovers structure, so it is a label-availability regime. C correct Deduction derives truth-preserving consequences from premises rather than naming a label-availability regime. D incorrect Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled data, so it is a label-availability regime.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 202 · NS0028
records.text: NS0028 Question 202 AI22 AI23 In adversarial search, what makes it different from traditional search? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A It only uses one agent B Multiple agents with conflicting goals compete in the same search space C It guarantees the optimal solution always D It does not use evaluation functions Competing agents with conflicting objectives. AI22 defines adversarial search by agents with competing objectives and gives minimax for opposition. That distinguishes it from a single-agent path search. It can use evaluation functions at cutoffs, and its best-outcome guarantee is conditional on the modeled game and opponent, not an unconditional guarantee that every implementation finds a globally optimal solution. A incorrect A single decision-making agent does not capture the competing-objective feature of adversarial search. B correct Competing agents and conflicting objectives are its defining distinction. C incorrect Guarantees depend on the algorithm, model and search depth, not merely the adversarial label. D incorrect Depth-limited adversarial search commonly uses heuristic evaluation functions.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 203 · NS0029
records.text: NS0029 Question 203 AI16 AI14 A Depth-Limited Search (DLS) is NOT complete in itself because: Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It uses too much memory B Solutions beyond the preset depth limit will be missed C It explores nodes in random order D It requires a heuristic function A solution beyond the fixed depth limit is missed. AI16 defines DLS as DFS stopped at depth ℓ and explicitly says it misses goals deeper than that. A fixed limit therefore does not establish completeness for arbitrary problem depths. This is independent of randomized ordering, heuristics or memory use; increasing limits through iterative deepening addresses the depth restriction under its stated assumptions. A incorrect Depth-limited DFS is memory-efficient; excessive memory is not the reason goals are missed. B correct A preset cutoff prevents exploring a solution whose depth exceeds that limit. C incorrect DLS need not use random order; the depth cutoff alone causes the limitation. D incorrect No heuristic is required for depth-limited DFS.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 204 · NS0030
records.text: NS0030 Question 204 AI29 AI24 AI-S06 Which probabilistic model represents knowledge in terms of conditional probabilities among variables? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Semantic Networks B Frames C Bayesian Networks D Ontologies Bayesian networks. AI29 defines a Bayesian network as a DAG with conditional probability tables and joint factorization by parents. That is the probabilistic knowledge representation in the stem. Semantic networks and frames encode relations or slots without inherently supplying conditional distributions, and ontologies specify conceptual structure rather than this particular probabilistic factorization. A incorrect Semantic networks encode labeled concept relations rather than inherently conditional probability distributions. B incorrect Frames encode slots, values and defaults rather than the named probabilistic dependency structure. C correct Bayesian networks explicitly store conditional probability relationships among variables. D incorrect An ontology’s conceptual organization is not itself the conditional-probability model specified.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 205 · NS0031
records.text: NS0031 Question 205 AI12 AI13 What is an 'expanded node' in a search algorithm? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A A node that has been visited but not explored further B A node selected for further exploration whose neighboring nodes have been generated C A node removed from the open list D A node that has reached the goal state A node whose successors have been generated. AI12 defines expansion as generating successors. B states that action, unlike mere visitation, removal from OPEN or reaching a goal. A node can be removed and goal-tested without expanding it, and discovered frontier nodes await expansion. The criterion is what was generated, not whether the node was seen or selected. A incorrect Visiting without generating successors does not meet the definition of expansion. B correct Generating the selected node’s neighboring successor nodes is expansion. C incorrect Removal alone may precede a goal test without generating any successors. D incorrect Goal status is not the definition of expansion; a goal may be accepted without expanding it.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 206 · NS0032
records.text: NS0032 Question 206 AI31 AI34 AI32 AI33 For which type of problem would Supervised Learning with CNNs be most appropriate? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Customer segmentation from unlabeled data B Classifying a large labeled image dataset C Learning chess actions from rewards obtained through trial-and-error play. D Finding hidden patterns in transaction data Classifying a large labeled image dataset The labeled images provide input–target pairs for supervised classification, and CNN filters exploit spatial image structure. Unlabeled customer segmentation and transaction-pattern discovery seek structure without class targets. Learning chess actions from rewards is a reinforcement objective. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 207 · NS0033
records.text: NS0033 Question 207 AI22 AI04 What does 'perfect information' mean in the context of game theory? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A The agent knows the future B Both players have complete and accurate knowledge of the entire game state C The game has no randomness D Each player can see only their own pieces The current game state and previous moves are visible to the players. AI22 defines perfect information as visibility of previous moves and the current state. This makes B the correct state-knowledge description. It does not reveal future choices and does not by itself remove chance from a game. Seeing only one’s own pieces instead describes hidden relevant state, inconsistent with perfect information. A incorrect Future choices are not known merely because the present game state is visible. B correct Complete visibility of current state and relevant move history is the intended information condition. C incorrect A game can include chance while still revealing the state and prior moves. D incorrect Seeing only one’s own pieces leaves relevant state hidden and is not perfect information.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 208 · NS0034
records.text: NS0034 Question 208 AI32 AI31 AI33 Semi-supervised Learning is typically used when: Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A All data is labeled B No data is labeled C Obtaining a fully labeled dataset is time-consuming or costly D The problem requires reinforcement feedback When labels are costly and some labeled data can be supplemented by unlabeled data. AI32 defines semi-supervised learning as combining some labels with additional unlabeled data. Costly full labeling provides the motivation described in C, provided at least some labeled targets exist. Fully labeled data is ordinary supervised learning; wholly unlabeled structure fits unsupervised learning, and environmental rewards specify reinforcement feedback rather than this mixed dataset regime. A incorrect A fully labeled dataset does not give the defining labeled-plus-unlabeled mixture. B incorrect With no labels at all, the described regime is unsupervised rather than semi-supervised. C correct Expensive labeling motivates using a limited labeled subset together with plentiful unlabeled examples. D incorrect Reward feedback defines reinforcement learning rather than a mixture of labeled and unlabeled examples.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 209 · NS0035
records.text: NS0035 Question 209 AI03 AI06 AI17 In the context of AI agents, what are 'effectors'? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Sensors that gather environmental data B Components that allow an agent to take actions in its environment C Internal memory modules D Heuristic evaluation functions Components through which an agent acts on its environment. AI03 uses actuators or effectors for acting components and sensors for perception. Therefore B gives the correct role. Memory stores internal information and heuristic functions estimate promise; neither is the acting interface. An effector may be physical hardware or a software action mechanism depending on the agent’s architecture. A incorrect Sensors gather percepts; effectors implement actions rather than observations. B correct Effectors are the components through which selected actions affect the environment. C incorrect Internal memory maintains information but is not the general acting interface. D incorrect Heuristic functions evaluate promise and do not themselves execute environmental actions.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 210 · NS0036
records.text: NS0036 Question 210 AI07 AI06 AI08 Which of the following best describes a Utility-Based Agent? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A It only reacts to current perceptions using condition-action rules B It selects actions that maximize expected utility, handling conflicting goals through trade-offs C It plans sequences of actions toward a single fixed goal D It learns entirely from environmental feedback Choose actions with maximum expected utility, balancing outcome trade-offs. AI07 defines utility-based agents by comparing desirability and trade-offs and maximizing expected utility over uncertain outcomes. This is broader than merely satisfying a fixed goal. Current-percept rule matching describes simple reflex behavior, and experience-based improvement describes learning, which may coexist with utility choice but does not define it. A incorrect Current-percept condition-action matching describes a simple reflex architecture. B correct Expected-utility maximization explicitly compares trade-offs among uncertain outcomes. C incorrect Goal-reaching planning alone does not rank degrees of desirability among outcomes. D incorrect Learning describes adaptation from feedback, not the utility-based decision criterion itself.

Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task. Language generation, robot mechanics and database indexing are separate task areas, although vision may be one component of a robot. B states the visual information-processing purpose directly.
