records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 212 · NS0038
records.text: NS0038 Question 212 AI23 In a zero-sum Tic-Tac-Toe terminal utility convention, MAX wins score +1 and MIN wins score −1. Which listed value represents a draw giving neither player an advantage? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A +1 B -1 C +Infinity D 0 0 The convention assigns equal and opposite utilities to the two decisive outcomes. A draw gives neither side an advantage, so its neutral utility is zero under that symmetric scale. Positive one favors MAX and negative one favors MIN; positive infinity would strongly favor MAX rather than indicate neutrality. This is an explicit utility convention, not an intrinsic numerical property of the game outcome. A incorrect Under the common stated scale, +1 is a win rather than a draw. B incorrect Under the common stated scale, −1 is a loss rather than a draw. C incorrect Positive infinity is not the draw value in the note’s common scale. D correct Zero is the neutral utility between +1 and −1 under this convention.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 213 · NS0039
records.text: NS0039 Question 213 AI09 Treat a whole independently reset chess match as one episode with no effects on later matches; treat the other options as ongoing tasks at the action level described. Which task is episodic under those units? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A A self-driving car navigating city traffic B A chess game (each individual match) C A robot cleaning a multi-room house continuously D A stock trading algorithm operating over months A chess game (each individual match) An episodic task has independent decision units. Under the stated convention, each whole chess match is reset and cannot affect later matches, so matches can be treated as episodes. Individual moves within a match remain sequential. Driving, continuous cleaning and continuing stock trading all have actions that affect later situations within the ongoing task. The classification therefore follows the explicit unit and independence assumptions. A incorrect Driving decisions affect later positions and traffic interactions, making the task sequential. B correct Whole independently reset matches are independent episodes under the stated convention. C incorrect Cleaning actions change later room states and decisions in the continuing task. D incorrect Trading decisions affect later holdings and opportunities, so the continuing task is sequential.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 214 · NS0040
records.text: NS0040 Question 214 AI17 AI18 AI12 The heuristic function h(n) in A* represents: Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A The exact cost from start to node n B The total path cost already traveled C The estimated cost from node n to the goal state D The branching factor at node n Estimated remaining cost from n to a goal. AI17 defines h as an estimate of remaining cost or promise, and AI18 adds it to accumulated g in A*. Thus C is the heuristic component. Exact start-to-node cost belongs to g, and branching factor b is a search-size parameter rather than a cost-to-go estimate. A incorrect Exact cost from the start belongs to g(n), not the heuristic h(n). B incorrect Already-traveled path cost is g(n), not estimated future cost. C correct h estimates the remaining cost from the current node to a goal. D incorrect Branching factor counts successor alternatives and is not the heuristic cost estimate.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 215 · NS0041
records.text: NS0041 Question 215 AI28 AI29 When a doctor proposes a disease as a plausible cause explaining observed symptoms, which term names this explanatory direction of reasoning, rather than a method for numerically ranking hypotheses? Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations. A Deductive Reasoning B Inductive Reasoning C Abductive Reasoning D Probabilistic Reasoning Abductive Reasoning Abduction proposes an explanation for observed evidence, such as a disease that could account for symptoms. Other causes may also fit, so the conclusion is not logically guaranteed. Probability can help rank the possible explanations, but that numerical method is distinct from the explanatory direction. Deduction preserves truth from premises, and induction generalizes patterns across cases. A incorrect Deduction follows truth-preserving implications from premises, not a merely plausible cause inferred from its effects. B incorrect Induction generalizes across observations rather than specifically proposing a cause that explains an observation. C correct Abduction proposes a plausible explanation for observed evidence. D incorrect Probability can rank disease hypotheses, but does not itself name the observation-to-explanation direction.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 216 · NS0042
records.text: NS0042 Question 216 AI40 AI34 AI04 What major ethical concern does AI raise related to decision-making systems? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A AI systems use too little data B Bias in algorithms leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes C AI always makes perfectly rational decisions D AI cannot process unstructured data Biased decisions causing unfair outcomes. AI40 says bias in data or evaluation can create unfair outcomes and calls for checking errors across groups, robustness and oversight. B states the ethical concern directly. Data scarcity may be a technical issue, but little data is not the stated general ethical principle; perfect rationality and inability to process unstructured inputs are false generalizations. A incorrect Using too little data is not the specific fairness concern described here. B correct Biased data or evaluation can produce unfair or discriminatory decisions. C incorrect AI is not guaranteed perfect rational decisions or error-free outcomes. D incorrect The note explicitly includes models that process images, sound and text.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 217 · NS0043
records.text: NS0043 Question 217 AI09 In a continuous environment like self-driving cars, what challenge does 'continuous' specifically pose? Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description. A A finite set of states makes decisions trivial B Infinite or large state/action spaces require more complex computations C The environment never changes D All outcomes are deterministic Real-valued state/action variables create large or infinite spaces to represent and search. AI09 defines continuous quantities as varying along real-valued ranges, unlike distinct discrete alternatives. Such ranges can create unboundedly many state/action possibilities, motivating approximation or richer computation rather than exhaustive finite enumeration. Continuity is separate from whether a world changes over time or whether outcomes are stochastic. A incorrect Continuous ranges do not reduce the task to a trivial finite set of alternatives. B correct Real-valued ranges can produce very large or infinite possibilities needing suitable representation and computation. C incorrect No world change defines static rather than continuous. D incorrect Determinism is a separate transition-property dimension and does not follow from continuity.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 218 · NS0044
records.text: NS0044 Question 218 AI22 AI11 AI23 The successor function in game search is responsible for: Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Evaluating terminal game states B Generating new states by applying legal moves to the current game state C Pruning unpromising branches D Calculating the heuristic value of each state Generate successor states by applying legal moves. AI22 lists legal actions and a successor function as game components; AI11 identifies successors as states reached by actions. In game search, applying each legal move yields its successor position. Terminal utilities and heuristic scores evaluate positions, while alpha-beta pruning avoids exploring branches; neither is the transition-generation function. A incorrect Terminal utility evaluation scores a completed outcome rather than generating the next position. B correct The successor function maps legal moves at the current position to resulting game states. C incorrect Pruning skips exploration under a bound; it is not state-transition generation. D incorrect A heuristic evaluation scores a state’s promise rather than producing legal successor states.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 219 · NS0045
records.text: NS0045 Question 219 AI16 AI13 AI14 For implicit-tree search with branching factor b and shallowest goal depth d, which is a key memory advantage of iterative deepening over BFS when each depth-limited pass stores pending siblings? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It finds deeper solutions faster B It requires storing all nodes at each level in memory C It uses O(bd) frontier space rather than storing an entire BFS level. D It does not guarantee completeness It uses O(bd) frontier space rather than storing an entire BFS level. Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited DFS while increasing the limit. A pass retains a depth-first path and pending siblings, giving O(bd) frontier space rather than BFS’s potentially exponential level frontier. It remains complete for finite branching and a finite-depth solution, although it repeats some shallow work. The option states the correct memory advantage without claiming that every implementation stores only the current path. A incorrect IDS repeats shallow work and does not universally find deeper solutions faster than BFS. B incorrect Storing all nodes at a level is BFS-style memory behavior, not the IDS advantage. C correct The stated implementation keeps only a depth-first frontier, requiring O(bd) rather than the BFS level frontier. D incorrect IDS is complete under finite branching and a finite-depth solution, so loss of completeness is not its benefit.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 220 · NS0046
records.text: NS0046 Question 220 AI34 AI43 AI24 AI-S06 Representation learning in Deep Learning refers to: Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Manually engineering input features B The ability to automatically discover and learn relevant features from raw data C Storing knowledge in frames and ontologies D Using labeled data with a teacher signal Automatically learning useful features from data. AI34 says deep models learn features from images, sound and text through multiple representation layers. That is representation learning rather than manually specifying every input feature. A label signal may guide training but is not required for every deep objective, and frames/ontologies are separate explicit knowledge structures rather than the learned representations meant here. A incorrect Manual feature engineering is contrasted with learning the representations automatically. B correct The model learns task-useful features or representations from the supplied data. C incorrect Frames and ontologies are explicit knowledge representations, not the deep feature-learning mechanism described. D incorrect Teacher labels define supervision; representation learning can also use unsupervised or reinforcement objectives.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 221 · NS0047
records.text: NS0047 Question 221 AI17 AI19 What makes Best-First (Greedy) Search non-optimal? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It always explores all possible paths B It relies entirely on heuristics and can overlook cheaper paths, making suboptimal choices C It uses actual path costs rather than estimates D It explores nodes in breadth-first order It uses only h and can ignore a cheaper route with a larger estimate. AI17 defines greedy best-first as f=h, ignoring cost already paid. AI19 demonstrates a route of cost 11 selected greedily while another route costs 4. The heuristic ranking can therefore prefer a worse total solution. Greedy is neither exhaustive nor breadth-first and does not order primarily by actual path cost. A incorrect Greedy search may stop at an early found goal rather than exploring every path. B correct Ignoring accumulated cost can favor a seemingly close but expensive route over a cheaper solution. C incorrect Using actual g alone describes UCS, whereas greedy uses h. D incorrect Breadth-first depth order is not the greedy minimum-heuristic policy.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 222 · NS0048
records.text: NS0048 Question 222 AI02 In AI, what does 'Acting Humanly' (Turing Test concept) primarily evaluate? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Whether a machine can solve math problems B Whether a machine's behavior is indistinguishable from a human's in conversation C Whether a machine can perceive visual stimuli D Whether a machine follows logical rules perfectly Humanlike conversational behavior judged by indistinguishability. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 223 · NS0049
records.text: NS0049 Question 223 AI34 AI33 Which of the following is the correct relationship between AI, ML, and DL? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 224 · NS0050
records.text: NS0050 Question 224 AI24 AI29 A recommendation system must directly represent products and labeled “frequently bought together” relationships, then traverse those relationships to find connected products. Which listed representation most directly fits that requirement? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 225 · NS0156
records.text: NS0156 Question 225 AI31 AI32 What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. Supervised learning fits labeled input–target examples; unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels. AI31 defines supervised learning through labels, with classification for discrete targets and regression for numeric targets. AI32 defines unsupervised discovery, including clustering, association and dimensionality reduction. The distinction is the supplied training feedback, not whether the data are images, text or numbers; the same modality can support either regime.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 226 · NS0157
records.text: NS0157 Question 226 AI18 Under what search and heuristic conditions does A* find a least-cost path, and why? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A* is optimal under its heuristic and search assumptions: admissible tree search, or consistent graph search without reopening; otherwise reopen improved states. With admissible h, A* tree search uses f=g+h as a lower bound on solution cost through each frontier node. Removing a minimum-f goal cannot skip a cheaper represented solution. Graph search that never reopens closed states normally requires consistency; with an admissible inconsistent heuristic, improved states must be reopened. Goal testing is on removal. Finite branching and positive lower-bounded step costs supply the usual infinite-space completeness conditions.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 227 · NS0158
records.text: NS0158 Question 227 AI02 What is the Turing Test and what does it measure? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. The conversational Turing test asks a judge to distinguish machine from human through dialogue; it measures humanlike behavior, not consciousness. AI02 sets the observable criterion: whether a judge can reliably tell a machine’s conversation from a human’s. Language use, knowledge, reasoning and often learning support the performance. Passing would meet this operational behavioral standard, but it does not prove consciousness, actual understanding or that the machine internally thinks in the same way as a human.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 228 · NS0159
records.text: NS0159 Question 228 AI36 What is the difference between precision and recall? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. Precision=TP/(TP+FP): how many predicted positives are correct. Recall=TP/(TP+FN): how many actual positives are found. AI36 distinguishes precision’s predicted-positive denominator from recall’s actual-positive denominator. False positives reduce precision; false negatives reduce recall. With TP=30, FP=10 and FN=20, precision is 30/40=75% and recall is 30/50=60%. The positive class and zero-denominator convention should be fixed before comparing scores.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 229 · NS0160
records.text: NS0160 Question 229 AI37 Why is tokenization important in natural language processing? Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task. Tokenization divides text into processing units such as words, punctuation or subwords so later NLP stages can operate on a consistent input sequence. AI37 defines tokenization as dividing text into processing units and lists several permitted granularities. Establishing that sequence lets later tagging, recognition and parsing refer to units consistently. Tokens need not equal whitespace-separated words, and tokenization by itself does not determine grammatical structure or resolve word meaning; those belong to later analyses.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 230 · NS0285
records.text: NS0285 Question 230 AI01 Which AI approach most directly supports understanding biological intelligence behavior as a scientific goal? Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources. A Weak AI B Applied AI C Cognitive AI D Strong AI Cognitive AI. AI01 explicitly describes cognitive AI as using computational models to investigate biological intelligence, making it the direct scientific-goal match. Applied AI emphasizes useful solutions. Narrow AI describes capability scope, while strong AI has a philosophical understanding sense; neither is the named research approach for testing models against biological behavior. A incorrect Weak AI denotes bounded capability rather than the specific scientific modeling goal. B incorrect Applied AI builds useful solutions rather than primarily explaining biological intelligence. C correct Cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence and behavior. D incorrect Strong AI concerns broad or actual-understanding claims, not this specific empirical modeling approach.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 231 · NS0291
records.text: NS0291 Question 231 AI17 AI19 Why is Greedy Best-First Search not guaranteed to be optimal or complete? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A It ignores path cost g( n) and relies only on h( n) B It always chooses the shallowest node C It expands nodes in FIFO order D It requires full knowledge of the goal state in advance It uses h alone, ignoring accumulated g. AI17 says greedy best-first chooses f=h and can take an expensive route or follow an infinite misleading branch. Ignoring g explains nonoptimality, while cycles or infinite paths without appropriate handling explain failure of completeness. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, so the lack of a general guarantee does not mean every implementation fails. A correct Using only h ignores total path cost and can follow misleading or unbounded branches. B incorrect Shallowest-first describes breadth-first order rather than greedy heuristic order. C incorrect FIFO is breadth-first queue behavior, not minimum-h priority selection. D incorrect Heuristics estimate promise; exact full goal-state knowledge is not required by the algorithm.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 232 · NS0305
records.text: NS0305 Question 232 AI17 AI15 AI18 AI14 Which search strategy tries to expand the node that is closest to the goal, on the grounds that this is likely to lead to a solution quickly; Thus, it evaluates nodes by using just the heuristic function: f ( n) = h ( n). Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A Uniform-cost search B Greedy best-first search C Depth-first search D A* search Greedy best-first search. AI17 explicitly defines greedy best-first by removing the smallest remaining-cost estimate h while ignoring paid cost g. This is exactly the stem’s equation. UCS uses g, A* combines g and h, and DFS uses depth/stack discipline rather than a minimum heuristic evaluation. A incorrect UCS orders by accumulated g rather than h alone. B correct Greedy best-first selects the node with the smallest heuristic estimate h. C incorrect DFS follows a LIFO/deepest-branch order rather than minimum h. D incorrect A* uses g+h, while the stem explicitly uses only h.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 233 · NS0312
records.text: NS0312 Question 233 AI17 AI12 Which of the following best defines a heuristic in the context of AI search? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A A function that estimates how close a state is to the goal B A guaranteed optimal path to the goal C A method that always avoids revisiting states D A brute-force enumeration of all possible states A problem-specific estimate of remaining cost or promise. AI17 defines a heuristic h(n) as estimating remaining cost or evaluating promise. A’s closeness wording captures that estimate rather than an exact path guarantee. A heuristic does not inherently prevent repeated states and is not exhaustive enumeration; those are separate search-policy or bookkeeping choices. Its quality and computation cost affect practical search. A correct Estimating closeness or remaining cost is the heuristic role defined in AI17. B incorrect An estimate is not itself a guaranteed optimal path. C incorrect Repeated-state avoidance requires duplicate handling rather than following from heuristic estimation. D incorrect Exhaustive enumeration is a search method, not the definition of a heuristic estimate.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 234 · NS0326
records.text: NS0326 Question 234 AI18 AI17 AI15 AI14 Which type of heuristic search strategy that evaluates nodes by combining g ( n), the cost to reach the node, and h ( n.), the cost to get from the node to the goal: f ( n) = g ( n) + h ( n) Since g( n) gives the path cost from the start node to node n, and h( n) is the estimated cost of the cheapest path from n to the goal, we have f ( n) = estimated cost of the cheapest solution through n ? Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies. A A* search B Greedy Best-First Search C Uniform-cost search D Depth-first search A* search. AI18 defines A* by f(n)=g(n)+h(n), exactly as the long stem specifies. The sum estimates the cheapest solution through the node when h estimates remaining cost. Greedy ignores g, UCS ignores h, and DFS does not prioritize this sum, so none of those matches the stated evaluation. A correct A* adds actual cost-to-node g and estimated remaining cost h. B incorrect Greedy best-first uses only h and omits accumulated path cost. C incorrect UCS uses only g and does not add a remaining-cost heuristic. D incorrect DFS uses stack/depth ordering rather than minimum g+h.

records.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Question 235 · NS0349
records.text: NS0349 Question 235 AI33 AI31 AI32 In which of the following Learning methods an agent receives feedback in the form of rewards or penalties to maximize cumulative reward? Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality. A Supervised learning B Reinforcement learning C Semi-supervised learning D Unsupervised learning Reinforcement learning. AI33 defines RL through interaction, rewards and improvement of a policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. The reward may be delayed and does not provide a correct-action label. Supervised and semi-supervised learning instead concern target labels, while unsupervised discovery lacks the defining action-reward interaction described here. A incorrect Supervised learning fits labeled targets rather than defining behavior through cumulative interaction rewards. B correct Reward or penalty feedback guiding cumulative-return improvement is the defining RL mechanism. C incorrect Semi-supervised learning mixes labeled and unlabeled examples, not necessarily action rewards. D incorrect Unsupervised learning discovers unlabeled structure rather than optimizing an interaction reward policy.

records.title: Computer Security — Course module
records.text: Computer Security

records.title: Computer Security — Study notes
records.text: Computer Security Security is reasoning about assets, threats, trust boundaries and justified controls. Learn mechanisms as well as names: identify the damaged property, explain the failure, choose a control and state its limits. The four blueprint outcomes include program security, evaluated trusted operating systems and database security. For each scenario identify the asset, actor, violated property, mechanism and most direct control. Practise key direction, classical cipher arithmetic and small RSA calculations; justify answers from the mechanism and arithmetic. Compare confidentiality with integrity models, function with assurance, detection with prevention, and backup with replication. Test assumptions before selecting one answer.

records.title: Computer Security — Practice questions
records.text: Computer Security

records.title: Computer Security — Revision outline
records.text: Computer Security

records.title: Computer Security — CIA and the property actually harmed
records.text: Confidentiality restricts disclosure: copying a credit-card database violates secrecy even if the original stays intact. Integrity restricts unauthorized or improper changes: altering a balance or inserting a false message damages correctness. Availability supplies timely, usable service to authorized users: crashes, resource starvation and denied access violate it. One event can harm several goals. Authentication establishes an identity or other claim; authorization decides permitted actions. Accountability links actions to responsible entities through reliable identity and protected logs. Non-repudiation supplies evidence supporting origin or receipt; signatures do not make denial physically impossible. Information assurance includes confidence, risk management, protection, detection, response and restoration across the information lifecycle. Data security protects information at rest, in use and in transit, including accidental corruption as well as intentional attacks. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Threat, vulnerability, risk and control
records.text: An asset is something valuable: data, software, hardware, service or reputation. A threat is a potentially harmful circumstance; a vulnerability is an exploitable weakness; an attack is an actual attempt; a control reduces likelihood or impact. A software flaw is not automatically an active attack. Risk concerns likelihood and consequence, not a universally meaningful numeric product of two unmeasured labels. Preventive controls block events, detective controls reveal them, corrective/recovery controls restore safe operation, and deterrents discourage attempts. Encryption is preventive for disclosure; an audit log is principally detective/accountability evidence. Physical, technical and administrative are control categories, not competing stages. An external firewall cannot replace a written policy or a locked equipment room. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Attack classifications and attacker intent
records.text: Interception copies or observes data, modification alters it, interruption blocks it, and fabrication inserts false material. The 4D classification uses disclosure, deception, disruption and usurpation, the last meaning unauthorized control. DoS primarily demonstrates disruption/availability loss; it need not give control of the victim. Passive attacks observe without changing the target exchange: sniffing and traffic analysis. Active attacks inject, alter, replay or disrupt. These are not synonyms for offline and online. Traffic analysis can infer relationships from timing/size even when content is encrypted. Neither category is universally easy to prevent or detect. White-hat testing requires authorization and scope; black-hat activity is malicious or unauthorized. A competitor may seek commercial secrets; hacktivists pursue a cause. “Hacker” alone does not establish legality. Insider versus outsider describes origin/trust position, not the specific mechanism. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Malware: propagation, disguise and payload
records.text: A virus replicates by attaching to a host program or document; execution of the infected host spreads it. A worm replicates independently, commonly across networks. A Trojan disguises malicious behavior as something useful and does not require self-replication. These labels describe different properties, so a malware package may contain several components. Spyware monitors users; a keylogger records keystrokes. Adware displays unwanted advertising and may also track users. Ransomware denies access through encryption/locking and extortion. A logic bomb waits for a trigger. A backdoor bypasses ordinary access paths; a rootkit hides malicious presence or privileged activity. A zombie/bot follows remote commands; a botnet is a collection. Malware is the umbrella term, not a specific replication method. Update, restrict execution, isolate compromise and maintain tested offline backups; no antivirus guarantees complete protection. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Social engineering, spoofing and sessions
records.text: Phishing impersonates a trusted source to obtain secrets or induce an unsafe action; spear phishing targets a specific person. Verify a request through an independently known channel. Shoulder surfing observes entry; pretexting invents a reason for disclosure. Monitoring software used with authorization is not necessarily an attack merely because it records activity. Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — DoS, wireless attacks and layer-specific defenses
records.text: DoS exhausts or disables a resource; distributed DoS uses multiple sources, often bots or reflected/amplified responses. A SYN flood leaves many incomplete TCP handshakes occupying state. DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers. Fragment floods abuse reassembly or packet-processing resources. Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering and upstream capacity controls address different bottlenecks. Rogue access points imitate or bypass approved wireless service. Bluesnarfing steals Bluetooth information; bluejacking sends unsolicited Bluetooth messages. Phishing is not specific to wireless. Match a defense to its layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data, TLS authenticates/protects application transport, and bounds-safe code prevents overflows. HTTPS cannot fix an unsafe memory copy in a server. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Identification, authentication and factors
records.text: A common access sequence is identify the subject, authenticate the claim, authorize the operation, then record relevant events. Identification is the username/claim, not its proof. When a sequence begins with authentication, distinguish it from the preceding identification stage. User-to-host means a user proves identity to a host; host-to-user means the host proves its identity to a user; the arrow names the prover and verifier. Knowledge is a password/PIN, possession is a token/card, and inherence is a biometric such as a fingerprint. Behavioral biometrics include typing rhythm or handwriting; some textbooks call these “something one does.” A body characteristic is not “three-factor authentication”: one biometric is one factor. Password plus PIN remains one factor class; card plus PIN is two. An OTP’s factor depends on its delivery/generation mechanism. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Passwords and delegated authorization
records.text: Brute force enumerates guesses; dictionary attacks prioritize likely words; credential stuffing tries previously leaked credentials on another service. Online attempts face server rate limits; offline attacks against stolen verifiers do not. Short passwords can fail in either setting. Use unique long secrets and password managers, rate limiting and suitable MFA; store salted slow password hashes, not reversible plaintext passwords. A salt prevents shared precomputed lookup, but is not secret. OAuth is an authorization framework: a client obtains limited access tokens, the authorization server authenticates/obtains approval from the resource owner, and the resource server validates tokens for protected data. The authorization server can delegate identity checks. OAuth alone does not define a complete end-user login identity protocol; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer. Computer Security module IETF RFC 6749

records.title: Computer Security — Access control and least privilege
records.text: Subjects request operations on objects. An ACL associates an object/resource with allowed subjects or actions; a network ACL matches traffic such as address, protocol and port. Classification and filtering are direct effects; high availability or malware detection is not guaranteed by an ACL. DAC lets owners grant permissions; mandatory control enforces labels and policy that ordinary owners cannot override. RBAC gives permissions to roles and assigns users to roles. ABAC evaluates subject, object, action and environment attributes. Rule-based controls apply explicit conditions, such as time or source network. Least privilege gives only needed rights, for needed time. Separation of duties splits sensitive steps across parties. Deny by default, mediate every access and revoke stale permissions. Allowing SELECT but denying UPDATE is an access-control decision that helps integrity; it does not by itself enforce all valid business-state transitions. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Confidentiality and integrity models
records.text: Bell–LaPadula protects confidentiality. The simple-security rule prohibits reading above a subject’s level; the star rule prohibits writing down. The strong-star variant permits writing only at the same level. With TS>S>C>U, an S subject can read C under the simple rule but cannot write C under star; compartments and discretionary restrictions may still deny access. Strict Biba protects integrity by preventing read down and write up: untrusted lower-integrity input should not contaminate higher-integrity results. Clark–Wilson protects integrity through certified well-formed transformations, integrity checks and separation of duties. It is not a confidentiality model. “MAC” is an enforcement category and does not force every system to use Bell–LaPadula rather than another label policy. Paul Krzyzanowski, Rutgers: Computer Security exam guide

records.title: Computer Security — Physical protection and resilient design
records.text: Protect equipment against theft, unauthorized connections, heat, humidity, water, electrical surges and fire. A UPS supplies temporary conditioned power; it is normally protective, but faulty installation/battery failure can itself be hazardous. A disconnected machine loses many network attack paths yet remains exposed to insiders, removable media, supply-chain attacks and physical access. There is no universal “most secure computer” without a threat model. Defense in depth layers independent controls. Minimization removes unnecessary software and services; compartmentalization limits blast radius. Fail securely means errors do not silently grant permission. Uniform configurations simplify patching and prediction but create correlated failures; diversity may reduce common-mode compromise while raising administration cost. Choose protection proportional to asset value and credible threats. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Cryptographic vocabulary and security assumptions
records.text: Plaintext is the original message, ciphertext its encrypted representation, a key is input to an algorithm, encryption computes C=E_k(P), and decryption recovers P=D_k(C). The five conventional symmetric ingredients are plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext and decryption algorithm. Cryptanalysis seeks recovery or other breaks without the authorized secret; cryptology includes cryptography and cryptanalysis. Steganography hides that a message exists; encryption hides its meaning. Assume the algorithm is known and protect keys: secrecy of implementation is not the main security argument. A b-bit key has 2^b possibilities; exhaustive search averages roughly half the space if keys are uniformly random. Security depends on algorithm, key size, randomness, mode and implementation. Symmetric cryptography is not inherently less secure than public-key cryptography, and speed ratios are not fixed constants. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Substitution, shift and affine ciphers
records.text: Substitution replaces symbols; transposition changes their positions. A monoalphabetic substitution preserves one mapping throughout the message and leaks frequency patterns despite a large nominal key space. Classical ciphers are teaching devices, not modern data protection. With A=0 through Z=25, Caesar encryption is C=(P+k) mod26 and decryption P=(C-k) mod26. A shift of 3 maps A→D and HELLO→KHOOR. Key25 moves back one: ATTACK→ZSSZBJ. Ensure negative results wrap into 0–25. A multiplicative cipher uses C=kP mod26 with gcd(k,26)=1; decryption uses k’s modular inverse. Affine uses C=aP+b mod26 and requires gcd(a,26)=1. The inverse-key relation, not simply the same numeric multiplication, recovers plaintext. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Vigenère, Playfair and Hill
records.text: Vigenère repeats or otherwise supplies shifts K_i and computes C_i=(P_i+K_i) mod26. The same plaintext letter may encrypt differently by position; repeated short keys still leak periodic structure. An autokey scheme extends its initial key using message material. Playfair uses a keyed 5×5 grid, commonly combining I/J, and encrypts letter pairs. Specify duplicate-letter fillers and padding. Same row moves right, same column moves down, and rectangle pairs take the other column in their original row; decryption reverses shifts. Hill uses C=KP mod26 for letter vectors. K needs an inverse modulo26, equivalently determinant coprime to26. It is linear: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal K=CP^-1 mod26. Hill is vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks; polygraphic substitution alone is not modern strength. Computer Security module Chris Christensen, Northern Kentucky University: Hill cipher

records.title: Computer Security — Transposition and one-time pads
records.text: Rail-fence writes along a specified zigzag and reads rails; columnar transposition writes rows and reads columns in a specified order. They preserve the symbols and their counts. Always state rows, column order, padding and direction before computing a transposition cipher. Two-rail zigzag for ABCDEF writes ACE on the first rail and BDF on the second, producing ACEBDF. A one-time pad XORs bits with an independent uniformly random secret key at least as long as the message and never reused. Its perfect secrecy depends on every condition. Reusing a pad leaks C1 XOR C2=P1 XOR P2. A Vernam XOR construction is not automatically a one-time pad: a predictable/reused keystream loses that guarantee. Key delivery and storage remain substantial costs. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Symmetric keys, AES and distribution
records.text: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret and efficiently protects bulk data. Pairwise independent keys for n users require n(n-1)/2 shared keys; a trusted key distribution center changes that architecture. A session key is temporary for a communication context; a master/key-encryption key protects subordinate keys. Distribute keys physically, via an authenticated protected channel, or through a trusted third party. An uncompromised old key can protect a new key, although this does not restore secrecy after the old key is stolen. AES is a 128-bit block cipher with 128/192/256-bit keys and 10/12/14 rounds. Its substitution/permutation design uses SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey; the final round omits MixColumns. Block ciphers need a mode and correct nonce/IV handling; authenticated encryption also detects tampering. A stream cipher combines data with a keystream. Never reuse a nonce when the chosen construction requires uniqueness. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — DES and Feistel mechanics
records.text: DES has a 64-bit block, 56 effective key bits (eight other bits serve parity), and 16 Feistel rounds. After initial permutation, each round computes L_i=R_(i-1), R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i). Its right-half expansion makes 48 bits, XOR mixes a 48-bit subkey, eight S-boxes each map six bits to four, and permutation rearranges the 32 output bits. The outer S-box input bits select a row and the inner four select a column. The nonlinear S-boxes resist simple linear descriptions. Feistel inversion uses the same overall structure with reversed round keys; f need not itself be invertible. Final swapping/permutation completes DES. DES and triple DES are legacy algorithms, not choices for new protection. Triple DES repeats DES operations but does not provide 168-bit effective security merely because three 56-bit keys are supplied. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Public keys and hybrid protection
records.text: For confidentiality to B, encrypt with B’s authenticated public encryption key; B decrypts with B’s private key. Do not encrypt to A’s public key if only B should read it, and never assume A possesses B’s private key. For a signature, A signs with A’s private signing key and others verify with A’s public key. These are distinct operations; not every public-key algorithm supports encryption. Public keys ease distribution but require authentic bindings to identities. Hybrid systems establish or encapsulate a symmetric secret with public-key mechanisms, then protect bulk data symmetrically. Diffie–Hellman agrees on a secret but unauthenticated DH permits intermediary substitution. With public p,g, A=g^a modp and B=g^b modp, both derive B^a=A^b=g^(ab) modp. Authenticate the exchange and derive separate traffic keys. For one-way public-key confidentiality the sender need not own a key pair; it needs the recipient’s authenticated public encryption key. A sender key pair is needed when the protocol requires its signature or separate recipient role. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — RSA arithmetic and key-validity conditions
records.text: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe. With p=7,q=19, n=133 and φ=108, e=5 is the smallest admissible e>1, but 7 and other coprime choices also work. For e=5, d=65 since 325≡1 mod108. With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key. Check key validity before treating arithmetic results as a working encryption/decryption pair. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Hashes, MACs and signatures
records.text: A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest. It is deterministic and designed to resist preimages and collisions; collisions must exist, so hashes are not mathematically unique fingerprints. An attacker can recompute an unkeyed hash of modified data, so a hash alone needs a trusted reference. A keyed MAC provides integrity and shared-secret authentication; both holders can create it, limiting third-party non-repudiation. A signature algorithm signs a message or its encoded digest with a private key and verifies with the public key. It is not generically “encrypting with a private key,” especially for DSA/ECDSA. Verification checks origin/integrity under key-identity and key-custody assumptions; it does not conceal content. Password verification uses a salt and deliberately expensive password hash. Historical MD5/SHA-1 examples do not justify their use for new collision-resistant signatures. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Certificates, TLS and HTTPS
records.text: A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature. Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy. A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest. TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel. A handshake negotiates parameters, authenticates the server and sometimes the client, and establishes keys; record protection uses symmetric authenticated encryption. Exact messages depend on TLS version: the old ChangeCipherSpec narrative is not a universal TLS1.3 sequence. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. It protects HTTP paths, headers and content on the channel, but does not hide all metadata such as IP endpoints and traffic timing, nor protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — SSH, IPsec, email protection and SET
records.text: SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods. IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer. AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys. Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header. A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel. PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS. One signed-and-encrypted S/MIME construction first signs the MIME entity, packages its content and signature, then encrypts that signed entity with a fresh symmetric content key. Protect a copy of that key for each recipient. A recipient recovers the key, decrypts the signed entity and verifies its signature using the validated signer certificate/public key. Signing is not generic private-key encryption. S/MIME permits other nesting orders; specify the order and resulting coverage. Computer Security module IBM KeyWorks service-provider interface S/MIME4.0 specification

records.title: Computer Security — Firewalls and protected boundaries
records.text: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN. Host firewalls protect individual machines; network firewalls segment networks and can create a DMZ for public-facing services. Rules should be explicit, ordered as implemented, least-privilege and logged appropriately. Stateful and next-generation devices can also filter ports; port filtering is not exclusive to one firewall category. Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection. Hardware firewall does not imply any fixed number of ports. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Detection, prevention and diagnostic measures
records.text: An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline. Host-based sensors examine host events, network-based sensors inspect traffic. Signature detection recognizes known patterns; anomaly detection compares with a baseline and may detect novel behavior. Neither guarantees every attack is detected; anomaly detection can raise many false positives, and signatures can sometimes match variants. A true positive is a real attack detected, false negative is a missed attack, false positive is innocent activity flagged, and true negative is innocent activity accepted. Recall=TP/(TP+FN); precision=TP/(TP+FP). Detecting 90 of 100 spam messages with five innocent messages flagged gives recall90%, precision90/95≈94.7%. Obfuscation makes code harder to understand and can hamper analysis, but does not reliably protect embedded secrets or remove vulnerabilities. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Memory safety and secure input handling
records.text: A buffer overflow writes beyond allocated bounds and can corrupt data or control information; code execution is a possible consequence, not its definition or an inevitable outcome. An array of eight bytes cannot store eight text characters plus a terminating zero. Bounds-check lengths and indexes, consider integer overflow, use safe abstractions and validate library return values. Canaries, non-executable memory and address randomization reduce exploitability but do not repair the underlying write. Validate expected type, length, range and structure at trust boundaries. Server validation is essential because clients are controllable. Encode output for its destination; validation is not a universal substitute for query parameterization or HTML-context encoding. Security patches repair known weaknesses; a zero-day may lack a vendor fix, but segmentation and other mitigations can still help. MITRE CWE-787

records.title: Computer Security — SQL injection, XSS and request forgery
records.text: SQL injection occurs when untrusted values alter SQL syntax through unsafe string construction. A tautology can change which rows match. Bind data values in prepared statements, allow-list identifiers that cannot be parameters, and restrict the application’s database account. Stored procedures/ORMs are safe only when they avoid unsafe dynamic SQL. XSS causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a victim’s browser under the site’s origin. Stored content persists; reflected content returns in a response; DOM-based XSS can arise from unsafe browser sinks. Use safe text insertion and context-specific encoding; carefully sanitize allowed HTML. CSP is added protection, not the sole fix. CSRF exploits ambient credentials to submit an unwanted authenticated action. Use unpredictable request tokens and suitable cookie/origin controls. HttpOnly restricts script access to cookies but does not stop every XSS effect. Fuzzing sends unexpected inputs to discover faults; it is a testing technique, not itself a category of injection. OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet OWASP Cross Site Scripting

records.title: Computer Security — Races, testing and secure development
records.text: A race occurs when correctness depends on timing/interleaving over shared state. In a check-then-open file operation, another actor may replace the file between the check and use. In a balance update, two workers can both read100 and each write90, losing one debit. Protect the whole invariant with suitable atomic operations, locks or database transactions; locking an unrelated variable does not help. Vulnerability assessment finds and prioritizes weaknesses; authorized penetration testing attempts to demonstrate consequences. Static analysis inspects code, dynamic testing executes it, and fuzzing varies inputs. Host/network/database scanners see different exposures and have false results. Correct findings, patch, test and recheck; testing is not proof of absence. Build threat modeling, review, least privilege, dependency management and safe error handling into development. Computer Security module MITRE CWE-362

records.title: Computer Security — Trusted OS requirements and reference mediation
records.text: A trusted OS is relied on to enforce a stated security policy. Relevant mechanisms include identification/authentication, process and memory isolation, controlled privileges, object access enforcement, protected auditing, safe resource reuse, trusted boot/update paths and recovery behavior. The trusted computing base comprises components whose failure can violate policy; smaller, analyzable boundaries simplify assurance. A reference monitor is an abstract access-checking mechanism: it must mediate every relevant access, resist tampering and be sufficiently small/simple to analyze. A security kernel implements core enforcement. A firewall can mediate its traversing traffic but cannot enforce every host-memory access. Assurance is justified confidence that controls implement the claims; functionality is what controls claim to do. A GUI or multitasking support alone does not establish trust. Computer Security module NIST SP800-53 Rev5 AC-25 Reference Monitor

records.title: Computer Security — Independent evaluation, certification and assurance
records.text: Under Common Criteria, define the Target of Evaluation (TOE), its configuration and environment. A Security Target (ST) states threats, assumptions, objectives, functional requirements and assurance requirements; a Protection Profile describes reusable requirements for a product category. Evaluators examine developer evidence, test and analyze vulnerabilities against those claims. A certification body oversees/reviews the evaluation and issues the certification decision; sponsors commission work and developers supply product/evidence. An Evaluation Assurance Level packages assurance requirements; EAL1–7 express increasing evaluation rigor, not a universal ranking of security functions. A higher number does not make a product with different scope automatically safer. CCRA is a mutual-recognition arrangement, not a single worldwide testing laboratory. A certificate applies to a specified product/configuration and claims, not immunity to all future attacks. Common Criteria 2022 Part 1 Indian Common Criteria Certification Scheme FAQ

records.title: Computer Security — Database secrecy, permissions and key boundaries
records.text: Database security needs confidentiality, integrity, availability and accountability together. Authenticate connections, give roles only necessary table/column/row privileges, restrict views and audit sensitive changes. A user allowed to read a report need not read the underlying full table. Check application-level authorization as well as database rights. Encryption at rest protects stolen storage/backups when keys remain separate; transport encryption protects the connection. Neither prevents a fully authorized query or guarantees correctness. Strong access controls, encryption and protected transmission can all contribute to secrecy; compare their roles and assumptions. Replication is useful for availability but also copies malicious updates unless separate recovery controls exist. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Database integrity and reliability mechanisms
records.text: Integrity requires valid data and valid transitions. NOT NULL rejects missing mandatory values; UNIQUE/primary keys prevent duplicate identifiers; foreign keys preserve references; CHECK enforces declared predicates. Transactions group a transfer’s debit and credit atomically; concurrency control prevents unsafe interleavings. Roles/ACLs limit who may update, but constraints and transaction logic determine whether an authorized update is valid. Write-ahead logging persists recovery records before dependent data-file changes, supporting recovery after a crash. Backups, restore tests and separately protected logs recover from deletion/corruption; replication provides alternate service capacity but does not replace backups. Redundancy improves availability only with appropriate failover and independent failure handling. Distinguish confidentiality controls from reliability controls and from integrity constraints. PostgreSQL constraints documentation PostgreSQL write-ahead logging documentation

records.title: Computer Security — Inference control and multilevel databases
records.text: Inference reveals protected facts by combining individually permitted outputs with other knowledge. If a report gives a two-person salary total and one salary is known, subtraction reveals the other. Blocking direct SELECT of a salary column does not stop that inference. Restrict small groups and overlapping queries, track query history, coarsen/suppress results, or introduce carefully designed noise; each trades utility against leakage. A multilevel database stores items at different labels and enforces mandatory policy using subject clearances, classifications and compartments. Bell–LaPadula-style read/write restrictions prevent direct downward confidentiality flow; trusted declassification is a separate controlled action. Views alone are not proof of multilevel isolation. Covert channels, query results and error messages may still reveal information, so evaluate both direct access and indirect inference. University of South Carolina, Information Security Lab

records.title: Computer Security — Policy, incident response and recovery objectives
records.text: A security policy states responsibilities and rules; a procedure supplies the steps. Policies coordinate protection, reduce risk and define acceptable use, access review, incident handling and recovery. They do not prescribe merely “passive system use.” Awareness training teaches reporting and independent verification; enforcement and usable procedures make it operational. Prepare response roles/tools, detect and analyze, contain the incident, eradicate the cause, restore verified service and learn from the evidence. Preserve useful protected logs. Disaster recovery restores IT after disruption; business continuity sustains business functions through workarounds and alternate facilities. RTO is a recovery-time target; RPO measures the tolerable age of lost data. A backup schedule must satisfy the required recovery point, and a restore test must demonstrate that data can actually be recovered. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Interpret security mechanisms and conditions precisely
records.text: Compare each security mechanism with the stated requirement and conditions. Check asymmetric-encryption key directions carefully; signatures do not generically encrypt whole messages with private keys. Body biometrics do not imply three factors. SSL and SSH can both describe protected channels; SSH specifically supports remote-shell services. Read the full option text before matching it to a security mechanism. Undefined “arbitrary code execution” does not uniquely identify buffer overflow: several mechanisms can produce that consequence. A database-security requirement can include both availability and confidentiality. Generic ACLs and RBAC both restrict unauthorized writes but neither independently enforces all integrity constraints. Evaluation organizations must be identified by the actual national scheme; CCRA is recognition, not an evaluator. An answer is supported only after the missing distinction is supplied. Computer Security module

records.title: Computer Security — Command injection and the data-to-command boundary
records.text: OS command injection occurs when an application lets untrusted input affect a command executed by the host operating system, often through unsafe construction of a shell command. The command runs with the application's effective privileges. This is an injection flaw in command interpretation, unlike fuzzing, which supplies varied inputs to discover defects. Prefer a suitable library API over constructing a shell command. Where command execution is required, keep the executable and arguments under strict control and validate against the expected permitted structure; merely blocking a few suspicious characters is not a general proof of safety. OWASP — Command Injection

records.title: Computer Security — WannaCry: ransomware and worm propagation
records.text: WannaCry, also known as WannaCrypt, is ransomware with worm-like propagation. It encrypts files and demands payment to restore access. Its name identifies malicious software rather than a network-security protocol. Malware names must be distinguished from defensive controls such as intrusion detection, intrusion prevention and physical protection. Microsoft Defender Security Research Team — WannaCrypt ransomware worm targets out-of-date systems CERT-EU — WannaCry Ransomware Campaign

records.title: Computer Security — Distinguish network roles and protocol names
records.text: A router forwards IP packets between networks; forwarding alone is different from detecting suspicious behavior or enforcing a firewall's security policy. SNMP means Simple Network Management Protocol and provides a framework for monitoring and controlling managed devices through management information. It is not a remote-shell service. AAA names authentication, authorization and accounting functions, rather than a particular remote-shell channel. SSH expands to Secure Shell and provides secure remote login and related network services. PGP expands to Pretty Good Privacy; its message-protection design combines conventional and public-key encryption with digital signatures. Protocol purpose matters when several technologies all contribute to security. RFC 1812 — Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers RFC 3411 — SNMP Management Frameworks RFC 2903 — Generic AAA Architecture RFC 4251 — The Secure Shell Protocol Architecture RFC 1991 — PGP Message Exchange Formats (historical terminology)

records.title: Computer Security — Question 1 · Q00002
records.text: Q00002 Question 1 SEC03 Which one of the following is an attack performed by wiretapping a network and illicitly copy files and programs? Classify the action actually described and distinguish observation, alteration, disruption and identity claims. A Interception B Fabrication C Interruption D Modification Interception Wiretapping and copying give an unauthorized party access without changing or destroying the resource. This is the disclosure/interception case on PDF p.4. A correct Interception directly matches unauthorized snooping/access. See PDF p.4. B incorrect Fabrication inserts a fake resource; no insertion is described. See PDF p.4. C incorrect Interruption makes the resource unavailable; copying does not imply loss of service. See PDF p.4. D incorrect Modification changes the resource; no change is stated. See PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 2 · Q00004
records.text: Q00004 Question 2 SEC11 Assuming the UPS is correctly installed and operating normally, which listed item is a protective power-supply control rather than an environmental hazard? Start with the stated attacker path or physical hazard and the limits of each control. A Improperly placed heater B Humidity C Lightning strikes D UPS(uninterruptible power supply) UPS(uninterruptible power supply) A working UPS supplies temporary conditioned power and normally protects equipment against power problems. The other entries name heat-placement, humidity or electrical-surge hazards that can impair operation. The revised question assumes normal installation and operation only for the UPS, rather than claiming it can never cause harm. Battery faults and installation failures remain possible in general, but they are outside this stated comparison. A incorrect An improperly placed heater can expose equipment to damaging heat. B incorrect Humidity is an environmental condition requiring protection. C incorrect Lightning can produce damaging electrical surges. D correct A correctly installed, working UPS supplies protective conditioned power.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 3 · Q00006
records.text: Q00006 Question 3 SEC18 Awgichew wants message confidentiality for Meron using asymmetric encryption, not a signature. KPRIV-A/KPUB-A are Awgichew’s keys and KPRIV-M/KPUB-M are Meron’s keys. Which statements are NOT correct for that confidential exchange? Select all that apply. Identify the intended recipient or signer and separate confidentiality from verification. A Awgichew uses Meron's private key KPRIV-M to encrypt his plain text B Awgichew uses his KPUB-A to encrypt his plain text C Meron can decode the encrypted text using her KPRIV-M D Meron can decode the scrambled text using her KPUB-M Awgichew uses Meron's private key KPRIV-M to encrypt his plain text; Awgichew uses his KPUB-A to encrypt his plain text; Meron can decode the scrambled text using her KPUB-M For confidentiality to Meron, the sender encrypts with Meron’s authenticated public encryption key and she decrypts with her private key. Awgichew should neither possess her private key nor encrypt to his own public key for a message only she should read. Her public key is not the secret decryption key. Thus A, B and D are incorrect directions; C describes the valid recipient decryption step and is not selected in this NOT-correct question. A correct Incorrect exchange step: the sender must not use or assume possession of Meron’s private key. B correct Incorrect exchange step: encrypting to Awgichew’s public key addresses the wrong recipient. C incorrect This is a valid decryption step, so it must not be selected as NOT correct. D correct Incorrect exchange step: Meron decrypts with her private key, not her public key.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 4 · Q00009
records.text: Q00009 Question 4 SEC18 SEC16 In a two-way confidential exchange, both participants send and receive encrypted messages. Which statement correctly describes symmetric versus asymmetric encryption key arrangements? Identify the intended recipient or signer and separate confidentiality from verification. A Both use the same shared secret as their sole confidentiality key B Symmetric key requires the sender and receiver to have a public and private key C Asymmetric encryption requires each participant, acting as a recipient, to have its own public/private encryption key pair D Both are recovery methods Asymmetric encryption requires each participant, acting as a recipient, to have its own public/private encryption key pair Symmetric encryption uses a secret shared by the communicating parties. For public-key confidentiality, a sender encrypts to the recipient's authenticated public encryption key, and that recipient decrypts with its private key. Because both participants receive encrypted messages in this two-way scenario, each needs its own encryption key pair. A sender in a strictly one-way exchange would not need a pair merely to send. Neither architecture is defined as a recovery method. A incorrect False: a shared secret describes symmetric confidentiality, not the asymmetric key arrangement. B incorrect False: symmetric encryption does not require each party to have a public/private pair. C correct Correct: each participant is a recipient in one direction and needs its own public/private encryption pair. D incorrect False: encryption key arrangements protect communication; they are not recovery methods.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 5 · Q00030
records.text: Q00030 Question 5 SEC13 A cipher replaces each plaintext letter with the next letter in the alphabet, wrapping Z to A. Which is the most specific standard cipher classification of this operation? Separate symbol replacement from position changes and apply the alphabet and modular direction. A Transliteration B Translation C Transformation D Substitution Substitution The operation changes each symbol's identity while leaving its position in the message unchanged. That is substitution, and using the next alphabet letter is a fixed Caesar shift. General text-conversion descriptions do not identify this specific cipher class. Transformation is especially broad and could include many cryptographic or noncryptographic changes. D is therefore the most precise classification, rather than a claim that ordinary language can never describe encryption using broader terms. A incorrect Incorrect: transliteration does not identify the specified fixed-alphabet-shift cipher class. B incorrect Incorrect: translation does not identify the specific cipher class defined by replacing symbols while retaining positions. C incorrect Incorrect: transformation is a broader description and does not distinguish substitution from other changes. D correct Correct: replacing symbol identities while keeping their positions is substitution.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 6 · Q00039
records.text: Q00039 Question 6 SEC02 SEC01 Which one of the following is an attack detection mechanism? Distinguish weaknesses, potential harmful events, actual attempts and the effect of a control. A Physical control B Audit log C Password D Encryption Audit log Logs preserve successful and failed authentication events (PDF p.4). Reviewing this evidence can determine that an attack occurred, matching the module’s detection objective; the other listed controls primarily restrict or protect. A incorrect Physical controls protect facilities; this option does not specify monitoring evidence. See PDF p.4. B correct An audit log records relevant events for identifying attacks after or during occurrence. See PDF p.4. C incorrect A password checker controls entry rather than recording evidence of attack by itself. See PDF p.4. D incorrect Encryption scrambles cleartext; it does not by itself identify an attack. See PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 7 · Q00048
records.text: Q00048 Question 7 SEC04 Which one of the following best describes for a program that seems friendly and legitimate but contains hidden malicious codes and harms a system? Separate propagation, disguise and payload when classifying malicious software. A Trojan B Malware C Virus D Worm Trojan The defining clue is apparent legitimacy hiding malicious behavior. SEC04 assigns that disguise property to a Trojan. Malware is the broad umbrella, while viruses and worms are distinguished by replication mechanisms. Because the stem asks what best describes the program, Trojan is more specific than the umbrella term and requires no unmentioned replication behavior. A correct A Trojan presents useful or legitimate behavior as cover for concealed malicious actions. B incorrect Malware is the broad umbrella and does not specifically capture the deceptive legitimate appearance asked for. C incorrect A virus is defined by attaching to a host and replicating, neither of which the stem specifies. D incorrect A worm independently replicates; that is different from the concealed malicious disguise described.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 8 · Q00055
records.text: Q00055 Question 8 SEC04 A malicious program that once installed on your machine can collect all keystrokes including username, password, emails, credit card numbers and other sensitive information is: Separate propagation, disguise and payload when classifying malicious software. A Rootkit B Worms C Key logger D Trojan Keylogger SEC04 directly assigns keystroke recording to a keylogger. Recording every entered character can capture passwords and other secrets typed by the user. Rootkits hide malicious presence, worms replicate independently and Trojans conceal malicious behavior under useful appearances; none of those names specifically denotes keystroke collection. A incorrect A rootkit hides malicious presence or privileged activity; keystroke capture is not its defining function. B incorrect Worms are defined by independent replication, not by collecting typed information. C correct A keylogger records keystrokes and can capture the sensitive values entered through the keyboard. D incorrect A Trojan describes deceptive packaging; it does not specifically name the keystroke-recording function.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 9 · Q00187
records.text: Q00187 Question 9 SEC07 Which authentication factor class uses a characteristic of the user’s body, such as a fingerprint? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A One-factor authentication B Two-factor authentication C Inherence (biometric) factor D Forth-factor authentication Inherence (biometric) factor An inherence factor authenticates using a biometric characteristic such as a fingerprint. That describes a factor class, not a count of independent classes combined by a procedure. One biometric alone is one factor, and biometrics may also participate in multi-factor authentication. The option identifies the factor class, while the numerical alternatives do not identify the bodily characteristic being requested. A incorrect One factor is a count and does not specify whether the factor is biometric. B incorrect Two-factor authentication is a combination count, not the body-based factor class. C correct Inherence identifies the biometric factor class. D incorrect Four-factor authentication is a count rather than the requested factor class.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 10 · Q00190
records.text: Q00190 Question 10 SEC24 SEC23 SEC04 SEC-S03 is a system that monitors traffic into and out of a network and automatically alerts personnel when suspicious traffic patterns occur, indicating a possible unauthorized intrusion attempt. Separate observation from blocking and sensor placement from detection method. A Anti-Virus Software B IDS C Firewall D Router SS Intrusion detection system The stem describes observing traffic and alerting on suspicious patterns rather than enforcing a block. SEC24 defines that as an IDS role. Antivirus focuses on malicious software, a firewall enforces traffic policy and a router forwards packets. A product can combine functions, but detection/alerting is the specific function requested. A incorrect Antivirus targets malicious software; it is not the generic traffic-pattern detection system defined by the stem. B correct An IDS observes activity and alerts personnel about suspected intrusion patterns. C incorrect A firewall’s defining role is traffic-policy enforcement rather than the stated intrusion-alerting function. D incorrect A router forwards packets between networks and is not defined by suspicious-pattern alerting.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 11 · Q00231
records.text: Q00231 Question 11 SEC06 SEC25 SEC04 Which attack category is defined by exhausting or disabling operating-system services so legitimate users cannot obtain service, regardless of the mechanism used? Match the resource bottleneck or wireless mechanism to the relevant protection layer. A Buffer Overflow B Malware C Denial of Service D Network Intrusion Denial of Service Denial of service is defined by exhausting or disabling a resource so legitimate users cannot use it. A buffer overflow is a memory-bounds violation that can have several consequences, including a crash in some cases; malware names malicious software, and network intrusion concerns unauthorized entry. Any of those mechanisms could participate in a service-denial incident, but they are not the availability-outcome category requested by the stem. C supplies that category. A incorrect Incorrect: a buffer overflow writes beyond allocated bounds; it is a possible mechanism rather than the service-denial category. B incorrect Incorrect: malware is an umbrella class of malicious software, not the requested availability outcome. C correct Correct: denial of service exhausts or disables a resource and blocks legitimate service.
