D incorrect Incorrect: network intrusion concerns unauthorized entry; the requested category is loss of service.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 12 · Q00234
records.text: Q00234 Question 12 SEC06 Which statement is false about network-traffic denial-of-service attacks? Treat NXDOMAIN flooding here as distributed and fragmentation as a fragment-flood attack rather than ordinary IP fragmentation. Match the resource bottleneck or wireless mechanism to the relevant protection layer. A Distributed NXDOMAIN flooding is a form of DDoS attack. B An IP fragment flood is a traffic-based attack. C DNS Flooding is a traffic-based attack. D TCP SYN Flooding is not a traffic-based attack. TCP SYN Flooding is not a traffic-based attack. The stated attacks exhaust resources through network traffic. Distributed NXDOMAIN flooding stresses resolver capacity using multiple sources; fragment floods abuse reassembly or packet-processing resources; DNS floods target query capacity. A SYN flood also uses network traffic, leaving incomplete TCP handshakes that consume connection state. Its mechanism differs from raw bandwidth exhaustion, but that does not make it non-traffic-based. D is therefore the false claim under the explicitly broad traffic-based meaning. A incorrect Multiple-source NXDOMAIN flooding qualifies as distributed denial of service. B incorrect Fragment flooding abuses processing or reassembly resources through traffic. C incorrect DNS flooding consumes query capacity through traffic. D correct SYN flooding is traffic-based, so this denial is false.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 13 · Q00235
records.text: Q00235 Question 13 SEC10 Which one of the following is true about Bell-LaPadula model security properties? Apply the named model's read and write restrictions separately. A The * (star) Security Property states that a subject at a given security level may not read an object at a higher security level. B Users can create content only at or below their own security level (i.e. secret users can create secret or confidential files but may not create top secret files; no write-up). C The Strong Star Property states that subjects may write to objects with only a matching security level. D The Simple Security Property states that a subject at a given security level may not write to any object at a lower security level. Strong-star permits writes only at the matching level SEC10 separates the properties: simple security is no read up, star is no write down and strong-star restricts writing to the same level. C correctly names the strong-star condition. A and D exchange the names of the simple and star properties, while B states no write up, contrary to Bell–LaPadula’s confidentiality direction. A incorrect No read up is the simple-security rule, not the star property. B incorrect Bell–LaPadula prohibits writing down; this option instead asserts no write up and allows downward disclosure. C correct Strong-star permits writes only to objects at the subject’s matching level. D incorrect No write down is the star rule, not the simple-security rule.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 14 · Q00236
records.text: Q00236 Question 14 SEC25 Which statement most precisely identifies the programming defect underlying a buffer overflow, rather than a possible exploit outcome or a broad claim about operating-system families? Identify the unsafe operation or input boundary rather than only a possible consequence. A An overflow may allow attacker-supplied instructions to execute B The age or family name of an operating system alone establishes that it contains an exploitable overflow C All other statements precisely define the underlying defect D Buffer-overflow may remain as a bug in apps if boundary checks are not done fully Buffer-overflow may remain as a bug in apps if boundary checks are not done fully A buffer overflow writes beyond allocated bounds. Missing or incomplete boundary checks can leave that defect in application code, which is the role described by D. Executing attacker-supplied code is a possible consequence, not the underlying definition or a necessary outcome. An operating-system family name or age alone does not establish a specific vulnerable component. The revised question distinguishes cause from consequence without endorsing unsupported historical vendor claims. A incorrect This is a possible consequence rather than the underlying bounds-checking defect requested. B incorrect A family name or age is not evidence of a specific exploitable out-of-bounds write. C incorrect The other statements are not all precise descriptions of the underlying defect. D correct Incomplete bounds checking can leave an application buffer-overflow bug.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 15 · Q00237
records.text: Q00237 Question 15 SEC23 Which one of the following is true about Firewalls? Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Prevent a TCP Session Hijacking attack B Prevent a virus or malicious code from entering to our network C Can be configured to limit access based on port number or protocol D Detects and prevent an attack if attacker is within our network segment Configure access limits by protocol and port SEC23 explicitly gives protocol/port matching as a firewall function. It also describes bypass paths, insiders and infected removable media as limits, so firewall deployment does not guarantee all hijacking, malware or same-segment attacks are prevented. C is the configurable capability supported without those absolute guarantees. A incorrect A firewall does not universally prevent every session hijack, especially traffic outside its inspected or enforced paths. B incorrect Malware can arrive through bypass paths or permitted traffic; a firewall cannot guarantee excluding all malicious code. C correct Protocol and port fields can be matched in traffic-policy rules to restrict access. D incorrect An attacker sharing an internal segment may bypass the firewall’s traffic path; detection/prevention is not guaranteed.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 16 · Q00238
records.text: Q00238 Question 16 SEC07 Which one of the following is true about means of authentication? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Something the individual does: recognition by voice pattern, handwriting characteristics, and typing rhythm. B Something the individual possesses: fingerprint, retina, and face. C Something the individual is: electronic keycards, smart cards, and physical keys. D Something the individual knows: possess a token. Behavioral characteristics: voice/handwriting/typing patterns SEC07 distinguishes knowledge, possession and inherence, and recognizes behavioral biometrics under the textbook “does” category. A matches that classification, including handwriting and typing rhythm. The remaining options exchange possession and biometrics or call a possessed token knowledge. Voice-pattern recognition is biometric behavior/characteristic recognition, not possession of an external object. A correct The examples describe biometric behavior/patterns consistent with the textbook something-one-does category. B incorrect Fingerprints, retina and face are body characteristics, not possessed token/card objects. C incorrect Keycards, smart cards and physical keys are possession factors, not inherent body characteristics. D incorrect Possessing a token is a possession factor; knowledge means a secret such as a password or PIN.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 17 · Q00269
records.text: Q00269 Question 17 SEC06 SEC21 SEC25 Which one of the following pairs is incorrect? Match the resource bottleneck or wireless mechanism to the relevant protection layer. A IP Spoofing - IPSec B TCP Session Hijacking - TLS C DNS Cache Poisoning - DNSSEC D Buffer overflow - HTTPS HTTPS does not fix buffer overflows SEC06 matches protections to the attacked layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and TLS protects application transport against interception/tampering. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; it cannot make an unsafe server memory copy bounds-safe. Thus D is the mismatched attack/defense pairing, without treating the other mechanisms as unconditional guarantees. A incorrect Authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, so this is a relevant defense pairing. B incorrect TLS protects authenticated transport against interception/tampering relevant to session hijacking, under correct endpoint validation. C incorrect DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and is relevant to resisting false cached DNS answers. D correct HTTPS protects the channel but does not repair writes beyond a server buffer’s allocated bounds.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 18 · Q00341
records.text: Q00341 Question 18 SEC01 SEC03 Which statement is NOT a property of integrity under the primary CIA-goal classification? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Integrity can be compromised by Deception B Integrity can be compromised by Disclosure C Requires permitted modifications to be authorized D Protects resources against unauthorized alteration Integrity can be compromised by Disclosure Integrity concerns the correctness of information and protection against unauthorized or improper changes. False data introduced through deception, unauthorized alteration and violations of modification permissions can therefore threaten integrity. Pure disclosure means an unauthorized party learns information without changing it; that directly violates confidentiality. Availability instead concerns timely, usable access. Classifying the direct effect avoids treating every active attack as an integrity attack or assuming that one incident can affect only one security goal. A incorrect An integrity concern: deception can introduce false information and corrupt correctness. B correct Correct selection: pure disclosure directly compromises confidentiality rather than integrity. C incorrect An integrity concern: modification permissions distinguish authorized changes from unauthorized ones. D incorrect An integrity concern: unauthorized alteration directly damages information correctness.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 19 · Q00342
records.text: Q00342 Question 19 SEC07 Assume, you went to the Ethiopian airport to catch a flight and told the airport personnel your name. For sure, they would ask you some questions like your passport number and your reservation ticket number for some proof of your identity. Then what do we call this process? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Authentication B Authorization C Access control D All Authentication The passenger first claims a name, then is asked for evidence supporting that identity. Proving who one claims to be is authentication (PDF p.4), rather than deciding what the passenger may do. A correct Passport/ticket evidence tests the claimed identity. See PDF p.4. B incorrect Authorization would grant permissions after establishing identity. See PDF p.4. C incorrect Access control is the broader restriction mechanism, while the described step is identity proof. See PDF p.4. D incorrect All incorrectly treats permission decisions as already described. See PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 20 · Q00343
records.text: Q00343 Question 20 SEC01 SEC07 Assume, you went to the nearby commercial bank's automatic teller machine (ATM) to withdraw money. You inserted your ATM card into the machine, and the machine asked you to enter your personal identification number (PIN). Then, when you type your password, someone intercepts your ATM card number, and which of your security goals is compromised? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Integrity B Authorization C Confidentiality D Availability Confidentiality Intercepting the ATM number discloses information to an unauthorized party. The module maps interception to confidentiality (PDF pp.3–4); neither data alteration nor service denial is described. A incorrect No modification is stated. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. B incorrect The event is disclosure rather than a permission-granting decision. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. C correct Unauthorized learning of the card number compromises confidentiality. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. D incorrect The user is not said to lose timely access to service. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 21 · Q00344
records.text: Q00344 Question 21 SEC04 SEC05 Which attack can be used for monitoring children's activity? Separate propagation, disguise and payload when classifying malicious software. A Spyware B Ransomwares C Worms D Adware Spyware-like monitoring capability The capability described is monitoring user activity, which SEC04 associates with spyware. Ransomware locks or encrypts for extortion, worms replicate and adware displays unwanted advertisements. SEC05 adds an important context limit: monitoring with authorization is not automatically an attack. A matches the functionality, but the child-monitoring use alone does not establish malicious intent. A correct Spyware’s monitoring function matches collection of user activity, subject to the authorization caveat. B incorrect Ransomware denies access and extorts payment rather than primarily monitoring user activity. C incorrect A worm independently replicates; monitoring is not the defining capability. D incorrect Adware primarily displays unwanted advertisements, although some packages may also track activity.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 22 · Q00345
records.text: Q00345 Question 22 SEC05 SEC06 _______is a type of data link layer attack in TCP/IP protocol stack Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused. A ARP spoofing B DNS spoofing C SYNC-FLOOD attack D All except c ARP spoofing ARP spoofing targets the local mapping between IPv4 and link-layer MAC addresses, making A the data-link-oriented attack among these choices. DNS spoofing targets name resolution rather than local link associations, and SYN flooding abuses TCP handshake state. D incorrectly includes DNS spoofing in the data-link category. A correct ARP spoofing poisons the local IPv4-to-MAC mapping at the network/link addressing boundary. B incorrect DNS spoofing falsifies name-resolution data rather than manipulating the local data-link association. C incorrect The likely SYN-flood reference concerns TCP handshake state at transport scope, not link addressing. D incorrect This includes DNS spoofing, which is not a data-link mapping attack.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 23 · Q00346
records.text: Q00346 Question 23 SEC04 Which statement correctly distinguishes the host-program dependence of viruses and worms? Here 'host' means a carrier program or document, not a computer. Separate propagation, disguise and payload when classifying malicious software. A Worms requires a host to spread while viruses doesn't require B Worms requires a user action for replicate while viruses doesn't require C Virus requires a host to spread while Worms doesn't require D Worms spreading speed is slower than Virus Spreading speed Virus requires a host to spread while Worms doesn't require A virus replicates by attaching to a carrier program or document and spreading when that infected host executes. A worm replicates independently of such a carrier. This makes C the correct direction and makes A a reversal. B wrongly makes user action a defining requirement for worm replication while denying the virus's dependence on infected-host execution. D proposes a general speed ranking, which is not a defining consequence of either replication mechanism. A incorrect Incorrect: this reverses the definitions; viruses need carrier programs/documents and worms replicate independently. B incorrect Incorrect: independent worm replication does not require a user to launch each copy; virus propagation depends on infected-host execution. C correct Correct: viruses attach to carrier hosts, whereas worms replicate independently of such carriers. D incorrect Incorrect: propagation speed does not follow from the carrier-versus-independent distinction and cannot define the requested host dependence.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 24 · Q00358
records.text: Q00358 Question 24 SEC23 SEC-S03 Which general security-control category enforces allow/block rules for incoming and outgoing network traffic? Choose the functional security category rather than a general forwarding or relay role. Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Proxy B Firewall C Gateway D Router Firewall A firewall is the general control that enforces a network traffic policy, allowing or blocking traffic according to rules. A router's basic role is forwarding IP packets; a proxy relays application requests, and gateway is a broader connection or mediation term. These devices can include firewall capabilities, so their hardware or networking names alone do not make mutually exclusive implementations. The stem asks for the functional security category, which makes firewall the precise answer. A incorrect A proxy's general role is relaying application exchanges; it may also implement firewall policy but is not the general category requested. B correct Correct: firewall names the general traffic-policy enforcement control. C incorrect Gateway is a broad networking or mediation role and does not by itself specify security-rule enforcement. D incorrect A router forwards IP packets; filtering added to a router is a firewall function rather than an implication of routing alone.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 25 · Q00642
records.text: Q00642 Question 25 SEC23 Firewall in computer network is Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A physical boundary of network B an operating system of network C A system designed to prevent unauthorized access D A web browsing software A system designed to prevent unauthorized access A firewall enforces rules controlling network traffic to prevent unauthorized access. It may be software or a network device and therefore need not be a physical boundary. An operating system is not the name of this specific traffic-policy function, and a web browser requests or displays web content rather than serving as the general network-access enforcement control. C captures the firewall's security purpose, subject to the normal limits of configured rules and available inspection. A incorrect Incorrect: traffic-policy enforcement is a logical control and need not be a physical boundary. B incorrect Incorrect: firewall names the traffic-policy enforcement function, not an entire network operating system. C correct Correct: preventing unauthorized network access through traffic rules is the firewall purpose. D incorrect Incorrect: browsing web content is different from enforcing network traffic policy.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 26 · Q00914
records.text: Q00914 Question 26 SEC09 SEC01 Assume that we are able to specify that Mr. Getahun can view the database record, but cannot change the value of the record. Which security management technique was used in this scenario? Identify subject, object and permitted operation before comparing policy models. A Access Control B Availability C ¢. Non-repudiation D Integrity Access Control Permitting read while denying write is a subject/object/operation permission assignment, exactly the access-enforcement model (PDF p.11). Integrity is a protected goal, not the mechanism requested. A correct Access control authorizes particular operations on an object. See PDF p.3, PDF p.11. B incorrect Availability means timely usable service and access for authorized users (PDF page3), rather than selecting the allowed operation on a particular record. C incorrect Non-repudiation concerns proving an event or action so sender or receiver cannot deny it (PDF page4), rather than assigning read/write permissions. D incorrect Integrity is the desired protection against unauthorized changes, not the permission-setting mechanism. See PDF p.3, PDF p.11.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 27 · Q00920
records.text: Q00920 Question 27 SEC20 SEC18 Which statement is NOT true about digital signatures? Separate a digest, shared-secret authentication and publicly verifiable signing. A A digital signature is not, by itself, a confidentiality-encryption mechanism B The sender signs a message or its encoded digest using its private signing key C The sender generates a digital signature using its public verification key D Digital signature provides authentication services The sender generates a digital signature using its public verification key A digital signature is generated with the signer's private signing key and checked with the corresponding public verification key. Signing may operate on a message or an encoded digest, depending on the algorithm. It is not generically private-key encryption, and it does not by itself hide the message. Under an authentic key binding and secure private-key custody, verification supports origin authentication and integrity. The public verification key cannot generate the signer's signature, making C false. A incorrect True: a signature supports origin and integrity checks without itself concealing the content. B incorrect True: signature generation uses the private signing key on the message or its encoded digest. C correct Correct selection: the public verification key verifies signatures; it does not generate them. D incorrect True: signature verification supports origin authentication under the stated key-binding assumptions.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 28 · Q00923
records.text: Q00923 Question 28 SEC29 Which one of the following party performs the technical evaluation work, using the evidence supplied by the developers, and additional testing of the product, to confirm that it satisfies the functional and assurance requirements specified in the security target? Distinguish requirements, technical evaluation, evidence and certification decisions. A Evaluator B Certifier C Sponsor D Developer Evaluator SEC29 assigns technical examination of developer evidence, testing and vulnerability analysis against Security Target claims to evaluators. The certification body oversees/reviews evaluation and issues the certification decision; sponsors commission the work and developers supply the product/evidence. A therefore names the party performing the actual technical evaluation rather than those adjacent roles. A correct Evaluators review developer evidence and perform tests/analysis against the stated functional and assurance claims. B incorrect The certifier oversees/reviews evaluation and issues the certification decision rather than being the named technical evaluator. C incorrect The sponsor commissions the work; that role does not itself perform the technical evaluation. D incorrect The developer supplies the product and supporting evidence for independent examination.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 29 · Q00941
records.text: Q00941 Question 29 SEC05 SEC03 SEC06 Compare two incidents at Registrar X. In incident I, Negesa composes a fresh request and presents it as coming from Dereje. In incident II, Negesa retransmits, without changing it, a valid request that Dereje genuinely sent earlier. Which statement correctly distinguishes the observed attack mechanisms? Compare the claimed origin, message freshness and whether an existing message was changed. A I makes the registrar unavailable, whereas II leaves the service available. B I alters the content of Dereje's existing request, whereas II leaves that request unchanged. C I creates a fresh message under Dereje's identity, whereas II repeats Dereje's authentic old message. D I repeats an authentic old message, whereas II creates a fresh message under a false identity. I creates a fresh message under Dereje's identity, whereas II repeats Dereje's authentic old message. Incident I introduces a newly composed message under another person's identity, which is masquerade. Incident II reuses a valid old message, which is replay. The relevant distinction is false origin for a fresh message versus reuse of an authentic earlier one. Neither incident describes service denial, and I does not modify an existing request. D reverses the two histories. Replay can also support impersonation in a larger attack, so this comparison classifies the specific observed mechanisms. A incorrect Neither history includes service exhaustion or interruption; service availability does not distinguish these incidents. B incorrect I creates a new request rather than altering an existing one; message modification is a different mechanism. C correct I's fresh false-origin request demonstrates masquerade, while II's unchanged reuse of an authentic earlier request demonstrates replay. D incorrect This reverses the observed histories: II reuses the old request, while I creates the fresh false-origin request.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 30 · Q00963
records.text: Q00963 Question 30 SEC23 SEC24 SEC22 Which general security-control category enforces allow/block rules on incoming and outgoing network traffic? Choose the general enforcement category rather than a relay, tunnel or observing role. Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Intrusion detection system (IDS) B Proxy server C Virtual Private Network (VPN) D Firewall Firewall A firewall is the general traffic-policy enforcement category that permits or blocks traffic under rules. An IDS observes and alerts, whereas a proxy relays application requests and may additionally implement policy. A VPN establishes a logical private connection whose security depends on its tunnel; that does not itself define allow/block filtering. Because implementations can combine these functions, the revised stem asks for the general enforcement category rather than treating all device types as mutually exclusive. A incorrect Incorrect: an IDS observes and alerts; the requested role enforces traffic permission decisions. B incorrect Incorrect: proxy names an application-relay role, even when a particular proxy also implements firewall policy. C incorrect Incorrect: a VPN provides a logical private connection; that role alone does not specify allow/block traffic enforcement. D correct Correct: firewall names the general traffic-policy enforcement category.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 31 · Q00972
records.text: Q00972 Question 31 SEC33 Which one of the following is WRONGLY stated about an importance of security policy? Distinguish organizational rules, operational steps and recovery goals. A To help minimize risk. B To ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data. C . To coordinate and enforce a security program across an organization. D To use the system in a passive way To use the system in a passive way A security policy regulates resource protection (PDF p.3); assurance reduces risk and preserves protection goals (p.2). Merely using a system passively neither establishes protection rules nor coordinates enforcement. A incorrect Minimizing risk is consistent with regulating protection. See PDF p.2, PDF p.3. B incorrect Protecting CIA is consistent with security and assurance goals. See PDF p.2, PDF p.3. C incorrect Coordinating and enforcing organizational protection is consistent with a common rule set. See PDF p.2, PDF p.3. D correct Passive system use is not a security-policy purpose derived from the definition. See PDF p.2, PDF p.3.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 32 · Q00975
records.text: Q00975 Question 32 SEC01 Which one of the following computer security goal prevents the disclosure of sensitive information to unauthorized users or systems on computer networks? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Confidentiality B Integrity C Cyberspace D Availability Confidentiality The stem restates prevention of unauthorized disclosure, the confidentiality definition on PDF p.3. It asks about secrecy rather than correctness or access timing. A correct Confidentiality is explicitly prevention of unauthorized disclosure. See PDF p.3. B incorrect Integrity prevents unauthorized writing/modification. See PDF p.3. C incorrect Cyberspace is not one of the module’s CIA goals. See PDF p.3. D incorrect Availability assures usable access for authorized users. See PDF p.3.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 33 · Q01175
records.text: Q01175 Question 33 SEC02 SEC09 SEC12 SEC07 Which of the following primarily provides detective evidence that can reveal an attack, rather than preventing access or disclosure? Distinguish weaknesses, potential harmful events, actual attempts and the effect of a control. A Access Control B Encryption C Audit log D Password authentication Audit log An audit log records events that can reveal suspicious activity during review or analysis and can support accountability. Its primary role in this comparison is detective evidence. Access control restricts permitted actions, password authentication checks an identity claim, and encryption limits disclosure to unauthorized readers. These are principally preventive roles in the question's comparison. A log does not automatically block an attack, and its usefulness depends on reliable recording, protection and analysis. A incorrect Access control primarily prevents actions that exceed a subject's permissions. B incorrect Encryption primarily prevents unauthorized disclosure rather than revealing attack activity through event records. C correct Correct: an audit log provides event evidence that can reveal attacks and support accountability. D incorrect Password authentication primarily checks identity before access; it is not the offered detective event record.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 34 · Q01189
records.text: Q01189 Question 34 SEC12 The process of recovering the original message without the detailed knowledge of the secret information is called: Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Decryption B Decipher C Cryptanalysis D A and B Cryptanalysis PDF p.6 distinguishes decryption (recovering plaintext) from cryptanalysis (breaking ciphertext without the key). The explicit absence of secret knowledge selects cryptanalysis. A incorrect Decryption is ordinary plaintext recovery and omits the without-key distinction. See PDF p.6. B incorrect Decipher is the same ordinary recovery operation. See PDF p.6. C correct Cryptanalysis explicitly concerns breaking ciphertext without knowing the key. See PDF p.6. D incorrect Combining two ordinary recovery synonyms does not supply the required without-key meaning. See PDF p.6.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 35 · Q01203
records.text: Q01203 Question 35 SEC03 SEC27 Which of the following statements is true about crackers? Classify the action actually described and distinguish observation, alteration, disruption and identity claims. A They attempt to break the system without permissions B They are legally employed to break into the system C They reveal the information after breaking into the system D All They attempt to break the system without permissions Cracking is malicious hacking; intrusion is unauthorized access (PDF p.5). By contrast authorized simulated attacks are penetration testing (p.10). A matches unauthorized breaking, and neither legal employment nor later disclosure defines a cracker. A correct Attempted unauthorized system breaking matches malicious intrusion. See PDF p.5, PDF p.10. B incorrect Legally authorized testing belongs to penetration testing, not the definition of cracking. See PDF p.5, PDF p.10. C incorrect Revealing information afterward is not a necessary defining property of malicious intrusion. See PDF p.5, PDF p.10. D incorrect B and C are not defining truths, so All cannot hold. See PDF p.5, PDF p.10.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 36 · Q01207
records.text: Q01207 Question 36 SEC23 Which basic firewall category makes stateless decisions from packet-header fields such as protocol and port numbers, without tracking connection state or terminating an application exchange? Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Packet Filtering B Proxy Service C Stateful Inspection D Threat-Focused NGFW Packet Filtering Stateless packet filtering matches packet headers such as addresses, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection adds connection context, while an application proxy terminates and relays application exchanges. Next-generation products can also filter ports, but that capability alone does not make them the basic stateless header-only category requested. The additional constraints distinguish the model rather than incorrectly claiming port filtering is exclusive to one product type. A correct This is the stateless header-matching category. B incorrect A proxy terminates and relays application exchanges. C incorrect Stateful inspection tracks connection context, which the stem excludes. D incorrect A next-generation firewall is not the basic header-only stateless category requested.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 37 · Q01213
records.text: Q01213 Question 37 SEC13 What will be the encrypted message if the message "ATTACK" is encrypted by Caesar's cipher with key = 25? Separate symbol replacement from position changes and apply the alphabet and modular direction. A ZSSZBJ B ZGGZXP C ZTTZAK D BGGBDL ZSSZBJ Using the additive shift on Z26 (PDF p.6), take A=0 and encryption C=(P+25) mod 26. ATTACK gives (0,19,19,0,2,10) -> (25,18,18,25,1,9) -> ZSSZBJ. This is a one-position backward shift because 25=-1 mod 26. A correct ZSSZBJ agrees at all six positions. See PDF p.6. B incorrect ZGGZXP has correct initial A->Z but T->G instead of S. See PDF p.6. C incorrect ZTTZAK leaves T unchanged and maps C incorrectly. See PDF p.6. D incorrect BGGBDL begins A->B, a forward-one shift rather than +25. See PDF p.6.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 38 · Q01247
records.text: Q01247 Question 38 SEC13 SEC16 All are properties of a substitution cipher except: Separate symbol replacement from position changes and apply the alphabet and modular direction. A The identity of the letters is changed in the encryption process. B The position of the letters is changed in the encryption process. C Uses the same key for the encryption and decryption process. D It has a secure key distribution problem. The position of the letters is changed in the encryption process. Substitution replaces symbol identities; transposition changes positions (PDF p.6). Classical encryption is shared-key with a key-distribution problem (p.7), so position change is the exception in the standard pure-substitution model. A incorrect Changing letter identity is the defining substitution action. See PDF p.6, PDF p.7. B correct Changing letter positions defines transposition, not pure substitution. See PDF p.6, PDF p.7. C incorrect The module classifies classical encryption as shared-key encryption/decryption. See PDF p.6, PDF p.7. D incorrect The module explains the need to distribute the shared secret securely. See PDF p.6, PDF p.7.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 39 · Q01282
records.text: Q01282 Question 39 SEC15 SEC14 SEC16 SEC18 Which statement is true? Assume a correctly used one-time pad and repeated-key Vigenère; compare the general cryptographic methods rather than one specially chosen implementation. Check the precise ordering or key-use assumptions rather than relying on a cipher's name. A A correctly used one-time pad provides perfect secrecy, unlike repeated-key Vigenère B Symmetric key cryptography has a slow encryption process than asymmetric key encryption technique C Hill cipher remains secure even with enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks D All of the above A correctly used one-time pad provides perfect secrecy, unlike repeated-key Vigenère A one-time pad has perfect secrecy only under its strict randomness, secrecy, length and nonreuse conditions; repeated-key Vigenère leaks periodic structure. Symmetric encryption supplies efficient bulk protection, while public-key mechanisms commonly handle keys in hybrid designs, so B reverses the general efficiency account. Hill is linear: enough independent known blocks allow recovery of its key matrix, contradicting C. Because B and C are false, the all-of-the-above selection is false and A is correct. A correct Correct: the stated pad conditions provide perfect secrecy; repeated-key Vigenère has periodic structure. B incorrect Incorrect: symmetric encryption is the efficient bulk-data component; the proposed general slowdown reverses that role in hybrid protection. C incorrect Incorrect: Hill's linear rule permits recovery of K = C P^-1 mod 26 from sufficient independent known blocks. D incorrect Incorrect: B and C are false, so not all statements hold.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 40 · Q01509
records.text: Q01509 Question 40 SEC09 SEC32 An access control mechanism which works by comparing security labels with security clearances Identify subject, object and permitted operation before comparing policy models. A Mandatory Access Control B Attribute Based Access Control C Discretionary Access Control D Role Based Access Control Mandatory Access Control Security labels and clearances identify the mandatory policy mechanism in SEC09, elaborated for multilevel databases in SEC32. Owners cannot override that centrally enforced label policy. RBAC assigns role permissions and DAC allows owner grants; generic ABAC can evaluate attributes, but the specified clearance/classification mechanism is the named mandatory control model. A correct Mandatory control compares classifications/clearances under a policy ordinary owners cannot override. B incorrect ABAC evaluates general attributes; the named security-label/clearance mechanism specifically identifies mandatory control. C incorrect DAC allows owners to grant permissions rather than enforcing nonoverridable classification labels. D incorrect RBAC bases permissions on roles and user-role assignments rather than security-label clearance comparisons.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 41 · Q01510
records.text: Q01510 Question 41 SEC05 SEC06 An attack in which the DNS queries are wrongly resolved in order to redirect the users to a malicious website. Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused. A DNS Flooding attack B NXDomain attack C SNMP Reflection attack D DNS Hijacking attack DNS hijacking/spoofed resolution Wrong name-to-address answers redirecting users match falsified DNS resolution, described as spoofing/cache poisoning in SEC05 and called hijacking in D. DNS and NXDOMAIN floods instead stress query capacity; they need not provide a malicious replacement destination. No SNMP reflection mechanism is described by the stem. A incorrect DNS flooding exhausts query-processing capacity rather than specifically supplying false destination records. B incorrect NXDOMAIN attacks generate nonexistent-name queries to stress resolvers, not the false successful answers described. C incorrect The stem describes DNS answer manipulation, not reflected traffic using a different management protocol. D correct Hijacking DNS resolution redirects a name to an attacker-controlled destination through false resolution data.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 42 · Q01511
records.text: Q01511 Question 42 SEC26 SEC-S01 The term injection attack refers to a wide variety of program flaws related to invalid handling of input data. Which one of the following is not a type of injection attack? Locate where untrusted data can become instructions and where they execute. A Cross site scripting B Input fuzzing C SQL injection D Command injection Input fuzzing is testing, not an injection-attack category SEC26 directly distinguishes fuzzing from injection: fuzzing varies unexpected inputs to discover defects. SQL injection changes SQL syntax and XSS introduces attacker-controlled script into a browser context. Command injection likewise names unsafe interpretation of input as commands. Fuzzing may discover those defects but does not itself identify that attack mechanism. A incorrect XSS injects attacker-controlled script/content into a browser execution context, so it is an injection-type attack. B correct Input fuzzing is a technique for finding faults with varied unexpected inputs, not an injection category. C incorrect SQL injection explicitly alters query syntax through unsafe handling of untrusted values. D incorrect Command injection names untrusted input interpreted as executable commands rather than merely a testing technique.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 43 · Q01590
records.text: Q01590 Question 43 SEC07 Using the convention prover-to-verifier, which statement correctly describes the direction of an authentication setting? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Host-to-host authentication allows the host to prove the identity of a user B User-to-user authentication allows the user to prove the identity of a machine C User-to-host authentication allows the user to prove the identity of a machine D Host-to-user authentication lets the host prove its identity to the user Host-to-user authentication lets the host prove its identity to the user The arrow convention identifies the entity supplying identity proof first and the verifier second. A user-to-host exchange therefore proves the user’s identity to the host, while host-to-user proves the host’s identity to the user. The corrected final option follows that rule. The other options describe proving a different entity’s identity from the one indicated as prover, so they do not match their stated authentication setting. A incorrect Host-to-host concerns a host proving identity to another host, not proving a user identity. B incorrect User-to-user concerns a user proving identity to another user, not a machine. C incorrect User-to-host proves the user’s identity, not the machine’s. D correct The host is the prover and the user is the verifier, as the convention requires.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 44 · Q01591
records.text: Q01591 Question 44 SEC10 SEC32 Which one of the following is not a correct match? Apply the named model's read and write restrictions separately. A Biba Model - Integrity B Bell-LaPadula Model - Confidentiality C Clark-Wilson Model - Confidentiality D Multiple Levels of Security (MLS) Model - Confidentiality Clark–Wilson protects integrity, not confidentiality SEC10 directly gives Biba and Clark–Wilson integrity goals, and Bell–LaPadula confidentiality. SEC32 describes multilevel label enforcement for confidentiality. C therefore mismatches the model and goal; the others are compatible with the note’s defined model purposes. A incorrect Biba is an integrity model, so this pairing is correct rather than the requested mismatch. B incorrect Bell–LaPadula protects confidentiality, making this pairing correct. C correct Clark–Wilson enforces integrity through well-formed transformations and separation of duties, not confidentiality. D incorrect Multilevel label restrictions can protect confidentiality, as SEC32 explains.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 45 · Q01634
records.text: Q01634 Question 45 SEC07 What is the first step of access control? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Subject identification B ACL verification C Subject authorization D Accountability logging Subject identification PDF p.4 says users must be identified and authenticated for access; p.11 then describes authorization of operations. Identification supplies the claimed subject before checking identity and permissions. A correct Subject identification supplies the identity on which subsequent checks operate. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. B incorrect ACL checking requires knowing the subject and request first. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. C incorrect Authorization decides permitted operations after the identity is established. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. D incorrect Accountability records actions and does not establish the initial identity. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 46 · Q01635
records.text: Q01635 Question 46 SEC08 SEC05 Which of the following is not a reason why using passwords alone is a poor security mechanism? Consider what the attacker can guess or steal, or which component validates a claim. A Short passwords can be discovered quickly in brute force attacks only when used against a stolen password database file. B When possible, users choose easy-to-remember passwords, which are therefore easy to guess or crack. C Passwords can be stolen through many means, including observation, recording and playback, and security database theft. D Randomly generated passwords are hard to remember, thus many users write them down. The “only” restriction to stolen-database brute force is false The negative stem asks which offered reason is not valid. A incorrectly restricts brute-force exposure of short passwords to stolen database files. SEC08 explicitly permits failure in online as well as offline settings, subject to rate limits. Guessable choices, theft and insecure recording are legitimate password-only weaknesses rather than exclusive claims. A correct Short passwords can be attacked online too; only against a stolen database is an unjustified restriction. B incorrect Predictable memorable choices enable likely-word guessing, a real weakness of password-only security. C incorrect Observed entry and stolen verifiers are real exposure paths, consistent with the note’s password and monitoring threats. D incorrect Difficulty remembering random secrets can encourage unsafe recording; password managers address that operational weakness.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 47 · SM0040
records.text: SM0040 Question 47 SEC01 SEC03 Which one of the following is a measure taken to ensure information and information systems' availability, integrity, authentication and confidentiality? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Wiretapping B Information security C Information assurance D Interception Information assurance PDF p.2 explicitly defines IA as measures protecting information and systems by ensuring availability, integrity, authentication, confidentiality and non-repudiation. This matches the stem’s list most closely. A incorrect Wiretapping is an interception behavior, not an assurance measure. See PDF p.2. B incorrect InfoSec is related but the exact enumerated measures definition is assigned to IA. See PDF p.2. C correct Information assurance matches the module’s definition almost verbatim. See PDF p.2. D incorrect Interception compromises confidentiality rather than ensuring these properties. See PDF p.2.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 48 · SM0044
records.text: SM0044 Question 48 SEC01 Which one of the following is a security service enforced to protect disclosure of information (stored in file or in transmission) from unauthorized entities? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Authentication B Integrity C Availability D Confidentiality Confidentiality Unauthorized disclosure of stored or transmitted information is precisely the confidentiality concern (PDF p.3), independent of storage location. A incorrect Authentication proves identity, not disclosure restrictions. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. B incorrect Integrity protects against unauthorized changes. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. C incorrect Availability protects timely access. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4. D correct Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure. See PDF p.3, PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 49 · SM0054
records.text: SM0054 Question 49 SEC23 SEC-S03 Which general security-control category creates a protected network boundary by enforcing allow/block traffic rules for a group of machines? Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Network operating system B Firewall C Router used only for forwarding, without security filtering D Switch used only for forwarding, without security filtering Firewall A network firewall protects a group of machines by enforcing traffic policy at a boundary. The decisive function is allowing or blocking traffic under security rules. A network operating system is not the name of that specific policy-enforcement role. The other two alternatives are explicitly limited to forwarding without security filtering, so their connectivity functions do not meet the requirement. Actual routers, switches or proxies can include firewall capabilities; the stated scope prevents that implementation overlap from making the choices ambiguous. A incorrect Incorrect: a network operating system does not name the specific boundary traffic-policy function requested. B correct Correct: a firewall enforces the allow/block rules protecting the group. C incorrect Incorrect: the explicitly forwarding-only router does not perform the required security filtering. D incorrect Incorrect: the explicitly forwarding-only switch does not perform the required security filtering.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 50 · SM0058
records.text: SM0058 Question 50 SEC03 Which one of the following best explains attackers who are motivated by financial gain and perform sabotage, IP theft and steal secrets of a rival company? Classify the action actually described and distinguish observation, alteration, disruption and identity claims. A Stealer B Competitor C Hacktivist D Activist Competitor The rival-company context and commercial-secret theft identify a competitor’s motive, as SEC03 states. Financial gain alone could describe many attackers, but the specific rival-company relationship distinguishes B. Hacktivists/activists pursue a cause, while stealer is a generic activity label rather than the specified commercial relationship. A incorrect Stealer describes taking information but does not identify the rival-company commercial motive. B correct A competitor can seek commercial secrets and advantage over a rival company. C incorrect Hacktivist motivation is a cause rather than the specified commercial competition. D incorrect An activist pursues a cause; the scenario instead identifies a financially motivated rival-company interest.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 51 · SM0060
records.text: SM0060 Question 51 SEC11 SEC23 SEC24 SEC04 Against an attacker whose only access is direct communication over the public Internet, which computer removes that attack path? Assume the disconnected computer has no Internet-reachable intermediary or other network route to the attacker. Start with the stated attacker path or physical hazard and the limits of each control. A A computer connected to the Internet with the latest firewall system B A computer connected to the Internet having strong intrusion detection C A computer that is not connected to the Internet D A computer connected to the Internet and the latest anti-virus installed on it A computer that is not connected to the Internet Disconnecting removes the Internet communication path available to the specified attacker. Firewalls, intrusion detection and antivirus can reduce particular risks, but they do not remove the fact that the other choices remain connected. The conclusion is deliberately limited to that attack path: the disconnected system can still face insiders, removable media or physical threats. Those are excluded from this scenario rather than silently treated as impossible. A incorrect A firewall-equipped Internet connection still exposes an Internet communication path. B incorrect Intrusion detection observes activity but does not remove connectivity. C correct The stated disconnected system has no path available to this attacker. D incorrect Antivirus does not remove the Internet communication path.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 52 · SM0072
records.text: SM0072 Question 52 SEC12 Suppose you have received a message from your friend but the message is scrambled for security. Your friend used a program to encode messages into scrambled text. In order to read the message, which program would you use? Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Encryption program B Ciphertext C Secret key D Decryption program Decryption program The received message is ciphertext; recovering its readable plaintext is deciphering/decryption on PDF p.6. The question asks for the program carrying out that inverse operation. A incorrect Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext, the opposite direction. See PDF p.6. B incorrect Ciphertext is data, not the recovery program. See PDF p.6. C incorrect A secret key may be an input but is not a program. See PDF p.6. D correct A decryption program performs plaintext recovery. See PDF p.6.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 53 · SM0081
records.text: SM0081 Question 53 SEC02 Which network security issue shows the level of weakness in networks and devices? Distinguish weaknesses, potential harmful events, actual attempts and the effect of a control. A Attack B Availability C Vulnerability D Treat Vulnerability A vulnerability is an exploitable weakness or fault in an information system or component (PDF p.3). The question asks about weakness, not the attack event or service goal. A incorrect Attack is an actual security violation. See PDF p.3. B incorrect Availability is a goal of usable access. See PDF p.3. C correct Vulnerability is the defined weakness. See PDF p.3. D incorrect Treat appears to mean threat, a potential harmful circumstance rather than the weakness. See PDF p.3.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 54 · SM0096
records.text: SM0096 Question 54 SEC12 Which one is a method used to obtain the meaning of encrypted information without access to the secret key? Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Cryptography B Crypto-analysis C Decryption D Encryption Crypto-analysis Obtaining meaning without the secret key matches cryptanalysis, which the module explicitly contrasts with ordinary decryption (PDF p.6). A incorrect Cryptography studies encryption methods rather than without-key breaking. See PDF p.6. B correct Crypto-analysis matches breaking ciphertext without knowing the key. See PDF p.6. C incorrect Decryption describes plaintext recovery but lacks the no-key distinction. See PDF p.6. D incorrect Encryption produces ciphertext rather than recovering meaning. See PDF p.6.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 55 · SM0221
records.text: SM0221 Question 55 SEC01 Which one of the following IS NOT a concern of availability? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Fault Tolerance B Alteration of resources C Usefulness of resources D Fair allocation of resources Alteration of resources Availability means timely, reliable, usable access for authorized users (PDF p.3). Altering resources is instead the integrity issue; fault tolerance, usability and fair allocation can support continued access. A incorrect Fault tolerance supports reliable service, consistent with availability. See PDF p.3. B correct Unauthorized alteration belongs to integrity rather than the access/continuity goal. See PDF p.3. C incorrect Useful/usable resources are expressly part of availability. See PDF p.3. D incorrect Fair allocation supports access for authorized users rather than denying service. See PDF p.3.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 56 · SM0223
records.text: SM0223 Question 56 SEC03 Person A sends a message to person B. While the message is transmitted, person C gains access to the message. Which category of attack is performed by person C? Classify the action actually described and distinguish observation, alteration, disruption and identity claims. A Modification B Interception C Interruption D Fabrication Interception C gains unauthorized access to the message in transit without any stated alteration, destruction or insertion. PDF p.4 calls this disclosure/interception. A incorrect No message change is specified. See PDF p.4. B correct Unauthorized message access matches interception. See PDF p.4. C incorrect No loss of service is specified. See PDF p.4. D incorrect No fake message is inserted. See PDF p.4.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 57 · SM0227
records.text: SM0227 Question 57 SEC12 Which one of the following terms refers to the techniques used for deciphering ciphertext without any knowledge of the enciphering mechanism? Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Cryptography B Cryptology C Cryptoanalysis D Decryption Cryptoanalysis The qualifier without knowledge distinguishes cryptanalysis from ordinary deciphering in PDF p.6. Cryptology includes both protective methods and codebreaking, but is not the specific technique requested. A incorrect Cryptography studies encryption principles. See PDF p.6. B incorrect Cryptology is the umbrella field including cryptography and cryptanalysis. See PDF p.6. C correct Cryptoanalysis is the offered spelling of the without-key codebreaking concept. See PDF p.6. D incorrect Decryption is ordinary plaintext recovery, not specifically without secret knowledge. See PDF p.6.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 58 · SM0258
records.text: SM0258 Question 58 SEC18 In asymmetric cryptography, the message is decrypted using ______. Identify the intended recipient or signer and separate confidentiality from verification. A Receiver's public key B Receiver's private key C Sender's private key D Sender's public key Receiver's private key For confidential public-key transmission, encryption uses the receiver’s public key and decryption the receiver’s private key (PDF p.8). The answer follows that communication model. A incorrect Receiver’s public key performs encryption in this model. See PDF p.8. B correct Receiver’s private key performs decryption. See PDF p.8. C incorrect Sender’s private key is not the recipient decryption key. See PDF p.8. D incorrect Sender’s public key belongs to signature verification, not confidential recipient decryption. See PDF p.8.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 59 · SM0272
records.text: SM0272 Question 59 SEC16 SEC18 Which one of the following cryptography systems uses the same key for encryption and decryption? Distinguish shared-key architecture, key distribution and bulk-data use. A Public key cryptography B Parallel cryptography C Asymmetric cryptography D Symmetric cryptography Symmetric cryptography PDF p.7 defines symmetric encryption as use of the same shared key for both directions; p.8 contrasts the public/private pair. A incorrect Public-key cryptography uses a key pair. See PDF p.7, PDF p.8. B incorrect Parallel cryptography is not a same-key class in the module. See PDF p.7, PDF p.8. C incorrect Asymmetric cryptography uses different paired keys. See PDF p.7, PDF p.8. D correct Symmetric cryptography explicitly uses the same shared key. See PDF p.7, PDF p.8.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 60 · SM0301
records.text: SM0301 Question 60 SEC07 SEC01 The first step in access control is ________. Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Audit B Authorization C Accreditation D Authentication Authentication The module requires identification and authentication before access and says NAC authenticates users then determines access/actions (PDF pp.4,11). Among these options authentication is the prerequisite, though identification would precede it if offered. A incorrect Audit records events rather than first proving identity. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. B incorrect Authorization determines allowed operations for an established identity. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. C incorrect Accreditation is not the identity-checking step defined in the module. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. D correct Authentication is the earliest listed access-control step. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 61 · SS110
records.text: SS110 Question 61 SEC23 SEC04 SEC11 A firewall is used in a system connected to a wide area network to Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A Stop unauthorized access by hackers B Scanning for viruses in various files C Avoid spreading of fire in the network D Fire spreading via network through cables Stop unauthorized access by hackers A firewall filters protected-network access to keep intruders out (PDF p.11). This is a logical security boundary, not a fire-suppression device. A correct Stopping unauthorized network access is an explicit objective. B incorrect File virus scanning is not the general firewall function. C incorrect Physical fire spread is unrelated to packet filtering. D incorrect Fire through cables is unrelated to the stated network security role.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 62 · SS112
records.text: SS112 Question 62 SEC08 Within OAuth, what component validates the user's identity? Consider what the attacker can guess or steal, or which component validates a claim. A "Gre. Authorization Server B Resource Server C d Oc. Client D Browser Authorization server SEC08 assigns resource-owner authentication/approval to the authorization server, which may delegate identity checks. The resource server checks access tokens for protected resources; the client seeks limited access and the browser is a user agent. OAuth is authorization rather than a complete login identity protocol, but A is the matching component role under the described flow. A correct The authorization server authenticates the resource owner or delegates that check and obtains approval. B incorrect The resource server validates access tokens for protected data rather than being the owner-authentication component. C incorrect The client requests limited access; it is not the trusted identity-validation role defined here. D incorrect The browser carries user interaction and redirects but is not the authorization server’s authentication authority.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 63 · SS136
records.text: SS136 Question 63 SEC22 SEC21 SEC-S03 Which protocol is specifically designed for secure remote login and remote command execution between a local client and a remote computer over an untrusted network? Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing. A Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) B Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) C Secure Shell (SSH) D Secure socket layer (SSL) Secure Shell (SSH) SSH provides secure remote login, command execution and related services over an untrusted network. SSL and its successor TLS provide protected channels but do not by themselves define the remote-login and command-execution service requested here. AAA names authentication, authorization and accounting functions rather than a remote-shell protocol. SNMP supplies network-management functions. Specifying the service, rather than merely a secure local-to-remote channel, makes SSH the unique answer among these choices. A incorrect AAA describes authentication, authorization and accounting functions, not a remote-login protocol. B incorrect SNMP provides device-management functions rather than the requested remote-login and command-execution service. C correct Correct: SSH directly provides secure remote login and remote command execution. D incorrect SSL/TLS protects communication channels but does not itself specify the requested remote-shell service.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 64 · SS150
records.text: SS150 Question 64 SEC01 Which of the following refers to unauthorized disclosure of information? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Integrity B Authorization C Confidentiality D Authentication Confidentiality is the property violated by unauthorized disclosure SEC01 defines confidentiality as restricting disclosure, so unauthorized disclosure is a breach of that property. Integrity concerns improper changes, authorization determines permitted operations and authentication establishes claims. The answer names the affected security goal rather than calling unauthorized disclosure itself a protective mechanism. A incorrect Integrity restricts improper changes, not disclosure of unchanged information. B incorrect Authorization decides which actions are permitted rather than naming the secrecy property harmed. C correct Confidentiality restricts disclosure and is directly violated when information is revealed without authorization. D incorrect Authentication establishes identity/claims rather than defining protection against disclosure.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 65 · SS152
records.text: SS152 Question 65 SEC09 SEC24 Which benefit follows directly from network ACL match-and-permit/deny rules, independently of optional traffic counters or malware-inspection features? Identify subject, object and permitted operation before comparing policy models. A Virus detection. B ACLs classify and organize network traffic. C ACLs provide high network availability. D ACLs monitor the number of bytes and packets. ACLs classify and organize network traffic. A network ACL matches traffic attributes such as addresses, protocols and ports and applies permission rules. Distinguishing the matching packet groups directly supports the offered classification and organization benefit. Malware inspection is a separate detection function, and a permission list does not guarantee high availability. An implementation may attach counters to rules, but those optional measurement features are outside the basic ACL permission function specified here. B is the direct consequence of that function. A incorrect Incorrect: matching permission rules is not malware-content detection. B correct Correct: matching packet conditions distinguishes traffic groups for permit/deny treatment. C incorrect Incorrect: a permission list does not by itself guarantee continued service availability. D incorrect Incorrect: byte/packet counters are optional measurement features, excluded from the basic permission-rule function asked about.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 66 · SS185
records.text: SS185 Question 66 SEC-S02 SEC24 SEC11 Which of the following is not an approach used by IT security specialists to enhance the security level of the network? Distinguish a malicious-software name from a defensive control's function. A Use of Intrusion detection system B Use of Intrusion prevention system C Use of Wana cry protocol D Use of physical security “Wana cry protocol” is not a defensive security approach IDS, IPS and physical controls are legitimate security approaches in SEC24 and SEC11. The option called “Wana cry protocol” supplies no defensive mechanism; treating a ransomware-like name as a security protocol is unsupported. SEC04 defines ransomware as denial/extortion, the opposite of a protective approach. Therefore C is the exception rather than a new protocol endorsed here. A incorrect An IDS observes and alerts on suspicious activity, a legitimate detective security approach. B incorrect An IPS can enforce blocking and is a legitimate preventive security approach. C correct The offered name establishes no security protocol or protective mechanism; ransomware is harmful rather than defensive. D incorrect Physical protection against unauthorized access and environmental hazards is an explicit security-control category.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 67 · AM0524
records.text: AM0524 Question 67 SEC01 What is the primary goal of computer security? Identify the property harmed: disclosure, improper change, unavailable service or lack of reliable attribution. A Confidentiality B Integrity C Availability D All of the above All of the above The module explicitly defines computer security around all three objectives confidentiality, integrity and availability (PDF p.2). Choosing only one omits other primary goals. A incorrect Confidentiality is included but incomplete alone. See PDF p.2. B incorrect Integrity is included but incomplete alone. See PDF p.2. C incorrect Availability is included but incomplete alone. See PDF p.2. D correct All three comprise the stated CIA objective set. See PDF p.2.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 68 · AM0525
records.text: AM0525 Question 68 SEC04 SEC23 SEC12 SEC22 What is the term used for a software program that attempts to gain unauthorized access to computer systems? Separate propagation, disguise and payload when classifying malicious software. A Firewall B Malware C Encryption D VPN Malware PDF p.5 calls software with malicious purpose malware and describes intrusion as attempted unauthorized access. A malicious program seeking unauthorized access therefore fits the broad malware class. A incorrect Firewall is a protective filtering mechanism, not the malicious program. See PDF p.5. B correct Malware is the umbrella for software with malicious purpose. See PDF p.5. C incorrect Encryption is a transformation for protected communication, not a malicious program class. See PDF p.5. D incorrect VPN is named as an application, not the malicious-software category. See PDF p.5.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 69 · AM0526
records.text: AM0526 Question 69 SEC12 SEC24 What is the practice of hiding confidential data within other data called? Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Encryption B Decryption C Steganography D Intrusion detection Steganography Hiding confidential data inside another data object aims to conceal the message’s existence. SEC12 calls that steganography and distinguishes it from encryption, which conceals meaning while leaving ciphertext observable. Decryption reverses encryption, and intrusion detection observes suspicious activity rather than embedding a hidden message. A incorrect Encryption conceals message meaning rather than specifically hiding its existence within another carrier. B incorrect Decryption recovers plaintext from ciphertext; it does not embed a hidden message. C correct Steganography conceals a message’s existence by hiding it within other data. D incorrect Intrusion detection observes and alerts about suspicious activity instead of hiding confidential content.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 70 · AM0527
records.text: AM0527 Question 70 SEC07 Which of the following authentication methods verifies a user's identity based on a unique physical characteristic? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Password authentication B Biometric authentication C Token authentication D Two-factor authentication Biometric authentication The module identifies face, retina, iris and fingerprint as biometrics (PDF p.11), and gives retina scanning as identity proof (p.4). A unique physical characteristic therefore selects biometrics. A incorrect Password authentication uses supplied secret knowledge, not a physical body trait. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. B correct Biometric authentication uses the listed bodily examples. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. C incorrect Physical tokens are cards, distinguished from biometrics. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. D incorrect Two-factor counts combined factors and does not name the body-trait method. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 71 · AM0528
records.text: AM0528 Question 71 SEC12 SEC20 SEC18 What is the process of converting plaintext into ciphertext called? Trace message transformations and separate data, keys, algorithms and codebreaking. A Encryption B Decryption C Hashing D Key exchange Encryption PDF p.6 directly defines encryption/enciphering as conversion of plaintext to ciphertext. Hashing instead produces a fixed-size digest (p.10). A correct Encryption exactly names the forward conversion. See PDF p.6, PDF p.10. B incorrect Decryption is the reverse conversion. See PDF p.6, PDF p.10. C incorrect Hashing produces a digest rather than the defined ciphertext representation. See PDF p.6, PDF p.10. D incorrect Key exchange distributes/agrees keys rather than converting this message. See PDF p.6, PDF p.10.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 72 · AM0529
records.text: AM0529 Question 72 SEC25 SEC05 SEC26 Which vulnerability writes beyond an allocated buffer and may thereby allow arbitrary code execution on the target system? Identify the unsafe operation or input boundary rather than only a possible consequence. A Phishing B Buffer overflow C SQL injection D Cross-site scripting Buffer overflow The decisive mechanism is an out-of-bounds write to a buffer. That is a buffer overflow, which can corrupt data or control information and may lead to code execution. Arbitrary code execution alone would not uniquely identify it. Phishing relies on deceptive interaction, SQL injection changes query syntax and XSS executes attacker script in a victim browser. The added memory-write condition distinguishes the mechanisms without claiming every overflow executes code. A incorrect Phishing deceives a user rather than defining an out-of-bounds memory write. B correct A buffer overflow is the specified write beyond allocated bounds. C incorrect SQL injection changes SQL syntax through unsafe input construction. D incorrect XSS concerns attacker script execution in a victim browser’s site context.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 73 · AM0530
records.text: AM0530 Question 73 SEC05 SEC06 SEC08 Which of the following is an example of a social engineering attack? Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused. A Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack B Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack C Phishing attack D Brute-force attack Phishing SEC05 defines phishing through deception: impersonating a trusted source to obtain secrets or prompt unsafe actions. That is social engineering. DoS/DDoS describe service disruption and brute force describes repeated credential guesses; neither requires the deceptive human interaction that distinguishes the requested example. A incorrect DoS exhausts or disables a service; that mechanism is not inherently social deception. B incorrect DDoS distributes service-disruption traffic and does not specifically describe manipulating a person. C correct Phishing deceives a user through trusted-source impersonation to induce disclosure or unsafe action. D incorrect Brute force enumerates credential guesses rather than persuading a person through impersonation.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 74 · AM0531
records.text: AM0531 Question 74 SEC23 SEC12 SEC04 SEC07 What is the purpose of a firewall in computer security? Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions. A To encrypt network traffic B To monitor and control network traffic C To detect and remove malware D To authenticate users To monitor and control network traffic PDF p.11 explicitly assigns monitoring and controlling incoming/outgoing traffic under security rules to firewalls. Encryption and identity proof are different operations. A incorrect Traffic encryption is not the firewall definition. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. B correct Monitoring and controlling traffic is the exact stated role. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. C incorrect Keeping malicious code out is an objective, not a general ability to detect and remove installed malware. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11. D incorrect User authentication is a separate identity-proof operation. See PDF p.4, PDF p.11.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 75 · AM0532
records.text: AM0532 Question 75 SEC07 A login already uses a password. Which listed input can add an independent possession factor when generated by a separate token controlled by the user? Separate identity claims from proof, and factor type from factor count. A Username B Password C Security question D One-time password (OTP) One-time password (OTP) A password supplies knowledge. A one-time password generated by a separate user-controlled token can supply possession, making the combination two-factor under the stated mechanism. Another password or secret security-question answer remains knowledge rather than adding an independent class. A username identifies the subject but is not proof. Specifying how the OTP is generated matters because an OTP’s factor class does not follow from the word one-time alone. A incorrect A username identifies the subject and is not possession proof. B incorrect Another password remains a knowledge factor. C incorrect A secret answer is another knowledge input, not an independent possession class. D correct A separately controlled token generating the OTP supplies possession under the assumption.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 76 · AM0533
records.text: AM0533 Question 76 SEC08 SEC06 SEC26 SEC05 What is the term for a malicious activity where an attacker tries all possible combinations of passwords to gain unauthorized access? Consider what the attacker can guess or steal, or which component validates a claim. A Brute-force attack B Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack C SQL injection D Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack Brute-force attack The module defines brute force as trying every possible key and separately names password guessing (PDF p.5). Applying that exhaustive-search method to all password combinations yields a brute-force password attack. A correct Exhaustive possible-combination testing is the brute-force method. See PDF p.5. B incorrect DoS blocks access rather than exhaustively guessing a secret. See PDF p.5. C incorrect SQL injection is not an exhaustive-password-search method in the module. See PDF p.5. D incorrect A man-in-the-middle is not the stated exhaustive-search process. See PDF p.5.

records.title: Computer Security — Question 77 · AM0534
records.text: AM0534 Question 77 SEC25 Which statement defines a buffer overflow by its underlying memory-write mechanism, rather than merely naming a possible consequence? Identify the unsafe operation or input boundary rather than only a possible consequence. A A vulnerability that allows unauthorized access to a system's memory B A vulnerability that allows attackers to intercept network traffic C A vulnerability in which a write exceeds an allocated buffer’s bounds D A vulnerability that allows unauthorized access to a system's files A vulnerability in which a write exceeds an allocated buffer’s bounds A buffer overflow is defined by writing beyond an allocated buffer’s bounds. That unsafe write can corrupt data or control information, and code execution is possible but not inevitable. Generic unauthorized memory or file access describes broader outcomes, while interception of network traffic describes a different kind of activity. The choice identifies the mechanism; the question asks for a definition rather than a consequence. A incorrect Generic unauthorized memory access is broader than the specific out-of-bounds write.
