records.text: Q00198 Question 10 AUT16 In a derivation graph whose root is S, whose vertices are sentential forms, and whose directed edges are single production applications, which property records the steps generating a terminal string? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Root of the graph B Degree of the vertex C Path of a vertex from the root D Parent vertex Path of a vertex from the root A derivation is a sequence of production applications beginning at S and ending at a terminal word. Under the specified graph model, each application is one directed edge, so the root-to-terminal-vertex path records the complete sequence. A root alone gives only the start; degree and an immediate parent give local information. This graph is not being treated as a parse tree. A incorrect The root identifies S but contains no sequence of applications. B incorrect Degree counts incident edges rather than their ordered traversal. C correct A root-to-vertex path lists the successive production applications. D incorrect A parent identifies one predecessor rather than the entire derivation.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 11 · Q00329
records.text: Q00329 Question 11 AUT18 A context free Grammar is called ambiguous if there exists a string that can have? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A only one parse tree B no parse tree C Partial parse tree D more than one parse tree more than one parse tree Ambiguity is witnessed by one terminal string having two distinct parse trees. It does not require every string to be ambiguous, and a string with no parse tree is simply not generated. A incorrect A unique tree is consistent with unambiguity. B incorrect No tree means failure to derive the string, not competing derivations. C incorrect A partial tree is unfinished and does not witness two full derivations. D correct Two or more full trees for the same string meet the definition.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 12 · Q00330
records.text: Q00330 Question 12 AUT13 A context free grammar with production rules: S->aS / ¢ is equivalent to the regular expression Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A a* B (atb)* C a(at+b)* D a+ a* The grammar is S→aS|ε. Applying the recursive rule n times followed by ε produces a^n for each n≥0, and no production creates any other terminal. This is exactly a*, including ε. Positive closure a+ omits ε. A correct Contains exactly all finite repetitions of a, including zero. B incorrect The expression (a+b)* also contains b. C incorrect The expression a(a+b)* contains ab and omits ε. D incorrect Requires at least one a, although S⇒ε is permitted.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 13 · Q00331
records.text: Q00331 Question 13 AUT21 AUT-S02 A push down automaton employs data structure. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Linked List B Stack C Hash Table D Queue Stack A PDA augments finite control with a stack. Push and pop operations supply its unbounded LIFO memory. A incorrect A linked list is an implementation possibility, not the abstract PDA storage discipline. B correct A PDA uses stack memory. C incorrect Hash lookup is not the PDA memory mechanism. D incorrect A queue is FIFO, unlike the required pushdown stack.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 14 · Q00332
records.text: Q00332 Question 14 AUT05 Which of the following Machine is Equivalent for Regular grammar? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Push down automata B Linear bounded automata C Finite state automata D Turing Machine Finite state automata Regular grammars generate exactly the regular languages, which finite-state automata recognize. The visual hierarchy pairs the innermost regular class with finite-state automata. More powerful models can accept those languages too but are not equivalent in class-wide expressive power. A incorrect PDA languages include nonregular CFLs, so the whole model is more powerful. B incorrect The diagram pairs LBAs with the larger context-sensitive class. C correct Matches exactly the class generated by regular grammars. D incorrect The outer Turing machine class is larger.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 15 · Q00333
records.text: Q00333 Question 15 AUT16 For a CFG G=(V,Σ,P,S), consider a production α→β. Treat a symbol also as its length-one string. Which statements hold? Select all that apply. Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A α∈(V∪Σ) B α∈V C α∈(V∪Σ)* D β∈(V∪Σ)* α∈(V∪Σ); α∈V; α∈(V∪Σ)*; β∈(V∪Σ)* A context-free production has exactly one variable on its left and a finite string of variables and terminals on its right. Therefore α∈V. Since V⊆V∪Σ, that same α belongs to the union and, as a one-symbol string, to its Kleene closure. The right-hand side β belongs to (V∪Σ)*, including the possibility of ε. All four memberships hold. A correct A variable is also an element of V∪Σ. B correct The left side of a CFG rule is one variable. C correct That variable is a length-one string in (V∪Σ)*. D correct The right side is a finite string over variables and terminals.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 16 · Q00334
records.text: Q00334 Question 16 AUT12 AUT13 AUT06 For the diagram, name the top-right state B and bottom state C. Use A as start and sole accepting state; transitions are A—a→B, A—b→C, B—a→C, B—b→A, C—b→B. Unshown transitions reject. Which regular expression denotes its language? Here + means union. Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A a*(a+b)ab(ab+bb+aa*(a+b)ab)* B ((a+bb)(ab)*b)* C (a+b)ab(ab+bb+aa*(a+b)ab)* D a*ab(ab+bb+aa*(a+b)ab)* ((a+bb)(ab)*b)* A return to A first reaches B either directly by a or via C by bb. While at B, the machine may make any number of ab detours through C. It returns to A by b. Thus one return has form (a+bb)(ab)*b, and any number of returns gives ((a+bb)(ab)*b)*. This also accepts ε and ab, as the accepting start and shortest return require. A incorrect Its mandatory prefix excludes ε, which must be accepted. B correct Its starred blocks describe exactly all excursions from A back to A. C incorrect Its mandatory prefix excludes the empty word. D incorrect Its mandatory ab suffix excludes ε.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 17 · Q00634
records.text: Q00634 Question 17 AUT12 Which one of the following regular expressions gives zero or one? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A r + =rr* B r* = r+ | ε C r? =r|ε D All The optional expression r? = r|ε. AUT12 defines r? as r|ε: one occurrence of a word matching r or no occurrence. Positive closure requires one or more occurrences; star permits arbitrarily many including zero. Their identities may be valid, but only the optional expression denotes the requested zero-or-one repetition count, so the aggregate is false. A incorrect Positive closure rr* requires at least one repetition and also allows more than one. B incorrect Star allows zero or arbitrarily many repetitions, not just zero or one. C correct The union with ε makes r optional: either one r match or none. D incorrect The positive and Kleene closures do not impose the zero-or-one bound.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 18 · Q00751
records.text: Q00751 Question 18 AUT18 If a grammar produces more than one leftmost derivation for a sentence, it is called as: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Ambiguous grammar B Perfect grammar C Associative grammar D Precedence Ambiguous grammar Each parse tree determines a unique leftmost sequence of expansions. Two distinct leftmost derivations of the same sentence therefore encode distinct parse trees and witness ambiguity under this definition. A correct Two leftmost derivations of one sentence witness two parse trees. B incorrect Perfect is not the relevant defined grammar property. C incorrect Associativity is an operator grouping convention, not this definition. D incorrect Precedence concerns ordering of operators; it does not name multiple leftmost derivations.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 19 · Q00752
records.text: Q00752 Question 19 AUT23 The intersection of a context-free language and a regular language is ________ Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A context-free B neither context-free nor regular. C regular but not context-free D both regular and context-free. Always context-free, but not necessarily regular. AUT23 constructs the intersection by combining PDA control with DFA control and retaining the original stack. It therefore guarantees a CFL. Regularity does not follow: intersecting {aⁿbⁿ} with a*b* gives the same nonregular CFL. Some individual intersections can be regular, but the question’s general result cannot assert that extra property. A correct Closure under intersection with a regular language guarantees that the result is context-free. B incorrect The stated closure theorem directly rules out a result outside the context-free family. C incorrect Every regular language is context-free, so regular but not context-free is impossible. D incorrect Some intersections are regular, but the counterexample in AUT23 shows regularity is not guaranteed.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 20 · Q00753
records.text: Q00753 Question 20 AUT27 Which one of the following is not part of Turing machine? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Finite control B Input C Tape D Head Input is data, not a separate hardware component. AUT27 lists finite control, a read/write head and an unbounded tape as the standard TM architecture. Input is initial tape content rather than a separate hardware organ. Thus input is the distinction requested by not part, under that structural reading; the other three options are actual machine components, not merely values processed by them. A incorrect Finite control is explicitly part of the standard machine’s architecture. B correct Input is initial tape content rather than a separate machine hardware component. C incorrect The unbounded tape is the standard TM’s storage component. D incorrect The read/write head is an explicit machine component used for tape access.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 21 · Q00891
records.text: Q00891 Question 21 AUT25 AUT24 Which automaton is powerful enough to recognize the language L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n > 1}, where n is an integer? Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A DFA B Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA) C NFA D Pushdown Automaton (PDA) Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA). The language contains equal numbers of a, b and c in that order. This family is context-sensitive but not context-free. Restricting n to integers greater than 1 does not remove the unbounded equal-count requirement. An LBA checks the order and repeatedly marks one a, one b and one c, using only the input-sized tape region. B therefore recognizes the stated language; DFA, NFA and single-stack PDA cannot. A incorrect A DFA recognizes regular languages; this three-equal-count language is not even context-free. B correct An LBA can mark matching a, b and c symbols while staying within space proportional to the input length. C incorrect An NFA recognizes exactly the regular languages, so nondeterminism does not give it the memory needed here. D incorrect A standard single-stack PDA recognizes context-free languages; the stated three-equal-count language is not context-free.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 22 · Q00917
records.text: Q00917 Question 22 AUT05 AUT29 AUT06 A recognizer reads input once from left to right and stores all its working memory in a fixed finite set of states. Which universal statement correctly explains why its language can also be described by a context-free grammar? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A Every regular language is context-free. B Every context-free language is regular. C Every context-sensitive language is regular. D Every recursively enumerable language is recursive Every regular language is context-free. A recognizer whose memory is a fixed finite state has regular-language power. Every regular language is context-free, so a context-free grammar can also describe its language. The reverse inclusion fails: equal-count matching such as {0^n1^n} is context-free but not regular. Context-sensitive languages need not be regular either. Finally, the halting language separates recognizable from decidable languages, so not every recursively enumerable language is recursive. A correct Every regular language has an equivalent context-free grammar. B incorrect {0^n1^n : n≥0} is context-free but not regular. C incorrect The context-sensitive family includes nonregular languages, including equal-count matching languages. D incorrect The halting language is recursively enumerable but undecidable, disproving this converse.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 23 · Q00934
records.text: Q00934 Question 23 AUT20 In the CNF-first route for converting a CFG into Greibach normal form, which initial normalization is performed before the later ordering, substitution and left-recursion work? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Convert the grammar into CNF B If any production rule in the grammar is not in GNF form, convert it. C . Convert the grammar into GNF D If the grammar exists left recursion, eliminate it. Convert the grammar into CNF The specified route begins by putting the grammar into Chomsky normal form. Later ordering and substitution arrange terminal-leading productions and eliminate left recursion as required for Greibach form. CNF is an intermediate normalization in this particular route, not a universal prerequisite for every GNF construction. The other conversion choices state the goal broadly rather than identify this route’s initial normalization. A correct CNF conversion is the initial normalization in the selected route. B incorrect Converting arbitrary offending rules does not identify the route’s initial normalization. C incorrect GNF conversion is the overall goal, not this preliminary operation. D incorrect Left recursion must be handled later in this chosen route.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 24 · Q00953
records.text: Q00953 Question 24 AUT05 Among the listed grammar families in the Chomsky hierarchy, which has the greatest expressive power? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Context-free B Context-sensitive C Unrestricted (Type 0) D Regular Unrestricted (Type 0) Unrestricted, Type 0 grammars generate the recursively enumerable languages, the family recognized by Turing machines. Context-sensitive, context-free and regular grammars generate successively smaller families. Asking for the most expressive listed family makes this an exact hierarchy comparison. It does not claim that every conceivable set of strings is recursively enumerable or that weaker grammars cannot generate complete languages of their own. A incorrect Context-free grammars generate a smaller family than RE. B incorrect Context-sensitive grammars generate a smaller family than RE. C correct Unrestricted grammars generate exactly RE. D incorrect Regular grammars generate the least expressive listed family.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 25 · Q00977
records.text: Q00977 Question 25 AUT04 ou have given that Grammar G1 —({S, A, B}, {a, b}, S, {S — AB, A— a, B—> b}). Which one is terminal symbol in the give? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A b B S C . S— AB,A—-a,B—b D S,A,B b The given terminal alphabet is {a,b}, so b is a terminal. S, A and B are variables, and the arrow expressions are productions. These categories match the four-component CFG definition. A correct b belongs to the given terminal alphabet. B incorrect S belongs to the variables and is the start symbol. C incorrect This is a set/list of productions, not one terminal symbol. D incorrect These are the variables, not the terminals.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 26 · Q00981
records.text: Q00981 Question 26 AUT22 Over Σ={a,b}, classify L={wwᴿ | w∈Σ*}, the unmarked even-length palindrome language, by the most specific listed description. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Regular B Non-deterministic CFL but not deterministic C Deterministic context-free D Context-sensitive but not context-free Non-deterministic CFL but not deterministic An NPDA can push a guessed first half, choose its midpoint nondeterministically, and pop matching symbols while reading the reverse half. This binary unmarked palindrome language is not deterministic context-free. It is context-free and nonregular. With exponent R denoting reversal, wwᴿ is the stated palindrome language; the forward-copy language ww would instead fall outside CFL. A incorrect Binary unmarked even palindromes are nonregular. B correct An NPDA recognizes them, but a DPDA cannot recognize this unmarked binary language. C incorrect The missing center marker prevents deterministic context-free recognition. D incorrect The language has a CFG, so the claim that it is not context-free is false.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 27 · Q01185
records.text: Q01185 Question 27 AUT05 Which of the following statements is false about classes of language in automaton theory? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Context-free language is the subset of context-sensitive language B Regular language is the subset of context-sensitive language C Recursively enumerable language is the superset of regular language D Context-sensitive language is a subset of context-free language Context-sensitive language is a subset of context-free language The inspected diagram nests regular inside context-free inside context-sensitive inside recursively enumerable. Thus A, B and C follow the depicted inclusions, while D reverses the middle inclusion. This uses the traditional hierarchy convention, which suppresses technical empty-word qualifications. A incorrect Context-free is drawn inside context-sensitive. B incorrect Regular is inside context-free and hence inside context-sensitive. C incorrect RE is the outer class surrounding regular. D correct Reverses the diagram: context-sensitive is not contained in the smaller CFL class.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 28 · Q01206
records.text: Q01206 Question 28 AUT08 Suppose you are asked to construct a DFA for the strings ending with an 'n' length substring. How many minimal states may the DFA require? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A n B n+1 C n+2 D n*2 n+1 states for a fixed valid suffix word. AUT08 gives n+1 states for a valid fixed suffix of length n: states remember the longest suffix of the consumed input that is a prefix of the target. Distinguishable prefixes establish the lower bound. The answer presumes the target word uses the declared alphabet; no extra rejecting sink is needed for a suffix matcher. A incorrect n states omit one of the n+1 necessary prefix-match stages. B correct The note gives one state for each matched-prefix length from zero through n. C incorrect An extra rejecting sink is unnecessary because later input may always form the required suffix. D incorrect Doubling n is not the general suffix-matching state bound; accidental numeric equality does not define it.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 29 · Q01223
records.text: Q01223 Question 29 AUT06 Under the standard total-DFA model, which statements about finite automata are NOT correct? Select all that apply. Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Finite automaton accept a string or word by final state B Finite Automaton has at least one final state C Finite Automaton has at least one initial state D Deterministic Finite Automaton has a single transition. Finite Automaton has at least one final state; Deterministic Finite Automaton has a single transition. A DFA requires a designated start state and accepts when the state after the complete input is accepting. Its accepting set may nevertheless be empty, producing the empty language, so B is false. Determinism requires one successor for each state/symbol pair, not one transition in the entire automaton, making D false as well. The two remaining statements describe standard acceptance and initialization. A incorrect Final-state acceptance after all input is consumed is correct, so A is not selected. B correct The accepting set can be empty, making the asserted minimum of one false. C incorrect A designated initial state is required, so C is not selected. D correct One successor per state/symbol pair does not mean one transition in the entire machine.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 30 · Q01253
records.text: Q01253 Question 30 AUT06 Finite automaton recognizes: Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Any class of language. B Context-free language. C Context-sensitive languages. D Regular languages. Regular languages. Regular languages are exactly those recognized by finite-state automata. This is an exact language-family question: some CFLs and context-sensitive languages happen to be regular, but the whole larger families are beyond finite automata. A incorrect The hierarchy shows larger families outside finite-state power. B incorrect All CFLs is too broad, though regular examples are CFLs. C incorrect All context-sensitive languages is too broad. D correct Exactly matches the finite-state/regular equivalence.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 31 · Q01273
records.text: Q01273 Question 31 AUT18 Which one of the following grammars is unambiguous? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A E → I; E → E + E; E → E * E; E → (E); I → ε | 0 | 1 | 2 | ... | 9 B S → aSb | SS; S → ε C E → E + T / T; T → T x F / F; F → id D S → A / B; A → aAb / ab; B → abB / ∈ E → E + T / T; T → T x F / F; F → id In C, F generates id, T is a nonempty sequence of Fs separated by ×, and E a nonempty sequence of Ts separated by +. The last + uniquely determines the top E→E+T split; each T is uniquely split at its last ×. Induction on operator count gives a unique parse. A allows different groupings of id-like operands through E+E and E*E. B already has two trees for ε: S→ε and S→SS→εε. D is also ambiguous: ab is generated by S→A→ab and S→B→abB→ab. A incorrect For 1+1*1, E→E+E permits a top + parse while E→E*E permits a top * parse; I→1 supplies the operands. These are different trees for the same string (PDF page 8). B incorrect ε has both a direct leaf expansion and an SS expansion with two empty children. C correct Operator levels fix the unique split at each stage, giving a unique tree. D incorrect ab is obtained via either A or B, yielding distinct root expansions.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 32 · Q01418
records.text: Q01418 Question 32 AUT05 Which language family is recognized exactly by nondeterministic pushdown automata? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Type 0 language B Type 1 language C Type 2 language D Type 3 language Type 2 language Nondeterministic pushdown automata recognize exactly the context-free languages, corresponding to Type 2 grammars. Regular languages are included in that family, but Type 3 is too narrow to describe all PDA languages. Context-sensitive and unrestricted languages include non-context-free languages that an ordinary single-stack PDA cannot recognize. The exact-family wording therefore makes Type 2 the unique classification. A incorrect Type 0 includes languages beyond PDA recognition. B incorrect Type 1 includes non-context-free languages beyond PDA recognition. C correct Type 2 is exactly the context-free family characterized by NPDAs. D incorrect Type 3 covers only the regular subfamily of PDA languages.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 33 · Q01419
records.text: Q01419 Question 33 AUT05 Among context-sensitive, context-free and regular grammar families, which is most expressive under the usual isolated-start ε convention? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Context-sensitive grammar B Context-free grammar C Regular grammar D All of these Context-sensitive grammar The hierarchy places regular languages strictly inside context-free languages and context-free languages strictly inside context-sensitive languages. Context-sensitive grammars are therefore the most expressive of the three named families. Unrestricted grammars would be stronger if included, but the question explicitly limits the comparison. The three named classes are not tied for maximum expressive power, so the aggregate alternative does not apply. A correct Context-sensitive is the largest of the three compared families. B incorrect Context-free is strictly below context-sensitive. C incorrect Regular is strictly below both other named families. D incorrect The three families are not equally most expressive.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 34 · Q01426
records.text: Q01426 Question 34 AUT16 In which derivation the right-most non-terminal symbol is replaced at each step? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Right look ahead B Right claim C Rightmost D Right non-terminal Rightmost At every derivation step choose the rightmost remaining variable and replace it by a production right side. That is a rightmost derivation. A incorrect Lookahead is not the name of the expansion order. B incorrect Right claim does not name a derivation method. C correct Names the specified rightmost expansion rule. D incorrect Names a symbol position but not the derivation method.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 35 · Q01427
records.text: Q01427 Question 35 AUT16 In which derivation the leftmost non-terminal symbol is replaced at each step? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Left recursion B Left non-terminal C Left pushdown D Leftmost Leftmost Choose the leftmost variable at each step, rather than arbitrarily choosing any remaining variable. This is precisely leftmost derivation. A incorrect Left recursion is a form of production, not the choice of variable at each derivation step. B incorrect A left nonterminal is a location, not the derivation name. C incorrect Left pushdown is not the defined method. D correct Matches left-to-right variable expansion.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 36 · Q01429
records.text: Q01429 Question 36 AUT04 Which symbol is not related to context-free grammar? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A End symbol B Start symbol C Non-terminal symbol D Terminal symbol End symbol A CFG consists of a start symbol, terminals, nonterminals and productions. A dedicated end symbol is not one of the four CFG components, even though a parser may add an input end marker for a separate purpose. A correct Not a required CFG component in the four-element definition. B incorrect The distinguished S is required. C incorrect Variables/nonterminals form V. D incorrect The alphabet Σ supplies terminals.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 37 · Q01432
records.text: Q01432 Question 37 AUT16 Which of the following tree is the pictorial identification of the derivation? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A The oct tree B The parse tree C The binary tree D None of the above The parse tree A parse/derivation tree labels nodes with grammar symbols and uses edges to show applications of productions. That is the pictorial representation asked for; it need not be a binary tree because productions may have arbitrary finite right sides. A incorrect An octree is not the grammar representation defined here. B correct A parse tree is this graphical representation. C incorrect Production right sides need not have two children, so binary tree is not the general answer. D incorrect The parse-tree option already supplies the defined representation.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 38 · Q01435
records.text: Q01435 Question 38 AUT14 Which grammar forms are guaranteed to have an equivalent DFA? Select all that apply. Use consistently linear orientations throughout each grammar. Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A Generic grammar (arbitrary unrestricted grammar) B Left Linear Grammar C Right-linear grammar D All of the above Left Linear Grammar; Right-linear grammar Consistently left-linear and consistently right-linear grammars both generate regular languages. Every regular language has an equivalent DFA; a right-linear grammar can first be converted to an NFA and then determinized. Arbitrary unrestricted grammars can generate nonregular languages and have no such guarantee. The all-of-the-above alternative fails because that generic case is not constrained to regular languages. A incorrect An arbitrary unrestricted grammar need not generate a regular language. B correct A consistently left-linear grammar generates a regular language. C correct A consistently right-linear grammar generates a regular language. D incorrect The generic-grammar case prevents all of the above from being true.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 39 · Q01437
records.text: Q01437 Question 39 AUT28 Classify FORTRAN’s computational power under an idealized model with ordinary loops and unbounded indexed read/write storage. Which description is intended, rather than a classification of its token patterns or source syntax? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Turing-complete language B Context-sensitive language C Context-free language D Regular language Turing-complete language Under the stated idealization, indexed writable storage can represent a Turing tape, with an index recording the head position and variables recording the finite control. A loop implements successive read, write, move and state-update steps. This gives the intended Turing-complete computational classification. The other choices classify word-language families rather than naming this general simulation capability; the conclusion depends on the explicit storage model. A correct Turing-complete describes the specified general computation capability. B incorrect Context-sensitive classifies formal word languages rather than this simulation capability. C incorrect Context-free syntax does not itself characterize general computation power. D incorrect Regular token structure does not describe Turing-machine simulation power.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 40 · Q01451
records.text: Q01451 Question 40 AUT06 DFA is an abbreviation of. Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Non Deterministic Finite set Automata B Deterministic Finite Automata C Non Deterministic Finite Automata D Deterministic Finite set Automata Deterministic Finite Automata DFA stands for deterministic finite automaton; deterministic specifies a unique next state for a given current state and input. A incorrect Adds nondeterministic and set, neither in the abbreviation. B correct This is the exact expansion of the abbreviation. C incorrect This is NFA, not DFA. D incorrect Inserts set, which is absent from the expansion.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 41 · Q01452
records.text: Q01452 Question 41 AUT09 NFA is an abbreviation of. Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Non Deterministic Finite set Automata B Deterministic Finite Automata C Non Deterministic Finite Automata D Deterministic Finite set Automata Non Deterministic Finite Automata NFA stands for nondeterministic finite automaton; it permits multiple possible next states and null moves. A incorrect Inserts set, which is absent from the abbreviation. B incorrect This expands DFA instead. C correct This is the exact expansion of the abbreviation. D incorrect This describes a deterministic model and inserts set.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 42 · SM0018
records.text: SM0018 Question 42 AUT-S01 Which branch of study deals with whether a problem can be solved at all or not, regardless of the resources required? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A Computability theory B Automata theory C Set theory D Complexity theory Computability theory The resource-independent question is whether an algorithm can decide the problem at all. Computability concerns membership algorithms and the limits of what Turing machines compute; computational complexity concerns resource estimates. A correct Matches existence of an algorithm regardless of cost. B incorrect Automata concerns abstract machines; computability specifically asks the solvability question. C incorrect Computability, rather than set theory, studies algorithmic solvability. D incorrect Complexity concerns time and space resources once solving a problem is considered.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 43 · SM0024
records.text: SM0024 Question 43 AUT17 Let a Grammar G = ({S}, {a, b}, S, P), where {S} is set of variables, {a, b} is set of terminal symbols, S is start variable and P is set of productions. Then which one of the following is not an element of the language (L) (L) which is generated from G. Given: P:S-— aSb, S-A Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A aabb B ab C X D a a is not generated. The image restores S→aSb|λ and option C as λ, not the extracted X. AUT17 derives exactly aⁿbⁿ for n≥0. Two recursions generate aabb, one generates ab, and the base rule gives λ. A lone a has unequal counts and cannot arise. The readable source resolves the OCR damage rather than changing the grammar by assumption. A incorrect Two recursive pair additions followed by the empty rule derive aabb. B incorrect One application of S→aSb followed by S→λ derives ab. C incorrect The image reads lambda here, and the empty base production derives it directly. D correct A lone a has no matching b and is outside the generated equal-count language.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 44 · SM0056
records.text: SM0056 Question 44 AUT28 Which type of Turing machine has two tapes: one tape read-only and the other read-write? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Multi-head Turing machine B Off-line Turing machine C Non-deterministic Turing machine D Multi-dimensional Turing machine An off-line Turing machine. AUT28 directly defines an off-line TM as having a read-only input tape and a separate read/write work tape. The question gives that architecture. Multiple heads, nondeterministic transition choices and multidimensional tape geometry are independent variants; none defines this input/work separation. The number of tape roles alone does not imply those other variants. A incorrect Multi-head describes head multiplicity rather than this read-only input and writable work-tape separation. B correct The off-line model explicitly separates a read-only input tape from a read/write work tape. C incorrect Nondeterministic describes transition choices, not which tape permits writes. D incorrect Multidimensional describes tape geometry rather than the two tape roles specified here.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 45 · SM0094
records.text: SM0094 Question 45 AUT03 Given input alphabet Σ = {a, b, c, d} and empty string λ, which one of the following is true about Σ*? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A Σ* = Σ¹ ∪ Σ² ∪ Σ³ ∪ Σ⁴ B Σ* = Σ⁺ C Σ* = Σ⁺ ∪ {λ} D Σ* = {λ} Σ* = Σ⁺ ∪ {λ} Σ* consists of all finite symbol sequences including zero occurrences; Σ+ supplies the positive-length sequences. Since the alphabet has no empty symbol, exactly λ separates the two sets. Thus Σ*=Σ+∪{λ}. A incorrect Only lengths 1–4 are included; both λ and words of length 5 are missing. B incorrect Positive closure omits λ, unlike star. C correct Adds exactly the missing zero-length word. D incorrect Star also contains a and every other nonempty finite word over the alphabet.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 46 · SM0095
records.text: SM0095 Question 46 AUT03 AUT01 Given input alphabet Σ = {a, b, c, d} and empty string λ, which one of the following is equivalent to Σ⁰? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A Σ⁺ B Σ* C Σ D {λ} The singleton set {λ}. AUT03 defines Σⁿ as all words of length n, including Σ⁰={ε}; AUT01 identifies λ with ε. There is exactly one length-zero word, so its set is {λ}. Σ, positive closure and Kleene closure contain nonempty words for the given nonempty alphabet and therefore are not equal to the zero power. A incorrect Σ⁺ contains positive-length words over the alphabet and excludes the empty word. B incorrect Σ* contains every finite-length word, not just the single empty word. C incorrect Σ contains four alphabet symbols, each forming a length-one word rather than a length-zero word. D correct λ denotes the empty word, and its singleton set is exactly the alphabet’s zero power.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 47 · SM0206
records.text: SM0206 Question 47 AUT27 a — b, L state transition in a Turing Machine means, Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A read a, write b and move left B delete a, read b and move left C write a, read b and move left D replace 6 by a and move left read a, write b and move left In an edge label (a,b,L), the first symbol is the scanned symbol, the second is written in its cell, and L moves the head left. The finite control also moves to the destination state of the arrow. A correct Exactly follows read, write, move-left order. B incorrect The scanned symbol is a, and b is written, not read. C incorrect Reverses reading and writing. D incorrect Reverses the direction of replacement; the cell changes a to b.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 48 · SM0234
records.text: SM0234 Question 48 AUT27 Which of the following IS NOT a component of a Turing machine? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Read-write head B Control Unit C Stack D Tape Stack The standard Turing machine uses an unbounded tape, a read/write head, and finite state control. Stack is the distinctive added memory of a PDA and is not a separate structural component required by this standard TM model. A incorrect Explicitly named as the reading/writing/moving device. B incorrect Finite states and transition rules provide control. C correct The standard TM model has tape storage, whereas the PDA description explicitly adds a stack. D incorrect The tape provides the TM’s memory.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 49 · SM0246
records.text: SM0246 Question 49 AUT19 AUT01 In a grammar, if the production S -> lambda (where S is a non-terminal) exists, such a production is called: Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A Null production B Unit production C Secondary production D Sigma production A null (epsilon) production. AUT19 defines a null production as A→ε, while AUT01 identifies λ as another notation for the empty word. Substituting S for A gives the displayed S→λ rule. A unit production instead has one nonterminal on the right; secondary and sigma production are not the defined names for an empty right-hand side. A correct The right-hand side is the empty word, exactly the definition of a null production. B incorrect A unit production has one nonterminal on the right, not the empty word. C incorrect Secondary production is not the defined term for a rule deriving the empty word. D incorrect Sigma denotes an alphabet conventionally, not the null-production category described here.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 50 · SM0256
records.text: SM0256 Question 50 AUT12 Which string from the following is a member of the language represented by the regular expression a*(b+c)? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A aab B bc C aaa D aaabc aab a* permits any number of initial a symbols; (b+c) then contributes exactly one b or c. aab factors as aa followed by b. No further suffix is allowed after that final symbol. A correct aa is in a*, followed by the permitted b. B incorrect Contains two symbols from the final alternative; the a* prefix cannot consume b. C incorrect Lacks the compulsory final b or c. D incorrect After aa a and b there is an extra c; the expression allows only one final alternative.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 51 · SM0303
records.text: SM0303 Question 51 AUT21 AUT05 Which class of languages is most suited to be represented by pushdown automata? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Context-free language B Regular language C Recursively enumerable language D Unrestricted language Context-free language PDAs and CFGs characterize the same family of context-free languages. Regular languages are included, but the question most suited asks for the full family rather than a subclass. A correct Exactly the class characterized by PDAs. B incorrect A smaller included family, already recognizable by finite automata. C incorrect The hierarchy places RE at the larger Turing machine level. D incorrect Unrestricted languages are not the PDA/CFG class.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 52 · AM0744
records.text: AM0744 Question 52 AUT04 Which statement correctly describes the generation and recognition roles of formal grammars and automata? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A Formal grammars generate formal languages, and automata recognize those languages. B Formal languages recognize automata, which are generated by formal grammars. C Formal grammars generate automata, which recognize formal languages. D Formal grammars recognize formal languages, which generate automata. Formal grammars generate formal languages, and automata recognize those languages. A formal grammar generates terminal words, collectively its language. An automaton processes words and accepts exactly those in the language it recognizes. Thus languages are generated by grammars and recognized by automata. The relationship concerns the same set of strings, not a claim that automata recognize grammar descriptions or that languages themselves perform machine operations. Option A states those roles explicitly. A correct It correctly assigns language generation to grammars and recognition to automata. B incorrect Languages do not perform recognition or generate machines. C incorrect Grammars generate word languages rather than automata in this relationship. D incorrect Grammars generate languages; languages do not generate automata.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 53 · AM0745
records.text: AM0745 Question 53 AUT04 AUT12 Which offered item is a precisely specified formal language, rather than a natural-language name? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A English B Spanish C L={w∈{a,b}* | w ends in a}, denoted by (a|b)*a D French L={w∈{a,b}* | w ends in a}, denoted by (a|b)*a A formal language is a set of strings with precisely defined membership. Option C gives the language of all words over {a,b} that end in a, denoted by (a|b)*a. English, Spanish and French are natural-language names in this comparison. A regular expression alone names a specification notation; explicitly naming its denoted word set provides the actual language example. A incorrect English is a natural-language name. B incorrect Spanish is a natural-language name. C correct This specifies a set of words over a fixed alphabet with an exact ending condition. D incorrect French is a natural-language name.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 54 · AM0746
records.text: AM0746 Question 54 AUT05 Which is the least expressive listed machine family that recognizes every regular language? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Turing machine B Pushdown automaton C Finite automaton D Nondeterministic Turing machine Finite automaton Finite automata recognize exactly the regular languages. Pushdown automata and Turing machines can also recognize regular languages, but their families recognize strictly more languages and are not the least sufficient choice. The nondeterministic Turing-machine alternative is likewise stronger than finite automata. This compares expressive power across machine families, rather than implementation size or execution speed. A incorrect Turing machines recognize a strictly larger family than REG. B incorrect Pushdown automata recognize all CFLs, exceeding REG. C correct Finite automata characterize REG exactly and are least sufficient here. D incorrect Nondeterministic Turing machines exceed finite-automaton recognition power.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 55 · AM0747
records.text: AM0747 Question 55 AUT05 Which statements follow from the Chomsky hierarchy and decidability? Select all that apply. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Context-free languages are a subset of regular languages. B Context-sensitive languages are a subset of recursive languages. C Regular languages are a subset of recursive languages. D Context-free languages are a subset of recursive languages. Context-sensitive languages are a subset of recursive languages.; Regular languages are a subset of recursive languages.; Context-free languages are a subset of recursive languages. The hierarchy is REG⊊CFL⊊CSL⊊DECIDABLE⊊RE under the stated ε convention. Recursive means decidable, so context-sensitive languages are recursive, and transitivity gives the same conclusion for regular and context-free languages. A reverses the first strict inclusion: every regular language is context-free, but not every context-free language is regular. Therefore the three recursive-containment statements are all true. A incorrect The REG/CFL inclusion is reversed. B correct CSL is contained in the decidable or recursive family. C correct REG is contained in CSL and therefore in the recursive family. D correct CFL is contained in CSL and therefore in the recursive family.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 56 · AM0748
records.text: AM0748 Question 56 AUT06 AUT09 AUT15 Which statement is true of ordinary DFAs? In D, the claim concerns every context-free language. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A DFAs can recognize all regular languages. B DFAs have multiple possible transitions for each input symbol. C DFAs can have empty transitions. D DFAs can recognize every context-free language. DFAs can recognize all regular languages. Ordinary DFAs recognize exactly the regular languages. Each state/input pair has one next state, and transitions consume an input symbol rather than ε. Some context-free languages are regular, but others, such as aⁿbⁿ, are not and cannot be recognized by a DFA. Making D explicitly universal removes its weaker existential reading and leaves A as the unique true statement. A correct Every regular language has a DFA. B incorrect A DFA has a unique successor for each state/symbol pair. C incorrect Ordinary DFAs do not have ε moves. D incorrect Nonregular CFLs such as aⁿbⁿ cannot be recognized by DFAs.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 57 · AM0749
records.text: AM0749 Question 57 AUT05 AUT21 AUT25 Which listed automaton family has recognition power strictly between finite automata and Turing machines and uses one unbounded stack as its auxiliary memory? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Pushdown automaton B Non-deterministic finite automaton C Turing machine D Nondeterministic linear bounded automaton Pushdown automaton A nondeterministic PDA adds one stack to finite control and recognizes the context-free languages. This family strictly contains REG and lies strictly below Turing-recognizable languages. NFAs have the same power as DFAs, while Turing machines are the upper endpoint. A nondeterministic LBA also lies between those endpoints, but uses bounded tape rather than the specified single-stack model. A correct A PDA has one unbounded stack and the required intermediate expressive power. B incorrect An NFA has no stack and recognizes only REG. C incorrect A TM is the upper endpoint, not strictly below it. D incorrect An LBA uses linearly bounded tape rather than the specified single stack.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 58 · AM0751
records.text: AM0751 Question 58 AUT36 Which statements about NP-complete decision problems are true? Select all that apply. In C, exponential time is an upper bound. Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A NP-complete problems are only solvable by nondeterministic algorithms. B NP-complete problems are a subset of NP problems. C NP-complete problems can be solved in exponential time. D NP-complete problems have no practical applications. NP-complete problems are a subset of NP problems.; NP-complete problems can be solved in exponential time. NP-completeness includes membership in NP and hardness for every NP language under polynomial reductions. Polynomial-size certificates permit finite deterministic exhaustive search, giving a 2^poly(n) upper bound. Thus B and C are true together. This does not show that exponential time is necessary. SAT, coloring and tour-decision formulations illustrate meaningful problems, so the blanket denial of applications is also false. A incorrect Deterministic exhaustive certificate search also decides these problems. B correct Membership in NP is part of the definition. C correct Enumerating polynomial-size certificates gives a deterministic exponential-time upper bound. D incorrect The note gives substantive SAT, coloring and tour-decision examples.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 59 · AM0752
records.text: AM0752 Question 59 AUT36 Which of the following complexity classes represents the hardest problems in NP? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P B NP-complete C NP-hard D PSPACE NP-complete: the problems both in NP and NP-hard. AUT36 defines NP-complete as NP membership together with hardness for every NP problem under polynomial reductions. That is the precise class described by hardest problems in NP. NP-hard alone can extend beyond NP, even to undecidable problems; PSPACE is a larger resource class, and P does not impose the required hardness. A incorrect P means deterministic polynomial time and does not define hardness for every NP language. B correct NP-completeness combines being in NP with being at least as hard as every NP problem. C incorrect NP-hardness alone does not ensure membership in NP, so it is broader than the class requested. D incorrect PSPACE is defined by polynomial space and can contain languages outside the specified NP-complete class.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 60 · AM0753
records.text: AM0753 Question 60 AUT30 Which of the following is true regarding the halting problem? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A The halting problem can be solved by a Turing machine. B The halting problem is decidable for all programs. C The halting problem is an undecidable problem. D The halting problem is only relevant to regular languages. The general halting problem is undecidable. AUT30 constructs a machine that contradicts a hypothetical universal halting decider when run on its own description. Hence no decider answers halting correctly for all machine/input pairs. HALT is recognizable by simulation, but that process need not terminate on nonhalting instances; recognizing some yes-instances is not solving the general decision problem. A incorrect Simulation recognizes halting yes-instances but no TM decides the general halting problem on every input. B incorrect The diagonal argument rules out a decider correct for all programs and inputs. C correct Undecidability is the exact result proved by the halting diagonalization argument in AUT30. D incorrect HALT concerns arbitrary computations and is not confined to regular languages or finite automata.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 61 · AM0754
records.text: AM0754 Question 61 AUT26 Which of the following is a regular language? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A {anbn | n ≥ 0} B {anbncn | n ≥ 0} C {an | n is a prime number} D {anb | n ≥ 0} {anb | n ≥ 0} Reading the powers as a^n b^n, a^n b^n c^n, a^n for prime n, and a^n b. D is a*b, a regular expression. A and B fail the pumping lemma’s condition: choose a^p b^p (or a^p b^p c^p); any nonempty pumped block in the first p positions consists only of a, so pumping changes only its count. For C choose a prime q at least p. If the pumped block has k≥1 a symbols, pumping with i=q+1 gives length q+qk=q(k+1), composite. Thus no pumping decomposition works. The argument uses the arithmetic fact that arbitrarily large primes exist. A incorrect Pumping only a symbols destroys equality with the b count. B incorrect Pumping only a symbols destroys equality with both later blocks. C incorrect Pumping the unary block q+1 times makes a composite length q(k+1). D correct a*b produces any number of a symbols followed by exactly one b.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 62 · AM0755
records.text: AM0755 Question 62 AUT05 Which is the least expressive listed grammar family capable of generating every context-free language? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Context-free grammar Context-free grammars generate exactly the context-free languages. Regular grammars are insufficient because CFL contains nonregular languages such as aⁿbⁿ. Context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars can also generate CFLs under the stated ε convention, but their expressive power is greater than required. The least-family qualifier distinguishes the exact defining family from stronger families that merely have the same capability as a subset. A incorrect Regular grammars fail for nonregular CFLs such as aⁿbⁿ. B correct Context-free grammars cover exactly the required family. C incorrect Context-sensitive grammars suffice but are stronger than required. D incorrect Unrestricted grammars suffice but are stronger than required.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 63 · AM0756
records.text: AM0756 Question 63 AUT05 Under the usual isolated-start ε convention, which statements about CFLs and CSLs are true? Select all that apply. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Every context-sensitive language is also a context-free language. B Every context-free language is also a context-sensitive language. C Context-free languages are a strict subset of context-sensitive languages. D Context-free languages are unrelated to context-sensitive languages. Every context-free language is also a context-sensitive language.; Context-free languages are a strict subset of context-sensitive languages. Every context-free language is context-sensitive under the stated ε convention. The containment is strict: aⁿbⁿcⁿ is context-sensitive but not context-free. Hence both the inclusive statement B and the stronger proper-subset statement C are true. A reverses the containment, and D denies an established relationship. Selecting the stronger statement alone would incorrectly discard a weaker statement that it logically entails. A incorrect The three-equal-count language is a CSL outside CFL. B correct Every CFL belongs to CSL. C correct CSL contains additional languages, making the inclusion strict. D incorrect The two families are related by strict containment.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 64 · AM0757
records.text: AM0757 Question 64 AUT05 AUT25 Which listed machine family can recognize every context-sensitive language? Interpret D as a nondeterministic finite automaton. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Finite automaton B Pushdown automaton C Turing machine D Nondeterministic finite automaton Turing machine Context-sensitive languages are recognized by nondeterministic linear bounded automata. An unrestricted Turing machine can simulate their bounded-tape computations, so it can recognize every CSL. Finite automata and NFAs recognize only regular languages, and ordinary PDAs recognize only context-free languages. Those weaker families cannot cover the three-equal-count CSL, so they fail the universal capability requirement. A incorrect Finite automata cannot recognize nonregular CSLs. B incorrect PDAs cannot recognize CSLs outside CFL. C correct A TM can simulate the LBA model for every CSL. D incorrect NFAs recognize only REG, not every CSL.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 65 · AM0758
records.text: AM0758 Question 65 AUT29 AUT05 Which listed term names exactly the recursively enumerable language family, rather than a proper subfamily? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A Regular language B Context-free language C Context-sensitive language D Turing-recognizable language Turing-recognizable language Recursively enumerable, Turing-recognizable and semidecidable are names for the same language family. Regular, context-free and context-sensitive languages are all contained in RE, but each is a proper subfamily. The exact-family wording therefore singles out Turing-recognizable. Recognizers must halt and accept members; on a nonmember they may either reject or loop, unlike deciders which halt on every input. A incorrect REG is a proper subfamily of RE. B incorrect CFL is a proper subfamily of RE. C incorrect CSL is a proper subfamily of RE. D correct Turing-recognizable is an exact synonym for RE.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 66 · AM0759
records.text: AM0759 Question 66 AUT05 Which class of languages is the most powerful in terms of generative power? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Regular languages B Context-free languages C Context-sensitive languages D Recursively enumerable languages Recursively enumerable languages Reading most powerful as largest generative family in the traditional hierarchy, the outermost region is recursively enumerable. It properly surrounds context-sensitive, context-free and regular classes. A incorrect Innermost family, hence smallest listed. B incorrect Contains regular but is inside context-sensitive. C incorrect Larger than CFL but still inside RE. D correct Outermost family in the diagram.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 67 · AM0760
records.text: AM0760 Question 67 AUT29 AUT30 Which statements about recursive and recursively enumerable languages are true? Select all that apply. Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A Every recursive language is also a recursively enumerable language. B Every recursively enumerable language is also a recursive language. C Recursive languages are a strict subset of recursively enumerable languages. D Recursive languages are unrelated to recursively enumerable languages. Every recursive language is also a recursively enumerable language.; Recursive languages are a strict subset of recursively enumerable languages. Every decider is also a recognizer, so each recursive language is recursively enumerable. The containment is proper: the halting language can be recognized by simulation but cannot be decided on every input. Thus both the inclusion statement and the strict-subset statement are true. The converse would turn every recognizer into a total decider, contradicting the halting example; describing the two families as unrelated also contradicts their inclusion. A correct A decider recognizes its language and halts on every input, establishing inclusion. B incorrect The recognizable but undecidable halting language is a counterexample. C correct The halting language belongs to RE but not to the recursive family, making inclusion strict. D incorrect The families are related by proper containment.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 68 · AM0761
records.text: AM0761 Question 68 AUT30 AUT26 AUT-S04 Which of the following is an example of an undecidable problem? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A Checking if a given number is prime B Sorting a list of numbers in ascending order C Solving a system of linear equations D Determining if a Turing machine halts on a given input Determining whether an arbitrary TM halts on its given input. AUT30 proves HALT undecidable, directly matching D. The other choices describe ordinary finite mathematical computation: primality can test finitely many candidate divisors, a finite list can be sorted, and an exact finite linear system can be processed by elimination. Their cost can vary, but no general undecidability follows from those ordinary formulations. A incorrect For an integer, testing finitely many candidate divisors decides primality; AUT26 uses bounded divisor testing. B incorrect A finite numeric list can be sorted by a terminating comparison procedure. C incorrect An ordinarily encoded finite linear system can be decided and solved by finite elimination steps. D correct This is the general halting decision problem proved undecidable in AUT30.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 69 · AM0762
records.text: AM0762 Question 69 AUT30 AUT26 Which offered language is nonrecursive (undecidable)? Use finite standard encodings and a fixed finite alphabet for mirror words. Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A HALT={⟨M,w⟩ | M halts on w} B {an | n is a prime number} C {wwR | w is any string} D {anb | n ≥ 0} HALT={⟨M,w⟩ | M halts on w} The halting language HALT contains encoded machine/input pairs for which the machine eventually halts. The diagonal argument in the note proves that no algorithm decides HALT on every input. The remaining examples are decidable: unary primality uses finite divisor testing, mirror words can be compared finitely, and aⁿb is regular. Thus nonregularity or an expensive test alone does not imply nonrecursiveness. A correct HALT is recognizable but undecidable by the diagonal argument. B incorrect Finite counting and divisor testing decide unary prime length. C incorrect A finite mirror comparison decides palindrome membership. D incorrect The language aⁿb is regular and hence decidable.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 70 · AM0763
records.text: AM0763 Question 70 AUT05 At the level of generated language families, what criterion orders the Chomsky hierarchy? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A It categorizes formal languages based on their computational complexity. B It categorizes formal languages based on their expressive power. C It categorizes formal languages based on their alphabet size. D It categorizes languages by the surface structure of individual input strings. It categorizes formal languages based on their expressive power. The hierarchy orders families by expressive power: regular languages form a proper subfamily of CFLs, then CSLs, then the stronger computable families. Grammar production restrictions define the corresponding types, but the resulting language-family comparison concerns generative capability. It is not a ranking of algorithm runtimes, alphabet sizes, or surface appearance of particular strings. That scope makes B the unique criterion. A incorrect The hierarchy is not a runtime or workspace ranking. B correct It compares the language families that the models can describe. C incorrect Alphabet size does not determine the family. D incorrect Surface structure of individual strings is not the language-family ordering criterion.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 71 · AM0764
records.text: AM0764 Question 71 AUT17 AUT15 AUT05 What is the least expressive listed grammar family that generates L={aⁿbⁿ | n≥0}? Use the usual isolated-start ε convention. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Context-free grammar The CFG S→aSb|ε generates exactly equal blocks of a and b: every recursive step adds one of each and the base supplies n=0. The pumping argument rules out regularity. Context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars can also generate this language, but are stronger than necessary under the ε convention. The least expressive sufficient family is therefore context-free. A incorrect Regular grammars cannot enforce these unbounded equal counts. B correct The displayed matched recursive CFG generates the language. C incorrect Context-sensitive grammars are stronger than necessary. D incorrect Unrestricted grammars are stronger than necessary.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 72 · AM0765
records.text: AM0765 Question 72 AUT26 Which listed language is context-sensitive but NOT context-free? Interpret the notation as powers and use the usual ε convention. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A {aⁿbⁿ | n≥0} B {aⁿbᵐ | n,m≥0} C {aⁿ | n is prime} D {aⁿb | n≥0} {aⁿ | n is prime} Unary prime length is context-sensitive because bounded-workspace counting and divisor testing decide it. It is not regular by the prime-length pumping argument, and every unary CFL is regular; consequently it is not context-free. In contrast, aⁿbⁿ is context-free, while independently chosen a/b counts and any number of a followed by one b are regular. These weaker examples are excluded by the explicit non-CFL condition. A incorrect Equal two-block counts form a CFL. B incorrect Independent counts give the regular language a*b*. C correct Unary prime length is CSL but not CFL. D incorrect Any number of a followed by one b is regular.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 73 · AM0766
records.text: AM0766 Question 73 AUT22 AUT15 What is the least expressive listed machine family that recognizes L={aⁿbⁿ | n≥0}? Interpret D as a nondeterministic finite automaton. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Finite automaton B Pushdown automaton C Turing machine D Nondeterministic finite automaton Pushdown automaton A PDA pushes one stack symbol for each a, then pops one for each b, accepting exactly when the blocks finish together. The language is nonregular, so neither deterministic nor nondeterministic finite automata suffice. A TM can simulate the matching procedure, but has greater expressive power than required. The least sufficient listed family is the pushdown automaton. A incorrect Finite automata cannot recognize the nonregular matched-count language. B correct A PDA stack matches each a with one later b. C incorrect A TM works but is stronger than necessary. D incorrect An NFA recognizes only regular languages.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 74 · AM0767
records.text: AM0767 Question 74 AUT22 Over Σ={a,b}, what is the least expressive listed grammar family generating L={wwᴿ | w∈Σ*}? Use the usual isolated-start ε convention. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Context-free grammar The grammar S→aSa|bSb|ε generates precisely binary even-length palindromes: matching symbols wrap a shorter mirror word until the empty center is reached. This language is context-free and nonregular over the stated two-symbol alphabet. Context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars also suffice but exceed the minimum expressive power required. Fixing the alphabet excludes the unary even-length case, which would be regular. A incorrect Binary unmarked even palindromes are nonregular. B correct The wrapping CFG generates exactly this mirror language. C incorrect Context-sensitive grammars are stronger than necessary. D incorrect Unrestricted grammars are stronger than necessary.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 75 · AM0768
records.text: AM0768 Question 75 AUT22 Over Σ={a,b}, what is the least expressive listed machine family recognizing L={wwᴿ | w∈Σ*}? There is no center marker; D means NFA. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Finite automaton B Nondeterministic pushdown automaton C Turing machine D Nondeterministic finite automaton Nondeterministic pushdown automaton An NPDA pushes the first half, guesses the midpoint and matches the remaining symbols against the stack in reverse order. That recognizes the binary even-palindrome language, which is nonregular. Finite automata and NFAs therefore fail, whereas a TM can recognize it but is stronger than necessary. The unmarked midpoint requires nondeterminism in the PDA family, as distinguished in the note. A incorrect A finite automaton cannot recognize binary unmarked even palindromes. B correct A nondeterministic PDA guesses the midpoint and matches using its stack. C incorrect A TM is sufficient but stronger than necessary. D incorrect An NFA still recognizes only regular languages.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 76 · AM0769
records.text: AM0769 Question 76 AUT25 AUT24 What is the least expressive listed grammar family generating L={0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ | n≥0}? Use the usual isolated-start ε convention. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Context-sensitive grammar Renaming the symbols in aⁿbⁿcⁿ gives 0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ without changing its classification. The three matched blocks form a context-sensitive language but not a context-free one. The isolated-start ε convention covers n=0. Regular grammars are weaker still, and unrestricted grammars can generate it but exceed what is needed. Thus the least sufficient listed grammar family is context-sensitive. A incorrect Regular grammars cannot generate this nonregular language. B incorrect The language lies outside the context-free family. C correct The context-sensitive family suffices and is the least listed family that does. D incorrect Unrestricted grammars suffice but exceed the required expressive power.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 77 · AM0770
records.text: AM0770 Question 77 AUT25 AUT24 Which listed machine family can recognize L={0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ | n≥0}? Interpret D as a nondeterministic finite automaton. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Finite automaton B Pushdown automaton C Turing machine D Nondeterministic finite automaton Turing machine A Turing machine verifies the 0*1*2* order, repeatedly marks one symbol from each block, and checks that none remains unmatched. Each round marks additional symbols, so the procedure halts. This is the three-equal-count language with renamed symbols, which is not context-free. Consequently neither a finite automaton, an NFA nor a single-stack PDA recognizes it, leaving the TM as the sufficient listed model. A incorrect Finite automata cannot recognize this nonregular language. B incorrect A single-stack PDA cannot recognize this non-CFL language. C correct A TM implements the terminating membership test described in the note. D incorrect An NFA recognizes only REG and cannot recognize this language.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 78 · AM0771
records.text: AM0771 Question 78 AUT26 What is the least expressive listed grammar family generating L={aⁿ | n is prime}? Use the usual isolated-start ε convention. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Context-sensitive grammar Unary prime length is nonregular by the pumping argument. Since every unary context-free language is regular, it is not context-free either. Bounded-workspace counting and divisor testing establish context sensitivity. Unrestricted grammars also suffice but are more expressive than necessary. The least sufficient listed family is therefore context-sensitive, rather than one of the two weaker grammar families. A incorrect Regular grammars cannot generate this nonregular language. B incorrect The language lies outside the context-free family. C correct The context-sensitive family suffices and is the least listed family that does. D incorrect Unrestricted grammars suffice but exceed the required expressive power.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 79 · AM0772
records.text: AM0772 Question 79 AUT26 Which listed machine family can recognize L={aⁿ | n is prime}? Interpret D as a nondeterministic finite automaton. Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. This procedure halts on every input. The language is nonregular, and every unary CFL is regular, so it is also outside CFL. Finite automata, NFAs and single-stack PDAs therefore fail, while the TM provides the required recognition procedure. A incorrect Finite automata cannot recognize this nonregular language.
