records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 80 · AM0773
records.text: AM0773 Question 80 AUT14 What is the least expressive listed grammar family generating L={aⁿb | n≥0}? Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A Regular grammar B Context-free grammar C Context-sensitive grammar D Unrestricted grammar Regular grammar A right-linear grammar S→aS|b generates any number of a symbols followed by exactly one b, including the word b for n=0. The language is therefore regular. Context-free, context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars can all generate regular languages too, but are more expressive than necessary. records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 81 · AM0774
records.text: AM0774 Question 81 AUT34 AUT39 Which class is defined as the decision languages decidable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P B NP C PSPACE D EXPTIME P P is defined by deterministic polynomial-time decidability. NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME all contain P, so broad containment would not distinguish the choices. They have different defining bounds: nondeterministic polynomial time, deterministic polynomial workspace and deterministic exponential time, respectively. The explicit deterministic-time definition uniquely identifies P without assuming any unresolved separation among neighboring classes. A correct P is defined by deterministic polynomial-time decisions. B incorrect NP is defined by nondeterministic polynomial time or polynomial verification. C incorrect PSPACE is defined by polynomial workspace. D incorrect EXPTIME is defined by exponential-time bounds rather than precisely the stated polynomial-time bound.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 82 · AM0775
records.text: AM0775 Question 82 AUT34 AUT38 AUT39 Which class consists of decision problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-size certificates checkable by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P B NP C PSPACE D EXPTIME NP NP is defined by polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification, equivalently nondeterministic polynomial-time decision. P instead names deterministic polynomial-time decision; its members also admit efficient verification, but P is not the name for the full verifier-defined class. PSPACE bounds deterministic working space by a polynomial, and EXPTIME bounds deterministic time exponentially. These are different resource-based definitions; their inclusion relationships do not make them alternative names for NP. A incorrect P is defined by deterministic polynomial-time decision, not by the full certificate-verification characterization. B correct The certificate-and-verifier definition is precisely NP. C incorrect PSPACE is defined by a polynomial bound on deterministic space. D incorrect EXPTIME is defined by exponential deterministic time bounds.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 83 · AM0776
records.text: AM0776 Question 83 AUT38 AUT34 AUT39 Which class is defined as the decision languages decidable using deterministic polynomial workspace? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P B NP C PSPACE D EXPTIME PSPACE PSPACE consists of decision languages decidable with deterministic workspace bounded by a polynomial in input length. P and NP use polynomial-time definitions, whereas EXPTIME uses an exponential-time definition and contains PSPACE. Those containments do not change which class the workspace condition defines. Nor is it necessary to assume unresolved strict separations among the classes to identify the definition. A incorrect P has a deterministic polynomial-time definition. B incorrect NP has a nondeterministic polynomial-time or certificate-verification definition. C correct PSPACE has exactly the stated deterministic polynomial-workspace definition. D incorrect EXPTIME contains PSPACE but is defined by a time bound.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 84 · AM0777
records.text: AM0777 Question 84 AUT35 Which concept is used to show that one problem can be reduced to another problem in order to prove hardness or completeness? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A Reductions B Hierarchy C Completeness D Complexity classes Reductions. AUT35 defines a polynomial reduction as a computable transformation preserving yes/no membership and explains how reducing a known hard problem to a new target proves target hardness. AUT32 supplies the computable version for undecidability. Thus reductions name the proof concept itself, while hierarchy, completeness and classes describe relationships or resulting properties rather than the transformation method. A correct A reduction transforms instances while preserving membership, enabling hardness or completeness arguments with the stated resource bound. B incorrect A hierarchy organizes classes; it does not itself supply the instance transformation used in a hardness proof. C incorrect Completeness is the property proved using membership and hardness, not the reduction method itself. D incorrect Complexity classes group problems by resources; reductions establish the required relationships between individual problems.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 85 · AM0778
records.text: AM0778 Question 85 AUT36 Which listed term denotes decision problems that belong to NP and are at least as hard as every NP problem under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P B NP-complete C PSPACE D EXPTIME NP-complete NP-completeness combines two conditions: the target problem belongs to NP, and every NP language reduces to it in polynomial time. That gives a precise meaning to hardest within NP under the chosen reductions. P, PSPACE and EXPTIME instead name resource-bounded language classes and do not by themselves assert that each member is hard for NP or belongs to NP. A incorrect P names a resource class, not the membership-plus-hardness condition. B correct NP-complete states both NP membership and hardness for all NP languages. C incorrect PSPACE membership alone does not give the specified NP completeness. D incorrect EXPTIME membership alone does not give the specified NP completeness.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 86 · CS0247
records.text: CS0247 Question 86 AUT17 Let a Grammar G = ({S}, {a,b}, S, P), where P: S -> aSb, S -> lambda. Which one of the following is NOT an element of the language L generated from G? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A aabb B ab C lambda (empty string) D a a After n applications of S→aSb and a final S→λ the word is a^n b^n. Induction preserves equal counts in block order, including n=0. a has one a and no b and cannot be generated. A incorrect S⇒aSb⇒aaSbb⇒aabb. B incorrect S⇒aSb⇒ab. C incorrect S⇒λ directly. records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 87 · CS0249
records.text: CS0249 Question 87 AUT03 Given input Alphabet sigma = {a, b, c, d} and empty string lambda. Which one of the following is true about sigma*? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A sigma* = sigma+ B sigma* = sigma+ union {lambda} C sigma* = sigma^1 union sigma^2 union sigma^3 union sigma+ D sigma* = {lambda} sigma* = sigma+ union {lambda} Star allows every finite number of alphabet symbols, including zero. Positive closure allows all positive numbers. Their union with the singleton zero-length word gives exactly star. In C, unioning positive powers with Σ+ still gives only Σ+, missing λ. A incorrect Σ+ omits λ, so it is smaller than Σ*. B correct Partitions all words by zero versus positive length. C incorrect All terms already have positive length; λ is absent. D incorrect Omits every nonempty word such as a.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 88 · CS0250
records.text: CS0250 Question 88 AUT03 Given input Alphabet sigma = {a, b, c, d} and empty string lambda. Which one of the following is equivalent to sigma+? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A sigma B sigma+ C {lambda} D sigma* sigma+ Taken literally, B is an identity: Σ+ equals itself. Since the alphabet is nonempty and contains no empty symbol, Σ contains only length-one words, Σ* additionally contains λ, and {λ} contains no positive-length word. The identical expressions make B a definite answer as printed. A incorrect aa is in Σ+ but not in Σ. B correct Identical expression on both sides. C incorrect λ has length zero and is not a positive repetition. D incorrect Σ* includes λ, unlike Σ+.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 89 · CS0251
records.text: CS0251 Question 89 AUT01 If Z=caddba, what is |Z|², the square of the numeric length of Z? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A 3 B 4 C 2 D 36 36 String length counts every symbol occurrence, including repetitions. The word caddba has six positions, so |Z|=6 and |Z|²=6²=36. Counting distinct symbols would give four, which is not string length. Concatenating two copies gives length twelve, but that computes |Z²| instead; the revised stem expressly preserves the original placement of the exponent outside the bars. A incorrect Three is neither the length nor its square. B incorrect Four counts distinct letters rather than the squared length. C incorrect Two is the exponent, not the squared length. D correct Six positions squared gives 36.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 90 · CS0252
records.text: CS0252 Question 90 AUT02 What will be the value of Z^R (reverse) if string Z = caddba? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A abddac B cad C abd D caddba abddac Reversal reads the characters in the opposite order without dropping any: c a d d b a becomes a b d d a c. A correct Produces every symbol in reverse order: abddac. B incorrect Only a three-symbol prefix; does not reverse the full word. C incorrect Only the first three reversed symbols; drops the remaining characters. D incorrect Original word differs from its reverse at the first symbol.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 91 · CS0253
records.text: CS0253 Question 91 AUT02 If we have two strings Z = cddc and W = ababb, then the concatenation ZW will be? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A ZW = cddcababb B ZW = cdab C ZW = ababbcddc D ZW = ca ZW = cddcababb. AUT02 defines xy as all of x followed by all of y, preserving order and every symbol. Appending ababb to cddc yields cddcababb, of length 4+5=9. Reversing the operands produces a different string; selecting prefixes or first letters discards symbols and is not concatenation. A correct This preserves cddc followed by ababb, giving the required nine-symbol concatenation. B incorrect cdab discards symbols from both operands instead of retaining both complete strings. C incorrect ababbcddc is WZ, reversing the specified operand order. D incorrect ca retains only initial symbols and is not the concatenation of the full strings.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 92 · CS0254
records.text: CS0254 Question 92 AUT01 AUT02 AUT03 Given input alphabet sigma = {a, b, c, d} and empty string lambda. Which one of the following is FALSE about lambda? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A lambda*ab = ab B For any string Z, Z^0 = lambda C lambda is an element of sigma* D lambda = 0 The empty word is not numeric zero. AUT01 distinguishes the empty word λ from the numeric symbol 0. AUT02 gives λx=x and Z⁰=λ, while AUT03 includes the empty word in Σ*. Thus the first three claims express the standard empty-word identities under the displayed concatenation notation, and D is the false equality. A incorrect Reading the displayed star as concatenation, the empty word followed by ab is ab. B incorrect Every string’s zeroth concatenation power is the empty word. C incorrect Kleene closure of the alphabet includes its zero-length word λ. D correct This equality is false: λ is a zero-length word, not the numeric symbol 0.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 93 · CS0255
records.text: CS0255 Question 93 AUT03 AUT02 AUT01 Which one of the following is FALSE about any language L? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A L^3 = L^1 * L^1 * L^1 B L^0 = lambda C L* = L^0 union L^1 union L^2 union L^3 ... D L+ = L^1 union L^2 union L^3 ... L⁰ is {λ}, not the word λ itself. AUT02 defines L⁰={ε}; AUT01 equates λ with ε. Thus the literal equality L⁰=λ confuses a set with its sole word and is false unless braces are explicitly understood. Reading the binary stars in A as the displayed concatenation separators, A is the third-power definition; C and D are the unions defining star and positive closure in AUT03. A incorrect With the displayed binary stars denoting concatenation, three copies of L form L³, so this is true. B correct This is the false statement: the zeroth power is the singleton language {λ}, not the word λ. C incorrect The union of all nonnegative language powers is the definition of Kleene closure, so this is true. D incorrect The union of positive language powers is positive closure, even if L itself contains ε.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 94 · CS0256
records.text: CS0256 Question 94 AUT03 Given input alphabet sigma = {a, b, c, d}, which one of the following is an element of set sigma^2? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A b B c C ac D aabbccdd ac. AUT03 defines Σⁿ as the words containing exactly n alphabet symbols. The given alphabet includes a and c, so ac has two permitted symbols and belongs to Σ². Single-symbol choices have length one; aabbccdd has length eight. Membership depends on length and symbol validity, not on including all alphabet symbols. A incorrect b uses an allowed symbol but has length one rather than the required two. B incorrect c is a one-symbol word and therefore belongs to Σ¹, not Σ². C correct ac has exactly two symbols, both drawn from the given alphabet. D incorrect aabbccdd has eight symbols; using each symbol twice does not make it a length-two word.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 95 · CS0260
records.text: CS0260 Question 95 AUT27 In a Turing Machine, the transition a -> b, L means: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Read a, write b and move left B Delete a, read b and move left C Write a, read b and move left D Replace b by a and move left Read a, write b and move left The TM transition reads the scanned a, replaces it with b, and moves the head one cell left. This is the transition ordering (read symbol, write symbol, movement), with next state specified by the destination vertex. A correct Matches the scanned symbol, replacement, and L direction. B incorrect b is written rather than read; no distinct delete-then-read instruction is specified. C incorrect Swaps read and write roles. D incorrect Replaces the wrong symbol in the wrong direction.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 96 · NS0161
records.text: NS0161 Question 96 AUT06 AUT09 AUT10 What is the difference between a DFA and an NFA? Are they equally powerful? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. DFA has one successor per state/symbol; NFA permits sets. They recognize the same languages. AUT09 permits an NFA to have zero, one or several next states and states that DFA and NFA recognize exactly REG. Subset construction simulates the simultaneous NFA possibilities by DFA states.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 97 · NS0162
records.text: NS0162 Question 97 AUT15 What is the pumping lemma used for? Demonstrate with an example. Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. The regular pumping lemma can disprove regularity, for example for aⁿbⁿ. AUT15 chooses aᵖbᵖ after assuming a pumping length p. Every legal nonempty y in the first p symbols contains only a, so pumping it out changes the a count without changing b. That contradicts regularity.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 98 · NS0163
records.text: NS0163 Question 98 AUT34 AUT36 What is the difference between P and NP? Why does it matter? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. P is deterministic polynomial-time decision; NP admits polynomial certificates. Equality remains open. AUT34 defines P by deterministic polynomial running time and NP by nondeterministic polynomial time or polynomial-size verifiable certificates. P is included in NP, and equality is unresolved. This matters for converting efficiently checked witnesses into efficiently found decisions.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 99 · NS0164
records.text: NS0164 Question 99 AUT30 Why is the halting problem undecidable? Explain the contradiction. Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A proposed halting decider yields a program contradicting its own prediction. AUT30 constructs D(x) to loop when H(x,x) predicts halting and to halt otherwise. On D’s own description, either prediction is contradicted. Therefore no general halting decider exists, although simulation recognizes halting instances.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 100 · NS0165
records.text: NS0165 Question 100 AUT05 AUT26 AUT30 What is the Chomsky hierarchy and why are the containments proper? Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. REG⊊CFL⊊CSL⊊RE by increasing generative power; separating examples witness proper inclusions. AUT05 supplies the proper family hierarchy. Equal pairs separate CFL from REG; equal triples separate CSL from CFL. CSLs are decidable by AUT25, while HALT is RE but undecidable under AUT30, separating CSL from RE.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 101 · NS0166
records.text: NS0166 Question 101 AUT05 Which of the following correctly orders automata from LEAST to MOST powerful? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A NFA < DFA < PDA < TM B PDA < NFA < DFA < TM C DFA = NFA < PDA < LBA < TM D TM < LBA < PDA < DFA DFA=NFA < PDA < LBA < TM in language-recognition power. AUT09 equates DFA and NFA power. AUT05 assigns finite automata, nondeterministic PDAs, nondeterministic LBAs and Turing recognizers to successively stronger language families. That gives C under the standard nondeterministic PDA/LBA family convention. The comparison is expressiveness, not a statement that stronger models always run faster. A incorrect NFA and DFA have equal power rather than the strict order shown. B incorrect PDAs recognize more than regular languages, so placing PDA below finite automata reverses the hierarchy. C correct This gives equal finite-automaton power followed by the standard strictly increasing PDA/LBA/TM families. D incorrect This reverses the standard language-recognition power hierarchy.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 102 · NS0167
records.text: NS0167 Question 102 AUT-S01 Complexity theory primarily studies: Check whether the required procedure must halt on every input, and distinguish solving a task from recognizing its yes-instances. A How to design finite automata B Resources (time and space) required to solve computational problems C How to convert NFA to DFA D The syntax of formal grammars Time and space resources for computational problems. AUT33 defines time as computation steps and space as memory cells, and AUT34 groups decision problems by polynomial resource bounds. Complexity studies these resource requirements as a function of encoded input size. Designing automata or transforming grammars may be objects of study, but neither is the general defining purpose. A incorrect Finite-automaton design is one specific task rather than the general study of computational resources. B correct Complexity theory classifies time and space requirements relative to input size. C incorrect NFA determinization is a particular construction, not the broad subject of complexity theory. D incorrect Grammar syntax concerns formal language description rather than resource requirements in general.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 103 · NS0168
records.text: NS0168 Question 103 AUT03 Given Σ = {a, b}, which of the following is in Σ² but NOT in Σ¹? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A a B b C ε D ab ab. AUT03 defines Σⁿ by exact word length. Over {a,b}, ab contains two permitted symbols and is not length one. The single letters a and b belong to Σ¹; ε has length zero. Thus only ab satisfies both membership in Σ² and exclusion from Σ¹. A incorrect a has length one and belongs to Σ¹ rather than Σ². B incorrect b has length one, violating the required exact length two. C incorrect Epsilon has length zero and is not in Σ². D correct ab has two permitted symbols and is not a one-symbol word.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 104 · NS0169
records.text: NS0169 Question 104 AUT03 The set Σ* for Σ = {0, 1} includes which of the following? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A ε (empty string) B All binary strings of length ≥ 1 only C Only finite-length strings starting with 1 D All strings NOT over {0,1} The empty string is included. AUT03 defines Σ* as the union of all nonnegative powers, including Σ⁰={ε}. Therefore the empty word belongs to the binary closure. Positive-length-only and starting-with-one descriptions exclude valid members, and strings using symbols outside {0,1} are outside this universe. The wording of B must not erase its restrictive only. A correct The zero power contributes epsilon to the Kleene closure. B incorrect The word only excludes epsilon, so this is not a complete description of Σ*. C incorrect Binary strings starting with 0 and epsilon also belong, so the starting-with-1 restriction is false. D incorrect Σ* consists of words over the specified binary alphabet, not words outside it.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 105 · NS0170
records.text: NS0170 Question 105 AUT03 What is the difference between Σ* and Σ⁺? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A Σ* excludes strings of length 2 or more B Σ⁺ includes the empty string but Σ* does not C Σ* includes the empty string (ε) but Σ⁺ does not D They are identical Σ* includes ε; Σ⁺ excludes it. AUT03 explicitly gives Σ*=Σ⁺∪{ε} for a nonempty alphabet. Both operations allow arbitrarily long finite words, but only star includes length zero. This statement concerns alphabet closure; the note separately cautions that positive closure of an arbitrary language containing epsilon can itself include epsilon. A incorrect Σ* contains words of every finite length, including length two and above. B incorrect This reverses which alphabet closure contains the empty word. C correct Star includes the zero-length word and positive alphabet closure omits it. D incorrect They differ at least by epsilon for the nonempty alphabet convention.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 106 · NS0171
records.text: NS0171 Question 106 AUT06 In the five-tuple M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) of an FSM, which component determines how the machine moves from state to state? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Q — the set of states B δ — the transition function C F — the set of accepting states D q₀ — the initial state δ, the transition function. AUT06 defines δ:Q×Σ→Q, mapping a current state and input symbol to the next state. That is precisely the movement rule asked for. Q lists available states, F marks acceptance and q₀ fixes the starting state; none of those alone specifies the transitions between states. A incorrect Q supplies state names but not the next-state rule for input symbols. B correct Delta maps the current state and input symbol to the next state. C incorrect F identifies acceptance rather than transitions between states. D incorrect The initial state specifies where processing starts, not how each symbol changes state.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 107 · NS0172
records.text: NS0172 Question 107 AUT06 What is the defining characteristic that makes an automaton 'deterministic'? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A It has exactly one accepting state B It processes input from right to left C It never enters a dead state D For every (state, input) pair, there is exactly ONE next state One next state for every state/input-symbol pair. AUT06 explicitly defines exactly one successor per state/symbol pair. Determinism does not constrain the number of final states, input-reading direction or whether a rejecting sink is reachable. The uniqueness concerns each transition choice, not the number of states or transitions in the entire automaton. A incorrect A DFA may have zero, one or several accepting states. B incorrect Right-to-left processing is not the definition of determinism. C incorrect Deterministic automata may legitimately have reachable rejecting sinks. D correct The next state is uniquely determined by the current state and current input symbol.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 108 · NS0173
records.text: NS0173 Question 108 AUT08 Over the alphabet Σ={a,b,c}, what is the minimum number of states in a complete DFA accepting exactly the strings that start with abc? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A 3 B 5 C 4 D 6 5 Before completing abc, the DFA must distinguish no matched symbol, a matched, and ab matched. It then needs an accepting state for all continuations after abc and a rejecting sink for any earlier mismatch. These five distinct situations require five states in a complete DFA. Including c in the alphabet makes the intended prefix language nonempty and the standard prefix-state construction applicable. A incorrect Three omits the accepting continuation and rejecting-mismatch situations. B correct Three incomplete-prefix stages plus accepting continuation and sink give five. C incorrect Four omits a necessary distinct situation in the complete DFA. D incorrect Six exceeds the five-state construction and is not minimal.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 109 · NS0174
records.text: NS0174 Question 109 AUT06 In a DFA, what happens after reaching a nonaccepting trap state while processing a finite input? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A It immediately accepts the input B It restarts processing from the initial state C It stays there for every remaining input symbol and rejects after the input ends. D It transitions to the initial state on the next input It stays there for every remaining input symbol and rejects after the input ends. A nonaccepting trap is a sink: every subsequent input symbol leaves the machine in that same state. It therefore cannot recover an accepting state. Once the finite remaining input is consumed, the DFA finishes and rejects. A self-loop transition does not imply an infinite computation after the input ends, nor does it restart processing or transfer to the start state. A incorrect The trap is nonaccepting, so it does not accept. B incorrect A sink stays in place rather than restarting. C correct It remains in the trap for the remaining symbols and rejects when input ends. D incorrect The next transition returns to the trap itself.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 110 · NS0175
records.text: NS0175 Question 110 AUT06 The transition function of a DFA is defined as: Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A δ: Q × Σ → Q B δ: Q × Σ → 2^Q C δ: Q × Σ × Γ → Q × Γ* × {L,R} D δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2^Q δ:Q×Σ→Q. AUT06 defines a total function from a state/input-symbol pair to one state. A set-valued codomain describes NFA choices; allowing epsilon in the input domain describes epsilon-NFA transitions. Stack alphabets and write/direction outputs belong to richer models and are not components of the ordinary DFA transition signature. A correct This is the exact state/symbol to unique next-state signature of a DFA. B incorrect A powerset codomain allows nondeterministic next-state choices. C incorrect The extra storage alphabet and write/direction outputs do not describe an ordinary finite automaton. D incorrect Epsilon input and set-valued successors describe an epsilon-NFA rather than a DFA.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 111 · NS0176
records.text: NS0176 Question 111 AUT03 AUT14 Which operation on regular languages gives all strings that are NOT in the original language? Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A Reverse (L^R) B Complement (Σ* - L) C Kleene Star (L*) D Concatenation Complement, relative to the fixed alphabet universe. AUT03 defines complement as Σ*−L and requires a fixed alphabet. This selects precisely the words in the universe absent from L. Reversal changes symbol order, star concatenates copies and concatenation joins words; none performs the required membership negation. Completing a DFA before swapping final states is the recognition construction in AUT14. A incorrect Reversal changes word order rather than selecting all words outside the language. B correct Complement contains exactly the universe’s words that are not members of L. C incorrect Kleene star concatenates zero or more language words and does not negate membership. D incorrect Concatenation joins words from languages rather than forming the universe-relative exclusion.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 112 · NS0177
records.text: NS0177 Question 112 AUT03 AUT02 The language L* (Kleene Star of L) is defined as: Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A L¹ ∪ L² ∪ L³ ∪ ... B L ∩ Σ* C All strings not in L D L⁰ ∪ L¹ ∪ L² ∪ ... (includes empty string because L⁰ = {ε}) The union of all nonnegative language powers. AUT03 defines L* by union over every n≥0, and AUT02 gives L⁰={ε}. Thus the zero power guarantees the empty word even when L is empty. A omits the zero power and instead describes positive closure; intersection with the universe and complement are different operations. A incorrect This omits L⁰ and defines positive closure rather than general Kleene star. B incorrect Intersecting a language with its word universe simply retains L. C incorrect All words outside L define complement, not repeated concatenation. D correct The nonnegative-power union is the definition and its zeroth term contributes epsilon.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 113 · NS0178
records.text: NS0178 Question 113 AUT09 In an NFA, the transition function maps each (state, input) pair to: Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A Exactly one next state B The initial state always C A SET of possible next states (including the empty set) D A symbol and a direction A set of possible successors, possibly empty. AUT09 defines an NFA transition as a mapping into the powerset of Q, so zero, one or several successors are permitted. The empty set represents a stuck branch, not an invalid machine. A uniquely determined singleton is only a deterministic special case; fixed resets and tape write/direction outputs do not describe the NFA signature. A incorrect One successor is permitted but not required; NFA transitions may have zero or several. B incorrect An NFA transition need not return to the initial state. C correct The powerset codomain permits any subset of states, including the empty set. D incorrect Write-symbol and direction outputs are tape-machine operations, not NFA state-set transitions.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 114 · NS0179
records.text: NS0179 Question 114 AUT09 An NFA accepts a string if: Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A ALL computation paths lead to an accepting state B AT LEAST ONE computation path leads to an accepting state C The majority of paths lead to accepting states D The last state visited is the accepting state At least one path consumes the whole word and finishes accepting. AUT09 states existential acceptance over finite computation paths, with the entire word consumed and permitted epsilon moves included. B expresses that existential condition, interpreted with the full-input requirement. Failed branches do not cancel an accepting branch, and counting a majority or asking every path to accept gives different, incorrect conditions. A incorrect Requiring all paths would wrongly reject words with one accepting branch and another failing branch. B correct One complete accepting path suffices; it must consume the whole input. C incorrect Path majority is irrelevant; the acceptance condition is existential rather than statistical. D incorrect There is no single global last state across nondeterministic branches, and unread input cannot be ignored.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 115 · NS0180
records.text: NS0180 Question 115 AUT09 AUT10 Which statement about DFAs and NFAs is CORRECT? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA recognizing the same language B NFAs are strictly more powerful than DFAs C DFAs can recognize languages that NFAs cannot D NFAs cannot recognize regular languages Every NFA has an equivalent DFA. AUT09 says both machine types recognize exactly regular languages, and AUT10 constructs equivalent DFA states as reachable NFA-state subsets. Nondeterminism may reduce representation size but does not add expressive power. Therefore A is true while each claim that one family recognizes languages inaccessible to the other is false. A correct Subset construction produces a DFA accepting exactly the NFA’s language. B incorrect Nondeterminism may improve succinctness but does not exceed regular-language power. C incorrect Every DFA is also an NFA special case, so no such exclusive DFA language exists. D incorrect NFAs recognize exactly the regular languages, the opposite of this claim.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 116 · NS0181
records.text: NS0181 Question 116 AUT09 What is an ε-transition in an NFA? Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model. A A transition that rejects the current input B A transition that only occurs at the end of input C A transition to the dead state D A transition that occurs without consuming any input symbol A move that consumes no input symbol. AUT09 explicitly defines epsilon moves as transitions without consuming input. They may occur before, between or after symbol-consuming transitions when the machine permits them. They do not inherently mean rejection or movement to a sink, and they do not waive the requirement that an accepting computation consume the full word. A incorrect An epsilon move is not intrinsically rejecting; its destination and later path determine acceptance. B incorrect Permitted epsilon moves can occur before or between input symbols as well as at the end. C incorrect Its destination need not be a dead state. D correct The machine changes state without consuming a symbol from the input.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 117 · NS0182
records.text: NS0182 Question 117 AUT10 When converting an NFA with n states to an equivalent DFA, the DFA may have at most how many states? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A n states B n² states C 2ⁿ states (the power set of Q) D n+1 states At most 2ⁿ states. AUT10 states the subset-construction bound explicitly. An n-element state set has 2ⁿ subsets, and each DFA state denotes one subset. Only reachable subsets need be included, so the bound need not be attained. Linear, quadratic and n+1 bounds are not general worst-case guarantees for NFA determinization. A incorrect A deterministic equivalent may require more than the original n states. B incorrect A quadratic bound does not cover the general powerset worst case. C correct There are 2ⁿ possible subsets of the n NFA states. D incorrect An n+1 bound is not sufficient for general subset construction.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 118 · NS0183
records.text: NS0183 Question 118 AUT12 What does the regular expression (0+1)*1 describe? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A All binary strings B All binary strings that END with '1' C All binary strings starting with '1' D All binary strings containing exactly one '1' All binary strings ending in 1. With + as union, (0+1)* generates any finite binary prefix, including empty. Concatenating the final 1 forces the whole word to end in 1. It does not constrain the beginning or total number of ones: 01 and 11 are included, while epsilon and words ending in 0 are not. A incorrect Epsilon and words ending in zero are binary strings excluded by the final mandatory 1. B correct An arbitrary binary prefix followed by 1 is precisely a binary word ending in 1. C incorrect The arbitrary prefix may begin with zero, as in 01. D incorrect The prefix may contain additional ones, so exactly-one is too restrictive.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 119 · NS0184
records.text: NS0184 Question 119 AUT13 Which regular expression describes the language of all strings over {a,b} with at least one 'a'? Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A (a+b)*a(a+b)* B b*ab* C (a+b)+ D a(a+b)* (a+b)*a(a+b)*. AUT13 gives this construction explicitly for at least one a. The middle a guarantees existence, while both stars permit additional a or b anywhere. b*ab* permits exactly one a; positive closure also permits all-b words, and a(a+b)* requires the first symbol rather than merely some symbol to be a. A correct The required middle a guarantees existence while unrestricted sides allow all other positions. B incorrect b*ab* excludes words with multiple a symbols and therefore denotes exactly one a. C incorrect Positive closure admits nonempty all-b words, which contain no a. D incorrect This requires a at the beginning and excludes valid words such as ba.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 120 · NS0185
records.text: NS0185 Question 120 AUT12 The regular expression 0*10* represents: Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A All binary strings B All binary strings starting with 1 C All binary strings containing exactly one '1' D All binary strings ending with '0' Exactly one 1, with any number of zeros on either side. AUT12 explicitly interprets 0*10* as exactly one 1. Both stars contribute only zeros, including none, so they cannot add another 1. The word 1 is accepted, while 11 and epsilon are not. No constraint forces the first symbol to be 1 or the final symbol to be zero. A incorrect Many binary words, including epsilon and 11, are excluded. B incorrect Leading zeros are permitted, so accepted words need not start with 1. C correct Only the mandatory middle symbol is 1; all other generated symbols are zeros. D incorrect The trailing zero star can be empty, so accepted words may end in 1.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 121 · NS0186
records.text: NS0186 Question 121 AUT15 Which of the following languages CANNOT be described by a regular expression? Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A All strings over {a,b} starting with 'a' B All binary strings of even length C All strings containing at least two 'b's D {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} — strings with equal a's and b's The equal-count language aⁿbⁿ is nonregular. AUT15 uses aᵖbᵖ and shows that pumping any permitted initial a block breaks equal counts. Classical regular expressions cannot describe this language. Starting with a fixed symbol, even length and a minimum number of b occurrences require only finite-state information, so the other descriptions are regular. A incorrect A fixed starting symbol can be recognized by finitely many prefix states. B incorrect Even length needs only two parity states and is regular. C incorrect Counting b occurrences up to a threshold of two needs finitely many states. D correct Unbounded equality of separated counts defeats regular pumping and therefore classical regular expressions.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 122 · NS0187
records.text: NS0187 Question 122 AUT05 In the Chomsky hierarchy, which grammar type corresponds to Finite Automata? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Type 0 — Unrestricted Grammar B Type 3 — Regular Grammar C Type 2 — Context-Free Grammar D Type 1 — Context-Sensitive Grammar Type 3 regular grammars. AUT05 directly pairs Type 3 regular grammars with finite automata. Other grammar types can generate regular sublanguages, but the question asks which family corresponds to the finite-automaton model, an exact-family comparison. Type 2, Type 1 and Type 0 correspond to progressively stronger stack, bounded-tape and unrestricted-tape recognition families. A incorrect Type 0 corresponds to unrestricted Turing recognition rather than exactly finite-automaton power. B correct Type 3 is the regular grammar family exactly matched by finite automata. C incorrect Type 2 corresponds to nondeterministic pushdown recognition. D incorrect Type 1 corresponds to nondeterministic linear-bounded recognition.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 123 · NS0188
records.text: NS0188 Question 123 AUT04 A formal grammar is defined as a 4-tuple G = (V, Σ, P, S). What does 'P' represent? Distinguish symbols, finite strings, their lengths and sets of strings. Apply the operation to its stated operands, including empty cases. A The set of all accepting states B The power set of the terminal alphabet C The set of production rules (A → β) D The pushdown stack alphabet The set of production rules. AUT04 defines V as variables, Σ as terminals, P as productions and S as the start variable. Productions specify the allowed rewriting steps used to generate terminal words. Accepting states and stack alphabets belong to machine definitions, while an alphabet powerset is not the meaning of P in this grammar tuple. A incorrect Accepting states are a recognizer component, not the production component of a grammar. B incorrect P is not the powerset notation for the alphabet in this tuple. C correct P denotes the allowed grammar-production rewrite rules. D incorrect A stack alphabet belongs to PDA storage rather than the grammar’s production set.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 124 · NS0189
records.text: NS0189 Question 124 AUT14 In a RIGHT-LINEAR grammar, production rules have the form: Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A A → aB or A → a (terminal before optional non-terminal on right) B A → Ba or A → a (non-terminal before terminal) C A → α where α is any string of terminals and non-terminals D αAβ → αγβ A→aB or A→a, with permitted ε rules where needed. AUT14 places the optional single variable at the right end after the terminal. That gives A; B is the opposite left-linear orientation. An unrestricted string on the right is CFG form rather than necessarily regular, and a context-sensitive rewrite with surrounding context is a different grammar restriction. Epsilon conventions are handled separately. A correct The optional nonterminal follows the terminal at the right end of the production. B incorrect Putting the nonterminal before the terminal gives a left-linear orientation. C incorrect An arbitrary right-hand string can contain multiple variables and need not be regular-grammar form. D incorrect The context-sensitive contextual rewrite is not the defining right-linear production form.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 125 · NS0190
records.text: NS0190 Question 125 AUT14 Which production rule form is VALID in a Context-Free Grammar but NOT in a Regular Grammar? Track mandatory symbols and factors that may repeat or disappear. Use short test words to check both directions of each proposed language description. A A → a B A → aB C A → ε D A → aBA (two non-terminals on right-hand side) A→aBA is context-free but not regular-grammar form. AUT14 explicitly identifies A→aBA as legal CFG form but not regular form. A CFG restricts the left side to one variable while permitting a variable/terminal string on the right. The other choices are regular productions or permitted epsilon cases. Two right-hand nonterminals violate the regular linear restriction. A incorrect A→a is an ordinary regular production as well as context-free. B incorrect A→aB is exactly a right-linear regular production. C incorrect An epsilon rule is allowed under the note’s regular-grammar convention. D correct The single-variable left side is CFG-valid, but two right-side variables violate regular linear form.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 126 · NS0191
records.text: NS0191 Question 126 AUT18 A grammar is said to be AMBIGUOUS if: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A It generates infinitely many strings B Some string in the language has more than one parse tree C It contains left-recursive production rules D It uses both left-linear and right-linear rules Some generated word has more than one parse tree. AUT18 defines ambiguity by two distinct parse trees for at least one word, equivalently two leftmost derivations. Infinite size, left recursion and mixed linear orientations concern other properties and do not establish this condition. One must exhibit competing trees, not merely different expansion orders of a single tree. A incorrect Infinite languages can have unambiguous grammars, so infinitude does not define ambiguity. B correct Multiple parse trees for one generated word are the precise ambiguity criterion. C incorrect Left recursion can encode unambiguous left associativity; it does not alone prove ambiguity. D incorrect Mixing linear orientations concerns grammar form and is not the parse-tree multiplicity definition.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 127 · NS0192
records.text: NS0192 Question 127 AUT16 In a derivation tree (parse tree), what do the LEAF NODES represent? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Non-terminal symbols that haven't been expanded yet B The start symbol S C Terminal symbols — the actual characters in the generated string D ε-transitions in the grammar Terminal symbols, with an explicit ε leaf where that convention is used. AUT16 describes complete parse trees with terminal leaves and sometimes an epsilon leaf for an empty production. Reading leaves left to right yields the generated word. Unexpanded variables belong to incomplete trees, and a start symbol is normally the root. Epsilon productions are not automaton transitions in this representation. A incorrect Unexpanded nonterminals indicate an incomplete tree rather than leaves of the completed derivation. B incorrect S is normally the root, not the general category of terminal leaves. C correct Terminal leaves spell the derived word; epsilon may be displayed for an empty production. D incorrect A parse tree records productions, not automaton epsilon-transition edges.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 128 · NS0193
records.text: NS0193 Question 128 AUT16 What is the key difference between left derivation and right derivation? Apply the stated transition, closure or equivalence rule step by step; distinguish a guaranteed bound from a value for one particular machine. A Left derivation always expands the LEFTMOST non-terminal; right derivation expands the RIGHTMOST B Left derivation produces left-linear grammars; right produces right-linear grammars C Left derivation is used only for regular grammars D They produce different final strings for the same grammar Expand the leftmost versus rightmost remaining nonterminal. AUT16 defines the two derivations by which remaining variable is rewritten. Both can describe the same final word and even the same parse tree. They do not determine whether the grammar itself is left-linear or right-linear, and the distinction applies to CFGs generally rather than only regular grammars. A correct The choice of the leftmost or rightmost remaining variable is the defining difference. B incorrect Derivation order does not convert the production system into a left-linear or right-linear grammar. C incorrect Leftmost derivation is used for context-free grammars generally, not only regular ones. D incorrect Different expansion orders can generate the same terminal word and the same tree.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 129 · NS0194
records.text: NS0194 Question 129 AUT17 AUT15 AUT05 The language {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} is: Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Regular — recognized by a DFA B Not a formal language C Context-Free but NOT Regular — recognized by a PDA, not a DFA D Context-Sensitive but not Context-Free Context-free but not regular. AUT17 generates aⁿbⁿ with matched recursive additions, using ab as the base for n≥1. AUT15 proves the family nonregular by pumping the initial a block. Thus a PDA suffices but a DFA does not. It remains a formal language and is also CSL, so a description denying context-freeness is wrong. A incorrect The regular pumping argument rules out any DFA for unbounded equal counts. B incorrect This is a precisely specified set of words and therefore a formal language. C correct A CFG/PDA handles matched counts, while the language is not regular. D incorrect It is context-sensitive too, but denying its context-free status is false.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 130 · NS0195
records.text: NS0195 Question 130 AUT05 Every regular language is a context-free language. This means: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Every CFL can be described by a regular expression B Any language recognizable by a DFA/NFA can also be recognized by a PDA C Regular grammars are more powerful than CFGs D CFGs and regular grammars generate the same set of languages A PDA can also recognize every DFA/NFA language. AUT05 places regular languages inside context-free languages, and AUT09 equates DFA with NFA power. Thus a PDA can recognize every finite-automaton language, for example by ignoring its extra stack. The containment is strict; it does not give regular expressions for every CFL or make regular and CFG language families equal. A incorrect The proper inclusion leaves CFLs that no classical regular expression describes. B correct Finite-automaton languages are included in the PDA-recognizable context-free family. C incorrect Regular grammars are less expressive, not more expressive, than CFGs. D incorrect The note gives a proper containment rather than equality of the two families.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 131 · NS0196
records.text: NS0196 Question 131 AUT21 AUT-S02 What additional component does a Pushdown Automaton (PDA) have that a Finite Automaton lacks? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A A set of accepting states B A transition function C An input tape D A stack (LIFO memory) A stack. AUT21 defines a PDA by adding a stack to finite control, with its own alphabet and initial symbol. Finite automata already have states, accepting states and transition rules and process input. The distinguishing unbounded LIFO storage is what supports matched-count recognition beyond finite-state memory. A incorrect Finite automata also have an accepting-state set. B incorrect Finite automata already use a transition function. C incorrect Both models process input; an input representation is not the added PDA memory. D correct The stack is the extra LIFO storage that distinguishes the PDA from finite control alone.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 132 · NS0197
records.text: NS0197 Question 132 AUT21 AUT-S02 The stack in a PDA operates as a: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure B First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure C Random access memory D Circular queue Last in, first out. AUT21 defines each PDA move using the current stack top and its replacement string. This top-only discipline means the most recently pushed item is the next removed: LIFO. A queue removes oldest items, random-access storage permits arbitrary addressing, and circular-queue organization is not the PDA stack model. A correct Top-only push/pop access removes the most recently pushed item first. B incorrect FIFO removes the oldest item and describes queue rather than stack behavior. C incorrect A PDA cannot arbitrarily access interior stack positions like random-access memory. D incorrect Circular queue organization does not express the top-only LIFO stack discipline.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 133 · NS0198
records.text: NS0198 Question 133 AUT21 A PDA formally defined as a 7-tuple includes which of the following that a DFA does NOT have? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A A set of states Q B An input alphabet Σ C A stack alphabet Γ and initial stack symbol Z D A set of accepting states F A stack alphabet and initial stack symbol. AUT21 gives the PDA tuple (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,Z₀,F). Compared with a DFA, Γ and Z₀ describe its added stack storage. States, input symbols and accepting states occur in both models. Their presence is not what expands the recognizer beyond finite-state control. A incorrect Both DFA and PDA models have a finite control-state set Q. B incorrect Both machines process symbols from an input alphabet Σ. C correct Γ and Z₀ specify stack storage, which an ordinary DFA lacks. D incorrect Accepting-state sets occur in both models and do not distinguish stack memory.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 134 · NS0199
records.text: NS0199 Question 134 AUT21 The transition function of a PDA takes which inputs and produces which outputs? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A (state, input) → next state B (state, input symbol or ε, top of stack) → (new state, new stack string) C (state, input) → set of states D (state, stack top, next input) → (write symbol, direction) State, input-or-ε and stack top map to possible new states and replacement stack strings. AUT21 defines a PDA move by the current state, consumed symbol or epsilon and top stack symbol. Its possible outputs combine a new state with a replacement stack string. Set-valued nondeterminism is understood even though B abbreviates an individual result. The alternatives lacking stack access or using tape directions describe other models. A incorrect This omits the stack top and replacement string essential to PDA behavior. B correct This includes the current stack top and replacement string; nondeterminism permits a set of such results. C incorrect A state-set output without stack operations describes finite-state nondeterminism instead. D incorrect Writing a tape symbol and moving a head is TM-style machinery, not PDA stack replacement.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 135 · NS0200
records.text: NS0200 Question 135 AUT22 AUT15 Which of the following languages can a PDA recognize but a DFA CANNOT? Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A All binary strings ending with '1' B All strings over {a,b} starting with 'ab' C {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} — strings with equal number of a's and b's D All strings of even length over {a,b} The nonregular equal-count language aⁿbⁿ. AUT22 supplies the push-one/pop-one PDA procedure for equal a/b counts, and AUT15 excludes a DFA. Fixed suffixes, fixed prefixes and length parity require only finite memory, so both machine types can recognize those. C alone describes a language in PDA capability but outside DFA capability. A incorrect A fixed final symbol is a regular condition recognized by a DFA. B incorrect A fixed starting prefix needs only finitely many match stages and is regular. C correct A PDA matches unbounded equal counts using its stack, while regular pumping rules out a DFA. D incorrect Even length needs only a finite parity state, so a DFA already suffices.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 136 · NS0201
records.text: NS0201 Question 136 AUT25 AUT24 The language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is NOT a context-free language. This means: Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A It can be recognized by a PDA B It can be described by a context-free grammar C It is not a formal language D No PDA can recognize it; it requires at least a Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA) No PDA recognizes it; an LBA suffices in the listed hierarchy. AUT24 proves three equal counts non-context-free, and AUT25 recognizes them by marking matched triples within the input region. Thus no ordinary single-stack PDA recognizes the language, while an LBA does. It is still a precisely defined formal language; non-context-freeness is a family boundary rather than failure to be a language. A incorrect PDA-recognizable languages are context-free, contradicting the stated non-CFL property. B incorrect A CFG would make it context-free, which the pumping proof rules out. C incorrect It remains a formal language despite lying outside the context-free family. D correct No PDA suffices; bounded triple marking provides an LBA recognizer in the next listed family.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 137 · NS0202
records.text: NS0202 Question 137 AUT25 In a Context-Sensitive Grammar, the production rule αAβ → αγβ requires: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A |γ| < |A| (right side shorter than left) B |αγβ| ≥ |αAβ| (right side no shorter than left side) C α and β must be empty strings D γ must be a single terminal symbol The complete right-hand side cannot be shorter. AUT25 explains contextual rules with a nonempty replacement γ, equivalently noncontracting full-side length under the isolated epsilon convention. The comparison must include the complete left and right sides, making B correct. Context α and β need not vanish, and γ may contain more than a single terminal. A incorrect A shorter replacement contradicts the noncontracting context-sensitive requirement. B correct The full right-hand side must be at least as long as the full left-hand side. C incorrect Context can be present; requiring empty α and β is not the context-sensitive rule. D incorrect Gamma is nonempty but need not be exactly one terminal.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 138 · NS0203
records.text: NS0203 Question 138 AUT27 The Turing Machine transition function δ(q, a) = (p, b, L) means: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A In state q reading symbol a: go to state p, write b, move head LEFT B In state q reading symbol a: go to state p, write b, move head RIGHT C In state q reading symbol a: go to state p, push b onto stack, move LEFT D In state q reading symbol a: delete b, move LEFT, enter state p Write b, move left, and enter p after reading a in q. AUT27 directly interprets δ(q,a)=(p,b,L). The current scanned symbol a is replaced with b, the head shifts one cell left and control enters p. L fixes the direction; there is no stack push operation, and deletion is not the meaning of writing b. A correct This exactly preserves the specified new state, written symbol and leftward head movement. B incorrect R would indicate right movement; the given L specifies left. C incorrect The TM writes b on tape rather than pushing onto a separate stack. D incorrect The transition writes b; it does not mean delete b.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 139 · NS0204
records.text: NS0204 Question 139 AUT28 Which of the following is TRUE about Turing Machines? Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A A TM has a finite tape of fixed length B A TM can only move the head in one direction C A TM can simulate any algorithm — it is the most powerful computational model D A TM is equivalent in power to a PDA A TM models general effective algorithmic computation. AUT28 identifies Turing completeness with simulating general TM computation and relates effective procedures to the Church–Turing thesis. C expresses this ordinary model comparison, not omnipotence over undecidable tasks or a speed guarantee. A standard tape is unbounded, heads may move both directions, and TMs exceed single-stack PDA recognition power. A incorrect A standard TM tape is unbounded rather than fixed to a finite length. B incorrect Standard TM transitions may move the head left or right. C correct Under the effective-algorithm interpretation, TM computation captures general algorithmic procedures. D incorrect TMs recognize languages beyond the context-free languages of ordinary PDAs.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 140 · NS0205
records.text: NS0205 Question 140 AUT15 Which option summarizes the pumping lemma for regular languages, rather than a separate consequence for a chosen recognizing DFA? Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A Every string in L can be pumped to produce longer strings still in L B Any sufficiently long string s in L can be split as xyz where the middle part y can be 'pumped' (repeated any number of times) and stay in L C L is infinite if and only if a string in L is longer than the number of states D All strings in L have the same length Any sufficiently long string s in L can be split as xyz where the middle part y can be 'pumped' (repeated any number of times) and stay in L For each regular language there is a pumping length p. Every accepted word of length at least p has a decomposition xyz with |xy|≤p and |y|>0 such that xy^iz remains accepted for every i≥0. The threshold and nonempty repeated part matter; short words need not be pumpable. The infinitude criterion involving a DFA’s state count is a separate consequence, while a regular language can contain words of many different lengths. A incorrect The lemma applies only above a length threshold and pumps a suitable part, not every word without qualification. B correct This states the sufficiently-long-word split and repeatable middle part; the formal bounds are supplied in the explanation. C incorrect A fixed-DFA infinitude criterion is a consequence rather than the pumping lemma’s quantified statement. D incorrect Regular languages need not have constant word length; 0* contains arbitrarily many lengths.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 141 · NS0206
records.text: NS0206 Question 141 AUT24 The language L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is NOT context-free. Which technique proves this? Respect the quantifier order and length constraints. A valid nonmembership argument must address every allowed decomposition, not one convenient split. A The Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages B The Chomsky hierarchy alone C Constructing a PDA and showing it fails D The Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages — any pumping violates the equal-count constraint The CFL pumping lemma, defeating every permitted decomposition. AUT24 chooses aᵖbᵖcᵖ and shows the bounded vxy window cannot cover both a and c blocks. Pumping changes at most two counts or breaks block order, defeating every allowed decomposition. A failed individual PDA is not a proof against all PDAs, and regular pumping excludes only regularity, not the stronger CFL property. A incorrect Regular pumping disproves regularity and does not by itself establish non-context-freeness. B incorrect The hierarchy alone does not prove the specific language lies outside CFL. C incorrect Failure of one proposed PDA does not rule out every possible PDA. D correct The CFL pumping proof breaks every legal decomposition by changing counts or symbol order.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 142 · NS0207
records.text: NS0207 Question 142 AUT28 'Turing Completeness' means a system: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass. A Can simulate a Turing Machine and thus compute anything computable B Solves problems in polynomial time C Uses an infinite amount of memory D Is equivalent to a Pushdown Automaton Ability to simulate general Turing-machine computation. AUT28 defines Turing completeness by general TM simulation. This says which effective computations can be expressed, not whether they run in polynomial time. A finite execution uses finitely many cells even though the model permits unbounded memory. Single-stack PDA equivalence is weaker than Turing universality. A correct Simulation of general TM computation is the definition of Turing completeness. B incorrect Universality does not guarantee a polynomial-time algorithm for every computable problem. C incorrect A finite run need not and cannot literally use infinitely many cells. D incorrect An ordinary PDA has less expressive recognition power than a TM.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 143 · NS0208
records.text: NS0208 Question 143 AUT34 The complexity class P contains problems that are: Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A Hard to solve and hard to verify B Solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing Machine C Solvable only by nondeterministic machines D Requiring exponential space to solve Deterministic polynomial-time decidable problems. AUT34 defines P by deterministic polynomial-time decision relative to input length. It is a solvability upper bound, not a requirement of hardness, nondeterminism or exponential space. A problem in P may also have nondeterministic algorithms, but it is the existence of a deterministic polynomial-time decider that establishes membership. A incorrect P is defined by efficient deterministic decision, not by hardness of solving or verification. B correct This is the exact deterministic polynomial-time definition of P. C incorrect Problems in P have deterministic algorithms and are not solvable only nondeterministically. D incorrect Exponential space is not a requirement for a polynomial-time computation.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 144 · NS0209
records.text: NS0209 Question 144 AUT34 The key property of problems in class NP is: Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A They can be solved in polynomial time by a deterministic TM B They require exponential time to verify solutions C Given a potential solution, it can be VERIFIED in polynomial time D They require polynomial space but exponential time Polynomial-time verification of polynomial-size yes-certificates. AUT34 equates NP with polynomially verifiable yes-instances using polynomial-size certificates. A verifier must not certify no-instances. Polynomial-time deterministic solving defines P and is not known for every NP problem; exponential verification or execution bounds are not part of NP’s defining certificate condition. A incorrect Deterministic polynomial-time solution defines P; whether it covers all NP is unresolved. B incorrect NP verification is polynomial for an appropriate certificate rather than requiring exponential time. C correct A polynomial-size yes-certificate can be checked in polynomial time, the equivalent NP definition. D incorrect NP does not require exponential running time; it includes the polynomial-time languages.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 145 · NS0210
records.text: NS0210 Question 145 AUT36 If a problem is NP-COMPLETE, it means: Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A It is in NP but not in P B It is the easiest problem in NP C It is NP-hard but might not be in NP D It is both in NP AND NP-hard; every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time Both NP membership and NP-hardness under polynomial reductions. AUT36 defines NP-complete as being in NP and hard for every NP language under polynomial reduction. It does not assert exclusion from P, since P versus NP is open. NP-hard alone need not even be decidable, while complete problems are the hardest in NP under the stated reduction, not its easiest members. A incorrect NP-completeness does not prove exclusion from P; that would settle the open P-versus-NP question. B incorrect Completeness concerns hardness for the whole class, not easiest membership. C incorrect This describes NP-hardness without the required NP-membership condition. D correct Both membership and polynomial-reduction hardness for every NP problem are required.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 146 · NS0211
records.text: NS0211 Question 146 AUT-S03 AUT36 Which is an established reason for the foundational significance of Boolean satisfiability (SAT) in NP-completeness theory? Distinguish a foundational hardness proof, efficient certificate verification and an unproved efficient solving algorithm. A It was the FIRST problem proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem); every NP problem reduces to SAT B It can be solved in polynomial time C It is in class P D It requires exponential space to verify It was the FIRST problem proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem); every NP problem reduces to SAT The Cook–Levin theorem made SAT the first problem proved NP-complete: its proof encodes an arbitrary nondeterministic polynomial-time computation as a Boolean formula. Hence every NP decision problem has a polynomial-time reduction to SAT. This starts the chain of later hardness reductions. A satisfying assignment can be checked in polynomial time. Whether SAT itself has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is unresolved, so neither membership in P nor such an algorithm is an established reason. A correct Cook–Levin established the first NP-complete problem and reductions from every problem in NP. B incorrect A general deterministic polynomial-time SAT algorithm is not established; one would imply P=NP. C incorrect SAT membership in P is unresolved, so this is not an established statement. D incorrect An assignment can be verified in polynomial time, without requiring exponential verification space.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 147 · NS0212
records.text: NS0212 Question 147 AUT39 Which containment chain is established unconditionally, without assuming answers to the open equalities among these classes? Here EXP means EXPTIME. Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A NP ⊆ P ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP B P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP C PSPACE ⊆ NP ⊆ P ⊆ EXP D EXP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ NP ⊆ P P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME. The established resource-class chain is P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME. These subset relations need not all be strict: the adjacent equalities named in the note remain unresolved. A reverse relation such as NP⊆P cannot therefore be selected as an unconditional theorem. Reversing the entire chain would additionally put EXPTIME inside P, contradicting the known strict separation P⊊EXPTIME. The revised scope asks for proved inclusion, not for a speculative equality. A incorrect This includes NP⊆P, which would settle the open P-versus-NP question rather than state a known unconditional chain. B correct P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME is the established chain. C incorrect This requires reverse containments that are not established unconditionally. D incorrect Reversing the entire chain would imply EXPTIME⊆P, contradicting the known strict time-hierarchy separation.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 148 · NS0213
records.text: NS0213 Question 148 AUT35 If problem A is REDUCIBLE to problem B in polynomial time (A ≤ₚ B), what can we conclude? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A A is at least as hard as B B A and B are in the same complexity class C B is at least as hard as A; an efficient algorithm for B gives an efficient algorithm for A D B can be solved in the same time as A B is at least as hard as A; solving B efficiently solves A efficiently. AUT35 defines A≤pB by a polynomial-time transformation preserving membership. Compute that transformation and run B’s algorithm to solve A. Therefore the target B is at least as hard under this reduction. The reduction does not force equal complexity classes, a reverse reduction or an algorithm for B from A alone. A incorrect This reverses the hardness direction implied by reducing A to B. B incorrect A one-way reduction does not place both languages in the same complexity class. C correct The polynomial mapping followed by a fast B solver gives a fast A solver. D incorrect A solver for A alone does not invert the reduction to provide a B solver.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 149 · NS0214
records.text: NS0214 Question 149 AUT36 For standard finite encoded instances, how is the exact optimization task of finding a shortest tour visiting every city once and returning to the start classified? Separate resource bounds, certificate verification and reduction requirements. Use proved containments without assuming unresolved class separations. A P — solvable efficiently B PSPACE-complete C Not a formal computational problem D NP-hard; this classification does not establish an exponential-time lower bound. NP-hard; this classification does not establish an exponential-time lower bound. Finding the shortest tour is an optimization problem and is NP-hard. The related question whether a tour of cost at most a given bound exists is a decision problem and is NP-complete. These statements do not prove that every exact algorithm must take exponential time or resolve P versus NP. The option retains the established hardness classification without overstating a lower bound. A incorrect A general polynomial-time exact algorithm is not the classification established in the note. B incorrect PSPACE-complete is not the supplied classification of this optimization task. C incorrect The finite encoded task is a well-defined computational optimization problem. D correct Shortest-tour optimization is NP-hard; hardness alone gives no exponential lower bound.

records.title: Automata and Complexity Theory — Question 150 · NS0215
