records.title: Compiler Design — Question 1 · Q01406
records.text: Q01406 Question 1 COMP10 Which grammar gives multiple parse trees for the same string? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Unambiguous B Regular C Ambiguous D All of the above An ambiguous grammar. COMP10 defines ambiguity by the existence of one terminal string with two different parse trees. This is exactly the property asked for. An unambiguous grammar excludes it. Being regular describes a grammar class rather than guaranteeing multiple trees, so it does not make all the listed descriptions correct. A incorrect Unambiguous means each generated string has a unique parse tree, directly contradicting the property. B incorrect Regularity restricts grammar form; it does not require multiple parse trees for a string. C correct Ambiguity is precisely the existence of multiple parse trees for the same terminal string. D incorrect Unambiguous grammars do not have the stated property, so all cannot be correct.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 2 · Q01416
records.text: Q01416 Question 2 COMP09 Leaf nodes in a parse tree indicate? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A sub-terminals B half-terminals C non-terminals D terminals terminals PDF p. 9 explicitly states that internal nodes are non-terminals and leaves are terminals. Thus the leaf labels in this module’s derivation trees are terminals, not the grammar variables expanded at internal nodes. A incorrect Sub-terminals is not a category in the module’s CFG or tree definitions (p. 9). B incorrect Half-terminals is not a category in those definitions (p. 9). C incorrect Non-terminals label internal nodes, not leaves (p. 9). D correct The module expressly assigns terminals to leaves (p. 9).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 3 · Q00047
records.text: Q00047 Question 3 COMP04 COMP09 Which one of the following is not the task of lexical analyzer? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Group characters into lexemes B Output a sequence of tokens C Read the input characters D Build syntax tree Build syntax tree Scanning reads characters and represents matched lexemes as tokens (PDF pp. 5, 8). Syntax analysis then groups those tokens and produces a parse tree. Building that tree is therefore the non-lexical task. A incorrect Grouping characters into matched lexemes belongs to scanning (pp. 5, 8). B incorrect A sequence of tokens is the scanner’s stated output (p. 8). C incorrect Reading the stream of source characters is explicitly lexical analysis. D correct Constructing the syntactic tree belongs to syntax analysis.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 4 · Q00054
records.text: Q00054 Question 4 COMP09 COMP39 Which statement is false about a compiler parser that constructs a parse tree and supports syntax-error diagnosis and recovery? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Parser builds the parse tree B Parser attempts to correct or recover few errors C Parser cannot perform context free syntax analysis D Parser produces appropriate error messages Parser cannot perform context free syntax analysis A parser analyzes the token stream against the context-free syntax and builds its structural representation. In a compiler with syntax diagnostics and recovery, it can report an unexpected token and try to resume at a useful boundary. Therefore the claim that it cannot perform context-free syntax analysis reverses its defining role. Building a parse tree, reporting syntax errors and attempting the specified recovery behavior are compatible responsibilities. A incorrect Building a parse tree represents the grammar structure recognized by syntax analysis. B incorrect Error recovery may skip to a synchronization token or make a limited local repair. C correct Context-free syntax analysis is the parser’s defining task, so denying it is false. D incorrect Syntax diagnostics identify unexpected or missing tokens with useful source locations.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 5 · Q00058
records.text: Q00058 Question 5 COMP25 For an infix source expression targeting a postfix stack evaluator, which notation conversion prepares it for evaluation? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Convert infix notation to postfix notation B Convert postfix notation to prefix notation C Evaluate infix notation to prefix notation D Convert postfix to infix notation Convert infix notation to postfix notation A postfix evaluator reads operands before the operator that combines them. Converting an infix expression to postfix therefore supplies the required input order for the specified stack target. For example, the tree for a−4+c yields a 4 − c + in postorder. This is a choice of representation for this evaluator, rather than a mandatory strategy for every compiler. A correct Infix-to-postfix supplies the required target order. B incorrect Neither source nor target matches this direction. C incorrect Prefix is not the specified target. D incorrect This reverses the specified translation direction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 6 · Q00335
records.text: Q00335 Question 6 COMP30 COMP32 COMP31 Which named transformation directly replaces an expression whose operands are compile-time constants with its computed value? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Pee hole optimization B Constant folding C Invariant computation D Code hoisting Constant folding Constant folding evaluates an expression from operands known at compilation and substitutes its value, such as replacing 3*4 with 12. This removes that expression’s run-time arithmetic. A peephole pass describes a small inspection region and may perform several transformations; it is not the particular evaluation rule. Loop-invariant computation can remain unknown until execution, and hoisting moves safe invariant work rather than necessarily computing a compile-time value. A incorrect Peephole identifies a short-window optimization method, not specifically constant-expression evaluation. B correct Constant folding computes a known constant expression during compilation. C incorrect An invariant may depend on a run-time input even though it stays unchanged across a loop. D incorrect Hoisting moves a computation to a preheader; it need not evaluate it at compilation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 7 · Q00337
records.text: Q00337 Question 7 COMP24 Which listed deterministic parser families can evaluate synthesized attributes for suitable grammars and semantic actions? Select all that apply. Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Ambiguous grammar B LR grammar C LL grammar D None LR grammar; LL grammar Synthesized attributes flow from child nodes to their parent. LR parsers naturally compute these during reduction, after the right-hand-side children have been recognized. Suitable LL implementations can also compute them after their recursive child calls return. Ambiguity is a property of grammar interpretation, not a deterministic parser family or attribute-evaluation method. Thus both LR and LL are valid families for this task. A incorrect Ambiguity is not a deterministic parser family or evaluation mechanism. B correct LR reduction actions can compute parent values from children. C correct Suitable LL actions can compute values after child processing. D incorrect Both LR and LL provide supported implementations.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 8 · Q00338
records.text: Q00338 Question 8 COMP05 Identifiers consist of one Letter followed by zero or more Letters or Digits. Which expressions denote exactly that language? Select all that apply. Here + means one-or-more, | alternation, and _ a literal underscore. Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A Letter(Letter+|Digit*)* B Letter(Letter|Digit)+ C Letter(Letter|Digit)* D Letter(_Digit)* Letter(Letter+|Digit*)*; Letter(Letter|Digit)* C directly expresses a leading letter followed by any sequence of letters and digits. A is equivalent: its outer star may take zero blocks, and repeated letter or digit blocks can generate every such suffix. B excludes a one-letter identifier because its suffix uses plus. D permits literal underscores and restricted digit blocks, so it does not denote the specified identifier language. A correct Its repeated blocks generate every allowed suffix, including the empty suffix. B incorrect The trailing plus excludes a one-letter identifier. C correct This directly states the required pattern. D incorrect Its literal underscores violate the specified alphabet and its restricted suffix misses identifiers.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 9 · Q00339
records.text: Q00339 Question 9 COMP09 What is the process of finding a parse tree for a string of tokens called? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Recognizing B Parsing C Tokenizing D Analyzing Parsing Parsing is explicitly the process of constructing a parse tree for a sentence generated by a grammar (PDF p. 10). That is the operation named in the question; token production precedes it (p. 8). A incorrect The module does not use Recognizing as the name of this construction (p. 10). B correct Parsing matches the express definition (p. 10). C incorrect Tokenizing produces the token stream, rather than its parse tree (p. 8). D incorrect Analyzing is a broad description; the defined specific process is Parsing (p. 10).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 10 · Q00340
records.text: Q00340 Question 10 COMP41 Which compiler phase groups source characters into lexemes and classifies them as identifier, keyword, literal or operator tokens? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Interpretation analysis B Lexical analysis C Syntax analysis D General syntax analysis Lexical analysis Lexical analysis groups the source character sequence into lexemes and emits token categories with attributes. Syntax analysis instead combines already recognized tokens into larger grammatical structures such as expressions and statements. Specifying characters and token categories resolves the original mixture of lexical classification and parsing terminology. The generic interpretation and syntax labels do not describe the requested character-to-token phase. A incorrect Interpretation executes a representation rather than classifying lexemes. B correct Lexical analysis turns character sequences into tokens. C incorrect Syntax analysis groups tokens into grammatical structures. D incorrect This syntax label concerns parsing rather than lexical classification.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 11 · Q00532
records.text: Q00532 Question 11 COMP34 For a register-based target compiler, which choice most completely lists general code-generator tasks? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Instruction selection B Register allocation and assignment C Instruction ordering D All All COMP34 separates selecting target operations, deciding storage in registers, assigning physical registers, and scheduling instructions. The three concrete choices name these standard code-generation tasks. Since the question offers an aggregate covering them, that aggregate is the complete answer; each individual choice supplies only part of the requested task list. A incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Instruction selection chooses which target instructions implement the intermediate operations. B incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Register allocation and physical assignment decide where values reside and which registers hold them. C incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Instruction ordering schedules computations while preserving data and control dependencies. D correct All three listed activities belong to the code-generator task set described in COMP34.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 12 · Q00537
records.text: Q00537 Question 12 COMP04 COMP41 What is the term for an actual occurrence of a character sequence in source text that matches a token pattern, such as total or 42? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Pattern B Lexemes C Tokens D All Lexemes A lexeme is the actual character sequence occurring in source text. A token is the category and optional attribute emitted for that occurrence, while a pattern defines which spellings are members of the category. For example, total is a lexeme classified as an identifier token. These are related but distinct objects, so the aggregate choice cannot name the concrete occurrence. A incorrect A pattern describes possible spellings. B correct Lexeme names the actual matched source sequence. C incorrect Token names the category and optional attribute. D incorrect The three concepts are distinct, not synonymous.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 13 · Q00561
records.text: Q00561 Question 13 COMP04 Which one of the following are the specific character strings that make up a token? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Token B Lexemes C Lexical units D Pattern Lexemes A lexeme is the sequence of characters matched by a pattern to form a token (PDF p. 8). A token instead denotes a class of similar lexemes, and a pattern specifies the rule. “Specific character strings” therefore identifies lexemes. A incorrect Token names the class in the module’s token/lexeme distinction (p. 8). B correct Lexemes are the actual matched sequences (p. 8). C incorrect Lexical units is not the defined name for specific strings in this passage (p. 8). D incorrect A pattern is the matching rule, not its particular match (p. 8).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 14 · Q00578
records.text: Q00578 Question 14 COMP21 Which one of the following are the program properties that can be checked at run time? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Static checking B Dynamic semantics C Other Static Checks D None Dynamic semantics Semantic checks are static when done during compilation and dynamic when done during run-time (PDF p. 14). Interpreting “Dynamic semantics” as the option’s name for run-time semantic checking, B fits; static checking and other static checks occur during compilation. A incorrect Static checking is done at compilation, not run-time (p. 14). B correct B corresponds to the module’s run-time dynamic semantic checks (p. 14). C incorrect Other static checks retain the compile-time timing (p. 14). D incorrect None does not fit because the dynamic check category is present (p. 14).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 15 · Q00610
records.text: Q00610 Question 15 COMP04 COMP39 For a language with insignificant whitespace and comments, which choice most completely lists the scanner’s secondary tasks? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Stripping out blanks, tabs, new lines B Stripping out comments C Error reporting D All All COMP04 says scanners usually skip whitespace and comments while retaining source positions. COMP39 adds that lexical analysis detects its own errors and that error handling is shared. These establish all three listed secondary scanner duties under the ordinary language convention. Layout-sensitive languages are an explicit exception in COMP04, not evidence that scanners never perform these tasks. A incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Ordinary scanners skip blanks, tabs and newlines while retaining positions; layout-sensitive languages need special handling. B incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Comments are normally discarded instead of being delivered as ordinary parser tokens. C incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Lexical errors require reporting, with positions retained to locate the offending source text. D correct Together the choices cover normal whitespace removal, comment removal and lexical error reporting.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 16 · Q00613
records.text: Q00613 Question 16 COMP24 Which one of the following is the parse tree showing the values of attributes at each node? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Inherited attribute B Synthesized attribute C Annotated parse tree D A&B An annotated parse tree. COMP24 directly calls a parse tree displaying computed attribute values an annotated parse tree. Inherited and synthesized classify how attribute information flows; neither is the name of the entire displayed tree. Combining those attribute categories still does not name the representation described in the question. A incorrect An inherited attribute carries contextual information; it is not a parse tree displaying values. B incorrect A synthesized attribute carries a value upward, rather than naming the annotated tree. C correct This is the note’s precise name for a parse tree showing attribute values at nodes. D incorrect Combining two attribute categories does not give the name of the displayed tree.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 17 · Q00631
records.text: Q00631 Question 17 COMP30 COMP31 Which one of the following can be applied directly after intermediate code generation to improve the intermediate representation? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Peephole optimization B Constant Propagation C Dead code elimination D All All Optimization changes intermediate code to remove inefficiencies (PDF p. 7). The module lists peephole transformations and constant propagation (p. 18), and elimination of never-executed or unreachable statements (p. 18). Each can improve an intermediate representation before target code is emitted; no exclusive ordering among those transformations is specified. A incorrect Peephole transformation improves instruction sequences (p. 18). B incorrect Constant propagation is a listed optimization technique (p. 18). C incorrect Removing unreachable intermediate statements is dead code elimination (p. 18). D correct All three fit the optimization of intermediate code described on p. 7.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 18 · Q00652
records.text: Q00652 Question 18 COMP19 COMP41 Which compiler structure associates declared identifier names or identities with attributes such as type, scope and storage location, irrespective of its container implementation? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Literal Table B Symbol table C Hash table D All Symbol table A symbol table maps identifier names or declaration identities to attributes such as type, scope and storage location. A hash table is one possible implementation of that mapping, not its semantic role. Literal tables concern literal values, and punctuation need not have symbol records at all. Restricting the question to identifier metadata avoids claiming that every token kind uses the same table. A incorrect A literal table concerns literal values. B correct The symbol table provides this mapping. C incorrect Hashing is an implementation technique rather than the semantic role. D incorrect The structures have different roles.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 19 · Q00754
records.text: Q00754 Question 19 COMP04 The output of lexical analyzer is* Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Syntax tree B Strings of characters C A set of tokens D set of regular expressions A set of tokens The output of lexical analysis is expressly a sequence of tokens (PDF p. 8). C is the only option naming that output, although “set” should be read informally: order matters, so the module’s precise word is sequence. A incorrect The parse tree is produced by syntax analysis. B incorrect Characters are the scanner input, not its classified output. C correct Tokens are the output elements (p. 8). D incorrect Patterns describe tokens; they are not the source-specific output sequence (p. 8).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 20 · Q00755
records.text: Q00755 Question 20 COMP26 COMP34 Which of the following is NOT the primary role of code generator in compiler design? * Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A instruction selection B Declaration of variables C instruction ordering D A Register allocation Declaration of variables Code generation lowers checked intermediate code into target operations. It selects instructions, allocates registers and orders instructions subject to dependencies. Declarations instead establish source names, types and storage information during analysis; generating code may use that information without declaring the variables again. Thus the declaration activity is outside the primary code-generator task set, while the other three choices describe target implementation decisions. A incorrect Instruction selection chooses target operations implementing the IR. B correct Processing source declarations belongs to analysis and symbol-table/type handling. C incorrect Instruction ordering schedules target computations while preserving dependencies. D incorrect Register allocation decides where intermediate values reside.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 21 · Q00756
records.text: Q00756 Question 21 COMP26 Which one of the following is different from the others? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A quadruples B triples C tree D indirect triples tree Quadruples, triples, indirect triples, trees and DAGs all implement three-address code (PDF p. 16). Quadruples and triples have numbered record fields, and indirect triples use pointers; tree is the hierarchical representation. C is the natural odd one out under that structural distinction. A incorrect Quadruples are instruction records with four fields (p. 16). B incorrect Triples are instruction records with three fields (p. 16). C correct Tree is the hierarchical structure among the options (p. 16). D incorrect Indirect triples retain a pointer-based triple representation (p. 16).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 22 · Q00757
records.text: Q00757 Question 22 COMP24 COMP25 COMP22 A compiler computes expression-type attributes and checks compatibility as grammar productions are processed. Which offered description most specifically identifies this mechanism? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A During lexical analysis B During syntax analysis C During syntax directed translation D During code optimization During syntax directed translation The compiler in the scenario evaluates type attributes and applies compatibility checks as grammar productions are processed. This is syntax-directed translation: semantic rules or actions are attached to grammatical structure. Pure lexical analysis only recognizes tokens, and pure syntax recognition alone does not establish operand-type compatibility. Optimization transforms an already analyzed representation. Parsing can invoke these semantic actions, so the mechanism is more precise than naming syntax analysis alone. A incorrect Token recognition alone does not compute full expression-type compatibility. B incorrect Pure syntax recognition checks grammar; the scenario additionally attaches semantic computations. C correct Syntax-directed semantic actions compute and check attributes associated with productions. D incorrect Optimization transforms analyzed code rather than naming the stated checking mechanism.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 23 · Q00758
records.text: Q00758 Question 23 COMP34 COMP26 In a conventional pipeline that lowers TAC further to native code or VM instructions, which representation is intermediate rather than the final emitted target? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A Three address code B Assembly language C Absolute machine code D Byte Code Three address code Three-address code is intermediate in the specified pipeline: analysis and optimization transform it before code generation lowers it further. Assembly, absolute machine code and VM bytecode can each be final target forms for an appropriate compiler. This pipeline-specific distinction does not assert that TAC could never be another translator’s target; it identifies the expressly stated intermediate role here. A correct TAC is lowered further in this pipeline. B incorrect Assembly can be a final emitted target. C incorrect Absolute machine code can be a final target. D incorrect VM bytecode can be a final target.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 24 · Q00759
records.text: Q00759 Question 24 COMP26 COMP34 Which of the following is NOT important property of intermediate code representation? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A Ease of generation B Ease of manipulation C Register allocation D Level of abstraction Register allocation An intermediate representation should be convenient to generate, analyze and transform, and its abstraction should suit optimization and target lowering. Those are design properties of the representation. Register allocation is an algorithmic backend task that chooses locations for values; it is not itself a property such as ease of generation or abstraction level. An IR can carry information useful to that task without making allocation a representation property. A incorrect Ease of generation is a useful IR design property. B incorrect Ease of manipulation supports analysis and transformation passes. C correct Register allocation is a backend decision over values rather than an IR property. D incorrect Abstraction level determines which source and target details the representation exposes.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 25 · Q00903
records.text: Q00903 Question 25 COMP24 What is the main purpose of syntax-directed translation in a compiler? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A To interleave semantic analysis with syntax analysis using attributes attached to grammar symbols B To generate optimized machine code directly C . To tokenize the source code D To replace the parser with a finite automaton To interleave semantic analysis with syntax analysis using attributes attached to grammar symbols A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes and rules; attributes attach to symbols and rules to productions (PDF p. 12). Actions execute according to the parsing mechanism. This is the grammar-based integration of semantic processing described in A, rather than a direct optimized-machine-code replacement for the remaining phases. A correct A matches the attribute/rule and parsing-action definitions (p. 12). B incorrect Machine-code conversion is a later code-generation task (p. 7), not the definition of SDT. C incorrect Tokenization is lexical analysis (p. 8). D incorrect The module retains the grammar/parsing mechanism; it does not replace it with an automaton (p. 12).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 26 · Q00908
records.text: Q00908 Question 26 COMP24 Straight directed translation uses: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Purely lexical rules B Backtracking algorithms C ¢. Grammar without attributes D Grammar with sematic rule Grammar with sematic rule Interpreting the apparent typo “Straight directed translation” as syntax-directed translation, the module defines it through actions on productions and a CFG with attributes and semantic rules (PDF p. 12). D is the only option that retains this grammar-plus-rule structure. A incorrect Pure lexical rules omit the production-associated semantic actions (p. 12). B incorrect Backtracking is not the defining mechanism; actions follow the chosen parser (p. 12). C incorrect A grammar without attributes omits the defining additions in a syntax-directed definition (p. 12). D correct A grammar with semantic rules matches the definition (p. 12).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 27 · Q00911
records.text: Q00911 Question 27 COMP11 COMP15 COMP-S01 Which one of the following is a top-down parser without backtracking? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LR parser B Brute force parser C Operator precedence parser D Predictive parser A predictive parser. COMP11 defines predictive parsing by choosing productions with lookahead without backtracking. This supplies both requirements in the stem: top-down direction and absence of backtracking. LR and operator-precedence parsing belong to bottom-up approaches; brute-force top-down trial does not provide the no-backtracking guarantee. A incorrect LR parsing reduces input bottom-up rather than expanding the start symbol top-down. B incorrect Brute-force production trials can require backtracking and do not meet the defining predictive constraint. C incorrect Operator-precedence parsing is a bottom-up technique rather than predictive top-down expansion. D correct Predictive parsing uses lookahead to choose productions without backtracking, exactly as COMP11 states.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 28 · Q00940
records.text: Q00940 Question 28 COMP25 If input is "a" is for syntax tree, which function is used to create tree? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A mknode(num, value) B mkleaf(num, value) C mkleaf(id, entry) D mknode(op, left, right) mkleaf(id, entry) For the expression a-4+c the first construction is P1=mkleaf(id,entrya) (PDF p. 13). Since a is an identifier, its node stores a pointer to the identifier’s symbol-table entry. Numeric leaf construction is instead used for 4; operator nodes connect child nodes. A incorrect The module uses mkleaf, not mknode, for a numeric constant, and a is not a number (p. 13). B incorrect This creates a numeric leaf, suitable for 4 rather than identifier a (p. 13). C correct This is exactly the identifier-leaf constructor used for a (p. 13). D incorrect This makes an operator node with two children, not an identifier leaf (pp. 12–13).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 29 · Q00945
records.text: Q00945 Question 29 COMP03 COMP34 Which statement is WRONGLY described about code generation? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation B The target program is the output of the code generator C Checked intermediate code is supplied as input to the code generator. D It used to produce the target code for three-address statements. Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation Lexical analysis begins the standard pipeline by recognizing tokens. Code generation occurs after analysis and IR construction, lowering checked IR to a target form. Its output is target code, which may be assembly or an object form, and it can translate three-address statements. Therefore calling code generation the start phase is the wrong description. The input option is read as checked IR suitable for lowering, without claiming a compiler can prove the absence of every program defect. A correct Code generation follows the frontend and IR; it is not the initial scanning phase. B incorrect The generator produces code in a target representation. C incorrect Checked intermediate code supplies the operations and metadata to lower. D incorrect Three-address statements can be lowered into target instructions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 30 · Q00973
records.text: Q00973 Question 30 COMP04 COMP09 Which of the following is NOT a task of the lexical analyzer? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Generating parse trees B Correlating errors with line numbers C Entering identifiers into the symbol table D Stripping whitespace and comments Generating parse trees Scanning turns characters into tokens, usually skips insignificant whitespace and comments, and retains source positions for diagnostics. A scanner may also intern identifier spellings in a symbol table; later semantic processing adds scope and declaration information. Parse-tree construction belongs to syntax analysis because it arranges the token stream according to grammar productions. It is consequently the activity outside the scanner’s listed responsibilities. A correct Parse trees represent grammar structure built by parsing. B incorrect Tracking token positions and line numbers supports scanner diagnostics. C incorrect Scanner-side interning can enter identifier spellings, distinct from later declaration analysis. D incorrect Ordinary scanners discard insignificant whitespace and comments.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 31 · Q01165
records.text: Q01165 Question 31 COMP04 Which analysis used to read the sequence of the characters from the source program? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A a | Lexical Analysis A B i? Syntax Analysis >< C /@| Semantic Analysis x D | All of the above x a | Lexical Analysis A PDF p. 5 explicitly says lexical analysis scans source code as a stream of characters; syntax groups tokens, and semantics checks meaningful compatibility (p. 6). A correct Lexical analysis explicitly reads the character stream. B incorrect Syntax analysis works on tokens grouped hierarchically. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 32 · Q01193
records.text: Q01193 Question 32 COMP11 COMP15 What is the bottom-up parsing method also known as? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 33 · Q01222
records.text: Q01222 Question 33 COMP07 How many tokens are in the C++ loop header for (int i = 0; i <= 10; i++)? Ignore whitespace and count <= and ++ as single operator tokens. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 42 · Q01403
records.text: Q01403 Question 42 COMP-S01 COMP17 Among these named deterministic parser methods, which has the broadest grammar coverage under the standard SLR(1), LALR(1) and canonical LR(1) comparison? A incorrect LALR is an LR bottom-up family, using merged LR item states. B incorrect LR recognizes input through bottom-up shifts and reductions. C incorrect Operator-precedence parsing reduces expressions bottom-up rather than expanding productions top-down. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 55 · Q01420
records.text: Q01420 Question 55 COMP26 In the compiler, the function of using intermediate code is: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A to improve the register allocation B to increase the error reporting & recovery. C to make semantic analysis easier. D to increase the chances of re-using the machine-independent code optimizer in other compilers. Reuse the machine-independent optimizer across compilers. COMP26 explains that IR separates source analysis from target implementation, making optimizers and backends reusable. This directly supports reusing a machine-independent optimizer in different compilers. An IR can support allocation and analysis, but none of the other proposed improvements is its defining architectural function, nor does merely introducing IR guarantee them. A incorrect Allocation may analyze IR, but improved allocation is not the portability function identified here. B incorrect Error reporting and recovery are shared compiler services, not the defining purpose of introducing IR. C incorrect Semantic analysis normally establishes source correctness before lowering; IR is not introduced chiefly to simplify it. D correct Separating source and target through IR enables reuse of machine-independent optimization passes.

records.text: Q01421 Question 56 COMP32 How many categories result when optimizations are divided solely by whether they depend on the target machine? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A two types B three types C four types D five types two types The stated criterion divides optimizations into machine-dependent and machine-independent categories, giving two categories. Other taxonomies use different criteria, such as local, global and loop scope, and need not have the same count. Individual transformations are not additional categories under this binary division. Naming the criterion fixes the count without claiming a universal number of optimization types across all classifications. A correct The two categories are machine-dependent and machine-independent. B incorrect Three fits another possible scope taxonomy. C incorrect This binary division does not yield four categories. D incorrect This binary division does not yield five categories.

records.text: Q01425 Question 59 COMP12 Which phenomenon happens when the non-terminal on the left side is repeated as the first symbol on the right side? records.title: Compiler Design — Question 65 · Q01436
records.text: Q01436 Question 65 COMP35 Which algorithm invokes a function GETREG()? Code motion and general optimization serve other transformation purposes; intermediate code is the input representation here rather than the algorithm making the register choice. B incorrect Optimization is broader, but COMP35 specifically locates getReg in the target code-generation algorithm. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 66 · Q01438
records.text: Q01438 Question 66 COMP34 The execution time of the code depends on? Select the most complete choice. Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A the usage of machine idioms B the way the registers are used C the orders in which the computations are performed D All of the mentioned All of the mentioned COMP34 states that machine idioms, register availability and instruction order affect execution time. These correspond to all three concrete choices. Better register use can reduce loads/spills; target idioms affect instruction cost, and legal scheduling changes execution efficiency. The aggregate is therefore the complete response rather than any one factor in isolation. A incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Choosing target machine idioms changes the operations emitted and their target costs. B incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. Register use affects memory traffic and spills, which can change execution time. C incorrect True as one component, but incomplete as the requested full selection. The scheduling of computations affects execution efficiency while dependencies constrain legal orders. D correct COMP34 explicitly includes all three factors, so the aggregate is the complete answer.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 67 · Q01439

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 68 · Q01440
records.text: Q01440 Question 68 COMP35 Which of the following term is used to keep track of the location where the current values of the name are stored? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Register descriptor B Address descriptor C Allocation descriptor D Flag register An address descriptor. COMP35 defines an address descriptor for a name as recording all current locations that contain its value, including memory and registers. That matches tracking where a name’s current value is stored. A register descriptor instead records values held in a particular register, reversing the direction of the association. A incorrect A register descriptor maps a register to its current values rather than a name to all locations. B correct An address descriptor records the current memory and register locations holding a name’s value. C incorrect Allocation descriptor is not the note’s defined bookkeeping structure for name-to-location tracking. D incorrect A flag register stores machine status flags rather than all locations of a named value.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 69 · Q01441
records.text: Q01441 Question 69 COMP09 In a nontrivial expression AST whose leaves are operands, which complete category of nodes carries operator symbols, including operators in nested subexpressions? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Root B Interior nodes C Leaves D Nodes Interior nodes In an expression AST, leaves carry operands such as identifiers and constants, while nonleaf nodes carry the operators that combine child expressions. A nontrivial tree’s root can also be an operator, but naming only the root omits nested operators. Naming all nodes includes operand leaves. The complete category requested is therefore the interior nodes, which includes an operator root and any other nonleaf operator nodes. A incorrect The root alone omits operators in nested subexpressions. B correct Interior nodes are the complete nonleaf category carrying operators in this expression AST. C incorrect Leaves carry operands rather than combining operators. D incorrect All nodes includes operand leaves and is too broad.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 70 · Q01443
records.text: Q01443 Question 70 COMP19 COMP03 Which of the following is used in various stages or phases of the compiler? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Records B Program C Symbol Table D Table Symbol Table The module stores semantic type information in the symbol table (PDF p. 6), puts identifier-entry pointers in syntax-tree leaves (p. 13), and enters names/types during declarations (p. 17). These uses support the symbol table as a shared structure across compiler work. A incorrect Records is only a generic storage term, not the shared named structure in these passages. B incorrect Program is the object being compiled, not the metadata table. C correct Symbol Table is explicitly used in several contexts (pp. 6, 13, 17). D incorrect Table is nonspecific; Symbol Table is the documented structure.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 72 · Q01445
records.text: Q01445 Question 72 COMP09 What is the conventional name for the compact expression representation with operand leaves and operator interior nodes? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Syntax tree B Parser tree C Structured tree D Sematic tree Syntax tree The conventional expression AST places operands at leaves and operators at interior nodes, removing grammar scaffolding and punctuation. A parse tree instead records grammar productions: its internal nodes are nonterminals, and its yield includes the terminals of the source phrase. The other two names do not identify the conventional expression representation in this comparison. The syntax-tree choice supplies the specific structure described by the question. A correct An expression syntax tree places operands at leaves and operators at nonleaf nodes. B incorrect A parse tree’s internal labels are grammar nonterminals, not generally expression operators. C incorrect This generic phrase does not specify the conventional expression AST representation requested. D incorrect Semantic annotation can be attached to representations, but this is not the conventional name for the described AST.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 74 · Q01447
records.text: Q01447 Question 74 COMP25 Which mapping is described by the implementation of the syntax-directed translator? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Parse table B Input C Output D Input-Output An input-to-output mapping. COMP25 distinguishes translation from recognition: semantic actions compute an output, such as values, ASTs or code, from an input program. Accordingly the implemented translator defines an input-to-output mapping. A parse table may drive an implementation, but neither the table nor either endpoint alone names that mapping. A incorrect A parse table can guide recognition; it is not the translation mapping itself. B incorrect Input is only the domain side and omits the translated result. C incorrect Output is only the result side and omits the mapping from source inputs. D correct Syntax-directed translation relates each processed input to its computed translation output.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 75 · Q01448
records.text: Q01448 Question 75 COMP16 Which transition function moves the dot over a grammar symbol and takes closure to build successor states in the canonical LR(0) item collection? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A FIRST B GOTO C COMPUTE D FOLLOW GOTO GOTO(I,X) advances the dot over X in eligible items and then takes closure, producing a successor item state. Repeating this over grammar symbols builds the canonical collection. The collection is the resulting set of item sets, not the function itself. FIRST and FOLLOW compute terminal sets for different parsing purposes; COMPUTE does not name the defined LR successor operation. A incorrect FIRST finds possible beginning terminals. B correct GOTO produces the successor item state. C incorrect COMPUTE is not the defined successor-state function. D incorrect FOLLOW finds possible following terminals.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 76 · Q01449
records.text: Q01449 Question 76 COMP15 Which of the following option is not a function of the shift-reduce parser? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Reduce B Accept C Go D Shift “Go” is not a standard shift-reduce ACTION. COMP15 lists shift, reduce, accept and error as standard shift-reduce actions. GOTO is essential after a reduction but is separate table machinery, not a distinct action called Go. Reading function as the standard action category yields the offered Go choice; the three other choices are explicitly standard actions. A incorrect Reduce is a standard action that replaces a recognized right-hand side by its left-hand nonterminal. B incorrect Accept is a standard action indicating successful completion of recognition. C correct Go is not one of the standard ACTION names; GOTO is separate transition-table machinery. D incorrect Shift is a standard action that consumes input and pushes a token with its state.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 77 · Q01450
records.text: Q01450 Question 77 COMP18 Which listed grammar classes guarantee no adjacent nonterminals on a production right-hand side? Select all that apply. Regular means consistently right-linear; irregular means arbitrary unrestricted. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Arbitrary unrestricted grammar B Right-linear regular grammar C Operator grammar Right-linear regular grammar; Operator grammar An operator grammar explicitly forbids adjacent nonterminals on a right-hand side. A consistently right-linear regular grammar has at most one nonterminal in such a rule, so it also guarantees the restriction. Arbitrary unrestricted grammars have no comparable adjacency guarantee. The property is therefore shared by the two specified classes and cannot be used to identify only operator grammar. A incorrect An unrestricted grammar can contain adjacent nonterminals. B correct A right-linear regular rule has at most one nonterminal. C correct Operator grammars forbid adjacent nonterminals by definition.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 78 · Q01488
records.text: Q01488 Question 78 COMP19 COMP04 In an implementation where the scanner interns identifier spellings in a symbol table before returning their tokens, which phase first interacts with that table? Under this explicit implementation convention, scanning is the first phase to interact with the table. Parsing and semantic analysis use or enrich this information later; semantic analysis resolves declaration identity and type. This establishes an ordering for the stated implementation rather than a universal compiler requirement. A incorrect Syntax analysis receives tokens after this scanner has interned identifiers. B incorrect Parsing is syntax analysis and occurs after the stated interning. C correct Scanning performs the stipulated initial interning. D incorrect Semantic analysis enriches name/type information after that initial interaction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 81 · SM0026
records.text: SM0026 Question 81 COMP30 COMP31 For const int x=8; const int y=16; if(x>y){int z=x+y;}, which techniques directly apply to evaluating the condition from known constants and removing its unreachable branch? Select all that apply. Distinguish constant evaluation from algebraic identity simplification. Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Arithmetic simplification B Dead code elimination C Code motion D Compile time evaluation Dead code elimination; Compile time evaluation With x=8 and y=16, the condition x>y evaluates to false during compilation. The branch body is consequently unreachable and can be removed. These are compile-time evaluation and dead-code elimination, respectively. No computation needs to move to another program location, and the decisive evaluation is not an algebraic identity such as x+0→x. Both direct transformations belong in the answer. A incorrect No algebraic identity rewrite is the decisive step. B correct The constant-false branch is unreachable and removable. C incorrect Code motion does not describe evaluating or deleting the branch. D correct Known constants permit compile-time evaluation of the condition.

records.text: SM0216 Question 85 COMP24 COMP09 Which output does syntax analysis produce when it retains every grammar production and terminal occurrence, including punctuation, without semantic attribute annotation? records.title: Compiler Design — Question 86 · SM0219
records.text: SM0219 Question 86 COMP11 COMP15 For a fixed suitable grammar, which listed approaches can be efficient top-down parsers using prediction without backtracking? Select all that apply. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Recursive-descent parser B Shift-reduce parser C Non-recursive predictive parser D LR parser Recursive-descent parser; Non-recursive predictive parser Recursive descent can use lookahead to predict productions without backtracking. Nonrecursive predictive parsing implements the same top-down strategy with an explicit stack and table. Both can run linearly for a fixed suitable grammar. Shift-reduce and LR instead work bottom-up, reducing input toward the start symbol, so they do not meet the specified parsing direction even if they are efficient. A correct Predictive recursive descent is a supported efficient top-down implementation. B incorrect Shift-reduce is bottom-up. C correct Nonrecursive prediction is a supported efficient top-down implementation. D incorrect LR is bottom-up.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 87 · SM0224
records.text: SM0224 Question 87 COMP41 COMP09 Which abstract data structure naturally represents hierarchical source-program constructs with parent/child relationships, as in a parse tree or AST? A 2D-array B Stack C Tree D Queue Tree A tree represents the hierarchy of program constructs through parent/child relationships. Parse trees preserve grammar detail, while ASTs retain the essential expression and statement structure. Arrays may implement node storage, and stacks or queues may support traversal, but those container roles do not make them the requested hierarchical model. The structure being represented, rather than the storage allocation technique, determines this answer. A incorrect A 2D array is not the requested abstract hierarchical model. records.text: SM0265 Question 89 COMP21 Which described check requires runtime values rather than being solely a static check? In D, the index depends on input and no static proof of its bounds is available. Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Type checking for compatibility B Uniqueness checks like redefined variables C Checking that break is inside an allowed loop or switch D Checking an input-dependent array index against runtime bounds, with no static proof available Checking an input-dependent array index against runtime bounds, with no static proof available Type compatibility, duplicate declarations and valid placement of break can be checked from the source program and its declarations. The specified array index depends on runtime input, and no static bounds proof is available, so its validity requires a runtime check. This does not claim that every memory access fault is inherently undetectable statically; the explicit value-dependent case supplies the distinction. A incorrect Type compatibility is a static semantic check. B incorrect Duplicate declarations can be checked statically within the relevant scope. C incorrect Placement in an allowed loop or switch is a static check. D correct The stipulated input-dependent bounds need runtime validation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 90 · SM0285
records.text: SM0285 Question 90 COMP02 Which tool is used to collect codes separately compiled or assembled in different object files into a file that is directly executable? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. An assembler translates assembly into object code before this combination. A loader places the resulting executable in memory and starts it. A preprocessor handles source directives before compilation. These tool roles distinguish object-file combination from translation, source expansion and program loading. A correct The linker combines object files, resolves symbols and performs relocation. B incorrect The loader maps an already produced executable into memory. C incorrect An assembler translates assembly source into object code. D incorrect A preprocessor handles source directives rather than combining object files.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 100 · AM0787
records.text: AM0787 Question 100 COMP10 For E→E+E|E*E|id, which technique resolves the ambiguity by requiring * to bind more tightly than + and both operators to associate left? records.title: Compiler Design — Question 104 · AM0793
records.text: AM0793 Question 104 COMP22 What is the main goal of the semantic analysis phase in compiler design? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. records.title: Compiler Design — Question 108 · AM0798
records.text: AM0798 Question 108 COMP26 What is the purpose of intermediate code in compiler design? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A To optimize the program's execution B To generate assembly code C To represent the program's semantics in a platform-independent form D To visualize the program's control flow Represent program meaning in a reusable, substantially platform-independent intermediate form. COMP26 identifies separation of source analysis and target implementation as IR’s architectural purpose, allowing reuse across targets. C expresses that purpose best. Optimization and assembly generation are operations enabled by the representation, while a control-flow graph is one possible representation aspect. Platform independence is a design benefit here, not a claim that every IR has no target details. A incorrect Optimization is enabled by IR, but it is not the general representational purpose distinguishing this choice. B incorrect Assembly is one possible later output; an IR need not be tied to assembly generation. C correct A reusable representation of program semantics separates front-end meaning from target-specific implementation. D incorrect Control-flow visualization is one possible use and does not exhaust the purpose of IR.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 109 · AM0799
records.text: AM0799 Question 109 COMP06 Which of the following is used to generate a lexical analyzer for a programming language? Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A Finite Automaton B Context-Free Grammar C Pushdown Automaton D Turing Machine A finite automaton. COMP06 describes converting regular expressions to an NFA and then a DFA. This is the automaton construction used for ordinary generated token recognizers. CFGs and pushdown machinery address nested syntax rather than the regular token-pattern mechanism; a Turing machine is not the specific scanner model in the supplied construction. A correct NFA/DFA finite automata implement recognition of regular token patterns in the stated generator pipeline. B incorrect CFGs describe nested syntactic structure rather than the regular scanner-automaton construction. C incorrect Pushdown machinery adds a stack for context-free structure and is not the ordinary token-recognizer construction. D incorrect A Turing machine is more general but is not the specific model used in this scanner-generation pipeline.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 111 · AM0801
records.text: AM0801 Question 111 COMP05 COMP-S02 COMP09 Which listed notation directly specifies ordinary token patterns using alternation, concatenation and repetition, rather than a general production notation or a tree of one program? Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A Regular Expressions B Context-Free Grammars C Backus-Naur Form (BNF) D Abstract Syntax Trees (AST) Regular Expressions Classical regular expressions combine alternation, concatenation and repetition to specify ordinary token patterns. CFGs and BNF are production-based grammar descriptions and can also describe regular languages, so mere expressive capability would not distinguish them. An AST represents the analyzed structure of a particular program. The revised comparison asks for the direct pattern notation characterized by its operators, making regular expressions the specific answer. A correct Regular expressions directly use the stated pattern-combination operators. B incorrect A CFG is a general production grammar, not the direct expression notation described. C incorrect BNF is a notation for context-free productions. D incorrect An AST represents one analyzed program structure rather than the permitted token patterns.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 112 · AM0802
records.text: AM0802 Question 112 COMP18 COMP-S01 Which listed parsing approaches can handle arbitrarily nested parenthesized expressions for suitable grammars and stack-based implementations? Select all that apply. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LL Parsing B LR Parsing C Recursive Descent Parsing D Operator Precedence Parsing LL Parsing; LR Parsing; Recursive Descent Parsing; Operator Precedence Parsing Nested parentheses require remembering unfinished surrounding expressions. LL and LR parsers use a parsing stack, recursive descent uses the call stack, and suitable operator-precedence expression parsing also uses stack structure and precedence relations. Each can therefore handle the stipulated nested expressions for an appropriate grammar. The existence of nesting alone does not distinguish one of these parser families from the others. A correct LL can parse a suitable nested-expression grammar using its stack. B correct LR can recognize the nesting with bottom-up stack actions. C correct Recursive descent processes nested expressions through recursive calls. D correct A suitable operator-precedence parser supports parenthesized subexpressions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 113 · AM0803
records.text: AM0803 Question 113 COMP11 COMP15 Which parsing technique builds the parse tree from the bottom-up? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LL Parsing B LR Parsing C Recursive Descent Parsing D Top-Down Parsing LR Parsing LR parsing constructs the parse tree bottom-up, reducing handles that correspond to a rightmost derivation in reverse. LL methods construct from the start symbol toward the input and are top-down. Recursive descent normally implements one procedure per nonterminal, also expanding top-down. The generic top-down option states the opposite construction direction. These are implementation and derivation distinctions, not a ranking of their execution speed. A incorrect LL parsing expands a leftmost derivation from the start symbol. B correct LR parsing reduces input handles and builds bottom-up. C incorrect Recursive-descent procedures expand grammar nonterminals top-down. D incorrect Top-down construction starts from the root, the opposite direction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 114 · AM0804
records.text: AM0804 Question 114 COMP18 COMP-S01 COMP11 Which is the most specific listed name for a stack-based expression parsing method using pairwise operator-precedence relations in a suitable conflict-free operator grammar? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Precedence Parsing B Operator Precedence Parsing C LR Parsing D LL Parsing Operator Precedence Parsing Operator-precedence parsing applies precedence relations to a suitable operator grammar to choose expression parsing actions. The question specifies that concrete method rather than asking for a universal cure for shift/reduce conflicts. Precedence parsing is a broader label, while LR and LL name larger parser families without supplying these particular relations. Therefore B is the most specific match to the described technique. A incorrect Precedence parsing is broader than the specific method requested. B correct Operator-precedence parsing directly names this method. C incorrect LR alone does not specify the operator-precedence method. D incorrect LL alone does not specify the operator-precedence method.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 115 · AM0805
records.text: AM0805 Question 115 COMP18 COMP11 Which listed parsing categories have a standard table-driven implementation that uses lookahead to select the next parsing action? Select all that apply. For C, mean ordinary procedure-based recursive descent with choices encoded directly in code. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LL Parsing B LR Parsing C Recursive Descent Parsing D Top-Down Parsing LL Parsing; LR Parsing; Top-Down Parsing A nonrecursive LL parser consults a nonterminal/lookahead table to select productions. LR parsers use ACTION and GOTO tables for shifts, reductions and state changes. Table-driven predictive parsing is also a top-down implementation, so the broader D category applies. The stipulated ordinary recursive-descent alternative encodes decisions directly in procedures instead of consulting an explicit parsing table. Thus A, B and D are selected. A correct Table-driven LL selects productions from lookahead entries. B correct LR uses ACTION/GOTO tables. C incorrect The stipulated implementation encodes decisions in procedures rather than an explicit table. D correct Nonrecursive predictive parsing is a table-driven top-down method.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 116 · AM0806
records.text: AM0806 Question 116 COMP12 Which parsing technique is more suitable for handling left-recursive grammar rules? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LL Parsing B LR Parsing C Recursive Descent Parsing D Top-Down Parsing LR parsing. COMP12 states that suitable left-recursive grammars are handled by LR parsers, while ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever without consuming input. LL/top-down prediction generally needs left recursion removed first. This directly supports LR as the suitable choice, without claiming LR accepts every possible left-recursive grammar. A incorrect Ordinary LL prediction requires eliminating left recursion rather than directly exploiting it. B correct LR can directly handle suitable left-recursive grammar rules using bottom-up recognition. C incorrect Unmodified recursive descent can recurse indefinitely before consuming input on a left-recursive rule. D incorrect Ordinary top-down prediction needs recursion removal; it is not the suitable direct handling choice.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 117 · AM0807
records.text: AM0807 Question 117 COMP11 COMP15 Which of the following is not a top-down parsing algorithm? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Recursive Descent Parsing B LL Parsing C Predictive Parsing D LR Parsing LR Parsing Recursive descent, LL parsing and predictive parsing all expand productions from the start symbol toward the input. Predictive parsing uses lookahead to avoid backtracking, while a general recursive-descent implementation may backtrack. LR parsing instead shifts input and reduces handles to build structure bottom-up. Its construction direction therefore excludes it from the top-down family, independent of whether either implementation uses a stack. A incorrect Recursive descent expands nonterminal procedures from the start symbol. B incorrect LL constructs a leftmost derivation top-down. C incorrect Prediction chooses a top-down production using lookahead. D correct LR is bottom-up, reducing handles from the input.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 118 · AM0808
records.text: AM0808 Question 118 COMP18 Which listed method can retain multiple parse possibilities for a general ambiguous CFG rather than requiring an ordinary deterministic LL/LR grammar? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LL Parsing B Generalized LR parsing (GLR) C Recursive Descent Parsing D Top-Down Parsing Generalized LR parsing (GLR) A general ambiguous grammar has multiple parse trees for at least one input. Generalized LR parsing can handle those possibilities, whereas ordinary deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous. A separate disambiguation policy may still be needed to select intended meaning. Recursive descent and top-down labels alone do not provide a generalized multi-parse method, so the GLR alternative uniquely answers the question. A incorrect Ordinary deterministic LL requires an unambiguous predictive grammar. B correct GLR is the generalized method identified for ambiguous grammars. C incorrect Ordinary recursive descent alone does not specify a generalized multi-parse algorithm. D incorrect Top-down direction alone does not handle general ambiguity.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 123 · AM0813
records.text: AM0813 Question 123 COMP19 Which data structure is commonly used in symbol tables during the compilation process? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Stack B Queue C Hash Table D Linked List A hash table. COMP19 explicitly says a hash table offers expected constant-time insertion and lookup with suitable hashing. That makes it the conventional structure for the name-to-attribute mapping. A stack can organize nested scope tables, and lists are possible implementation choices, but the common keyed lookup structure asked for here is the hash table. A incorrect A stack manages nested scope order, while the keyed mapping within a scope commonly uses hashing. B incorrect FIFO queue order does not directly provide the keyed lookup role of a symbol table. C correct Hashing commonly implements efficient name-to-attribute insertion and lookup. D incorrect A linked list is possible but does not provide the expected constant-time keyed lookup highlighted in COMP19.

records.text: AM0814 Question 124 COMP30 Which phase of the compiler performs optimization techniques to improve the efficiency of the generated code? records.title: Compiler Design — Question 125 · AM0815
records.text: AM0815 Question 125 COMP30 COMP32 COMP03 Which of the following is not a typical optimization performed by a compiler? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Constant Folding B Loop Unrolling C Dead Code Elimination D Syntax Analysis Syntax Analysis Constant folding evaluates known expressions, loop unrolling replicates a loop body to reduce branch overhead, and dead-code elimination removes unnecessary computation when effects permit. Each transforms an existing program while preserving its required behavior. Syntax analysis instead checks and organizes grammatical structure in the frontend. It is necessary compiler work, but it is not an optimization transformation of the kind named by the other alternatives. A incorrect Constant folding replaces constant expressions with computed values. B incorrect Unrolling replicates loop iterations, handling remainders and code-size costs. C incorrect Dead-code elimination removes unreachable or unused effect-free computations. D correct Syntax analysis recognizes grammatical structure rather than optimizing code.

records.text: AM0816 Question 126 COMP34 Which phase of the compiler generates the target code? Identify each activity’s input and output. A Lexical Analysis B Syntax Analysis C Semantic Analysis D Code Generation Code Generation PDF p7 states that code generation converts intermediate code to machine code, the target in this question. A incorrect Lexical analysis emits tokens (p8). B incorrect Syntax analysis emits a tree (p5). C incorrect Semantic analysis checks compatibility (p6). D correct Machine-code output is the explicit code-generation role (p7).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 127 · AM0817
records.text: AM0817 Question 127 COMP26 Which of the following is an advantage of using an intermediate representation during the compilation process? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A Faster compilation speed B Improved error detection C Portability across different platforms D Reduced memory usage Portability across platforms. COMP26 explains that IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. This supports retargeting and portability across platforms. Introducing IR does not inherently promise faster compilation, better error detection or lower memory use; it can add processing stages and data structures while improving architecture. A incorrect An extra representation and processing stage do not inherently guarantee faster compilation. B incorrect Error detection depends on analyses and language rules; it is not the stated architectural advantage. C correct Separating source meaning from target lowering enables reuse across different platforms. D incorrect IR introduces storage and does not guarantee reduced compiler memory consumption.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 128 · AM0818
records.text: AM0818 Question 128 COMP39 What is the shared compiler service that supports detecting, recovering from and reporting lexical, syntax and semantic errors? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Lexical Analysis B Syntax Analysis C Semantic Analysis D Error Handling Error Handling Error handling and reporting is a shared service supporting multiple compilation phases. Scanning detects malformed tokens, parsing detects invalid token arrangements, and semantic analysis detects name, scope or type violations. These are contributors rather than one phase responsible for every error category. Naming the shared service makes D the appropriate complete answer without denying the diagnostic responsibilities of the other phases. A incorrect Lexical analysis handles lexical errors but is not the complete shared service. B incorrect Syntax analysis handles parsing errors but is not the complete shared service. C incorrect Semantic analysis handles semantic errors but is not the complete shared service. D correct Error handling names the shared support service.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 129 · AM0819
records.text: AM0819 Question 129 COMP25 Which of the following is true about syntax-directed translation? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A It only involves the lexical analysis phase. B It involves the generation of intermediate code from the parse tree. C It is concerned with the optimization of the generated code. D It is performed during the code generation phase. It can generate intermediate code using parse-tree structure and semantic actions. COMP25 says syntax-directed actions may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. Generating IR from grammatical structure is therefore a supported use of syntax-directed translation. B describes that standard use without limiting it to lexical analysis or a single final phase. Optimization may use other analyses, and syntax-directed translation is not defined solely by optimization. A incorrect Syntax-directed translation is tied to grammatical productions and semantic actions, not solely tokenization. B correct Semantic actions associated with parsed structure can compute and emit an intermediate representation. C incorrect Optimization is not the defining task; translation actions can construct many forms of semantic output. D incorrect It is not restricted to final target-code generation; actions can run while parsing and constructing IR.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 130 · AM0820
records.text: AM0820 Question 130 COMP24 What is the general defining role of semantic rules attached to productions in a syntax-directed definition, rather than one possible specialized use? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A To define the syntactic structure of the language. B To define computations of attributes such as types, values, environments and generated code. C To perform optimization techniques on the intermediate code. D To define the order of evaluation of expressions. To define computations of attributes such as types, values, environments and generated code. The grammar productions define syntactic structure, while semantic rules define computations of attributes associated with grammar symbols. Those attributes may represent types, values, environments or generated code. Assigning types and constraining evaluation dependencies are examples rather than exhaustive definitions. Optimization may occur in a particular translation, but is not the general defining role of all such rules. A incorrect Productions, rather than semantic rules, specify the grammatical structure. B correct Computing attributes is the general defining role. C incorrect Optimization is a possible specialized transformation, not the general definition. D incorrect Evaluation order is a specialized concern rather than the complete role.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 131 · AM0821
records.text: AM0821 Question 131 COMP22 Which phase of the compiler is responsible for type checking? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Lexical Analysis B Syntax Analysis C Semantic Analysis D Code Generation Semantic Analysis PDF p6 explicitly names type checking as a major task of semantic analysis.
