A incorrect Lexical analysis recognizes tokens (p5). B incorrect Syntax analysis checks grammatical hierarchy (p5). C correct Type checking is explicitly assigned here (p6). D incorrect Code generation converts IC to machine code (p7).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 132 · AM0822
records.text: AM0822 Question 132 COMP22 What is type checking in a compiler? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Verifying the syntax of the program. B Detecting lexical errors in the program. C Ensuring that the operations on variables are well-defined and compatible. D Generating the intermediate code for the program. Ensuring that the operations on variables are well-defined and compatible. PDF p14 defines type checking as enforcing type safety and lists incompatible operands; p15 makes assignment produce type_error when the identifier and expression types differ. Thus C expresses compatible operations. A incorrect Grammatical syntax is handled by parsing (p5). B incorrect Token recognition is lexical analysis (p8), not type compatibility. C correct Compatible operations and assignments match pp14–15. D incorrect Intermediate generation is distinct from semantic checking (pp6,15).

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 133 · AM0823
records.text: AM0823 Question 133 COMP22 Which of the following is an example of a static type checking technique? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Type inference B Dynamic typing C Run-time type checking D Operator overloading Type inference. COMP22 defines type inference as deriving types from constraints and explicitly calls it static even without explicit type annotations. Dynamic typing and runtime checks concern execution-time behavior. Operator overloading defines several meanings for an operation, but is not a replacement for the checking technique itself. Thus only type inference is the named static technique. A correct Type inference derives expression types from constraints before execution and is explicitly a static technique. B incorrect Dynamic typing does not name the requested before-execution type-inference technique. C incorrect Runtime type checking occurs during execution, so it is not static checking. D incorrect Overloading supplies operation meanings; COMP22 distinguishes it from type checking itself.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 134 · AM0824
records.text: AM0824 Question 134 COMP19 Which attribute is specifically recorded for each variable in a type-oriented symbol table and distinguishes its typing information from the name that identifies the entry? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A To store the types of variables used in the program. B To store the names of variables used in the program. C To store the intermediate code generated during parsing. D To store the syntax rules of the programming language. To store the types of variables used in the program. A symbol table associates a name or declaration identity with attributes. In a type-oriented table, the relevant attribute is the variable’s type, used to check whether operations and assignments are compatible. Names identify the records but do not themselves give typing information. Intermediate instructions and grammar rules belong to other representations and are not the per-variable typing attribute requested. A correct Variable types provide the requested typing attribute. B incorrect Names identify entries but are not their type attributes. C incorrect IR instructions are not the per-variable type attribute. D incorrect Syntax rules describe the language rather than variable types.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 135 · AM0825
records.text: AM0825 Question 135 COMP22 In ordinary C++ with no custom conversions, which offered example is specifically a type mismatch rather than a syntax, value-domain or layout issue? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Syntax error in an if-else statement. B Division of a number by zero. C int x="hello"; D Incorrect indentation in the program. int x="hello"; An ordinary C++ declaration int x="hello" attempts to initialize an integer from a string literal and is a type mismatch under the stated rules. Division by zero can involve correctly typed operands and is instead a value-domain fault. Incorrect indentation is layout, while malformed if-else syntax concerns grammatical arrangement. The option illustrates an incompatible-type example. A incorrect This explicitly describes a syntax error rather than a type mismatch. B incorrect A zero divisor is a value issue even with compatible numeric types. C correct A string literal is not a compatible ordinary integer initializer. D incorrect Indentation does not establish an incompatible operand type.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 136 · AM0826
records.text: AM0826 Question 136 COMP22 Which advantage of static type checking specifically concerns detecting incompatible operations before the program executes? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Improved program performance. B Enhanced code optimization. C Early detection of potential runtime errors. D Simplified debugging process. Early detection of potential runtime errors. Static type checking can reject an incompatible operation during compilation, before that operation causes a run-time type error. This is the direct timing benefit asked for. Type information may also aid optimization, and diagnostics may make debugging easier, but those are additional consequences rather than the specific before-execution detection property. Type checking does not by itself guarantee faster code or eliminate all possible run-time errors. A incorrect Faster execution is not guaranteed and does not state detection before execution. B incorrect Optimization may use types but is a different benefit from the requested early rejection. C correct Compile-time rejection detects incompatible operations before execution. D incorrect Debugging may be easier, but that broad consequence does not specify the requested detection timing.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 137 · AM0827
records.text: AM0827 Question 137 COMP22 What is the primary goal of type checking in a compiler? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A To ensure syntactic correctness of the program. B To generate efficient machine code. C To enforce programming language rules and constraints. D To provide support for code reuse through libraries. To enforce programming language rules and constraints. PDF p14 defines type checking as semantic checks enforcing type safety and says the compiler checks source-language semantic conventions. C is the offered broad rule-enforcement description, limited here to type constraints. A incorrect Syntax correctness is the parsing task (p5). B incorrect Machine-code efficiency is an optimization goal (pp7,17). C correct Type-related semantic conventions and constraints match p14. D incorrect Library reuse is not a type-checking goal stated in the module.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 138 · AM0828
records.text: AM0828 Question 138 COMP23 Which of the following is an example of a type coercion or type conversion? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Assigning a floating-point value to an integer variable. B Assigning a value to an uninitialized variable. C Declaring a variable without specifying its type. D Using an undeclared variable in the program. Converting a floating-point value when assigning to an integer variable, where the language permits it. COMP23 gives C++ int x=3.14 as an ordinary conversion yielding 3 when representable. That is the listed example of conversion, with the language caveat that Java needs a permitted cast and C++ brace initialization rejects narrowing. The remaining choices concern initialization, inference or undeclared names rather than converting one value type to another. A correct Floating-to-integer assignment performs conversion where permitted; exact legality and precision loss depend on the language. B incorrect First assigning to a variable is initialization or assignment, not inherently a change of value type. C incorrect Omitting an explicit declaration type may invoke inference; it does not itself convert a value. D incorrect An undeclared name is a name-resolution problem rather than an example of value conversion.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 139 · CS0121
records.text: CS0121 Question 139 COMP11 COMP15 Which listed approaches are bottom-up and therefore are not top-down parsers? Select all that apply. Assume predictive recursive descent for A. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Recursive-descent parser B Shift-reduce parser C Non-recursive predictive parser D LR parser Shift-reduce parser; LR parser Shift-reduce parsing starts from the input and reduces recognized handles toward the start symbol. LR is a bottom-up family using that strategy. Recursive descent and nonrecursive prediction instead expand productions top-down for suitable grammars. Therefore both B and D fail the top-down description. This directional distinction avoids an unsupported efficiency ranking between recursive and table-driven predictive implementations. A incorrect Predictive recursive descent is top-down. B correct Shift-reduce is bottom-up. C incorrect Nonrecursive prediction is top-down. D correct LR is bottom-up.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 140 · CS0267
records.text: CS0267 Question 140 COMP02 Which one of the following is a type of compiler that compiles only the changed lines from source code and updates the object code accordingly? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Retargetable compiler B One pass compiler C Incremental compiler D Parallelizing compiler An incremental compiler. COMP02 defines incremental compilation as recompiling affected fragments or dependent units after edits. This is the compiler category intended by updating code after source changes. The question’s only changed lines wording is simplified: real dependency tracking can require recompiling more than literal edited lines. Retargeting and one-pass organization describe different properties. A incorrect Retargetable compilers support changing target descriptions rather than selecting edited source fragments. B incorrect One pass counts traversals of the program, not whether edits trigger selective recompilation. C correct Incremental compilation updates affected fragments after edits, accounting for dependencies beyond literal changed lines. D incorrect Parallelizing compilation is not the category defined by selective recompilation after source changes.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 141 · CS0268
records.text: CS0268 Question 141 COMP30 Which technique of code optimization shifts computations from run time to compile time by evaluating constant expressions at compile time and replacing them with their values? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Copy propagation B Compile time evaluation C Code motion D Dead code elimination Compile time evaluation PDF p18 lists constant folding and illustrates R2 = 3 * 2. Evaluating this constant expression early gives 6, eliminating that runtime computation. B describes this operation as compile time evaluation, although constant folding would be the module’s exact name. A incorrect P18 copy propagation example copies r1 into r2, not evaluates a constant arithmetic expression. B correct Evaluating 3 * 2 to 6 is the constant-folding example on p18, matching the stem. C incorrect P18 code movement relocates a block outside a loop, not necessarily evaluating it at compilation. D incorrect P18 dead-code elimination removes unreachable statements, rather than computing constant values.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 142 · NS0222
records.text: NS0222 Question 142 COMP30 COMP31 For const int x=8; const int y=16; if(x>y){int z=x+y;}, which techniques directly evaluate the known condition and remove its unreachable body? Select all that apply. Arithmetic simplification means algebraic identity rewriting here. Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Code motion B Dead code elimination C Compile time evaluation D Arithmetic simplification Dead code elimination; Compile time evaluation Both x and y are known constants, so evaluating 8>16 at compile time yields false. The body can never execute and dead-code elimination can remove it. These are distinct but compatible transformations, corresponding to B and C in this option order. Code motion relocates computations, while algebraic identity simplification is not the decisive operation on this constant-false condition. A incorrect No relocation is needed to evaluate or delete the branch. B correct The unreachable branch body can be removed. C correct The condition is evaluated from known constants at compile time. D incorrect No algebraic identity rewrite is the decisive step.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 143 · NS0223
records.text: NS0223 Question 143 COMP01 What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A compiler translates; an interpreter executes a representation. COMP01 distinguishes translating source into an equivalent target from executing a program representation. Bytecode systems may combine compilation, interpretation and JIT, so the distinction is not simply all-at-once versus line-by-line execution.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 144 · NS0224
records.text: NS0224 Question 144 COMP04 COMP09 What is the difference between lexical analysis and syntax analysis? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens; syntax analysis groups tokens into structures. COMP41 separates character-to-token classification from token-to-expression or statement structure. The scanner recognizes lexemes such as identifiers and operators and emits an ordered token stream. The parser checks how those tokens form grammatical constructs and can build a parse tree or AST; legal tokens can still appear in an illegal syntactic arrangement.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 145 · NS0225
records.text: NS0225 Question 145 COMP19 What is the purpose of a symbol table? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A symbol table associates names with declaration attributes. COMP19 maps names or identities to type, scope, width, offsets, signatures and linkage information. These records support declaration lookup and semantic checks; a hash table is one implementation rather than the purpose itself.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 146 · NS0226
records.text: NS0226 Question 146 COMP11 COMP15 What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. Top-down expands from the start symbol; bottom-up reduces input toward it. COMP15 describes bottom-up recognition as input reductions toward S, reversing a rightmost derivation. COMP11 describes top-down expansion from S toward the input, normally a leftmost derivation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 147 · NS0227
records.text: NS0227 Question 147 COMP26 What is intermediate code and why is it used? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. IR separates source analysis from target lowering and enables reuse. COMP26 defines IR’s role in separating source meaning from target implementation so analysis, optimization and backends can be reused. ASTs, graphs, TAC and bytecode are possible forms. A useful IR is easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower; portability does not require every IR to exclude all target-specific details.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 148 · NS0228
records.text: NS0228 Question 148 COMP04 Which of the following is NOT a valid token type produced during lexical analysis? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Keyword | B Parse tree node C Identifier | D Numeric literal Parse-tree node is not a lexical token type. COMP04 lists keywords, identifiers and literals among token classes. A parse-tree node belongs to the grammatical structure built after scanning, not the lexical class of a source lexeme. Consequently only parse-tree node is the invalid token-type choice, while the other three are ordinary scanner output categories. A incorrect Keywords are explicitly listed as a valid lexical token class. B correct Parse-tree nodes represent grammatical structure, not a lexical token category emitted by a scanner. C incorrect Identifiers are an ordinary lexical token class. D incorrect Numeric literals are literals and therefore valid token categories.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 149 · NS0229
records.text: NS0229 Question 149 COMP06 COMP-S02 What algorithm is commonly used to convert a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) to a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) in lexer construction? Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A Thompson's construction | B Subset construction (Powerset construction) C Cocke-Younger-Kasami (CYK) | D Earley's algorithm Subset (powerset) construction. COMP06 distinguishes Thompson construction, which builds an NFA from a regular expression, from subset construction, which determinizes the NFA. Each DFA state represents an NFA-state subset, with epsilon closure when needed. CYK and Earley are grammar-parsing algorithms rather than this automaton determinization, so the powerset option is the relevant stage. A incorrect Thompson construction goes from regular expression to NFA rather than NFA to DFA. B correct Subset construction creates DFA states from sets of NFA states. C incorrect CYK performs CFG membership parsing and does not determinize a lexical NFA. D incorrect Earley is a grammar-parsing method rather than the stated NFA-to-DFA construction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 150 · NS0230
records.text: NS0230 Question 150 COMP10 Given the grammar: E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | id — this grammar enforces: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Right-associativity for both + and * | B Left-associativity for both + and *, with * having higher precedence than + C Right-associativity for + and left-associativity for * | D No precedence or associativity rules Both operators associate left; multiplication has higher precedence. COMP10 states exactly these productions and their effect. Multiplication occurs within T below the addition level E, so it binds more tightly. The recursive operand on the left of E→E+T and T→T*F enforces left association for each operator. Parentheses in F can override the default grouping. A incorrect The recursive nonterminal is on the left, producing left rather than right association. B correct Separate T multiplication and E addition levels give higher multiplication precedence and left association. C incorrect Addition is left-recursive too, so it does not have the claimed right association. D incorrect The grammar explicitly encodes both precedence levels and associativity.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 151 · NS0231
records.text: NS0231 Question 151 COMP14 COMP12 COMP18 For a reduced CFG (all symbols reachable and productive), which conditions prevent it from being LL(1)? Select all that apply. In A, overlap means a shared terminal in competing RHS FIRST sets. Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Two productions for the same non-terminal have overlapping FIRST sets | B The grammar contains a left-recursive rule C The grammar is ambiguous | D A and B only Two productions for the same non-terminal have overlapping FIRST sets |; The grammar contains a left-recursive rule; The grammar is ambiguous | A shared FIRST terminal for alternatives of one nonterminal creates a predictive-table collision. Reachable left recursion prevents ordinary LL(1) prediction, and an ambiguous useful grammar cannot have a unique LL(1) parse. Thus A, B and C are all obstructions. The combined D alternative wrongly says only A and B, excluding ambiguity, so it is not a complete correct selection. A correct Shared FIRST terminals create competing table entries. B correct Reachable left recursion rules out ordinary LL(1) parsing. C correct A useful ambiguous grammar is not LL(1). D incorrect The word only wrongly excludes the valid ambiguity obstruction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 152 · NS0232
records.text: NS0232 Question 152 COMP24 Which of the following is an example of a synthesized attribute in attribute grammars? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A The type of an expression computed from its sub-expressions | B The scope environment passed down to a block C The inherited type context for a function body | D The enclosing loop level passed to a break statement Expression type computed from subexpressions is synthesized. COMP24 defines synthesized attributes by flow from children to a parent. Computing an expression’s type from its subexpressions fits this direction. Scope, type context and enclosing-loop information passed down from surrounding constructs instead supply inherited context. The direction of dependency, rather than the fact that types are involved, distinguishes these choices. A correct The parent expression derives its type from child subexpressions, which is synthesized upward flow. B incorrect A scope environment passed down to a block is inherited contextual information. C incorrect A type context supplied to a function body flows from its surroundings, so it is inherited. D incorrect Enclosing-loop context is passed inward to a break statement rather than synthesized from its children.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 153 · NS0233
records.text: NS0233 Question 153 COMP26 What is the primary purpose of Three-Address Code (TAC) as an intermediate representation? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A To directly execute on the target CPU | B To provide a machine-independent representation suitable for optimization and code generation C To replace the symbol table | D To encode only arithmetic expressions An optimization-friendly intermediate representation for later target generation. COMP26 gives reuse and separation as the purpose of IR and describes TAC as simple instruction records. TAC is normally not directly executed by a native CPU, does not replace declaration metadata and is not limited to arithmetic: branches and assignments are also representable. B states its architectural optimization/code-generation role most directly. A incorrect TAC is normally intermediate and requires lowering rather than direct execution on the target CPU. B correct TAC provides analyzable intermediate operations supporting reuse, optimization and later target-code generation. C incorrect A symbol table retains declaration metadata and is not replaced by the instruction representation. D incorrect TAC can encode control transfers and other operations, not only arithmetic expressions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 154 · NS0234
records.text: NS0234 Question 154 COMP07 The 'maximal munch' rule in lexical analysis means: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A The lexer always produces the shortest possible token | B The lexer always produces the longest possible token matching the current position C Keyword tokens are prioritized over identifiers | D Comments are included in the token stream Choose the longest matching lexeme at the current position. COMP07 defines longest matching lexeme selection at each input position. Equal-length matches use rule order, which is a separate tie-breaking rule; keywords do not override a longer identifier such as ifx. Comments are normally skipped rather than retained merely because maximal munch is used. This establishes B as the definition. A incorrect Shortest-match selection is the opposite of maximal munch. B correct The lexer consumes the longest available match beginning at the current input position. C incorrect Keyword priority can break equal-length rule ties but does not define longest match. D incorrect Comment retention is independent of longest match; ordinary comments are skipped.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 155 · NS0235
records.text: NS0235 Question 155 COMP17 In bottom-up parsing, a 'shift-reduce conflict' occurs when: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A There are two possible reductions for the same stack top | B The parser cannot decide whether to shift the next input token or reduce the current stack contents C The grammar is left-recursive | D The FOLLOW set is empty A competing shift and reduction on the same situation. COMP17 defines a shift/reduce conflict as a choice between consuming a token and reducing. Two competing reductions describe reduce/reduce instead. Left recursion may be entirely acceptable to LR, and an empty FOLLOW set is not the definition of this table conflict. The conflict concerns competing actions for the same state and lookahead. A incorrect Two possible reductions define a reduce/reduce conflict, a different conflict type. B correct The same parser situation permits both shifting input and reducing the recognized right-hand side. C incorrect LR can handle suitable left recursion; that property does not itself define a shift/reduce conflict. D incorrect FOLLOW-set emptiness does not express competing shift and reduction actions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 156 · NS0236
records.text: NS0236 Question 156 COMP32 Which optimization technique moves loop-invariant computations outside the loop body? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Strength reduction | B Loop unrolling C Loop-invariant code motion (LICM) | D Dead code elimination Loop-invariant code motion. COMP32 explains that an expression whose inputs remain unchanged can be moved to a preheader when safe on newly executed paths. That is loop-invariant code motion. Strength reduction changes operation cost, unrolling replicates the body, and dead-code elimination removes unused or unreachable work. Hoisting also requires safety, not merely unchanged operands. A incorrect Strength reduction substitutes a cheaper equivalent operation rather than necessarily moving it outside a loop. B incorrect Unrolling replicates loop bodies instead of hoisting invariant computations. C correct LICM moves invariant computations to an appropriate outside location when executing them there is safe. D incorrect Dead-code elimination removes unnecessary computations rather than relocating a needed invariant value.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 157 · NS0237
records.text: NS0237 Question 157 COMP36 What does 'register spilling' mean in the context of register allocation? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Allocating the same register to two variables | B Storing a variable in memory instead of a register because no register is available C Using floating-point registers for integer values | D Eliminating unnecessary register copies Store selected values in memory and insert loads/stores when registers do not suffice. COMP36 says spilling places selected values in memory when the register assignment cannot fit available registers. Loads and stores then connect memory-resident values to instructions needing registers. Register sharing can be legal for nonoverlapping live ranges, while copy elimination and choosing a different register class are separate operations rather than this storage fallback. A incorrect Register sharing may be legal for disjoint live ranges and does not itself describe spilling. B correct Spilling moves selected values to memory because a feasible register-only assignment is unavailable. C incorrect Using another register class is not the definition of writing spilled values to memory. D incorrect Removing redundant register copies is a different optimization from memory-backed spilling.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 158 · NS0238
records.text: NS0238 Question 158 COMP23 For Java numeric conversions such as int→long and int→float, which statement correctly describes widening? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Converting a wider type to a narrower type, possibly losing information | B Converting to a numeric type with a wider representable range; some widening conversions can still lose precision. C Declaring a variable with an explicit type annotation | D Assigning a value to a pointer of a different type Converting to a numeric type with a wider representable range; some widening conversions can still lose precision. Java int→long is widening and exact, while int→float is also widening even though some large integer values round. Widening therefore does not universally guarantee preservation of every bit of precision. Narrowing goes toward a more restricted representation; type annotations and arbitrary pointer changes are separate concepts. Option B captures the relevant larger-range conversion without making the false no-loss promise. A incorrect This describes narrowing rather than widening. B correct Widening can increase range while still losing precision, as int→float illustrates. C incorrect An explicit annotation declares a type rather than converting a value. D incorrect An arbitrary pointer-type change does not define Java numeric widening.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 159 · NS0239
records.text: NS0239 Question 159 COMP19 Which of the following data structures is most commonly used to implement a symbol table for fast insertion and lookup? Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens. A Sorted linked list | B Hash table C Binary search tree | D Stack A hash table. COMP19 directly identifies hashing as giving expected constant-time insertion and lookup under suitable hashing. A stack supports nested scope order but is not the primary keyed mapping. Lists and trees are possible alternatives, yet neither is the specific common expected-constant-time structure emphasized in the note and requested by the stem. A incorrect A sorted linked list generally requires linear search and does not supply the highlighted expected constant lookup. B correct Hash tables commonly implement expected O(1) symbol insertion and lookup. C incorrect A search tree is possible, but the note specifically identifies hashing for the usual fast keyed implementation. D incorrect A stack organizes scope nesting rather than providing fast arbitrary name lookup within a scope.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 160 · NS0240
records.text: NS0240 Question 160 COMP12 A grammar is said to be 'left-factored' when: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A All productions are left-recursive | B Productions for the same non-terminal that share a common prefix are rewritten to factor out the prefix C The grammar has no ε-productions | D The grammar can be parsed by a bottom-up parser only Common prefixes are factored out of alternatives. COMP12 rewrites A→αβ|αγ as A→αA′ and A′→β|γ. The transformation postpones the alternative choice until after consuming the common prefix. It does not mean making productions left-recursive, removing all epsilon rules or restricting parsing to bottom-up methods; left factoring alone also does not guarantee LL(1). A incorrect Left recursion and left factoring are distinct properties and transformations. B correct Factoring extracts shared prefixes and delays selection between the remaining suffix alternatives. C incorrect Factoring does not require removing every epsilon production. D incorrect Factored grammars can support top-down prediction; bottom-up exclusivity is not a defining condition.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 161 · NS0241
records.text: NS0241 Question 161 COMP30 What is 'constant propagation' in compiler optimization? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Evaluating constant expressions at compile time | B Replacing uses of a variable with its known constant value at each program point C Removing code that has no effect on program output | D Moving constants from memory to registers Replace uses with their known constant values. COMP30 gives x=3; y=x+2 becoming y=3+2 before folding. Replacing x by its known value is propagation; evaluating 3+2 is folding. Removing unnecessary code or choosing register locations addresses different transformations. The program-point qualification matters because the value must still be known on all relevant incoming paths. A incorrect Evaluating an already constant expression is constant folding, which can follow propagation. B correct Propagation substitutes a variable’s established constant value at uses where that fact holds. C incorrect Removing effect-free unused or unreachable work is dead-code elimination. D incorrect Memory-to-register placement is not the substitution of a known compile-time value.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 162 · NS0242
records.text: NS0242 Question 162 COMP17 In an LR parsing table, what does a 'reduce/reduce conflict' indicate? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A Two different productions can both be used to reduce the same stack contents with the same lookahead | B The parser must both shift and reduce on the same input symbol C The grammar has a dangling else problem | D The grammar contains ε-productions Two competing reductions for the same parser state/lookahead. COMP17 defines reduce/reduce as two reductions being available. In a parsing table that means the same state and lookahead permit different completed productions. A shift competing with reduction is another conflict type. Dangling else is a grammar ambiguity example, and epsilon productions alone do not guarantee any reduce/reduce collision. A correct The table offers two different production reductions for the same state and lookahead. B incorrect Simultaneous shift and reduce actions define shift/reduce rather than reduce/reduce. C incorrect Dangling else commonly creates an attachment ambiguity, not the definition of two competing reductions. D incorrect Epsilon rules can appear in conflict-free grammars and do not alone imply this collision.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 163 · NS0243
records.text: NS0243 Question 163 COMP08 COMP22 Which compiler phase is primarily responsible for detecting the incompatible assignment in the Java declaration int x = "hello";? Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning. A Lexical analysis | B Syntax analysis C Semantic analysis | D Code generation Semantic analysis | The declaration has recognizable tokens and a valid declaration-shaped syntax, but assigns a string to an integer variable. Under Java’s type rules this violates assignment compatibility, so semantic analysis and type checking identify the error. Scanning recognizes the identifier, type keyword and literal; parsing organizes them. Code generation uses the checked representation later. The named language removes any assumption that every statically typed language has identical implicit conversions. A incorrect The individual tokens are recognizable; the error is their type compatibility. B incorrect The declaration’s grammar structure is not the primary problem. C correct Semantic type checking rejects the string-to-integer assignment. D incorrect Code generation follows the frontend type check rather than defining this compatibility rule.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 164 · NS0244
records.text: NS0244 Question 164 COMP06 In Thompson's construction for building an NFA from a regular expression, the NFA for the concatenation r1r2 is built by: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A Merging the start states of both NFAs | B Adding an ε-transition from the accepting state(s) of the NFA for r1 to the start state of the NFA for r2 C Creating a new start state with ε-transitions to both NFAs | D Taking the cross product of the two NFAs Connect the first fragment’s accepting end to the second start with ε. COMP06 directly gives the concatenation rule: connect r’s final state to s’s start by epsilon. This forces any complete path through the first fragment to continue through the second in order. Branching epsilon paths instead implement alternation; merged starts and product constructions do not implement the specified Thompson concatenation step. A incorrect Merging starts does not force a complete r1 match followed by an r2 match. B correct The epsilon connection joins the first accepting end to the second start without consuming input. C incorrect A new branching start with epsilon alternatives implements union rather than concatenation. D incorrect A state cross product is not the Thompson fragment connection for concatenation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 165 · NS0245
records.text: NS0245 Question 165 COMP10 What is the 'dangling else' problem? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A An else branch that can never be reached due to preceding conditions | B Ambiguity in grammars that allows an else to be matched with either of two if statements C An else clause that lacks a body | D An else used outside an if statement Ambiguous attachment of else to one of two nested ifs. COMP10 describes an else that can attach to either nested if and resolves it with nearest-unmatched-if policy or a grammar rewrite. That grammatical ambiguity is the dangling-else problem. It does not mean unreachable code, a missing body or an else outside any if, which are different semantic or syntactic situations. A incorrect Unreachability concerns control-flow feasibility, not the competing grammatical attachment of else. B correct The ambiguity is whether else belongs to the inner or outer unmatched if. C incorrect A missing else body is a syntax defect rather than the classic attachment ambiguity. D incorrect An else outside any if is not the two-attachment situation defining dangling else.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 166 · NS0246
records.text: NS0246 Question 166 COMP28 Which representation explicitly uses basic blocks as vertices and possible transfers as edges, making it the direct structural basis for dominator and natural-loop analysis? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) | B Three-Address Code (TAC) C Static Single Assignment (SSA) form | D Control Flow Graph (CFG) Control Flow Graph (CFG) A control-flow graph explicitly records basic blocks and their possible successor transfers. Dominator relationships describe which blocks occur on every path to another block; back edges to dominating headers identify natural loops. TAC can populate the blocks, and SSA can coexist with this graph, but neither alone names the requested vertex/edge structure. An AST emphasizes source syntax rather than this control-flow representation. A incorrect An AST represents source hierarchy rather than the specified block-transfer graph. B incorrect TAC gives instructions, not by itself the requested graph. C incorrect SSA is a definition-naming discipline that can coexist with a CFG. D correct A CFG explicitly provides the specified blocks, edges and path structure.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 167 · NS0247
records.text: NS0247 Question 167 COMP27 In Static Single Assignment (SSA) form, what is the purpose of a 'φ (phi) function'? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A To represent a conditional branch in the control flow graph | B To select the correct version of a variable at join points where multiple control flow paths merge C To mark the entry point of a function | D To represent a loop-back edge in the CFG Select the incoming variable version corresponding to the predecessor taken. COMP27 defines phi at a join as choosing an incoming value according to the actual predecessor path. It is not a conditional branch instruction, a function-entry marker or a back edge, and does not average its operands. The function reconciles distinct definition names when different paths reach the same use. A incorrect A phi function selects an incoming value; it does not transfer control between blocks. B correct It merges definition versions by selecting the value associated with the predecessor actually taken. C incorrect Function entry is a control-flow location, not the value-selection purpose of phi. D incorrect A back edge represents loop control transfer rather than a merge of SSA values.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 168 · NS0248
records.text: NS0248 Question 168 COMP13 The FOLLOW set of the start symbol S always contains: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A ε (epsilon) | B The end-of-input marker $ C The first terminal of every production | D Nothing; FOLLOW(S) is always empty The end-of-input marker $. COMP13 explicitly places $ in FOLLOW(S), representing that a completed start-symbol derivation can be followed by end of input. FOLLOW never contains epsilon. Possible initial terminals belong to FIRST, not automatically FOLLOW. Therefore the marker is guaranteed even when other following terminals depend on the grammar. A incorrect FOLLOW contains terminals and possibly the end marker, never epsilon. B correct The end-of-input marker is placed in FOLLOW of the start symbol by initialization. C incorrect Initial terminals are FIRST information and are not automatically following terminals. D incorrect FOLLOW(S) is not empty because it contains the end marker.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 169 · NS0249
records.text: NS0249 Question 169 COMP31 COMP33 COMP32 For an unsigned fixed-width integer x with width greater than three and modular arithmetic, which optimization replaces x = x * 8 with x = x << 3? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Constant folding | B Dead code elimination C Strength reduction | D Loop unrolling Strength reduction | The transformation replaces multiplication by a power of two with an equivalent shift under the stated unsigned model. This is strength reduction when the target makes that replacement cheaper. It does not evaluate a constant-only expression because x remains variable, does not remove an unused statement, and does not replicate loop iterations. The explicit arithmetic model matters because signed-language overflow or shift rules can make a superficially similar rewrite invalid. A incorrect The operand x remains variable, so this is not evaluation of an all-constant expression. B incorrect The assignment remains and still computes a needed result. C correct Replacing an operation by an equivalent cheaper form is strength reduction. D incorrect No loop body is replicated.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 170 · NS0250
records.text: NS0250 Question 170 COMP37 In a compiler's code generator, 'calling convention' refers to: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A The order in which source files are compiled | B The agreed-upon protocol for how functions pass arguments, return values, and manage the stack C The naming convention for generated labels | D The format of debug information in the object file The protocol for arguments, results, registers and stack management. COMP37 defines the locations of arguments/results, saved-register responsibilities, stack alignment and frame duties as the calling convention. These permit caller and callee to agree on the runtime call interface. Source-file build order, label spelling and debug format concern other compiler/toolchain conventions rather than this execution protocol. A incorrect Compilation order concerns build organization rather than the runtime interface between callers and callees. B correct The calling convention specifies argument/result passing and register/stack responsibilities. C incorrect Label naming is separate from the runtime storage and control-transfer call protocol. D incorrect Debug information format is not the protocol used to invoke and return from functions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 171 · NS0251
records.text: NS0251 Question 171 COMP31 What does 'peephole optimization' involve? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Optimizing entire functions at once | B Examining and replacing small sequences of generated instructions with more efficient equivalents C Inlining small functions at call sites | D Eliminating unreachable basic blocks Examine short instruction sequences and replace them with better equivalents. COMP31 defines peephole optimization by short instruction windows and lists redundant-load removal, machine idioms and jump-chain shortening. B states that method directly. Whole-function optimization has a broader scope; inlining changes calls to bodies, and unreachable-block removal is a particular control-flow simplification rather than the definition of examining small windows. A incorrect Whole-function scope is broader than the short instruction windows defining peephole optimization. B correct The optimizer inspects short instruction sequences and substitutes equivalent more efficient forms. C incorrect Inlining expands calls into bodies rather than defining the local instruction-window method. D incorrect Unreachable-block removal is one control-flow optimization, not the defining peephole inspection mechanism.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 172 · NS0252
records.text: NS0252 Question 172 COMP17 Which statement correctly compares LALR(1) with SLR(1) and canonical LR(1), allowing the case where no equal-core canonical states need merging? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LALR(1) is weaker than SLR(1) | B LALR(1) has no more states than canonical LR(1) and can resolve some conflicts SLR(1) cannot. C LALR(1) and SLR(1) produce identical parsing tables for all grammars | D LALR(1) requires more lookahead than SLR(1) LALR(1) has no more states than canonical LR(1) and can resolve some conflicts SLR(1) cannot. LALR combines lookaheads of canonical LR(1) states with equal LR(0) cores. This gives no more states than the canonical machine, with a reduction when distinct equal-core states merge. LALR can handle some grammars beyond SLR because its lookaheads are more precise. Both use one lookahead token, and their tables are not identical for every grammar. A incorrect The hierarchy places SLR within LALR rather than the reverse. B correct This states both the correct state-count bound and the greater parsing capability. C incorrect The methods can use different reduction lookaheads and tables. D incorrect Both use one lookahead token.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 173 · NS0253
records.text: NS0253 Question 173 COMP29 In data flow analysis, 'live variable analysis' is a: Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation. A Forward may-analysis | B Backward may-analysis C Forward must-analysis | D Backward must-analysis Backward may-analysis. COMP29 explicitly calls liveness backward may-analysis. A value is live if some future path reads it before redefinition, so information flows backward from successor uses and combines possible uses rather than requiring every path. This distinguishes both the direction and may-versus-must dimensions requested by the options. A incorrect May is appropriate, but liveness propagates from future uses backward rather than forward. B correct Liveness asks whether some future path uses a value before redefinition, a backward may property. C incorrect Both direction and must quantification differ from the liveness definition. D incorrect Backward direction fits, but liveness requires a possible use, not use on every path.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 174 · NS0254
records.text: NS0254 Question 174 COMP06 The 'closure' operation in NFA-to-DFA subset construction computes: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases. A The set of all NFA states reachable from a given set of states using only ε-transitions | B The set of all NFA states reachable using any number of any transitions C The minimal DFA equivalent to the NFA | D The FIRST set of a non-terminal States reachable by zero or more ε transitions. COMP06 defines epsilon closure as all states reachable without consuming input through zero or more epsilon edges. Zero moves includes the starting set itself. Arbitrary labeled transitions would consume symbols and belong to a different reachability relation; minimization and FIRST-set computation are separate algorithms. A therefore matches the closure used in subset construction. A correct Epsilon closure includes the starting set and every state reachable using only epsilon edges. B incorrect Arbitrary symbol transitions consume input and are not part of epsilon closure. C incorrect Closure supplies subsets during determinization; it does not itself minimize the resulting DFA. D incorrect FIRST is a grammar lookahead set, not epsilon reachability among NFA states.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 175 · NS0255
records.text: NS0255 Question 175 COMP-S04 For a real-machine backend, which listed optimization chiefly depends on the target’s instruction latencies and execution resources? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Constant folding | B Dead code elimination C Instruction scheduling | D Loop-invariant code motion Instruction scheduling | Instruction scheduling chooses a legal instruction order while considering target resources and latencies. It is therefore the target-dependent backend choice in this comparison. Constant folding computes known expressions, dead-code elimination removes unnecessary computation while preserving effects, and loop-invariant motion relocates safe unchanged expressions. Their validity depends on program semantics, but these three need not be organized around a particular processor’s scheduling resources. A incorrect Folding evaluates known expressions from program semantics rather than scheduling machine resources. B incorrect Dead-code elimination uses reachability, use and side-effect information. C correct Instruction scheduling considers target execution resources and instruction latencies. D incorrect Invariant motion uses loop values, paths and safety conditions rather than target issue scheduling.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 176 · NS0256
records.text: NS0256 Question 176 COMP09 In a context-free grammar, a 'sentential form' is: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A A string consisting only of terminal symbols | B Any string of terminals and non-terminals derivable from the start symbol C A string that cannot be further reduced | D The right-hand side of a production rule Any terminal/nonterminal string derivable from the start symbol. COMP09 defines a sentential form as any string of terminals and nonterminals derivable from S. Terminal-only sentences are a special case, not the full definition. A production right side need not itself be reachable from S, and irreducibility does not define derivability. B captures the required reachability and permits both kinds of symbols. A incorrect Terminal-only strings are sentences, a subset of sentential forms rather than their full definition. B correct Derivability from the start symbol with terminals and possibly nonterminals is the defining property. C incorrect A sentential form can still contain expandable nonterminals; inability to reduce is not required. D incorrect A right-hand side is not necessarily reachable from the grammar’s start symbol.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 177 · NS0257
records.text: NS0257 Question 177 COMP38 What is 'function inlining' and what is its primary risk? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Replacing a function call with the function body; risk is incorrect semantics | B Replacing a function call with the function body; risk is increased code size (code bloat) C Moving a function to a different module; risk is linker errors | D Specializing a function for specific argument values; risk is type errors Replace a call with its body; excessive code size is a risk. COMP38 defines inlining as substituting a suitably renamed body while preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects. It can remove call overhead but increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. Correct inlining preserves semantics; corruption is an implementation bug rather than its defining trade-off. Moving modules or specializing arguments describes different transformations. A incorrect Inlining must preserve semantics; incorrect behavior is a bug rather than the normal primary trade-off stated here. B correct Body substitution can reduce call overhead while increasing generated code size. C incorrect Moving a function between modules is not call-site body substitution. D incorrect Argument specialization is a different optimization and does not define general function inlining.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 178 · NS0258
records.text: NS0258 Question 178 COMP15 Which of the following best describes the 'handle' in bottom-up parsing? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A The leftmost terminal in the input string | B A substring of the current sentential form that matches the right-hand side of a production and whose reduction leads to a valid parse C The top element of the parsing stack | D The lookahead token used for parsing decisions The RHS occurrence whose next reverse-rightmost reduction leads toward the valid parse. COMP15 defines a handle as a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next reverse-rightmost derivation step. B is the closest complete description: its valid-parse condition must mean that next legitimate step, not merely any matching substring. Neither a single stack item nor the lookahead alone specifies that contextual production occurrence. A incorrect The leftmost terminal need not be the handle and does not identify a production RHS occurrence. B correct Read valid reduction as the next reverse-rightmost step; contextual validity distinguishes a handle from arbitrary matches. C incorrect A handle can span multiple symbols and is not simply the top stack element. D incorrect Lookahead guides action selection but is not the substring being reduced.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 179 · NS0259
records.text: NS0259 Question 179 COMP28 In the context of code generation, what is a 'basic block'? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A A block of memory allocated on the heap | B A maximal straight-line sequence of instructions with one entry point and one exit point C A function or procedure in the source code | D A group of related variable declarations A maximal straight-line sequence with entry at the beginning and exit at the end. COMP28 directly defines this sequence as a basic block. Maximality means it is not arbitrarily shortened while retaining the same entry/exit structure. Heap allocation, whole functions and related declarations describe different entities; a function may contain many basic blocks separated by branch targets and control transfers. A incorrect A heap memory region is storage, not a straight-line control-flow unit. B correct This matches the maximal straight-line single-entry, end-exit definition in COMP28. C incorrect A function may contain branches and multiple basic blocks rather than one straight-line block. D incorrect Related declarations are not the instruction sequence defined by control-flow boundaries.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 180 · NS0260
records.text: NS0260 Question 180 COMP33 What is 'alias analysis' and why is it important for optimization? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Determining which variables have the same name in different scopes; important for scope resolution | B Determining whether two pointer expressions can refer to the same memory location; important because aliasing restricts reordering and CSE C Detecting variables with the same type; important for type coercion | D Finding duplicate function names; important for linking Determine whether references may denote the same memory, constraining transformations. COMP33 asks whether references can designate the same memory. A write through p can invalidate a value loaded through q unless nonaliasing or another proof permits reuse. Therefore alias facts constrain CSE and reordering. Identical spellings, types or function names concern scope, typing or linkage rather than memory-location overlap. A incorrect Equal spelling in different scopes concerns declaration identity rather than whether references share memory. B correct Potential shared locations determine whether writes can invalidate reused loads or reordered memory operations. C incorrect Equal types do not prove shared addresses and are not the alias-analysis question. D incorrect Duplicate linker names concern symbol resolution rather than potential overlap of referenced memory.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 181 · NS0261
records.text: NS0261 Question 181 COMP12 Which statement about recursive-descent parsers is TRUE? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A They cannot handle left-recursive grammars without modification | B They inherently support all context-free grammars C They require a parsing table to function | D They build the parse tree bottom-up Ordinary recursive descent needs modification to handle left recursion. COMP12 explains that ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever on left recursion before consuming a token. Removing left recursion or changing the algorithm is therefore necessary for that direct implementation. Recursive descent is top-down and normally procedural, so it does not inherently require an explicit table or support every CFG unchanged. A correct Without transformation or algorithmic modification, left recursion can cause infinite recursive calls before input consumption. B incorrect Ordinary recursive descent is not an unrestricted parser for every context-free grammar. C incorrect Procedures can encode production choices directly; an explicit parsing table is not required. D incorrect Recursive descent expands productions top-down rather than constructing a reverse-rightmost bottom-up parse.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 182 · NS0262
records.text: NS0262 Question 182 COMP24 In attribute grammar terminology, which of the following is an 'inherited' attribute? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A The value of an expression node computed from its children | B The type environment passed from a function declaration down to its body C The size of an array determined from its element type and length | D The result type of an arithmetic operation A type environment passed from a declaration into its body is inherited. COMP24 explicitly gives the declaration’s type environment passed into its body as an inherited attribute. This carries context inward rather than computing a parent from child values. Expression values, array sizes computed from components and arithmetic result types are ordinarily synthesized examples when obtained from the node’s own child information. A incorrect Computing an expression from its children is synthesized upward flow. B correct The surrounding declaration supplies type context to the nested body, matching the explicit inherited example. C incorrect Computing size from element information and length is a synthesized result, not supplied surrounding context. D incorrect An operation’s result type derived from operands is normally synthesized from its child information.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 183 · NS0263
records.text: NS0263 Question 183 COMP29 A compiler emits the error 'variable used before initialization'. This is detected during: Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation. A Lexical analysis | B Syntax analysis C Semantic analysis / data flow analysis | D Code generation Semantic/data-flow analysis. COMP29 distinguishes definite assignment, which asks whether initialization occurs on every incoming path, from reaching definitions alone. Such control/data-flow facts go beyond recognizing legal tokens or grammar. The error therefore belongs to semantic/data-flow analysis before target emission, even though exact acceptance and diagnostic rules depend on the language. A incorrect Scanning recognizes identifier tokens but does not prove initialization along every control-flow path. B incorrect A grammatically valid variable use can still occur before initialization. C correct Semantic data-flow analysis checks that required initialization precedes each use on every relevant path. D incorrect Target generation ordinarily consumes checked input rather than supplying the primary definite-assignment analysis.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 184 · NS0264
records.text: NS0264 Question 184 COMP36 In graph-coloring register allocation, what is an 'interference graph'? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A A graph where nodes represent machine instructions and edges represent data dependencies | B A graph where nodes represent variables and edges connect pairs of variables that are simultaneously live C A graph where nodes represent registers and edges represent compatibility | D A graph representing the control flow of the program A graph connecting values that must coexist in distinct registers. COMP36 models concurrently needed values as vertices joined by interference edges, with physical registers represented by colors. Thus the variable/live-range graph in B is the intended model. Instruction dependencies and control-flow edges have different meanings; a graph of register compatibility reverses the allocation model’s vertices and does not express live-value interference. A incorrect Instruction-dependency edges constrain scheduling rather than describing interference among live values. B correct Variables or live ranges form vertices; an edge requires distinct registers for simultaneously needed values. C incorrect Registers are colors in this model, not the vertices whose live ranges interfere. D incorrect A CFG connects basic blocks by possible transfers, not values by register interference.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 185 · NS0265
records.text: NS0265 Question 185 COMP30 What is 'dead code' in the context of compiler optimization? Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions. A Code that causes a runtime error | B Code that is syntactically incorrect C Code that is unreachable or whose computed results are never used | D Code that depends on uninitialized variables Unreachable code or unused computations without required effects. COMP30 permits removing unreachable code and unused computations only when evaluation has no necessary side effects. C states the intended two dead-code categories, with this semantic caveat. Runtime faults, syntax defects and uninitialized uses are different error categories, not definitions of code being safely removable. An unused volatile read or effectful call may still be required. A incorrect A runtime fault does not make arbitrary reachable code safely removable as dead code. B incorrect Syntactically invalid code is a compilation error, not the definition of dead computation. C correct Unreachability or unused results identify candidates, provided necessary observable side effects are preserved. D incorrect An uninitialized dependency is an analysis or correctness issue, not automatically dead code.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 186 · NS0266
records.text: NS0266 Question 186 COMP01 What is the precise relationship between the general term compiler and the term transpiler? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler; compilers can also target assembly, machine code or bytecode. B A compiler is faster than a transpiler C A transpiler performs more optimizations than a compiler | D There is no meaningful distinction A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler; compilers can also target assembly, machine code or bytecode. A compiler translates a source program to an equivalent target representation, which may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. A transpiler is the source-to-source subtype of compiler. This gives a meaningful target-based distinction while retaining the shared category. Speed and optimization count depend on implementations and workloads; neither defines the relationship between the two terms. A correct A transpiler is a compiler whose target is another source language. B incorrect There is no universal speed ordering. C incorrect Optimization count does not define the subtype. D incorrect The source-to-source target is a meaningful distinction.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 187 · NS0267
records.text: NS0267 Question 187 COMP04 In the context of lexical analysis, 'lexeme' vs 'token' means: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Lexeme is the abstract category; token is the actual text | B Lexeme is the actual sequence of characters in the source; token is the abstract category with optional attribute value C They are synonymous terms | D Lexeme refers to keywords only; token refers to all other units Lexeme is the source text; token is its category with optional attributes. COMP04 directly distinguishes the actual character sequence from its token category and optional attribute. For example, total is a lexeme that may produce an ID token associated with a symbol entry. Neither term is restricted to keywords; the same distinction applies to identifiers, numeric literals, operators and other lexical units. A incorrect This reverses the roles: the lexeme is concrete text and the token identifies its class. B correct The concrete source sequence is the lexeme; category and optional information form the token. C incorrect The note explicitly separates the two abstractions rather than treating them as synonyms. D incorrect Lexemes include identifiers, literals and operators, not just keywords.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 188 · NS0268
records.text: NS0268 Question 188 COMP36 Under the general interference-graph model with fixed k≥3, which task is an NP-complete decision problem? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Converting an NFA to a DFA | B Constructing a LL(1) parsing table C Deciding whether an arbitrary interference graph can use k registers without spilling, for fixed k≥3 D Computing FIRST sets for a CFG Deciding whether an arbitrary interference graph can use k registers without spilling, for fixed k≥3 In the general interference model, simultaneously needed values are adjacent and registers are colors. Deciding whether the graph can be colored with k registers without spilling is general graph k-colorability, NP-complete for fixed k≥3. Optimal allocation is instead an optimization task. The other alternatives are construction or fixed-point tasks and do not state this membership-plus-hardness decision problem. A incorrect NFA determinization is a construction task, even when its output is exponential. B incorrect LL(1) table construction is not the specified graph-coloring decision task. C correct No-spill allocation is k-colorability under the stipulated general model. D incorrect FIRST-set computation is a fixed-point task rather than this NP-complete decision form.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 189 · NS0269
records.text: NS0269 Question 189 COMP29 What is the 'reaching definitions' data flow problem used for? Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation. A Determining which variables are live at each program point | B Determining which variable assignments might reach a given program point without being overwritten C Determining which expressions are available at each program point | D Determining which functions can be called from a given call site Assignments that may reach a point without being overwritten. COMP29 directly defines reaching definitions as assignments that can arrive at a point without a replacement definition on the path. Its join is union because one possible path suffices. Liveness asks about future uses, available expressions asks about previous computations on every path, and possible call targets is a separate analysis question. A incorrect Future reads before redefinition are the liveness question, not reaching definitions. B correct This is the exact assignment-and-no-overwrite property defined for reaching definitions. C incorrect Available expressions concerns prior computations with unchanged operands, not assignment definitions. D incorrect Possible function targets concern call-graph or points-to analysis rather than reaching assignment definitions.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 190 · NS0270
records.text: NS0270 Question 190 COMP14 In predictive (LL(1)) parsing, when should the parser use an ε-production A → ε? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A When the lookahead token is in FIRST(A) | B When the lookahead token is in FOLLOW(A) and no other production for A begins with that token C When the stack is empty | D Whenever the next token is not a keyword Use ε on an appropriate FOLLOW(A) lookahead with no competing alternative. COMP14 enters a nullable alternative under the left-hand nonterminal’s FOLLOW symbols and requires no conflicting production in that cell. An epsilon reduction consumes no input. FIRST(A) alone can refer to a nonempty alternative, while stack emptiness and token being a keyword do not define nullable-alternative selection. Thus B supplies the correct lookahead rule. A incorrect A FIRST terminal may require a nonempty alternative; FIRST(A) alone does not select epsilon. B correct FOLLOW lookahead selects the nullable alternative when its predictive table cell has no competing production. C incorrect An empty stack is not the rule for selecting a production for a pending nonterminal. D incorrect Keyword status has no general relation to a nonterminal’s nullable-production table entries.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 191 · NS0271
records.text: NS0271 Question 191 COMP28 Which of the following correctly describes a 'dominator' in a control flow graph? Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task. A A node that is executed before all other nodes unconditionally | B Node D dominates node N if every path from the entry node to N must pass through D C The node with the most outgoing edges | D The unique successor of every conditional branch Every entry-to-N path passes through D. COMP28 defines domination relative to a particular node N: every path from entry to N must pass D. This is not a claim that D precedes every node in the program, nor is domination measured by out-degree or being a unique successor. The definition concerns unavoidable traversal on paths reaching the specified node. A incorrect A dominator is defined relative to a node, not necessarily as preceding all program nodes. B correct This exactly states the all-entry-to-N-paths definition in COMP28. C incorrect The number of outgoing edges does not establish unavoidable traversal on paths. D incorrect Branch successor uniqueness is unrelated to the general dominator definition.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 192 · NS0272
records.text: NS0272 Question 192 COMP17 In SLR(1) parsing, the reduce action for production A → α is triggered when the lookahead is in: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A FIRST(A) | B FOLLOW(A) C FIRST(α) | D FOLLOW(α) FOLLOW(A), once the item for A→α is complete. COMP17 says SLR uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. The completed item establishes that the right side has been recognized; FOLLOW restricts which lookaheads permit reducing it. FIRST information predicts beginnings instead, and FOLLOW of an arbitrary right-hand string is not the table rule used here. A incorrect FIRST(A) concerns beginnings of derived strings rather than lookaheads after a completed A. B correct SLR places a completed A-production reduction under the lookaheads in FOLLOW(A). C incorrect FIRST of the right side predicts starting tokens, not permitted post-recognition reduction lookaheads. D incorrect SLR uses FOLLOW of the left-hand nonterminal A, not this right-side expression.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 193 · NS0273
records.text: NS0273 Question 193 COMP37 What is 'escape analysis' and how does it help optimization? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Analysis to detect out-of-bounds array accesses; helps prevent security vulnerabilities | B Analysis to determine whether an object's reference can 'escape' the function where it is created; enables stack allocation of non-escaping objects C Analysis to find unreachable exception handlers; enables dead code elimination | D Analysis to track pointer arithmetic; enables bounds checking elimination Determine whether references outlive or escape a region, enabling safe allocation changes. COMP37 asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside its allocating region. A proven nonescaping object may use stack storage or be eliminated when lifetime and identity are preserved. Bounds checking, exception reachability and pointer arithmetic are separate analyses and do not define the reference-escape property described. A incorrect Array bounds concern index validity rather than whether references leave their allocation region. B correct Reference escape information can justify stack allocation when lifetime and identity remain correct. C incorrect Unreachable exception handlers concern control-flow reachability, not reference lifetime or external access. D incorrect Pointer arithmetic tracking does not by itself define escape beyond a function or allocation region.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 194 · NS0274
