records.text: NS0274 Question 194 COMP17 Which of the following is a valid reason why LALR(1) parsers may have reduce/reduce conflicts that canonical LR(1) parsers do not? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A LALR(1) uses a larger parsing table than canonical LR(1) | B LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core but different lookaheads, potentially merging incompatible lookahead sets C LALR(1) does not support left-recursive grammars | D LALR(1) computes FOLLOW sets incorrectly Merging equal-core LR(1) states can combine incompatible reduction lookaheads. COMP17 directly explains that LALR merges canonical states with identical LR(0) cores while unioning their lookahead sets. Distinctions that prevented competing reductions in separate states can disappear, creating reduce/reduce conflicts. This is not due to incorrect FOLLOW computation or rejection of left recursion; the loss comes from deliberate state merging. A incorrect Merging aims to reduce state count, and a larger table is not the reason for new conflicts. B correct Combining lookaheads of equal-core states can make previously separated reductions compete. C incorrect LALR can handle suitable left-recursive grammars, as other LR methods can. D incorrect The conflict can arise from correct merging, without any erroneous FOLLOW-set computation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 195 · NS0275
records.text: NS0275 Question 195 COMP38 Which is a common implementation mechanism for runtime virtual dispatch in an object-oriented language, when the receiver’s class cannot be resolved statically? Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage. A Static binding of function calls at compile time | B A virtual method table (vtable) per class, with function pointers resolved at runtime C Inline expansion of all polymorphic calls | D Name mangling to distinguish overloaded functions A virtual method table (vtable) per class, with function pointers resolved at runtime A common implementation stores virtual-method entries in a per-class vtable and lets an object refer to the appropriate table. A virtual call selects the entry using the receiver’s runtime class. Static binding alone does not provide that selection for an unknown class. Mandatory inlining is not generally possible, and name mangling distinguishes linker symbols rather than selecting overrides at runtime. A incorrect Static binding alone does not choose by an unknown runtime class. B correct A per-class vtable is the common mechanism described in the note. C incorrect Unknown runtime receivers prevent mandatory inlining of all polymorphic calls. D incorrect Name mangling identifies symbols rather than selecting overrides.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 196 · NS0276
records.text: NS0276 Question 196 COMP14 Which of the following is true about a 'well-formed' grammar for LL(1) parsing? Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them. A It may contain left recursion | B For every non-terminal A with productions A → α1 | α2 | ... | αn, no two alternatives share a common token in their FIRST sets, and if any αi derives ε, then FIRST(αj) and FOLLOW(A) are disjoint for all j ≠ i C It must be ambiguous | D It must have at least one ε-production Disjoint predictive selections, including nullable FIRST/FOLLOW constraints. COMP14 requires that alternatives for a nonterminal select disjoint lookahead sets. B gives the standard FIRST separation and nullable-alternative FOLLOW restriction; shared epsilon alternatives would also violate pairwise FIRST disjointness. Left recursion and useful ambiguity are not acceptable LL(1) properties, and epsilon productions are optional rather than required. A incorrect Ordinary LL(1) grammars cannot retain left recursion that recurs without input consumption. B correct Disjoint alternative selections prevent multiple productions from occupying the same predictive table cell. C incorrect A useful ambiguous grammar cannot give a unique deterministic LL(1) parse. D incorrect A grammar may be LL(1) without any epsilon production.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 197 · NS0277
records.text: NS0277 Question 197 COMP01 The primary difference between a 'compiler' and a 'just-in-time (JIT) compiler' is: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A A JIT compiler produces faster code than an ahead-of-time compiler always | B A JIT compiler compiles code at runtime (during program execution), allowing it to use runtime profiling information for optimization, while an AOT compiler compiles before execution C A JIT compiler does not perform any optimization | D A JIT compiler only works for interpreted languages JIT compiles during execution; AOT compiles before execution. COMP01 defines AOT before execution and JIT during execution, possibly using runtime profiles. Both are compilation, so the heading compiler versus JIT is better understood as AOT versus JIT. The timing contrast in B is correct, while no universal speed guarantee, absence of optimization or restriction to interpreted languages follows. A incorrect Neither AOT nor JIT is universally faster; startup and workload affect the comparison. B correct Runtime compilation can use execution profiles, whereas AOT performs compilation before the run. C incorrect JIT may optimize using runtime information rather than performing no optimization. D incorrect JIT is an execution-time compilation strategy, not a technique restricted to a separately defined interpreted-language category.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 198 · NS0299
records.text: NS0299 Question 198 COMP24 COMP25 What is the main purpose of syntax-directed translation in a compiler? Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A To interleave semantic analysis with syntax analysis using attributes attached to grammar symbols B To generate optimized machine code directly C To tokenize the source code D To replace the parser with a finite automaton Associate semantic computations with grammatical structure and attributes. COMP24 attaches attributes and semantic rules to grammar symbols and productions; COMP25 executes translation actions during processing. This permits semantic work to follow parsing structure, as A states. It does not inherently bypass IR to optimized machine code, reduce to tokenization, or replace the parser with a finite automaton. A correct Attributes and rules connect grammatical structure to semantic computations during translation. B incorrect Direct optimized machine-code production is not the required or exclusive purpose of syntax-directed translation. C incorrect Tokenization is lexical analysis rather than grammar-directed semantic computation. D incorrect Finite automata recognize ordinary token patterns and do not replace general nested-syntax parsing.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 199 · NS0303
records.text: NS0303 Question 199 COMP24 COMP25 Straight directed translation uses: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information. A Purely lexical rules B Backtracking algorithms C Grammar without attributes D Grammar with sematic rule Grammar with semantic rules, reading the misspelled term as syntax-directed translation. The stem’s Straight directed translation appears to be a damaged rendering of syntax-directed translation. Under that explicit reading, COMP24 defines a CFG with attributes and semantic rules, and COMP25 embeds translation actions in productions. D expresses that structure despite its spelling error. The other choices omit semantics or prescribe unrelated implementation details. A incorrect Pure lexical rules do not supply grammar-directed semantic attributes and computations. B incorrect Backtracking is a parsing implementation choice, not the defining translation structure. C incorrect A grammar without semantic attributes or rules does not describe the syntax-directed definition requested. D correct Reading sematic as semantic, this is the grammar-plus-semantic-rules structure of syntax-directed translation.

records.title: Compiler Design — Question 200 · NS0331
records.text: NS0331 Question 200 COMP03 COMP34 A compiler has produced checked three-address code for a function. Which description incorrectly places the ensuing target-lowering task within the standard compilation pipeline? Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation. A Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation B The target program is the output of the code generator C Checked intermediate code is supplied as input to the code generator. D It used to produce the target code for three-address statements. Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation Code generation uses checked intermediate code to produce target instructions after the frontend has analyzed the source. It can lower each three-address operation into a suitable target sequence. Lexical analysis, not code generation, begins the standard pipeline. The input condition here means checked IR suitable for lowering; it is not a claim that all possible program bugs have been proved absent. A correct Target lowering follows scanning, parsing, semantic checks and IR construction; it does not start compilation. B incorrect The generator’s output is target code. C incorrect Checked IR is the stated input to target lowering. D incorrect Three-address statements can be translated into target instructions.
